signals.title: [RFC] Nullable(Array) support: staged implementation
signals.text: ## Status Accepted design, staged implementation in progress. Supersedes #105192. This RFC replaces the earlier draft RFC #105192 by @zhanglistar. That document, together with the exploratory implementation in #104816, is the direct ancestor of everything below: the stream-naming approach, the framework treatment of null rows, the gating strategy and a large body of tests all originate there. #104816 was closed in favour of a staged implementation by the core team, and its code is reused with attribution (`Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits that carry it). Thanks also to @Avogar for the original blocker analysis, which shaped the design, and to @alexey-milovidov for the resolutions to it. ## Goal Allow the array value itself to be `NULL`, distinctly from an empty array: ```sql NULL::Nullable(Array(UInt32)) != []::Array(UInt32) ``` This is not the same as `Array(Nullable(T))`, which already works and makes *elements* nullable. Arrow, ORC, Parquet, Spark, Hive and JSON producers all distinguish "list field absent or NULL" from "list present but empty", and ClickHouse currently cannot represent the difference, so those reads are lossy. ## Non-goals - `Nullable(Map(...))`. `Map` is physically `Array(Tuple(keys, values))`, so it depends on this work, but it is out of scope. - Changing the rule that `Map` keys cannot be nullable. - Flipping `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()`. See below — this is a deliberate and load-bearing decision, not an omission. ## Core design **`DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()` keeps returning `false`, permanently.** `Nullable(Array(T))` is constructible only through `makeNullableAllowingArray`, which reaches a private `DataTypeNullable` constructor via a friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. This is the single most important property of the design, and the reason is not the one an earlier revision of this document gave. It is not primarily about blast radius during the rollout. `canBeInsideNullable` is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and those places do two different jobs: 1. **Handle a `Nullable(Array)` that already exists** — serialization, subcolumn extraction, the nullable subcolumn creator, `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple`. 2. **Decide whether to *produce* a `Nullable`** — `getLeastSupertype`, `makeNullableSafe`, cast resolution. Only the second kind would behave differently if the predicate were flipped. The first kind needs explicit `Nullable(Array)` handling either way, because once the type can be created at all, this code has to cope with it. And the second kind is where flipping the predicate becomes a user-visible result-type change for queries that have nothing to do with this feature. This was measured rather than reasoned about: `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()` was flipped to `true` on a scratch branch, the server rebuilt, and the same queries run against both binaries with every gate off. | Expression | predicate `false` (today) | predicate `true` | | --- | --- | --- | | `splitByChar(',', materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(String)')))` | `Array(String)`, value `['']` | `Nullable(Array(String))`, value `NULL` | | `extractAll(materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(String)')), '.')` | `Array(String)` | `Nullable(Array(String))` | | `bitmaskToArray(materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(UInt8)')))` | `Array(UInt8)` | `Nullable(Array(UInt8))` | These are ordinary functions on ordinary types. No `Nullable(Array)` column is involved and nothing experimental is enabled. The mechanism is `makeNullableSafe` in `IFunctionOverloadResolver::getReturnTypeWithoutLowCardinality`: with the predicate `false` it returns the array type unchanged, and with the predicate `true` it wraps it. Every function that uses the default nulls implementation and returns an array is affected, and the change is semantic, not cosmetic — `splitByChar(',', NULL)` yields `['']` today and `NULL` after. **That change cannot be gated.** The `compatibility` setting is implemented by replaying old *setting values* — `SettingsChangesHistory` entries are `{setting, old value, new value, description}` — so a behaviour change is only reversible if a setting is read at the point of decision. Function return-type computation reads no settings, and `canBeInsideNullable()` is a property of a type object rather than of a call site: a `DataTypePtr` does not know which session created it, and the predicate is consulted during background merges, metadata load and distributed query fragments, where a session setting is not a defined concept. The exploratory work tried to make an equivalent predicate settings-aware for the `Tuple` case and had to reach for `Context::getGlobalContextInstance()`, documenting that "config changes for global context settings are applied after server restart" — global state with a restart caveat, which is not gating. So flipping the predicate would be an unconditional result-type change with no `compatibility` value and no individual setting that restores the previous behaviour. Conversely, building genuine dual behaviour would mean keeping the explicit per-site decisions described here *and* adding a second branch at each — more code than the current design, not less. `Nullable(Tuple)` is the cautionary example rather than a counter-example. Its predicate is `true`, and the consequence is observable today, by a different route — the `Tuple` branch of `getLeastSupertype`: ```sql SET enable_nullable_tuple_type = 0; SELECT if(0, tuple(1), NULL); -- \N, of type Nullable(Tuple(UInt8)) ``` The gate does not contain the type: with the setting explicitly disabled you still get real `Nullable(Tuple)` values, because type inference never consults it. We are deliberately more conservative in light of how much corner-case work that feature required after merge. For the avoidance of doubt, one thing that does **not** change when the predicate is flipped is array-versus-`NULL` supertype resolution. `if(1, [1], NULL)` returns `Variant(Array(UInt8))` with the predicate either way, and `NO_COMMON_TYPE` either way when the `Variant` fallback is disabled, because the array branch of `getLeastSupertype` bails at "some of them are Array and some of them are not" before any nullable wrapping. An earlier revision of this document claimed otherwise; see the correction log. ### What this costs `canBeInsideNullable()` now returns `false` for a type that demonstrably *is* inside `Nullable`. That is a permanent, accepted cost rather than a transitional one: - Any guard of the form `if (t->canBeInsideNullable())` reachable by a `Nullable(Array)` value must be extended with `|| isArray(t)`. We already missed one — see the known-defect section below. - `makeNullableSafe` returns its argument unchanged for `Array`, silently degrading `Nullable(Array)` to `Array` rather than throwing. There are 32 such call sites. - **Every `canBeInsideNullable` guard added anywhere in the codebase from now on is wrong for `Nullable(Array)` by default.** This is the real long-term price, and the Stage 4 audit is what bounds it. Do not attempt to "clean this up" later by flipping the predicate. There is no gated path back. Identifying every reachable instance is the **call-site audit**, delivered in Stage 4 (below). This is the audit @Avogar asked for in #104816, reframed: the question is not "are 75 files correct" but "which sites can a `Nullable(Array)` value actually reach, and which of those need to change". ### Gating A single session setting, `allow_experimental_nullable_array_type`, gates **every user-facing path that can produce the type** — not only DDL. That includes `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER`, table-function column lists, and the functions that accept a type by name (`toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST`). Internal C++ construction is ungated. This makes the gate a single clean seam between internal machinery and external interface, which is what the staging below is built around. ## MergeTree serialization ### The collision Stream names come from `getNameForSubstreamPath`. `Nullable` appends `.null`; `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1`, …; array *elements* add no name component at all, only a nesting level. ```text Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.null c <-- collision ``` Two distinct null maps would share one file name. Shipping that would corrupt data. ### Resolution A second, *structured* naming scheme, used only for columns whose type requires it (`needsStructuredSubstreamNames`), which inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements: ```text Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.null element null map c.array.nested element data Nullable(Array(UInt32)): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.nested element data Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))): c.size0 outer array offsets c.array.null inner nullable array's null map c.array.array.size0 inner array offsets c.array.array.nested.null element null map c.array.array.nested element data ``` Note that the outer null map and the array offsets keep their plain `.null` and `.size0` names; only the streams below an array element acquire the `.array` component. This is the naming the implementation actually produces, verified by driving real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than by reasoning about substream paths — see the correction note at the end of this issue. Every currently-legal type keeps byte-identical legacy names, so existing parts remain readable with no migration and no format version bump. Selection is **per column, from the type as stored in the part**, on both read and write, so a single query can span old and new parts, and unaffected columns inside a part that contains a structured column keep their legacy names. `columns_substreams.txt` records the actual on-disk substream names for Compact parts and is the source of truth on read. Not in `serialization.json`, which describes serialization kinds and statistics rather than physical file names. Not a global part format version bump, since the change is column-scoped and must coexist with legacy names in the same part. ### Requirements this must meet These are the acceptance criteria for Stage 2, and they are stronger than what #104816 demonstrated: 1. **No legacy stream name changes for any currently-legal type.** The property is that the structured scheme is never *selected* for such a type, neither by the type nor by any path enumerated for it: the legacy naming code is then the only code that runs, and it is not modified. The corpus must reach the shapes where a stream name is decided, and a corpus of static types enumerated from the top level does **not** reach all of them. Two that it misses, both of which produced real regressions: - types materialised at runtime inside `Dynamic` and `Object` columns — a JSON dynamic path holding `Array(Nullable(T))` carries an array and a null map on one path, exactly like `Nullable(Array(T))` but in the opposite nesting; - subcolumn serializations produced by `NullableSubcolumnCreator`, which are not the column's own streams. Treat "proven over a corpus" as a claim about the corpus, and state which shapes it reaches. 2. **Collision-free names for arbitrary nesting** of `Array`, `Nullable`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic` and `Object`, including substream cache keys and prefix/suffix substreams. 3. **A single source of truth for names.** #104816 duplicated the substream-to-name switch, and `Object`/JSON substream types are added to `master` continuously, so a duplicate will drift. 4. **The column type is required, and losing it must not fail silently.** *(Revised — see the correction log.)* This was originally stated as "one naming oracle, or a proven equivalence between two". That is not achievable: the path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The same path requires different names for different types, so no path-only oracle exists and the two arms are not competing answers to one question — the path-based arm covers `Dynamic`/`Object` columns whose static type does not reveal the runtime variant. The hazard is therefore not disagreement between arms but a caller that supplies no type at all: it silently receives legacy names for a structured column. What is required instead: - where the substream path *proves* a type was needed, resolving a name without one raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than returning a name no writer produced; - the divergent case above is pinned by a test, so the reason the type is required is documented where a reader will look; - a test asserts the guard never fires for any currently-legal type; - **every MergeTree caller passes the column type** — an explicit obligation for Stage 3, verified there rather than assumed. ## Subcolumns The outer null map must propagate into subcolumns: ```sql SELECT a.null FROM t; -- UInt8 SELECT a.size0 FROM t; -- Nullable(UInt64), not UInt64 ``` `NullableSubcolumnCreator` handles this, **in Stage 6 rather than alongside the naming work**. Note that bare `Array(T).null` must stay an invalid Dynamic subcolumn path: the null map belongs to the `Nullable` wrapper, not to the array, so `getSubcolumn(42::Dynamic, 'Array(UInt64).null')` must keep failing rather than returning an all-ones map. `.size0` needs none of this — it resolves to `Nullable(UInt64)` through the ordinary path, because `UInt64` passes `canBeInsideNullable`. The creator's array case only matters when the extracted subcolumn is *itself* an array, such as a tuple-element subcolumn inside a nullable array. Two constraints on that work, both learned the hard way: - It must not change the subcolumn type of `Nullable(Tuple(... Array ...))`, which is legal today. Wrapping arrays unconditionally moves `Nullable(Tuple(x Array(T)))`.`x` from `Array(T)` to `Nullable(Array(T))`. - Reaching the *outer* null map of a `Nullable(Array)` as a subcolumn is still an open question. Marking hidden null maps as subcolumn-bearing is not the answer: `NullMapHidden` exists to let a nested `null` subcolumn win, and un-hiding it makes the null map shadow `Nullable(JSON).null`. ## Function execution framework `defaultImplementationForNulls` unwraps nullable arguments, runs the function on the nested columns and patches the result. When the result type cannot be `Nullable` — historically true for `Array` — it substitutes defaults for null rows. Left alone, this silently turns a `NULL` array into `[]` for roughly 70 unmigrated array functions. The contract: - For an array-returning function with a `Nullable(Array)` argument, the result type becomes `Nullable(Array(...))`. - Array arguments are normalised to empty at null rows before the call, so functions that have not been individually migrated still see well-formed offsets. - The row null map is the OR of the input null maps, and is re-applied to the result. - A function may opt in to producing the nullable result itself via `preserveNullableArrayResultForDefaultNulls`, for cases like `arrayElementOrNull` where the function's own null semantics must win. This is deliberately narrower than #105192 proposed. That draft sketched four separate framework capabilities; one opt-in virtual plus automatic normalisation turned out to be sufficient, and the smaller surface is easier to reason about. **Ordering constraint:** the framework must land before the gate opens. Otherwise the type is storable but silently lossy through most functions, which is worse than not having it. ## Semantics | Expression | `NULL::Nullable(Array(T))` | `[]::Array(T)` | `[x]::Array(T)` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `isNull(a)` | `1` | `0` | `0` | | `length(a)` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `empty(a)` | `NULL` | `1` | `0` | | `a.size0` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `arrayElement(a, 1)` | `NULL` | default | `x` | | `arrayElementOrNull(a, 1)` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `x` | | `arrayMap(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | `[f(x)]` | | `arrayFilter(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | filtered | Questions #105192 left open, now resolved: - **`arrayJoin` / `ARRAY JOIN` over `Nullable(Array)` is explicitly unsupported** and throws `TYPE_MISMATCH`. Row-cardinality semantics for a NULL array have no obviously correct answer, and silently treating it as `[]` would defeat the purpose of the type. Revisitable later; not blocking. - **Aggregate functions treat a NULL array as any other NULL value.** Aggregates that skip nulls skip null arrays; those that collect values may collect them where the result type can represent them. This falls out of the existing `Null` combinator rather than needing per-function work. - **Formats never infer the type by default.** Inference is behind its own separate setting, `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`. ## Staged implementation One pull request per stage, each targeting `master`, merged before the next opens. | # | Stage | Content | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Type and column foundation | `makeNullableAllowingArray`, private constructor, `ColumnNullable` exception. `DataTypeFactory` still rejects the type string, so the type is constructible from C++ only and unreachable from any query. | | 2 | Serialization and substream naming | Structured naming, cache keys, deserialization order, plus the four requirements above. Still unreachable from SQL. | | 3 | MergeTree wiring, gate opens | Typed stream names, wide and compact readers and writers, `columns_substreams.txt`, merges, mutations, `ALTER`. `DataTypeFactory` starts accepting the type string, and `validateDataType` / `InterpreterCreateQuery` begin enforcing the gate: the factory is permissive and the entry points are restrictive. Paths not yet migrated throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. | | 4 | Function framework and audit | The framework contract above, the full call-site audit, and the `unwrapNullableTuple` fix. | | 5 | Array functions and aggregates | Migration by category; `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` throws replaced with real behaviour. | | 6 | Remaining creation paths | The functions that take a type by name — `toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST` — each gated. User documentation. | | 7 | Formats, explicit schema only | Arrow, Arrow IPC, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON, Native, plus the `Native` format specification. | | 8 | Schema inference | Behind `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`, including schema-cache keys. | | 9 | Stabilisation | Fuzzing, performance and storage overhead, beta decision. | Stages 1 and 2 are verifiable by unit tests only, since the type cannot be named in a query. That is deliberate: it makes "internal machinery only" a checked property rather than an intention, and Stage 3 flipping it becomes a visible change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. Stage 3 introduces the gate rather than Stage 6 so that Stages 4 to 9 are testable with ordinary stateless tests. Between Stages 3 and 5 the type is reachable only with the experimental setting explicitly enabled, and any path not yet migrated **throws** rather than returning a wrong answer. Substituting `[]` for `NULL` in the interim was considered and rejected: it would ship exactly the defect this feature exists to remove. ## Known defect inherited from the exploratory work `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple` substitutes defaults for an `Array` field of a `Nullable(Tuple(...))`, so a NULL struct's list field becomes `[]`. It is reached from the ORC, Arrow and Arrow IPC readers when a nullable struct sits inside a list. Reproducer, against an Arrow file holding `Array(Nullable(Tuple(x Array(Int32))))` whose second element is `NULL`: ```sql SET allow_experimental_nullable_array_type = 1; SELECT a FROM file('nt.arrow', Arrow, 'a Array(Tuple(x Nullable(Array(Int32))))'); -- [([1,2]),([])] -- expected [([1,2]),(NULL)] ``` The requested type *is* honoured (`toTypeName` reports `Nullable(Array(Int32))`) but the value comes back as `[]` with `isNull() = 0`. Cause: the branch tests `elem_type->canBeInsideNullable()`, which is `false` for `Array` by design, so the default-substitution path is taken before the hinted type is applied. Fixed in Stage 4. This is not a regression — with the gate disabled the same hint is rejected outright — but it is an instance of the exact conflation the feature exists to remove, occurring inside the feature. It was found by chasing a single `canBeInsideNullable` call site, which is the argument for completing the audit before the gate widens. ## Testing matrix - **Types:** `Nullable(Array(T))`, `Nullable(Array(Nullable(T)))`, `Array(Nullable(Array(T)))`, multidimensional, inside `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic`, `Object`, `Nested`. - **Storage:** wide and compact parts, old-part reads, merges, mutations, projections, materialised views, `ALTER`, `columns_substreams.txt` integrity. - **Subcolumns:** `.null`, `.size0`, nested `sizeN`, tuple subcolumns inside arrays. - **Functions:** every array function by category; `if`, `multiIf`, `CAST`, `accurateCastOrNull`, `IN`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`. - **Aggregates:** `groupArray`, `groupUniqArray`, `arrayReduce`, combinators, state serialization. - **Formats:** `Native`, `Values`, `JSONEachRow`, CSV, TSV, Arrow, ArrowStream, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON. - **Fuzzing:** AST fuzzer, function stress, serialization round-trip. ## Related - Supersedes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 ## Correction log **2026-08-19, stream names.** The stream-name example in *MergeTree serialization → Resolution* originally showed `c.array.size0` for the array offsets and `c.array` for the element data. Both were wrong. They were carried over from #105192 and the exploratory implementation's own documentation, and had never been checked against the code. The cause is worth recording, because it also invalidated the exploratory work's unit tests for this area. The naming decision for a stream depends on what precedes the final substream in its `SubstreamPath` — in particular on whether a null map precedes it. `SerializationNullable::enumerateStreams` emits the null-map substream, then **pops it** before recursing into the nested type, so the path seen while naming the array's own streams contains no null map. A hand-built path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs in production; the real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and it takes a different branch. Expectations written against hand-built paths were therefore self-consistent and simultaneously wrong about two of the four streams. Combined with a shell test whose `Before drop:` listing was never actually emitted, the on-disk naming for this feature had no accurate test and no accurate documentation. The fix on our side is to derive every naming expectation from a real `enumerateStreams` walk, and to state the acceptance criteria as properties over a corpus of types rather than as spot checks on constructed paths: - the structured scheme is never selected for any type that is legal today, which is what makes "no existing stream name changes" a proof rather than a sample; - a caller that has the column type and one that does not must produce identical names for a legal type; - all stream names of a type containing `Nullable(Array)` are distinct, at arbitrary nesting depth. **2026-08-19, criterion 4.** Restated. The original wording asked for a single naming oracle or a proven equivalence between two, which is not achievable — the naming of a stream genuinely depends on the column type and not only on the substream path. The revised criterion and its rationale are in *Requirements this must meet* above; the reasoning and what replaced it are in the Stages 1–2 comment on this issue. **2026-08-20, the rationale for `canBeInsideNullable`.** The *Core design* section originally justified keeping the predicate `false` as a blast-radius decision: 105 call sites, too many to audit safely. That reasoning is real but weak, and it would expire once the feature reached GA, inviting a future contributor to flip the predicate as cleanup. The section now gives the argument that actually holds. The call sites split into those that must handle an existing `Nullable(Array)` (unchanged by a flip) and those that decide whether to create one (changed by a flip) — and the second group is precisely where a flip becomes a user-visible result-type change, from `Variant(Array(T))` to `Nullable(Array(T))`, that the `compatibility` mechanism cannot express, because that mechanism replays setting values and a type-level predicate cannot read a setting. The consequence is that the decision is permanent, and that the explicit opt-in call sites are the correct long-term shape rather than debt to be repaid. **2026-08-20, the mechanism behind the `canBeInsideNullable` decision — previous correction was wrong.** The 2026-08-20 revision above claimed that flipping the predicate would change `if(1, [1], NULL)` from `Variant(Array(UInt8))` to `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, via the nullable wrapping in `getLeastSupertype`. That was incorrect, and it does not reproduce. The `canBeInsideNullable` check in question is in the `Tuple` branch of `getLeastSupertype`; the `Array` branch exits earlier with "some of them are Array and some of them are not" and never reaches a nullable wrap. The claim was checked the direct way — flipping the predicate on a scratch branch, rebuilding, and running the same queries against both binaries. `if(1, [1], NULL)` is `Variant(Array(UInt8))` with the predicate either way. The same experiment found the mechanism that does hold, and it is a stronger argument than the one it replaces: `makeNullableSafe` in `IFunctionOverloadResolver::getReturnTypeWithoutLowCardinality` starts wrapping array return types, so ordinary functions change their result type and their semantics — `splitByChar(',', NULL)` moves from `['']` to `NULL` — for every user, with nothing experimental enabled and no setting read anywhere on that path. The section above now states the measured before-and-after and names the correct mechanism. **2026-08-20, criterion 1 and the placement of subcolumn null-map propagation.** Criterion 1 was described as proven over a corpus. It was proven over the corpus that existed, which enumerated static types from the top level and therefore reached neither `Dynamic`/`Object` paths materialised at runtime nor subcolumn serializations produced by `NullableSubcolumnCreator`. Both shapes turned out to decide stream names, and both produced regressions in existing tests. The criterion now says which shapes a corpus has to reach. The *Subcolumns* section also read as though `NullableSubcolumnCreator`'s array handling belongs with the naming work. It is now scheduled for Stage 6, with the two constraints that the first attempt violated.

signals.title: RESTORE DATABASE ... AS ... corrupts/crashes views using FROM table AS alias FINAL,  other_table
signals.text: ### Company or project name Critical Manufacturing S.A. ### Describe what's wrong Restoring a database backup under a different name (`RESTORE DATABASE src AS dst FROM ...`) mishandles views whose `SELECT` uses a table alias immediately followed by `FINAL` in a multi-table (comma-joined) `FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b`. This is valid, documented syntax (["When a table has an alias, FINAL must come after the alias, not before it"](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/select/from#final-modifier)), and views are created and queried correctly before any rename-restore. Depending on the query's complexity, this produces one of two failures only when the database is renamed during restore: 1. Silent alias drop (minimal repro below): the restored view's stored definition loses the alias(es) entirely, silently corrupting the view — it then fails when queried. 2. Hard crash (seen on a more complex, real production view with CTEs/multiple joins — full trace below): the restore itself fails with a `SYNTAX_ERROR` while ClickHouse tries to re-resolve the qualified table name for the rename. No issue occurs if the database is restored under its original name (no `AS `) or if the `CREATE VIEW` is executed directly (not via backup/restore) — pointing at the backup-restore-time table-name rewrite (`DB::BackupMetadataFinder::findTableInBackupImpl`) as the common cause, not the general SQL parser. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Tested and reproducible in these versions: - 25.3.6.56 - 26.3.9.8 - **26.3.19.3** ``` CREATE DATABASE testdb; USE testdb; CREATE TABLE t1 (id UInt32, val String) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE t2 (id UInt32, label String) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1, 'a'); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (1, 'x'); CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT a.id, b.label FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b WHERE a.id = b.id; -- Works fine so far: SELECT * FROM v1; BACKUP DATABASE testdb TO Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); --Restoring under a DIFFERENT name silently drops both aliases from the view definition: RESTORE DATABASE testdb AS restoredtestdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE restoredtestdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM restoredtestdb.t1 -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are gone, but the WHERE clause still references them) SELECT * FROM v1; -- Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression identifier `a.id` in scope -- SELECT a.id, b.label FROM restoredtestdb.t1 FINAL, restoredtestdb.t2 WHERE a.id = b.id. -- Maybe you meant: ['t1.id']. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- Restoring under the ORIGINAL name works correctly (no alias loss): DROP DATABASE testdb; RESTORE DATABASE testdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE testdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM testdb.t1 AS a -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 AS b -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are present) SELECT * FROM v1; ``` ### Expected behavior Aliases are kept when restoring with a rename. Fix expected for 26.3 LTS. ### Error message and/or stacktrace Complete statements and error messages present as comments in the reproduction example. ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Parts written by an INSERT concurrent with DROP PROJECTION keep the dropped projection; after any mutation CHECK TABLE permanently fails with UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` that is still running when `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PROJECTION` commits keeps using its metadata snapshot from query start, so the parts it writes after the drop still materialize the dropped projection (`.proj` directory on disk and an entry in the part's `checksums.txt`). Nothing ever reconciles those parts: the drop's cleanup mutation was created before their block numbers, so it never rewrites them, and every later ordinary mutation hardlinks the orphaned `.proj` directory into the new mutated part. Beyond the false alarm, merges are blocked wherever affected and clean parts coexist in one partition: merge assignment refuses ranges whose parts have differing projection sets, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `OPTIMIZE ... PARTITION` permanently fail with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE` (`Parts have different projection sets: {} in '...'`), and the partition can never merge down. In that mixed state nothing non-destructive heals it: `DETACH PARTITION` + `ATTACH PARTITION` re-attaches the part still carrying the orphaned `.proj` (renumbered, still failing `CHECK`), `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR PROJECTION <dropped name> IN PARTITION` completes without removing the directories, and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. `OPTIMIZE FINAL` heals only the uniform case where every part in the partition carries the same orphaned projection set (they merge together and the merge drops the unknown projection). The lasting symptom appears as soon as any mutation rewrites such a part: `CHECK TABLE` permanently fails for the mutated part with `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` (`Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj`), although every data file is intact and all rows are readable. The un-mutated ancestor part passes `CHECK TABLE` (it is covered by the unknown-projection tolerance), so the table degrades from "checks clean" to "permanently reports broken parts" at the first mutation, which for an operator is a corruption alarm that never clears. On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the background part-check thread (`ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix`) logs the same `Part has broken projections` for the part, on every replica that has it. The unknown-projection tolerance in `checkDataPart` (added for parts that legitimately carry a projection dropped while they were detached) removes the unknown `.proj` entries from the in-memory checksums and sets `is_broken_projection` with a comment saying the caller can then handle it gracefully — but the entries are not erased from `projections_on_disk`, so the `require_checksums && !projections_on_disk.empty()` branch right below throws `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` anyway (`src/Storages/MergeTree/checkDataPart.cpp`, "Found unexpected projection directories"). A mutated part takes the `require_checksums` path, which is why the throw fires exactly for the mutation descendants. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Reproduces on 26.8.1.1708 (official master build) and on 26.4.1.1, so it is long-standing, and on both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree` (2-replica cluster: `CHECK TABLE` returns 0 on both replicas). ### How to reproduce Against any running server (the race window is the INSERT's runtime, ~5 s here, so the interleaving is reliable): ```bash clickhouse-client -q "CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id" clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t ADD PROJECTION p1 (SELECT part, sum(val) GROUP BY part)" # slow INSERT: the metadata snapshot is taken at query start clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, sleepEachRow(0.05)*0 + number, 0 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS max_block_size=10, min_insert_block_size_rows=10, max_insert_threads=1" & sleep 1.5 # DROP PROJECTION commits while the INSERT is still running clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t DROP PROJECTION p1" wait # any ordinary mutation over the affected parts clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t UPDATE val = val + 1 WHERE id < 50 SETTINGS mutations_sync=2" clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t" # 100 - data is fine clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1" # 0 clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=0" | grep $'\t0\t' ``` The same end state is reached with asynchronous mutations (`mutations_sync=0`); the synchronous form above is only for determinism. In this repro all parts of the partition carry the orphaned projection, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` merges them and heals the check. When the partition mixes affected and clean parts (one more concurrent INSERT after the drop is enough), `OPTIMIZE` fails with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE: Parts have different projection sets` and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. It survives server restarts. ### Expected behavior Either the INSERT does not materialize a projection that was dropped before its parts were committed, or parts that legitimately carry a since-dropped projection keep passing `CHECK TABLE` after mutations, matching the graceful-handling intent already present in `checkDataPart` for the un-mutated case. A part whose data files are all intact must not be reported broken forever, and its presence must not permanently block merge assignment in its partition. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0_8_8_0_12 0 Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) (version 26.8.1.1708 (official build)) ``` On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the same error surfaces through the background part check: ``` Part `0_7_7_0_11` has broken projections. It will be ignored. Broken projections info: Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) 5. DB::checkDataPart(...) 7. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartImpl(String const&, bool) 8. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix(String const&, std::optional<long>*, bool) 9. DB::StorageReplicatedMergeTree::checkDataNext(std::shared_ptr<DB::IStorage::DataValidationTasksBase>&) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct from #100413: that issue covers a fetch-side flavor where `checksums.txt` references a `.proj` directory that was never transferred (`NO_FILE_IN_DATA_PART`). Here no detach, attach or fetch is involved — an `INSERT` racing `DROP PROJECTION` plus one mutation is enough, and the direction is inverted: the `.proj` directory exists on disk but is unknown to the table metadata.

signals.title: CSVWithNames and CSVWithNamesAndTypes Incorrectly exports NULL Tuple as single column but defines multiple columns
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse/pg_chdb ### Describe what's wrong In 26.7 (but not 26.5), exporting values for a `Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))` column breaks the value up into multiple columns, but when the value is `NULL`, only one of the columns is populated. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Using `clickhouse client --allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1`: ``` CREATE TABLE boxes ( id Int32 PRIMARY KEY, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point)) ); INSERT INTO boxes VALUES (1, NULL); INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SELECT * FROM boxes SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 ``` ### Expected behavior As seen in 26.5: ``` ┌─id─┬─box──┐ 1. │ 1 │ ᴺᵁᴸᴸ │ └────┴──────┘ ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace In 26.7: ``` Received exception: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '\n': (at row 1) : Row 1: Column 0, name: id, type: Int32, parsed text: "1" Column 1, name: <SKIPPED COLUMN>, type: Nothing, parsed text: "<BACKSLASH>N" ERROR: Line feed found where delimiter (,) is expected. It's like your file has less columns than expected. And if your file has the right number of columns, maybe it has unescaped quotes in values. : (in file/uri /tmp/geos-tmp.csv): While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat: While executing File. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context The content of `gens-tmp.csv` on 26.5 is: ```csv "id","box" 1,\N ``` But on 26.7 it's: ```csv "id","box.high.1","box.high.2","box.low.1","box.low.2" 1,\N ``` Not sure why the tuple was converted to multiple columns on export, but `NULL` is not properly mapped to that pattern.
