signals.title: Shipped sort gate ignores WITH FILL: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1`, any `SELECT ... ORDER BY <col> WITH FILL` fails with `Code: 48. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED)`. The same query on the same binary returns rows with `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 0` (classic parallel replicas) and with `enable_parallel_replicas = 0`.** - **Root cause:** `sortingCanBeShipped` delegates the shippability decision to `SortingStep::isSerializable()` (SortingStep.h:160-163), which inspects only the sort TYPE and `scatter_partitions` - never the sort DESCRIPTION. A `WITH FILL` sort is `Type::Full` with `scatter_partitions == 0`, so it passes the gate although `serializeSortDescription` hard-rejects it. `subtreeIsShippable(parent_node)` cannot catch it either: the unserializable `FillingStep` sits ABOVE the sorting node, outside the checked subtree. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** applyParallelReplicas.cpp:307 accepts the lift when `sortingCanBeShipped` (:377-379) is true -> the sort is cloned into the fragment at :320 -> the fragment is serialized for the replicas -> `SortingStep::serialize` (SortingStep.cpp:730) calls `serializeSortDescription`, which throws for any element with `with_fill` (SortDescription.cpp:310-311). **Affected locations:** - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:379`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L379) — sortingCanBeShipped - gate that lets a WITH FILL sort into the shipped fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:320`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L320) — partial_sorting_node.step = sorting_step->clone() - puts the WITH FILL sort description into the fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h:160`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h#L160) — isSerializable() checks only type and scatter_partitions, not the sort description - [`src/Core/SortDescription.cpp:310`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Core/SortDescription.cpp#L310) — serializeSortDescription throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED for desc.with_fill **Impact:** Every `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` query (with or without LIMIT, with or without INTERPOLATE, with `parallel_replicas_local_plan` 0 or 1) is rejected outright once `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled. `WITH FILL` is a common gap-filling idiom for time-series dashboards, so enabling the setting breaks those queries wholesale. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `a4efc96a3f8ce`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL under plan-based parallel replicas returns the same rows as local execution. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_pr_with_fill; CREATE TABLE t_pr_with_fill (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO t_pr_with_fill SELECT number * 4 FROM numbers(5); SET enable_analyzer = 1; SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1; SET parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1; SET max_parallel_replicas = 3; SET cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost'; SET parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1; SET parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1; -- CI randomizes automatic_parallel_replicas_mode; pin the manual mode so the split engages. SET automatic_parallel_replicas_mode = 0; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_replicas = 0; SELECT '---'; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2; DROP TABLE t_pr_with_fill; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19020. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) (query 14, line 20) (in query: SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2;) ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Reject a sort whose description carries `WITH FILL` before shipping it. Narrow fix: add `&& std::none_of(desc.begin(), desc.end(), [](const auto & c) { return c.with_fill; })` to `sortingCanBeShipped`. Broader fix (also covers `tryMakeDistributedSorting` and any future consumer): make `SortingStep::isSerializable()` return false when any element of `result_description`/`prefix_description` has `with_fill`, mirroring the check `serializeSortDescription` already enforces. Trade-off: the broader fix costs read-in-order for WITH FILL queries under plan-based parallel replicas - the same state as before this PR. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - A window pre-sort WITHOUT `PARTITION BY` (`OVER (ORDER BY a)`) is also newly shipped by this rule and is not covered by 04909 (which only tests the excluded partitioned case). It planned cleanly in EXPLAIN here, but could not be executed locally. Found during automated review of [PR #114315](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114315). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114315_001` </details> cc @devcrafter @nickitat (from #114315)
signals.author: clickgapai

signals.title: Lossy-codec rejection skips partition-key columns; pruning drops matching rows
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With a lossy codec (`SZ3`) on a column used in the partition key, the same predicate returns fewer rows when partition/part pruning is used than when the rows are scanned: `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400` returns 91 while `SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t` over the same table returns 92. 6 of 1000 rows sit in a partition that contradicts their own read-back value.** - **Root cause:** The new check's column set is the sorting key only, although the failure mode it guards against (a value derived from the pre-compression block being stored separately from the lossily-compressed data) applies identically to the partition key, whose value and minmax index are also derived pre-compression. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `MergeTreeData::checkProperties` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033)) iterates only `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()`. `getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()` ([`src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h:247`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h#L247)) is never consulted, so `PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)` with `i CODEC(SZ3(...))` is accepted. The partition value and the part-level `minmax_i.idx` are computed by the writer from the pre-compression block, while the data stream is written lossily - so `KeyCondition` prunes on values the part no longer contains. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033) — new lossy-codec check iterates only getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey() - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1052`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1052) — throw BAD_ARGUMENTS; the message names only the sorting key **Impact:** Silent wrong results: a query whose predicate touches the partition-key column returns fewer rows than the same predicate evaluated over a full scan, and rows are stored in a partition their own value contradicts (so `DROP PARTITION`, `_partition_id` filters and partition-wise merges all act on the wrong rows). No error is raised at any point. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `6c8e5b1397b5f`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a4e07fd3-1f5d-45c5-a666-4202ab5427be) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- no-fasttest: needs sz3 library -- no-random-settings, no-random-merge-tree-settings: SZ3 is lossy and its output depends on how the data -- is split into compressed blocks -- A lossy codec on a column of the partition key: the partition value and the part minmax index are -- computed before compression, so they contradict the values that are read back. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; CREATE TABLE t_lossy_partition_key (k Int64, i Float64 CODEC(SZ3('ALGO_INTERP_LORENZO', 'REL', 0.01))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100); INSERT INTO t_lossy_partition_key SELECT number, number * 1.1 FROM numbers(1000); SELECT countIf(toString(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)) != _partition_id) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3; SELECT countIf(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400; SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 0 91 91 91 91 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 6 91 92 91 92 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Extend the loop's column set to the partition key: iterate over the union of `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()` and `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()`, and generalise the message to name the key that the column belongs to. Alternatively, restrict the PR title/changelog to the sorting key and file the partition-key hole separately. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - Secondary skip indexes on a lossy column are the same shape of hazard (index built pre-compression); three probe shapes failed to produce a divergence because the codec error stayed inside the granule range, so this is unproven rather than ruled out. Found during automated review of [PR #114531](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114531). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114531_001` </details> cc @groeneai @rschu1ze (from #114531)
signals.author: clickgapai

signals.title: Cascades node count still re-read from ambient context; subquery SETTINGS rejected
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With no stateless worker cluster configured, a scalar subquery that scopes `make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4` in its own `SETTINGS` clause is rejected with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` ("make_distributed_plan with enable_cascades_optimizer cannot determine how many nodes will run the query"). The identical settings on the top-level query run fine and return the right answer.** - **Root cause:** `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount` derives the planning node count from the ambient query context instead of the settings the plan is being built with. This is the same ambient re-read of `distributed_plan_execute_locally` that this PR removes from `createExchangeLookup`, `createDistributedQueryExecutor` and `TaskToHostMap`; the planner-side consumer was left behind. `buildContext` itself takes the plan's value two lines later (`context.distributed_plan_execute_locally = optimization_settings.distributed_plan_execute_locally`, Optimizer.cpp:93), so one function reads the same setting from two different sources. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `optimizeTreeSecondPass` -> `CascadesOptimizer::CascadesOptimizer` -> `buildContext` ([`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp:80`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp#L80)) calls `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount(query_context)` where `query_context` is `CurrentThread::get().tryGetQueryContext()` (Optimizer.cpp:51) -> [`src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1190`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp#L1190)/1193 reads `distributed_plan_workers_num` and `distributed_plan_execute_locally` from that ambient context. For a separately-planned subquery the ambient context is the outer query's, so both settings read their outer values (0/0), the function falls through to the configured worker cluster size (0 on a plain server), and Optimizer.cpp:83 throws. **Affected locations:** - [`src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1193`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp#L1193) — getCascadesPlanningNodeCount: ambient read of distributed_plan_execute_locally and distributed_plan_workers_num - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp:80`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp#L80) — buildContext passes the CurrentThread query context, while line 93 uses optimization_settings for the same setting **Impact:** On a server with no `stateless_worker_client` cluster - the configuration the error message itself names as supported for `distributed_plan_execute_locally` - a valid query is refused purely because its distributed-planning settings sit in a subquery's `SETTINGS` clause instead of the outer query's. Where a worker cluster IS configured the query is not refused but is planned for the cluster's node count instead of the requested `distributed_plan_workers_num`, i.e. the wrong parallelism. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `90a20ccf81cd3`). ### How to reproduce ```python On a server with a default config (no `stateless_worker_client` section): CREATE TABLE t1 (key UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY key; CREATE TABLE t2 (key UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY key; INSERT INTO t1 SELECT number FROM numbers(100); INSERT INTO t2 SELECT number FROM numbers(100); -- works, returns 100: SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0; -- same settings scoped to the subquery, fails with SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED: SELECT (SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0); -- repeating both settings on the outer query makes it succeed again, proving the ambient read: SELECT (SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0) SETTINGS distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4; Or run: cd tests/integration && pytest test_distributed_plan_subquery_settings/test.py -v ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 100 100 (both the query-level and the subquery-scoped form return 100) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Client failed! Return code: 88, stderr: Received exception from server (version 26.8.1): Code: 344. DB::Exception: Received from 172.18.0.2:9000. DB::Exception: make_distributed_plan with enable_cascades_optimizer cannot determine how many nodes will run the query. Configure a stateless worker cluster, or set `distributed_plan_workers_num` (also required for `distributed_plan_execute_locally` with ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Take the node count from the settings the plan is built with: add `distributed_plan_workers_num` (alongside the existing `distributed_plan_execute_locally`) to `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings` and have `buildContext` pass those values to `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount`, leaving only the config lookups (worker cluster / discovery service) on the context. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount` also sizes Cloud discovery leases (`#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1197); switching its source of `distributed_plan_workers_num` changes that path too and should be reviewed by someone with Cloud context. - DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1220 reads `distributed_plan_workers_num` from a context as well; that call is on the execution path where the context is the query's own, so it was not investigated further. Found during automated review of [PR #113422](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113422). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr113422_001` </details> cc @groeneai @alexey-milovidov @davenger (from #113422)
signals.author: clickgapai

signals.title: ReplicatedMergeTree replica becomes permanently readonly (Code 122) when power loss reverts an applied ALTER's local metadata commit; force_restore_data / RESTART REPLICA / RESTORE REPLICA all fail to recover
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong When a `ReplicatedMergeTree` replica applies an `ALTER` (its `/replicas/<r>/metadata_version` znode is durably advanced in [Zoo]Keeper) but the local side of that commit — the rename that replaces `metadata/<db>/<table>.sql` — is reverted by a power loss, the replica can never start again: `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread` fails initialization with `Code: 122` `Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and logs `Initialization failed, table will remain readonly`. The state is permanent across restarts, and none of the documented recovery paths repair it: | Recovery attempt | Result | |---|---| | restart the server | same `Code: 122`, still readonly | | `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t` | still readonly | | `flags/force_restore_data` + restart | still readonly (the flag only skips part sanity checks) | | `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` | refuses: `Replica path is present at ... - nothing to restore` | The only way out is `SYSTEM DROP REPLICA` plus re-creating the replica (or hand-editing the `.sql` file to match ZooKeeper). The window is real on default settings: the `ALTER`'s local metadata commit is `writeMetadataFile` of an fsynced `.sql.tmp` (`fsync_metadata = 1` covers only the file content) followed by `DatabaseAtomic::commitAlterTable` doing `renameExchange`/`replaceFile` with no fsync of the file or parent directory — the same never-made-durable commit rename described in #111348, and the code itself carries `/// NOTE: replica will be lost if server crashes before the following rename` right at that spot. On ext4 the rename becomes durable only when the journal happens to commit, so a power cut within that interval rolls the local file back to the pre-`ALTER` structure while the replica's own `metadata_version` znode (updated durably in Keeper as part of applying the `ALTER_METADATA` entry) stays advanced. On the next start the replica's recorded metadata version claims the new structure while the local file carries the old one, and the attach thread refuses. A normal lagging replica (killed before applying the `ALTER`) recovers fine — its local structure and its `metadata_version` znode are consistently old, so the queued `ALTER_METADATA` entry replays. The brick needs exactly the torn state this unfsynced rename produces: znode ahead, local file behind. Since initialization refuses before the queue is even loaded, the `ALTER_METADATA` replay that would repair the structure never gets a chance to run. Secondary effects observed while the replica sits in this state: its `/replicas/<r>/parts` set keeps hundreds of stale entries for parts that no longer exist locally (the startup fetch-or-remove reconciliation also never runs), and the broken local parts accumulate in `detached/`. Observed organically first: a 3-replica cluster under a concurrent INSERT/mutation/DDL workload where one replica's data directory sat on a dm-flakey device that lost power (drop_writes + remount) while the other replicas and Keeper stayed durable — 2 of 5 such runs on 26.8 ended with the recovered replica permanently readonly with `Code: 122`. The deterministic reproduction below simulates only the rename rollback, which is what the device power loss does by itself. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — 26.8.1.1708 (official master build), deterministic with the reproduction below; also observed under real device power loss. ### How to reproduce Two `ReplicatedMergeTree` replicas (`r0`, `r1`) of one table over one Keeper, each server with its own data directory: ```sql -- on both replicas: CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/t', '{replica}') PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id; -- on r0: INSERT INTO t SELECT number, number, 0 FROM numbers(100); ``` 1. Save a copy of r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. 2. `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c UInt32` (on either replica); wait until r1's `t.sql` contains the new column (the `ALTER_METADATA` entry applied; r1's `/replicas/r1/metadata_version` znode advanced). 3. Kill r1's server (`kill -9` — any crash). 4. Write the saved pre-`ALTER` content back into r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. This simulates the power-loss rollback of the never-fsynced commit rename (#111348's mechanism); under a real device power cut inside the filesystem journal window this step happens by itself. 5. Start r1. r1 logs `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread: Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and `system.replicas.is_readonly` stays `1` forever. `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t`, the `flags/force_restore_data` flag and `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` all fail as in the table above. A control run without step 4 recovers to `is_readonly = 0` immediately. ### Expected behavior An applied `ALTER` whose local metadata commit was lost to power loss leaves the replica in a state its own queue already knows how to repair — the replica's structure is simply behind ZooKeeper's. The replica should reconcile the local metadata from ZooKeeper (or reapply the `ALTER_METADATA` diff) instead of refusing initialization forever, or at minimum `force_restore_data` / `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA` should cover this state. Alternatively, making the metadata commit rename durable (fsync the parent directory when `fsync_metadata` is enabled) closes the window at its source. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` <Error> default.t (ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread): Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure. Local columns: ... ``` `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t`: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Replica path is present at /clickhouse/tables/t/replicas/r1 - nothing to restore. If you are sure that metadata is lost and that replica path contains some garbage, then use SYSTEM DROP REPLICA query first.. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct open reports of the same unfsynced-commit-rename mechanism with different consequences: #111348 (table-level `DROP`/`RENAME`/`EXCHANGE` on an Atomic database silently revert) and #111802 (`ON CLUSTER` DDL marked finished in Keeper while one host's local effect is lost, never retried). This report is the `ReplicatedMergeTree` column-`ALTER` flavor, where the outcome is not a silent revert but a replica that permanently refuses to initialize, with no working documented recovery short of dropping and re-creating the replica.
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: Role settings profiles are not enforced on SET ROLE only at session-start
signals.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour `SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO <role>` silently has no effect if the role activated with `SET ROLE` (or HTTP `?role=`) mid-session. It fails to change settings imposed by the profile and fails to enforce `CONST`ness of settings that the settings profile locks. The settings profile is only applied if the role is active when the session is initiated. This is surprising and undocumented. <details> <summary>Detailed explanation</summary> Attaching a settings profile to a role via `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO <role>` causes the profile's settings and constraints to be applied **only when the role is enabled at connect time** (typically via `DEFAULT ROLE`). When the same role is activated in an existing session with `SET ROLE <role>` (or in an HTTP request with the `?role=<role>` query parameter) the role's privileges and row policies engage, but the profile does not: neither its settings values, nor its `CONST` / `READONLY` / `MIN` / `MAX` constraints, nor its `readonly = N` enforcement take effect. This is not documented on the [`CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE`](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/settings-profile), [`SET ROLE`](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/set-role), or [Settings profiles](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/settings-profiles) pages. It has security implications for anyone building a trusted-gateway pattern where a single service user connects, activates a per-request role, and expects the role's profile (e.g. `readonly = 1 CONST`) to confine the session. </details> ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce On Clickhouse 26.3.17.1 or 26.8.1.1731 (tested), such as the default clickhouse container image. Configuration should have `custom_settings_prefixes: SQL_,custom_` (only required for the `CONST` demo): ```sh mkdir -p ~/ch-config.d cat > ~/ch-config.d/custom-prefixes.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <custom_settings_prefixes>SQL_,custom_</custom_settings_prefixes> </clickhouse> EOF docker run -d --name ch \ -p 8123:8123 -p 9000:9000 \ -v ~/ch-config.d:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d:ro \ clickhouse/clickhouse-server:latest ``` ### `readonly = 1 CONST` profile is not applied on `SET ROLE` ``` -- Setup CREATE ROLE ro_role; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ro_profile SETTINGS readonly = 1 TO ro_role; CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role TO probe; ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE NONE; -- role is granted but not default ``` Reconnect as `probe` and observe: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --query " SET ROLE ro_role; SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'; SET some_random_setting = 1; " 0 -- readonly is still 0 (profile not applied) -- SET succeeded (would fail with READONLY if readonly = 1 were engaged) ``` Compare with the connect-time variant: ```sql ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role; ``` ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --query " SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'; SET some_random_setting = 1; " 1 -- readonly is now 1 (profile applied) Code: 164. DB::Exception: ... : Cannot modify 'some_random_setting' setting in readonly mode. ``` ### HTTP `?role=` has the same behaviour <details> <summary>Show repro steps for http connections</summary> Same setup as Reproducer 1, with `probe` reverted to `DEFAULT ROLE NONE`. Send an HTTP request activating the role via query param: ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "role=ro_role" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT value FROM system.settings WHERE name = 'readonly'" 2 ``` Note: the HTTP interface reports `readonly = 2` by default for URL-supplied queries (its own convention), not `1`. The role's profile pinning `readonly = 1` should would override this but the profile actually had no effect. Confirm this with a `SET`: ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "role=ro_role" \ --data-urlencode "query=SET max_threads=3" # (empty body, exit 0 - the SET succeeded) ``` Under a real `readonly = 1` the `SET` would fail with code 164 `READONLY`. Compare with the connect-time variant (`ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role`): ``` $ curl -sS -G 'http://localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "user=probe" --data-urlencode "password=x" \ --data-urlencode "query=SET max_threads=3" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` The role's grants let the query run. Only the former engages the profile. Dropping `?role=ro_role` on the first URL still returns `SELECT count() FROM system.one` correctly via HTTP-interface defaults, so the test uses `SET` rather than `SELECT` to distinguish "role activated" from "profile applied". </details> ### `CONST` binding on a custom setting is not enforced under `SET ROLE` When connecting directly as a role with a settings profile that enforces a setting as `CONST` and trying to `SET` the a setting, clickhouse reports an error like ``` Code: 452. DB::Exception: Setting custom_pinned_value should not be changed. ``` When switching to the role with `SET ROLE` instead, the setting change is permitted. <details> <summary>Show reproducer</summary> > [!NOTE] > Requires `custom_settings_prefixes` to include `custom_` server-side. Setup: ```sql CREATE ROLE ro_role_custom; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role_custom; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ro_custom_profile SETTINGS custom_pinned_value = 'pinned' CONST TO ro_role_custom; CREATE USER probe2 IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role_custom TO probe2; ALTER USER probe2 DEFAULT ROLE NONE; ``` As `probe2`: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe2 --password x --query " SET ROLE ro_role_custom; SET custom_pinned_value = 'overridden'; SELECT getSetting('custom_pinned_value'); " overridden ``` The profile pins the setting `CONST 'pinned'` on the role, but the user is free to rewrite it after `SET ROLE`. Compare with connect time: ```sql ALTER USER probe2 DEFAULT ROLE ro_role_custom; ``` ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe2 --password x --query " SET custom_pinned_value = 'overridden'; " Code: 452. DB::Exception: Setting custom_pinned_value should not be changed. ``` Cleanup: ```sql DROP USER probe2; DROP SETTINGS PROFILE ro_custom_profile; DROP ROLE ro_role_custom; ``` </details> ### Related: `readonly = 1` does not restrict role membership changes Moved to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 ### Expected behavior | Path | Expected (from current docs) | Actual (26.3.17.1 and 26.8.1.1731) | |---|---|---| | `DEFAULT ROLE role_with_profile` at connect | Profile applies | Profile applies ✓ | | `SET ROLE role_with_profile` mid-session | Profile applies (unstated) | Profile does NOT apply ✗ | | HTTP `?role=role_with_profile` | Profile applies (unstated) | Profile does NOT apply ✗ | | `SET ROLE NONE` under `readonly = 1` | Refused (unstated) | Succeeds ✗ | ### Error message and/or stacktrace As shown in repro steps above ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context A "trusted gateway" pattern is to: 1. Connect once as a service user. 2. Stamp a per-request setting (`SET somecustomsetting_confining_access = 'some_confining_scope'`). 3. Activate a role that carries a row policy reading that setting (`SET ROLE <reader_role>`). 4. Trust the role's attached profile to have engaged `readonly = 1 CONST` and to enforce the custom setting `CONST`, so user-supplied SQL forwarded on the same session cannot rewrite either to escape the safeguard 5. Use `somecustomsetting_confining_access` in row-security policies. The undocumented behaviour above makes step 4 silently a no-op. I worked around it. The gateway forces `readonly = 1` itself and relies on grants to confine roles. But the workaround isn't obvious and the failure mode is silent. An incorrectly-designed gateway looks correct, passes casual functional tests, and only fails against a knowledgeable attacker or deeper exploration.
signals.author: ringerc

signals.title: Mixing lightweight and heavyweight mutations permanently wedges a MergeTree table (`NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK: _row_exists`)
signals.text: ## Describe the bug After a lightweight `DELETE` and a heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` have both run on a MergeTree table, a subsequent heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` fails with ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _row_exists in block. There are only columns: k, v, g, s, t, ver, sign, _block_number, _block_offset. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` The mutation is **retried forever**. It never completes and never gives up, so every later mutation on that table queues behind it and the table can no longer be mutated at all. The statement itself returns `Code: 341 ... (UNFINISHED)`, but the entry stays in `system.mutations` with `is_done = 0`. No TTL, skip index, projection, replication or concurrency is required. ## How to reproduce ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sh SYNC; CREATE TABLE sh (k UInt64, v UInt64, g UInt32, s String, t DateTime, ver UInt64, sign Int8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY (k % 4) ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO sh SELECT number, number * 7 % 1000000, number % 50, concat('s', toString(number % 200)), now() + INTERVAL 10 YEAR, 1, 1 FROM numbers(60000); SET mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2, lightweight_deletes_sync = 2; DELETE FROM sh WHERE k % 3 = 0 SETTINGS lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'; ALTER TABLE sh UPDATE v = v + 1 WHERE k = 1; DELETE FROM sh WHERE k = 1 SETTINGS lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'; ALTER TABLE sh DELETE WHERE k = 1; -- Code: 341 ... (UNFINISHED) SELECT mutation_id, is_done, parts_to_do, latest_fail_reason FROM system.mutations WHERE table = 'sh' AND NOT is_done; ``` **Actual** ``` mutation_13.txt 0 1 Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _row_exists in block. There are only columns: k, v, g, s, t, ver, sign, _block_number, _block_offset. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` The row stays in `system.mutations` indefinitely with a growing retry count. **Expected:** the `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` completes, exactly as it does when the preceding lightweight `DELETE`s are absent. ### It is not merely "still running" The mutation makes no progress and never will. `parts_to_do` is unchanged after minutes, while `latest_fail_time` keeps advancing, i.e. it is looping on the same failure: ``` mutation_id: mutation_13.txt is_done: 0 parts_to_do: 2 <-- same value 140 s later age_s: 140 since_last_fail_s: 66 <-- still actively re-failing ``` And the table is no longer mutable — the next statement fails immediately, naming the wedged mutation: ```sql ALTER TABLE sh UPDATE v = 1 WHERE k = 99999 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; -- Code: 341. DB::Exception: Exception happened during execution of mutations -- 'mutation_13.txt, mutation_14.txt' ``` Recovering the table requires `KILL MUTATION`. ## Notes on the shape of the trigger - Both mutation styles are needed. A table that only ever receives lightweight mutations, or only ever receives heavyweight ones, never wedges. - Only the **first** lightweight `DELETE` needs a broad predicate; the other three statements work with `WHERE k = 1`. It also has to be non-aligned with the partition key: with `PARTITION BY (k % 4)`, `k % 3 = 0` reproduces but `k % 2 = 0`, `k % 100 = 0` and `k < 30000` do not. So what matters is that the first lightweight delete masks off a partial, non-partition-aligned subset of *every* part. - `lightweight_delete_mode` may be either `'lightweight_update'` or `'lightweight_update_force'`; both reach it. - Independent of `TTL`, of `minmax` / `set` / `bloom_filter` skip indexes, of projections, and of `ReplicatedMergeTree` — first observed on a replicated table with indexes and projections, then reduced to the plain table above. ## Impact The table becomes permanently unmutable: no further `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `ALTER UPDATE` or `ALTER DELETE` will complete, because the failing mutation is never retired and blocks the queue. Recovery requires `KILL MUTATION`. Because the failure is a retry loop rather than a terminal error, it also burns a background mutation slot indefinitely. ## Root cause Two places independently decide whether a mutation "updates the `_row_exists` mask", and they disagree when the only signal is a pending patch rather than an explicit assignment: - `MutateTask.cpp::isDeletedMaskUpdated`, which decides the **new part's physical column list** (`getColumnsForNewDataPart`), treats a synthesized `READ_COLUMN(_row_exists, read_for_patch=true)` command as "yes, the mask is updated". That command is added whenever a part has an unresolved patch touching `_row_exists` (a pending lightweight delete). So `_row_exists` is kept in the new part's schema. - `MutationsInterpreter::prepare()`, which decides what the **pipeline actually writes**, explicitly excludes that same signal: ```cpp /// The _row_exists mask is handled by APPLY_DELETED_MASK, not as a data column. if (command.type == MutationCommand::READ_COLUMN && command.read_for_patch && command.column_name != RowExistsColumn::name) patch_updated_columns.insert(command.column_name); ``` Its own `deleted_mask_updated` flag only flips on an explicit `UPDATE _row_exists = ...` assignment, never on this `READ_COLUMN` signal. For a plain `UPDATE`, the mismatch is harmless: untouched columns are hardlinked from the source part, so `_row_exists` never goes through the writer. It only surfaces when the mutation is `DELETE` / `APPLY_DELETED_MASK` / `REWRITE_PARTS` (`affectsAllColumns() == true`), which forces a full rewrite (`MutateAllPartColumnsTask`) that writes every declared column through the pipeline. `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::addStreams` then expects `_row_exists` in the block and throws `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` when it isn't there. Confirmed against a live repro: the server-side stack trace resolves the throw to `block_sample.getByName("_row_exists")` inside `addStreams`, and `system.mutations` / `system.parts` / `system.parts_columns` show exactly the state this explanation predicts — an active patch on `_row_exists` sitting on the one part the failing `DELETE` touches. ## Suggested fix Teach `MutationsInterpreter::prepare()`'s command scan to also set `deleted_mask_updated = true` for the excluded case, mirroring `isDeletedMaskUpdated`: ```cpp // src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp, around line 741 if (command.type == MutationCommand::READ_COLUMN && command.read_for_patch) { if (command.column_name == RowExistsColumn::name) deleted_mask_updated = true; else patch_updated_columns.insert(command.column_name); } ``` `deleted_mask_updated` is already a member used the same way for the explicit-assignment case a few dozen lines below, so this is a single-function, single-file change (~6-line diff hunk), plus a regression test. **Not yet verified**: this is a proposed direction from static analysis of the two disagreeing code paths, not a built and tested patch — I have not compiled ClickHouse with this change or confirmed it resolves the repro without regressing anything else. ## Related - #67314 — same `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK: _row_exists` error on v24.6, triggered by lightweight deletes followed by `MATERIALIZE PROJECTION`. Closed; the final comment attributes it to a mutation still running asynchronously. The case here involves no projection at all, and the evidence above shows the mutation is looping rather than progressing. - #61985 — same error message on v24.3 while changing a TTL column, closed without a repro ("should be verified in a recent version"). This report is that verification, on 26.8, with a deterministic reproducer.

signals.title: [RFC] Text index: fuzzy token search (typo-tolerant)
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115446 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108802 ## Use case Typo tolerance on a text index: find rows containing a token *close* to the search term. No function expresses this today. Users either scan every row, or hand-write a two-step query that reads the index dictionary through `mergeTreeTextIndex`, filters it with `editDistanceUTF8` and feeds the surviving tokens to `hasAnyTokens` — much faster than a scan, but it has to be written out for every query and must repeat the index's tokenizer and preprocessor by hand. ## Proposed solution ### New functions ```sql hasAnyTokensFuzzy(input, needles [, distance] [, algorithm => <string>] [, tokenizer => <literal> | <string>]) hasAllTokensFuzzy(input, needles [, distance] [, algorithm => <string>] [, tokenizer => <literal> | <string>]) ``` `input` and `needles` are positional. `distance` is optional, defaults to `'auto'`, and may be positional or named. `algorithm` and `tokenizer` are named-only. Named parameters follow the positional ones and are otherwise order-independent. ```sql hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark') -- 'auto' distance, index tokenizer hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', 1) hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', distance => 1) hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', 1, algorithm => 'levenshtein') -- either option alone hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', 2, tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' '])) ``` All the same query: ```sql hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', distance => 1, algorithm => 'levenshtein', tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' '])) hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' ']), distance => 1, algorithm => 'levenshtein') hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', algorithm => 'levenshtein', tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' ']), distance => 1) ``` Semantics hold with or without an index: - `input` is tokenized with `tokenizer` (default `splitByNonAlpha`); `needles` is a `String` (tokenized) or an `Array(String)` (used as-is) — same conventions as `hasAnyTokens`. - Returns 1 if at least one (`hasAnyTokensFuzzy`) / every (`hasAllTokensFuzzy`) needle has an input token within `distance`, in UTF-8 code points. - `distance` is `'auto'` or 1 to 8; larger is `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. `'auto'` follows Elasticsearch's `AUTO:3,6` — 0 edits up to 2 code points, 1 for 3 to 5, 2 above. - `algorithm` is a bare name from a closed set: `'damerau'` (default, optimal string alignment, so `hte` → `the` costs 1) or `'levenshtein'` (transposition costs 2, what `editDistanceUTF8` computes). **Damerau as default.** Adjacent transposition is among the commonest typos and costs 2 under Levenshtein, so it is invisible at `'auto'`'s budget of 1 for short needles. Damerau strictly dominates, and matches Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch (`transpositions = true`). The choice has to be made before the first release, since changing it afterwards silently changes results. **`'auto'` as default.** Lucene caps at 2 and Elasticsearch defaults to length-dependent `AUTO`; neither uses a constant. A fixed 1 would be broad on a 3-character needle and stingy on a 15-character one, while `'auto'` also keeps short needles under control as part of the semantics. The set of dictionary tokens within `distance` of a needle — the expansion — grows explosively with distance, so the ceiling of 8 is a guard rather than a recommendation. Useful values are 1 to 2, which is why Lucene and Elasticsearch stop there. ### Supported tokenizers `splitByNonAlpha`, `splitByString`, and `array`/`keyword`: each splits text into non-overlapping tokens and tokenizes a needle the same way in isolation as inside a document, so a dictionary hit implies a row-level hit. ### Preprocessors and postprocessors Both work unchanged. A text index may declare a preprocessor applied to the column before tokenization (`lower`, `normalizeUTF8NFKCCasefold`) and a postprocessor applied to each token afterwards (`stem`), so the dictionary holds already-transformed tokens. The needle goes through the same transformations, as `hasAnyTokens` already does, and indexed and non-indexed evaluation therefore agree. Case folding matters more here than for exact search: `editDistanceUTF8('ClickHouse', 'clickhouse')` is 2, so case alone exhausts a budget of 2. One trap: the preprocessor applies to `String` needles but not to `Array(String)` ones, so that dictionary tokens can be fed back verbatim — `['Warking']` misses where `'Warking'` hits. A stemming postprocessor lowers recall, since a typo in a suffix stops the stemmer's rule from firing and the needle keeps a suffix the dictionary entry has already lost. Worth documenting alongside the functions. ## Syntax The signature above needs named arguments. Three layers, in order of necessity. **L1 — named arguments**, `f(a, b, opt => value)`, proposed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108802. Everything in this RFC depends on this alone. **L2 — bare literals as option values**, so `tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' '])` needs no quoting and matches how index DDL already spells it (`text(tokenizer = splitByString([';', ' ']), …)`). **L3 — an options bag**, `hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', { distance => 1, algorithm => 'levenshtein' })`, in brace or parenthesis form. Deferred. With L1 and L2, index DDL could share the same grammar (`text(tokenizer => splitByString([';', ' ']), …)`, `=` still accepted), removing the split where a tokenizer is `splitByString([';', ' '])` in DDL and `'splitByString([\';\', \' \'])'` in a function. #108802 is on hold, so a first version can ship with positional arguments only — `hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark')` and `hasAnyTokensFuzzy(body, 'wark', 1)`, using the default algorithm and the index's tokenizer. That already covers https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115446; `algorithm` and an explicit `tokenizer` arrive later with L1, without changing any existing call.

signals.title: GRANT has no TO ALL, while CREATE ROW POLICY / SETTINGS PROFILE / QUOTA all accept it
signals.text: ### Company or project name Multi-tenant application built on ClickHouse's native access control (RBAC). ### Use case Building multi-tenant applications on ClickHouse's own access control means expressing "any authenticated principal may write here" -- the mail-slot pattern, where many principals may `INSERT` into a table and only the owner may `SELECT` from it. There is currently no way to grant a privilege or a role to every user. `GRANT ... TO ALL` is rejected as an unknown role, even though the same server accepts `ALL` as a live all-users target in three neighbouring statements, and as a live all-roles set in `SET DEFAULT ROLE`. **Version:** `26.7.1.1315` (official build). Also reproduced on `26.7.3.19` and `26.7.1.706`. All refused with `Code: 511 UNKNOWN_ROLE`: ```sql GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; -- Code: 511. There is no role `ALL` in `user directories` GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; -- Code: 511 GRANT pub TO ALL; -- Code: 511 (granting a role, not a privilege) ``` Accepted on the same server, same session: ```sql CREATE ROW POLICY rp ON t.reg USING 1 TO ALL; -- ok CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE sp SETTINGS max_threads = 4 TO ALL; -- ok CREATE QUOTA q FOR INTERVAL 1 hour MAX query_inserts = 9 TO ALL; -- ok SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO g1; -- ok (all *roles*, live) ``` Full reproduction: ```sql CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS t; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t.reg (h String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY h; CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS pub; CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS g1 IDENTIFIED WITH no_password; -- accepted: ALL as a live target set CREATE ROW POLICY IF NOT EXISTS rp ON t.reg USING 1 TO ALL; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE IF NOT EXISTS sp SETTINGS max_threads = 4 TO ALL; CREATE QUOTA IF NOT EXISTS q FOR INTERVAL 1 hour MAX query_inserts = 9 TO ALL; SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO g1; -- refused: the same word as a grantee set GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; GRANT pub TO ALL; ``` ### Describe the solution you'd like `TO ALL` and `TO ALL EXCEPT ...` on `GRANT`, matching the sibling statements: ```sql GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; GRANT pub TO ALL; ``` The storage machinery for a live "all users" marker appears to exist already. ClickHouse stores two such sets today, both flag-based and future-proof rather than expanded at execution time: - `SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO alice` is stored as `default_roles_all = 1` in `system.users`; a role granted to alice next month auto-activates. - `CREATE ROW POLICY / SETTINGS PROFILE / QUOTA ... TO ALL` applies to users created after the statement ran. Only the `GRANT` grammar refuses the same concept for grantees. Alternatively, if the asymmetry is deliberate -- e.g. the rule is *`ALL` is accepted where an object is applied to users (a policy, a profile, a limit) and refused where a capability is given to them* -- a sentence in the `GRANT` documentation recording that decision, and the recommended pattern instead, would resolve this entirely. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Without `TO ALL`, "everybody" has to be an application-maintained role granted at every `CREATE USER`. That is workable but fragile in a specific way: **one missed grant makes the role silently mean "everybody created before the omission."** There is no error, and the only way to detect the drift is to audit every account against the role (e.g. a cron diffing `system.users` against `system.role_grants`). ### Additional context The grant grammar has broadening syntax on two of its three positions and none on the third -- `GRANT <privileges> ON <objects> TO <grantees>`: | Position | Syntax | Semantics (verified on 26.7) | |---|---|---| | objects | `db.*` | live wildcard -- future tables covered | | privileges | `ALL` | snapshot -- expands to 45 rows in `system.grants` at grant time; privilege types added by later upgrades not included | | grantees | -- | nothing; `TO ALL` refused with Code 511 | So `ALL` currently has four meanings in the access-control grammar: a privilege set (snapshot), a granted-roles set in `SET DEFAULT ROLE` (live), an all-users target on row policy / settings profile / quota (live), and a grantee set on `GRANT` -- the only one that does not exist. A note on the documentation: https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/grant gives the grammar as `TO {user | role | CURRENT_USER}`, so the behaviour matches the documented syntax. The confusion is that the same page documents the *privilege* `ALL` -- easy to read as a grantee at a glance. Nothing on the page mentions that the sibling statements accept `TO ALL` as a target set.
signals.author: ramazanpolat

signals.title: `count()`/`sum()` without `GROUP BY` returns zero rows instead of one when a single-shard `Distributed`/`Remote` table's only shard is skipped via `skip_unavailable_shards`
signals.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** An aggregate query with no `GROUP BY` is supposed to always return exactly one row, even over zero input rows (e.g. `SELECT count() FROM emptyTable` returns a single row containing `0`). This invariant breaks when the query reads directly from a `Distributed`/`Remote` table that has exactly one configured shard, and that shard gets skipped at runtime via `skip_unavailable_shards = 1` (e.g. because its target table doesn't exist). The query returns **zero rows** instead of one row with the aggregate's default value. Wrapping the exact same access in a derived subquery does *not* trigger the bug — it correctly returns one row. **Which ClickHouse versions are affected?** Confirmed on `26.8.1.1733` (master-built). The relevant code (`StorageDistributed::getQueryProcessingStage`'s `nodes == 1` shortcut) predates 26.8 and is unrelated to #100134's fix, so earlier versions are very likely affected too. **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE t0 (c0 Int) ENGINE = MergeTree() PRIMARY KEY tuple(); CREATE TABLE t1 ENGINE = Remote('localhost:9000', default, t0) SETTINGS skip_unavailable_shards = 1; DROP TABLE t0; SET prefer_localhost_replica = 0; -- force the query through the remote/TCP path, not the local-execution shortcut SELECT count() AS s0 FROM t1; -- returns zero rows SELECT count() AS s0 FROM (SELECT c0 FROM t1) AS sub; -- returns one row: 0 ``` Not specific to `count()` — reproduces the same way with `sum(c0)`, and with `count(DISTINCT ...)` (which is how this was originally found, via BuzzHouse's `ifNull(count(DISTINCT expr), 0)` vs. `count()` over a `SELECT DISTINCT ... WHERE expr IS NOT NULL` consistency oracle — the two forms disagree on row count, and the oracle correctly flags it as a wrong-result bug). **Expected behavior** Throws an error, the same way it does with `skip_unavailable_shards = 0`: ``` Code: 279. DB::Exception: All connection tries failed. Log: There is no table `default`.`t0` on server: localhost:9000 : While executing Remote. (ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED) ``` **Error message and/or stacktrace** None — that's the problem. The query completes "successfully" with the wrong row count and no diagnostic. **Related issues and pull requests** Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100134 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100141 **Additional context** Root cause: `StorageDistributed::getQueryProcessingStage` decides purely from the *static* configured shard count (`getClusterQueriedNodes`, from `cluster->getLocalShardCount() + getRemoteShardCount()`), with no knowledge of `skip_unavailable_shards`: ```cpp // src/Storages/StorageDistributed.cpp if (nodes == 1) return std::max(to_stage, QueryProcessingStage::Complete); // "the shard will finish this aggregation itself" if (nodes == 0) return QueryProcessingStage::FetchColumns; // "nobody to delegate to — aggregate on the initiator" ``` A single-shard `Remote`/`Distributed` table always takes the `nodes == 1` branch and gets `Complete`, so no local `Aggregating` step is ever built (confirmed via `EXPLAIN PIPELINE`: the plan is just `(ReadFromRemote)`, vs. `(Aggregating) → (ReadFromRemote)` for the subquery-wrapped form). When that one shard is skipped at runtime, there's nothing left to enforce the "≥1 row" invariant, and — unlike the case #100141 fixed — `query_plan.isInitialized()` is still `true` (a `ReadFromRemote` step *was* added), so the `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED` guard #100141 added in `StorageDistributed::read()` never fires either. The gap isn't in the plan-build-time guard from #100141; it's at execution time, where the "all connections gone, skip silently" shortcut doesn't know whether the pipeline had a local finalization step to fall back on: ```cpp // src/QueryPipeline/RemoteQueryExecutor.cpp, read() (~line 627) and needToSkipUnavailableShard() (~line 1221) if (context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::skip_unavailable_shards] && (0 == connections->size())) return ReadResult(Block()); // silent "no data", regardless of what stage was requested ``` `RemoteQueryExecutor` already tracks its own `stage` member. Proposed fix — reject silently when the requested stage was `Complete` (meaning the shard was trusted to fully compute the result, with no rescue path), reusing the same exception #100141 introduced for the sibling case: ```cpp if (context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::skip_unavailable_shards] && (0 == connections->size())) { if (stage == QueryProcessingStage::Complete) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED, "No available shards to query"); return ReadResult(Block()); } ``` at both call sites. This only changes behavior in the actual failure case — normal single-shard queries where the shard stays reachable are untouched, so it shouldn't cost the "push the whole aggregate to the shard" optimization in the healthy path. cc @alexey-milovidov

signals.title: A view whose projection is an unaliased scalar subquery cannot be read
signals.text: 🕵 **Describe what's wrong** A view whose only projection is a scalar subquery without an explicit alias cannot be read. Reading it always throws `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Yes. Reproduced on 26.7.1.1362 and on `master` (26.8.1.1). **How to reproduce** ```sql CREATE TABLE source (id UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT (SELECT max(id) FROM source); SHOW CREATE v; -- CREATE VIEW default.v (`_subquery_1` Nullable(UInt64)) AS SELECT (SELECT max(id) FROM default.source) SELECT * FROM v; -- Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression identifier `_subquery_1` in scope -- SELECT _subquery_1 FROM (SELECT (SELECT max(id) FROM default.source)). -- Maybe you meant: ['_subquery_2']. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` **Expected behavior** `SELECT * FROM v` returns the value of the scalar subquery. **Additional context** The view's column list is named after the alias the analyzer generates for the scalar subquery (`_subquery_1`), but that generated alias is not persisted into the view query. When the view is read, the query is analyzed again and the scalar subquery gets a different generated name (`_subquery_2`), so the stored column name no longer resolves. Giving the projection an explicit alias avoids it: ```sql CREATE VIEW v2 AS SELECT (SELECT max(id) FROM source) AS v; SELECT * FROM v2; -- works ``` No `SQL UDF` is involved; it is not specific to `CREATE FUNCTION` even though it is easy to hit that way, because a `SQL UDF` body is a bare expression. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114923

signals.title: clickhouse-local: HTTP/TCP listener aborts the whole process on a routine client socket error (KillingErrorHandler)
signals.text:
**Component:** clickhouse-local · **Version:** 26.8.1.1774 (official build, arm64 macOS; the listener feature is new in 26.8) · **Severity:** crash / DoS of the local server ## Summary `clickhouse-local` can now expose network listeners with `SYSTEM START LISTEN TCP/HTTP` (new in 26.8). When it runs **non-interactively** (piped/non-TTY stdin — i.e. exactly how you'd run it as a background server), it installs Poco `KillingErrorHandler`, whose handler calls `std::terminate()` on **any** exception that reaches a Poco thread's error handler. A connection-handler thread routinely throws on benign client behaviour — e.g. a client that resets a keep-alive socket mid-response. `clickhouse-server` swallows these via `ServerErrorHandler` (log-and-continue). In `clickhouse-local` the same exception hits `KillingErrorHandler` → `std::terminate()` → `abort()`, killing the entire process (and, with a persistent `--path`, taking down the served database). A **single** client doing "keep-alive request → RST" in a loop kills the listener in ~4 seconds. ## Reproduction Fully self-contained (no auth, no data, no special query). Needs `clickhouse` ≥ 26.8 and `python3`. ```bash CH=/path/to/clickhouse DIR=$(mktemp -d) cat > "$DIR/cfg.xml" <<EOF <clickhouse><logger><level>trace</level><log>$DIR/ch.log</log><errorlog>$DIR/ch.err</errorlog><console>0</console></logger></clickhouse> EOF # keep stdin open (non-interactive server path) so the listener stays up mkfifo "$DIR/in"; ( exec 9>"$DIR/in"; sleep 120 ) & "$CH" local --path "$DIR/data" -C "$DIR/cfg.xml" --http_port 18124 --interactive \ -q "SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP" < "$DIR/in" & SRV=$! sleep 2 curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18124/ping" # -> Ok. SRV=$SRV python3 - <<'PY' import socket, struct, threading, os, time def alive(): try: os.kill(int(os.environ["SRV"]),0); return True except OSError: return False REQ=b"GET /?query=SELECT%201 HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: keep-alive

" LINGER0=struct.pack("ii",1,0) # SO_LINGER on, 0s -> hard RST on close def churn(): while True: try: s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1",18124),timeout=2) s.sendall(REQ); s.recv(20) # read part of the keep-alive response... s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_LINGER,LINGER0); s.close() # ...then RST except Exception: pass threading.Thread(target=churn,daemon=True).start() # ONE thread is enough t0=time.time() while time.time()-t0<20: if not alive(): print(f"*** clickhouse-local ABORTED after {time.time()-t0:.1f}s ***"); break time.sleep(0.2) PY ``` Observed: `*** clickhouse-local ABORTED after 4.3s ***`, and the parent shell reports `Abort trap: 6` for the clickhouse process. Reproduced consistently at 1, 2, 4, 8, and 48 concurrent connections (always ~4.3s). Originally hit organically with an ordinary application using `clickhouse-connect` and a keep-alive connection pool pointed at a `clickhouse-local` listener — it crashed within a few requests under concurrency. ## Crash Two escaping exceptions observed, both the same scenario (client reset mid-response), both fatal via the same handler: ``` Terminate called for uncaught exception: Poco::Exception. Code: 1000, e.code() = 22, Invalid argument: Invalid argument 0. Poco::Exception::Exception(...) 1. Poco::InvalidArgumentException::InvalidArgumentException(...) 2. Poco::Net::SocketImpl::error(int, String const&) 3. Poco::Net::SocketImpl::<socket op> # EINVAL on the reset keep-alive socket ... 7. Poco::ErrorHandler::handle(Poco::Exception const&) # -> KillingErrorHandler 8. Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start() 9. Poco::Net::TCPServerDispatcher::run() ``` and ``` Terminate called for uncaught exception: 5. DB::WriteBufferFromHTTPServerResponse::cancelWithException(...) # "Write buffer has been canceled" 6. DB::HTTPHandler::trySendExceptionToClient(...) # sending an error to a reset socket throws 7. DB::HTTPHandler::handleRequest(...) 8. DB::HTTPServerConnection::run() # exception escapes the handler 9. Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start() 10. Poco::Net::TCPServerDispatcher::run() ``` Then `signalHandler → abort → terminate_handler → std::__terminate → Poco::ErrorHandler::handle → TCPServerConnection::start` (SIGABRT). ## Root cause `programs/local/LocalServer.cpp` (v26.8.1): ```cpp is_interactive = stdin_is_a_tty && (... ); if (!is_interactive) { /// We will terminate process on error static KillingErrorHandler error_handler; // :1152 Poco::ErrorHandler::set(&error_handler); // :1153 } ``` `src/Common/ErrorHandlers.h`: ```cpp class KillingErrorHandler : public Poco::ErrorHandler { void exception(const Poco::Exception &) override { std::terminate(); } // :15 void exception(const std::exception &) override { std::terminate(); } void exception() override { std::terminate(); } }; class ServerErrorHandler : public Poco::ErrorHandler { void exception(const Poco::Exception &) override { logException(); } // :26 <- log & continue ... }; ``` `clickhouse-server` installs the tolerant handler — `programs/server/Server.cpp:2007`: ```cpp static ServerErrorHandler error_handler; Poco::ErrorHandler::set(&error_handler); ``` `KillingErrorHandler` was a reasonable choice while non-interactive `clickhouse-local` was a one-shot batch tool (fail the run on any error). But now that the **same non-interactive path** can start network listeners, a per-connection socket exception — which `Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start()` catches and forwards to the global `Poco::ErrorHandler` — terminates the whole process instead of dropping one connection. Note the interaction: `--interactive` is downgraded to non-interactive whenever stdin isn't a TTY, so any scripted/daemonized invocation that serves connections gets `KillingErrorHandler`. ## Suggested fix When listeners are (or can be) active, connection-thread exceptions must not be fatal. Options, smallest first: 1. Install `ServerErrorHandler` instead of `KillingErrorHandler` once `SYSTEM START LISTEN` brings servers up (or whenever `server_ports`/listeners are configured). ~2 lines at the listener-start site; preserves `KillingErrorHandler`'s batch-mode semantics for the pure one-shot path. 2. Or ensure the HTTP/TCP connection handlers never let socket exceptions (`SocketImpl` errors, `WriteBufferFromHTTPServerResponse::cancelWithException`) escape `HTTPServerConnection::run()` in local mode, so the global error handler is never reached for routine client resets. Option 1 matches how `clickhouse-server` already behaves and is the minimal change. ## Impact Anyone using the new `clickhouse-local` listener as a lightweight embedded/loopback ClickHouse server (the emerging "clickhouse-local as a server" pattern) can have the process aborted by ordinary client-side connection resets — trivially triggered, no auth required. With a persistent `--path`, the served database goes down with it (data is safe on disk; availability is not). --- *Verified end-to-end on 26.8.1.1774 (official build), macOS arm64.* --- > *Generated by [Nerve](https://github.com/ClickHouse/nerve)*

signals.title: readonly>0 does not restrict SET ROLE
signals.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour With `readonly = 1` set on the session by any means, `SET ROLE NONE` and `SET ROLE <other granted role>` still succeed. The [permissions-for-queries doc](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) describes `readonly = 1` as > you can only run read queries ... and lists which statement classes are refused, but doesn't explicitly say anything about `SET ROLE`. As `SET` is confined unless a settings profile explicitly permits it to be set in read-only mode, a reader would reasonably expect and assume that `SET ROLE` should also be confined. Users building read-only, locked-down sessions could easily rely on this unintentionally. But this allows an attacker to simply `SET ROLE NONE` or `SET ROLE` to another known role their session has access to in order to escape confinement. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce Deploy a basic clickhouse container, and: ### Setup **Setup (as admin user):** ```sql CREATE ROLE ro_role; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role; CREATE ROLE other_role; CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role, other_role TO probe; ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role; ``` ### Variant A: `readonly = 1` at connect time (`--readonly 1`) ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --multiquery --query " SET ROLE NONE; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " [] $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --multiquery --query " SET ROLE other_role; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " ['other_role'] ``` `SET` enforcement for variables works: ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --query "SET max_threads = 3" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` ### Variant B: `readonly = 1` applied mid-session via `SET readonly = 1` This is what a gateway that wants to drop into a less-privileged session before executing user queries might do - but it doesn't actually work either. ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET ROLE NONE; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " [] $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET ROLE other_role; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " ['other_role'] ``` Again `SET` enforcement for session variables and configuration works: ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET max_threads = 3; " Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` ### HTTP API and readonly=2 Similar behaviour for the HTTP API when running the queries using session-ids, if a settings profile is used to allow the initial connection to connect without the default `readonly=2` enforcement. Because the HTTP API's default `readonly=2` does allow `SET`, it's arguably more reasonable that it should permit `SET ROLE`, though still surprising. (Surprisingly, though, `readonly=2` does not permit the session to transition to the seemingly more-restrictive `readonly=1` mode). But it still isn't documented behaviour and is IMO still surprising. With the same `probe` user setup as above, using stateless GET (no sessions): ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE NONE' # expected given readonly=2: refused under readonly; actual: 200 OK $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE other_role' # expected given readonly=2: refused; actual: 200 OK ``` The same can be seen with HTTP sessions: ```console $ SID=$(uuidgen) $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' ['ro_role'] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE NONE' # succeeds $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' [] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE other_role' # succeeds $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' ['other_role'] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly') FORMAT TSV" 2 ``` The last query confirms `readonly = 2` is in effect. ### Expected behavior Either both `SET ROLE` statements are refused with `READONLY` (code 164) once `readonly = 1` is in force, matching the treatment of `SET max_threads = …`, _or_ the docs for `readonly = 1` explicitly call out that role membership is not covered. In the latter case another mechanism for one-way role transitions would be strongly desirable. ### Error message and/or stacktrace N/A ### Related issues and pull requests Related to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 which covers issues with role transitions and `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO ROLE ...` Also to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115697 which flags issues in the docs around readonly mode. ### Additional context This isn't strictly a security bug because there's no documented claim about the interaction of `readonly = 1` and `SET ROLE`, but it's close.

signals.title: GRANT is extremely slow for users with many per-table grants
signals.text: ### Environment - ClickHouse version: **26.6.1.1193** (self-hosted, 4-shard × 2-replica cluster, 8 nodes) - Access storage: `local_directory` (`DiskAccessStorage`), ~366k grants total across 66 users - Affected user: `userX` with **~11.6k per-table grants** (11,683 GRANT statements, concentrated in one database) ### Symptom A single `GRANT ON CLUSTER xx_cluster SELECT, INSERT, ... ON db.table TO userX` takes **5–28 seconds** on some replicas, while completing in **~100 ms** on others. Because `ON CLUSTER` waits for the slowest replica, the whole cluster's GRANT is blocked for tens of seconds. ### Root cause (confirmed via trace_log) `system.trace_log` shows the hot spot is the **recursive deep copy of the `AccessRights` tree**: ``` DiskAccessStorage::writeAccessEntityToDisk -> serializeAccessEntity -> getGrantQueriesImpl -> AccessRights::operator= -> Node::operator= (recursive, 15+ levels) ``` `AccessRights` is a radix tree (`AccessRights.cpp`). `Node::operator=` copies every child recursively: ```cpp if (src.children) children = std::make_shared<Container>(*src.children); ``` For a user with ~11.6k per-table grants the tree is large, and a single `GRANT` triggers **three** deep copies / full traversals: 1. `update_func`'s `entity->clone()` (InterpreterGrantQuery.cpp:491) 2. `getGrantQueriesImpl`'s `AccessRights access = grantee.access` (InterpreterShowGrantsQuery.cpp:97) 3. `access.getElements()` traversal (AccessRights.cpp:903) ### Evidence For the same `GRANT` on the same table: | Node | Duration | MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheck | UserTime | |------|----------|-----------------------------|----------| | slow replica | 20–28 s | ~500 MB (116 allocs) | 99.9% of duration | | fast replica | ~100 ms | ~19 MB (16 allocs) | ~0.1% | `SYSTEM RELOAD USERS` temporarily resets the in-memory tree and drops the duration to ~20–46 ms, confirming the in-memory `AccessRights` tree size is the driver. ### Suggested fix Avoid the deep copy in `getGrantQueriesImpl` when the tree is only read (`final == false`): ```cpp const AccessRights & access = grantee.access; if (final) { AccessRights access_copy = grantee.access; unionAccessFromRoles(access_copy, grantee, access_control); getGrantsFromAccess(res, access_copy, grantees, access_control, attach_mode, with_implicit); } else { getGrantsFromAccess(res, access, grantees, access_control, attach_mode, with_implicit); } ``` This removes one of the three deep copies (the one in `serializeAccessEntity`/`SHOW GRANTS`). A more complete fix would be copy-on-write for `AccessRights::Node` (only copy the modified path), but that is a larger change. ### Workaround for users - Aggregate per-table grants into a role and `GRANT role TO user`, so the deep-copied object is the (smaller) role. - Periodically run `SYSTEM RELOAD USERS` after large batches of GRANTs.
