signals.title: readonly=2 blocks transition to more-restrictive readonly=1
signals.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When a session/connection is in `readonly=2` mode, it is restricted from transitioning to `readonly=1` even though `readonly=1` should have a strict subset of `readonly=2`'s capabilities, and thus be a reduction in privileges. **What the docs say about it:** [The docs for readonly](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) do not make any claims about transitions restricted by `readonly=2`. They claim for `readonly=1` that: > After setting `readonly = 1`, the user can’t change `readonly` and `allow_ddl` settings in the current session. > When using the `GET` method in the HTTP interface, `readonly = 1` is set automatically. To modify data, use the `POST` method. > Setting `readonly = 1` prohibits the user from changing settings. There is a way to prohibit the user from changing only specific settings. Also there is a way to allow changing only specific settings under `readonly = 1` restrictions. For details see [constraints on settings](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/constraints-on-settings). But: 1. The **documentation is actually wrong**, as the HTTP interface sets `readonly=2` not `readonly=1` by default; 2. The **documentation makes no specific claims about what `readonly=2` constrains**; it only says > 2 — Read data and Change settings queries are allowed. which isn't particularly specific and doesn't describe if/whether `readonly=2` confines transitions to `readonly=1` or even to `readonly=0`. 3. The breakout passage about not being able to escape readonly once it is set only applies to `readonly=1`; it says nothing at all about `readonly=2` This ticket focuses on the IMO surprising inability to switch from a less to more restrictive readonly mode. I raised https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115697 for the wrong docs about the HTTP readonly mode etc. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce ### Setup On a generic clickhouse docker container, assuming default no-auth admin: ```bash clickhouse-client --query " CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; " ``` ### HTTP API test cases Using the HTTP API, which defaults to `readonly=2`: ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'readonly=1' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT 1 FORMAT TSV' Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET readonly = 1' Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` Show that `readonly=2` is in effect by default: ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly') FORMAT TSV" 2 ``` ### Native protocol test cases Same underlying issue as HTTP. `SettingsConstraints` refuses to modify `readonly` while any nonzero `readonly` is in effect. **From `readonly = 2` (HTTP-default-equivalent)** Single statement refused with `Code: 164 READONLY`: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 \ --query "SET readonly = 1" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` **Multi-statement has the same error and `SELECT` never runs:** ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 --multiquery \ --query "SET readonly = 1; SELECT getSetting('readonly')" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) (query: SET readonly = 1;) ``` Sanity check showing `readonly=2` really is in effect, and other settings can still be changed under it (as that's how `readonly=2` is distinct from `readonly=1`): ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 \ --query "SELECT getSetting('readonly')" 2 $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 --max_threads 3 \ --query "SELECT getSetting('readonly'), getSetting('max_threads')" 2 3 ``` ### Expected behavior I **expected** the following state-transitions to be permitted: a. `readonly=0` -> `readonly=1` or `readonly=2` b. `readonly=2` -> `readonly=1` and all others blocked. The reality is that only (a) is allowed, and (b) is blocked: | Start state | Attempted transition | Result | |-----------------------------------|----------------------|----------------------------| | `readonly=0` (default) | `SET readonly=1` | ✅ succeeds | | `readonly=0` (default) | `SET readonly=2` | ✅ succeeds | | `--readonly 2` | `SET readonly=1` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 2` | `SET readonly=0` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 1` | `SET readonly=2` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 1` | `SET readonly=0` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 2` + `--max_threads 3`| (query time) | ✅ both settings applied | This is true for both HTTP and native protocols but because `readonly=2` is the default on the native protocol, it's easier to hit the issue. ### Error message and/or stacktrace `DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY)` ### Related issues and pull requests Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 ### Additional context This overlaps somewhat with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 in which `readonly=1|2` fails to restrict `SET ROLE`, and with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 where session profiles are not applied when role-transitions occur mid-session. All three are problems with confinement, privilege dropping and access control.
signals.author: ringerc

signals.title: "Permissions for queries" docs for `readonly` mode falsely claims readonly=1 default for HTTP and is incomplete for readonly=2
signals.text: ### Documentation page /concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the issue The [documentation for `readonly` mode](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) is both incorrect and incomplete: ### Incorrect claim about HTTP GET using `readonly=1` [The docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) claim that HTTP `GET` queries use `readonly=1` by default. In reality, HTTP `GET` use `readonly=2` by default unless overridden by settings profiles. `POST` uses `readonly=0`, which is implied but not explicitly stated. E.g. with a default clickhouse docker container (`clickhouse/clickhouse-server:24.8`, clickhouse 24.8.14.39) with no config overrides or custom env-var injection: ```console $ curl -G 'http://localhost:8123/' --user 'default:' --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly')" 2 ``` It looks `HTTP GET` has used `readonly=2` since the beginning of the repo's history; see commit a33ab9cbe1a. It'd also make sense to explicitly mention that while GET _defaults to_ `readonly=2` if not otherwise set, this can be overridden by settings profiles (but _not_ by http listener configuration or http authentication server responses). With test cover for the assertions. ### `readonly=2` behaviour is unclear and underspecified The docs describe `readonly=1` fairly clearly, but the box-out section that carries most of the details has no mention of `readonly=2`. Nothing says that `readonly=2` disallows changing `readonly` mode, and the description for 2 says > When set to 2, allows the above plus: SET [...]" ... which doesn't exclude `SET readonly` so it's open to interpretation whether `readonly=2` blocks changing `readonly` at all, or what to. I actually suggest _not_ fixing this immediately. Instead I'd leave it under-specified and implement https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115695 to _permit_ `readonly=2` to transition to `readonly=1`, _then_ document the new behaviour and add a state-transition-table showing the permitted and blocked transitions. ### Confusing mention of `allow_ddl` for `readonly=1` in the boxout By explicitly naming two settings, this: > After setting readonly = 1, the user can’t change `readonly` and `allow_ddl` settings in the current session. implies that other settings may be changeable. This is clarified shortly after by: > Setting readonly = 1 prohibits the user from changing settings. but it's confusing. I suggest removing the first paragraph entirely, and instead adding to the main description that _Once readonly=1 is set in a session the user cannot change the `readonly` setting. Once readonly=2 is set in a session the user cannot set readonly=0._ ... with a note that currently readonly=2 prohibits a transition to readonly=1 too, but that's subject to change in future per https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115695 ### Additional context **There is duplicate documentation for the readonly setting at https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/constraints-on-settings#read-only** which is better overall, but doesn't mention or link to the docs for HTTP mode. Based on the `git blame` for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blame/master/src/Common/SettingConstraintWritability.h the `readonly=2` setting has existed for at least 4 years. I wasn't immediately able to find when the HTTP GET method started using `readonly=2`; it seems to have been the case as early as a33ab9cbe1a which is as close to the start of the repo's history as I could usefully get.
signals.author: ringerc

signals.title: index_granularity_bytes is a per-block average, not a per-granule cap: a skewed insert block makes Array(FixedString(N)) parts permanently unreadable and unmergeable (TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE)
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse (found while investigating a support escalation). ### Describe what's wrong `index_granularity_bytes` is documented as *"Maximum size of data granules in bytes"*. It is not a maximum — it is an average. The MergeTree writer computes **one** granule size for a whole block from the block's *average* row size, then applies that same row count uniformly across the block: `src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexGranularity.cpp`, `computeIndexGranularity`: ```cpp else if (index_granularity_bytes != 0 && bytes_uncompressed >= index_granularity_bytes) { size_t granules_in_block = bytes_uncompressed / index_granularity_bytes; index_granularity_for_block = rows / granules_in_block; } ``` `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::fillIndexGranularity` then appends marks of exactly that size for every row of the block. So when a single block mixes tiny rows with large rows, the *average* comes out perfectly within `index_granularity_bytes` while the granules covering the large rows are orders of magnitude over it. For a block of `R` rows containing `D` contiguous large rows of `b` bytes each, the worst granule holds ``` min(D*b, R * index_granularity_bytes / D) <= sqrt(R * index_granularity_bytes * b) ``` so with `R = 8192` and the default 10 MiB cap, one granule crosses 1 GiB as soon as a single row reaches roughly 13 MB. This is bad on its own (read amplification, query memory). For `Array(FixedString(N))` it is worse than that: it produces a part that **cannot be read or merged at all, ever**. `SerializationFixedString::deserializeBinaryBulk` refuses any bulk read over 1 GiB: `src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationFixedString.cpp`, `deserializeBinaryBulk`: ```cpp if (unlikely(max_bytes > MAX_STRINGS_SIZE)) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE, "Too large sizes of FixedString to deserialize: {}", max_bytes); ``` Once such a granule exists, `SELECT` fails, `OPTIMIZE` fails, and every mutation fails, because merges and mutations always read exactly one whole granule at a time and have no setting to read less: `src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp`: ```cpp void MergeTreeSequentialSource::updateRowsToRead(size_t mark_number) { const auto & index_granularity = read_task_info->data_part_info->getIndexGranularity(); if (mark_number < index_granularity.getMarksCountWithoutFinal()) current_rows_to_read = index_granularity.getMarkRows(mark_number); } ``` The part is not corrupt — the data is still reachable through a `SELECT` with a short enough read span — but nothing in the server can rewrite it, so the only recovery is `INSERT SELECT` into a fresh table. What makes this hard to notice is that every metric says the table is healthy. In the reproducer below the part reports `data_uncompressed_bytes / marks = 10420732` against a `10485760` cap, i.e. 0.6% *under* budget, while one of its granules holds 1.25 GiB. There is no per-granule size exposed in `system.*`, so the first symptom is the error. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce ### 1. The invariant violation, cheaply (6.6 MB, runs in 0.2 s) 100 rows of exactly `index_granularity_bytes` each, preceded by 4000 empty rows, all in one insert block. Every one of the large rows is one full cap's worth of data, so each must get its own granule. ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS skewed_granule; CREATE TABLE skewed_granule (k UInt64, arr Array(FixedString(16))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, index_granularity_bytes = 65536, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO skewed_granule SELECT number, arrayMap(x -> toFixedString('0123456789abcdef', 16), range(if(number >= 4000, 4096, 0))) FROM numbers(4100) SETTINGS max_block_size = 10000, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0; SELECT 'average looks compliant' AS what, round(data_uncompressed_bytes / marks) AS avg_bytes_per_granule, 65536 AS index_granularity_bytes FROM system.parts WHERE table = 'skewed_granule' AND active AND database = currentDatabase(); SELECT 'but one granule is not' AS what, max(rows_in_granule) AS rows_in_worst_granule, max(rows_in_granule) * 65536 AS bytes_in_worst_granule, 65536 AS index_granularity_bytes FROM ( SELECT rows_in_granule, sum(rows_in_granule) OVER (ORDER BY mark_number) AS end_row FROM mergeTreeIndex(currentDatabase(), skewed_granule, with_marks = 1) ) WHERE end_row > 4000 AND rows_in_granule > 0; ``` Result on 26.7.4.58 and on master: ``` average looks compliant 63646 65536 but one granule is not 40 2621440 65536 ``` 40 large rows in one granule, 2621440 bytes, 40x the cap. ### 2. The unreadable part (1.25 GiB) ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS poisoned; CREATE TABLE poisoned (k UInt64, arr Array(FixedString(16))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, index_granularity_bytes = 10485760, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; -- one insert block: 130048 empty arrays, then 1024 arrays of 81920 elements (1.25 MiB each) INSERT INTO poisoned SELECT number, arrayMap(x -> toFixedString('0123456789abcdef', 16), range(if(number >= 130048, 81920, 0))) FROM numbers(131072) SETTINGS max_block_size = 200000, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0, max_insert_block_size = 200000, max_memory_usage = 0; SELECT rows, marks, data_uncompressed_bytes, round(data_uncompressed_bytes / marks) AS avg_bytes_per_granule FROM system.parts WHERE table = 'poisoned' AND active AND database = currentDatabase(); -- 131072 129 1344274432 10420732 <- average is *under* the 10485760 cap SELECT sum(cityHash64(arr)) FROM poisoned; -- Code: 131 OPTIMIZE TABLE poisoned FINAL; -- Code: 131 -- the data is still there, reachable only with a short read span SELECT sum(cityHash64(arr)) FROM poisoned SETTINGS max_block_size = 512, use_query_condition_cache = 0; -- 13584573267723215872 ``` `1342177280 = 1024 rows * 81920 elements * 16 bytes`. Note that `SELECT sum(length(arr)) FROM poisoned` succeeds, because it only reads the `.size0` subcolumn — a useful way to inspect an affected table without touching the broken stream. ### Notes on reachability * No unusual settings are required. Disabling the insert squashing above only makes the reproducer deterministic. With completely default insert settings the same failure appears as soon as one incoming block spans the whole skewed range (source block of 131072 rows fails, 100000 rows does not) — `min_insert_block_size_bytes` merges small blocks but never splits a large one, so any client sending one big mixed block is exposed. * Under default `min_bytes_for_wide_part = 1 GiB` an affected part is always Wide, since exceeding the 1 GiB read limit requires more than 1 GiB of uncompressed data in the part. * Merges are also a source, though the default `merge_max_block_size_bytes = 10 MiB` normally prevents it. With an `AggregatingMergeTree` column of type `SimpleAggregateFunction(groupUniqArrayArray, Array(FixedString(16)))`, four individually readable parts merge into an unreadable one as soon as `merge_max_block_size_bytes` is set to `0` or to a large value; at the default, and with `merge_max_block_size = 512` alone, the merge output is fine. * `Array(String)` with an identical layout is unaffected: `SerializationString::deserializeBinaryBulk` has no equivalent cap. The oversized granules still exist, they just do not throw. * Reducing `index_granularity` does **not** help, because the reader coalesces consecutive granules into a single deserialization call (`MergeTreeRangeReader::DelayedStream`). With `index_granularity = 512` the same table still fails, on a read span of 33792 rows (66 granules). ### Expected behavior No granule should exceed `index_granularity_bytes` by more than one row, regardless of how row sizes are distributed inside the block being written. Secondarily, a large-but-valid read span should not be a hard error. The 1 GiB check guards a single up-front `data.resize` before `readBig` (added in e3dafdb865d12dbc9ad0ed38378cbfa574b15d99, "More hardening", 2022-09-18); it is not an on-disk format constraint, and `SerializationString` has no equivalent. Reading the span in bounded steps would preserve the hardening (a corrupt length would no longer cause any up-front allocation at all) while letting existing affected parts be read and merged again without a manual rebuild. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 131. DB::Exception: Too large sizes of FixedString to deserialize: 1342177280: (while reading column arr): (while reading from part .../all_1_1_0/ in table default.poisoned located on disk default of type local, from mark 127 with max_rows_to_read = 1024, offset = 0): While reading part all_1_1_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPool, algorithm: Thread). (TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108243 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/20013 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108297 ### Additional context ### Relationship to #108243 / #108297 That fix addresses a different defect with the same symptom family: `ColumnAggregateFunction::byteSize` reports only pointers plus its own arena, so the writer under-measured the *input* to the averaging formula. It corrects the average for aggregate-state columns and does not touch the averaging itself, so intra-block skew still produces oversized granules there. It is unrelated to this report: `Array(FixedString(16))` and `SimpleAggregateFunction(..., Array(FixedString(16)))` are both `ColumnArray(ColumnFixedString)`, whose `byteSize` is exact — the writer here already saw the correct 1.34 GB — and the failure reproduces on builds that contain the fix. ### Recovery for an affected table No server-side operation can repair the part, because everything that rewrites data reads whole granules. `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` and `CLEAR COLUMN` succeed (they never read the column), lightweight `DELETE` succeeds, and everything else fails. `index_granularity_bytes` is readonly for all MergeTree engines, so it cannot be lowered in place either. The working recovery is a rebuild through a `SELECT` with a bounded read span: ```sql INSERT INTO new_table SELECT * FROM affected_table SETTINGS max_block_size = 512, use_query_condition_cache = 0, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0, max_insert_block_size = 512, max_threads = 1; ``` Both settings are needed: `use_query_condition_cache = 1` forces reads to round up to complete granules (`ceilRowsToCompleteGranules` in `MergeTreeRangeReader::startReadingChain`), so `max_block_size` alone does not shorten the span for a filtered read. Verified byte-for-byte: symmetric difference between source and rebuilt table is 0 rows, and the rebuilt table reads with default settings and survives `OPTIMIZE FINAL`. One case is unrecoverable by any means: a single row whose elements exceed 1 GiB (67108865 elements of `FixedString(16)` = 1073741840 bytes) cannot be read even at `max_block_size = 1`, since a granule cannot be smaller than one row. Worth checking before attempting a rebuild with `SELECT max(length(arr)) * 16 FROM t`, which is safe to run on an affected table because it only reads the offsets subcolumn.

signals.title: [Easy Money] ClickHouse Bug Bounty Program
signals.text: ### ClickHouse has a bug-bounty program. Apply at https://bugcrowd.com/clickhouse Note: it is not necessary to use the Bugcrowd service. This is optional and only needed if you need a chance to get a monetary reward. If you just want to report a vulnerability, you can send it to security@clickhouse.com, and we will ensure you get a proper acknowledgment after disclosure. See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/SECURITY.md) for more details. We want to encourage researchers to find and report security vulnerabilities, stability issues, and bugs in ClickHouse. The reports are qualified for a bug bounty program if the following conditions are met: 1. The report should contain a description of the error and step-by-step instructions for reproducing it. 2. The issue should be reproducible in the latest official release and the latest build from the master branch. 3. Unmodified source code and binaries have to be used in reproducing scenarios. 4. The issue should not be already published. If the issue is already found by another researcher, it is not qualified for the bug bounty program. 5. The issue should be reproducible on Linux, x86_64 platform and should not depend on the Linux kernel version, libc version, and configuration of environments like DNS resolvers, SSL certificates, filesystem, and block devices configuration, etc. It should not depend on hardware failures. 6. The issue should be reproducible without the installation of additional software on the machines with clickhouse-server. 7. If the issue requires the usage of features marked as experimental in the documentation or code or enabling experimental flags (settings, configurations), it is not qualified for the bug bounty program. 8. The issue should be reproducible with the release builds from ClickHouse CI infrastructure. Debug and sanitized builds, builds with another compiler, or compiler options - can be used to help find the issues, but are not qualified. 9. The issue should be related to the clickhouse-server component. If the issue is not qualified for the bug bounty program, it still should be reported to security@clickhouse.com or publicly on GitHub issues. The bugs are classified by severity according to the following guidelines: - High severity: RCE, write-what-where, reading and exposing uninitialized memory, invalid memory writes (except nullptr dereference), unexpected data corruption or loss, access control bypass (except information leakage in side-channel attacks). - Medium severity: invalid read memory access, crash (except OOM), SSRF. - Low severity: unexpected resource exhaustion, DoS. The severity is considered lower if the issue: 1. Requires a user with write access to the database. 2. Is related to the code in third-party libraries. 3. Requires manual modification of the data in the filesystem or in ZooKeeper/Keeper. 4. Requires interaction with external data sources. 5. Requires unrealistic configuration changes (corner cases in the server configuration). The reports are also classified by the number of details. If finding a bug requires a special testing methodology or tools, we would appreciate it if these will be described in the report, so we can improve our infrastructure. If the report covers mitigation guidelines or a fix, it is also appreciated.

signals.title: Mac OS security dialogs due to self-extracting binary distribution
signals.text: The official Mac OS builds are currently shipped as self-extracting executables (e.g. `clickhouse-macos-aarch64`). Recent Mac OS releases have additional checks for unsigned/untrusted executable files, which means you have to go through multiple hoops (four dialogs and a non-obvious button in Settings) to allowlist the binary, and this has to be done after each minor upgrade. (With previous Mac OS versions, it was two dialogs which was slightly more bearable.) Clickhouse's self-modification appears to reset and drop the permission needed to execute. So you end up with a non-executable `clickhouse` after `brew upgrade`. Possible low-friction solution is to just ship the Mac OS binaries as a standard non-self-modifying gzip executable. (Alternatively, it might be possible to make the Mach-O header look like a valid gzip stream and locate the data such that you can gunzip it, or might be possible to preserve the security metadata while self-extracting, or might be possible for the homebrew packager to pre-run the binary once and re-install the permissions on the result, but life's too short.)

signals.title: Database context not preserved in distributed queries when using dictGet function
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong When executing a distributed query that uses the dictGet function to access a dictionary, the database context is lost on remote nodes, causing "**Dictionary not found**" errors even when the dictionary exists. **Version Affected**: ClickHouse 25.7.1.3997 (still reproduces on 26.3) ### How to reproduce **​Cluster Configuration**: 2 shards, 1 replica ​**Component**: Distributed query execution with dictionary functions ### Steps to Reproduce ```sql -- Create database demo CREATE DATABASE demo on cluster 'all' ENGINE = Replicated('/clickhouse/default/demo', '{shard}', '{replica}'); -- Create test Dict CREATE DICTIONARY demo.dict_test ( code Int32, value String ) PRIMARY KEY code SOURCE(FILE(path './user_files/test.ndjson' format 'JSONEachRow')) LAYOUT(COMPLEX_KEY_HASHED) LIFETIME(0); -- Create local table CREATE TABLE demo.test_local(code Int32) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree() ORDER BY code; -- Create Cluster table CREATE TABLE demo.test(code Int32) ENGINE = Distributed('demo', 'demo', 'test_local', rand()); -- Execute sql use demo; SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; ``` ### Expected behavior The query should successfully resolve the dictionary reference on all cluster nodes since: - The dictionary exists in the same database on all nodes - The query is executed within the demo database context ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- Exception: /** Received exception from server (version 25.7.1): Code: 36. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000. DB::Exception: Received from ch-2:9000. DB::Exception: Dictionary (`dict_test`) not found: In scope SELECT __table1.code AS code, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', __table1.code) AS `dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code)` FROM demo.test_local AS __table1. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) **/ select hostname,type,current_database,query,databases,tables from cluster('demo','system.query_log') where initial_query_id='4c9b4549-be34-4c37-b635-024eb53fa70d'; /** Row 1: ──────the space key to toggle the display of the progress table. hostname: ch-1 type: QueryStart current_database: demo query: SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; databases: ['demo'] tables: ['demo.test','demo.test_local'] Row 2: ────── hostname: ch-1 type: ExceptionWhileProcessing current_database: demo query: SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; databases: ['demo'] tables: ['demo.test','demo.test_local'] Row 3: ────── hostname: ch-2 type: ExceptionBeforeStart current_database: default query: SELECT `__table1`.`code` AS `code`, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', `__table1`.`code`) AS `dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code)` FROM `demo`.`test_local` AS `__table1` databases: [] tables: [] **/ ``` ### Additional context The database context from the initiating node is not properly propagated to remote nodes during distributed query execution, particularly when resolving dictionary references. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115541 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1789` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Release pull request for branch 26.3
signals.text: This PullRequest is a part of ClickHouse release cycle. It is used by CI system only. Do not perform any changes with it. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > Touches query analyzer/optimizers and network I/O/SSL code paths, plus introduces new distroless Docker images/entrypoint logic; regressions could affect query semantics/perf or connectivity. Broad dependency/build/CI updates increase integration risk despite many changes being incremental. > > **Overview** > **Adds distroless Docker images for `clickhouse-server` and `clickhouse-keeper`** and introduces a new compiled `clickhouse docker-init` program to replace shell-based entrypoints, including initdb script execution and user/db bootstrapping. > > **Improves robustness and compatibility across runtime/query execution:** fixes partial-write handling in Poco stream buffers and HTTP chunked writes, tightens `Content-Length` enforcement, and surfaces SSL read/write/handshake timeouts as `TimeoutException`s. Extends analyzer optimizations (notably rewriting `Map` key lookups to dynamic key subcolumns in filters) and adds plumbing for `MATERIALIZED` CTE metadata through the query tree/identifier resolution. > > **Refines optimizations and correctness checks:** makes quantile fusion stable with duplicate levels, hardens inverse dictionary lookup rewrites with semantic-safety guards and set overflow settings, and fixes several aggregate-function edge cases (self add/sub in BSI, safer `quantileTiming` deserialization, legacy null-adapter handling for `sumCount`, correct signedness in LLVM codegen). > > **Updates CI/build and dependencies:** switches stateless tests to Node 20 + npm `azurite`, adds distroless to docker build matrix/tests, disables backport-branch automerge, and bumps/adjusts bundled deps and build flags (e.g., OpenSSL `3.5.6`, xz updates, jemalloc LTO disable). Documentation is updated for `MATERIALIZED` CTEs, Map bucketed serialization, and related notes. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit c04e83b7958da5876b5f8e4b66344cad2ef6a0ff. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signals.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signals.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. signals.title: Add `borrow_from_cache` object storage and `memory` metadata types
signals.text: Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache using ephemeral `FileSegment`s. signals.title: Auto-escape XML special characters in from_env config substitutions
signals.text: ### What this PR does When direct config values loaded via `from_env` contain XML special characters (`&`, `<`, `>`), the `ConfigProcessor` failed with `SAXParseException` because the raw value was concatenated directly into an XML string. Direct values are now escaped before being embedded into the XML DOM, so an environment variable can hold any XML-1.0-legal value — including one that looks like an XML fragment (taken as literal text) and one that contains the `]]>` sequence the XML grammar forbids in character data. Existing `<include from_env="..."/>` substitutions continue to interpret their value as an XML subtree. Upgrade note: a direct `from_env` value that was XML-entity-encoded for the old XML parser (for example `a&b`) now resolves to its exact literal bytes and must be set raw (`a&b`) instead. This migration is documented and covered by an integration regression. The contents of a ZooKeeper node referenced via `from_zk` may be a whole subtree. A value beginning with `<` is parsed as an XML fragment (both for a structural `<include>` and for a leaf substitution), which is kept for backward compatibility because earlier versions always interpreted a `from_zk` value as XML. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` parses a non-`<` value as a YAML subtree. Without `yaml="true"`, the value remains literal text, so `<include>` is also the generic "replace this element with the node contents" form and may carry a leaf value such as a secret. Whitespace surrounding that `<include>` becomes part of the leaf value, so direct leaf substitutions such as `<password from_zk="..."/>` or `<some_setting from_zk="..."/>` are recommended when exact bytes matter. Those direct leaf substitutions keep a non-`<` value as literal text using its exact original bytes, so existing *plain-text* scalar substitutions and secrets keep working unchanged on upgrade. There is one deliberate behavior change on upgrade: a leaf value that was XML-entity-encoded to satisfy the old parser (which reparsed every `from_zk` value as XML and rejected a raw `&`, `<` or `>` as not well-formed) is now kept as its exact original bytes. A value stored as `a&b` used to decode to `a&b`, but now resolves to the literal `a&b`; such values must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. This is documented in `docs/concepts/features/configuration/server-config/configuration-files.mdx` and covered by an integration regression. Upgrade note: the same literal-text behavior applies to direct ordinary-element `from_env` substitutions such as `<profiles from_env="..."/>`. Existing XML-subtree imports in that form must migrate to `<profiles><include from_env="..."/></profiles>`; this is documented and covered by an integration regression. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78835 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry: Fixed direct config substitutions via `from_env` failing when XML-1.0-legal values contain XML special characters like `&`, `<`, `>`, or the `]]>` sequence; existing `<include from_env="..."/>` XML-subtree substitutions are unchanged. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` substitution can read a YAML subtree wherever the generic `<include>` form is used, including inside a leaf element, so it must not be used for a literal secret or setting. Without the explicit `yaml="true"` attribute, a non-`<` value is literal text, but direct non-`<` leaf `from_zk` substitutions are recommended for exact-byte secrets/settings, because surrounding whitespace of an `<include>` becomes part of a leaf value. Values beginning with `<` continue to be interpreted as XML fragments for backward compatibility. Upgrade note: a direct `from_env` value or a non-`<` leaf `from_zk` value that was previously XML-entity-encoded (for example `a&b`) now resolves to its exact literal bytes and must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101773&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101773](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101773+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Print invisible characters as escape sequences in Vertical format
signals.text: ### What this PR does Non-printable characters (NUL, SOH, etc.) were silently swallowed in `Vertical` output format. Since `Vertical` is a "pretty" format, C0 control characters (`0x00`..`0x1F`) and `DEL` (`0x7F`) are now displayed as Unicode "Control Pictures" (`U+2400`..`U+2421`, e.g. `␀`, `␉`, `␊`, `␡`), which unlike C-style escape sequences cannot be confused with the literal characters they represent. The new setting `output_format_vertical_display_control_characters` (enabled by default) restores raw-byte output when disabled. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85179 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Display non-printable control characters as Unicode "Control Pictures" in `Vertical` format by default; the new setting `output_format_vertical_display_control_characters` can be disabled to restore raw-byte output. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101774&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101774](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101774+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Ask for continuation in single-line mode when query is incomplete
signals.text: ### What this PR does In single-line interactive mode, pressing Enter on an incomplete query (one where the parser reaches the end of input still expecting more tokens) no longer sends it and shows a syntax error. Instead, a newline is inserted into the same edit buffer, exactly like pressing Alt+Enter, so the whole query stays under a single prompt and the arrow keys can navigate and edit across all of its lines. A trailing `;` still forces submission (for example, to deliberately submit an incomplete query and see its syntax error). This replaces the earlier approach that printed a separate `:-] ` continuation prompt and read additional lines, which prevented cross-line editing and could split pasted queries. The completeness check is now passed to `ReplxxLineReader` as a callback and consulted from the `commit_action` bound to Enter. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/64886 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): In single-line interactive mode, `clickhouse-client` now keeps an incomplete query under a single prompt and lets you continue it on the next line (like pressing Alt+Enter) instead of sending it immediately. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (not required for this change) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101785&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101785](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101785+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: feat(promql): Parse Prometheus Query API POST bodies as urlencoded form
signals.text: The Prometheus Query API (`QueryAPIImpl`) read parameters only from `HTMLForm(settings, request)`, which parses the URL query string. For POST requests with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, the PromQL `query` and range parameters live in the body, so they were empty and clients such as `prometheus/client_golang` saw failed or empty evaluations. `QueryAPIImpl` now uses `HTMLForm(settings, request, *request.getStream())` for POST and PUT so the body is merged with any query string (same behavior as `HTMLForm::load`). `RemoteWriteImpl` and `RemoteReadImpl` keep the default path so the raw body stream is not consumed before protobuf handling. Added `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_query_api_post_body.py` comparing GET and POST for instant and range queries. Using the [prometheus/compliance](https://github.com/prometheus/compliance) PromQL harness, the reported pass count rose from **4 / 539 (~0.7%)** to **205 / 539 (~38%)** in one full run—about **+37 percentage points** and **~51×** more passing queries versus that baseline, consistent with POST clients no longer sending an empty `query` from the server’s perspective. Fixes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/93191. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Prometheus Query API ignoring POST form bodies <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.4.1.813` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Not a fix: "Not-ready Set" exception when buildOrderedSetInplace fails
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 `FutureSetFromSubquery::buildOrderedSetInplace` (the speculative set build run during primary key analysis for `IN` subqueries) used to consume the subquery `source` plan up front. If the in-place build then failed silently (e.g. due to subquery timeout with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'`, where the executor stops without throwing and without setting `is_created`), the set remained permanently unbuilt and `FunctionIn` threw "Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument". The core fix — running the in-place pipeline against a clone of the source plan so that `DelayedCreatingSetsStep::makePlansForSets` can still build the set after a silent failure — has meanwhile been merged in #107924, which falls back to the original destructive build when the source plan contains a step that does not implement `IQueryPlanStep::clone`. After merging master, this PR carries the remaining hardening on top of #107924: - `clone` implementations for eleven more query-plan steps: `JoinStep`, `FillingStep`, `ExtractColumnsStep`, `FractionalLimitStep`, `FractionalOffsetStep`, `MergingAggregatedStep`, `NegativeLimitStep`, `NegativeLimitByStep`, `NegativeOffsetStep`, `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep`, `ReadFromQueryResultCacheStep`. `IN` subqueries whose plans contain these steps (e.g. `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL`, joins planned as `JoinStep`, subqueries going through the query result cache) previously took the destructive fallback, where a silent in-place failure still reproduces the "Not-ready Set" exception; with clone support they take the non-destructive path and recover. - `JoinStep::clone` covers only the join algorithms whose `IJoin` implementation supports cloning: `HashJoin`, `ConcurrentHashJoin`, `ConstantJoin` and `FullSortingMergeJoin`. `JoinSwitcher` (`join_algorithm = 'auto'`), `SpillingHashJoin`, `MergeJoin` / `PartialMergeJoin` and `GraceHashJoin` keep the pre-existing destructive fallback: `IJoin::isCloneSupported` also gates `optimizeJoin`, `convertOuterJoinToInnerJoin` and `QueryPipelineBuilder`, so widening it would silently enable join swapping and outer-to-inner conversion for never-validated stateful spilling algorithms. This limitation is documented at the throw site, and `04649_not_ready_set_with_non_clonable_join_algorithms` pins that those algorithms still produce correct results (the `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` stays internal). - `FilledJoinStep` (`StorageJoin` and dictionary joins) and `JoinStepLogicalLookup` (direct key-value joins) intentionally remain non-clonable as well: they wrap live storage-backed join state with no safe copy semantics (`IJoin::clone` constructs an empty join rather than copying the filled state). The constraint is documented at both classes. - Copying a `QueryResultCacheWriter` (which is what `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep::clone` does) now carries over both the original's `query_start_time` and its `skip_insert` decision. On the successful in-place build path the copy is the only writer that is ever finalized, so otherwise `query_cache_min_query_duration` would be measured from the clone point and an already cache-resident key would be buffered into a throwaway buffer instead of being skipped. Pinned by `04652_query_result_cache_subquery_clone_min_query_duration` and `04653_query_result_cache_subquery_clone_skip_insert`. - `QueryPlan::clone` now preserves `max_threads` and `concurrency_control`, so a pipeline built from a cloned plan runs under the same resource contract as the original instead of defaulting to `max_threads == 0` with concurrency control disabled. - The Planner no longer plants query result cache steps into a *logical* plan. A logical plan is not executed where it is built: it is serialized and shipped to another node (parallel replicas with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, see `createRemotePlanForParallelReplicas`), while `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep` and `ReadFromQueryResultCacheStep` hold node-local state (a `QueryResultCacheWriter`, or the cached chunks) that has no serialized representation. Before this, `query_cache_for_subqueries = 1` together with parallel replicas and `serialize_query_plan = 1` failed the whole query with `Method serialize is not implemented for StreamInQueryResultCache`. The cache is still populated and read by the plan the initiator executes itself. - Regression tests using the `prepared_sets_build_ordered_set_inplace_fail` failpoint: `04095_global_not_in_parallel_replicas` (the original parallel-replicas reproducer), `04492_not_ready_set_with_fill_subquery` (a `WITH FILL` subquery source plan), `04550_not_ready_set_with_join_subquery`, `04648_not_ready_set_with_query_result_cache_subquery` (both the cache write and the cache read path) and `04649_not_ready_set_with_non_clonable_join_algorithms`. The original failure was observed in the [Stress test (amd_tsan)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=d0432097aed783bd35054dce2edcefe0c4e5122c&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29) on master, where `considerEnablingParallelReplicas` triggers `selectRangesToRead`, which calls `buildOrderedSetInplace` for primary key analysis. Note on the changelog category: the "Not-ready Set" exception is a `LOGICAL_ERROR`, so reproducing it on the unfixed build aborts the server on the sanitizer builds that the per-arch Bugfix validation jobs run on, and the validation harness deliberately treats a mid-run server death as inconclusive rather than as a reproduced bug. Automated bugfix validation is therefore structurally impossible for this fix, and the user-visible bug fix for the common plan shapes already shipped with #107924; the remaining hardening here is classified as an Improvement. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Extend the non-destructive speculative in-place set build for `IN` subqueries (introduced in [#107924](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924)) to more query-plan shapes: `clone` is implemented for eleven more query-plan steps, including clone-supported joins via `JoinStep`, `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` via `FillingStep`, and the query result cache steps. Such subqueries now preserve the original source plan and can recover from a silent in-place build failure instead of throwing "Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument". A cloned query plan now preserves `max_threads` and `concurrency_control` of the original plan. Also fixed `Method serialize is not implemented for StreamInQueryResultCache` when `query_cache_for_subqueries = 1` is used together with parallel replicas and `serialize_query_plan = 1`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=102192&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/102192](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F102192+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Added Parquet Shredded VARIANT Support to ParquetReaderv3
signals.text: This PR introduces the parquet Shredded VARIANT standard to CLickHouse. duckdb has this already and the main benefit is that it can read less bytes from disk. This is of course critical for a main parquet use case, which is remote reads from S3. signals.title: Fix KQL parser depth and backtracks counter propagation
signals.text:
This is a dedicated PR created from commit `8f9090355e872a3cea1f1c54df7f030a8b76e9dd`. It fixes KQL parser logic where depth and parser-backtracks counters could be lost while passing through KQL parser components, which could weaken parser-limit accounting and error behavior for complex KQL queries. Reference PR with related recent parser/CI context: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99740 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved KQL parser robustness by preserving parser depth and backtracks counters across KQL parser stages, so parser limits are tracked consistently for complex KQL queries. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: ReaderExecutor: pipeline-based read orchestration
signals.text: Builds on top of #103234 (ReadPipeline). Gated by `SET use_reader_executor = 1` (experimental, default off). This commit replaces the matryoshka of `ReadBuffer` wrappers with a `ReaderExecutor` that owns offset mapping, cache decisions, prefetch and decryption in one place. Caches plug in via a uniform `ICacheProvider` / `ICacheHandle` API. ## What this brings **Zero-copy page-cache hits.** Reads served from `PageCache` reach the caller as a `shared_ptr` into the mmap'd cell — no `memcpy` between cache and working buffer (compare to `CachedInMemoryReadBufferFromFile`'s per-block copy). **Connection reuse across remote read calls.** Sequential reads against the same S3/Azure/HTTP object reuse an open buffer instead of issuing a new HTTP request per window. `SourceBufferLimit` caps live connections globally (`max_remote_read_connections`, default 1000); over-limit reads fall back to stateless open-read-close. Visible via `system.remote_read_connections`. **Coordinated cache + prefetch decisions.** The matryoshka design had each layer making independent choices (prefetch ahead in `AsynchronousBoundedReadBuffer`, decide what to cache in `CachedOnDiskReadBufferFromFile`, gather across objects in `ReadBufferFromRemoteFSGather`). The executor sees the whole window: - prefetches only what isn't already cache-hit - retains source over-read only when paired with a live connection (drops it otherwise) - knows which bytes are user-requested vs cache-fill, so it doesn't account cache-fill bytes against the user's read budget **Per-object cache identity, not per-pipeline.** `DiskCacheProvider` derives `FileCacheKey` / `FileCacheOriginInfo` per `StoredObject` (etag-keyed caching for `StorageObjectStorageSource`, segment-key-type classification for `Data` vs `System` queues). The old single-key-per-executor approach silently shared cache identity across all objects in a gather-mode read. **Foundation for new cache backends.** New caches (vector cache, distributed cache, etc.) implement one interface (`ICacheProvider::lookup`) and plug into the chain without touching read paths. ## Observability - `system.remote_read_connections` — open connections (path, query id, position, elapsed) - `system.reader_executor_log` — per-executor stats (cache hit/miss/populate bytes, prefetch hits/cancellations, source request count, decrypt time, …) - `ProfileEvents`: `ReaderExecutor*` counters and microsecond timers; `LiveSourceBuffer*` counters - `HistogramMetrics`: cache get/populate/source-read/prefetch-wait latencies ## Server settings - `reader_executor_prefetch_pool_size` (default 8) — shared prefetch thread pool size - `reader_executor_prefetch_queue_size` (default 0 = `pool_size * 10`) — pool queue depth - `max_remote_read_connections` (default 1000) — live-buffer slot count, reload-able ## Internals - `Rope` / `RopeNode` / `OwnedRopeBuffer` — refcounted buffer chains with mixed provenance (owned, page-cache-pinned), built-in cursor (`peek`/`advance`/`tryRewind`), sorted-on-insert nodes, disjoint-interval coverage tracking. - `ICacheProvider` / `ICacheHandle` — uniform cache API (lookup → status/get/put). Two implementations: `PageCacheProvider` (file-level, zero-copy), `DiskCacheProvider` (per-object, FileCache-backed). - `ISourceReader` — stateless range-read interface. `LocalSourceReader`, `ObjectStorageSourceReader`, `BufferSourceReader` (adapter for backup / `BufferCreator`). - `OffsetMap` — replaces `ReadBufferFromRemoteFSGather`'s gather logic with a logical-to-(object, object-offset) lookup; supports single-object unknown-size (S3 `HEAD` without `Content-Length` → streams to EOF). - `ReaderExecutor` — owns: position, offset map, cache chain, prefetch handle, live buffer, over-read tail, source-buffer slot. - `PipelineReadBuffer` — thin `ReadBufferFromFileBase` exposing the executor through `BufferBase::set/next/seek` (so legacy callers see no change). - `PrefetchThreadPool` — shared bounded pool, returns `nullptr` on overflow (sync fallback), task cancellation is race-free. ## Testing ~3,700 lines of tests (≈46% of the PR), 130+ gtest cases: - `gtest_rope` — 31 cases (append / peek / advance / tryRewind / slice / copyTo / coverage queries / shift). - `gtest_reader_executor` — 41+ cases (cache-chain combinations, per-object lookup, prefetch races, EOF release, slot leak fixes, unknown-size streaming, …). - `gtest_filecache` — 22 cases including over-read / bypass-mode / partial coverage scenarios. - `gtest_read_pipeline` — known/unknown size selection through the executor. - Functional: `04262_reader_executor_observability` plus opt-outs (`SET use_reader_executor = 0`) on tests that intentionally exercise the legacy path. ## Load I need to optimize the work with caches. Need to stream data from available cache segments without any additional costs. sha -- dd4ae00fdaac (26.7.1.1) ``` ┌──────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐ │ regime │ baseline QPS │ executor QPS │ exec/base │ ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤ │ cold │ 0.230 │ 0.328 │ 1.43× (+43%) │ ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤ │ warm │ 0.244 │ 0.302 │ 1.24× (+24%) │ ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤ │ partial │ 0.332 │ 0.325 │ 0.98× (−2%) │ ├──────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤ │ populate │ 0.348 │ 0.384 │ 1.10× (+10%) │ └──────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘ ``` First build with every regime at parity or better. The warm coordination-CPU tax and the populate cache-write regression are both gone; populate over-read down to 14%. Run under production-default networking (`disk_connections_rcvbuf=204800`, `max_remote_read_connections=1000`), with `reader_executor_use_long_connections=1` set explicitly (its default flipped to 0 on this build). Long-connection hit rate 99.5–100% on all regimes. sha -- fcccec1c7e6c (26.7.1.1) — equal-workload methodology ``` ┌──────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐ │ regime │ baseline wall │ executor wall │ speedup │ ├──────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤ │ cold │ 959 s │ 705 s │ 1.36× (+36%) │ │ warm │ 665 s │ 450 s │ 1.48× (+48%) │ │ partial │ 592 s │ 540 s │ 1.10× (+10%) │ │ populate │ 552 s │ 516 s │ 1.07× (+7%) │ │ evict │ 601 s │ 565 s │ 1.06× (+6%) │ └──────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘ ``` Methodology fix: both arms now run the identical query multiset (`--iterations`, sequential — no `--randomize`), metric = total wall time. The earlier windowed-QPS numbers systematically penalized the faster arm (a free benchmark worker draws a new random query, so the faster arm attracts more heavy queries) — warm was reported −9…−14% but is actually **+48%**; `evict` = new regime with the FileCache as a transit buffer (continuous eviction, no cross-query hits). The executor is faster in all five cache regimes; the 128-thread stress arm now completes without stuck queries (previously required `KILL QUERY`), with 4× fewer sockets than legacy. No correctness errors or crashes across the campaign since `c089b7e5`. Known remaining costs (per-query analysis): (1) cold/partial S3 over-read 2.2–2.8× from prefetch speculation; (2) on mixed cache regimes small queries regress 2-3× — `cache_get` returns zero bytes for data that is present (`FileSegmentWait` on DOWNLOADING segments, then reads from source anyway) plus block-granular request amplification on narrow columns (~90 MiB requested for a 5 MiB column), paid at S3 first-byte latency with ~90% of prefetches cancelled. sha -- 018c0257567b (26.7.1.1) — plan-look-ahead window build ``` ┌──────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐ │ regime │ baseline wall │ executor wall │ speedup │ ├──────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤ │ cold │ 810 s │ 619 s │ 1.31× (+31%) │ │ warm │ 477 s │ 450 s │ 1.06× (+6%) │ │ partial │ 785 s │ 518 s │ 1.52× (+52%) │ │ populate │ 532 s │ 478 s │ 1.11× (+11%) │ │ evict │ 579 s │ 581 s │ 1.00× (par) │ └──────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘ ``` Same equal-workload methodology (identical 186-query multiset per arm). Since the workload is fixed, executor wall times are directly comparable across builds: vs `fcccec1c` the executor improved on cold (705→619 s, −12%), populate (516→478 s, −7%) and partial (540→518 s, −4%) — the plan-window changes helped. Baseline wall times swing between rounds (legacy path + master merge + day variance), so cross-build conclusions should use the executor-vs-executor columns, not the ratios. Also corrected with the fixed workload: the true equal-work S3 over-read is ~2.0× on cold and ~2.3× on partial (the earlier 2.8–2.9× figures were inflated by the windowed methodology — the faster arm simply ran more queries per window). Stress arm self-completed again (4th consecutive build). No `Code: 33`, no crashes. sha -- 2b43930ebbcf (26.8.1.1) — read-path log cut + settings-history dedup ``` ┌──────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐ │ regime │ baseline wall │ executor wall │ speedup │ ├──────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤ │ cold │ 496 s │ 315 s │ 1.57× (+57%) │ │ warm │ 223 s │ 226 s │ 0.99× (par) │ │ partial │ 326 s │ 254 s │ 1.28× (+28%) │ │ populate │ 242 s │ 240 s │ 1.01× (par) │ │ evict │ 281 s │ 304 s │ 0.92× (−8%) │ └──────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘ ``` Two rounds this cycle. The morning round (head `a6465d03`) exposed a hot-read-path logging tax: `PipelineReadBuffer` logged one `Trace` message per window advance (6.3M messages per warm arm) plus ~1M per-buffer `Debug` "Created" messages, costing 795 s of thread time per arm (baseline: 6.7 s) — roughly 14% of the CPU budget on cache-served regimes, which showed as warm/populate 0.95×. The same-day fix (`da34b431`) is verified by this round: logger time dropped 795 → 170 s, allocation volume dropped 5.85 → 1.94 TB ≈ baseline's 1.84 TB (most of the long-standing "executor allocates ~4× more" observation was log-message formatting), and executor `UserTime` is now below baseline on warm. Populate flipped to parity-plus; warm is at 0.99× with the residual logger time still 34× baseline — a few more sites may be worth demoting. S3 over-read: populate 1.01× and evict 1.03× (the executor no longer over-fetches where the cache absorbs writes), cold 1.20× while making 7× fewer GETs at ~11 MiB each (this is what buys the 1.57× cold wall), partial 1.38× — the remaining cost item. The evict 0.92× turned out to be regime noise: a clean repeat pair on the settled cluster came back 323/279 s = 1.16× in the executor's favor, matching the morning round's 1.17× (evict has a history of single-pair swings — 0.78× → 1.18× between two runs of one build earlier). Verdict: executor ≥ baseline in all five regimes. Environment notes for cross-entry comparison: starting with this cycle the staging instance's default profile `compatibility` was bumped `25.12` → `26.8`, which changes effective defaults for both arms — all walls in this entry are ~2× faster than in previous entries for that reason; compare ratios, not walls, across entries. Relatedly, the settings-history dedup in this head means Cloud `compatibility` no longer resurrects the pre-release 8 MiB `reader_executor_plan_look_ahead_max_window` introduction default on private builds. Zero failed queries, no `Code: 33`, no crashes across all 20 arms of both rounds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental `ReaderExecutor` for pipeline-based read orchestration with unified cache API (`PageCacheProvider`, `DiskCacheProvider`), connection reuse for remote reads, shared prefetch pool, and `system.remote_read_connections` / `system.reader_executor_log` observability tables. signals.title: Fix `MultiVolnitsky` fallback for failed UTF-8 ngram inserts
signals.text:
The PR now contains only the `MultiVolnitsky` fix. For UTF-8 case-insensitive search paths, a failed `putNGram` call could leave partial hash inserts for a needle and continue with inconsistent state. This change handles the failure explicitly: it rolls back hashes inserted for the current needle and routes that needle to fallback searchers. Context from CI investigations: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99740 and this PR thread https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103864. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `MultiVolnitsky` UTF-8 case-insensitive search handling by rolling back partial `putNGram` inserts on failure and switching failed needles to fallback searchers to avoid inconsistent state and sanitizer exceptions. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signals.title: Transform JOIN hash table payload to row major
signals.text: Resolves [#97883](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/97883) Introduce an alternative layout for hash table payload in hash joins, where fixed and contiguous columns under a certain size are transformed into one row-major block of data. Before the change: ``` col1 Int32 col2 String col3 UInt8 col4 Float64 ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └────────────┘ └──────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┘ row N → col1[N], col2[N], col3[N], col4[N] ``` After the change: ``` ROW STORE (col1 + col3 + col4, contiguous per row) col2 String (columnar) ┌──────────┬──────────┬────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ col1 │ col3 │ col4 │ ← row N (record) │ .... │ ← col2[N] ├──────────┼──────────┼────────────┤ ├──────────┤ │ col1 │ col3 │ col4 │ │ .... │ └──────────┴──────────┴────────────┘ └──────────┘ ``` ### Rational: The row-major format allows the output construction to be a tight loop over each column, basically one pointer load and data copy: ``` for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) { const char * row_store_ptr = row_store_ptrs[i]; col->insertData(row_store_ptr + value_offset, value_size); } ``` In comparison the columnar version has to do more work: load columns[j], row_numbers[j], replicated_columns access, insertFrom ... For the following query `SELECT * FROM rs_probe_200m l JOIN rs_right_10m r ON (l.k % toUInt64(10000000 / 0.9)) = r.k FORMAT Null` from `04054_hash_join_with_row_store.sql` the perf counters for `LazyOutput::buildOutput` in `AddedColumns` look as follows: ``` ┌─variant────────────────────────────┬─query_id─────────────────────────────┬─runtime_ms─┬───────instr─┬──────cycles─┬──────cmiss─┬──brmiss─┬───ipc─┬─cmiss_per_kinstr─┬─brmiss_per_kinstr─┐ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 9d2d6886-2ad7-430f-af2c-6c7cd32f3808 │ 1621 │ 11393048228 │ 31974507197 │ 1470246364 │ 5892574 │ 0.356 │ 129.05 │ 0.517 │ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 56b33013-8bec-4d7a-a415-2a06beb14bf6 │ 1633 │ 11547943445 │ 31874206968 │ 1484117664 │ 6265932 │ 0.362 │ 128.52 │ 0.543 │ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 65583fa7-9ce0-4426-95eb-977251d38f75 │ 1708 │ 11338601601 │ 31825721703 │ 1468670383 │ 5921051 │ 0.356 │ 129.53 │ 0.522 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 5ff1b154-3c3f-40c6-bae9-f6cf0feafe81 │ 2548 │ 15453833738 │ 58322156979 │ 2636461094 │ 9533242 │ 0.265 │ 170.6 │ 0.617 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 6e92c1d4-8432-4a79-a6cc-85e38232116d │ 2580 │ 15400954730 │ 58683032344 │ 2623136775 │ 9455570 │ 0.262 │ 170.32 │ 0.614 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 133f384f-c09a-4e12-9e69-85b61272a360 │ 2686 │ 15419169622 │ 59548322941 │ 2647601264 │ 9746405 │ 0.259 │ 171.71 │ 0.632 │ │ row-major-enabled-single-threaded │ 20039e91-b5dc-4b4a-8e22-f4451f6067be │ 30610 │ 9046504977 │ 16964398066 │ 995568814 │ 3235355 │ 0.533 │ 110.05 │ 0.358 │ │ row-major-disabled-single-threaded │ a3f9a822-dae6-45c1-9a4e-63e87a3592e8 │ 56821 │ 15279361788 │ 27940919919 │ 1167368997 │ 4694553 │ 0.547 │ 76.4 │ 0.307 │ └────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴─────────┴───────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────┘ ``` ### Changes: - A `RowDataStore` that takes a set of columns and lays them in row major format. It exposes access to individual rows and the layout of each row (offset and size of fields in a row). - New `IColumn` interfaces that handle building the output columns from the row store, used manly by `AddedColumns.cpp`. - Two new settings to control the row-major transformation: - min_columns_for_hash_join_row_store: the minimum number of columns that must be suitable to the transformation to apply. - min_rows_ratio_for_hash_join_row_store: Minimum estimated ratio of join output rows to build-side rows to enable transforming hash join payload to row-major. Used in the planner to decide when to enable the optimization. - A runtime feedback loop that tracks the number of hash table matches from a join and feeds it to the next execution of the join instead of relying on the estimated join output: - The match count is only published when the probe phase fully completes. - Only joins that went through the join reorder optimizer get a cache key. - Plans serialized to distributed workers don't collect or use the feedback. ### Limitations: 1. Only supports fixed and contiguous types and nullable version of them. Supporting non fixed rows would make the row-major layout non-uniform between rows and output column construction loop would not be as tight anymore. Also transforming unbounded unfixed types to row major could be very heavy. 2. ColumnReplicated might get materialized. The decision is made based on the column state the join sees in the first block. If it's ColumnReplicated the column is excluded from the row store, if it's not the column is included and it's replicated in a future block it get's materialized. 3. If spilling occurs, the row stored data is split back into columns for now. In a follow up we can make the row store a column and spill it as is. ### Build overhead: | Type | Rows | Columns | avg per worker thread (ms) | |---|---|---|---| | Int64 | 2M | 8 | 28.2 | | Int64 | 1M | 16 | 31.9 | | FixedString(16) | 1M | 8 | 24.6 | | FixedString(16) | 2M | 4 | 21.5 | ### Benchmarks: #### from `04054_hash_join_with_row_store.sql`: | # | Right table | Match | Join | Before (s) | After (s) | Speedup | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 0 | `rs_right_100k` | 0.9 | INNER | 0.265 | 0.237 | 1.12× | | 1 | `rs_right_100k` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.182 | 0.178 | 1.02× | | 2 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.108 | 0.525 | 2.11× | | 3 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.532 | 0.335 | 1.59× | | 4 | `rs_right_100k_nullable` | 0.9 | INNER | 0.350 | 0.249 | 1.41× | | 5 | `rs_right_100k_nullable` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.216 | 0.183 | 1.18× | | 6 | `rs_right_10m_nullable` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.607 | 0.553 | 2.91× | | 7 | `rs_right_10m_nullable` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.698 | 0.357 | 1.95× | | 8 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.9 | FULL | 1.652 | 0.916 | 1.80× | | 9 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.3 | FULL | 1.424 | 0.861 | 1.65× | | 10 | `rs_right_1m_x10` | 0.9 | INNER | 2.239 | 1.554 | 1.44× | | 11 | `rs_right_1m_x10` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.825 | 0.641 | 1.29× | | 12 | `rs_right_1m_nullable_x10` | 0.9 | INNER | 3.771 | 1.820 | 2.07× | | 13 | `rs_right_1m_nullable_x10` | 0.3 | INNER | 1.372 | 0.771 | 1.78× | | 14 | `rs_right_mixed_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.596 | 1.249 | 1.28× | | 15 | `rs_right_mixed_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.759 | 0.628 | 1.21× | | 16 | `rs_right_wide_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 6.158 | 1.979 | 3.11× | | 17 | `rs_right_wide_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 2.563 | 1.111 | 2.31× | ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Introduce an alternative layout for hash table payload in hash joins, where qualifying columns are transformed into one row-major block of data in order to speed up join output reconstruction. Controlled by two new settings: `min_columns_for_hash_join_row_store` (default 3, the minimum number of fixed-size payload columns that triggers the row-major layout; set to 0 to disable) and `min_rows_ratio_for_hash_join_row_store` (default 2, the minimum estimated ratio of join output rows to build-side rows to enable the transformation).

signals.title: Support column matcher expansion for default value expressions and index expressions
signals.text: This PR closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92266 Support column matchers in column `DEFAULT`, `ALIAS`, `MATERIALIZED`, and `EPHEMERAL` expressions, and in data skipping index expressions. This allows expressions such as `*`, `COLUMNS('...')`, `COLUMNS(a, b)`, `EXCEPT`, `APPLY`, and `REPLACE` to be expanded before expression validation and execution. ~~The change also adds `namedTuple` function to make matcher-expanded named tuple expressions ergonomic in tests and user queries.~~ The tests cover these use cases, direct and indirect cyclic default-expression dependency detection, and nested matcher expansion. ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry: - Support column matchers such as `*` and `COLUMNS` in column default value expressions, `DEFAULT`, `ALIAS`, `MATERIALIZED`, and `EPHEMERAL` expressions, and in data skipping index expressions. ### Note ~~About the newly added `namedTuple` function: I read the previous discussions in [1], [2], and [3], and my impression is that the existing `enable_named_columns_in_function_tuple` setting is not very discoverable. A separate function name may make the intention clearer and the feature easier to use, especially in this use case. It also avoids changing the behavior of the existing tuple function, so it should not introduce compatibility issues. Please let me know if this direction is not desirable.~~ [1] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/63524 [2] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54921 [3] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/54881 <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches core expression/DDL validation paths (defaults, aliases, ALTER, mutations, skip indexes), which can affect query planning and error behavior if matcher expansion or cycle detection is incorrect. > > **Overview** > Enables column matchers (e.g. `*`, `COLUMNS(...)` plus `EXCEPT`/`APPLY`/`REPLACE`) inside column `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS`/`EPHEMERAL` expressions by expanding matchers before validation/execution, honoring `asterisk_include_*` settings and rejecting qualified matchers. > > Updates DDL/default validation, alias expansion, read-order optimization, merge/SELECT paths, and mutation/materialize flows to use a shared `cloneAndExpandColumnDefaultExpression` helper and adds cycle detection that accounts for matcher-expanded dependencies. > > Extends skip index parsing/analysis to normalize matcher and alias usage (including cyclic-alias detection) before `TreeRewriter` analysis, and adds docs + comprehensive stateless tests covering matcher expansion, errors, and ALTER/mutation/index scenarios. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 48ab80fd074599c63f967f624435e0a2e7f166ed. signals.title: Use text index for LIKE/ILIKE with ESCAPE
signals.text: Follow-up to #99774 (qoega's LIKE ESCAPE clause). Before this change, a query like `... WHERE col LIKE pattern ESCAPE 'c'` silently bypassed the primary key (`KeyCondition`), the text index (`TYPE text`), and the bloom-filter text indexes (`ngrambf_v1`, `tokenbf_v1`, `sparse_grams`), falling back to a full scan even on tables with such an index defined or with `col` in the sorting key. Root cause: `LIKE pattern ESCAPE 'c'` is parsed into a 3-argument function call `like(col, pattern, escape_char)`. `MergeTreeIndexConditionText::traverseAtomNode`, `MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText::extractAtomFromTree`, and `KeyCondition::extractAtomFromTree` only accepted 2-argument forms; any 3-arg `like`/`ilike` was rejected without ever reaching the LIKE handler. The execution layer in `FunctionsStringSearch::executeImpl` already calls `likePatternWithCustomEscapeToLikePattern` to fold the custom escape into standard backslash escapes before matching, so result correctness was never affected, only performance. Apply the same fold at index-condition time: - Text index (`MergeTreeIndexConditionText`): handles 3-arg `like` and `ilike` (the same arities `isSupportedFunction` allows for the index). - Bloom-filter text indexes (`MergeTreeConditionBloomFilterText`, for `ngrambf_v1` / `tokenbf_v1` / `sparse_grams`): handles 3-arg `like` and `notLike` (the like-family forms this index supports; `ilike` is not supported by this index type). - Primary key (`KeyCondition`): handles 3-arg `like` and `notLike` (the like-family forms present in `atom_map`). Case-insensitive `ilike`/`notILike` are not in `atom_map` and continue to fall back to row-level evaluation, same as the existing 2-arg behavior. In all paths the pattern must be a constant String and the escape argument a constant String of length 1; otherwise we bail out. Invalid escape sequences cause analysis to skip the index/key so row-level evaluation throws the same error the user would have seen before. The `nextInStringLike` tokenizer used by both text-index variants drops the backslash for an unknown escape `\c` while row-level matching keeps it, so an unknown/trailing backslash is declined (the `likePatternHasUnknownBackslashEscape` guard) and falls back to row-level matching to avoid wrongly pruning a matching granule. In the bloom-filter path this guard is placed in the shared `traverseTreeEquals`, so it protects both the folded 3-argument form and the pre-existing 2-argument `like` / `notLike` / `mapContainsKeyLike` / `mapContainsValueLike` paths. Regression tests use `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` to assert that pruning now happens: - `04277_text_index_function_like_escape.sql` covers the `TYPE text` index for `LIKE`/`ILIKE`, both `splitByNonAlpha` and `array` tokenizers, and both the operator form and the functional form `like(a, p, 'c')`. - `04292_105885_primary_key_like_escape.sql` covers the primary key for `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE` (with a remaining wildcard so the perfect-prefix extraction succeeds) and the functional form. - `04351_bloom_filter_text_index_like_escape.sql` covers the `ngrambf_v1` / `tokenbf_v1` / `sparse_grams` text indexes for `LIKE`/`NOT LIKE` ESCAPE and the functional form, including a consumed escape character, `force_data_skipping_indices`, and the unknown/trailing-backslash decline for both the 2-argument and 3-argument forms. The tests FAIL on master without this change and PASS with it. Closes #105885 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` and `ILIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` predicates (added in #99774) now use `TYPE text` skip indexes to prune granules; `LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` and `NOT LIKE ... ESCAPE 'c'` additionally use the `ngrambf_v1`, `tokenbf_v1`, and `sparse_grams` skip indexes, and the primary key when the column is in the sorting key, instead of falling back to a full scan. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is unchanged (the existing text-index docs already describe LIKE-based pruning; this change only fills a coverage gap for the recently added ESCAPE clause).
