signals.title: [#76518] Fix the input table function hint when the column is used twice in insert select
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/76518 `INSERT ... SELECT` from a table function that infers its schema (`file`, `url`, `s3`, `s3Cluster`, `input`, ...) failed when the same source column was selected more than once: ```sql INSERT INTO http (x, y) SELECT size AS x, size AS y FROM s3Cluster(...); -- Cannot add column size: column with this name already exists. (ILLEGAL_COLUMN) ``` The structure of the table function is guessed from the insertion table by mapping every `SELECT` expression to the insertion table column at the same position. When the same identifier is selected twice, the same column was added to the hint twice, which is not allowed. Now the column is added to the hint only once. A source column has a single type, so when the insertion table columns it is mapped to disagree on the type, the hint is ambiguous: it is dropped and the structure is inferred from the data instead, the same way it already happens when an asterisk is mixed with a column list. With `use_structure_from_insertion_table_in_table_functions = 1`, where the hint is mandatory, the ambiguity is reported as an error. Both the analyzer (`QueryAnalyzer::resolveTableFunction`) and the old query interpretation path (`Context::executeTableFunction`) are fixed, because the query failed with `enable_analyzer` set to both `0` and `1`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the error `Cannot add column ...: column with this name already exists` on `INSERT SELECT` from a table function such as `file`, `s3` or `input`, when the same source column is selected more than once. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105982&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/105982](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F105982+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Parquet: map TIME logical type to Time64
signals.text: The native Parquet reader currently maps both `logical.TIMESTAMP` and `logical.TIME` (and the deprecated converted types `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`/`TIMESTAMP_MICROS`/`TIME_MILLIS`/`TIME_MICROS`) to `DataTypeDateTime64`. That was fine before ClickHouse 25.6, when there was no time-of-day type, but it now produces the Parquet analogue of #104038: when the target column is `Time64` and `session_timezone` is non-UTC, the `DateTime64 -> Time64` cast (PR #90310) shifts the value by the timezone — silent data corruption for a value that has no date/timezone to begin with. This PR splits the schema-converter branch so that: - `logical.TIME` / `TIME_MILLIS` / `TIME_MICROS` → `DataTypeTime64(scale)` (timezone-unaware). - `logical.TIMESTAMP` → `DataTypeDateTime64(scale, timezone)` (unchanged). It also extends `is_output_type_decimal` to recognize `Time64` so min/max stats stay enabled when the output column is `Time64`, and removes the stale comment that claimed ClickHouse has no time-of-day type. While covering explicit type hints in the test (`SELECT * FROM file(..., 'Parquet', 't Time')`), I hit a second pre-existing gap from 25.6: `Time64 -> Time` was never registered as a cast — it threw `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` because `IsDataTypeNumber<DataTypeTime>` is `false` (it inherits `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>`, not `DataTypeNumber<Int32>`). Before this PR the path went `DateTime64 -> Time` and returned a wrong, timezone-shifted value; after the Parquet fix it would have thrown. The second commit adds an inline `Time64 -> Time` branch in `ConvertImpl` that divides by the scale multiplier — no timezone offset, because both Time64 and Time are timezone-unaware seconds-of-day. A new stateless test `04277_parquet_time_of_day` covers: - Schema-less inference (Parquet `time32[ms]`/`time64[us]`/`time64[ns]` → `Nullable(Time64(3/6/9))`; `TIMESTAMP` stays `Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC'))`). - Import into `Time64(scale)` columns under `session_timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai'` (values must not shift). - Explicit type hints under non-UTC session: `Time64(3)` / `Time` / `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')` / `Int64`. Review follow-up: making `Time64 -> DateTime` legal also exposed that `ToDateTimeMonotonicity` treated `Time64` sources as monotonic, while the cast wraps negative time-of-day values with the default `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'ignore'` (`-00:00:01` -> `2106-02-07 06:28:15`), i.e. it drops at zero. `toDateTime` now reports non-monotonic for `Time`/`Time64` sources; the regression test `04828_time64_to_datetime_not_monotonic` shows that without the guard the key condition prunes every granule and range/point queries over a `Time64` key silently return empty results. The Parquet docs (`docs/reference/formats/Parquet/Parquet.mdx`) are updated for the new `TIME` -> `Time64` mapping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Parquet `time32`/`time64` columns being read as `DateTime64` and then silently shifted by `session_timezone` when inserted into a `Time64` target column. Parquet `TIME` logical types now map directly to `Time64`, and a previously-missing `Time64 -> Time` cast is added. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106019&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106019](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106019+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads for parallel manifest decoding
signals.text: Reading an Iceberg snapshot's data files requires walking the snapshot's manifest list and decoding each manifest file. `IcebergIterator` currently does this with a single background producer thread, so for tables with many manifest files the manifest walk is serial and can dominate query planning time. This adds an opt-in, experimental setting `iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads` (`UInt64`, default `1`). At the default value of `1` behavior is unchanged. With a value greater than `1`, `IcebergIterator` builds N data-file iterators that share one atomic counter over the snapshot's `manifest_list_entries` and spawns N producer tasks; each producer claims the next manifest index via `fetch_add`, so manifests are decoded cooperatively with no overlap, and the last producer to finish closes the queue. The effective thread count is clamped to the number of manifest files. Delete-file manifests are still drained serially, since data-file pruning depends on the full delete set. A new `ProfileEvent` `IcebergParallelManifestDecodeThreadsSpawned` reports how many producer threads were spawned. Tests: a unit test for the shared-index claim contract, a stateless test for the setting, and an integration test asserting result parity across thread counts (including a query with an `IN` filter, which exercises concurrent lazy materialization of the shared filter set). ### Changelog category: - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads` that decodes Iceberg manifest files using multiple threads during query planning, speeding up reads of tables with many manifest files.

signals.title: Fix signed integer overflow in condition_variable::wait_for with huge timeouts
signals.text: A wait-timeout setting that reaches `std::condition_variable::wait_for` unchecked overflows the chrono conversion inside it. libc++ evaluates `wait_for(d)` as `steady_clock::now() + d` in nanoseconds, multiplying a millisecond duration by 1000000: a timeout above ~9.2e12 ms overflows Int64, and one above the Int64 millisecond range even turns into a negative duration, so the wait returns at once and the caller busy-loops instead of waiting. UBSan aborts the server; a release build silently wraps. The setting that reaches it in practice is `interactive_delay`, a plain unbounded `UInt64` of microseconds: the server waits `interactive_delay / 1000` milliseconds for the next result chunk in `ConcurrentBoundedQueue::popImpl`, through the lazy output format, on both the `TCPHandler` and the `clickhouse-local` path. Found by serverfuzz on master, and again in the stress test of an unrelated pull request — https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112177&sha=e601607e228ad5d736ad491220ebf4b62d531d51&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20s3%29 (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112177): ``` /ClickHouse/contrib/llvm-project/libcxx/include/__chrono/duration.h:93:79: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 18584892780430 * 1000000 cannot be represented in type '_Ct' (aka 'long long') ... #6 ConcurrentBoundedQueue<DB::Chunk>::popImpl<true>(...) src/Common/ConcurrentBoundedQueue.h:73 #8 DB::LazyOutputFormat::getChunk(unsigned long) src/Processors/Formats/LazyOutputFormat.cpp:25 #11 DB::TCPHandler::processOrdinaryQuery(DB::QueryState&) src/Server/TCPHandler.cpp:1540 SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior ``` Reproduces deterministically: ``` clickhouse-local --query "SELECT 1 SETTINGS interactive_delay = 100000000000000000" ``` Fix: clamp the timeout to one year before constructing the chrono duration, via a small shared helper `saturatedMilliseconds`. The same cap is already used for `CancellationChecker` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96450); it is applied here to the remaining `wait_for` sites that take a user-controlled millisecond timeout, and `saturatedSeconds`/`saturatedSecondsFrom` cover the seconds-typed timeouts and the query cache expiry built as `now() + seconds(query_cache_ttl)`. A `Milliseconds`- or `Seconds`-typed setting can no longer carry such a value in the first place: `SettingFieldTimespan` rejects a value that does not fit into Int64 microseconds, so the clamp there is only defence in depth. That check landed on master after this branch was cut and supersedes the saturating conversion this pull request originally added to `SettingsFields`, which is dropped along with its unit tests in favour of master's stricter ones. What is left for the clamp is every setting that is not a timespan — above all `interactive_delay`. Keeper has its own coordination waits with a different bound; they are handled separately in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112088. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112088 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112177 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a signed integer overflow when a wait-timeout setting, such as `interactive_delay`, was set to a huge value: the wait could time out immediately instead of waiting, and the server could abort under the Undefined Behavior Sanitizer. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106961&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106961](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106961+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add query plan cache for complex queries (views, joins, subqueries)
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add an experimental query plan cache supporting complex `SELECT` queries: views (including nested views), joins, `UNION`, `IN` subqueries and multiple tables over supported local table engines. When `allow_experimental_query_plan_cache = 1` and `enable_query_plan_cache = 1`, repeated identical queries skip query analysis and logical planning (the query is still parsed) while still executing against current data. `SYSTEM DROP QUERY PLAN CACHE` clears the cache; events `QueryPlanCacheHits`/`QueryPlanCacheMisses`/`QueryPlanCacheValidationMisses`/`QueryPlanCacheStaleMisses` and metrics `QueryPlanCacheBytes`/`QueryPlanCacheEntries` provide observability. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) --- ### Description An experimental **query plan cache** for `SELECT` queries that supports **complex queries** — views (including nested views), joins, `UNION`, `IN` subqueries and multiple tables over supported local table engines. It complements https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99309, which covers single-table `MergeTree` queries with a universalize/materialize design; this PR takes a different approach to reach query shapes where planning cost is actually concentrated (deep view chains, many joins). Unlike the query result cache, a plan cache hit still executes the query: only query analysis and logical planning are skipped (the query is still parsed, since the cache key is built from the parsed AST), so hits are transactionally consistent and always see current data. #### Design On a miss, the plan is built in the planner's existing `build_logical_plan` mode (the machinery used by distributed plan shipping), with a new `SelectQueryOptions::cacheable_logical_plan` mode that makes the logical plan self-contained: - Leaf reads are storage-agnostic `ReadFromTable` placeholders for any eligible local engine. - **Views are expanded at plan time** (only `StorageView`; a materialized view stays a leaf and is read from its target table like an ordinary table), recursively in logical mode (propagated through `StorageView::readImpl` via `SelectQueryInfo::build_logical_plan`), so the cached plan embeds the analyzed view bodies instead of deferring the expensive expansion to execution. - Key-value direct-join lookup steps (`JoinStepLogicalLookup`), which bind live storages into the plan, are not used; a regular join is planned instead and the physical join algorithm is chosen at materialization. Distributed and parallel-replicas logical plans do not set this mode and are unaffected. - The plan is serialized with the standard query plan serialization and built with `compile_expressions = 0` (JIT-fused function nodes cannot be serialized; the JIT still applies when pipelines are built from the plan). Both hits and misses execute through `QueryPlan::resolveStorages`, which re-binds every leaf to a fresh storage snapshot. #### Cache key and invalidation The key is the normalized AST hash, a hash of plan-affecting settings, the current database, the user and the sorted role set. Each entry stores a **dependency fingerprint over every referenced storage**, discovered from the plan's `ReadFromTable` leaves plus an AST closure through view definitions (which also catches tables referenced only from scalar subqueries): UUID, metadata version (or a schema content hash including the view body), and the row policy hash. Every hit revalidates all dependencies and re-checks `SELECT` access, so `DROP`/`CREATE`, `ALTER`, view redefinition (including **nested** views), row policy changes and permission revocation are handled transparently. #### Eligibility - Non-deterministic functions anywhere — including inside expanded view bodies — make a query uncacheable (`arrayJoin` is exempt: it is multi-valued but pure). - Scalar subqueries are evaluated during analysis and baked into the plan as constants, so they are gated behind the opt-in setting `query_plan_cache_allow_scalar_subqueries`. - Table functions, temporary tables, system tables (except `system.one`), remote/`Merge` storages and views whose SQL security is not `INVOKER` (`DEFINER` and `NONE`) are rejected. - Plans containing steps without serialization support (e.g. window functions) execute normally and are simply not stored. #### Performance, proven on DOOMbench [DOOMbench](https://github.com/cedardb/doombench) is a DOOM-like raycasting engine implemented entirely in SQL; its `screen` query renders a frame through a deep chain of views over joins, unions, array joins and scalar subqueries. Ported to ClickHouse SQL, the workload is **query-analysis-bound**: profiling showed `IQueryTreeNode::getTreeHash` and analyzer resolution dominating, and `SELECT ... LIMIT 0` was as slow as the full query. With the plan cache (local server, single connection): | DOOMbench frame render | median | speedup | | --- | --- | --- | | cache off | 551-577 ms | — | | cache on (hit) | 227-246 ms | **2.4x** | | cache on, `max_threads = 4` | 148-176 ms | **3.3x** | On hits the analyzer cost disappears from profiles (`getTreeHash`: 25.8k samples → 174); the remaining time is genuine execution. Correctness validated on the same workload: frames are byte-identical between cache off/miss/hit, game-state mutations are visible on every cached render (HTAP freshness), nested view redefinition is picked up immediately, and `rand()` inside a view body refuses to cache. #### Notes - This PR includes the `ActionsDAG` input-constant serialization fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107124 as its first commit; it will be rebased once that PR is merged. - The miss path executes through the same logical-plan machinery as hits, so hit and miss behavior is identical by construction; storage-specific planning shortcuts (e.g. trivial `count()`) are not applied to cache-enabled queries. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99309 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107124 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107125&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107125](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107125+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Test: merge memory is not bounded by max_memory_usage (merge OOM repro)
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107389 --> Draft. A test demonstrating that a background merge's memory is **not** bounded by the per-query `max_memory_usage` setting. ### Motivation In the AST fuzzer run for #107389 ([CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107389&sha=ec12cb3ce0a49a403226cb0668b092f02a2fa3f6&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29)) the server was OOM-killed even though the fuzzer runs queries **sequentially** and no single query peaked above 1.69 GiB. During the steepest part of the memory climb there were *zero* foreground queries running — only background merges. The fuzzer's `INSERT`s left behind parts (large arrays from `arrayResize`, very wide schemas up to 1796 columns) that the background merge subsystem then combined; that memory accumulates across query boundaries and is governed by the global / background-pool trackers, not by the per-query limit. A merge runs under its own memory tracker — a child of the global `Background process (mutate/merge)` tracker — created in `ThreadGroup::createForMergeMutate`. `configureMemoryTrackerFromSettings` never installs `max_memory_usage` as the merge tracker's hard limit, so the per-query limit does not constrain a merge at all. ### What the test does - Creates a `MergeTree` table and inserts two parts of large arrays (forcing a horizontal merge). - Sets a tiny `max_memory_usage` (20 MB). - Runs `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` — the merge **completes** despite the limit. - Confirms via `system.part_log` that the merge's `peak_memory_usage` (~110 MiB observed) is far above the per-query limit. The test asserts behavior with a generous margin, so it does not literally OOM-kill the CI server (that would be destructive and flaky). It reliably reproduces the *condition* that leads to OOM: a merge consuming memory the per-query limit never sees. It is intended as the regression/repro basis for extending the memory-overcommit mechanism to merges (today `OvercommitTracker` only selects victims from `ProcessList`, i.e. user queries; merges — which are restartable and therefore cheaper to cancel than queries — do not participate). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107410&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107410](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107410+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: TTL CLEAR INDEX for MergeTree parts
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107804 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78714 TTL CLEAR INDEX lets a MergeTree table keep secondary indexes for recent parts while dropping the physical index files from old parts. I recommend reviewing commit-by-commit. The motivating case is Observability log storage. For log tables, the raw data is not always the dominant cost. Text indexes can be very large, and most queries only touch recent data. We want to keep the index where it helps and stop paying for it on old parts that are rarely searched. Example syntax: ```sql TTL timestamp + INTERVAL 7 DAY CLEAR INDEX message_text ``` This follows the existing meaning of `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR INDEX`: remove the per-part index files, but keep the index definition in table metadata. Queries remain correct. Parts without the index just fall back to scanning. ## What this changes The patch adds a new table TTL action, `CLEAR INDEX`, and stores its per-part min/max TTL info in `ttl.txt` as `index_clear_ttl`. When a part is fully past the TTL for a target index, future maintenance may remove that index’s files from the part. If the table later reads that part, the secondary index reader already handles missing index files and simply does not use that index for that part. The patch also adds system table visibility: ```text system.parts.index_clear_ttl_info.{index_name,expression,min,max} ``` ## Merge behavior There are two cases. First, normal merges apply the TTL policy to their output. If a merge output is fully past the `CLEAR INDEX` TTL, the merge should not retain the target index files. This is important for late-arriving data: a tiny old insert should not cause a merge that rebuilds a huge old text index. Second, there is a dedicated TTL maintenance merge type: `MergeType::TTLClearIndex`. This is used for the case where a single old part has expired index files and does not otherwise need a merge. The first implementation is intentionally conservative: it selects one source part and produces one replacement part. Dedicated `TTLClearIndex` selection obeys the normal full-part merge byte and row limits. This keeps cleanup conservative when preserving the part would require copying unchanged files rather than hardlinking them. For eligible full-storage parts, the implementation uses a fast path: hardlink or copy unchanged files, omit the expired index files, rewrite checksums and metadata, and publish the replacement part. Projection directories are copied wholesale because the row set is unchanged. This avoids reading and rewriting the raw data. If the fast path is not safe, the code falls back to the normal rewrite path. The fallback may rewrite the part, but it still must not retain expired index files in the final output. Parts with incomplete TTL metadata are not selected for dedicated cleanup; `MATERIALIZE TTL` or an ordinary merge must first recalculate the current TTL rules. The fast path currently opts out for cases like packed part storage, UUID parts, legacy parts without metadata-version files, metadata version mismatches, patch parts, part-format changes, and projection subdirectories it cannot copy as-is. On remote or zero-copy storage, it copies unchanged files instead of hardlinking them. It handles packed skip-index archives by excluding dirty `skp_idx.packed` files from the hardlink/copy set and rewriting the archive for surviving packed entries. ## Rollout safety `TTLClearIndex` is a new merge type, and merge types are serialized in replicated MergeTree log entries. Older replicas would not understand a new merge type. For that reason, generation is gated by a setting: ```sql enable_ttl_clear_index_merge_type_generation ``` The default is off. The binary can parse and execute `TTLClearIndex`, but a server will not write that merge type to the replicated log unless the setting is enabled. The intended rollout is: 1. deploy code everywhere; 2. once every replica that can read the log understands `TTLClearIndex`, enable generation; 3. later we can consider changing the default. With the gate off, replicas will not schedule dedicated `TTLClearIndex` maintenance work. Regular merges can still apply the clear-index TTL to their outputs, which is safe because missing per-part index files are already supported. ## Interaction with `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` `CLEAR INDEX` is a TTL effect, so it respects the TTL merge blocker. If TTL merges are already stopped before a regular merge starts, the merge continues without applying clear-index TTL effects. If TTL merges are stopped after a merge has already decided to apply clear-index TTL effects, the merge is cancelled, matching existing TTL-delete behavior. ## Validation and edge cases covered The tests cover: - invalid target index names - per-part `index_clear_ttl_info` in `system.parts`, including the target index name - minmax index clearing - text index clearing - the late tiny insert case, where an old cleared part later merges with a small old part - adding `CLEAR INDEX` TTL to a table that already has old indexed data - TTL dependency recalculation after mutating a column used by the TTL expression - replicated execution with embedded Keeper - generation off vs generation on ## Things deliberately left conservative The fast path is narrow on purpose. Physically unsupported parts use the regular fallback, while parts with incomplete TTL metadata wait for recalculation. We can broaden the fast path later once we are comfortable with storage-specific details. The generation gate is also conservative. It is there to make rolling upgrades safe, not to disable all `CLEAR INDEX` TTL behavior. Possible follow-ups: - share more code with the existing `ALTER ... CLEAR INDEX` mutation path - add more schema-evolution tests around dropping or changing target indexes - add more direct instrumentation around which files were hardlinked vs copied in the fast path ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree tables now support `TTL ... CLEAR INDEX index_name`, which clears secondary index files from parts once all rows in the part are past the TTL. This can help to manage the lifecycle of large indexes on older data, to conserve disk space. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108069](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108069+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid copying data for the NONE compression codec when writing
signals.text: Avoid copying data for the `NONE` compression codec when writing. For `CODEC(NONE)` the compressed block on disk is byte-identical to the input, so the payload does not need to be copied between the compressor's working buffer and the output buffer. When a `CompressedWriteBuffer` exclusively owns its output buffer, the working buffer is now pointed directly into the output buffer (reserving room for the checksum and header in front of the data), so the caller writes the uncompressed data straight to where it will be flushed; `nextImpl` only fills in the header and checksum in place, with no payload copy. The header is written by a new `ICompressionCodec::writeHeader` helper factored out of `compress`. When the output buffer is too small, the writer falls back to the previous owned-buffer copy path. This is the same zero-copy buffer-aliasing technique that `HashingWriteBuffer` already uses. The zero-copy path (`out_buffer_is_exclusive`) is enabled only where the compressor is the sole, sequential writer of its output buffer: the wide-part column data streams, the primary-index stream, and the temporary-data buffer. It is intentionally left off where the output buffer is shared and written interleaved — the per-column streams of compact parts (which share one `plain_hashing`) and the network protocol buffer (interleaved with raw packet framing) — because there the reserved window could be overwritten by another writer. It is also left off for the marks streams of wide and compact parts: their `marks_file` has a small fixed-size buffer (4096 bytes), so the direct path would clamp `NONE`-coded mark blocks to it instead of the configured `marks_compress_block_size`; the regression test `04539_marks_compression_codec_none_block_size` covers this. Note: for `NONE`, compressed block sizes become bounded by the output buffer size, so the on-disk byte layout can differ slightly from before (an occasional shorter block at buffer boundaries). This is deterministic and does not affect reads. The read side already decompresses `NONE` data directly into the destination column via `readBig`, so no change is needed there. ### Performance evidence Measured with two `clickhouse` binaries built from the same base commit, differing only by this PR (cherry-picked onto the same parent), so the comparison isolates exactly this change. Isolated write-path microbenchmark — 4 GiB through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with the `NONE` codec into a discarding sink (no disk), 1 MiB blocks and output buffer, toggling only `out_buffer_is_exclusive`: | `out_buffer_is_exclusive` | throughput | |---|---| | `false` (old copy path) | ~8.5–9.2 GB/s | | `true` (zero-copy path) | ~13.6–14.0 GB/s | | **speedup** | **~1.5–1.6x** | End-to-end `INSERT` of 8 wide `String CODEC(NONE)` columns (3M rows, single insert thread, no dedup/squashing/sparse, merges stopped; baseline = exact parent commit; median of interleaved reps): **2.96s → 2.62s (~1.13x, ~13% faster)**. The end-to-end gain is below the disk-free microbenchmark because disk I/O and data generation (equal in both binaries) dominate the rest of the insert. A focused performance test, `tests/performance/codec_none_read.xml`, is added. It scans `CODEC(NONE)` columns, so in the PR-vs-master comparison the table is filled by each side's own write path (old vs new block layout) and then read by the identical read code. This guards against a read regression from the slightly changed `NONE` block layout, and tracks `NONE` read throughput in general (relevant for incompressible data such as vector embeddings). Measured read time is unchanged before/after (~0.62s vs ~0.61s for 100M rows, single thread), confirming the write-path change is read-neutral. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid an extra data copy when writing columns and temporary data compressed with the `NONE` codec by writing the data directly into the output buffer. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108096](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108096+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid per-row heap allocations in blocked Myers edit distance
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved the performance of `levenshteinDistance` (and `editDistance`) for medium-length strings on ARM by avoiding per-row heap allocations in the blocked Myers code path. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 Fixes the ARM regression reported in #106595: `string_similarity` query `0` (`SELECT avg(levenshteinDistance(randomString(300), randomString(300))) FROM numbers(10000)`) was about +12.6% slower on Neoverse-V2. Root cause: the blocked Myers path (`BlockMyersEditDistance`, used for byte needles of 257..8192 bytes) allocated its per-row scratch buffers on the heap once per row through `VectorWithMemoryTracking`: the pattern-mask table `tbl` and the `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` bit vectors. Each allocation pairs a `malloc`/`free` with a `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomic update. On ARM those atomic updates are comparatively expensive, so this per-row churn showed up as the regression. Only this path was affected: the single-word Myers widths (`ByteEditDistanceMyersImpl`, needles up to 256 bytes) already use fixed stack scratch, which is why the other `string_similarity` queries did not regress. Fix: hold the per-row buffers in `PODArrayWithStackMemory`. It keeps an allocation up to its inline capacity in an inline buffer (no heap allocation, no `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomics) and transparently spills to a tracked allocation above it. The per-row allocation is therefore eliminated across each buffer's inline range, and the buffer management is a single idiomatic type instead of a hand-rolled stack-array + tracked-vector + raw-pointer split (suggested by @ nikitamikhaylov). The inline range differs per buffer because their shapes differ: - `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` hold one `Word` per block (1 KB each), so a 128-block inline buffer covers the full 8192-byte blocked-Myers range. - `tbl` is the ASCII pattern table, `256 * num_blocks` words (one row per byte value), so it is 256x larger per block. Its inline buffer covers needles up to 8 blocks (512 bytes, 16 KB); a full-range inline table would be about 256 KB, so longer needles transparently spill `tbl` to a tracked allocation while the bit vectors stay inline. The reported regression (300-byte needles, 5 blocks) is fully on the inline path for every buffer. Correctness: distances are unchanged. `02884_string_distance_function`, `03369_function_arrayLevenshtein` and `04125_array_levenshtein_types` pass, and a differential check of `editDistance` and `editDistanceUTF8` against a brute-force DP reference (1392 random pairs) matches exactly, including the block and inline/spill boundary lengths (64/128/192/256/512/8192). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Deny mergeTreeProjection and mergeTreeIndex reads that bypass a SELECT row policy
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> No related public open issue found. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading projection data with the `mergeTreeProjection` table function no longer bypasses a SELECT row policy defined on the parent table. Such a read is now denied with `ACCESS_DENIED` when a non-trivial SELECT row policy exists. The `mergeTreeIndex` table function is likewise denied when the row policy references one of the index columns being read. ### Description `mergeTreeProjection(db, table, projection)` reads a projection's parts directly. Projection parts contain materialized rows of the parent table, so the read returned rows that a SELECT row policy on the parent is meant to hide. Any user with `SELECT` on the table could read hidden rows. `mergeTreeIndex` had the same gap, exposing per-granule index metadata (marks, primary key and column min/max). PR #95480 added the missing `SELECT` grant check to these functions but did not consider row policies. Reproduction (before this PR the last query returns all 4 rows): ```sql CREATE TABLE users (id UInt64, name String, department String, salary UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'Alice','engineering',100000),(2,'Bob','finance',120000), (3,'Carol','engineering',110000),(4,'Dave','hr',90000); ALTER TABLE users ADD PROJECTION proj (SELECT id, name, salary ORDER BY id); ALTER TABLE users MATERIALIZE PROJECTION proj; OPTIMIZE TABLE users FINAL; CREATE USER restricted NOT IDENTIFIED; GRANT SELECT ON default.users TO restricted; CREATE ROW POLICY rp ON users FOR SELECT USING department = 'engineering' TO restricted; -- as restricted: returns only Alice, Carol (policy enforced) SELECT * FROM users; -- as restricted, before this PR: returns all 4 rows (policy bypassed) SELECT * FROM mergeTreeProjection('default', 'users', 'proj'); ``` Fix: - `StorageFromMergeTreeProjection::read()` denies the read when a non-trivial SELECT row policy exists on the parent. The policy cannot be re-applied here: a projection may aggregate rows or omit the policy's filter columns entirely (as in the example above, where `department` is absent from the projection), so hidden rows still leak even when those columns are absent. A column-overlap check is therefore insufficient for projections; a full deny is required. - `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl()` exposes only index metadata, so it gets the narrower column-overlap guard already used by `mergeTreeTextIndex`: deny only when the policy filter references one of the storage columns whose index data is being read. An always-true policy (`isAlwaysTrue()`) does not trigger the deny, and reads without a row policy are unaffected. Test: `tests/queries/0_stateless/04401_mergetree_projection_row_policy.sh`.

signals.title: Switch the default compression to ZSTD(3) for table data and network
signals.text: Switch the default compression in ClickHouse from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`, for both on-disk table data and network communication. ### Motivation `LZ4` has been the default for a long time and optimizes for speed, but `ZSTD(3)` gives substantially better compression ratios at a still-modest CPU cost, reducing both storage footprint and network traffic out of the box. ClickHouse Cloud already uses a stronger default; this aligns the self-managed defaults. ### What changes - **On-disk table data.** `CompressionCodecFactory::getDefaultCodec` now returns `ZSTD(3)` instead of `LZ4`. For `MergeTree` column data the built-in default is *size-aware*: when a column specifies no codec and no `<compression>` server-config case matches, `CompressionCodecSelector::choose` uses the faster `LZ4` for parts smaller than 100 MB and `ZSTD(3)` for larger parts, so freshly inserted data starts as `LZ4` and the bigger parts produced by background merges switch to `ZSTD(3)`. The direct `getDefaultCodec` users — the `Log` family, part checksums, the HTTP `compress=1` output, the `StripeLog` data stream, and the persistent `Set`/`Join` files — are not size-aware and switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. External temporary (spill) files are unaffected: they keep their own `temporary_files_codec` default (`LZ4`). - **Network.** The defaults of `network_compression_method` (`LZ4` → `ZSTD`) and `network_zstd_compression_level` (`1` → `3`) are changed, so the native client/server and Distributed (server/server) protocol uses `ZSTD(3)` by default. The changes are recorded in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so the `compatibility` setting restores the previous behavior for these paths. The distributed-query streaming exchange (`StreamingExchangeSink`) does not read `network_compression_method` and always uses the server default codec; this is safe because each frame is self-describing (the receiver auto-detects the codec) and the exchange is a transient, same-version channel — `StreamingExchangeProtocol` rejects peers on a different protocol version, so a stream is never read back by a node expecting a different codec. - **Upgrade safety.** The append-only `Log`/`TinyLog`/`StripeLog` engines resolve the default codec at write time, so a table written before the upgrade (`LZ4`) and appended to after it (`ZSTD(3)`) ends up with mixed-codec blocks in one file. Their readers now pass `allow_different_codecs = true` (as the `MergeTree` reader already does) so such files still read back correctly. The legacy custom-frame Keeper snapshot format (`compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format = false`) is pinned to `LZ4` so it stays the documented format. Columns, tables, and connections that specify a codec or method explicitly are unaffected — with one exception: streams written through the built-in default codec directly, which ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config. The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files (written by `SetOrJoinSink` and `StorageJoin::mutate` through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with no codec), and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`, via `MergeTreeDataPartChecksums::write`) always follow the new default; see the changelog entry below for the per-path rollback. ### Validation Built locally and verified against the new binary: - A `MergeTree` table created with no explicit codec follows the size-aware default: small parts report `LZ4` and parts larger than 100 MB report `ZSTD(3)` as their `default_compression_codec` in `system.parts`. Direct `getDefaultCodec` streams (e.g. `StripeLog`) report `ZSTD(3)` regardless of size. - `system.settings` shows `network_compression_method = ZSTD` and `network_zstd_compression_level = 3`. - End-to-end `SELECT`/`INSERT` over the native protocol with default (now `ZSTD`) network compression work; all of `LZ4`/`lz4hc`/`zstd`/`none` still work and an invalid method still errors with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. - The `02995_new_settings_history` consistency check passes (both setting changes are recorded). - The on-disk byte-dump tests (`02047_log_family_*_data_file_dumps`) were regenerated for the new default: `Log`/`TinyLog` keep `LZ4`-pinned columns, while `StripeLog`'s shared `data.bin`/`index.mrk` reflect the `ZSTD(3)` default (it uses `getDefaultCodec` and ignores the per-column codec). Size-sensitive stateless and integration tests that assert compressed byte sizes were pinned back to `LZ4` (cache segment sizes, distributed-batch corruption offsets, full-disk thresholds, frozen-part checksums). The CI performance comparison does **not** measure this tradeoff: the harness pins the built-in default codec to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/config.d/compression.xml`) and `network_compression_method` to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/users.d/perf-comparison-tweaks-users.xml`) on *both* the reference and the tested server, deliberately, so the report measures query logic rather than drowning in expected codec regressions. It therefore serves only as a regression filter for the non-codec parts of this change; the storage/network-vs-CPU tradeoff of `LZ4` → `ZSTD(3)` itself is a well-known property of the two codecs and is not measured by this pull request's CI. Documentation updated accordingly, including the `Native` format and protocol specifications and the `<compression>` config examples. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The default compression method is changed from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. For client/server and server/server network communication it switches uniformly to `ZSTD(3)`. For on-disk table data, `MergeTree` column data now uses a size-aware built-in default — parts smaller than 100 MB use `LZ4` and larger parts use `ZSTD(3)` — while the direct built-in-default streams (the `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and part checksums) switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. This improves compression ratios and reduces storage and network usage out of the box, at a modest increase in CPU usage. None of the on-disk or HTTP paths are controlled by `compatibility`; the previous behavior can be restored per path as follows. For client/server and Distributed network compression, use the `compatibility` setting (or set `network_compression_method = 'LZ4'`). For `MergeTree` column data, set a column/table `CODEC(LZ4)` or configure the server `<compression>` default to `LZ4`. For the `Log`/`TinyLog` engines, set a column `CODEC(LZ4)` (their default does not consult the `<compression>` config). The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`) use the built-in default codec directly — they ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config — so they always use the new `ZSTD(3)` default and have no runtime rollback; reading stays correct because every compressed frame is self-describing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108786&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108786](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108786+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Use bloom filter skip index for arrayJoin(col) IN (set) and arrayJoin(col) = const
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109516 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109844 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A `bloom_filter` skip index on an `Array` column is now used for `arrayJoin(column) IN (set)`, `arrayJoin(column) GLOBAL IN (set)` and `arrayJoin(column) = const`, the same way it was already used for `hasAny(column, set)` and `has(column, const)`. Previously these `arrayJoin ...` forms fell back to a full scan. ### Description `MergeTreeIndexConditionBloomFilter` only accepted the argument of `IN` / `=` as an indexed column directly or one of a few wrappers (`tuple`, map subcolumns, JSON paths). `arrayJoin(tags)` matched none, so the atom became `FUNCTION_UNKNOWN` and nothing was pruned, while `hasAny(tags, ...)` / `has(tags, ...)` already pruned. This PR recognizes `arrayJoin(indexed_array_column)` on the left side and maps: - `arrayJoin(arr) IN (set)` (and `GLOBAL IN`) to the same granule test as `hasAny(arr, set_elements)` (`traverseTreeIn`); - `arrayJoin(arr) = const` to the same granule test as `has(arr, const)` (`traverseTreeEquals`). `arrayJoin` only multiplies rows, so a granule matches only if one of its array elements belongs to the set / equals the constant, which is what the bloom filter evaluates for `hasAny` / `has`. `NOT IN` / `!=` are intentionally not handled: a granule containing a set element / the constant can still yield rows whose value is outside the set / differs. Both derivations hash the constant after converting it towards the indexed element type, and SQL comparison coerces more widely than that conversion does. Where the two disagree the index was probed with bytes the predicate never compares, or the conversion threw during index analysis. Both are now gated on a proven-matching hash domain: an identical element and constant type, or integer against integer. Everything else is declined, leaving a full scan and keeping a conversion error reachable at execution rather than turning it into pruned granules. Integer widening and a `LowCardinality` wrapper stay admitted, so the pruning this PR adds is unchanged. Verified with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the `arrayJoin ...` forms prune like `hasAny` / `has`, that `NOT IN` / `!=` do not prune, and that results are identical with the skip index on and off for every declined domain and for the `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` case. Test: `04365_bloom_filter_arrayJoin_in`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109536&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109536](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109536+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Remove CatBoost integration
signals.text: Removes the CatBoost integration: the `catboostEvaluate` function, the `system.models` table, the `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S)` queries and the matching `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` privilege, together with their documentation, tests and the bundled model artifacts. The `CANNOT_LOAD_CATBOOST_MODEL` and `CANNOT_APPLY_CATBOOST_MODEL` error codes are intentionally kept so their numbers are not reused. Refs: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/70771 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/45052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Removed the CatBoost integration. The `catboostEvaluate` function, the `system.models` table and the `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S)` queries are no longer available. Queries, views and grants referring to them have to be migrated before the upgrade: in particular, revoke `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` from all users and roles beforehand, because an access entity whose grants still mention the removed privilege cannot be parsed on startup. Also let any in-flight `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S) ON CLUSTER` entries drain from the distributed DDL queue before the upgrade: upgraded hosts can no longer parse such entries and will finish them with an error status instead of executing them. The same applies to persisted table metadata: a table whose column `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS` expressions, secondary indices, constraints, projections, partition/order/sample keys, or TTL expressions still reference `catboostEvaluate` cannot be loaded after the upgrade (`UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`), so drop or rewrite such definitions beforehand. The revoke also has to cover every other carrier of serialized grants: a `GRANT SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` line in the `grants` section of `users.xml` must be removed as well, because it can no longer be parsed and the server then refuses to load the users configuration at startup; on clusters with replicated (Keeper-backed) access storage, revoke the privilege before upgrading any replica, because with the default `access_control_improvements.throw_on_invalid_replicated_access_entities = 0` an upgraded replica that reads a user or role still carrying `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` from ZooKeeper cannot parse it and silently drops that entity from its in-memory copy (set `throw_on_invalid_replicated_access_entities = 1` to fail loudly instead); and access backups (`BACKUP ... ACCESS`) taken while the grant was still present cannot be restored with `RESTORE ... ACCESS` on the new version, so re-create such backups after the revoke. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109710&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109710](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109710+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid server abort on type mismatch during partial result evaluation
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110048 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97411 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Constant folding during query planning no longer executes a function whose argument type differs from the type the function was resolved for during analysis. Such a mismatch used to raise a `LOGICAL_ERROR` while the output header was being computed, which is an assertion failure in debug and sanitizer builds. Folding is now skipped instead, and a genuinely invalid query still reports a recoverable `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` error from the normal execution path. ### Description `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` matches header columns to DAG input nodes **by name only**, then runs `evaluatePartialResult` to compute the output header. A function node, by contrast, is resolved once during analysis: the overload is picked and the return type computed for a fixed set of argument types. If partial evaluation is handed an input column whose type differs from the one the function was resolved for, `executeActionForPartialResult` used to execute the function anyway. That trips a `LOGICAL_ERROR` inside the function body (for example `FunctionUnaryArithmetic`: "`negate`'s argument does not match the expected data type"), and because `handle_error_code` routes `LOGICAL_ERROR` to `abortOnFailedAssertion`, a debug or sanitizer build aborts the whole server process during planning rather than failing the one query. **Fix.** Before executing a `FUNCTION` node in partial evaluation, compare each argument column's type against the type recorded in `function_base->getArgumentTypes()`. If any of them differs, skip the fold: it is only an optimization, and the node's declared result type is already known from analysis. - With `input_rows_count == 0` (header computation) an empty column of the declared result type is produced, so header computation proceeds. - With `input_rows_count == 1` (the callers reached from JOIN rewrites, shard skipping and virtual-column path extraction) the column is left null. Those callers treat any non-null output as a definitive folded value, so a fabricated one could silently change a JOIN rewrite or skip the wrong shards; a null routes them through their existing "unknown value" path. The comparison is exact rather than wrapper-stripped, because `isNullable` derives its value from the argument type alone: its result type is `UInt8` either way, so a wrapper-only difference would produce a definitive but wrong value that no result-type check can catch. `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` need the same treatment, because both used to pass a value through while keeping the declared type computed during analysis. That hid the mismatch from the check above and let a downstream function execute on an incompatible column anyway. Both now carry the argument's actual type, which is what `ExpressionActions::executeAction` already does in its own `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` cases. One result type cannot be instantiated: `DataTypeFunction`, the result type of a captured lambda, inherits `IDataTypeDummy::createColumn`, which throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. The column is left null in that one case. Since a capture is normally a child of the higher-order function consuming it, that function then reports a recoverable `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, whereas executing the stale capture raises `Cannot capture column N because it has incompatible type`, another `LOGICAL_ERROR` abort. (`DataTypeNothing` and `DataTypeSet` derive from the same base but do override `createColumn`, so they are built normally.) **Scope.** In production the mismatch was produced by a concurrent `EXCHANGE TABLES`. The query does hold its table object, lock and metadata snapshot for its whole lifetime (`InterpreterSelectQuery.cpp:635-656`), so the held storage is never swapped. What drifts is that the old analyzer resolves the table name a second time for the analyzed column types (`getTableExpressions.cpp:118`, reached from `joined_tables.resolveTables()`), and an exchange changes what that second resolution returns. The per-query storage cache from #97411 is what keeps those two resolutions consistent; #108728 defeated it and #110048 restored it, which is what `03915_exchange_tables_race` races for. This change is therefore no longer the fix for that race; it hardens the planning path itself so that any argument-type mismatch degrades to "do not fold" instead of aborting the server. I left the changelog category as `Bug Fix` because the abort was user-visible on released builds before #110048, but I am happy to move it to `Not for changelog` if you prefer, given that the root cause is now fixed upstream. **Testing.** Coverage is a unit test rather than a functional one, because the race is an inherent TOCTOU and cannot be reproduced deterministically. Since `updateHeader` binds header columns by name only, the mismatch can be injected directly, single-threaded, with no race at all. `src/Interpreters/tests/gtest_actions_dag_partial_result_type_drift.cpp` covers a strict function (`Float64` resolved, `Int256` supplied), a wrapper-only difference through `materialize`, the same mismatch behind an `ALIAS` and behind an `ARRAY_JOIN`, the wrong-value hazard via `isNullable` at `input_rows_count == 1`, a captured lambda both as a terminal output and consumed by `arrayMap`, and a non-mismatched constant that must still be folded. Verified in both directions on a debug build. Against master's `executeActionForPartialResult` the first case aborts the test binary with `Logical error: 'Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Int256'` through `updateHeader` -> `evaluatePartialResult` -> `executeActionForPartialResult`; with the fix all eight cases pass. Each hunk was also reverted individually and fails only its own case, and forcing the guard to fire unconditionally fails only the still-folds-a-constant case. Full unit suite: 22357 tests pass. `03915_exchange_tables_race` passes 10 out of 10 runs. **Known residuals, both pre-existing on `master` and deliberately not addressed here.** I measured each one against a build with this branch's `ActionsDAG.cpp` replaced by master's, and the behaviour is identical, so neither is caused or widened by this change: - The add-time fold in `tryFoldFunctionToConstant` does not perform this check. Handing `addFunction` a `function_base` resolved for one type together with a differently typed constant child raises `Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Const(Int256)`. This diff does not touch that path, and adding the check there would alter DAG construction for every query on a scenario I could not reach from SQL. - At `input_rows_count == 1` with `allow_unknown_function_arguments`, a type-sensitive folder above a node whose column is unknown can still fold from the type alone. Two shapes: `identity -> isNullable` over a `Nullable(String)` yields `0` where the real chain would yield `1` (unchanged from `master`), and an `ARRAY_JOIN` whose argument stopped being an array leaves the declared nested type in place, so `isNullable` above it also folds to `0`. Closing this properly needs an explicit "unknown" marker propagated through descendants, which changes the `evaluatePartialResult` contract for every caller. I tried the two local shortcuts and neither works: clearing the type outright makes the unit-test binary abort and then segfault, because a null type in a `ColumnWithTypeAndName` breaks downstream consumers; handing up the argument's own type does not help, because the parent compares against the type it was itself resolved for. So this is a separate design decision rather than part of an abort-avoidance fix. Happy to follow up on any of these if you would like them in scope. This branch also takes master's version of `03915_exchange_tables_race` verbatim: master rewrote that test after this branch forked it (pinning `enable_analyzer` and capping concurrent clients so the flaky check does not run out of memory), and those changes belong with #110048's coverage rather than here.

signals.title: Supply `_sample_factor` to the per-part read path used by mutations and merges
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78465 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78465 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a mutation that references the `_sample_factor` virtual column failing mid-execution with `Unexpected const virtual column: _sample_factor` and leaving the mutation stuck. A mutation now reads it as `1`, the same value a query without `SAMPLE` returns. ### Description `_sample_factor` is registered with `VirtualsMaterializationPlace::Reader`, so a reader is expected to supply its value. `ReadFromMergeTree` publishes it into `shared_virtual_fields` and the normal read pool copies that map into every read task, which is why `SELECT` resolves it. The per-part path used by mutations and merges does not: `createMergeTreeSequentialSource` seeds only `_part_index` and `_part_starting_offset`, so `fillVirtualColumns` falls through to a throw. `ALTER TABLE t UPDATE u = _sample_factor WHERE ...` therefore starts, then fails per part with `Code 341` wrapping `Code 16`, and the mutation entry stays stuck. The fix seeds the field where the sibling already does. The value is `1` because no `SAMPLE` clause reaches this path: `used_sample_factor` is declared `1.0` and is overwritten only for an actual `SAMPLE` clause, which a mutation predicate cannot carry. It is a literal constant, identical on every replica, so it is safe on ReplicatedMergeTree and SharedMergeTree. The net change against master is 3 lines of source plus one test. This replaces the analysis-time rejection this PR previously carried, so the guard it added earlier is gone and `MutationsInterpreter.cpp` is now untouched. That guard decided column identity from raw AST identifier names, which cannot distinguish an `ALIAS` over a virtual column from an `ALIAS` over a real `Tuple`, because `ColumnsDescription` deliberately omits alias subcolumns. One of the six holes measured rejected `a Tuple(_table UInt8) ALIAS tup` over a real `tup`, which master and 26.7.2 both accept, so dropping the guard also removes that regression. Scope is `_sample_factor` only, which is what the issue reports. `_table` and `_database` derive from the local storage id, and a mutation persists what it reads, so seeding them could diverge replicas, while rejecting them for every MergeTree would be a new restriction. That design is filed separately, and their current mid-execution failure is unchanged here.

signals.title: Support arrayElement and arraySlice for QBit
signals.text: arrayElement(qbit, n) (and the qbit[n] operator) reconstructs the n-th vector element at the full precision of the QBit element type, reading only the bit planes of the stride group that contains the element. Out-of-range indices follow the Array semantics: default value for arrayElement, NULL for arrayElementOrNull, negative indices count from the end. arraySlice(qbit, offset[, length]) returns a QBit over the selected dimensions (projection to a subset of dimensions). The offset and length must be constants because the dimension of a QBit is part of its type. A slice aligned to stride-group boundaries keeps the stride and reuses the stored bit-plane streams without copying; an octet-aligned slice is a pure byte move; any other slice repacks the bits, reading only the planes of the stride groups it overlaps. Possible follow-up: an analyzer pass (similar to DistanceTransposedPartialReadsPass) could rewrite these functions to read only the needed bit-plane subcolumns from disk, extending the "only needed strides" guarantee from the in-memory execution down to storage I/O. Closes #109942 ### Changelog category - New Feature ### Changelog entry Functions `arrayElement` (the `vec[n]` operator) and `arraySlice` now work for the `QBit` data type: `qbit[n]` returns the n-th vector element at full precision, and `arraySlice(qbit, offset, length)` returns a projection to a subset of dimensions. Both read only the bit planes of the stride groups they need, and slices aligned to stride-group boundaries reuse the stored streams without copying. This closes #109942. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109953&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109953](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109953+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Allow creating a Distributed table over a table function
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106189 Allow creating a `Distributed` table over a table function, in the same way the `remote`/`cluster` table functions already accept an arbitrary table expression. Previously `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Distributed(...)` only accepted `Distributed(cluster, database, table[, sharding_key[, policy_name]])`, where `database` and `table` had to be string literals or identifiers. `StorageDistributed` itself already supported being backed by a table function (`remote_table_function_ptr`), but that capability was only reachable through the `remote`/`cluster`/`clusterAllReplicas` table functions. This change lets the engine take a table function directly: ```sql CREATE TABLE t ENGINE = Distributed(cluster, table_function()[, sharding_key[, policy_name]]); -- e.g. CREATE TABLE distributed_numbers ENGINE = Distributed(test_cluster_two_shards, numbers(100)); ``` mirroring the `cluster('cluster_name', table_function())` signature. The second engine argument is treated as a table function only when it is a call to a registered table function; any other expression is still interpreted as a database name, so the existing `Distributed(cluster, database, table, ...)` form is unaffected. The structure is inferred from the table function when the columns are omitted. `INSERT` into a table-function-backed `Distributed` table is rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, since there is no concrete remote table to route rows to. As a side effect, `INSERT INTO FUNCTION cluster('cluster', table_function())` now fails with this clear error instead of silently building a broken `INSERT INTO <empty>` query for the shards. ### Relationship to #106189 This is complementary to #106189 (`Remote`/`RemoteSecure` storage engines): that PR adds address-based engines over an ad-hoc cluster, while this one lets the configured-cluster `Distributed` engine take a table function. The table-function `INSERT` guard in `StorageDistributed::write` is aligned with #106189 (identical exception message, guard placed only in `write`). The `read` path here additionally handles the case where the remote database/table names are empty (a table-function-backed `Distributed` stores empty names rather than the `system.one` placeholder that #106189's engines inherit from the `remote` table function); this also makes the shared `read` path robust for #106189's engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Allow creating a `Distributed` table over a table function, e.g. `CREATE TABLE t ENGINE = Distributed(cluster, numbers(100))`, in the same way as the `cluster`/`remote` table functions accept a table function. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110073&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110073](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110073+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add UUID2 data type with correct sorting
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110066 Introduces `UUID2`, a variant of the `UUID` data type with correct (lexicographic) sorting. ## Motivation For historical reasons, the `UUID` data type sorts by the *second half* of the value. This is unexpected and, in particular, hurts the performance of primary indexes built on `UUIDv7` columns, whose most significant bits are a timestamp: with sorting by the second half, primary-key analysis cannot prune granules by the timestamp. ## What this does `UUID2` stores the 128-bit value as a plain big-endian integer of the 16 canonical bytes, so that natural integer comparison of the underlying value matches the textual (lexicographic) order and the canonical byte order used by most other systems. It reuses the `UUID` column and `Field` representation (like `DateTime` reuses `UInt32`), so sorting is correct with no extra comparison code, and its binary/interchange serialization is the canonical big-endian byte order. - `UUID1` is an alias of the current `UUID` type. - A new setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) controls whether the bare name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` (`1`) or `UUID2` (`2`) at `CREATE`/`ALTER` time. The resolved concrete type is materialized into the stored table definition (including nested types such as `Array(UUID)`), so reads never depend on the session setting and existing tables are never rewritten. The default will be flipped to `2` in a later, separate change. - Conversions to/from `String`, `UInt128`, `FixedString(16)` and `UUID`, plus `toUUID2` / `toUUID2OrZero` / `toUUID2OrNull`. - Parity across functions (`hex`/`bin`, `reinterpretAs*`, `UUIDv7ToDateTime`, `UUIDToNum`, `empty`/`notEmpty`, `min`/`max`, hashing, `uniq`), formats (`RowBinary`, `Native`, `JSON`, `CSV`, `TSV`, `Arrow`, `Parquet`, `Avro`, `BSON`, `MsgPack`, `Protobuf`, `CapnProto`, `JSONExtract`) and storage (`generateRandom`, `bloom_filter` skip index). The `UUID` type is unchanged (verified: still sorts by second half, identical conversions, default `uuid_type_version = 1`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new data type `UUID2`, a variant of `UUID` that sorts by its textual (lexicographic) representation instead of by the second half of the value. The setting `uuid_type_version` (default `1`) selects whether the type name `UUID` resolves to `UUID` or `UUID2`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110084&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110084](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110084+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support per-authentication-method GRANTS clause in CREATE USER and ALTER USER
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117 Implements per-authentication-method grant limits, the first part of the linked issue: ```sql ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY 'WYmdFyas8PftrHbHQQo8' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table) ``` When a user logs in with such a method, the access rights of the session are the intersection of the user's access rights (including granted roles) with the listed elements. The clause never adds rights: a listed privilege that is not granted to the user stays unavailable. This provides a way to create tokens for applications: an additional credential with an expiration date and a limited set of grants, which is tied to the user — it is displayed in `query_log` and `processlist` as the user, stops working if the user is deleted, and is narrowed when the user loses grants. Details: - The clause is parsed after the per-method `VALID UNTIL`, works with `CREATE USER`, `ALTER USER [ADD] IDENTIFIED`, and `NOT IDENTIFIED`, is shown by `SHOW CREATE USER`, and persists through the SQL serialization of access entities (and therefore backups). Elements without a database name are bound to the current database when the query is interpreted. - The intersection erases all grant options (the clause cannot express them), so such sessions cannot `GRANT` anything. Role administration is denied entirely (fail-close), including per-role admin option. `EXECUTE AS`, `ALTER USER`, `CREATE USER` and similar escapes require the corresponding rights to be listed explicitly and granted to the user. - Reattaching to a named session (`session_id`) with a different credential re-applies the limit of the credential used by the new connection, so a limited credential cannot pick up the full rights of a session created by an unrestricted one. - The limit is captured at login: `ALTER USER` affects new sessions, not established ones (same as `VALID UNTIL`). - A new `auth_grants` column in `system.users` exposes the limit of each authentication method. - `ContextData`'s copy constructor now preserves `external_roles` and the new field: previously a recalculation of access rights on a copied context silently dropped external roles; for the new field that would mean silently widening the rights. - `EXECUTE AS <user> <statement>` now keeps the current database of the caller's session. `Context::setUser` sets the current database from the target user's `DEFAULT DATABASE`, so the wrapped statement used to be re-scoped and an unqualified table name resolved in a different database; the session form (`EXECUTE AS <user>` without a statement) already preserved it. Test `04907_execute_as_preserves_current_database` covers both forms. Known limitations (consistent with `VALID UNTIL` and external roles): the limit is not propagated to other nodes of a cluster in distributed queries or `ON CLUSTER` DDL (the query is checked on the initiator), and the clause is not available in `users.xml`. The `CREATE TOKEN` syntactic sugar and the separate grant for self-service `ADD IDENTIFIED` mentioned in the issue are left for a follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Authentication methods in `CREATE USER` and `ALTER USER ... ADD IDENTIFIED` support a `GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table, ...)` clause which limits the access rights of sessions authenticated with that method to the intersection with the listed grants. This allows using additional credentials as tokens for applications: `ALTER USER vasya ADD IDENTIFIED WITH password BY '...' VALID UNTIL '2026-12-31' GRANTS (SELECT ON db.table)`. Closes [#109117](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109117). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110144&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110144](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110144+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
