signals.title: Add the `default_session_user` server setting
signals.text: Adds a way to configure which user is assumed when a client connects without specifying a user name, instead of the hardcoded `default`. - A new server setting, `default_session_user` (default `default`), is applied when the user name is empty: an HTTP request without the `user` parameter and `X-ClickHouse-User` header (including Basic credentials with an empty username and a key without a user), a native protocol `Hello` packet with an empty user name (previously rejected, now accepted), MySQL and PostgreSQL handshakes with an empty user name, a gRPC query without `user_name`, an Arrow Flight call without an `authorization` header (or with Basic credentials with an empty user name), and the web terminal auth message without a user field. Setting the value to an empty string prohibits connections without a user name. HTTP handlers with a fixed user (the `user` key inside `handler` of an `http_handlers` rule, or the `user` key of a `prometheus` protocol) authenticate as their configured user and ignore the setting, including the empty reject mode. - Composable protocol endpoints (the `protocols` section) can override the setting per endpoint with a `default_session_user` key, so different listening ports can serve different anonymous users. The key is looked up from the endpoint's module through `impl` references, and the endpoint is restarted on config reload when the value changes. - Interserver connections never use the default session user: they identify themselves with a special marker instead of a user name and are authenticated by the cluster secret and the initial user. Configuring `default_session_user` on an `interserver` composable protocol is rejected as a configuration error. The `NativeProtocol.md` specification and the composable protocols documentation are updated accordingly. Covered by the new integration test `test_default_session_user` (all protocols including gRPC and Arrow Flight, per-endpoint overrides, the explicit reject mode, fixed-user handlers on an endpoint with the reject mode, and a two-node cluster with a secret verifying that remote queries still run as the initiating user). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `default_session_user` server setting: the user to authenticate as when a client connects without specifying a user name (previously hardcoded to `default`; the native, MySQL, and PostgreSQL protocols now accept an empty user name instead of rejecting it, and Arrow Flight honors the setting instead of its own hardcoded `default`). Composable protocol endpoints in the `protocols` section can override it per endpoint with a `default_session_user` key, so different listening ports can serve different anonymous users. Setting it to an empty string prohibits connections without a user name. Interserver connections never use the default session user. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110179&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110179](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110179+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Check access rights in EXPLAIN QUERY TREE and EXPLAIN SYNTAX
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78938 `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE` and `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` (in the analyzer) resolve the query and dump table metadata such as column names and types, but unlike `EXPLAIN PLAN` they do not build a query plan. The `SELECT` access check that the planner performs in `prepareBuildQueryPlanForTableExpression` was therefore skipped, so a user with no privileges could read the column names and data types (including `Enum` element lists) of tables they are not allowed to access, while `SELECT`, `EXPLAIN PLAN` and `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` are correctly rejected. This adds a `SELECT` access check for every table referenced anywhere in the query tree (including tables inside subqueries in expressions such as `WHERE x IN (SELECT ... FROM t)`). The check mirrors the planner: it validates access to the columns that are actually read, with the trivial-count fallback (access is granted if at least one column is accessible) for queries that read no specific column, e.g. `SELECT count() FROM t`. As a result, a user with a column-level grant sees the same behavior as for a plain `SELECT` (`EXPLAIN QUERY TREE SELECT granted_col FROM t` is allowed, `... other_col ...` is denied). `buildQueryTree` only builds the tree; table identifiers are bound to storages and columns are resolved by the query analysis pass. The check runs on the resolved tree: on `query_tree` directly when the passes already resolved it, or on a throwaway resolved copy otherwise (e.g. `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE run_passes = 0`, which intentionally dumps the unresolved tree, so the tree that gets dumped is unchanged). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE` and `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` not checking access rights on the referenced tables, which allowed a user without privileges to read table column names and data types. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110180&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110180](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110180+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support INSERT ... VALUES in the polyglot SQL dialect
signals.text: Enable `INSERT ... VALUES` with inline data in the polyglot SQL dialect (`dialect = 'polyglot'`). Previously, running e.g. `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3)` with `dialect = 'polyglot'` failed with `Multi-statement queries are not supported in polyglot dialect mode`. The underlying problem is that transpiling inside the parser cannot deliver inline data to the executor: the transpiled buffer is transient, and the executor overwrites `ASTInsertQuery::tail` with the external input stream, so the inline-data pointers (`data`/`end`) must reference a live query buffer. This transpiles the query up front instead of inside the parser: - The server (`executeQuery`) transpiles a foreign-dialect query to ClickHouse SQL before parsing, keeps the transpiled text alive on the query context, and parses it with the standard parser. Inline INSERT data then points into a live buffer and is processed by the normal machinery. `SET` queries are still parsed as-is so `dialect`/`polyglot_dialect` can always be changed back. - The client (`clickhouse-client`/`clickhouse-local`) parses a non-ClickHouse-dialect query into an AST — which, for a foreign dialect, means transpiling it locally only to drive client-side handling (statement classification, output format, INSERT detection) — but then sends the *original* query text verbatim, without splitting off inline data. The server performs the authoritative transpilation whose result is actually executed, so inline INSERT data lives in a server-owned buffer and survives parsing. The client-side transpilation is throwaway; note this means the transpiler must also be available on the client (a client built without `USE_POLYGLOT` fails locally with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`), and the client and server transpilers are assumed to agree — acceptable for this experimental dialect. Every parse-time setting the query was parsed under (`dialect`, `allow_experimental_polyglot_dialect`, `polyglot_dialect`, `allow_settings_after_format_in_insert`, `implicit_select`, and the parse limits `max_query_size`, `max_parser_depth`, `max_parser_backtracks`) is pinned in the per-query settings sent along with the verbatim text, so the query's own `SETTINGS` clause cannot change how the server reparses that same text (it still applies to the query's execution, and a `SET` still takes effect for subsequent queries). All changes are gated on the dialect, so ordinary ClickHouse INSERTs are unaffected. Validated over the HTTP interface, the native client, and `clickhouse-local` (multi-row and single-row `VALUES`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, and PostgreSQL literal transpilation such as `true`/`false`); `SET` passthrough and multi-statement rejection are preserved. External insert data combined with a foreign-dialect `INSERT` is rejected with `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` instead of being silently dropped, on both surfaces: the client rejects piped stdin and `INFILE` (it sends the query verbatim and cannot forward a data tail), and the server rejects a non-empty HTTP request body appended to a streaming `INSERT` (`POST /?query=INSERT ... &dialect=polyglot` with a body). A foreign-dialect `INSERT` is transpiled as a whole, so the body would go through neither the transpiler nor the `max_query_size` guard, mixing two parsing rules in one `INSERT`. An empty body still works, which is the normal way to run a polyglot `INSERT` over HTTP. Limitations (scoped, experimental): because a foreign-dialect query is transpiled as a whole (the transpiler rewrites the inline data too and cannot know where the SQL header ends without parsing the dialect), the inline `INSERT ... VALUES` data counts towards `max_query_size` — unlike a native ClickHouse `INSERT`, whose inline data is streamed and is not bounded by `max_query_size`. An oversized payload fails-close with a dedicated, actionable error rather than silently changing the `INSERT` size contract; increase `max_query_size` to submit larger inline payloads. Only `INSERT ... VALUES` inline data is transpilable by the bundled dialects. `INSERT ... FORMAT ...` is not: `FORMAT` is a ClickHouse-only extension, so a foreign-dialect parser rejects the query at the inline data that follows (empirically, `postgresql`/`mysql`/`sqlite`/`duckdb`/`snowflake`/`bigquery` all fail at the first data row after `FORMAT`; a hypothetical identity transpiler even drops the raw `FORMAT` payload rather than re-emitting it). A foreign-dialect `INSERT ... FORMAT` therefore fails cleanly with a syntax error and inserts nothing — like `EXPLAIN INSERT ... VALUES`, which is also not transpilable by the bundled dialects (rejected at the `VALUES` token). The server-owned transpiled buffer that carries the inline data is itself format-agnostic and would handle `FORMAT` data if a transpiler ever produced such a query; the parser also defensively clears the inline-data pointers of an `EXPLAIN`-wrapped `INSERT` — the same way the client unwraps it — so both forms are safe if a future transpiler supports them. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `INSERT ... VALUES` with inline data when using the experimental `polyglot` SQL dialect. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110321&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110321](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110321+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix reading `Arrow` files that validate the arbitrary bytes of unobservable slots
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111996 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111534 The Arrow specification leaves the value bytes of unobservable slots undefined: slots that are null at their own or an ancestor level (a struct's nulls do not have to be repeated in its children's validity), slot ranges no list offset references, and union child slots not selected by their row's type id. The native `Arrow` IPC reader ran value-level validation — the `Date32` range check, dictionary index bounds, `BinaryView` view checks, the raw-byte width sniff for `IPv6` and the big integers — over every slot before applying null maps, so spec-valid files failed to read. It also copied those undefined bytes into the result, so they surfaced as values whenever an ancestor null map is dropped, which is what reading a nullable struct as a plain `Tuple` does. ClickHouse produces such files itself: `Date32` arithmetic does not clamp the stored day number and `nullIf` keeps the original payload under the new null mask, so the writer stores an out-of-range day number under a null slot and the reader then refuses to read it back. ```sql INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('t.arrow', 'Arrow') SELECT nullIf(x, x) AS d FROM (SELECT toDate32('9999-12-31') + 100 AS x); SELECT * FROM file('t.arrow', 'Arrow'); ``` ``` Code: 321. DB::Exception: Arrow IPC date32 value 2932996 is out of the allowed Date32 range [-719528, 2932896] ... (VALUE_IS_OUT_OF_RANGE_OF_DATA_TYPE) -- but should work fine ``` The same failure occurs one level deeper with a nullable struct read as `Nullable(Tuple)` (with `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type`): the child of a NULL struct row can hold garbage while its own validity marks it valid, so only the composed ancestor validity reveals the value is unobservable. Both reading paths are now driven by one composed invisible-rows mask: value-level validation skips those rows, and every leaf decodes them as the type default instead of copying the undefined bytes — including the `fixed_size_binary` leaves the ClickHouse writer uses for `UUID`, `IPv6` and the 128/256-bit integers, and the self-describing Arrow `uuid` extension type. `04513` covers the crafted `pyarrow` files where the garbage is reachable only through composed visibility; `04512` covers the ClickHouse round trip. Two notes on scope: - The first version of this pull request fixed the Apache Arrow library reader as well. That reader was removed from the `Arrow` formats in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111996, so those changes are gone and `input_format_arrow_use_native_reader` no longer selects anything. `ArrowColumnToCHColumn` still validates the bytes of null slots the same way, but it is now reachable only through `ArrowFlight` and DeltaLake, so that is left for a separate change with its own coverage. - Reading a nullable struct as a plain `Tuple` drops the struct null map, and the NULL row's element values now read as type defaults rather than as the payload the producer left behind — `04493` records that (`ORC`, whose null map does reach the tuple elements, shows `NULL`s for the same file, so the defaults are the closer of the two answers). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading `Arrow` and `ArrowStream` files that carry arbitrary bytes in unobservable slots: values hidden by null rows (at their own or an ancestor level), unreferenced list ranges and unselected union children are no longer validated and no longer surface as values, but decode as type defaults. Previously such spec-valid files could fail with errors like `VALUE_IS_OUT_OF_RANGE_OF_DATA_TYPE`, including files written by ClickHouse itself. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110531&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110531](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110531+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add support for S3Queue mode='exclusive'
signals.text: This patch adds a third mode to the S3Queue engine: `exclusive` mode turns off all file tracking and synchronization in ZooKeeper. S3 file processing will be tracked only locally via in-memory structures of this ClickHouse server process. This mode is meant to support high-throughput, high-volume ingestion scenarios. In our particular case, we have a minio instance on each of our ClickHouse nodes, with S3Queue pointing to 127.0.0.1. Exclusive mode allows ingesting many terabytes of data per day while avoid file framing boundary and buffering issues. (S3 multipart uploads solve the buffering issue for ingestion clients.) We have been running our ClickHouse cluster with these patches for many years with no issues. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds support for mode='exclusive' in S3Queue engine, for high-throughput and self-hosted scenarios. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110552&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110552](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110552+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix logical error in optimize_or_like_chain with aggregate/window function on LIKE LHS
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error (`Function node with name '...' is not resolved as ordinary function`) that could occur with `optimize_or_like_chain` enabled when an aggregate or window function appeared on the left-hand side of a `LIKE`/`ILIKE`/`match` inside an `OR` chain. ### Description Found by the BuzzHouse fuzzer (STID 3477-117d) on [this CI run](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107567&sha=16ccfffe167f14e51996ce4ec16384f92e4d15d0&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29). Not caused by that PR — it is a trunk analyzer bug the fuzzer happened to surface there. `isExpressionNonDeterministic` in `ConvertOrLikeChainPass` guarded its `getFunctionOrThrow()` call with `FunctionNode::isResolved()`. `isResolved()` returns true for aggregate and window functions too (it only checks that the function pointer is set), but `getFunctionOrThrow()` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` when the function kind is not `ORDINARY`. So a resolved aggregate (e.g. `count()`) or window function nested under a `LIKE` argument in an `OR` chain tripped the assertion — an exception in release builds, an abort in debug/sanitizer builds. Fix: guard with `isOrdinaryFunction()` instead, matching the existing correct guard in `PlannerExpressionAnalysis`. Aggregate/window functions are never non-deterministic-in-scope-of-query at this point, so recursing into their children is sufficient. Minimal reproducer (aborts before the fix on a debug build): ```sql SET optimize_or_like_chain = 1; SELECT toString(count()) LIKE '%1%' OR toString(count()) LIKE '%2%' FROM numbers(3); ``` Covered by `tests/queries/0_stateless/04545_optimize_or_like_chain_aggregate_lhs.sql` (aggregate and window variants, plus an ordinary-function control that must still collapse). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110641&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110641](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110641+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add IPv4/IPv6 auto-inference for JSON shared data insertion
signals.text: Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110761 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `input_format_try_infer_ipv4` and `input_format_try_infer_ipv6` settings (both disabled by default) that allow ClickHouse to automatically infer `IPv4`/`IPv6` types from string fields during schema inference for text formats, following the same pattern as `input_format_try_infer_dates`. --- ## What does this PR do? Adds two new opt-in format settings that allow ClickHouse to automatically infer `IPv4`/`IPv6` types from string values during schema inference for text formats, following the same pattern as the existing `input_format_try_infer_dates` / `input_format_try_infer_datetimes` settings. ## New settings | Setting | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `input_format_try_infer_ipv4` | `false` | Infer `IPv4` from strings matching IPv4 address format | | `input_format_try_infer_ipv6` | `false` | Infer `IPv6` from strings matching IPv6 address format | ## How it works In `insertIntoSharedData` (`JSONExtractTree.cpp`), after the existing Date/DateTime inference chain, two new blocks attempt to parse the string as IPv4/IPv6 using the already-existing `IPv4Node::tryParse` / `IPv6Node::tryParse` methods. On a match, the value is encoded with its native binary type (`BinaryTypeIndex::IPv4`/`IPv6`) instead of falling back to `String`. ## Storage benefit | Value | As String | As IPv4 | |---|---|---| | `"192.168.100.200"` | 15 bytes | 4 bytes | | `"10.0.0.1"` | 8 bytes | 4 bytes | <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110766&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110766](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110766+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: MaterializedPostgreSQL: coordinated Replicated/Shared nested tables for HA
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/47655 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` can now create its nested tables as `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree`/`SharedReplacingMergeTree` for high availability, using a new Keeper-based single-active-worker coordination of the replication slot. Controlled by the new settings `materialized_postgresql_table_engine`, `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and `materialized_postgresql_replica_name`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The three new settings and the coordinated-failover mechanism are documented in the embedded `Documentation` blocks of `DatabaseMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp` and `StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp`, from which the published engine pages are generated. --- ## Problem The nested tables that `MaterializedPostgreSQL` auto-creates were hardcoded to plain `ReplacingMergeTree` ([`StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/src/Storages/PostgreSQL/StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp)), so the engine could not be made highly available (issue #47655). Simply allowing `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` is unsafe on its own: a PostgreSQL logical replication slot permits only **one** active consuming session, so two ClickHouse replicas consuming the same slot would race on `pg_replication_slot_advance` and silently drop WAL. ## Solution Allow the nested engine to be `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` / `SharedReplacingMergeTree`, **gated** behind a new Keeper-based coordination that elects exactly one active worker — the same pattern used by `S3Queue`, the Keeper-coordinated `Kafka` engine and refreshable materialized views: - The active worker holds an ephemeral `/leader` node under `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and is the only replica that consumes the slot. - Standby replicas create the nested tables as replicas of the same replicated tree and receive data (including the initial snapshot) through ClickHouse replication, without touching the slot. - When the active worker's Keeper session ends, a standby wins `/leader` and resumes consuming from the slot's `confirmed_flush_lsn` — no reload, no duplication. PostgreSQL's own single-active-session rule on the slot is the ultimate backstop against double-advance during a handover. A graceful stop of the active worker (`DETACH`, a non-last `DROP`, server shutdown) does not wait for that: it releases `/leader` with a **confirmed** removal - the node lives under the server's shared Keeper session, which outlives the database, and nothing re-enters the election on that replica after shutdown, so an unconfirmed (lost-response) removal is resolved on the spot with owner- and version-checked re-checks instead of leaving a stale node that would keep every peer on standby for as long as that session lives. - The slot and the publication are **shared state**, and the whole lifecycle honors that: - A durable `snapshot_completed` marker in Keeper records that the initial snapshot loaded every table. A new leader may resume from `confirmed_flush_lsn` only when the marker exists; otherwise the previous worker died mid-snapshot, and the new one **clears the nested tables**, drops the slot and redoes the snapshot from scratch, so pre-slot rows cannot be lost. Clearing first is required for correctness: a row the dead worker had copied and that PostgreSQL then `DELETE`d has no counterpart in the new snapshot, so without a clear the stale copy would survive (a `ReplacingMergeTree` collapses duplicate keys by `_version` but never turns a now-absent row into a tombstone). The marker is fenced on the live leadership session: it is written through the Keeper session that backs `/leader` (in a multi-request with a check on `/leader`), the snapshot load aborts as soon as that session is lost, and a consumer is never started over a dead leadership session - so a worker deposed mid-snapshot can never mask its successor's replacement snapshot with a stale marker. The redo of the snapshot is fenced the same way: a worker whose leadership session is no longer alive aborts before truncating the nested tables (re-checked per table) and before dropping or recreating the shared slot, so a deposed worker cannot wipe the tables its successor has already reloaded or discard the slot the successor just created. A startup attempt that fails before a consumer got running (most importantly, a coordinated single-table engine whose one snapshot load failed) aborts instead of starting a consumer with nothing to apply - which would advance the shared slot's `confirmed_flush_lsn` while applying no rows - and releases the leadership so a healthy peer can take over. That release never leaves a stale leadership claim behind: a `remove` of `/leader` that could not be confirmed does not prove the node survived, so the claim is dropped in either case, and a leader node this replica created under the current Keeper session but no longer tracks is recognized (by its stored replica name and its owning session) and removed on its next election attempt - a replica never keeps acting as the active worker, or touches the shared slot and snapshot state, without provably holding `/leader`. - A second coordinated `CREATE DATABASE` adopts an existing publication instead of dropping it from under the active worker. - Every replica registers itself under `<keeper_path>/replicas`; dropping the database on one replica keeps the shared slot/publication for the others, and only dropping the last replica removes them from PostgreSQL (fail-close when Keeper is unavailable). The last-replica decision is fenced on the shared `replicas` node so concurrent `DROP DATABASE` on different replicas cannot both act as last, it removes the replica's registration only atomically with winning that fence - a replica that is not the last one keeps its registration until its local nested tables are actually gone, so even a server killed mid-drop stays visible to every later last-replica check - and it runs even for a `DROP DATABASE` issued immediately after a restart, before the background startup task has rebuilt the replication handler. - Recreating a coordinated database right after dropping it is safe: the nested tables are dropped without the delayed-drop window (so their shared Keeper subtrees do not outlive the `DROP DATABASE`), the snapshot insert is never silently deduplicated against block hashes surviving from a previous incarnation of the shared table, a publication leaked by an incompletely dropped setup (no surviving coordination state in Keeper) is dropped by a fresh `CREATE` instead of silently adopted with its stale table set, and a refused (failed) drop never leaves the replica silently dead: every refusable Keeper step of the pre-data teardown runs before the replica's consumer is stopped, and if the drop still fails after that point - the last replica's removal of the shared coordination nodes, or the deletion of this replica's own local nested tables (e.g. Keeper disappearing while a nested replicated table removes its own Keeper metadata) - replication is rebuilt in the background - for the database engine through a new generic `IDatabase::onDropDatabaseFailed` hook that discards the stopped handler and re-runs the startup task, for the single-table engine by re-arming the handler's retrying startup path - so the replica rejoins the setup once Keeper is reachable again. - All replicas of one coordinated setup must agree on the naming-affecting settings (`materialized_postgresql_table_engine`, `materialized_postgresql_schema`, `materialized_postgresql_schema_list`, `materialized_postgresql_tables_list_with_schema`) and must replicate the same PostgreSQL source — the same source database and, for the single-table engine, the same source table (so a single-table engine and a database engine can never share one keeper path): these determine how the ClickHouse names of the shared nested tables and the names of the shared slot and publication are derived. The first replica publishes a canonical fingerprint of them at `<keeper_path>/naming`; a disagreeing replica is rejected — synchronously at `CREATE` time when the setup already exists in Keeper, and fail-close at startup before it registers itself — instead of adopting the same publication yet building a disjoint replicated tree that never receives the other replicas' data. - The shared **table set** is fenced the same way, *before* any nested table is built: the first replica publishes its derived set at `<keeper_path>/table_set`, and a replica whose derived set differs is refused fail-close (the shared publication - from which joining replicas later derive their set - is only created by the elected active worker, so without this fence two fresh replicas starting concurrently could silently build diverging nested tables on one keeper path). The refusal converges by itself once the publication exists, because joining replicas then derive their set from the publication, which was created from the fenced set. - The last-replica teardown is generation-safe: winning the last-replica fence atomically (in one Keeper multi-request) creates an ownership token at `<keeper_path>/teardown`, which is removed only after the shared PostgreSQL slot/publication have actually been dropped. While the token exists, a fresh coordinated `CREATE` on the same keeper path is rejected (synchronously by validation and fail-close at startup), so the pending by-name drops can never delete a new setup's freshly created slot/publication. A replica recovering its own refused drop reclaims its own token, and a retried drop resumes its earlier teardown instead of leaking the slot. - Per-table and database-wide destructive changes are refused (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`) in coordinated mode: `ATTACH TABLE` / `DETACH TABLE PERMANENTLY` / `DROP TABLE` / `RENAME TABLE` / `EXCHANGE TABLES`, and a database-wide `TRUNCATE DATABASE` / `TRUNCATE ALL TABLES FROM`. Each would only change the local replica (or wipe its copy of the shared replicated data) while the shared publication, tables list, slot/snapshot marker and peer replicas keep the old state, silently diverging the replicas. Recreate the database with an updated `materialized_postgresql_tables_list` instead. New settings (both the database engine and the single-table engine): | Setting | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `materialized_postgresql_table_engine` | `ReplacingMergeTree` | `ReplacingMergeTree` / `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` / `SharedReplacingMergeTree` | | `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` | (empty) | opt-in gate that enables coordination; supports the `{shard}` macro; a per-replica/per-server macro (`{replica}`/`{server_uuid}`, including reached through a config macro) is rejected at `CREATE` time, and so is `{uuid}` unless the DDL carries the UUID (`ON CLUSTER`, a table inside a `Replicated` database, or an explicit `UUID '...'` clause) so that it is provably identical on every replica, and so is a misspelled/unsupported macro (in this path or in `materialized_postgresql_replica_name`) — both settings are macro-expanded during validation exactly as the handler expands them later | | `materialized_postgresql_replica_name` | `{replica}` | replica identity for coordination and the nested replicated engine; must resolve to a distinct value on every replica, which is enforced: the `/replicas/<name>` registration node stores the owning replica's identity, and a name already registered by another replica is rejected (synchronously at `CREATE` time when the registration is already visible); it must also resolve to a single Keeper node name (empty or containing `/` is rejected, since a nested path under `/replicas` would break the last-replica bookkeeping); together with `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` it forms the coordination identity of the replica, which is treated as immutable once the setup exists: a configuration-only change of a macro these settings expand through is refused at startup, while a `DROP` tears down the identity persisted in the nested tables; a name change made in the one window where the registration already exists while no nested table does yet is recovered from the registration itself, which stores an owner identity no macro feeds into, so the stale registration is removed (on startup and on drop) instead of keeping `<keeper_path>/replicas` non-empty forever and stopping every future drop from becoming the last-replica drop | The replicated/shared engines require `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and vice versa (coordination with a plain `ReplacingMergeTree` would leave the standbys without data), and coordination is mutually exclusive with `materialized_postgresql_use_unique_replication_consumer_identifier` (which gives each replica its own slot). Coordination also requires Keeper/ZooKeeper to be configured on the server: a coordinated `CREATE DATABASE` on a server with no Keeper is rejected synchronously at `CREATE` time rather than being accepted and left retrying in the background. All of this validation also applies to a user `ATTACH DATABASE` / `ATTACH TABLE` that spells out the full definition - it is fresh user input, exactly like a `CREATE`; only replaying an already-persisted definition (server startup, and the short `ATTACH` syntax, which re-reads the stored definition) is exempt. Behaviour is unchanged when coordination is not configured. ## Testing - Added integration test `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_coordination.py`: convergence + single leader, leader failover with no data loss/duplication, rejoin, takeover before snapshot completion redoes the snapshot without losing pre-slot rows, a mid-snapshot takeover after a row is deleted in PostgreSQL drops the stale copy (`test_takeover_after_partial_snapshot_drops_stale_deleted_rows`), a second `CREATE` adopts the publication, `ATTACH`/`DETACH`/`DROP`/`RENAME`/`EXCHANGE`/`TRUNCATE` rejection, shared Added `test_plain_single_table_engine_refused_drop_recovers` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_3.py`: the plain (non-coordinated) single-table engine now drops its local nested table before the authoritative PostgreSQL teardown, so a refused (thrown) nested-table drop keeps the replication slot/publication and re-arms the handler to resume from the existing slot, instead of leaving the table mounted but dead with the PostgreSQL objects already removed. - Added `test_rename_and_exchange_table_are_rejected`, `test_database_wide_truncate_is_rejected` and `test_drop_of_individual_table_is_rejected` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_1.py`: `RENAME TABLE` / `EXCHANGE TABLES`, a database-wide `TRUNCATE`, and a `DROP` / `TRUNCATE` of an individual table are now also rejected for a plain (non-coordinated) `MaterializedPostgreSQL` database, which previously fell through to the generic `Atomic` DDL and silently diverged the local tables from the replication state (a dropped table stayed in `materialized_postgresql_tables_list` and in the publication, so the consumer marked it skipped while the slot kept advancing); `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` remains the supported removal path. - Added `test_count_does_not_include_deleted_rows` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_1.py`: `SELECT count()` reads the cheapest column of the nested table - the one-byte `_sign` column itself - and the wrapped read used to skip its `_sign = 1` filter whenever the sign column was among the requested columns, so a count included the durable tombstones a PostgreSQL `DELETE` leaves in the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` table and disagreed with `SELECT *`. The filter is now applied unconditionally (an explicit read of `_sign` is filtered the same way). - Added `test_failed_attach_rolls_back_setting_and_table` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_2.py`: a failed `ATTACH TABLE` now rolls back the already persisted `materialized_postgresql_tables_list` extension and the published table wrapper together with the nested table, so the database does not keep claiming a table is attached that never joined the publication; a retry starts from a clean state. - Added `test_failed_attach_with_failed_cleanup_keeps_table_attached` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_2.py`: when the cleanup of a failed `ATTACH TABLE` cannot drop the nested table it created either, the attach deliberately stays visible instead of leaving an invisible leftover that every retry would collide with, and `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` followed by a retried `ATTACH TABLE` recovers it. - Added `test_attached_table_can_be_detached_permanently` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_2.py`: a table added by `ATTACH TABLE` gets a freshly built wrapper that never went through the database's replication startup, so it has to be marked as belonging to an already started database - otherwise the startup-window guard refuses every later `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` of it and the supported attach/detach round trip is broken. - Added `test_failed_detach_rolls_back_and_table_keeps_replicating` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_1.py`: a `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` whose local nested-table drop throws is now rolled back completely - the table is re-added to replication through a fresh snapshot and the persisted `materialized_postgresql_tables_list` is restored - so the table keeps replicating and the `DETACH` can simply be retried, instead of stranding a live nested table outside the logical database. - Added `test_detach_database_and_reattach` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_1.py`: `DETACH DATABASE` used to fail half-way (the generic detach path had already stopped replication when the per-table walk hit the unconditional `DETACH TABLE not allowed` guard), leaving the database mounted but no longer replicating. The internal walk is now let through, so `DETACH DATABASE` unmounts the database cleanly and `ATTACH DATABASE` resumes replication, catching up on changes made while it was detached. - Added `test_detach_permanently_of_last_table_is_rejected` to `test_postgresql_replica_database_engine/test_1.py`: detaching the last replicated table would persist an empty `materialized_postgresql_tables_list`, and an empty list does not mean "replicate no tables" - the table set would be re-derived from the current PostgreSQL schema on the next startup, so the detach would not stick. It is now refused up front, leaving the table replicating. - Verified end-to-end against a locally built binary with two real `clickhouse-server` nodes + `clickhouse-keeper` + PostgreSQL (`wal_level=logical`): coordinated `CREATE DATABASE` builds the `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` nested tables with correctly macro-expanded per-table Keeper paths; snapshot + ongoing INSERT/UPDATE are consumed by the single leader; a standby serves the same data via ClickHouse replication; killing the leader triggers takeover (~8s) that resumes consumption with matching row/key counts (no loss, no duplication); and a restarted node rejoins as a standby without stealing leadership. Note: `SharedReplacingMergeTree` is only available in ClickHouse Cloud; open-source runs are covered with `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110886&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110886](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110886+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix LOGICAL_ERROR in OPTIMIZE ... DRY RUN racing a concurrent merge
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107114 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114399 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception (`Temporary part ... already added`) when `OPTIMIZE ... DRY RUN` runs concurrently with a real merge, or with another `DRY RUN`, on the same parts. ### Description `MergeTreeData::optimizeDryRun` executes a real `MergeTask` but, unlike the real optimize/merge paths, takes no `CurrentlyMergingPartsTagger` and no merge lock, so it never registers its source parts as "being merged". A concurrent real merge on the same parts computes the same result part name and reserves the same `tmp_merge_<result>` directory. The second reservation trips `TemporaryParts::add` -> `LOGICAL_ERROR "Temporary part ... already added"`, aborting the server on debug and sanitizer builds. Seen on 17 unrelated PRs over the 30 days to 2026-08-11 (CIDB `default.checks`, 17 rows / 17 distinct PRs), never on master. The dry-run part is throwaway, so its directory need not be named after the result part. It is now `tmp_merge_dry_run_<uuid>`, making the collision impossible on both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree`. A UUID rather than a counter, because the directory can live on storage shared with other servers, where a process-local counter restarts and repeats itself. Leaving the part name out also avoids a length trap: appending a token to it can exceed the 255-byte filename limit while the real merge of the same parts still succeeds. Part names are not length-capped (an all-integral partition key spells its values out, so ten `Int64` fields plus an `IPv4` reach 226 bytes) and `MergeTree` prepends `delete_tmp_` before removal, leaving 8 bytes. The new name has a fixed size. It is never parsed back into a part name and still starts with `tmp_merge_`, which the cleaner and the startup skip logic select by. Only a `dry_run_` suffix takes the new path, so top-level and projection merges keep byte-identical names. Not a duplicate of the `DRY RUN` fix linked above (rows_sources under a soft timeout). Tracking issue: #114399. Test `03823_optimize_dry_run_merge_race` races two `DRY RUN`s on the same parts via a new failpoint pausing after the directory is reserved, at part-name lengths 7, 9 and 226, asserting the real merge succeeds at 226 and each `DRY RUN` really merged. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110916&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110916](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110916+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Promote exponentialTimeDecayed window-functions to aggregate-functions
signals.text: ## Motivation `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` already exist and are documented as aggregate functions, but their current implementation is a special window-function implementation in `WindowTransform`. They do not provide mergeable aggregate states that can be persisted and combined with aggregate combinators such as `-State` and `-Merge`. This prevents incremental time-decayed aggregation in engines such as `AggregatingMergeTree`: data has to be evaluated through the window path instead of being aggregated independently in multiple batches and merged later. This PR adds regular, mergeable aggregate implementations for those three names while preserving the existing window implementation and its behavior. ## What changes For the regular aggregate form, each state keeps the weighted sum and sum of weights at the greatest timestamp observed by that state, plus that timestamp. When a row or another state has an older anchor, it is moved to the newer anchor with: `exp((older_time - newer_time) / decay_length)` The existing semantics are unchanged: `decay_length` is the interval after which a contribution has weight `1/e`. It is not a half-life. With the default `exponential_time_decay_aggregate_function_calculation_budget = 0`, the state representation makes independently built states mergeable with the same calculation. Input rows do not need to be timestamp ordered, and different row orders and batch distributions produce the same mathematical result subject to normal `Float64` rounding. A positive calculation budget opts into approximate aggregation using calculation index timestamps. For sums, the index is the time when the absolute contribution or state reaches unit magnitude; counts use the corresponding total-weight index; averages consider both numerator and denominator indexes. A state more than the configured number of decay lengths behind the dominant state is discarded before evaluating `exp`. This makes the cutoff depend on remaining significance rather than source age. Approximate results near the cutoff can depend on row order or merge grouping, and signed sums that nearly cancel can have larger relative error. The aggregate forms accept numeric timestamps, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64`. ### Finalized decaying values The sum and count aggregate forms return the experimental parameterized type: `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` The decay length is part of the type. Its tuple-compatible storage is canonicalized as `(sign, signed_unit_time, decay_length)`, where `unit_time = anchor_time + decay_length * ln(abs(value))` is the timestamp at which the curve has unit magnitude and `signed_unit_time = sign * unit_time`. Zero has the canonical form `(0, 0, decay_length)`. This representation makes native sorting and relative comparisons match the curve values at any common timestamp for values with the same decay length. Comparisons across different decay lengths are rejected. The redundant decay-length marker is checked against the type parameter when a value is evaluated or combined, preventing incompatible values from being silently mixed through layout-compatible custom-tuple paths. Values can be constructed/aggregated with: `exponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)(value, time)` A finalized decaying value can be aggregated again without repeating the decay length: `exponentialTimeDecayedSum(decaying_value)` When the input is `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)`, the decay length is inferred from its type and the result has the same parameterized type. This gives the closure property required by `SimpleAggregateFunction`, so it can be stored directly in `AggregatingMergeTree`: ```sql CREATE TABLE decaying ( key UInt64, value SimpleAggregateFunction( exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(60)) ) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree ORDER BY key; ``` The scalar helpers are: - `exponentialTimeDecayingValueAt(value, target_time)` — evaluate the same exponential curve before, at, or after its anchor, including at `now()` / `now64()`; - `exponentialTimeDecayingDecayLength(value)` — read the decay length encoded in the type; - `exponentialTimeDecayingAdd(a, b)` — combine two values at their greatest anchor. The `+` operator uses the same addition logic for two decaying values. Different decay lengths are rejected. `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg` continues to return `Float64`. All new regular-aggregate and decaying-value behavior is experimental and disabled by default behind `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. ## Effect on the existing window functions The existing window-function implementation remains in place. Window calls continue to use the previous frame-based implementation, retain their `Float64` result, and do not require `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. This PR also corrects the function documentation to consistently call the parameter `decay_length` and describe the existing `1/e` decay semantics. ## Correctness and tests Stateless tests cover: - regular aggregation and `-State` / `-Merge`; - direct aggregation of finalized `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` values; - direct `SimpleAggregateFunction(exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length))` storage and merging in `AggregatingMergeTree`; - different input orders and batch distributions, including reproducibly generated randomized inputs; - numeric, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` time arguments; - the experimental setting in enabled and disabled forms; - forward and backward value evaluation, addition, decay-length lookup, and rejection of inconsistent/mixed decay lengths; - native sorting and all relative comparison operators, including negative, zero, and positive values; - exact-default, bounded-cutoff, and state-merge calculation-budget behavior; - signed values, empty input, nullable paths, canonical reconstruction, and large-time decay/underflow cases. The implementation uses `Float64` accumulation. As with other floating-point reductions, large signed values that nearly cancel can expose order/grouping-dependent rounding. Stronger reproducibility for that case is intentionally left for a separate improvement if feedback shows it is important in practice. ## Benchmark status There are no end-to-end ClickHouse benchmark results yet. The benchmark already posted in the PR discussion is a standalone C++ microbenchmark of the decay formulas. It showed the expected benefit from avoiding redundant `exp` evaluations in the merge/value paths, but it excludes ClickHouse aggregation, column access, serialization, scheduling, and `AggregatingMergeTree` overhead and therefore is not evidence of end-to-end query throughput. An end-to-end benchmark, preferably a ClickHouse performance test covering state creation and state merging, is still pending. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental mergeable `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` aggregate forms, including a parameterized decaying-value type that can be stored directly with `SimpleAggregateFunction` in `AggregatingMergeTree`, while preserving the existing window-function behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110934&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110934](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110934+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: perf(native-proto): batch protocol messages by default
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Native protocol: Make batching protocol messages default and `sync()` api to ship immediately. This enables to send the end-of-query message sequence like (profile info, progress, profile events, end-of-stream, …) as one socket write instead of one packet per message. Removes a full round-trip of latency per query for clients on high-latency links whose connections idle between queries. ### Background and Rationale NOTE: **This is driven by one of the customer (low-latency system). Saw this additional RTT and saw latency spike. Their setup is egress is 30 ms DELAY from client -> server (RTT). They notice additional RTT between client and server.** The native protocol runs with `TCP_NODELAY`, so every buffer flush becomes its own small TCP packet. At the end of every query the server sends a burst of tiny messages back-to-back (profile info, progress, profile events, an empty block, logs, end-of-stream). Flushed one at a time, each takes a slot in the TCP congestion window. That is usually invisible, but not always. After a connection sits idle between queries, Linux resets the congestion window back to the route's `initcwnd` (`net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle`). If the end-of-query burst is longer than that window, the server has to stop and wait for an ACK before sending the rest (a full extra round trip). On a high-latency link this shows up as roughly 2x query latency for clients that idle between queries, which is exactly what a customer hit. The fix groups the whole end-of-query suffix into a single socket write instead of one write per message, so the burst fits in one flight. A `GroupedMessagesGuard` (see `src/Server/TCPHandler.h`) accumulates the messages and flushes once at end-of-stream. This covers every path that emits the suffix: the pulling `SELECT` path, the synchronous and asynchronous `INSERT` epilogues, and the completed-pipeline branch. Tested with an integration suite (`test_native_protocol_grouped_writes`) that counts the server's socket writes per query via the `NetworkSendCalls` profile event, plus an end-to-end latency test over a simulated 500ms-RTT link with a small `initcwnd`. ### See it in action You can use [Go program](https://gist.github.com/kavirajk/62dfcc661ba004cb09f5f59ea5d52750) with following environment setup (simulating customer setup) to reproduce the latency spike (additional RTT) #### Setup (Linux) ```bash # A private network stack named "chsrv" for the server process. sudo ip netns add chsrv # A virtual cable. One end (veth-host) stays on your machine; the other (veth-ch) # is pushed into the namespace. Traffic between them really crosses this "cable" # (two local IPs WITHOUT a namespace would short-circuit over loopback - that's # why the namespace is needed at all). sudo ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-ch sudo ip link set veth-ch netns chsrv # Addresses: your side is 10.99.0.1, the server side is 10.99.0.2. MTU stays 1500, # so segment sizes behave like a real network (loopback's 64KB MTU would not). sudo ip addr add 10.99.0.1/24 dev veth-host sudo ip link set veth-host up sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip addr add 10.99.0.2/24 dev veth-ch sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip link set veth-ch up sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip link set lo up # The fake WAN: delay every packet leaving the server by 32ms => client-observed # RTT = 32ms. (Requires the sch_netem kernel module - loads automatically now # that your kernel and /lib/modules match.) sudo ip netns exec chsrv tc qdisc add dev veth-ch root netem delay 32ms # THE LEVER: the server's initial congestion window, as a route metric. # 10 is the Linux default; 8 reproduces the customer; 4 is pathological. sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip route change 10.99.0.0/24 dev veth-ch \ proto kernel scope link src 10.99.0.2 initcwnd 8 ``` Validate the 30ms egress delay by a ping ```bash ping -c 3 10.99.0.2 ``` You should see ~30 ms ```bash PING 10.99.0.2 (10.99.0.2) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=4 ttl=64 time=32.2 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=5 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms ``` #### Performance issue with CH 26.3 1. Run the 26.3 CH server (without the patch) ```bash mkdir -p /tmp/chdata cd ~/chbin wget https://builds.clickhouse.com/26.3/amd64/clickhouse sudo ip netns exec chsrv sudo -u "$USER" \ ./clickhouse server -- --listen_host=0.0.0.0 --path=/tmp/chdata/ ``` 2. Create the dataset ```bash ./clickhouse client --host 10.99.0.2 -q \ "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS benchmark_test (id UInt64) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY id" ./clickhouse client --host 10.99.0.2 -q \ "INSERT INTO benchmark_test SELECT number FROM numbers(939)" ``` 3. Run the Go script to see the latency ``` # save the gist as main.go, then: go mod init repro && go get github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-go/v2 go run . addr=10.99.0.2:9000 sleep=2s profile_events=true query: SELECT max(id) FROM benchmark_test query 1: first_row= 34.99ms eos= 67.26ms tail= 32.27ms (rows=1) query 2: first_row= 34.79ms eos= 65.98ms tail= 31.20ms (rows=1) query 3: first_row= 34.80ms eos= 66.21ms tail= 31.41ms (rows=1) query 4: first_row= 77.76ms eos= 108.90ms tail= 31.14ms (rows=1) query 5: first_row= 34.25ms eos= 65.79ms tail= 31.54ms (rows=1) ``` #### Performance fix with this PR 1. Run the binary from this PR (with patch) ```bash mkdir -p /tmp/chdata-patched cd ~/src/clickhouse/build/programs/ sudo ip netns exec chsrv sudo -u "$USER" \ ./clickhouse server -- --listen_host=0.0.0.0 --path=/tmp/chdata-pathced/ ``` 2. Run the Go script to see the latency ``` # save the gist as main.go, then: go mod init repro && go get github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-go/v2 go run . addr=10.99.0.2:9000 sleep=2s profile_events=true query: SELECT max(id) FROM benchmark_test query 1: first_row= 34.53ms eos= 35.65ms tail= 1.12ms (rows=1) query 2: first_row= 34.79ms eos= 35.58ms tail= 0.79ms (rows=1) query 3: first_row= 35.23ms eos= 36.12ms tail= 0.90ms (rows=1) query 4: first_row= 34.72ms eos= 35.95ms tail= 1.23ms (rows=1) query 5: first_row= 34.98ms eos= 36.26ms tail= 1.27ms (rows=1) ``` You see the tail latency goes away (no extra ~30ms) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111034&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111034](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111034+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Lower KeeperTCPHandler 'Client has not sent any data' log from warning to info
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/18005 `KeeperTCPHandler` logs `Client has not sent any data` at `LOG_WARNING` when a connection is opened but no data is received (the `in->eof()` branch). The same message in the server's `TCPHandler` was lowered from warning to info in #18005, but `KeeperTCPHandler` — a separate copy of the same pattern — was never updated, so it still logs at warning. Any TCP health check against the Keeper client port trips this on every probe. In particular, the ClickHouse Keeper operator's default `tcpSocket` liveness probe opens and closes a connection to the client port every few seconds, producing a steady stream of warning-level lines. This brings `KeeperTCPHandler` in line with `TCPHandler`. The nearby `LOG_WARNING` for a genuine protocol-header read error is intentionally left unchanged. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ClickHouse Keeper now logs the "Client has not sent any data" event at `Information` level instead of `Warning`, matching the server's TCP handler. signals.title: Refactor columns deserialization to avoid all assumeMutable calls, simplify the substreams cache, and remove rows_offset
signals.text: PR #109105 replaced `assumeMutable` with `IColumn::mutate` in the some pars of the deserialization code. When a column is shared via the substreams cache, `IColumn::mutate` clones the whole accumulated column, giving O(rows × granules) cost and a 3–4× deserialization slowdown. Rework the deserialize path so it never clones: - `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams` and its helpers take `IColumn &` instead of `ColumnPtr &`. - The substreams cache never shares a `ColumnPtr`; consumers copy the current range out via `insertRangeFrom`. - `assumeMutable`/`IColumn::mutate`/`const_cast` are removed from the deserialize paths; mutable children come from non-const accessors. - Cache-shared members are dropped from the `Deserialize*State` structs. - The MergeTree reader stack reads into `MutableColumns`. Additionally, remove `rows_offset` from the deserialization API. `rows_offset` (the number of leading rows to skip while deserializing a range) is provably always `0` for every caller, so it is dropped from `deserializeBinaryBulkWithMultipleStreams`, `deserializeBinaryBulk` and all their helpers. This deletes the read-side skip machinery: - the skip loops / `istr.ignore(size * rows_offset)` seeks; - the `Map` bucketed reorder-with-skipped-rows path (which also removes a latent substreams-cache over-count on bucketed `Map`); - the `Object` shared-data `granules_offsets` / `last_incomplete_granule_offset` cursors (the load-bearing `StructureGranule` continuous-read state is kept); - the `SerializationArrayOffsets` helper (`rows_offset`-only); - assorted dead offset arithmetic. <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. signals.title: Fix lazy materialization OOB and a Merge LOGICAL_ERROR from unused text index virtual columns
signals.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an out-of-bounds read (release) / logical error (debug) in the lazy materialization optimization, and a logical error in `Pipe::unitePipes` for `Merge` tables, when the direct-read-from-text-index optimization leaves an unused index virtual column in the read header of a `MergeTree` table with multiple `text` indexes. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 `TextIndexDAGReplacer::replace` rewrites text-search predicates into `__text_index_*` virtual columns, recording one per rewritten node, then runs `removeUnusedActions()`. When the rewrite keeps a different index's virtual column (or the original expression), the first virtual's input becomes unreferenced, but `result.added_columns` was not re-filtered, so `createReadTasksForTextIndex` still appended that orphaned column to the `ReadFromMergeTree` output header. `removed_columns` was already reconciled against the surviving inputs; `added_columns` was not, and that asymmetry is the bug. The fix collects the rewritten virtuals as candidates while walking the DAG and only populates `added_columns` after `removeUnusedActions()`, keeping a candidate when its input is in the surviving-inputs set already computed for `removed_columns`. The reading step's header then matches what the plan consumes, and a redundant index read goes away. One orphaned column causes two user-visible failures, both fixed: 1. **Lazy materialization out-of-bounds read** (the reported issue). `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` builds its `required_columns` mask positionally from the input headers above the reading step, which never contain a read-only virtual column. The mask ends up shorter than that step's header and the pass indexes a `std::vector<bool>` past its end: out-of-bounds read in release, `cols.size() == required_columns.size()` assertion in debug. 2. **`Merge` table logical error.** With `text` indexes on both `mapKeys(map)` and `mapValues(map)`, the `mapKeys` virtual wins the predicate and the `mapValues` one is left registered but unreferenced. Under `SELECT count()` nothing else is read, so the dead virtual becomes the indexed child's only output column while a non-indexed sibling's header stays empty. `Pipe::getCommonHeader` picks the first non-empty header and `unitePipes` asserts the empty sibling against it: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream`, a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds. `02346_text_index_bug111422` covers the first shape. The new `04563_text_index_merge_heterogeneous_children` covers the second, which the first cannot reach (no `merge()`, no bare `count()`). It pins the two runner-randomized settings it depends on per setting, not with a blanket tag. <details> <summary>Validation of the new test</summary> Debug build of this branch, memory-capped server, per-slot ports. | arm | build id | result | |---|---|---| | master `f9801d5649` (no fix) | `c29b56ab…` | aborts: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream: different number of columns` (`Block.cpp:308` <- `Pipe.cpp:316` <- `QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:263`) | | this branch, reconciliation loop removed | `fd96fd28…` | aborts: `Column __text_index_idx_map_values_equals_… already added for reading` (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4765`); via the test runner: `ClickHouse server died` | | this branch, unmodified | `a0a422da…` | passes byte-for-byte, and 50/50 randomized runs | The pre-fix signature differs between the two bases because this branch's merge-base predates the `already_has_direct_read` re-entry gate (`optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex.cpp`, `6253632d8da4`): without that gate the pass visits the step twice and the same over-registration trips the duplicate guard before a pipe is united. Same defect, two assertions. Both pinned settings were verified load-bearing and effective: with the pins removed, a client injecting `query_plan_direct_read_from_text_index=0` or `query_plan_text_index_add_hint=0` turns the `EXPLAIN` assertion vacuous (`1 0` -> `0 0`); with the pins present the test matches the reference under either injection and under both together. Full `text_index` suite on this branch, base vs with the new test: 157 -> 158 tests, 7 -> 6 failures, **zero new failures**. All shared failures are environmental on a bare slot server (missing stateful `test.hits` dataset, no `localhost:9000`, and four debug-build 600s timeouts). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111467&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111467](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111467+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111552&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111552](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111552+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Reject truncated/incomplete AI text function responses
signals.text: The AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) could silently return a truncated answer. When a provider stops early — most commonly by hitting the `max_tokens` limit — it reports this in the response, but the shared base class `FunctionBaseAI` never inspected the signal and returned whatever partial text came back. For example, `aiGenerate('Write three sentences about the ocean.', map(..., 'max_tokens', '5'))` returned the fragment `The ocean covers more than` with no error. This change normalizes each provider's native stop reason (OpenAI `finish_reason`, Anthropic `stop_reason`) into a canonical `FinishReason` enum, so the base class can make a single completeness decision without knowing the provider dialect: - `Truncated` (token/context limit) → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_TRUNCATED`. - `ContentFilter` (OpenAI `content_filter`, Anthropic `refusal`) and `ToolCall` → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_INCOMPLETE`. - `Complete` (natural end, or a caller stop sequence such as Anthropic `stop_sequence`) and `Unknown` (unrecognized reason) are accepted, so benign non-`stop` reasons are not misclassified as truncation. The rejection is thrown inside the existing per-row `try`, so it is non-retriable (retrying would hit the same limit) and honors `ai_function_throw_on_error`: with `1` the exception propagates; with `0` the row becomes the column default. `aiEmbed` is unaffected (embeddings have no finish reason). Integration tests in `test_ai_functions` cover truncation (throw + graceful), content-filter, an accepted unknown reason, and the Anthropic `stop_sequence` (must not throw) and `max_tokens` (must throw) cases. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) now reject truncated or otherwise incomplete provider responses (e.g. when the model hits the `max_tokens` limit) instead of silently returning partial output. Behavior follows the `ai_function_throw_on_error` setting. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111830&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111830](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111830+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
