signals.title: Hash the type-derived parameter in the ALP, FPC and GCD codecs
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `ALP`, `FPC` and `GCD` omitting their type-derived parameter from the codec hash. In a Compact part the writer shares one compressed stream per distinct codec hash, so two columns of different value width under the same codec collided and shared one codec object carrying the wrong width. This rejected valid inserts with `CANNOT_COMPRESS` when the widths disagreed, and otherwise compressed one of the columns worse than it should have. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 `MergeTreeDataPartWriterCompact::addStreams` keys compressed-stream reuse on `codec->getHash()` with no key-equality fallback, so a hash collision is an object-identity collision. Three codecs resolve a parameter from the column type, keep it out of the codec description AST, and hash only that AST, so two columns of different width shared one codec object and the loser of the race got the other's width: - `ALP` and `FPC` derive `float_width`. With `Float64` declared first the shared codec carries `float_width = 8`, a `Float32` granule is not a multiple of 8, and `ALP` throws `Code: 270 ... data size 404 is not aligned to 8 (CANNOT_COMPRESS)`. A mixed-width `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)` reaches the same throw, since the codec is resolved per substream. `FPC` ceil-divides instead of throwing, so its half is ratio-only: measured +10.0%. - `GCD` derives `gcd_bytes_size`, so the divisor width depended on declaration order and the ratio suffered. Data round-trips either way, because the width is in the GCD block header. Added on review request so the class stays revertable as one change; #113798 fixes the same `updateHash` for its own `is_signed_type` and goes forward independently. The fix adds the missing field to each hash, matching `SZ3`, `DoubleDelta`, `Gorilla`, `T64` and `Delta`, which already hash their type-derived width. Wide parts were never affected: one stream per column. Two consequences worth noting. Codec hashes also gate `can_substitute_codec_arguments`, a whole-codec flag, so `Tuple(Float32, Float64) CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` now shows as `CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` rather than `CODEC(FPC(12), LZ4)`; `Delta` and `Gorilla` already behave this way, same-width tuples still resolve, and a bare `CODEC(FPC)` still means level 12. No format change: each codec records the parameter in its own block header, so existing parts stay readable both ways. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, base `f9dd35fa7f57bbd8ec97be53c15acd82848a98f1`. ALP/FPC (build id `a0327326e75c88c307e5efda56857c3df38552c7`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `INSERT`, default table, f64 then f32, 101 rows | `Code: 270 ... 404 is not aligned to 8` | 101 rows, Compact part | | `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)`, default table | `Code: 270 ... 12012 is not aligned to 8` | 1001 rows, values round-trip | | ALP mixed vs two single-column tables | 234896 vs 228332, order dependent | 228332 == 228332 | | FPC mixed vs two single-column tables | 238887 vs 217185 | 217185 == 217185 | GCD (build id `bb612f0c6681bdde02436c553770393ff66f63fe`, pre-fix control `0a3b06892a5a9cafc8bc2c68a19d5fe9dff3f312`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `UInt16` + `UInt64` mixed vs two single-column tables | 80815 vs 80830 | 80830 == 80830 | | declaration order invariance (`u16, u64` vs `u64, u16`) | 160544 vs 160540 | identical | | round-trip on the mixed table | 20000/20000 | 20000/20000 | | same tables as Wide parts (control, no stream sharing) | already equal | already equal | `04861_codec_hash_type_derived_params` (renamed, since it no longer covers only float width) fails on the parent commit and passes with the fix; the two new GCD assertions were verified to redden independently, 5/5 runs failing before and 10/10 passing after under randomized settings, and 4-way self-parallel runs pass. A control build patching only `ALP` left the `FPC` numbers at exactly 238887, confirming the `FPC` measurement is not leaking from the `ALP` change. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114189&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114189](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114189+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Lazy materialization for reading local Parquet files (`file` / `File`)
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110970 Follow-up to the lazy materialization for object storage (#110970), as discussed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110970#issuecomment-5247858385: implement it for plain local Parquet files read through `StorageFile` — the `file` table function and the `File` table engine. For `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` queries, the columns that are not needed for sorting and filtering are read only for the `n` rows that survive the `LIMIT`. The format side (row-selective Parquet reads via `FormatFilterInfo::rows_to_read`) and the plan split (`JoinLazyColumnsStep`, `LazyMaterializingTransform`) from #110970 are reused as-is; this PR adds the `StorageFile` counterpart of the two branches: - The main pass appends a `__global_row_index` column (file index in a per-query `LazyFileRegistry` + physical row numbers from `ChunkInfoRowNumbers`) in `StorageFileSource::generate`. - The lazy branch (`LazilyReadFromFile` → `LazyReadFromFileSource` → `StorageFileLazyRowsSource`) reopens only the surviving files (at most `LIMIT n` of them) with a per-file set of rows to read and `parquet.preserve_order`. - The storage-agnostic column-split logic of `ReadFromObjectStorageStep::keepOnlyRequiredColumnsAndCreateLazyReadStep` (which columns can be deferred: `DEFAULT` expression dependencies, PREWHERE inputs, hive partition and virtual columns) is extracted into the shared `splitLazilyReadColumnsFromFormatInfo` and reused by both storages. **Generation safety.** POSIX has no conditional read, so the reread cannot be pinned the way `If-Match` pins it on S3. Instead the reread fails close with the new `FILE_CHANGED_DURING_READ` error when the file's generation token — sub-second mtime + inode + size, reusing `computeFileCacheVersionToken` from the query condition cache integration — no longer matches the one captured when the main pass opened the file. The token is validated at file registration time in the main pass, and both before and right after the reopen in the lazy pass. Replace-by-rename (the common atomic-update pattern) is always caught since it changes the inode; an in-place rewrite is caught up to the filesystem timestamp tick (and already tears a single-pass read today). **Gates** (`ReadFromFile::canUseLazyMaterialization`): Parquet format only, no file descriptor reads (stdin cannot be reopened), no archive entries, no `distributed_processing`, no `--rename_files_after_processing`, uncompressed files only. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization_for_file` (enabled by default), on top of `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization`. **Bug fix for #110970 shared via the helper:** deferring a requested subcolumn (e.g. of a `JSON` column) left the lazy branch's format header empty and the query failed with `Not found column or subcolumn ... in block`, because the format header contains the parent column of a requested subcolumn while the split filtered it by subcolumn names. The split now maps requested columns to their storage-level names — the parent of a deferred subcolumn moves to the lazy branch, and stays in the main branch as well when a sort key still needs another subcolumn of it. Covered for both storages by the new tests. On a 1 GB local Parquet file (2M rows × 105 columns equivalent shape: two 300-byte strings), `SELECT * ... ORDER BY k DESC LIMIT 5` runs 3× faster (0.15 s vs 0.45 s, page-cache warm), with results verified identical with the optimization on and off. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Lazy materialization for `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` queries (#110970) now also applies to local Parquet files read with the `file` table function and the `File` table engine: the columns that are not needed for sorting and filtering are read only for the `n` rows that survive the `LIMIT`. The second read of a surviving file fails close with the new `FILE_CHANGED_DURING_READ` error if the file was modified between the two passes. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization_for_file` (enabled by default). Also fixes lazy materialization for object storage failing with `Not found column or subcolumn ... in block` when a requested subcolumn (e.g. of a `JSON` column) is deferred. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114262&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114262](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114262+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Don't build a set to estimate its selectivity
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Bounded the cost of estimating the selectivity of `col IN (...)` from column statistics, which could add hundreds of milliseconds to the planning of a single query. The estimator no longer runs the subquery behind `col IN (subquery)` to fill a set it only needs one selectivity number from — an unbuilt set is skipped instead. For a set larger than the new `statistics_max_set_size_for_exact_selectivity_estimation` setting (default 10000), the selectivity is now derived from the size of the set and its bounding range. --- Some measurements on sf=100 could be found [here](https://clickhouse-inc.slack.com/archives/C02F2LML5UG/p1786527589000709?thread_ts=1786399008.205189&cid=C02F2LML5UG). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114389&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114389](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114389+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add SHARED REGEXP path placement policy to JSON
signals.text: Adds `SHARED REGEXP 'pattern'` to `JSON` type declarations so matching root-relative flattened paths are always stored in shared data instead of competing for dedicated dynamic-path subcolumns. This is useful for high-cardinality path families whose promotion would displace more useful paths. Matching is partial by default, like `SKIP REGEXP`. Set the persisted `JSON` type parameter `shared_regexp_use_partial_match=0` to require full-string matching. Typed paths take precedence over `SHARED REGEXP`; `SKIP` and `SKIP REGEXP` continue to discard matching data. Rules are evaluated against the complete path from the original `JSON` root, including derived sub-objects. The rules are compiled once into an immutable `RE2` matcher, with bounded rule count and pattern sizes. A single rule uses direct `RE2` matching and multiple rules use `RE2::Set`. `JSON` columns without rules keep a null matcher, their existing binary type encoding, and their existing row-placement path. Metadata snapshots are copied lazily only when retained placement provenance actually changes a type. Placement provenance is stored in part column metadata and retained by default through horizontal and vertical merges, wide and compact mutations, column renames, lightweight-update patch materialization, and `Array`/`Nullable`/`Tuple`/`Map` wrappers. Removing a rule therefore does not unexpectedly promote already-shared paths during a later rewrite. Set the `MergeTree` table setting `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` to opt into reconsidering those paths. Policy-only metadata changes inside `Variant` are documented as unsupported. The `Native` binary type encoding uses `JSON` encoding version 1 only when a policy is present; ordinary `JSON` types remain byte-identical version 0. The canonical `JSON` documentation and `Native` format specification are updated accordingly. Testing includes 18 focused unit tests and 9 stateless scenarios covering syntax, partial/full matching, root-relative sub-objects, all supported wrappers, flattened `Native` and `RowBinary` paths, horizontal/vertical merges, compact/wide mutations, renames, statistics, and both lightweight-patch application paths. An 88.6 MB real Elasticsearch `indices_stats` document produced 143,555 flattened paths; all 143,290 paths targeted by `^indices[.]` remained in shared data and none became dynamic. A one-run end-to-end smoke comparison was 1.66 s without the policy and 1.69 s with it, with a 0.055% max-RSS difference; these small differences are noise-level, not a statistical benchmark. **Scope note:** `SKIP`/`SKIP REGEXP` already applied inconsistently between array-shaped and object-shaped occurrences of the same path on `master`, independent of `SHARED REGEXP` (a path skipped when the value at that path is an object could still surface when the value is an array of objects). This PR's fix for `SKIP REGEXP` on dynamically inferred nested objects closes one instance of that inconsistency; the underlying array-vs-object gap predates this PR and is not otherwise addressed here. **Scope note:** for a value dynamically inferred as its own nested `JSON` object (an inconsistent-shape array/object under a dynamic path), a policy-only `ALTER` followed by a plain read correctly picks up the new `SHARED REGEXP`/`SKIP REGEXP` rules for that nested object. A `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` merge or mutation that rewrites such a part afterward does not: it reconstructs the nested object's dynamic-path structure from cached per-column type state that a policy change doesn't refresh, so paths inside it can still be placed according to the rule in effect when the object was first materialized. This is opt-in (`allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion` defaults to off) and not fixed by this PR. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `SHARED REGEXP` rules to the `JSON` data type to keep matching paths in shared data, with configurable full-string matching and explicit control over re-promoting paths after rules are removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114414&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114414](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114414+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix wrong results for non-boolean conditions taken out of `and`
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112236 `and` implicitly converts its arguments to booleans, so any non-zero value is true. When a query plan optimization takes a part of a conjunction away and a single conjunct is left as the new predicate, that conjunct was converted with a cast to the type of the original predicate. A cast is not a boolean conversion: it maps values like 256 or 0.1 to 0, so rows whose condition value is a non-zero multiple of 256 silently disappeared. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(600); SELECT count() FROM t AS l LEFT JOIN t AS r ON l.id = r.id WHERE r.id AND l.id = r.id; ``` returned 597 instead of 599, the rows with `id = 256` and `id = 512` were dropped. `mergeFilterIntoJoinCondition` moves `l.id = r.id` into the JOIN and leaves `CAST(r.id, 'UInt8')` as the filter: ``` Filter column: CAST(id AS UInt8) ``` The same happens in `ActionsDAG::removeUnusedConjunctions` when a conjunct is pushed down and the filter column is still needed in the result. That one is reachable without a JOIN, and the value of the condition was wrong there as well (the raw value instead of a boolean): ```sql SELECT count(), sum(f) FROM ( SELECT id, (id != 1000 AND s) AS f FROM (SELECT id, sum(id) AS s FROM t GROUP BY id) WHERE id != 1000 AND s ); ``` returned `597 597` instead of `599 599`. It only converted floating point types, now every non-boolean type is converted. Both places now wrap the remaining conjunct into `and(x, true)`, the same way `toBoolIfNeeded` does it in `JoinStepLogical.cpp`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a non-boolean condition, such as a bare integer column in `WHERE`, is left alone after the other conditions are merged into the JOIN condition or pushed down. Rows whose condition value was a non-zero multiple of 256 were skipped. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: Reject Delta Lake partition column absent from the table schema
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114462 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` when reading a Delta Lake table whose `metaData.partitionColumns` names a column that `metaData.schemaString` does not declare. Such metadata is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS` on the delta-kernel reader and `INCORRECT_DATA` on the legacy reader, whenever the table or its schema is read from a snapshot, not only when the query carries a predicate. ### Description Requested by @ PedroTadim in #114462. `partitionColumns` and `schemaString` are independent fields of externally supplied metadata and nothing cross-checked them, so a mismatch was reported as `LOGICAL_ERROR`, which aborts on debug and sanitizer builds. Paimon already threw `BAD_ARGUMENTS` here. - delta-kernel reader: validate in `TableSnapshot::initOrUpdateSchemaIfChanged`, where both values first exist, beside the existing empty-schema rejection. Previously an unfiltered `SELECT *` succeeded and only a predicate threw, since `PartitionPruner` is built only when a filter exists. That site keeps `LOGICAL_ERROR`, now a genuine internal invariant. - legacy reader: `LOGICAL_ERROR` -> `INCORRECT_DATA` where an `add` action's `partitionValues` names an undeclared key, in the JSON-log and checkpoint branches. It also validates `partitionColumns` where `metaData` is loaded, in both branches, so a snapshot with no `add` action to resolve is rejected too. That check compares logical names: a parsed legacy schema is keyed by column-mapping physical names, so comparing against it would reject well formed column-mapped tables. Iceberg is unaffected: it resolves partitions by numeric `source_id` field ids, not by name. Change-data-feed reads go through `TableChanges`, which resolves no partition name, and are out of scope. Behaviour change: such a table was readable without a predicate, and on the legacy reader also with no `add` action; it is now rejected for every query that reads it. It is malformed per the Delta protocol. One case is left alone, unchanged from master: on a table with an explicit column list a bare `count()` is answered from transaction-log row counts, which resolve no column name, so it is not rejected, while reading any column from it is. Validated with the new stateless test `04877`: every failure arm fails on a targeted revert of the line it covers, including a well formed column-mapped control that must keep reading. Also 50/50 randomized runs and the `delta_lake` suite. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1554` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Never cancel a query before its `max_execution_time` has elapsed
signals.text: `CancellationChecker::appendTask` derived a query's cancellation deadline from the current time truncated to whole milliseconds, and then aligned it up to the 100 ms grid the worker batches deadlines on. The alignment normally hides the truncation, but when the deadline already sits on the grid - one query in a hundred - it adds no padding, and the deadline lands up to 1 ms before `now + max_execution_time`. The query is then cancelled ahead of its own timeout and fails with a self-contradictory message: ``` Code: 159. DB::Exception: Timeout exceeded: elapsed 999.672 ms, maximum: 1000 ms. (TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED) ``` The current time is now rounded up to a whole millisecond instead, which is the direction the code around it already promises: *"Tasks may be cancelled slightly later than their exact timeout, but never before"*. Only the `throw` overflow mode was affected: in `break` mode the checker re-reads the elapsed time before acting on the deadline, so an early wake-up does nothing. This is what makes `02122_join_group_by_timeout` flaky - it asserts that a `max_execution_time = 1` cancellation takes at least 1000 ms, and `query_duration_ms` is measured from a stopwatch that starts before the deadline is computed. The failure shows up as `query_duration 1` becoming `query_duration 0`, always on one of the two `throw`-mode queries and never on the `break`-mode ones. In the server logs of both `Fast test` runs below, the query was cancelled early - at 999.672 ms and at 999.630 ms of its 1000 ms timeout. The deadline computation moved into `CancellationChecker::taskDeadlineMs` so that the invariant can be tested directly: the new unit test checks every sub-millisecond phase of `now` against every phase of the grid, for a range of timeouts, and fails with the old truncation. CI reports of the flaky test: - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=gh-readonly-queue/master/pr-113021-93e2851fddb5add7bad5b28bcef780be2f6ff7bb&sha=bef88e3d96ecb0f57a0f8d81f6b7ee2117db19fd&name_0=MergeQueueCI&name_1=Fast%20test - https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=gh-readonly-queue/master/pr-110451-2f02abe52a79c02fb554728f14d8fa847dcbc1e6&sha=2eba84a8a12a21c36516158d4fbe9530d3f0af8c&name_0=MergeQueueCI&name_1=Fast%20test The truncation is as old as the checker itself. Before deadlines were aligned to a grid in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/95563 the deadline was plainly `floor(now) + timeout`, i.e. early for every query rather than for one in a hundred; and the assertion that catches it was only sharpened from `round(query_duration_ms / 1000) BETWEEN 1 AND 60` to `query_duration_ms BETWEEN 1000 AND 60000` in daf1b4980b1, which is why the flake is recent. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A query could be cancelled up to 1 ms before its `max_execution_time` had passed, failing with a self-contradictory `Timeout exceeded: elapsed 999.672 ms, maximum: 1000 ms`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114559&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114559](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114559+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix stale MATERIALIZED column values read through a chain while a mutation is pending
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100613 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/50237 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99281 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103182 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115371 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115372 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115638 **Scope changed.** The staging half of this pull request — recomputing a chain of `MATERIALIZED` columns one dependency level at a time during a mutation — landed on master in the meantime via #103182, which also generalizes it to `APPLY PATCHES`, so all of it was dropped here. What remains is the read path, which master still gets wrong: the read set is closed in `AlterConversions`, and `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` keeps a single line of change, resolving `MATERIALIZED` defaults against the whole table instead of the read task's columns. The two defects that belong to the staging path are split out into #115371 and #115372. ## Problem With a mutation still pending, reading a `MATERIALIZED` column that reaches the updated column only through another `MATERIALIZED` column returns the stale on-disk value, while reading the whole chain returns the recomputed one: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, y Int32, m1 Int32 MATERIALIZED x + 1, m2 Int32 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1, m3 Int32 MATERIALIZED m2 + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t (x, y) VALUES (10, 0); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; SET alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0, apply_mutations_on_fly = 1; ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; -- stays pending ``` ``` SELECT m2 FROM t; -- 12 (stale; must be 22) SELECT m3 FROM t; -- 13 (stale; must be 23) SELECT x, m1, m2, m3 FROM t; -- 20 21 22 23 (correct) ``` - The result of a query depends on which columns it selects, so the same value read two ways disagrees. - The same happens for a `MATERIALIZED` column defined over a subcolumn (`m1 MATERIALIZED t.a + 1` with a pending `UPDATE t = ...`): `SELECT m1` returns the stale value unless the query happens to select `t` as well. - Selecting a `MATERIALIZED` column together with a column the mutation updates fails outright with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` whenever the first one's dependencies are not in the select list, even when that column has nothing to do with the mutation. - Once the mutation finishes, the values are correct — only the pending window is affected. ## Root cause Reading with `apply_mutations_on_fly` builds the pending commands into the read pipeline. `AlterConversions::addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` decides which extra columns must be read so that the `MATERIALIZED` columns being selected can be recomputed, and it only looked one hop deep: ```cpp for (const auto & column_name : read_columns_set) if (default is MATERIALIZED) for (const auto & dependency : TreeRewriter(context).analyze(expression, source_columns)->requiredSourceColumns()) if (all_updated_columns.contains(dependency)) required_source_columns.insert(dependency); ``` For `m2 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1` the only dependency is `m1`, which is not in `all_updated_columns`, so nothing is added, `filterMutationCommands` drops the `UPDATE x` command as irrelevant to the read set, and `m2` is returned from disk. Two further details of the same analysis: - the default expression is not normalized with `replaceSubcolumnsToGetSubcolumnFunctionInQuery`, so `m MATERIALIZED t.a` is seen to depend on `t.a` rather than on `t`, and a pending `UPDATE t` is filtered out (or the analysis fails with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` when the subcolumn does not resolve against `source_columns`); - a `MATERIALIZED` column whose expression reads an `EPHEMERAL` column can never be recomputed outside `INSERT`, so analysing it against physical columns must be avoided rather than attempted. ## Solution Two sites, because the read set has two consumers that must agree. ### `AlterConversions::addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` — close the read set 1. **Transitive closure.** A breadth-first walk seeded with the read columns replaces the single pass, so the `MATERIALIZED` columns in between are read too and the interpreter recomputes the whole chain instead of `filterMutationCommands` dropping the `UPDATE` as irrelevant. 2. **Only a column that is recalculated pulls in dependencies, and it pulls in all of them.** The walk asks of the column it visits whether the interpreter recalculates it, and if so takes its whole expression, because the stage that rewrites it evaluates that expression against the block — including the part reading a column no mutation touches (`c MATERIALIZED m1 + y`, where `y` is untouched). A column that keeps its stored value contributes nothing, so a chain whose value cannot change is not read. 3. **Subcolumn rewrite.** Dependencies are analysed after `replaceSubcolumnsToGetSubcolumnFunctionInQuery`, matching what `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` does before analysing the same expression. Without it `m MATERIALIZED t.a + 1` is seen to depend on `t.a` while `all_updated_columns` holds `t`; the names do not match and a pending `UPDATE t` is filtered out. This is a one-hop defect, independent of the chain. 4. **`EPHEMERAL` columns added to the analysis source list.** `getAllPhysical` excludes them, so analysing `me MATERIALIZED x + e` threw `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` inside this function. Measured on master, `SELECT me` with any pending `UPDATE` fails this way. Also a one-hop defect, and analysing every hop of a chain would have multiplied its reach. 5. **The `EPHEMERAL` test mirrors the interpreter's policy, and keeps a pass of its own.** `MutationsInterpreter` never recomputes a `MATERIALIZED` column that reads an `EPHEMERAL` one, so such a column is not treated as recalculable here either — the read set must not promise a recomputation the interpreter refuses. It cannot share the loop that looks for a changed dependency: that loop stops at the first one it finds, while this test quantifies over all of them, so interleaving them skips it exactly when a dependency is updated. 6. **Memoised lookups.** `getMutationSteps` runs per read task per part, so each default expression is analysed at most once per call and each reachability question answered at most once. ### `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` — resolve defaults against the whole table `available_columns` was serving two different roles: which `MATERIALIZED` columns need recalculating, and which columns their expressions may be resolved against. For a plain `UPDATE` the two coincide. A table carrying a `MATERIALIZED` column the mutation does not affect breaks the coincidence — its dependencies are legitimately outside the read set — and the analysis failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, taking the query with it: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, y Int32, m Int32 MATERIALIZED x + 1, n Int32 MATERIALIZED y + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; -- stays pending SELECT m, n FROM t; -- Missing columns: 'y' while processing: 'y + 1' SELECT x, n FROM t; -- the same, and this one fails on master too ``` Deciding whether a column has to be recalculated must not require reading what it reads, so the default expressions are now resolved against every column of the table. Only an on-fly read has a narrow list: a materialising mutation passes `getNamesOfPhysical()`, so the only columns this adds there are virtual ones, which a `MATERIALIZED` default cannot reference — `CREATE` and `ALTER` both reject that. The list is built on first use. Copying it costs a node per column of the table, the loop needs it only for a `MATERIALIZED` column the task reads, and an on-fly read reaches it per part. Widening `need_materialized_analysis` instead would have been wrong: `validateUpdateColumns` runs at the end of the same block, so guarding the block would drop the check that rejects an `ALTER UPDATE` of a key or `MATERIALIZED` column on every table without `MATERIALIZED` columns. ### Taken from #115638 @Avogar tried an alternative on top of this branch in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115638 and asked for it to be moved here. It is in as of `4bec5ca8a1a`, applied verbatim — the test files this branch already carried are byte-identical in it, and `Settings::apply_on_fly_for_read` is kept. What it adds over the two sites above: - **`MaterializedColumnDependencies`** — the dependency graph over a table's `MATERIALIZED` columns, built once and shared by the read path and `MutationsInterpreter` instead of being derived separately in each, so the two can no longer disagree about how a dependency is spelled. This is also the graph @Avogar needs in #112717. - **The closure and the command filter now run to a fixed point.** `filterMutationCommands` puts the columns a surviving command reads into the read set, and one of those can itself be a `MATERIALIZED` column of a chain (`DELETE WHERE m2 > 100`), which can in turn keep an older command alive. Closing and filtering used to run once each, in that order, so a chain reached from a `DELETE` predicate or an `UPDATE` expression stayed stale. They now iterate until the set stops growing; it only grows and is bounded by the width of the table, so it terminates. - **A command may name a subcolumn as written (`t.a`)** while the read set is keyed on storage columns, which made every read of the table fail with `NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE`. Names now go through `getNameInStorage` on the way in. This one reproduces on master. - **One `buildMutationChainForRead`** shared by `getMutationSteps` and `getMutationActions`, instead of each recomputing the read set and the command filter. ### A `MATERIALIZED` column over an `ALIAS` column Also fixed here, in `aeda9610380`, because after the extraction there is exactly one place to do it. A `MATERIALIZED` default may read an `ALIAS` column, and that made **every** mutation on the table throw, including one updating a column the expression never mentions: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, z Int32, a Int32 ALIAS x + 100, m Int32 MATERIALIZED a + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); ALTER TABLE t UPDATE z = 5 WHERE 1; -- Code: 47. Missing columns: 'a' while processing: 'a + 1' ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` The list the default is analysed against is the physical one and an `ALIAS` is physical-excluded. Merely adding aliases to it would let `TreeRewriter` resolve the name, but the expression would then still read `a` at execution time and no part has such a column, so the recompute stage would fail on it instead. The reference is replaced by the expression it stands for, with `ReplaceAliasByExpressionMatcher` — the same visitor `IndexDescription::initExpressionInfo` uses so a skip index can reference an `ALIAS` column. `MaterializedColumnDependencies` hands the same expression to the dependency analysis and to the recompute stage, so one expansion reaches both; it runs before the subcolumn rewrite, so a subcolumn reached through an alias is normalised too. Unlike the `EPHEMERAL` case next to it there is no trade-off: `m` recalculates correctly from the stored `x`, and an `ALIAS` column is recomputed per query so it can never itself be stale. ### Not proposed for backport The change started as a narrow read-path fix, but with the dependency graph extracted into a new component shared by two subsystems it is no longer a good backport candidate, and it is not labelled for one. ### Coverage Regression test `04869_materialized_chain_on_fly_read` covers six cases, each measured individually against master `5bd006cd298`: - the plain chain read tail-only — returns the stale value; - the chain read next to the updated column, without the intermediate hop — throws `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, because the surviving command makes the interpreter analyse a default whose dependency is not in the read set; - one command assigning two columns, with the query reading the other assignment target — throws for the same reason, after the command is narrowed and loses the assignment the chain depends on; - a pending `DELETE` that keeps a command alive while the set of updated columns stays empty — returns the stale value, since the analysis is skipped entirely; - columns the mutation does not affect, read on their own and next to the updated column, and a recalculated column reading an untouched one — stale value or `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` depending on the select list; - the subcolumn default and the `EPHEMERAL`-derived column — stale value and `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` respectively. `04926_on_fly_mutation_read_set_closure` covers the cases the read-set closure loop repairs: the chain reached from a pending `DELETE` predicate, a subcolumn spelled as written in a command, and the cases that must not move. `05024_materialized_over_alias_column_mutation` covers the `ALIAS` case, measured both ways on a Debug build: without the expansion `UPDATE z = 5` and `UPDATE x = 20` both throw `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`; with it the first leaves `m` alone and the second gives `x, a, m = 20, 120, 121`, on the settled part and on the on-fly read alike. `05023_materialized_ephemeral_stale_warning` is unchanged and still passes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed reading a table while a mutation is in progress: a `MATERIALIZED` column could return a stale value, and selecting one together with an updated column could fail with an error. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114561&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114561](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114561+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add `/dialect`, `/lang`, `/language` client commands
signals.text: Adds client-side `/dialect`, `/lang` and `/language` commands - an equivalent of `SET dialect = '...'` that is handled before parsing, so it also works when the current dialect cannot express a `SET` query (for example, to leave `kusto` or `promql`). The active non-default dialect is shown in the prompt, and a plain `SET dialect = '...'` keeps the prompt in sync. Implementation notes: - The prompt is rendered by `getPrompt` on every line from a template that keeps the `{display_name}` placeholder: the current dialect is appended to the display name in parentheses (with a separating space if the display name is non-empty), and the `:) ` smiley is appended at the end, preserving the previous behavior for the default dialect. A custom prompt without `{display_name}` gets the dialect appended at its end. - The command works in `clickhouse-client`, `clickhouse-local`, and the embedded client (SSH/web terminal). - `clickhouse-local` also recognizes the command in noninteractive scripts: a standalone dialect-command line splits the script, so each chunk is parsed with the dialect selected before it. A line that belongs to inline `INSERT ... FORMAT` data or to an unfinished statement (an open string literal or bracket) stays a part of the SQL, and the other text-level meta-commands keep working. A rejected command aborts the script, exactly like a rejected `SET dialect`. - Documentation: a new "Switching the SQL dialect" section on the client page. - Test: `04892_client_dialect_command.expect`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added client-side commands `/dialect`, `/lang`, and `/language` to `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local`, so you can switch the active SQL dialect before parsing - it also works when the current dialect cannot express a `SET` query, for example to leave `kusto` or `promql`. The current non-default dialect is now shown in the prompt, and a plain `SET dialect = ...` keeps the prompt in sync. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114568&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114568](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114568+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Mongo queries: keep whole documents in a JSON column
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58394 Adds two ways to run MongoDB queries against ClickHouse: - a **wire protocol endpoint** (`mongo_port`), so MongoDB drivers and tools such as `pymongo` and `mongosh` can connect to ClickHouse as if it were a MongoDB server; - a **query dialect** (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`), so MongoDB shell syntax can be sent over the usual ClickHouse interfaces. This continues @scanhex12's https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 - it holds all of its commits - and changes how a collection is stored, which is what the review of that pull request asked for (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493#discussion_r3771132310): a collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in one `JSON` column rather than a column inferred per field of the first document. ```sql CREATE TABLE db.users (`_id` String, `json` JSON) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY `_id` ``` The document goes into the `JSON` column, whose paths are its fields, and its object id into the `_id` column, which is the primary key. A document may then hold a field that no document before it had, may leave out a field another one has, and `$exists` answers what it means. A table that was created in ClickHouse keeps its own columns, and a field of a query names the column of the same name there, so an application can also be pointed at a table that already holds the data. A read of the documents as they are stored selects them next to the types of their paths, so a date reads back as a BSON date and an integer as an `int32`/`int64` of its width. The integration tests of `test_mongo_protocol` say what each shape answers now - a collection of documents where that is what is tested, a table created in ClickHouse where the test is about a column - and 75/75 of them pass. **This is a draft** because a few things of a document collection are an explicit error rather than an answer: an `update` of it, an index over a path, the `mongo` dialect over it, the element-wise match of an array by equality or `$in`, `$unwind` of a path, and the accumulators that read a number. They are the next commits; every one of them is listed in `docs/en/interfaces/mongo.md` and pinned by a test in the meantime. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol endpoint (the `mongo_port` server setting) and a MongoDB query dialect (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`) for basic collection operations. A collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in a `JSON` column. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114577&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114577](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114577+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix a renamed and dropped column being read from the wrong file while the mutation is pending
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114562 ## Problem A column that is renamed, dropped and added again in one `ALTER` silently returns the **dropped** column's data instead of its own default, while the mutation is still pending: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, h UInt8 DEFAULT 0) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t SELECT number + 100, 0 FROM numbers(1000); SET alter_sync = 0; -- mutation left pending ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b, DROP COLUMN b, ADD COLUMN b UInt64 DEFAULT 7; SELECT count(), min(b), max(b) FROM t; -- 1000 100 1099 <- the old `a` values -- expected: 1000 7 7 ``` No error and nothing in the log; it affects `Wide` and `Compact` parts alike. The added `b` is a different column from the one that was dropped, so its rows have to come from its `DEFAULT`. **Scope.** This fixes the answer while the mutation is pending. Once the mutation has materialised a `Wide` part still returns the dropped column's data — a separate, pre-existing defect that lives in `MutateTask`, see the follow-ups at the end. ## Root cause `AlterConversions` records a pending drop under the name the command used: ```cpp else if (command.type == DROP_COLUMN) { dropped_columns.emplace(command.column_name); } ``` while every consumer of `isColumnDropped` asks about a column under the name it has **in the part**: - `IMergeTreeReader::isColumnDroppedByPendingMutation` takes the name out of `columns_to_read`, which is built from `getColumnInPart` and therefore already has the rename mapping applied (`IMergeTreeReader.cpp:81`); - `injectRequiredColumnsRecursively` passes `column_name_in_part` (`MergeTreeBlockReadUtils.cpp:119`). Without a rename the two names are identical, so the hazard those checks exist for — a column dropped and re-added under the same name, whose data in the part is stale — behaves correctly. That is why this was never noticed. With a rename they diverge: the part holds `a`, the drop is recorded for `b`, the check asks about `a`, finds nothing, and the reader streams the `a` file into the new `b`. ## Solution Consume the ordering in `DROP_COLUMN`, where both halves of it are needed anyway. Commands arrive as issued, so the renames recorded so far are exactly those preceding the drop; the entry that gives the drop its part-side name is also the entry the drop makes obsolete, so one lookup does both: ```cpp auto name_in_part = command.column_name; auto it = std::ranges::find(rename_map, command.column_name, &RenamePair::rename_to); if (it != rename_map.end()) { name_in_part = it->rename_from; rename_map.erase(it); } dropped_columns.emplace(std::move(name_in_part)); ``` Every existing caller of `isColumnDropped` already passes a part-side name, so all of them become correct at once and none of them changes. Retiring the mapping matters on its own. `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b` used to leave **two** entries pointing at `b` — from the dropped `a` and from the live `c` — and the lookup returns whichever comes first, so `b` read the wrong column. Writing a `RenamePair` as `to <- from`, where `to` is the name in the metadata and `from` the name in the part, and remembering that `dropped_columns` now holds part-side names: | # | command | what happens | `rename_map` | `dropped_columns` | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | `RENAME a TO b` | not chained, insert | `[b <- a]` | `{}` | | 2 | `DROP b` | `b <- a` gives the part's `a` and is erased in the same step | `[]` | `{a}` | | 3 | `RENAME c TO b` | `b` is free, insert | `[b <- c]` | `{a}` | `getColumnOldName("b")` then answers `c`, and `a` stays dropped so nothing reads it. Both halves are needed to get this right: | variant | `min(b), max(b)`, want `5000 5999` | |---|---| | `master` | `100 1099` — the **dropped** column's data | | part-side drop only | `0 0` — the default | | both | `5000 5999` ✔ | ### Why in the drop and not when the name is taken over Retiring the entry in `RENAME_COLUMN` instead — erase whatever maps onto the new target and is already dropped — reads as the more targeted fix, and it is where the first two commits of this PR put it. It has to cover two paths, though, because a rename can reach the freed name through a chain: `RENAME c TO d, RENAME d TO b` updates the existing `d <- c` entry in place rather than appending, so an erase placed on the appending path alone leaves `[b <- a, b <- c]` again. That variant does not misread — it fails outright, because `b` resolves to the dropped `a` and the part-side name reaches the storage snapshot: ``` Code: 16. DB::Exception: There is no column a in table. (NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE) ``` Reaching it takes `ReplicatedMergeTree`: a single `ALTER` rejects transitive renames (`Transitive renames in a single ALTER query are not allowed`), and `StorageMergeTree::alter` always waits for the previous mutation before a metadata change (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:548`, *"alters should be executed in sequential order"*), so two of them can never both be pending there. Doing it in the drop is the same thing one step earlier and needs no case analysis: a mapping onto a dropped name simply never exists, so `RENAME_COLUMN` has nothing to clean up and the chained path needs no special handling. The two were measured equivalent on both the read path (all of `04872`) and the materialisation path (the mutation run to completion with `alter_sync = 2` for `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, ADD b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` and the chained Replicated case — byte-identical results). ### Why not fix it in the reader Checking the renamed-to name in the reader as well looks equivalent and is wrong. The opposite command order produces exactly the same `AlterConversions` state, and `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames` already pins the required behaviour for it: ```sql ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN value2_old, RENAME COLUMN value2 TO value2_old; ``` Here the drop hit a *different* column that merely carried that name, and `value2`'s data is live and must be readable as `value2_old`. The only thing separating the two situations is where the drop sits among the renames, which the readers cannot see. Measured with the reader-side variant applied, live data is replaced by defaults: ``` dropped, then the name reused by a rename -1000 100 1099 +1000 0 0 ``` Hence the ordering has to be consumed at construction time. ### Tests `tests/queries/0_stateless/04872_read_renamed_then_dropped_and_readded_column.sh` — seven cases: the defect on `Wide` and on `Compact`, the `RENAME/DROP/RENAME` case above and its chained variant, plus three controls that must not move — drop-and-re-add without a rename (what the check was written for), a pending rename with no drop, and the mirror case. The chained case runs the `ALTER`s with the partition detached and then attaches the part carrying the old column names to a table whose merges are stopped, so the mutations stay unapplied while it is read — the same shape as `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`. Verified on a local server that it is load-bearing: with the retirement placed on the appending path of `RENAME_COLUMN` it fails with `NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE`, while the non-chained control passes either way. Because the two possible wrong answers fail in opposite directions, the result is checked three ways: | variant | the defect | the mirror case | |---|---|---| | `master` | `1000 100 1099` ✗ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | | reader-side variant | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 0 0` ✗ | | this change | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames`, `01278_alter_rename_combination`, `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`, `04053_alter_add_rename_column_in_single_query` and `04011_detach_rename_attach_column` all pass. ### Notes for reviewers - **The retirement relies on the command sequence reaching `AlterConversions` without gaps, and it does.** Metadata mutations are exempt from every `params` switch — `needIncludeMutationToSnapshot` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:653`, *"Metadata mutations must be included into the snapshot regardless of the parameters"*) and `addSupportedCommands` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:704`) both admit `RENAME_COLUMN` and `DROP_COLUMN` unconditionally, so no caller can ask for a snapshot holding the renames but not the drops. Per-part filtering then takes a contiguous suffix, never a middle slice: both `getOnFlyMutationCommandsForPart` implementations walk in reverse and *stop* at the first mutation at or below the part's version (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:3549`, `ReplicatedMergeTreeQueue.cpp:2355`). A gap would need `RENAME a TO b` in the window with `DROP b` cut out, but the drop is the newer of the two, so cutting it necessarily cuts the rename that created the entry as well. Order is a documented contract: *"@return list of mutation commands in order: oldest to newest"* (`MergeTreeData.h:617`). The chained-rename collapsing that predates this PR rests on the same property. The replicated loop iterates by `mutation_version` while testing `alter_version`, so the suffix is contiguous only if the two are co-monotonic, and they are: the single site that creates a mutation entry with `alter_version != -1` (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7092`) does so in one `tryMulti` that also carries `set /metadata` with a CAS on the current metadata version (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7001`, and `alter_version` is that version plus one) and `set /mutations` with a CAS on its own version. Either CAS makes two of them serialise, and the sequential number is assigned inside that atomic commit, so the k-th alter mutation to commit gets both the larger sequence number and the higher metadata version. `mutate` — the other creator — leaves `alter_version` at `-1` and is handled by the loop's other branch. Confirmed by reading the raw znodes through `system.zookeeper`: with `ALTER UPDATE`s interleaved between the renames the metadata subsequence is `1, 2, 3, 4` in znode order, and ten concurrent renames from separate clients land as `alter_version` `1..9` matching the znode sequence exactly. - `isColumnDropped` now consistently answers about part-side names. That matches all four existing call sites, so it is a fix rather than a contract change for them, but a future caller holding a metadata name would have to resolve it first. - **Overlaps with #114562, in a way that is safe in either merge order.** That PR adds a second lookup in the empty-candidate accounting loop of `injectRequiredColumns`, mapping a part name forward to its renamed-to name and testing the drop under that, so that a single-statement `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` is recognised as accounted for. This change makes the *first* lookup answer that correctly, because the drop is then already recorded as `a`, so the second lookup becomes dead code once both are in. It is deliberately left in place here rather than removed pre-emptively: while only #114562 is merged the second lookup is what makes that case work. A small cleanup to delete it belongs after this merges. Checked on a scratch branch carrying both changes with that lookup deleted — `04870`, `04871`, `04872`, `03830`, `04011` and `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames` all still pass, so the cleanup is safe. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a column that was renamed, dropped and added again in one `ALTER` returning the dropped column's values instead of its own default while the mutation was still pending. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114601&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114601](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114601+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> ### Follow-ups found while testing, not fixed here Both are pre-existing, live in `MutateTask` rather than `AlterConversions`, and were measured identical on the pre-PR base and on this branch, so they are out of scope. Filed for follow-up: - `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, ADD b UInt64 DEFAULT 7` still returns `1000 100 1099` after the mutation has materialised. This PR fixes the answer only while the mutation is pending. Measured: `Wide` parts only (a `Compact` part gives the correct `7 7`), plain `MergeTree` **and** `ReplicatedMergeTree`, with default `alter_sync` and no fault injection at all; `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `DETACH`/`ATTACH` do not repair it. The same statement without the `ADD` leaves `b.bin` orphaned in the part while neither the table nor the part lists the column any more. - `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b` with `alter_sync = 2` makes the mutation fail permanently with `Code: 424 ... b.bin already exists and has a different inode ... (CANNOT_LINK)`, because the retired `a -> b` rename and the live `c -> b` collide on one destination file.

signals.title: Find a LowCardinality needle equal to the type's default value
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112953 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`, `indexOf`, `countEqual`, `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue` and `Map` subscript returning "not found" for a constant `LowCardinality` needle equal to the element type's default value, such as an empty `String` or a zero number. ### Description **The problem.** A constant needle equal to the element type's default value is never found in an `Array(LowCardinality(T))` or a `Map` with a `LowCardinality` key. No exception, so a `WHERE` on such a predicate silently drops rows: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a Array(LowCardinality(String))) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t VALUES (['', 'a']); SELECT has(a, '') FROM t; -- 0, expected 1 ``` Likewise for `0` over the numeric types, a NUL-padded `FixedString` and the `1970-01-01` `Date`, while `m['']` returns `''` instead of the stored value. Any non-default needle is correct. Reproduces on 26.5 to 26.7. **Root cause.** A `LowCardinality` dictionary reserves prefix slots for the default and NULL values, and `ReverseIndex` is built with `num_prefix_rows_to_skip`, so the reserved slot is never indexed. `ColumnUnique::uniqueInsertData` compensates for that on the write path; the read path had no counterpart. **The change.** `ColumnUnique::getOrFindValueIndex` now performs the same default-slot match as the write path. `ReverseIndex` is untouched, so no write behaviour moves. That slot becoming reachable brings two equality details. The lookup casts the constant into the element type without reporting loss, so `UInt64(256)` arrived as `UInt8(0)` and would match the default; that slot now answers only if the element type can represent the constant. And a dictionary can hold `-0.0` and `0.0` as separate entries while the shortcut has room for one index, so a zero constant over a float element type is left to the value-comparing path, as `indexOfAssumeSorted` already is. The new test covers both call sites. Lookup timing is unchanged. **Overlap with #112953.** That open PR declines this same shortcut for every float element type, subsuming the float-zero decline here, and the two conflict textually; whichever merges second should keep the broader decline and drop this one, collapsing the duplicated representability predicate to one copy. Non-float types are independent of it.

signals.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114629&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114629](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114629+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Re-land aggregate function `gini` in the `sum` family
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113868 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112280 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New aggregate function `gini`, which calculates the [Gini coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient) of a column of finite, non-negative numeric values. The result ranges from `0` (all values equal) towards `1` as inequality grows; for a sample of `n` values the maximum is `(n - 1) / n`. `NaN` values are skipped, while infinite and negative values are rejected. The function returns `Float64` and consumes `O(n)` memory. ### Description Re-lands the `gini` function that #113868 reverted, following the option-2 spec @ Manerone gave in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5217284116. `gini` now registers and folds exactly like `sum`. Relative to #112280 it drops the `getArgumentsThatCanBeOnlyNull` override, `.returns_default_when_only_null = true`, and the `argument_type->onlyNull()` branch in the creator, and touches no file under `src/AggregateFunctions/Combinators/`. The property was doing the work: it made `AggregateFunctionFactory::getImpl` skip its only-null guard and build a real `gini` over `Nullable(Nothing)`, so `gini(NULL)` returned `Float64` `nan` where every `sum`-family function folds to `Nullable(Nothing)`. Without it the fold happens in the `Null` combinator first, which is why `createAggregateFunctionSum` has no equivalent. It also drops `getOwnNullAdapter`, at @ Manerone's request in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114643#issuecomment-5354588069. Keeping it left `gini` the only function in the family whose plain and wrapped forms disagreed on nullability: the `Null` combinator consults that hook only on the object it wraps directly, and for `giniIf` / `giniDistinct` that is `AggregateFunctionIf` / `AggregateFunctionDistinct`, whose own adapters win. So `gini(x)` stayed `Float64` while `giniIf(x, c)` became `Nullable(Float64)`. Dropping it gives parity on the runtime axis too: over a `Nullable` column every form returns `Nullable(Float64)`, `NULL` when no non-`NULL` value qualifies and `nan` when fewer than two do. Non-nullable input is unchanged. Validated against `sum` on the same binary: every literal-`NULL` and `Nullable`-column cell matches its `sum` counterpart, and non-nullable results are unchanged from #112280. Docs: `gini.mdx` plus its slug-map, navigation and redirect entries are restored from their merged state in #114314, which #113868's revert had removed as collateral; the generated region is regenerated from the `FunctionDocumentation` block by `ci/jobs/scripts/docs/autogenerate/autogenerate_docs.py` (`--check` clean) and the page keeps its hand-written header. The slug-map row is needed, not cosmetic: without it the nightly generator resolves no Mintlify destination and fails for this page. The `pr-autogenerated-docs` label is what lets a page carrying the markers pass the generated-region guard, as the guard's own message asks for. cc @Manerone <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114643&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114643](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114643+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Revert "Revert "NATS: add inline credentials setting""
signals.text: Reverts https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178, restoring the `nats_credentials` setting of the `NATS` table engine (originally added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733), and fixes the reason of the original revert: the possibility of referencing arbitrary server paths through `nats_credential_file`. `nats_credential_file` is a path on the server filesystem: the server opens it with its own privileges, and during authentication the credentials are sent to `nats_url`, which comes from the same query. So a path taken from SQL lets anyone who can define a `NATS` source probe the local filesystem (the error text distinguishes a missing file, a permission error, and a file without a seed), and exfiltrate files the server can read to a NATS server they control (the part of the file before the seed line is sent verbatim in the `CONNECT` frame's `jwt` field). See the analysis in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733#discussion_r3750203599. This hole predates #110733 (`nats_credential_file` exists since 24.2), but with the inline `nats_credentials` setting restored, the path form is no longer needed in SQL at all. The restriction, modelled on `StorageMySQL::getSSLParams` (`e700bbec4c84c585`): `nats_credential_file` is accepted only from a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. Every SQL spelling — the `SETTINGS` clause, an engine-argument override `NATS(collection, nats_credential_file = ...)`, or a named collection created by `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` — throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with a message directing to `nats_credentials`. It is rejected on provenance, whether the query assigned the key at all, rather than on the resulting value, so an override with the empty string cannot silently drop the credentials the operator configured. Loading from previously-validated metadata (server startup, force-restore, and short-syntax `ATTACH`) is exempt via `isLoadingFromExistingMetadata`, so existing tables keep working after an upgrade; a user-issued full `ATTACH TABLE` query is still checked. `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` is not a bypass: the `NATS` engine does not support settings alter. The server-global `<nats>` credentials (`nats.user`, `nats.password`, `nats.token`, `nats.credential_file`) keep their established behavior of authenticating tables which define no authentication of their own, including tables whose destination comes from SQL. Whether a table defines its own authentication is decided on provenance, not on the resulting values: a query which clears the authentication a named collection carries (`nats_username = ''`) has decided it too, so the global account is not resurrected for the destination that query selected. Replacing a configured path with inline `nats_credentials` from the query remains allowed — the path itself is not used then — as long as the named collection permits it. Because the contents are the only spelling a query has, `nats_credentials` inherits the override permission of the path key it replaces, the same way `ssl_ca_pem` does for `ssl_ca` in `findOverrideForbiddingKey`: credentials the operator pinned with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">` cannot be replaced through the contents form either, in either spelling, while the contents form stays usable when `allow_named_collection_override_by_default` is disabled (it is not a new key, it replaces one the collection defines). The `SETTINGS` clause is applied on top of the collection values without passing through the named-collection override check, so `resolveCredentialSource` enforces the same permission for both spellings. An empty `nats_credentials` is refused as well: it can only drop the credentials a collection carries, in either form, never replace them with other ones. Tests: a new stateless test `04891_nats_credential_file_path_restriction` covers all rejected SQL spellings and the accepted configuration-file sources, using `NATS` named collections added to the stateless-test server configuration (`tests/config/config.d/named_collection.xml`, with `nats_url = '127.0.0.1:1'`, so passing the validation surfaces as `CANNOT_CONNECT_NATS`) — one with a plain `nats_credential_file`, one where it is locked with `overridable="false"`, and one without credentials at all; `04665_nats_credentials_named_collection` is updated — the `nats_credential_file` query-override direction is now rejected. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85213 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `NATS` table engine accepts credentials inline in the new `nats_credentials` setting (the same payload as a `.creds` file), and no longer accepts `nats_credential_file` from SQL: the path is a reference to a file on the server filesystem, which the server opens with its own privileges, so it can only be specified in a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. A query may replace such a configured path with inline `nats_credentials`, unless the operator pinned it with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">`. Tables created before this restriction keep working after an upgrade. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114644&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114644](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114644+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Speed up `IN (subquery)` set building by pre-deduplicating each `MergeTree` partition independently
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108326 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105126 The set for `IN (subquery)` is built by a single `CreatingSetsTransform`: all streams of the subquery are merged into one and every row is hashed serially, no matter how many threads read the data. If the partition expression of the subquery's table is a function of the subquery's output columns (the set is keyed on all of them), the reading will now emit each partition through a single port and each stream is deduplicated independently before the filling transform. Because a key then lives in exactly one stream, per-stream deduplication is complete, and the single filling transform only hashes unique rows — the serial part of the build shrinks from all rows to distinct rows, and the deduplication itself runs in parallel. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() PARTITION BY a % 8; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000000 FROM numbers(100000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t) SETTINGS allow_creating_set_partitions_independently = 1, max_threads = 8; ``` ```response (CreatingSets) DelayedPorts 9 → 8 (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (Aggregating) Resize 1 → 8 AggregatingTransform (Expression) ExpressionTransform (Filter) FilterTransform (ReadFromSystemNumbers) NumbersRange 0 → 1 (CreatingSet) CreatingSetsTransform <- the single filling transform now hashes ~1M unique rows instead of 100M Resize 8 → 1 DistinctTransform × 8 <- new: parallel pre-deduplication on partition-disjoint streams (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (ReadFromMergeTree) MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 8 0 → 1 <- per-partition reading (8 partitions → 8 streams) ``` On the table above (100M rows, 1M distinct keys, 8 balanced partitions; 64-core machine, average of 3 runs after 2 warm-ups): | query | off | on | speedup | |------------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------| | `SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t)` | 0.643s | 0.113s | 5.7× | ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up set building for `IN (subquery)` on partitioned `MergeTree` tables by keeping each partition's rows within a single stream and deduplicating each stream independently, so the single set-filling transform — previously hashing every row serially — only sees unique rows. This applies when the partition expression is a deterministic function of the subquery's output columns. The optimization is not applied when the largest partition holds more than twice the rows of the average partition; the new setting `force_creating_set_partitions_independently` (disabled by default) bypasses this check. Controlled by the new setting `allow_creating_set_partitions_independently` (enabled by default). --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114645&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114645](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114645+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]
