signals.title: Avoid overflow in the `uniq` aggregate function at cardinalities above ten billion
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/6078 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `uniq` aggregate function returned garbage (e.g. `18446743978444128518`) for cardinalities above roughly thirty billion, because its state kept only 32 bits of each hash and the correction formula overflowed. The state now additionally keeps a small sample of full 64-bit hashes (state version `1`) which the estimate switches to at about two billion elements: `SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000)` returns `99642145106` (−0.36%), and the estimate stays accurate (about 1%) up to trillions. Below two billion nothing changes: the estimates, the memory usage and the state format are exactly as before, and states written by older versions remain readable and merge correctly in mixed-version clusters. --- ### The bug The `uniq` state (`UniquesHashSet`, a BJKST-style adaptive sampling set) keeps hashes truncated to 32 bits. Beyond a few billion distinct values all `2^32` hash values fill up, and the collision-correction formula computes `round(2^32 * (log(2^32) - log(2^32 - res)))` with `res >= 2^32` — `log` of a non-positive number, and the cast of the resulting infinity/NaN to an integer is undefined behavior that produced the values reported in the issue. ### The fix The main sample stays in the historical 32-bit format, bit for bit — below two billion elements nothing changes at all: same estimates, same memory, same serialized bytes. In addition, the state maintains a small sample of full 64-bit hashes (the "wide" set): only one hash in `262144` enters it, and it is bounded by 16384 values (256 KiB), thinned out further beyond that. For normal states it is empty or tiny — about 4 values per million distinct elements — and `size()` switches to it once it has at least 8192 values, i.e. at about two billion elements, where its statistical error (~1%) meets the degrading precision of the 32-bit sample. The legacy formula is also clamped, so a saturated 32-bit estimate returns its saturation limit (~9.5e10) instead of the garbage above. The wide sample must be fed from the very first insertion — the high bits of the hashes of already-consumed elements are unrecoverable. This also rules out the reviewer-suggested variant of converting the state at a threshold: with parallel or distributed aggregation every partial state stays below any threshold, no 64-bit information is ever captured, and the merged estimate stays capped (~9.5e10) no matter the real cardinality — I implemented that variant and measured exactly this on `numbers_mt(50000000000)`. Feeding a heavily pre-thinned sample from the start gets the same memory profile without that trap. **State versioning** follows the `quantileDeterministic` scheme (#112052) exactly: version `1` (a flags byte, the main sample in the legacy layout, then the wide sample if present) is spelled out in fresh state types and pinned at DDL time; the default version stays `0` so unversioned persisted data keeps its layout; the wire version is derived from the negotiated revision (new constant `DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_UNIQ_STATE_VERSION_1 = 54493`), so an old peer receives plain version-`0` states. A version-`0` state simply carries no wide sample, and merging it degrades only the merged-in elements to the old 32-bit precision. ### Results ``` SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(2000000000) -- 2006192184 (+0.31%, still the 32-bit sample) SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(4000000000) -- 3979938734 (-0.50%, the 64-bit sample) SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(50000000000) -- 50090681348 (+0.18%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000) -- 99642145106 (-0.36%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(1000000000000) -- 1016359869734 (+1.6%) ``` Cross-version compatibility was verified against a real 26.7 server: all six mixed-version scenarios (raw state columns and partial aggregation states, both directions, plus a two-shard mixed `remote`) return exactly the value the old server computes natively (`1001943` for `numbers(1000000)`), since the main sample is identical. ### Costs - Memory and serialized size are unchanged below ~1 million distinct elements per state (the wide sample is empty for almost all states; `sizeof` of the state grows by one pointer). From there the wide sample adds `n / 16384` bytes, up to +50% (256 KiB over the 512 KiB main table) for multi-billion-cardinality states. - The insertion hot path gains one branchless check per value. The batched path detects the rare candidates without calls inside the loop, and the instruction count of `SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers(100000000)` is within 0.1% of master (wall-clock comparison on my machine was inconclusive due to load; the perf tests will tell). - Above two billion the estimate error is ~0.8-1.1% (8192-16384 samples) versus ~0.6% below — and versus garbage before this change. ### Two latent bugs of #112052 fixed on the way Both reproduce with `quantileDeterministic` on current master and were exposed by the new `uniq` version: - `ColumnBLOB::toBLOB` (parallel block marshalling) serialized the payload with the state version resolved from the local type, while `NativeWriter::write` announces the version derived from the negotiated revision, so the receiver lost sync inside the blob: `SELECT medianDeterministic(n, n) FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', default, t) GROUP BY n % 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_blocks_marshalling = 1, prefer_localhost_replica = 0` failed with `Skip degree in quantileDeterministic state is 120` (an exception, in a release build). - A view of a `ColumnAggregateFunction` (the result of a sort, filter, or index operation) and a plain copy of it dropped the state version, so `SELECT arraySlice(groupArray(x), 1, 1) FROM (SELECT medianDeterministicState(number, number) AS x FROM numbers(10) GROUP BY number ORDER BY number)` failed with `Cannot read all data`. ### Tests - A `gtest` suite for `UniquesHashSet`: the estimator at a simulated cardinality of `10^11`, the saturation clamp of the legacy formula, round trips of both formats, wide-sample merges with thinning, merges with legacy states, the insertion path feeding the wide sample, and rejection of corrupt states. - `05023_uniq_state_version_64bit_hashes`: version pinning, wire round trips of both versions, cross-version merges, and that the values below two billion are identical across versions. - `05024_aggregate_state_version_parallel_marshalling`, `05025_aggregate_state_version_in_column_views` for the two bugs above (covering both `uniq` and `quantileDeterministic`). - `05026_uniq_64bit_sample_above_two_billion` (`long`): an end-to-end four-billion-row check of the switch to the 64-bit sample; the result does not depend on the distribution of rows between threads. - Since the 32-bit sample is bit-identical to master, only the tests that print state type names or raw state bytes needed reference updates; all `uniq` value references below two billion are untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115393&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115393](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115393+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Enforce settings constraints on nested SETTINGS and SET name = DEFAULT
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109473 Two code paths mutated session or query settings without calling `checkSettingsConstraints`, so an authenticated user could override a setting an administrator had locked with `CONST`, `readonly`, `MIN`/`MAX`, or a feature tier. Where those constraints are the tenant-isolation boundary, this breaks multi-tenant isolation. ### A nested `SETTINGS` clause was applied unchecked `QueryTreeBuilder::buildSelectExpression` applied a `SELECT` node's `SETTINGS` clause to the per-node context copy with no constraint check. A clause on an outer query is validated by `InterpreterSetQuery::applySettingsFromQuery`, but a clause inside a subquery, a CTE, or a view's inner query reached only the analyzer. The Planner then read the mutated context, so with `additional_table_filters` - a documented row-level isolation mechanism - the user read other tenants' rows: ```sql -- rejected SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}; -- accepted before this change, returning every tenant's rows SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}); ``` There were no `checkSettingsConstraints` call sites anywhere in `src/Analyzer`, `src/Planner` or `src/Processors`. The legacy interpreter has always checked the same clause in `InterpreterSelectQuery`, so the analyzer becoming the default silently dropped the check. ### `SET name = DEFAULT` was applied unchecked The parser stores `SET k = v` in `ASTSetQuery::changes` and `SET k = DEFAULT` in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, and only the former was validated before `Context::resetSettingsToDefaultValue` applied the compiled-in default. So `SET readonly = DEFAULT` cleared a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile and re-enabled `INSERT`, `CREATE` and `DROP`, and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` cleared a resource cap. The same gap existed in the Arrow Flight `SetSessionOptions` reset branch, whose value-assignment branch already checked. ### A `profile` change was not checked against the constraints it installs A `SET` statement was validated as a whole before it ran, but a `profile` change among its settings replaces the constraint set halfway through it. So a single statement overrode the very constraint that the profile it names installs, while the same settings applied as two separate statements were rejected: ```sql -- rejected SET profile = 'p'; SET max_execution_time = 999; -- accepted before this change, for a profile p with max_execution_time = 10 CONST SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = 999; SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = DEFAULT; ``` ### The fix A new `SettingsConstraints::checkCanReset` validates a reset request, reached through `Context::checkSettingsConstraintsForDefaults` from both `InterpreterSetQuery` entry points, the Arrow Flight reset branch, and the analyzer: * For a built-in setting the compiled-in default is checked as the new value, via the new `Settings::getDefaultValue`, so min/max, `CONST`, tier and source restrictions all apply. Resetting a setting that already holds its default stays allowed, including under `readonly = 1`, because the constraint checker skips a change equal to the current value. * A custom setting has no compiled-in default - resetting it erases it - so only its writability is checked. This matters: erasing a `CONST` custom setting that a row policy reads through `getSetting` is exactly how the reported isolation boundary was broken. `buildSelectExpression` also no longer ignores a nested `SETTINGS name = DEFAULT`, which was previously a silent no-op; it is now checked and applied as a reset. It is applied to the subquery's context only and is not recorded on the `QueryNode`, so it stays invisible to the consumers that read a subquery's settings off the query tree - as it was when the clause was dropped outright. That limitation is documented at the call site and tracked in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115415. For the `profile` case, `InterpreterSetQuery` now checks the rest of the statement against the constraints the profile installs. That requires the profile to have been applied first, so the checking runs on a scratch copy of the context and nothing is applied to the real one until all of it passes: a rejected statement leaves the session alone rather than applying the profile and dropping its own tail. The changes are then applied in one call with the original list, so the order in which they take effect - and therefore which assignment wins - is unchanged. ### Behaviour change A `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view - the default for `CREATE VIEW` - whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails. This restores the behaviour of the legacy interpreter, which has always checked that clause. An administrator can keep such a view working with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER`, because `getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext` switches to the definer, whose constraints then apply. Note the limit of that workaround: it copies the invoker's changed setting *values* while switching the user, so a `CONST`/`MIN`/`MAX` constraint does not travel and the view works, but a `readonly = 1` value does travel and the inner clause is rejected even under `DEFINER`. A `readonly` user reading a view whose inner query sets a setting therefore has no workaround other than removing the clause from the view. ### Testing `05019_settings_constraints_reset_and_nested` covers, in a `CONST`-constrained session: a rejected `SET x = DEFAULT`; a no-op reset of an already-default setting still being allowed; a `CONST` custom setting resisting erasure; a nested `SETTINGS` clause rejected in a subquery, in a CTE, and in the `= DEFAULT` form; an unconstrained nested clause still working; and a `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view still reading while its `INVOKER` equivalent is rejected. It also pins down that a `SETTINGS` clause written after a nested `UNION` or `INTERSECT` is rejected: the parser attaches such a clause to one of the member `SELECT`s rather than to the compound query, so it is covered by the same check, whichever member it lands on. `05021_settings_constraints_set_profile_in_same_query` covers the `profile` case: an explicit value and a reset after the `profile` change both rejected against the profile's constraints, the profile left unapplied by a rejected statement, an assignment before the `profile` change still allowed, the profile's constraints in force afterwards, and an unconstrained setting after the change still applying. `05020_settings_constraints_readonly_user` covers a user under a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile: `SET readonly = DEFAULT` and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` both rejected, the session still readonly afterwards, and a nested `SETTINGS` clause unable to lift the user's row filter. One existing test needed a fix. `04102_hash_join_stress_test` used `SETTINGS max_joined_block_rows = 100` inside a subquery; the setting is called `max_joined_block_size_rows`. The misspelling went unnoticed because `Settings` accepts custom settings, so `Settings::set` stores an unrecognised name instead of rejecting it, and the `SQL_`/`custom_` prefix validation lives in `AccessControl::checkSettingNameIsAllowed`, reached only from `SettingsConstraints::checkImpl`. The same clause on a top-level query has always been rejected with `UNKNOWN_SETTING`; only the nested form escaped. The name is now spelled correctly. The Arrow Flight reset branch is not covered by a test: there is no functional-test harness for the Arrow Flight server, and the change there is the same three lines as its sibling value-assignment branch. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a settings-constraint bypass. A `SETTINGS` clause inside a subquery, a CTE or a view's inner query, `SET <name> = DEFAULT`, and a setting assigned or reset after a `profile` change in the same `SET` statement, now all enforce settings constraints, so none of them can be used to leave readonly mode or to override a `CONST`, `MIN` or `MAX` constraint. Note that a `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails, matching the behaviour of the old analyzer; use `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for such a view. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115397&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115397](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115397+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Bound the Cascades cluster node count by the distributed-read bucket limit
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A very large `distributed_plan_workers_num` no longer makes the server abort with a `std::length_error` when the experimental `make_distributed_plan` and `enable_cascades_optimizer` are enabled. Such a node count is now rejected with `INVALID_SETTING_VALUE`. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109770 That PR capped the sibling setting the same way. Found by `AST fuzzer (arm_asan_ubsan)`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105987&sha=58887a838b23240918d8f9e717a4bed777136134&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) (unrelated carrier PR). Reproduces deterministically: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t SETTINGS enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, make_distributed_plan = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 9223372036854775807; -- std::length_error in sliceMarksAcrossBuckets; the server dies in a debug build ``` `buildContext` resolves `cluster_node_count` from the internal query parameter, from `distributed_plan_workers_num`, or from the configured worker cluster, checking only for zero. The `ParallelRead` rule passes it through as the read's bucket count, and `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets` sizes a vector to it as its first statement, before the 256 ceiling already threaded in is consulted. `buildContext` now also rejects a resolved count above `max_distributed_read_buckets`, beside the existing zero check. Bounding the resolved value covers all three sources of the count and every consumer of it: the read buckets, the layer budget `FINAL` derives from them, and the exchange fan-out sized from the count. Not inside `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets`, which `FINAL` legitimately calls with `target_buckets * 16`-derived counts before grouping the layers into at most 256 tasks. Behaviour change: a count above 256 that did not reach the plain slicer (`257`, a `FINAL` read, or a worker cluster above 256 replicas) is planned today and is now refused. Such a plan reads serially but can still scatter to that many exchange destinations, which is the memory cost this same ceiling already bounds for the sibling settings. @ davenger, say so if you would rather bound the setting itself (a worker lease count) or clamp. `04320_distributed_plan_read_rejects.sql` gains seven arms: both sources of the count, both read paths, and three positive controls (256 accepted on the plain and `FINAL` paths, plus a rule-based query with a huge `workers_num` untouched). It fails on unpatched master with `server died`, and passed 50/50 runs with the fix. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115398&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115398](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115398+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Wait for the worker cleanup before force-killing the test workers
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113393 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description No related open issue; found while investigating `Stress test (*)` jobs failing with only ` script exit code: 1`. `do_run_tests` stopped a run by SIGTERMing each worker and waiting `join(timeout=10)` before SIGKILLing it. That worker's SIGTERM path reaches `kill_process_group`, which on a sanitizer build sleeps **60** seconds, so every worker got 10 seconds for a 60 second cleanup and died inside that sleep. Two consequences. The sanitizer report is truncated, which is what the grace in `1a76ce9b81ce3fc` exists to collect. And `p.kill()` reaches only the worker, not the test's process group, whose PGID file is already unlinked, so the test's `bash` and `clickhouse-client` survive. The harness's random query killer then kills that leaked client and the orphaned `bash` writes `Terminated` into the log descriptor it inherited. Landing while the job packages the logs, `tar` exits 1 on `file changed as we read it`, killing the job *before* the hung check. The wait is now derived from the delays cleanup sleeps for, so the two cannot drift apart again; `ddc6bcfbd68a761`'s SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL, wait escalation is unchanged. Workers clean up concurrently, so the grace is one monotonic deadline for all of them, and a ceiling rather than a sleep. It bounds one cleanup invocation, not the whole cleanup: a worker owning several process groups pays the sleeps per group and its later groups are still cut short. No wait is shorter than the previous 10 seconds, so nothing regresses. Remaining gaps below. Aggregate shutdown grows: N wedged workers cost 70 + (N-1)*10 seconds on a sanitizer lane, 80 + (N-1)*10 with stacktrace capture, against N*10 before, so about +60s on 16 workers. Cheap against losing a report, but it is CI wall-clock. A unit test pinning the budget was removed on review request, so it rests on the CI stop-path runs. <details> <summary>Affected runs, validation, #113393</summary> All four are sanitizer lanes over three weeks, `base_ref=master`. In each the worker log stops after the `SANITIZED`-gated print, never reaching `Killing process group`, and the archived log is 11 bytes short. Release and debug lanes, which skip that sleep, show none. Also uncovered: the stacktrace collection, an uninterruptible sleep, and `spawn` workers (`aarch` names), which have no cleanup. - [`57ffb33`, PR 111575, `arm_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111575&sha=57ffb330ff3e3da66a99a2c8dfa6f4a49ffddc27&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) - [`5639d68`, PR 107736, `arm_tsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107736&sha=5639d68fe32623687d7dba60a6f72a58ffd1603b&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29) - [`542bb86`, PR 112951, `arm_msan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112951&sha=542bb86022afb31800274d59fcd836d8c7dfc159&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_msan%29) - [`6e15957`, PR 114695, `amd_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114695&sha=6e159579fc017f42673653cf0db45fc03ac9090d&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29) Before the test was removed, eleven mutations each reddened it distinctly (flat 10s, no `kill()` escalation, unbounded wait, sleep instead of ceiling, per-worker budget, either delay dropped, floor gone, wall-clock deadline, call site reverted). End to end with real processes, the pre-change shape leaks the `bash` and writes those 11 bytes 3/3; this change eliminates it 3/3. #113393 (mine, open) extracts this same sequence into `quiesce_workers_and_reap()` and keeps `p.join(timeout=10)` verbatim, relocating this defect without fixing it. Complementary (that one reaps orphaned groups, this one stops creating them) but textually conflicting. I can rebase onto it or fold this in there. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115403&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115403](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115403+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.text: Support distributed `GROUPING SETS` aggregation in the Cascades optimizer. Follow-up to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114950, which added it to the rule-based distributed planner; with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` such an aggregation stayed on a single node. - `TwoStageAggregationTransformation` accepts grouping-set aggregations: every worker builds partial states for every grouping set over its share of the data, and one node merges them per set. signals.title: TimeSeries: optional TTL'd recent samples table preferred by PromQL for short time ranges
signals.text: On a large `TimeSeries` table the most frequent queries — alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards — pay primary-key analysis over the whole multi-billion-row samples table and read one full granule per series: on a 71.4B-sample corpus a bare instant selector takes 0.85 s cold to return a few hundred points. When the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a fourth target table (`RECENT SAMPLES`) mimicking the samples table, plus an inner materialized view `.inner_id.recentsamplesmv.<uuid>` copying `id`, `timestamp`, `value` into it on every insert. The recent table adds `PARTITION BY` from `recent_samples_partition_by` (default `toDate(timestamp)`), `TTL toDateTime(timestamp) + toIntervalSecond(<ttl>)` with `ttl_only_drop_parts = 1`, and `recent_samples_index_granularity` (default 8192). PromQL selector reads (`prometheusQuery`, `prometheusQueryRange`, the HTTP API, remote read) prefer it whenever the selector's whole range fits in the TTL window (`min_time >= now() - TTL`) — safe because `ttl_only_drop_parts` drops a part only when all its rows have expired. The preference can be disabled with the new query setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. Off by default; not supported in `Replicated` databases yet (the inner materialized view would get a different UUID on every replica). Measured on a 71.4B-sample / 30-day / 413k-series corpus (40 PromQL queries, cold geomean vs the same binary without the feature): rules 5x (bare selector 0.85 s → 0.03 s, alert 1.9 s → 0.20 s), 30m dashboards 3.5-4.3x, 6h 1.4x, 24h 1.1x, overall 1.6-1.7x; results value-identical to 1e-15. A TTL of ~3 days is the sweet spot: it covers the intraday horizon including `offset 24h` panels at +10% disk, and avoids the regression seen with a 10d TTL, where 7d-range queries switch to the recent table and get 15% slower than on the single sorted part. Hourly partitioning is a wash overall and multiplies part count 24x, so day partitioning is the default. The cost is ingest: a fresh remote-write load of 1.3B samples slows from 324 s to 455-475 s (−30% throughput) — hence opt-in; a dedicated batched sink instead of the generic materialized-view chain is a possible follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TimeSeries` tables can now keep a "recent samples" table: when the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a TTL'd copy of the samples table (partitioned by `recent_samples_partition_by`, by day by default) fed by an inner materialized view, and PromQL queries whose time range fits in the TTL window automatically read from it, making alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards several times faster on large tables. The preference can be disabled with the new query-level setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115441&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115441](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115441+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Nullable(Array) stages 1-2: type foundation and collision-free substream names
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115394 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 Stages 1 and 2 of the staged `Nullable(Array(T))` implementation described in the RFC, ClickHouse/ClickHouse#115394. Internal machinery only: **the type is still unreachable from any query**, and there is no user-visible change. `DataTypeFactory` continues to reject the string `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, so this cannot be reached through DDL, a table function's column list, or any function that takes a type by name. That boundary is itself pinned by a test, so opening it in a later stage is a deliberate change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. The two stages ship together because Stage 1 alone has no production caller — `makeNullableAllowingArray` would land exercised only by unit tests. Stage 2 is the first thing that uses it. They are separate commits. ### Stage 1: the type-level foundation `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable` keeps returning `false`, permanently. That predicate is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and each encodes an assumption about which types can be wrapped. Leaving its meaning untouched means no existing code path can begin producing `Nullable(Array(...))` on its own; only code that explicitly opts in can. `makeNullableAllowingArray` is that opt-in and it is the only door — the constructor it uses is private, reachable through a single friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. The cost is that `canBeInsideNullable` now answers `false` for a type that can in fact sit inside `Nullable`. Two consequences are pinned by tests so they are deliberate rather than discovered later: `makeNullable` rejects an array, and `makeNullableSafe` silently returns the array unwrapped instead of throwing. The second is how a `Nullable(Array)` could be quietly degraded to `Array`; the sites where that matters are audited in a later stage. ### Stage 2: collision-free substream names `Nullable` appends `.null` to a stream name and `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1` and so on, while array *elements* contribute no component at all. A `Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))` column would write two different null maps to the same file. A second, structured naming scheme inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements, and is selected per column from the type as stored in the part: ```text Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.nested Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.null c.array.nested Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))) -> c.size0 c.array.null c.array.array.size0 c.array.array.nested.null c.array.array.nested Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c (unchanged) ``` Types legal today keep byte-identical names, so existing parts stay readable with no migration and no format version bump. ### Testing Expectations are derived from real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than hand-built substream paths. That distinction turned out to matter: `SerializationNullable` emits its null-map substream and pops it before recursing, so a path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs. The real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and the naming code branches on whether a null map precedes the final substream. Expectations written against constructed paths can be entirely self-consistent and still disagree with what is written to disk. The criteria are stated as properties over a corpus rather than as spot checks: - **No existing stream name changes.** Asserted as a proof rather than a sample: for 28 currently-legal types the structured scheme is never selected, neither by type nor by any enumerated path. If it is never reached then the legacy naming code is the only code that runs, and this change does not modify it. - **Typed and untyped callers agree** for every legal type, so a column cannot be written under one set of names and read under another. - **All names distinct** for thirteen shapes placing `Nullable(Array)` inside arrays, tuples, maps and variants — including their substream cache keys and their prefix/suffix substreams. - **Subcolumn reads resolve to files the writer produced.** 31 unit tests across the three suites; the full `unit_tests_dbms` suite is green at 22732 passed, 0 failed. ### Two things worth a reviewer's attention **The substream-to-name mapping existed in three places** — `getNameForSubstreamPath`, a full copy, and a partial per-element copy — and the full copy had already drifted: it was missing `MapBucketIndexes`, so a bucketed `Map` holding a `Nullable(Array)` would have lost that name component and could have written two streams under one file name. Both copies are gone, replaced by `ISerialization::getLegacyNameForSubstreamPath`. **The naming scheme cannot be decided from the substream path alone.** The path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The column type is load-bearing, and a caller that does not supply one cannot be answered correctly. Where the path proves a type was needed — `NullableElements` above an array substream can only come from a `Nullable` directly over an `Array` — resolving a name without one now raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than quietly returning a legacy name no writer produced. A test asserts this guard never fires for any currently-legal type. Ensuring every MergeTree caller passes the type is an explicit obligation for the next stage. ### Attribution The design and a substantial amount of the code originate in ClickHouse/ClickHouse#104816 by @zhanglistar, which was closed in favour of this staged implementation. Both commits carry a `Co-authored-by` trailer. The blocker analysis that shaped the design is @Avogar's, and the resolutions to it are @alexey-milovidov's. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115464&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115464](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115464+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Perf: Optimize PromQL unless for exact groups
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL `unless` expressions with an exact group key skip redundant matching stages. ## What changed - add an **exact-group fast path** for the PromQL set operator `unless` - use it when both inputs already dropped `__name__`, there is no `on(...)`, and `ignoring()` is empty or absent - join the unique left and right `VECTOR_GRID` inputs directly on `group` - remove the RHS `GROUP BY`, `countForEach`, and transformed `join_group` work from this path - preserve the full LHS array when the RHS group is missing - preserve each LHS sample when the matching RHS sample is NULL - keep `on(...)`, `on()`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, and other transformed matching keys on the existing general path ## Why this is safe `VECTOR_GRID` guarantees one row per `group`. The fast path is enabled only when the matching rules leave the original `group` column unchanged on both sides, so the join key is already unique and exact. The RHS projection adds a literal group-present marker. This keeps a missing RHS row distinct from a real RHS row whose values are NULL at some timestamps. The exact path then applies the same element-wise `unless` behavior as the existing lowering. The generic path is unchanged for matching rules that transform or collapse the group key. Empty `ignoring()` is treated like default matching when both inputs already have exact groups. ## Benchmark fixture `tests/performance/promql_set_operators_unless.xml` uses the same workload as the related set-operator benchmarks: - 8,000 series - 4,000 matching groups - 300 samples per series - exact-group `unless` compared with an equivalent `unless on(instance)` control The default query uses the new fast path. The `on(instance)` query keeps the existing general implementation. ## Tests - add grouped exact-output coverage for `unless` - add exact-output coverage for empty `ignoring()` - keep the existing default and non-empty `ignoring(...)` coverage on the general path - add the paired performance fixture - run focused Python, XML, and diff checks Related: #115219, #115374 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115476&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115476](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115476+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add with_source parameter to the JSON type storing the JSON text in the __source sub-column
signals.text: ## Motivation Reading a whole `JSON` value as a `String` (`toString(json)`, or just selecting the column in a text format) is expensive: it reads every sub-column of the JSON column — all typed paths, all dynamic paths and the shared data structure — and constructs the JSON object back for every row. Applications that store JSON documents and ship them back verbatim pay this on every query. ## What was added The `JSON` type accepts a new parameter `with_source`. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in a separate `String` sub-column `__source`: ```sql CREATE TABLE test (json JSON(with_source=1)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO test VALUES ('{"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42}'); SELECT json, json.__source FROM test; ``` ``` ┌─json─────────────────┬─json.__source─────────────┐ │ {"a":42,"b":"Hello"} │ {"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42} │ └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ ``` Reading `json.__source` reads a single sub-column. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such a column write the stored text instead of constructing it from the object (it saves the construction, not the reading of the column). The text is stored exactly as it was inserted. Where the original text is not available it is created from the object itself, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON: values restored from an aggregation or `JOIN` key, binary input without the JSON text (structured `RowBinary`), nested `JSON(with_source=1)` type hints (only the top level column gets the original text), and results of functions creating JSON objects such as `mergedJSONPatch`. `__source` is reserved in such types: a top level JSON key with this name is rejected during parsing, and the name cannot be used as a type hint or in the `SKIP` section. Nested keys with this name are fine. Adding or removing the parameter with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` always rewrites the data. The stored text is not a part of the value: it doesn't participate in comparison, so two values with the same content but different formatting stay equal and are grouped together. ## Implementation notes - The text is stored in a separate `String` column inside `ColumnObject` and serialized into its own named `ObjectSource` sub-stream, so `json.__source` is a static sub-column resolved the same way a named tuple element is. The sub-stream exists in all `Object` serialization versions except `STRING`, where the JSON text is the payload itself, and no `Object` serialization version was bumped. - In binary type encoding the JSON type version is bumped to `1`, and version `1` is written only for types that actually have `with_source=1`, so encodings of all other types stay byte-identical and readable by older servers. - `ColumnObject` keeps its type to create the text when the original is not available; the serialization for it is built lazily on first use, so nothing is built for columns that never need it. - The aggregation key representation (`serializeValueIntoArena`) deliberately stays canonical, i.e. it doesn't include the text; otherwise values differing only in formatting would form different `GROUP BY` groups while comparison says they are equal. ## Limitations - Text created from the object is written without the settings used during parsing, so with `json_type_escape_dots_in_keys` enabled keys with dots appear in it escaped (`{"a%2Eb" : 42}`). - `Native` in JSON-as-string mode transmits the constructed text unless `output_format_json_type_use_source` is set. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `with_source` parameter to the `JSON` data type. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in the reserved `__source` `String` sub-column, so reading the whole value as a string is a single sub-column read instead of reading every path and constructing the JSON back. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such columns write the stored text. The text is kept as it was inserted; where the original text is not available (for example for values restored from an aggregation key) it is created from the object, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON. A top level JSON key named `__source` is not allowed in such types. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115477&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115477](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115477+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Use the primary key index for first-tuple-element conditions and `pointInEllipses`
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54805 Follow-up to #112956, which taught `KeyCondition` to use the primary key index for `pointInPolygon(coord, [...])` with a `Point` key column. This PR closes the remaining gaps of the same shape: 1. **Conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column** (`coord.1 < 100`, `tupleElement(coord, 1) = 5`, or access by element name for named tuples) now use the primary key index. Tuple values are ordered lexicographically, so the first element is a non-strictly monotonic function of the tuple; it is analyzed through the regular monotonic-functions chain (`FunctionFirstTupleElementOfKey`), so composed chains such as `coord.1 + 1 <= N` and `NOT` also work. Other elements are not monotonic w.r.t. the tuple order and remain unanalyzed. 2. **`pointInEllipses(x, y, x0, y0, a, b, ...)`** over key columns now uses the primary key (and minmax) index. The analysis stores the union bounding box of the ellipses as a rectangle ring and reuses the existing `pointInPolygon` evaluation unchanged, in both the regular and the lightweight analysis paths. The box follows the function's exact semantics: an ellipse with a non-positive or `NaN` parameter matches no point (the function's own bounding-box check never passes for it); if all ellipses are empty, the condition folds to `ALWAYS_FALSE`; a non-finite box declines the analysis. The atom only ever reports `{maybe, maybe}` or `{no match, maybe}`, so `NOT pointInEllipses` stays correct. 3. **`pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), ...)` and `pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, ...)`** — the point written as the two elements of one tuple-typed key column — resolve to the single-key-column form from #112956, deriving the point's bounding box from the range of the tuple key column. Previously this natural rewrite silently disabled the index. ```sql CREATE TABLE points (coord Point) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY coord; INSERT INTO points SELECT (number, number) FROM numbers(100000); SELECT count() FROM points WHERE coord.1 <= 25000; -- Before: 100000 rows read (full scan). After: 26/100 granules. SELECT count() FROM points WHERE pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, 0., 0., 5000., 5000.); -- Before: full scan. After: 6/100 granules. ``` Note: the reference outputs of the two new tests were computed analytically (counts from the data distribution, granule counts from `index_granularity = 1000`); if CI reports a formatting difference in the `EXPLAIN` lines, I will update the references from the CI output. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Use the primary key index for conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `coord.1 < 100` for a table ordered by a `Point` column), for `pointInEllipses` over key columns, and for `pointInPolygon`/`pointInEllipses` with the point written as the two elements of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), [...])`). Follow-up to [#112956](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115482&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115482](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115482+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Stop resolving the UTC time zone in `TimezoneMixin`
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> While profiling `clickhouse local --query "SELECT 1"` it turned out that almost all of the run happens before the query: the query itself took 1ms of a 45ms run. This is one of the sources of that startup work, split out of #112496. `TimezoneMixin` resolved the UTC time zone in its constructor, in addition to the named or default one. Building a `DateLUTImpl` walks ~146k days through cctz, about 70M instructions, and `DataTypeDateTime` / `DataTypeDateTime64` get constructed just to name a column type — for example when building the schemas of the system tables — without ever touching UTC. Only the serializations need UTC, for ISO output and for the `best_effort` parsers, so `SerializationDateTime`, `SerializationDateTime64` and the `DateTime` / `DateTime64` nodes of `JSONExtractTree` declare their own `utc_time_zone` member instead. The cost is then paid once per formatter rather than once per named type. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Naming a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` type no longer builds a UTC time zone lookup table that nothing reads, which makes constructing these types — and therefore starting up `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` — faster. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115488&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115488](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115488+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1780` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Stop copying a system table's metadata twice to set its comment
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> Noticed while profiling start-up for #112496. Attaching a system table fetched the table back from `DatabaseCatalog` and copied its whole `StorageInMemoryMetadata` — which carries the full `ColumnsDescription` — twice, only to fill in the comment. Since there are ~164 system tables, every start-up copied every system table's schema two extra times. `IStorage::setInMemoryMetadataComment` replaces only the comment, and it is now applied to the storage before it is attached, so the catalog lookup goes away as well. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Attaching the system tables no longer copies each table's metadata, including its full column description, twice just to set the table comment. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115490&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115490](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115490+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Resolve the client hostname in `ClientInfo` on demand
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> Split out of #112496. `ClientInfo::fillOSUserHostNameAndVersionInfo` resolved the local FQDN through `getFQDNOrHostName`, a blocking `getaddrinfo` that also dlopens the NSS modules. Every `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` invocation paid for it even when nothing ever asked for the name, and a resolver that is slow or unreachable sat on the startup path with no short timeout. `getClientHostName` resolves it on first use instead, and `getFQDNOrHostName` caches process-wide, so the readers — `system.processes`, `query_log`, `session_log` and the TCP handshake — see the same value as before. When the name arrives from a peer in `ClientInfo::read` it describes that peer rather than us, so it is kept as received and never re-resolved locally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The client hostname is now resolved when it is first reported instead of on every `clickhouse client` and `clickhouse local` invocation. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115491&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115491](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115491+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: macOS binary signing: prod key via dedicated signing runner
signals.text: Cuts macOS cask signing over to the prod Apple Developer ID key. signals.title: Support safe type conversions in correlated subquery equivalence substitution
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113407 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101863 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Correlated subqueries with an equality on columns that differ only in nullability (e.g. `Int64` vs `Nullable(Int64)` under `data_type_default_nullable = 1`, as in TPC-DS Q35), or on native-number columns having a least common type (e.g. `Int32` vs `Int64`), are now decorrelated via equivalent-expression substitution instead of falling back to a CROSS JOIN with a post-join filter, avoiding severe memory growth on such queries. Closes #113407. --- ## Motivation The equivalent-expression substitution in `PlannerCorrelatedSubqueries` recorded an equivalence only when both sides of the correlated `equals` had exactly the same type. A correlated `EXISTS` whose join condition compares `Int64` with `Nullable(Int64)` therefore decorrelated through the CROSS JOIN fallback; at TPC-DS SF100 (Q35 with `data_type_default_nullable = 1`) the cross-joined intermediate grew without bound (35+ GiB and climbing before being killed, versus 1.72 s / 1.70 GiB with aligned column types). ## Approach The exact-type guard was load-bearing: correlated columns are `PLACEHOLDER` nodes typed with the outer column's type, and every decorrelated DAG declares that type for its inputs, so a substituted column of a different runtime type is a logical error during execution. The substitution therefore cannot simply alias a column of another type, nor cast to the common supertype — it must produce exactly the placeholder's type. Equivalence classes now track `(column name, type)` pairs. The recording guard admits, besides equal types, two verified-safe families: - nullability-only differences (any base type) — the equality predicate rejects `NULL`s; - native-number pairs with a least supertype — for them `equals` is mathematically exact (`9007199254740993 :: Int64 = 9007199254740992.0 :: Float64` is `0`), the supertype exists only when every type embeds losslessly, and `accurateCastOrNull` is exactness-checking, so value equivalence is transitive across a class. At substitution the chosen equivalent column is converted to exactly the correlated type: `toNullable` / lossless `CAST` when widening, `assumeNotNull` / `accurateCastOrNull` when narrowing. For the narrowing conversions a `FilterStep` is inserted below the renaming that drops rows whose value is `NULL` or does not convert exactly — such rows can never satisfy the recorded equality (a top-level AND-conjunct of an ancestor filter), and dropping them before `assumeNotNull` is required so that its arbitrary result for non-converting values cannot leak into aggregation keys (the aggregation decorrelation appends correlated identifiers as group keys). Pairs whose comparison semantics are not consistent with `CAST` keep the previous CROSS JOIN fallback: `Decimal` vs `Float` (comparison converts to `Float` and is inexact), `String` vs `FixedString` (comparison ignores padding), and supertype-less numeric pairs such as `Int64` vs `UInt64` or `Int64` vs `Float64`. ## Verification - The issue's reproducer plans with zero `cross` nodes and returns the same result as the fallback. - New stateless test `05023_correlated_subquery_equivalence_type_conversion` (12 cases: both nullability directions, widening/narrowing/sideways/float numerics with adversarial boundary values, scalar-subquery aggregation with an outer `0` vs inner `NULL`, guarded fallbacks) passed 6/6 runs under harness setting randomization. - A cross-check over 16 type pairs compared `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` / scalar `count()` results between substitution and the CROSS JOIN fallback on value pools with boundary values (`2^31±1`, `2^32±1`, `2^53`, `2^53+1`, non-integer floats) and `NULL`s — identical everywhere, and plan probes confirmed the substitution fires exactly for the admitted pairs. - The existing `correlated` stateless subset passes (3 environment-only failures in the local scratch setup: MinIO, test cluster, writable access storage). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix AI SQL generation failing on prompts that need several schema lookups
signals.text: Supersedes #113959 (carries @cwurm's commits unchanged; opened from a maintainer fork to finish the review items). ## Summary AI SQL generation (`??`) failed on any prompt needing more than one schema lookup: the bundled `ai-sdk-cpp` rebuilt every step's request from the initial options, so the model lost all earlier tool results and kept re-requesting the same schemas until the step limit — and the client then prepopulated the model's explanatory text as if it were the generated query, claiming success. On top of #113959's fixes (multi-step SDK update, `<sql>`-anchored extraction, honest no-query reporting, `ai.max_steps` default of 10), this PR: - **Pins `contrib/ai-sdk-cpp` to its `main` branch directly.** Upstream replaced its nested git submodules with pinned CMake FetchContent (ClickHouse/ai-sdk-cpp#57), so the separately maintained flattened integration branch is no longer needed. The new pin also carries: - the `GenerateResult::response_messages` terminal-reply fix requested in review (ClickHouse/ai-sdk-cpp#55), - GPT-5-family request normalization — the family rejects `temperature`/`top_p` (hard 400 on e.g. `ai.temperature`) and defaults to reasoning, which can consume the entire completion budget without producing visible text on small `ai.max_tokens`; the SDK now omits sampling params with a warning and pins `reasoning_effort` (`none` on gpt-5.6, `minimal` floor on earlier gpt-5 models) (ClickHouse/ai-sdk-cpp#58), - the provider refresh and streaming overhaul (ClickHouse/ai-sdk-cpp#49–#53). - Adds the SDK's new `src/providers/http_sse_stream.cpp` to the explicit source list in `contrib/ai-sdk-cpp-cmake` (link failure otherwise). - Replaces `LOGICAL_ERROR` with `NETWORK_ERROR` for failed AI generations — a provider/API error is external, and `LOGICAL_ERROR` aborts debug builds on any API failure (observed as SIGABRT in `unit_tests_dbms`). - Adds an untrusted-SQL-fragments rule to the generation system prompt: without it, current models faithfully reproduce statement stacking / `UNION SELECT ... FROM passwords` when the "request" embeds them (observed deterministically on claude-haiku-4-5 at temperature 0), and `AITestFixture.SQLInjectionProtection` asserted behavior nothing instructed. - Updates live-test model IDs that referenced retired models (`gpt-4o-mini`, `gpt-4`, `claude-3-haiku-20240307`, `claude-3-opus-20240229` — these 404 today) to current ones, and scopes the injection test's comment assertion to quote-terminated statement stacking (models may legitimately echo the user's own comment text; the result is prepopulated for review, not executed). Note: the effective default model (used when `<ai><model>` is unset) follows the SDK defaults forward: `gpt-4o` → `gpt-5.6` and `claude-sonnet-4-5` → `claude-sonnet-5`. "Bugfix validation" remains structurally inconclusive for this PR: the fix lives partly in the submodule, and the validator cannot build a "before" binary at the merge-base's submodule state. ## Local validation - `unit_tests_dbms` (Debug, clang 22): offline AI suites 16/16 (`AISQLGenerator.*`, `AIClientFactory.*`) - Live `AITestFixture` (real APIs): **8/8 with OpenAI** (gpt-5-mini / gpt-5.6) and **8/8 with Anthropic** (claude-haiku-4-5 / claude-sonnet-5), including the multi-step `SchemaExploration` case this PR exists to fix - ai-sdk-cpp upstream: 240/240 unit/offline tests, plus its own live streaming/tool-calling checks ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Fixed AI SQL generation (`??` in `clickhouse-client`) failing on prompts that require several schema lookups: the model lost earlier tool results between steps and re-requested the same schemas until the step limit was reached. The client now reports honestly when no query was generated, works with current GPT-5-family models (which reject sampling parameters and default to reasoning), no longer aborts debug builds on provider errors, and the default `ai.max_steps` matches the documented value of 10. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115509&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115509](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115509+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Reject a bare carriage return in HTTP header names and values
signals.text:
`HTTPHeaderFilter::checkAndNormalizeHeaders` rejected an embedded line feed (`
`) in HTTP header names and values, but not a bare carriage return (``). A lone `` also terminates a header line, so a value such as `tokenX-Injected: evil` could still smuggle a second header into an outgoing request (request/response splitting). This rejects `` alongside `
`, for both header names and values, in the shared filter. This covers the callers that route header names/values through `HTTPHeaderFilter` — the SQL-facing paths where headers are supplied per query: the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, S3/Web configuration, and the DataLake/REST catalogs. Outbound HTTP clients that build headers without this filter (for example the AI providers and the BigQuery client, whose header values come from named collections, OAuth tokens, or DDL configuration) are not affected by this change; enforcing the same invariant at the shared HTTP send path for those clients is left to a separate follow-up. Deferred from #110313 to keep that pull request focused on refactoring. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110313 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reject a bare carriage return (``), in addition to a line feed (`
`), in HTTP header names and values that pass through the HTTP header filter. This closes an HTTP header injection (request/response splitting) gap for features that pass user-provided headers, such as the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, and data lake catalogs. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1790` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Keep the SeaweedFS mini admin gRPC port out of the ephemeral range
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109368 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109368 Related: https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/10838 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `test_database_iceberg_seaweedfs_catalog` can fail in fixture setup with a `Connection refused` reading as "the catalog never started" ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109368&sha=4443610796f2ef985ff5615a261456a7ea4155ea&name_0=PR&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%205%2F6%29), tagged `retry_ok`). It did start: it answered 200 on all 314 polls; the refusal is the last poll, after the container exited 255. Its log shows why. ``` E mini.go:1583 Admin server error: failed to listen on port 33646: bind: address already in use F mini.go:1598 Admin server readiness check failed ... after 240 attempts ``` `weed mini` derives the admin gRPC port as `admin.port + 10000` = 33646, inside the Linux ephemeral range (floor 32768), so one of mini's own startup dials can take it as a source port before admin binds it. It is the only derived gRPC port above the floor; the other four land in 18333..19340. The failure hides itself: `glog.Fatalf` skips `defer close(allServicesReady)`, and the call creating `-tableBucket=analytics` runs only after `<-allServicesReady`. S3 and Iceberg keep answering 200 while `analytics` is never created, so `"analytics" in buckets` never becomes true and a longer wait cannot help. `-admin.port=12646` derives 22646: below the floor, and below the 22768 cap SeaweedFS derives for this same problem in its own test port allocator (seaweedfs/seaweedfs#10209, which left the `mini` default alone). That default is 23646 on 4.41, 4.42 and master, so an image bump does not help; it is filed upstream. Raising `ip_local_port_range` via `sysctls`, as the Kafka composes do, would work too, but for every dial mini makes. It reaches users too: the SeaweedFS catalog guide and connector page both document `mini` on `image: latest`, so the bucket each tells the reader to use never appears. Both are pinned here; the guide's locale copies are left to the translation workflow. Validated with `docker run --sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="33646 33646"`: unpinned reproduces the CI log verbatim, pinned creates the bucket, a default-range control is green. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115512&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115512](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115512+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1762` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Add memory_eviction_score query setting for memory reservation eviction order
signals.text: Adds an experimental per-query `memory_eviction_score` setting (`Int32`, default `0`) that controls the order in which queries' memory reservations are evicted when their workload is under memory pressure. A query with a higher `memory_eviction_score` is evicted first; queries with an equal score keep the existing largest-reservation-first order. Negative values make a query less likely to be evicted. The eviction victim is now selected by `(memory_eviction_score, reservation size)` instead of reservation size alone. When every query keeps the default `memory_eviction_score = 0` the selection is identical to before, so there is no behavior change unless the setting is used. The setting only has an effect when a `MEMORY RESERVATION` resource is configured for the workload (experimental workload scheduling). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110876 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/82414 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `memory_eviction_score` query setting that controls the order in which queries' memory reservations are evicted under workload memory pressure (a higher score is evicted first). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115515&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115515](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115515+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix SLRU cache admitting no new entries once max_count entries were used twice
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed caches configured by a maximum number of entries (`SLRU` policy) silently stopping to admit new entries once that many entries had been accessed at least twice. Affected caches include the Iceberg and Paimon metadata file caches, the Parquet metadata cache, the text index caches, the vector similarity index cache, the compiled expression cache and the ObjectStorageQueue file status cache. ### Description Found by reading `SLRUCachePolicy`'s eviction arithmetic; there is no public issue for it. The case below rests only on the source and on the added test, which fails on unpatched master. `SLRUCachePolicy` bounds its protected queue by bytes (`max_protected_size`) but has no count equivalent, so the protected arm of `removeOverflow` compares the protected queue's size against `max_count`, the *total* entry limit. The probationary arm runs last on every `set()` and already enforces `cells.size() <= max_count`, which makes that comparison unsatisfiable: the protected queue is never shrunk under count pressure. Once `max_count` entries have each been accessed twice (a second `set`, or any `get`, promotes an entry), the protected queue holds all of them. The next insertion overflows, and the only eviction candidate in the probationary queue is the entry just inserted. Lowering `max_entries` at runtime reaches the same state at once, because `setMaxCount` demotes the protected queue to exactly `max_count` entries. The fix bounds protected count the way protected bytes already is: `max_protected_count = min(trunc(max_count * size_ratio), max_count - 1)`, so the probationary queue always keeps one slot, and recomputes it in `setMaxCount`. `SLRUFileCachePriority` ratio-splits both `max_size_` and `max_elements_` the same way. `cells.size() <= max_count` is unchanged, so `max_entries` keeps its meaning and no setting is added. Eviction behaviour does change for the affected caches: a protected entry can now be demoted to probationary under count pressure, where previously only byte pressure could. That is what makes these caches admit new entries at all. Splitting the count bound by `size_ratio` mirrors the byte side rather than following from a measurement. The existing suite exercised the count limit only with distinct keys, where entries stay probationary and the protected queue stays empty, so the defect was unreachable. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115517&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115517](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115517+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1771` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Perf: bulk copy dense values in timeSeriesFromGrid
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **`timeSeriesFromGrid` bulk-copies values for dense rows.** ## What changed - Add a **dense-row fast path** to `timeSeriesFromGrid`. - Use **one `insertRangeFrom` call** for dense values. - Remove repeated **per-sample `insertFrom` calls** on that path. - Use ClickHouse’s existing **`memoryIsZero()` null-map helper** for nullable rows. - Keep the **existing sample-by-sample path** for rows containing NULLs. - Keep **timestamp generation** unchanged. - Keep **row ordering and result offsets** unchanged. - Add **mixed dense and sparse multi-row coverage**. - Add a **dense nullable row after a sparse row** to cover a nonzero nested-array offset. - Add a **dense negative-timestamp case**. - Add an **all-NULL case** for the sparse fallback. ## Why this is safe - **Input length validation is unchanged.** Every row still needs exactly `num_steps` values. - **Non-nullable rows are always dense**, so they can use the range copy directly. - **Nullable rows check only their row slice** of the null map before taking the bulk path. - Rows with **any NULL stay on the existing path**, including sparse and all-NULL rows. - For nullable values, the fast path copies the already-unwrapped **nested `T` column into the non-nullable result `T` column**. - The optimization changes only **how dense values are copied**. - **Timestamps, NULL filtering, row order, and offsets keep the existing behavior.** ## Benchmark Focused `timeSeriesFromGrid` benchmark on Apple arm64 with **Release/O3 binaries**. The baseline and patch used the same remaining build objects and differed only in `timeSeriesRange.cpp` (`std::none_of` versus `memoryIsZero`). Each case ran **10 identical queries in one `clickhouse local --multiquery` process**, with `max_threads = 1`, 4,096 grid points, 10,000 input rows, and `arraySum` over the returned values so the value payload was consumed. Times below are total wall time for the 10 queries. | Workload | Baseline | Patch | Change | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Non-nullable dense | 2.98 s | 2.51 s | **15.8% faster** | | Nullable dense | 2.24 s | 2.17 s | **3.1% faster** | | One NULL at first position | 3.49 s | 3.47 s | **flat** | | One NULL at final position | 3.55 s | 3.55 s | **flat** | | 10% NULL | 3.78 s | 3.80 s | **0.5% slower** | | 50% NULL | 2.66 s | 2.66 s | **flat** | A sample-width sweep at **256, 1,024, 4,096, and 16,384 points** showed the same shape. The sparse nullable cases stayed within normal run-to-run noise, including the late-NULL case. ## Tests - Add **dense and sparse rows in the same function call** to `03254_timeseries_range`. - Add a **sparse-first, dense-second** row pair to exercise `values_base_offset != 0`. - Cover **dense values**. - Cover **sparse values**. - Cover **nullable values**. - Cover **all-NULL values**. - Cover **dense negative timestamps**. - Compile the changed translation unit with **Ninja**. - Run **direct output checks** for mixed, offset, all-NULL, sparse, nullable, and negative-timestamp inputs. - Run **`git diff --check`**. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115518&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115518](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115518+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
