signals.title: Fix read_rows/read_bytes/written_rows/written_bytes in system.query_thread_log
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105246 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `read_rows`, `read_bytes`, `written_rows` and `written_bytes` in `system.query_thread_log` reporting a thread lifetime running total instead of the values for the logged query. Rows of long-lived pooled threads, in particular the query's initiating `HTTPHandler` thread, were affected. ### Description `ThreadStatus::progress_in` and `progress_out` live as long as the OS thread, and the four progress columns are read straight off them. Nothing ever cleared them, so for a pooled thread the row reported everything that thread had ever served. Worker threads get a fresh `ThreadStatus`, so the victim is the row with `thread_id = master_thread_id`. `ThreadStatus::initPerformanceCounters()` already exists for this, runs on attach to a thread group, and says "Clear stats from previous query if a new query is started". It resets `performance_counters` and `memory_tracker` but never these two members, which predate it. The fix adds them. Before the fix, over HTTP on one connection, four identical `SELECT`s each reading 200000 rows: | `query_log.read_rows` | `query_thread_log.read_rows` | same row's `ProfileEvents['SelectedRows']` | |---|---|---| | 200000 | 1000000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1200000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1400000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1600000 | 200000 | After the fix all three agree. Four identical `INSERT`s behaved the same way on `written_rows`, and are covered. One semantic point to confirm, since it is a choice: this reset runs per attach to a thread group, not per query, so a thread logged on several rows for one query reports each attach cycle separately. `ProfileEvents` on the same row already behaves this way, so the two become consistent rather than gaining a new convention. Populating the columns from `SelectedRows`/`InsertedRows` instead was rejected: it redefines them and would tie them to `log_profile_events`. Query-level accounting is untouched: `query_log`, `system.processes`, `max_rows_to_read`, leaf limits, throttling and quotas read the separate `QueryStatus` object, and I checked each of those. The test drives the queries over HTTP on one keep-alive connection: over the native protocol the reads happen on a separate pipeline thread, so the initiating thread's row would assert nothing. It fails on master. @PedroTadim <details> <summary>Validation</summary> - Negative control on a pristine master binary: all four assertion lines move (distinct `read_rows` 1 to 4, distinct `written_rows` 1 to 4, and every column comparing a progress value against `ProfileEvents` moves on both arms). Reproduced under randomized settings too. - New test passes on the fixed build, 50 of 50 randomized runs, and 12 concurrent copies over 6 workers. - Of the ten other stateless tests touching `query_thread_log`, the eight runnable in my sandbox still pass; the remaining two need a listener this sandbox does not provide, and neither reads the four columns. - Verified `progress_in`/`progress_out` on `ThreadStatus` have two writers (`CurrentThread::updateProgressIn`/`Out`), one reader (the log site), and no other reference in `src/`, `programs/`, `base/`, `utils/`. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115596&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115596](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115596+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Normalize the plan check in 04061_analyzer_inline_view
signals.text: `04061_analyzer_inline_view` pinned the full `EXPLAIN` output, including the step description of `ReadFromRemoteParallelReplicas`, which embeds the whole query sent to the replicas. That makes the reference sensitive to unrelated changes in query formatting, and it breaks outright once reading with parallel replicas is planned differently: the step is then called `ReadFromParallelReplicas` and it is not wrapped into `Expression (Convert distributed names)`. Print the plan with `description = 0`, drop the `Expression` steps and fold both names of the reading step into one, so the check keeps asserting what the test is about - the shape of the plan built for an inlined view - without depending on how reading from the replicas is planned. signals.title: Fix out-of-bounds read of the LowCardinality saved-hash array
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/29782 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114993 Reported on master, no issue open for it, by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)` as a ThreadSanitizer heap-use-after-free at `src/Common/ColumnsHashing.h:248` on thread `MergeMutate`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=a753fdf104bb824600ebd63fd8fe20fc8deabbf2&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an out-of-bounds read of the cached dictionary hashes when aggregating or joining on a `LowCardinality(String)` key whose dictionary grows while it is being aggregated, reachable from `TTL ... GROUP BY`. It could yield a wrong hash, and a reported heap-buffer-overflow in sanitizer builds. ### Description `IColumnUnique::tryGetSavedHash()` memoized the dictionary hash array on first use and returned a bare `const UInt64 *` with no length. `ReverseIndex::calcHashes()` sizes it from the dictionary size at that moment, and `ReverseIndex::insert()` afterwards grows only the internal copy, so nothing extended the published one. Consumers cached the bare pointer and indexed it with a current dictionary position, past the end. Only String and FixedString keys have such an array. `TTL ... GROUP BY` reaches this from ordinary SQL: `TTLAggregationAlgorithm` builds its aggregate columns once per block, grows the dictionary in place row by row, and aggregates once per key run, so later runs index positions the first run's snapshot never covered. This publishes the array as a `std::span` derived from a single owned column, so data and length always describe the same buffer, and bounds-checks all six read sites: a position inside the span uses the memoized hash, one outside takes the existing branch that hashes from the key. That branch runs today for every numeric dictionary, so no new code path appears. Both consumers are fixed: `HashMethodSingleLowCardinalityColumn` (aggregation, where it was reported) and `LowCardinalityKeyGetterForJoin` (joins, same unbounded pointer), as is the dictionary cache, which would otherwise resurrect an unbounded pointer on a hit. I did not produce a join query that overflows. #29782 fixed the lifetime half of this contract; this fixes the bounds half. Validation: a new stateless test kills the server during `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` on master under a sanitizer build and passes with this change, 50 of 50 runs under randomized settings. The sanitizer build is the oracle, not the SQL assertion. Reverting only the bounds check brings the report back, and results are byte-identical before and after. <details><summary>Validation detail</summary> Reproduced locally with the same frames as the linked report, under ASan, which additionally attributes the overflowed region to `ReverseIndex::calcHashes` via `tryGetSavedHash` on the first `executeOnBlock` and reports the read as exactly 8 bytes past a 144-byte (18-slot) allocation. Instrumenting the out-of-range branch on the reproducer shows it taken over a thousand times with a snapshot of 2 entries while positions reach 9 and beyond, so without the check those reads are all out of bounds. Reproducer: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (k LowCardinality(String), d DateTime, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k TTL d + INTERVAL 1 SECOND GROUP BY k SET v = sum(v), d = max(d) SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, index_granularity = 1024, merge_with_ttl_timeout = 100000; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000, now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY, number FROM numbers(200000) SETTINGS max_insert_block_size = 200000; OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; ``` Existing coverage could not reach this: `03774_ttl_group_by_lowcardinality.sql` uses numeric LowCardinality types, where there is no saved-hash array. Taking the fallback branch cannot split a group: the memoized value comes from `StringViewHash`, which is also the `HashMap` default hash for these keys, over the same bytes `getDataAt` returns. GROUP BY and join results over String, Nullable(String), FixedString and numeric keys are byte-identical on both binaries. Eight concurrent clients running GROUP BY, spilling GROUP BY, `uniqExact` and a `parallel_hash` join over one shared dictionary return identical correct results with no sanitizer reports, exercising both sides of the publication exchange. #114993 changes the mapping caches in the same file without touching the saved hash, so the mechanisms are independent, but it extends cache lifetime across blocks here and will likely conflict textually. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115604&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115604](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115604+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1799` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Unify `hash` and `parallel_hash` into a single join implementation
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111307 `hash` and `parallel_hash` were two separate join classes running the same algorithm. Every fix, every new JOIN kind, every setting had to be done twice, and they still drifted apart. That is the motivation for this PR. The speedups are a side effect. Behaviour changes: 1) `join_algorithm`: listing `hash` or `parallel_hash` picks the same implementation and no longer decides anything by itself. 2) `parallel_hash_join_threshold` now decides whether a hash join may run in parallel. Two consequences: `hash` on a large right table now builds in parallel where it used to be single-threaded, and `parallel_hash` on a right table estimated below the threshold now runs single-threaded where it always ran parallel. 3) Parallel build and parallel non-joined-row emission cover `INNER`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT` and `FULL`. `SEMI`, `ANTI` and `ASOF` keep the single-slot layout. 4) Multi-clause (`OR`) joins can use the parallel layout. More than one disjunct used to force the serial path. 5) `parallel_non_joined_rows_processing` applies to hash joins in general, not only to `parallel_hash`. Unmatched right rows of a `RIGHT`/`FULL` join can come out in a different order than before. 6) `EXPLAIN` prints `Algorithm: HashJoin` where it printed `Algorithm: ConcurrentHashJoin`. 7) `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` can show a different number of `FillingRightJoinSide` processors, because the join now caps its own build threads. 8) `system.metrics` loses `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreads`, `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreadsActive` and `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreadsScheduled`. `HashJoinDestroyThreads`, `HashJoinDestroyThreadsActive` and `HashJoinDestroyThreadsScheduled` are added for the pool that frees a large join's blocks. 9) `system.events` gains `HashJoinBuildMicroseconds`, `HashJoinBuildScatterMicroseconds`, `HashJoinBuildInsertMicroseconds`, `HashJoinBuildLockWaitMicroseconds`, `HashJoinProbeMicroseconds`, `HashJoinProbeLookupMicroseconds` and `HashJoinProbeGatherMicroseconds`. 10) The hash table size statistics cache now feeds the whole hash family, so plain `hash` also preallocates from it. 11) The multiple-ORs rejection message is now "Only `hash` and `parallel_hash` joins support multiple ORs for keys in JOIN ON section". Defaults are unchanged. The changes: 1) One `HashJoin`, `parallel_hash` is an alias of it. Parallelism moved inside: build threads take per-slot locks over a `TwoLevelHashTable` whose bucket count is a template parameter, and 0 buckets gives back exactly the old single-level layout. So serial and parallel are one code path now, and which of the two names you list no longer decides anything - `parallel_hash_join_threshold` is what controls whether the build runs in parallel. `ConcurrentHashJoin` is deleted. On master the same query could cost 1.02s via `hash` and 4.20s via `parallel_hash`; now there is one path and one number. One `HashJoin` now owns the maps, so it has to grow machinery `ConcurrentHashJoin` never had: * Per-bucket locks on a shared table, instead of a mutex per child `HashJoin`. * `WorkerStoredData` + one `Arena` per slot. Stored blocks and string/list nodes used to be "free" because each child `HashJoin` already had its own `columns` and pool. One object needs that split made explicit, because `Arena` is unsynchronized and two build threads cannot bump the same one. * `SlotScatter` into buckets of that one table, instead of scatter into N join objects. * `PartitionedFixedHashMap`. The direct-addressed maps (`key8`/`key16`) had no two-level variant, so a shared-table build had nothing to lock. Buckets now partition the one fixed buffer by key range: 256 under the parallel layout, 1 under the serial one, which is exactly the old `FixedHashMap` layout. `parallel_hash` used to build these as per-slot private maps and scatter the probe across them; now they run on the one shared map like every other type. * `freezeMapsForProbing`. After concurrent inserts, cell numbering for used flags (and min/max on a direct-addressed map) has to be settled once. The old merge did that implicitly by finishing in slot 0, then calling `onBuildPhaseFinish` on a quiet map. * Atomics for `rows_to_join` / `keys_to_join` / `bucket_bytes`. The old code summed after the merge; summing buckets while another thread is inserting would race. 2) Multi-clause (`OR`) JOINs gain parallelism. More than one disjunct used to force the serial path, so the build stayed single-threaded no matter how many threads the query had. Now it scales: on a build-heavy join master is flat at ~2.5s from 8 threads up, while this builds 3.4x faster at 8 threads, 7.3x at 16 and 11.2x at 32. The flip side: a probe-heavy multi-clause join below ~32 threads pays 8-16% for the two-level layout; raising `parallel_hash_join_threshold` above the right table's size gives back the serial map. 3) The per-lookup once-guard on two-level offsets is gone: the prefix sums are computed once when the build finishes, so the flagged probe reads them directly where master re-checks a `once_flag` on every found row. `RIGHT JOIN ... count()` over 1e8 x 2e6 rows at one thread: 9.9% faster than master, parity at 8 threads. Single-clause probes are at parity with master. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `hash` and `parallel_hash` join algorithms are now one implementation, with `parallel_hash` kept as an alias. Listing `hash` or `parallel_hash` in `join_algorithm` no longer controls how parallel the join is: `parallel_hash_join_threshold` decides whether a hash join may run in parallel, so `hash` on a large right table builds in parallel where it used to be single-threaded, and `parallel_hash` on a right table estimated below the threshold runs single-threaded where it always ran parallel. Multi-clause (`OR`-joined) JOINs can use the parallel layout, so their build scales with threads instead of staying single-threaded (up to 11x faster at 32 threads on a build-heavy join). `RIGHT`/`FULL` probes got cheaper per matched row. `parallel_non_joined_rows_processing` applies to hash joins in general rather than only to `parallel_hash`, so unmatched right rows of a `RIGHT`/`FULL` join can be emitted in a different order. `EXPLAIN` now prints `Algorithm: HashJoin` instead of `Algorithm: ConcurrentHashJoin`. The `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreads`, `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreadsActive` and `ConcurrentHashJoinPoolThreadsScheduled` metrics were removed; `HashJoinDestroyThreads` and its `Active`/`Scheduled` companions were added, along with seven `HashJoin*Microseconds` profile events. Setting defaults are unchanged. --- ### Addendum `parallel_hash` was N private `HashJoin`s. Each child already had its own map, arena, stored blocks and used flags, so scatter-then-merge was cheap. One object owning one map has to make that split explicit. 1) Serial and parallel are the same template. `bits_for_bucket = 0` is one bucket, routing folds, it compiles as the old single-level table. That's why `JoinHashMap` is a `TwoLevelHashMap` even when the join is serial. Serial grower stays `HashTableGrowerWithPrecalculation` -> `TwoLevelHashTableGrower` starts a 1-bucket map too small. 2) Locks are per slot, not per bucket. `slotCountForThreads` is `bit_ceil(max_threads)` capped at 256. A build thread scatters its own block and take the slot locks; two threads collide only when both have rows for the same slot. `insertIntoSlots` try_locks from `block_no` and yields rather than stacking everyone on slot 0. 3) `WorkerStoredData` is per `worker_id` (stored blocks, nullmaps) and needs no lock. Master has no such id: concurrent fill meant calling a different child join. Now it's one object, so `addBlockToJoin` takes the id. Concurrent callers pass distinct ids in `[0, getMaxBuildThreads())`. Single-threaded filler passes `0`. Grace / spilling / `FillingRightJoinSide` forward it. 4) One `Arena` per slot. `Arena` is unsynchronized; string keys and `RowRefList` nodes have to go somewhere. Neither kind needs contiguity, so splitting is fine. 5) `SlotScatter` routes with the map's own `bucketRoutingHash`, so scatter and insert can't disagree. For `key8`/`key16` it also gathers keys per slot so the insert loop is sequential. 6) `PartitionedFixedHashMap`. Direct-addressed maps had no two-level variant, and hashing the key itself dumps a dense range into one bucket. Routing hashes the key's cache line: the range spreads, and two keys on the same line can't sit under two locks. Storage is still one flat buffer; buckets only partition the locks. Min/max is off during the concurrent fill and restored in `freezeMapsForProbing`. 7) `freezeMapsForProbing` after the last insert. Used flags are indexed by cell number, and those numbers are only well-defined once no bucket is still growing. Probe then uses `offsetInternalUnsafe` (master re-checked a `once_flag` on every found row). Direct-addressed min/max restored in the same call. 8) `rows_to_join` / `keys_to_join` / `bucket_bytes` are atomics. Summing buckets while another thread is inserting would race. 9) Per-row used flags (`RIGHT`/`FULL` with extra ON filters etc) go to `pending_per_worker` during the build and get compacted once. Resizing a shared vector from several fill threads would race. `SEMI` / `ANTI` / `ASOF` stay 1-bucket: their non-joined / used-flag model doesn't partition across buckets. `StorageJoin` is filled on 1 thread then shared, so serial. `JoinSwitcher` dumps blocks into `MergeJoin`, same. `GraceHashJoin` already parallelizes by file bucket and builds each in-memory table serial: 256 empty two-level buffers would count against `max_bytes_before_external_join` and wouldn't shrink as Grace adds file buckets. Pipeline caps `FillingRightJoinSide` at `getMaxBuildThreads()`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115605&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115605](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115605+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: CI: raise Config Workflow timeout to avoid killing submodule cache prep
signals.text: Raise the `Config Workflow` job timeout from 600s to 1800s. On a submodule-cache miss, the `Config Workflow` job performs a full shallow clone of all submodules in `_prepare_submodule_cache` (`git submodule update --depth=1 --single-branch --jobs 64`), which can take well over 10 minutes. The previous 600s job timeout killed the job mid-clone: ``` [2026-08-19 20:24:44] Submodule path 'contrib/rocksdb': checked out ... [2026-08-19 20:24:54] Submodule path 'contrib/rust_vendor': checked out ... [2026-08-19 20:24:56] WARNING: Timeout exceeded [600] for [10399] [2026-08-19 20:24:56] WARNING: Job timed out: [Config Workflow], timeout [600], exit code [-15] ``` The clone itself is already parallel (`--jobs 64`); the only remaining fix is a more generous timeout so the config job survives a cache-miss clone. On a cache hit (the common case) the archive is restored from S3 and the job stays fast. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115614&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115614](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115614+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1778` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Perf: reserve TimeSeries tag vectors by row
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reserve the final per-row capacity when converting TimeSeries tag arrays.** ## What changed - Count the separate tag name/value pairs already present in the function arguments. - Reserve array tags and separate tags together for each row. - Cover empty `Array(Nothing)` and `NULL` arrays when separate tags are provided. ## Why this is safe - The array offsets contain the exact number of array tags in each row. - The number of separate tag pairs is known from the validated arguments. - `reserve()` does not change tag order, sorting, duplicate removal, or output. - Empty and `NULL` array paths only reserve when separate tags are present. ## Benchmark Local Release build with `max_threads=1` and `max_block_size=65536`. The benchmark used 2M rows and three measured runs after one warmup per case. Each row used the same tag value modulo 10,000, and only the number of array tags changed. | Array tags per row | Before | After | Change | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 0.35 s | 0.35 s | 0% | | 4 | 0.93 s | 0.62 s | 33% faster | | 8 | 1.38 s | 1.00 s | 28% faster | | 16 | 2.75 s | 2.25 s | 18% faster | | 32 | 6.06 s | 5.10 s | 16% faster | These are array-only calls, where the extra-tag count is zero, so the measured hot path is unchanged by the mixed-tag fix. The end-to-end ingest gain depends on how much time is spent in this path. ## Tests - Run `git diff --check`. - Existing `03779_time_series_tags_functions` coverage includes array tags with separate tags and empty arrays with separate tags. - The revised helper is included in the PR CI build.

signals.title: CI: refuse LLVM coverage verdicts on incomplete measurements, make coverage profiles kill-safe
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The `LLVM Coverage` gate fails a PR when total line coverage drops more than 0.3 pp below the master baseline. Both totals are merged from 21 per-shard `.profdata` artifacts that are deliberately `optional=True`, and nothing verified that either side had all of them. A shard profile can vanish while every check stays green (a corrupt `.profraw` aborts the producer merge, `-failure-mode=warn` silently discards a corrupt input, a zero-length `.profraw` is accepted silently). Both error directions occur: - A short PR side fails an unrelated PR. Observed twice in the last 60 days, both times the same missing file `it-amd_llvm_coverage_4_8.profdata` with all 21 shard jobs green: [PR 110186](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110186&sha=0b33f54bc8089ea3560397c589e93dc6aec92d47&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage) ("dropped 0.50 pp" on a 102-line PR) and [PR 105844](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105844&sha=66107bb44ab45a490e839225eb096e46204e5e86&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage). - A short master run writes a low baseline into the CI DB, so a later real regression passes. This direction produces a PASS and is invisible in any failure count. The invariant established here: a verdict comes only from two complete measurements. - Every coverage producer (functional, integration, unit) names its profile after its own artifact (`<artifact>.profdata`), so the filename carries the shard identity. Producer merges use `--failure-mode=any` and skip zero-length `.profraw` inputs: a shard with invalid data publishes nothing instead of a silently short profile. Artifacts stay `optional=True`, so a missing profile never reddens a green test job. - The `LLVM Coverage` job compares the expected file set against what arrived and merges an explicit file list instead of a `*.profdata` glob. On a missing or invalid shard it reports `SKIPPED` naming the shard, and withholds every comparative output: no verdict, no GitHub comment, no `llvm_coverage.info` artifact, no CI DB row. A genuine tooling failure (report generation) still stays RED. - Baseline completeness needs no metadata: the diff script already selects the first master ancestor that has an `llvm_coverage.info`, and after this change such an `.info` exists only for complete runs. (Transitional: for the first ~30 master commits after merge, pre-change ancestors are still selectable, which is exactly today's behaviour.) - Under coverage, the integration sequential test phase runs regardless of how many parallel tests failed (`MAX_FAILS_BEFORE_DROP`), so a green shard cannot silently publish a profile that is short by the whole sequential phase. - Root cause of the recurring shard 4/8 loss: `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` in merge mode writes the profile only at process exit, and integration tests `SIGKILL` servers on purpose; a kill inside that multi-second write leaves a half-written `.profraw` whose header makes `llvm-profdata` abort with `LLVM ERROR: out of memory` ([llvm/llvm-project#50970](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/50970), open since 2021). Coverage builds now compile with `-mllvm -runtime-counter-relocation` and run with `%c` (continuous mode): the counters are memory-mapped into the profile, which is valid at every instant, so a kill at any moment loses nothing and corrupts nothing. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832, which establishes the same invariant via a completeness sidecar published next to `llvm_coverage.info`, a manifest fingerprint, and a two-pass baseline selector. Withholding the `.info` on incomplete runs makes the sidecar unnecessary, and the profile naming plus set check shrink to ~40 lines. Accepted residuals of the simpler design: a session-timeout-truncated shard can still publish a valid short profile, and on the rare day the coverage artifact manifest itself changes, verdicts are unreliable until master republishes. Not covered here (pre-existing, unchanged): the diagnostics of the diff-report script, addressed separately by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115225. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115623&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115623](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115623+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Reject a lossy codec on columns backing the partition key
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114406 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115533 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114531 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER TABLE` now reject a lossy codec such as `SZ3` on a column used in the partition key. ### Description Follow-up to #114531, which added this check for the sorting key only. #115533 reported the same problem for the partition key, and @rschu1ze asked for it to be covered too. A partition value and a part minmax index are both computed from the block before compression, so they record the exact input while the data on disk decompresses to a different value. Pruning trusts that metadata and discards parts that do hold matching rows. With `i Float64 CODEC(SZ3('ALGO_INTERP_LORENZO', 'REL', 0.01))` and `PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)` over 1000 rows, 6 rows read back a value contradicting their own partition, and a pruning query returns 91 rows where a full scan returns 92. Not a regression from #114531: the same numbers reproduce on an earlier build. The change extends the existing loop in `MergeTreeData::checkProperties` to the partition-key columns and generalises the message. Per-substream lossiness resolution is reused unchanged, so type wrappers and codec chains behave as before. `CREATE` and `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` both reach the check; `ATTACH` stays exempt, so existing tables stay loadable. Two costs, both already carried by the shipped sorting-key check, verified. The check is keyed on column names, since neither key accessor exposes substreams, so a provably exact key such as `PARTITION BY length(arr)` over `Array(Float64) CODEC(SZ3(...))` is now rejected although only the lossless sizes substream is read (measured: 82611 payload values differ from what was written, yet no row lands in the wrong partition and pruning is exact). And a table created earlier with a lossy partition-key column refuses further `ALTER`s while that codec remains, the metadata entry stalling on an upgraded replica in a mixed-version cluster. Tests were added to `04791_lossy_codec_key_column`: the partition key through a plain expression, through an `Array` element and through a `MATERIALIZED` column, plus the `ALTER` path and accepted cases. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115626&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115626](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115626+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Allow unknown settings in query plan serialization
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114184 Adding a plan setting has meant bumping `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION` and gating the write on it — twice already, for versions 5 and 7 — because the settings of a step were written as a name and a typed binary value. A reader that met a name it did not know could not tell where the value ended, so `QueryPlanSerializationSettings::readBinary` threw `UNKNOWN_SETTING`. That fenced off far more than the feature being added: the name goes into every plan that touches the step, so a setting a given plan cannot even use made that plan unreadable to the previous release. Fencing a feature is what the step registry does, by rejecting an unknown step. Plan settings are now written the way query settings have always travelled between client and server (`SettingsWriteFormat::STRINGS_WITH_FLAGS`): name, flags, and the value as a string of its own length. A reader steps over a name it does not know and keeps its own default for it, and rejects the plan only when the name carries `IMPORTANT` — the flag that already means "affects query results, cannot be ignored by older versions". Which form is written is decided by the version of the stream, which `QueryPlan::serialize` already negotiates as the minimum of ours and the peer's, so a peer below version 9 keeps receiving the old form and nothing changes for it. The plan settings that decide a result rather than a way of producing it are marked `IMPORTANT` accordingly: the row and byte limits of `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` with their overflow modes, the two-level aggregation thresholds, `empty_result_for_aggregation_by_empty_set`, `join_any_take_last_row`, `totals_auto_threshold`, and the two settings that decide how aggregation states are laid out. The existing per-setting gates stay — peers below version 9 still need them — but a setting added from now on needs one only when it belongs in that group. `gtest_query_plan_settings_skippable` covers the round trip of every declared setting type through its string form, the old form at the previous version, an unknown setting being skipped, and an unknown `IMPORTANT` setting being rejected. The 58 stateless tests that set `serialize_query_plan` were run against the new format locally (56 pass; two fail only for want of `s3_disk` and `https_port` in the local server config). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A query plan serialized with `serialize_query_plan = 1` no longer becomes unreadable to a peer that does not know one of the plan's settings: a setting the peer can ignore is skipped, and only one whose absence would change the query result is rejected. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115627&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115627](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115627+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Detect stream filename collisions within a single column
signals.text: `MergeTreeData::checkColumnFilenamesForCollision` only compared stream file names *across* columns. Two streams of one column that render to the same file name were silently deduplicated before that comparison, so the column was accepted at CREATE/ALTER and the part was then written with both streams in one file: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (c Nullable(JSON(`null` Int64))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES ('{"null":1}'), (NULL); SELECT c FROM t; -- Code: 33. Too many marks in file .../c.null.cmrk2 ... (CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA) ``` The same collision spread over two columns was already rejected, so this only removes an asymmetry. The new branch follows the existing convention: `BAD_ARGUMENTS` at CREATE and ALTER, a logged error on attach so an already broken table still attaches and can be repaired manually. Columns whose streams collide only as *subcolumn* names, not as file names, stay allowed (``Array(Tuple(`size0` UInt64))``, ``Tuple(`a` String, `a.size` UInt64)``) - they read back correctly, and such tables may already exist. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed accepting a column whose two serialization streams map to the same file name (for example ``Nullable(JSON(`null` Int64))`` or ``Tuple(`a` Tuple(`b` UInt64), `a.b` UInt64)``). Such a table was created successfully, but its parts were written with both streams in one file and could not be read, merged or checked. Creating such a column now fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, as a collision between two different columns already did. Existing tables still attach, with the collision logged. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115632&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115632](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115632+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.text: Brings the `MemoryPressureMonitor` from the ReaderExecutor redesign to master as a self-contained, experimental slice (gated by the existing experimental `ReaderExecutor`). signals.title: Make Jepsen node setup wait for apt's dpkg locks
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The nightly `ClickHouse Keeper Jepsen` check reported ERROR for **all 24 workloads** on master `90a20ccf` ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=90a20ccf81cd348372f1406facf7544efa445f75&name_0=NightlyJepsen&name_1=ClickHouse%20Keeper%20Jepsen)): `0 successes / 24 crashed` and no `:valid?` line anywhere, so it produced no linearizability signal while reporting a red that reads like a Keeper defect. All 24 died in `jepsen.os.ubuntu/setup!` (`ubuntu.clj:22` -> `debian.clj:117`) before any test body ran: `E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend ... (unattended-upgr)`. **Root cause.** `debian/install` runs a plain `apt-get install` with no lock-wait option, and apt's default `DPkg::Lock::Timeout` is `0`, so it exits 100 the instant the lock is held. Nodes are scaled 0 -> 3 at job start, so each is seconds old, and Ubuntu's apt-daily timers carry `Persistent=true`, firing the missed run at once on boot. **Change.** A new `jepsen.clickhouse.os` wraps `ubuntu/os`: stop the two apt-daily timers (best effort, never the services), write a `DPkg::Lock::Timeout "600"` drop-in, assert via `apt-config dump` that apt resolves that timeout, fetch the package lists once per node, then delegate. The three `:os` sites point at it; `server/db.clj` reaches its Keeper node via `(:os test)`, so that 4th node is covered too. **Validation.** Nightly-only and PR-gated on `jepsen-test`, so it cannot go green here. Holding the lock with `fcntl.lockf` and running Jepsen's exact argv: without the drop-in `rc=100` in 0.06 s with that error; with it `rc=0` after the 30 s hold, package installed. Pinning the timeout back to `"0"`, or malforming the file, re-breaks it. Checked on Ubuntu 20.04/22.04/24.04 through Jepsen's real sshj remote. Post-merge: 3 nightlies at 0 of 24 failures, with neither error string in `job.log`. **Not fixed, deliberately.** 2026-07-16's 15/24 is a different cause (SSH `session-error`, no dpkg-lock hits). Baking the packages into the AMI would be more robust, but is unreachable from here. <details> <summary>Why the lists lock needs a separate step, and why neither apt's cache nor its exit status is the postcondition</summary> `DPkg::Lock::Timeout` covers the dpkg frontend lock only. The same automatic apt run also holds `/var/lib/apt/lists/lock` during its update phase, and 6 of the 26 historical lock hits on this check are lists-lock ones, so the lists are fetched by a step that retries only while apt reports that lock held. Four candidate apt-native timeouts for that lock were tested and all fail in 0-1 s. Its postcondition is neither apt's cache files nor its exit status. Measured: an `apt-get update` that failed to take the lock still *creates* `/var/cache/apt/pkgcache.bin` having fetched zero indexes, so a freshness check reads that as success and suppresses the update `ubuntu/setup!` would run. And the status misreports both ways: **0** when every fetch failed and no index was written, **100** when one configured source is broken while every index that matters was fetched. So the step counts the *package* indexes apt can read afterwards (`apt-get indextargets`, restricted to `Created-By: Packages`; needs no root, takes no lock), and a non-lock failure is judged by that count rather than being fatal on its own. The restriction matters because apt lists one record per target, so Translations/DEP-11/CNF appear beside the package indexes: a node with the Release files but no package index reports a positive *total* while `apt-get install ntpdate faketime` finds no installation candidate. Measured on apt 2.8.3, as targets/package-indexes: 30/15 populated (install resolves) - 22/11 one mirror host unreachable (accepted) - 30/15 a 404 suite made the update exit 100 (accepted) - 15/**0** package indexes missing, auxiliary ones present (rejected) - 0/0 lists emptied, and after the lock-failed update above. `Created-By:` is present on apt 2.0.10, 2.4.14 and 2.8.3, and in the stock state package-indexes equals the total on all three. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115637&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115637](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115637+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility with redundant parentheses
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility during rolling upgrades when equivalent primary keys were serialized with different redundant parentheses. ### Problem KeeperMap stores the table definition in Keeper and previously compared its primary-key expression as formatted text. Builds that serialize the same expression as either `key` or `(key)` therefore reject an otherwise compatible shared table definition during a rolling upgrade, including during ATTACH/startup. ### Implementation - keep the existing writer spelling and never rewrite compatible shared metadata, so patched nodes do not strand unpatched peers during a rolling deployment; - parse stored and local primary-key expressions and normalize only redundant outer parentheses that wrap one complete expression; - require the remaining input to be exact normal formatter output, preserving strict rejection of malformed, terminated, commented, or genuinely different definitions; - use the same compatibility check in CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup; - split columns from the primary-key section using its structural newline-delimited header. The reader-side implementation uses parser and formatter APIs present in both current master and 26.4. It does not depend on `formatIgnoringRedundantParentheses()` added by #114188, so the same compatibility rule can be backported to 26.4. ### Tests The stateless SQL regression covers both directions (`key` stored with `(key)` local and `(key)` stored with `key` local), verifies that compatible CREATE and ATTACH do not rewrite the Keeper znode, and checks data access after ATTACH. It also verifies rejection of a different key, malformed `(key`, and terminated `key;` metadata, plus a primary-key expression containing the metadata header text. Red-before was reproduced with embedded Keeper on official ClickHouse 26.4.5.143 and 26.7.1.1315: after changing stored metadata from `key` to `(key)`, DETACH + ATTACH left the table in `INVALID_STATE` (Code 668). Local `git diff --check` and a snapshot-bound hostile review passed. Green-after remains a CI gate for this commit and for the future 26.4 backport. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115642&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115642](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115642+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix flaky 04511_reader_executor_disk_cache
signals.text: `04511_reader_executor_disk_cache` fails on master with ``` cold_read_from_source 1 executor_populated_cache 1 -warm_served_from_cache 1 +warm_served_from_cache 0 ``` CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=2101f9b0850389d7fddfefd04d2577162c8958c3&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20sequential%2C%202%2F2%29 It also fails on unrelated pull requests in `Stateless tests (amd_msan, WasmEdge, sequential, 2/2)` (4 of 14 reruns there). No tracking issue exists. ### What goes wrong The third check asserted `warm < cold`, comparing the `ReaderExecutorBytesFromSource` totals of a cold and a warm `SELECT`. That is a proxy, and a partially populated cache inverts it. With more than one reading thread each stream builds its own `ReaderExecutor` over the same file. `DiskCacheWriter` appends only at the segment's live write offset, so whichever stream loses the downloader race contributes nothing, and the cold read leaves the segment partially populated. The warm read then re-fetches such a segment from its start — `claimLeadRole`'s `available` prefix is deliberately unused, see the *\"Coarse by design\"* note in `ReaderExecutor::readThroughCaches` — so it can move *more* source bytes than the cold read did. The failing job's server log and `query_log` show exactly that: the cold read populated 285856 of the 801126-byte segment and read 1658884 bytes from source; the warm read then read 2480460. Across the 28 runs of that job the cold total was a constant 1658884 while the warm total was 0, 801126, 1372817, 1479995 or 2480460, purely as a function of how the streams interleaved. ### The fix Pin the reads to a single thread, so the cold read populates the segment completely, and assert the strong property instead of the proxy: the warm read must touch the source not at all (`warm = 0`). Verified over 54 runs of the test with randomized settings against a local minio: `cold` is now a stable 800461 (one clean pass over the file instead of two or three overlapping ones) and `warm` is 0 in every run. The re-fetch-from-segment-start behaviour itself is left alone — it is a documented limitation of the experimental `ReaderExecutor` with a follow-up already noted in the code, not something to change in a CI fix. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115643&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115643](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115643+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix flaky test `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit`
signals.text: Fix a flaky test. Without `exact_rows_before_limit`, `rows_before_limit_at_least` is set from `LimitByTransform`, which counts the rows it emitted before `LIMIT` stopped the pipeline. That count depends on the block size of the sorted stream, and `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit` pins it with `max_block_size = 1`. When settings randomization enables external sorting, `MergeSortingTransform` merges its spilled runs into blocks of at least 128 rows, so `LIMIT BY` sees a whole batch of groups at once and the counter reports a larger value — 5 instead of 3 on the failing run. The queries in the test are tiny (50 rows), but `max_block_size = 1` makes `MergeSortingTransform` account for 50 single-row chunks by their allocated size, which crosses the randomized `max_bytes_before_external_sort` threshold and spills to disk (confirmed by `ProfileEvents['ExternalSortWritePart'] = 2`). The fix disables external sorting in the test. Minimal reproducer of the CI failure: ``` --optimize_read_in_order 0 --max_bytes_before_external_sort 156659 --max_bytes_ratio_before_external_sort 0 --allow_merge_tree_settings --ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization 0.0 ``` Verified locally: with the fix, 210 runs of the test over randomized combinations of `max_block_size`, `max_threads`, `optimize_read_in_order`, external sort/group-by thresholds, `prefer_external_sort_block_bytes` and MergeTree serialization settings all match the reference; without it, the same sweep reproduces the mismatch (including on the "unsorted" query, which reported 9). The sibling tests `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit_mem` and `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit_dist` were checked under the same sweep and are not affected. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=bddae8d728ac67d24e7c4f102e87b4a3c552322b&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_msan%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%201%2F3%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115644&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115644](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115644+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Keep table aliases in stored query bodies when restoring under a new name
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115479 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug where restoring a database or table under a new name dropped the table aliases from the bodies of stored views, so reading a restored view failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`. Closes #115479. ### Description Closes: #115479 A renaming restore rewrote the table references inside a stored view body but discarded the alias on each one, so the view was permanently broken: its `FROM` named a table with no alias while its projection still qualified columns by that alias. ```sql CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT a.id FROM testdb.t1 AS a; BACKUP DATABASE testdb TO Disk('backups', 'r'); RESTORE DATABASE testdb AS renamed FROM Disk('backups', 'r'); SELECT * FROM renamed.v; -- Code: 47. UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER: Unknown expression identifier `a.id` ``` Root cause: the alias is state on the reference node itself, not on the `ASTTableExpression`. `DDLRenamingVisitor::visitTableExpression` substituted a freshly built `ASTTableIdentifier` for the reference, so every field other than the name was lost, and the formatted body was persisted into the restored metadata. The fix renames the reference in place with `ASTTableIdentifier::resetTable`, so the alias, `parametrised_alias` and `prefer_alias_to_column_name` survive by construction. This is option 2 from the issue. Its `has_uuid` caveat does not apply on master: `ASTTableIdentifier` has no `formatImplWithoutAlias` override there and nothing reads `has_uuid` on the node past parse time, so a stale flag is inert; #114277 already carries the clearing line, so either merge order is correct. `resetTable` itself is untouched, and its only other caller, `InJoinSubqueriesPreprocessor`, requires a non-empty alias. Sibling carrier, so you do not have to ask: `replaceTableNameInArgument` rebuilds the reference the same way for `joinGet`/`dictGet`/`IN`. An alias does parse there but is not resolvable (`SELECT 1 IN (db.t AS a), a` already fails with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`), so dropping it has no reachable consequence and is left alone. `RESTORE TABLE db.v AS other.v` alone does not reproduce: only the view is remapped, so the visitor early-returns. Already-written backups are not repaired. Validated by a new `.sh` test: five aliased shapes plus four boundary controls, red before and green after, plus 50/50 randomized runs. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115645&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115645](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115645+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not treat a cast to String from a type that can hold NULL as safe
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115294 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Code: 349. Cannot convert NULL value to non-Nullable type` when a `has` or `notHas` predicate carries a NULL array element and the primary key is a `String`, `Array(String)` or `Map(String, String)`, and fixed wrong results when that element is a `Dynamic` or `Variant` holding NULL. The NULL is now dropped from the set during key analysis, as it already was for other key types. ### Description No related open issue. Reproduces on 26.7.4.55: ```sql CREATE TABLE a3 (k String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO a3 VALUES ('a'); SELECT count() FROM a3 WHERE has([CAST(NULL, 'Nullable(String)')], k); -- Code: 349. Cannot convert NULL value to non-Nullable type. ``` `ENGINE = Memory` answers `0` for the same data, and key analysis raises the error, so no rewrite avoids it. `canBeSafelyCast` declared `Nullable(X) -> String` safe, but `String` cannot hold a NULL. `tryPrepareSetColumnsForIndex` trusts that and exits early through the non-accurate `castColumn`, which throws. Every other target answers "not safe" and routes to `castColumnAccurateOrNull`, which filters unrepresentable elements out; this pair never reached it. `Array` and `Map` inherit it by recursion. The switch made the same claim for `Dynamic` and `Variant`, which carry NULL in a discriminator. There it gave wrong results rather than an error: the NULL became `''`, entered the set index and pruned away rows keyed `''`. A `Nullable` target represents it, so those two stay safe against one. That routes more targets into `castColumnAccurateOrNull`, which refuses a target it cannot wrap in `Nullable`. All four guards over such a cast tested only the outer type, so a `Tuple(Array(String))` key passed and then raised `Code: 43`; the `EmbeddedRocksDB`/`KeeperMap`/`Redis` helper had no check at all. Each now asks the cast about the target, and that helper also strips the `LowCardinality` encoding, as the key-analysis guards did. Scalar, `Nullable`, `LowCardinality` and plain `Tuple` keys keep their pruning; a container key scans when its element is Nullable-nested. Both tests fail without this change and pass with it, 50/50 under randomization. Two of my open PRs touch this. #115294 is orthogonal but appends to the same test, so the second to merge rebases it. #112890 makes two of the same `canBeSafelyCast` changes without these guards, so alone it raises that `Code: 43` for a container key. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115647&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115647](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115647+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Text index: accept arbitrary LIKE/ILIKE patterns for the array tokenizer
signals.text: The `array` tokenizer stores the whole value as a single token, so a pattern matches a token exactly when it matches the value. signals.title: Do not qualify an expression alias in the right argument of IN with the default database
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/94894 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/76356 `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` when the view query used an expression alias as the right argument of `IN`: ```sql CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW myview TO mydestination AS SELECT 'foo' AS object WHERE (object IN ('foo', 'bar') AS objects) AND object IN objects; ``` ``` Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression or table expression identifier `default.objects` in scope SELECT 'foo' AS object WHERE ((object IN ('foo', 'bar')) AS objects) AND (object IN (default.objects)). (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` assumed that an identifier in the right argument of `IN` is a table name and qualified it with the current database, so the stored view query could not be resolved, while the same plain `SELECT` worked. The similar code in `MarkTableIdentifiersVisitor` checks the query aliases before marking such an identifier as a table; now `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` does the same: it collects the expression aliases of each select query (visible in nested queries, but not leaking into the enclosing query) and leaves matching identifiers intact, so that a real table name in the right argument of `IN` is still qualified. #76356 fixed the same problem for aliases defined in the `WITH` clause; this covers aliases defined elsewhere in the query. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` error when creating a materialized view whose query uses an expression alias as the right argument of `IN`. Closes [#94894](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/94894). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115651&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115651](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115651+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Infer a physically nullable Parquet struct as Nullable(Tuple)
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112427 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed wrong results when reading a Parquet file with a nullable struct column without an explicit schema. Schema inference pushed the nullability down to the tuple elements and returned `Tuple(Nullable(...), ...)`, which cannot hold a struct-level NULL, so a NULL struct was read as a tuple of NULLs. Such a column is now inferred as `Nullable(Tuple(...))` when `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` is enabled. That setting was also added to the Parquet schema inference cache key, so a schema cached under one of its values is no longer reused under the other. ### Description Reading a Parquet `optional group` (a nullable struct) without a schema returned wrong data: ```sql DESCRIBE file('np.parquet', Parquet); -- p Tuple(`1` Nullable(Float64), `2` Nullable(Float64)) SELECT * FROM file('np.parquet', Parquet); -- (1,2) -- (NULL,NULL) <- the file holds NULL here ``` **Root cause.** `SchemaConverter::processSubtreeTuple` already reads such a group correctly, but only with a `Nullable` type hint. Without a hint each leaf takes its own def-level nullability and the assembled type is a bare `Tuple` of `Nullable` elements. Writing and hinted reading were already correct; `ORC`, `Arrow` and `Native` infer `Nullable(Tuple(...))` from the same data. **The change.** Inference now names `Nullable(Tuple(...))` for an `OPTIONAL` group with an all-`REQUIRED`, non-array subtree. Only the type is named: the read-time null-map machinery stays hint-only, because the inferred type reaches the read as its type hint and the existing hinted path re-derives that state itself. Inference mode is selected by `sample_block == nullptr`, the converter's own mode invariant, rather than by a missing node type hint, which in read mode a `JSON` hint on a struct also produces. Gated on `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type`, matching `ArrowColumnToCHColumn` so inference cannot return a type `CREATE TABLE` rejects, and on `schema_inference_make_columns_nullable`. `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` defaults to `false`, so inferred types at default settings are unchanged and no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry is needed. Every other group shape keeps a plain `Tuple`; the table lists them with the reason. Nested-optional and optional-leaf groups are rejected with a hint today too, so those remain a separate pre-existing limitation. <details> <summary>Invariant carriers, all measured</summary> | Carrier | Before | After | |---|---|---| | top-level `optional group`, all-required subtree | `Tuple(Nullable,...)` -> `(NULL,NULL)` | `Nullable(Tuple(...))` -> `\N` | | named elements | same defect | fixed | | `Array` element struct | `Array(Tuple(...))` -> `[(1,2),(NULL,NULL)]` | `Array(Nullable(Tuple))` -> `[(1,2),NULL]` | | `Map` value struct | `Map(String, Tuple(...))` | `Map(String, Nullable(Tuple))` | | `Map` `key_value` tuple | plain Tuple | unchanged (`DataTypeMap` requires `Tuple(keys, values)`) | | `Map` key that is an `optional` group | plain Tuple | unchanged (`DataTypeMap` rejects a `Nullable` key) | | `optional` group whose only child is a childless group | plain Tuple | unchanged (no leaf carries the null map) | | `JSON` hint over a struct with a nested `optional` group | reads the struct | unchanged | | nested optional group | plain Tuple | unchanged (rejected with a hint too) | | optional leaf under an optional group | plain Tuple | unchanged (same) | | `REQUIRED` group | `Tuple(...)` | unchanged | | GeoParquet geometry column (a WKB binary leaf, resolved by the geo path) | `Point` | unchanged | | `schema_inference_make_columns_nullable = 0` | `Tuple(Float64, Float64)` | unchanged | | `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type = 0` | `Tuple(Nullable,...)` | unchanged | | tuple element subcolumn read | leaf read | unchanged | | hinted read, all elements missing | `TYPE_MISMATCH` | unchanged | | optional group, all children skipped as unsupported | silently skipped, `Tuple()` | unchanged | | schema cache key | 2 entries for 4 setting combinations | keyed on the setting | </details> `04065_tuple_inside_nullable_parquet_roundtrip.reference` pinned the buggy `(NULL,NULL)` output as a limitation; that reference change is the fix, not a weakened assertion. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115653&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115653](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115653+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Extend test 04307_add_to_enum with MergeTree and ReplicatedMergeTree coverage
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93830 PR #93830 added `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... ADD ENUM VALUES`, but its test used only the `Memory` engine. The test now carries the `no-replicated-database` tag, because it creates two replicas with an explicit ZooKeeper path, which a `Replicated` database does not allow. signals.title: Read the global settings under a lock in Context::getReadSettings
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62025 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a data race on the global `Context`'s settings. `Context::getReadSettings()` and `Context::getWriteSettings()` read the settings without a lock while the writers on that path hold `Context::mutex` exclusively, so a background thread opening a file during a settings change could read a torn value, including a `std::string_view` into a `String` setting being reallocated. `Context::setDefaultProfiles()` also adjusted settings outside the lock. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62025 ### Description `Context::getReadSettings()` reads 51 settings through `getSettingsRef()`, an unsynchronized inline accessor, while the writers on that path hold the exclusive `Context::mutex` - a missing reader-side lock (the `checkSettingsConstraints`/`clampToSettingsConstraints` overloads are the exception, disclosed below). `getWriteSettings()` has the same shape, and the four throttler getters read their bandwidth setting the same way. Two of those settings are `SettingFieldString`, and the getter holds a `std::string_view` into the heap `String` while a concurrent assignment can reallocate it, so the consequence exceeds a torn scalar. `setDefaultProfiles()` was the other half: `applySettingsQuirks`, `adjustSettingsForMakeDistributedPlan` and `doSettingsSanityCheckClamp` ran after `setCurrentProfile` released the mutex, so a reader-side lock alone would exclude nothing. Free `getReadSettings()` falls back to the global context when there is no query context - the documented `system_profile` path for background work - so a background thread opening a file during startup reaches it. The report came from a Keeper changelog reader racing `setDefaultProfiles`, but the defect is in `Context`. Both getters now take a shared lock over the settings extraction and release it before the calls that follow, because this mutex cannot be upgraded and the throttler getters re-enter it exclusively. The throttler getters' own bandwidth reads are synchronized the same way, and `setDefaultProfiles`' trailing mutations move under the exclusive lock. The effective settings a server reports are byte-identical before and after. Scope is narrow: it makes the reported pair race-free, not all access to the global settings. Still unsynchronized and not addressed here: the five `checkSettingsConstraints`/`clampToSettingsConstraints` overloads reaching `doSettingsSanityCheckClamp` under a shared lock only, `reloadClusterConfig()`, `getBackupsThrottler()`, and 29 sites outside `Context` reading the global settings via `getSettingsRef()`. <details> <summary>Provenance and validation</summary> Issue #62025 reports this same race, also on a `String` setting; it was closed by #62309, which reordered one `clickhouse-local` caller and left the accessor unsynchronized. This report is from an internal ThreadSanitizer stress run, with no public CIDB hits for the stack in 90 days: it is rare, and the argument is the mechanism. Two tests in the existing `gtest_context_race.cpp`, neither carrying signal outside ThreadSanitizer. `GetReadSettingsRace`: reader threads calling both getters against a writer changing a `String` setting and an integer one; it reports on the unpatched tree in 3 of 3 runs, naming `getReadSettings` as the read and `setSettingWithLock` as the write, and is silent in 5 of 5 with the fix. `SetDefaultProfilesRace` covers the other half, where the trailing pass is the unlocked reader. Of the seven locks added, six were removed one at a time with the matching test required to report, at six distinct addresses; the seventh is `getWriteSettings`' own, driven by the same test through `s3_allow_parallel_part_upload`, which only it reads. Since this locks a hot accessor, deadlock was the main concern. `Context::mutex` is private and no `Context` method calls either getter, so there is no reverse entry, and the callees inside the locked region do not take it. Dynamically, a server with embedded Keeper and all four bandwidth settings non-zero, so the throttler getters reach their exclusive branch, served 263,251 queries at 2920 QPS under mixed load with no hang. Also green under ThreadSanitizer: `Context.*` (9), `Coordination*` (43), `Threading.*SharedMutex*` (12), and the Keeper suites `test_keeper_and_access_storage` (which guards the startup ordering `setDefaultProfiles` takes part in), `test_keeper_session`, `test_keeper_incorrect_config`, `test_keeper_block_acl`. An alternating A/B benchmark showed no measurable throughput change (base 3464 QPS, patched 3520, overlapping ranges). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115659&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115659](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115659+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not re-read a partially cached segment's committed prefix from the source
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115070 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `ICacheProvider.h:107-109` puts the derivation of a tier's uncommitted tail on the caller: given `Lead::available`, fetch `[available.end(), range.end())`. `readThroughCaches` bound `lead.available` to a local, used it only for the covers-the-head early return, then dropped it - `MissTier` had no field for it. `fetch_lo` came from the miss range instead, and on the populating path a partial segment's miss spans its whole extent from `seg_left` (`DiskCacheProvider.cpp:651`), that range being the writer's fill geometry. So a partially cached read re-read that prefix; `write`'s append-only check discarded those bytes, making it wasted I/O, not wrong data. The read-only sibling emits the miss from `committed_end` (`:600-601`). This carries `available` into `MissTier` and derives the tail once, for `fetch_lo`/`fetch_hi` and the write loop. A tier whose prefix spans its range yields an empty tail and is skipped, so it cannot pull `fetch_lo` back to the segment start. The new coverage is a unit test because a segment committed to an arbitrary mid-point is not deterministically reachable from SQL - which is why 04511 was flaky rather than failing. Its five cases each fail on master; the suite is 44/44 here. Measured on `s3_cache_04511`, `ReaderExecutorBytesFromSource` on the warm reread: **1,325,913 -> 276,057** bytes, cold unchanged at 1,588,547. With `reader_executor_use_long_connections` a held connection can still bridge over the prefix; untouched here. Surfaced by two [`04511_reader_executor_disk_cache`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113518&sha=758c46640f6193b9a9770c3e76a599688e574b15&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_msan%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20sequential%2C%202%2F2%29) failures on 2026-08-20, one on master, both diffing only `warm_served_from_cache 1 -> 0`. That test and its `.reference` are unchanged: its `warm < cold` assertion was correct and was reporting this bug, having been adjusted for flakiness four times. It passes 50/50 under randomized settings and under those runs' settings. #115643 pins it to one thread so its oracle can be strict; measured here, the two compose - `warm = 0` needs the pin, and this cuts the multi-thread warm read it leaves. <details> <summary>Validation detail: warm-read source bytes per configuration, and the release-branch check</summary> Same fixture and probe each time; `warm/cold` ratio of `ReaderExecutorBytesFromSource`. The test's assertion is `warm < cold`, so a ratio near 1.0 is a near-failure. | threads / window | master | this PR | |---|---|---| | 8 / 1 MiB | 0.835 | 0.174 | | 8 / 256 KiB | 0.668 | 0.448 | | 8 / 64 KiB | 0.575 | 0.377 | | 4 / 1 MiB | 0.504 | 0.174 | | 16 / 256 KiB | 0.502 | 0.116 | | worst case | **0.835** | **0.504** | Build IDs: master `c877fb06499b8acdfd053c38051b7fd4c7e79737`, this PR `2ffe0b96223a5b47c2099d92b26cbbb4768786fd`; server identity asserted with `SELECT lower(buildId())` before each arm. `readThroughCaches`, `DiskCacheProvider.cpp` and `ICacheProvider.h` are absent from every active release branch (26.7 / 26.6 / 26.5 / 26.3 / 25.8), so the read-through cache path has never shipped. `use_reader_executor` was added in `996c1850` (2026-06-09), defaults to `false`, tier `EXPERIMENTAL`. No backport. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115664&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115664](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115664+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix a wedged mutation after a patch-mode lightweight delete
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115570 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` (`Not found column _row_exists in block`) that permanently blocked all further mutations of a `MergeTree` table after a lightweight `DELETE` run with `lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'` was followed by a heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` and then by another mutation rewriting all columns. Closes #115570. ### Description Closes #115570. A lightweight `DELETE` in patch mode supplies `_row_exists` from a patch part, not from the source part's own columns, so `MutateTask` synthesizes a `READ_COLUMN{read_for_patch = true}` command for it. For a mutation that rewrites all columns, `MutationsInterpreter` correctly omits the mask from its output header: that mutation applies the mask on read and physically drops the masked rows, so the new part must not carry a mask. `getColumnsForNewDataPart` disagreed with it. Its `_row_exists` entry derived the answer from a command proxy, which is true for that synthetic command, so the mask was added to the new part's column list while the pipeline block did not contain it. The part writer enumerates the column list and looks each name up in the block, so it threw on the first write and the mutation was re-queued forever. Every later mutation queued behind it, leaving the table unmutable until `KILL MUTATION`. `_row_exists` was the only entry in that loop asking a command proxy. Its siblings `_block_number` and `_block_offset` already ask the pipeline header, and two other sites in this file already treat the header as the mask authority, so I made `_row_exists` ask it too. The second disjunct is kept: it preserves an existing on-disk mask for a partial rewrite. I validated by row-set equality against `lightweight_delete_mode = 'alter_update'`, the mode that does not wedge, rather than by the exception disappearing: same rows, same checksum, same per-part mask layout. A partial `ALTER UPDATE` still materializes the mask and hides the deleted rows, so no lightweight-deleted row is resurrected. All three commands that rewrite all columns (`DELETE`, `APPLY DELETED MASK`, `REWRITE PARTS`) reproduce and are fixed. Not addressed here: a deterministically failing mutation is still re-queued indefinitely. That is a separate retry policy question, and fixing the exception removes the wedge. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115665&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115665](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115665+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
