signals.title: Fix out-of-bounds read in `formatRowNoNewline` with empty rows
signals.text: Fixes a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline`. When a row is formatted to an empty result (for example, an empty string with the `RawBLOB` format), the newline-stripping logic could rewind the shared write buffer into the previous row's bytes, producing non-monotonic `ColumnString` offsets and a `size_t` underflow in the string size. Functions consuming the result could then return incorrect results or raise a logical error. The trailing newline is now stripped only when the current row actually emitted at least one byte, which keeps the offsets monotonic. The cursor is also kept within the current working buffer so the decrement never moves it before the buffer start after a flush. Added a regression test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/04512_format_row_no_newline_empty_row_underflow.sql`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline` that could produce incorrect results or a logical error when a row is formatted to an empty result. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115669&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115669](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115669+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix substreams cache key collision between streams of one column
signals.text: The substreams cache was keyed by the subcolumn name, which escapes nothing, so two streams of one column could share a cache slot even when their files differ: for `Array(Tuple(`size0` UInt64))` the array sizes are written to `c.size0` and the tuple element to `c%2Esize0`, and both render to the cache key `size0`. The reader then handed the wrong column to the wrong deserializer - wrong values, `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` or a logical error - and such a table could not be merged. The data on disk is correct, so existing parts read correctly after this fix. Affected are a `Tuple` element named like an automatic substream of an enclosing `Array` or of a sibling element, and a `JSON` typed path named like a substream of a sibling path or like one of `JSON`'s internal streams. The wide reader uses the cache for every read, the compact reader only for subcolumn reads. `StorageLog` and `StorageTinyLog` use the same cache and are fixed too. Both caches are now keyed by the file name rendering minus the column prefix, which is injective. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115632 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading a column that has two streams whose names differ only by escaping, for example a `Tuple` element named `size0` inside an `Array`, or a `JSON` typed path named like a substream of a sibling path. Such columns returned wrong values, failed with `CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA` or a logical error, and made the table unmergeable. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115670&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115670](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115670+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Publish the standalone WebAssembly SQL parser as a CI artifact
signals.text: ## Motivation `utils/wasm-parser` builds `src/Parsers` on its own, for a browser: a WASI reactor that answers whether a query parses, reports the error with a position, and pretty-prints, in 1.2 MB (280 KB brotli). Nothing in CI published it, so the only way to get the module was to build it — a wasi-sdk download and a few hundred translation units of full LTO. The module *was* built in CI, inside `tests/integration/test_wasm_parser`, but in a container that was torn down at the end of the test, with the result thrown away. ## What this does Adds a `Build (wasm_parser)` job that builds the two extreme configurations, runs `ctest` on each - `parser-cases` drives the module through `test.mjs` under Node.js, `parser-size` asserts the byte ceiling - and publishes both modules as the `CH_WASM_PARSER_BIN` artifact: ``` https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/REFs/master/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser.wasm https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/REFs/master/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser-no-formatting-no-dcl.wasm https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/PRs/<pr>/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser.wasm ``` There is no JavaScript sidecar to go with them, unlike the Emscripten `Build (wasm64)` artifact: a consumer instantiates the `.wasm` itself and supplies the WASI preview1 imports. It is a job of its own rather than another `BuildTypes` entry in the `Build` matrix, because the project cross-compiles to `wasm32-wasip1` with a wasi-sdk toolchain that cannot be mixed into a tree configured for the host. So it runs in `clickhouse/wasm-builder` instead of `binary-builder`, and the two post hooks the other build jobs carry are left off - neither the master-head binary nor the build profile has a counterpart here. The job takes over from `tests/integration/test_wasm_parser`, which existed because nothing else notices when this module stops compiling, which it did within a day of being merged, twice over. It built the same two configurations and discarded them; it, its compose file and its `TEST_CONFIGS` entry are removed, so CI no longer performs the same full-LTO build twice. `clickhouse/wasm-builder` moves out of `ci/docker/integration` - it is a build-job image now, not a service an integration test spins up - and gains `python3`, which praktika needs in order to run the job script inside it. ## Verification The job was run locally through praktika, against this branch after merging `master`: | configuration | ctest | published | bytes | ceiling | | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | everything | 2/2 passed | `parser.wasm` | 1234449 | 1290000 | | no-formatting-no-dcl | 2/2 passed | `parser-no-formatting-no-dcl.wasm` | 805553 | 840000 | Both are ~3.5% above the size table in `utils/wasm-parser/README.md`, which has drifted from what `master` produces; still inside the ceilings, so `parser-size` passes. Re-measuring all four configurations to refresh that table is left for a separate change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not required for this category. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115673&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115673](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115673+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Take the Cascades sort limits from the plan, not the ambient context
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115571 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the sort limits the Cascades optimizer applies to a sort it adds for a subquery. `max_rows_to_sort`, `max_bytes_to_sort`, `sort_overflow_mode`, the external-sort thresholds and `min_free_disk_space_for_temporary_data` were read from the ambient query context, which for a separately-planned subquery holds the enclosing query's values, so a subquery's `SETTINGS` clause was silently discarded in both directions: a tightened limit was not enforced, and a raised one was overridden by the outer query's stricter value. ### Description A scalar subquery gets its own `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings`, but `buildContext` seeded `OptimizerContext::sort_settings` from `CurrentThread::get().tryGetQueryContext()`, the enclosing query's context while the subquery is planned. `SortingEnforcer` builds its `SortingStep` from that copy, so every sort limit it carries came from the wrong scope. Further down, the same function already read four other settings from `optimization_settings`, so this was also a two-source inconsistency. Measured on `cc440c911383a00`: a subquery asking for `max_rows_to_sort = 10, sort_overflow_mode = 'throw'` under a permissive outer query returns a value instead of throwing; reversed, an outer query at `10, 'throw'` with the subquery raising it to `1000000, 'break'` throws instead of returning. Both invert with this change, while the no-Cascades control and the top-level-limit arm are unaffected. Every setting involved is experimental and off by default, so this needs an unusual but supported configuration. Same defect class as #113422 (merged) and #115571, at a third consumer; this is the residual I disclosed on #115571. The fix extends that seam: `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings` carries the sort limits and `buildContext` builds `SortingStep::Settings` from them. `max_bytes_ratio_before_external_sort` stays a raw ratio there and is resolved inside `buildContext`: resolving it reads the memory trackers and rejects an out-of-range value, so doing it in the settings constructor would widen that error to all queries. The new test's last two statements pin the surface. The new test covers both directions plus two controls. It fails on master, and reverting only the seeding line while keeping the new fields reddens it again. Also noticed, not fixed here: one `OptimizerContext` holds one `sort_settings` for the whole memo, so a plan with sorts from two scopes uses one of them, where the non-Cascades path is per-sort. Separate root cause, unmeasured under Cascades. The statistics hint and cost-config there remain ambient; those are query parameters, with no per-subquery scope to inherit. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115674&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115674](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115674+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add stateful storage memory profiler
signals.text: Adds a stateful storage memory profiler alongside the existing AST memory profiler in `clickhouse-examples`. signals.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114867 Implements the `/api/v1/series` endpoint of the Prometheus HTTP API for `TimeSeries` tables. This is a minimal rewrite of the PR above (by @fallintoplace, kept as co-author) reusing the existing primitives of the query endpoints: - each `match[]` value is parsed with the regular PromQL parser and must be an instant selector; - the matching series are found by the same tags-table query the query path builds (exposed as `StorageTimeSeriesSelector::makeSelectIDsQuery`), including the `min_time`/`max_time` overlap conditions for the optional `start`/`end` parameters — ignored when the tags table does not store the bounds, as allowed by the approximate `/series` contract; - the label sets are returned via `timeSeriesIdToTags` and serialized with the existing `writeTags`. Repeated `match[]` parameters produce the union of the matched series. The optional `limit` parameter caps the number of returned series; a truncated response carries the Prometheus `results truncated due to limit` warning. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Implement the `/api/v1/series` endpoint of the Prometheus HTTP API for `TimeSeries` tables: `match[]` series selectors (repeated values are a union), an optional `start`/`end` time range, and an optional `limit` parameter. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115676&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115676](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115676+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Compute the transformed header once per step instead of per stream
signals.text: `ExpressionTransform` and `FilterTransform` recomputed their output header in every instance via `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` (constant folding over the whole DAG, one column per node), and `ExpressionStep` / `FilterStep` create one transform per stream — so pipeline construction paid O(streams × DAG size). `FilterTransform` even ran updateHeader twice per instance: once for the output header and once for the pre-removal `transformed_header` member. This came out of profiling why ClickBench Q29 (90 `SUM(ResolutionWidth + N)` aggregates, which the analyzer collapses into a single `sumCount` plus 89 scalar projections) still takes ~25 ms hot: on a 96-core machine, the single largest item of pipeline construction was `ActionsDAG::evaluatePartialResult` called from the `ExpressionTransform` constructor once per each of the 89 streams (~8 ms of ~23 ms total query overhead), via `ExpressionStep::transformPipeline` → `Pipe::addSimpleTransform` → `transformHeader`. ## Changes All output ports of a `Pipe` share one header, so the transformed header is now computed once in `ExpressionStep::transformPipeline` and `FilterStep::transformPipeline` and shared by all instances through new `ExpressionTransform` / `FilterTransform` constructor overloads that accept a precomputed header. The legacy constructors are kept for the remaining call sites; the legacy `FilterTransform` constructor now delegates and runs updateHeader once instead of twice. ## Results On the 96-core machine (12 runs, steady state, 100M-row table): - hot Q29 `SELECT`: ~24 ms → ~17 ms - `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` of Q29: ~19 ms → ~13 ms - `EXPLAIN PLAN`: unchanged (as expected) - `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` output and query result checksums are identical before/after; a 140-test stateless smoke run (filter/totals/`EXPLAIN PIPELINE`-heavy tests, including `02210_processors_profile_log*`) shows no regressions. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up query pipeline construction for queries with large expressions or many streams: the output header of `ExpressionTransform` and `FilterTransform` is now computed once per query plan step instead of once (twice for filters) per stream. For a ClickBench Q29-like query on a 96-core machine, this removes about a third of the hot query time. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115677&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115677](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115677+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix PromQL query_range step validation for equal start and end
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject zero and negative `step` values in one-point Prometheus range queries.** ### Summary Prometheus rejects zero and negative query resolution steps for `/api/v1/query_range`, including requests where `start == end`. ClickHouse currently skips step validation when the timestamps are equal. This means a request such as: `query=vector(1)&start=10&end=10&step=0` can return a successful one-point matrix instead of an error. This change validates `step` for `QUERY_RANGE` independently of the timestamp range. Instant queries keep their internal `step=0` behavior. ### Why this matters Prometheus-compatible clients expect the same validation for one-point range queries. Returning a successful result for an invalid request can hide client-side errors. ### Tests - Add HTTP integration coverage for `step=0` and `step=-1` when `start == end`. - Keep coverage for a valid positive-step one-point range. - Validate the changed C++ translation unit and Python test syntax. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115679&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115679](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115679+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Expand `url` glob patterns lazily
signals.text: A pattern passed to `url` was expanded into the full direct product before the query started, so `glob_expansion_max_elements` limited how large a pattern was allowed to be rather than how much of it a query needed. A query that stops early paid for the whole address space up front, and was rejected outright when that space was large: ```sql SELECT * FROM url('https://clickhouse-public-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/wikistat/original/pageviews-20200101-{0..10000}{0..10000}00.gz', LineAsString) LIMIT 3 -- Code: 36. DB::Exception: first argument generates too many result addresses. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` `RemoteDescriptionGenerator` produces the addresses of a pattern one at a time instead. Numeric intervals stay symbolic, so `{0..10000}{0..10000}` costs two factors rather than a hundred million strings, and the odometer over them walks the same order the materializing code produced - the last factor varies fastest. `parseRemoteDescription` is now a thin wrapper that checks the arithmetic total and drains the generator, so there is still one parser of the syntax, and `remote`, `mysql` and `postgresql` - which need every address at once to build a cluster - behave exactly as before, down to the error messages. Three places on the `url` path stopped materializing: - `getSampleURI` takes a single address. It only reads hive partitioning and virtual columns off a path, and used to expand the whole pattern to look at its first element. - `StorageURLSource::DisclosedGlobIterator` generates in batches and applies the `_path` / `_file` filter to each. A pattern that fits into one batch keeps the exact post-filter size, which is what empty-glob detection and the number of streams are derived from, so nothing observable changes for it. - Schema inference pulls addresses through a producer and stops at the first one it can read. The limit therefore applies to the addresses a query actually reads. The batch is `min(1000, glob_expansion_max_elements)` and the default limit is 1000, so every pattern that works today is still served in a single batch and behaves bit for bit as it did; only patterns that used to be rejected behave differently. Reading a huge pattern in full is still rejected. Groups holding the separator, such as `{a,b}` in `{a,b}{c,d}`, are still expanded eagerly and bounded by the limit, because the direct product needs their alternatives up front. A `..` anywhere inside braces makes the whole group a numeric interval, so such a group can only hold literal text. Verified against a locally built server: the query above now returns rows; `{1..1000}` at the default limit still reads exactly 1000 addresses; `_path` filtering, failover options, `remote`, `mysql` and every malformed-pattern error message are byte-identical to an unmodified `master` binary. The `url` over-limit message now names `url` instead of `remote`, which is the only intentional difference. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/49234 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115581 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `url` table function and the `URL` table engine now expand glob patterns lazily instead of materializing every address before the query starts. `glob_expansion_max_elements` now limits how many addresses a query actually reads rather than how large the pattern is, so a query that stops early - for example under a `LIMIT` - can use a pattern that describes far more addresses than the limit. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115680&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115680](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115680+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Disable 1MB Head prefetch for small random access files (Parquet)
signals.text: ClickHouse have an throughput optimization. If object is small (<20MB), there is 1MB prefetch of object beginning. But there are formats, (Parquet specifically), which are being read from footer. And quite commonly, you don't even need to read rest of object, if statistics in footer says so. So, making prefetch of first 1MB, if it doesn't cover footer as well (whole file <1MB) is not helpful. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid a redundant object-storage GET request when reading random-access formats from object storage. The generic from-start read-ahead is no longer issued for files larger than a single read buffer, where it could not reach the footer. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115681&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115681](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115681+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix PromQL timestamp and duration overflow at Int64 boundary
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject PromQL timestamps and durations that exceed the Int64 range.** ### Summary PromQL timestamps and durations can be passed as floating-point values. ClickHouse scales them and converts them to Int64. `INT64_MAX` is rounded to `2^63` when represented as `Float64`. The previous upper-bound check used `>` and allowed that value to reach the conversion even though `2^63` is outside the Int64 range. Converting it to Int64 is undefined behavior. The upper-bound check now rejects equality as well. ### Tests - Add a timestamp regression for the finite floating-point boundary. - Add a duration regression for the same boundary. - Compile the changed C++ translation unit. - Run `git diff --check`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115682&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115682](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115682+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Perf: write sampling keys directly to output column
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Write TimeSeries sampling keys directly into the result column.** ## What changed `timeSeriesGroupToSamplingKey` used to: - ask the collector to build a temporary `VectorWithMemoryTracking<UInt64>`; - allocate the result `ColumnUInt64`; - copy every sampling key into the result column. This change lets the collector fill `ColumnUInt64::getData()` directly. - Removes the temporary vector. - Removes the second per-key copy loop. - Keeps the existing lookup and output values unchanged. - Uses the same direct output-buffer pattern as `timeSeriesIdToGroup`. ## Why this is safe - The collector still uses the same group lookup and lock. - The destination buffer is resized before it is filled. - Output type, order, duplicate-group behavior, and empty-input behavior are unchanged. ## Benchmark Added an isolated performance workload that materializes 20 million sampling-key rows from a repeated vector of 4,096 groups. It uses one thread and a large block size so the temporary allocation and copy are easier to measure without spending most of the query on group setup. ## Tests - Added functional coverage for repeated groups, distinct groups, and empty input in `03779_time_series_tags_functions`. - Syntax-checked the changed translation units. - Ran `git diff --check`.

signals.title: Prune the unasked-for right keys of a multi-disjunct join under the old analyzer too
signals.text: Follow-up to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115465, which stopped a join with several disjuncts (`... ON a = b OR c = d`) from adding right key columns the query does not ask for. That pruning was gated on `enableAnalyzer()`, out of caution about a path I had not measured, so on the legacy planner every right key is still added. `TableJoin::requiredRightKeys` works on both paths: the planner fills `columns_added_by_join` through `setUsedColumns`, and `TreeRewriter::collectJoinedColumns` fills it through `addJoinedColumn`. So the gate can go. It matters beyond the columns themselves: the key-only join hash tables of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115301 are chosen for `LEFT SEMI` only when the join produces no right value at all, so with `enable_analyzer = 0` a query like `SELECT count() FROM l SEMI LEFT JOIN r ON l.k = r.k OR l.s = r.s` would stay on the mapped tables while the same query on the analyzer gets the key-only ones. With this change it gets them on both. Checked against a build of the parent commit, all with `enable_analyzer = 0`: - seven `OR` join shapes - `ALL`/`SEMI`/`ANTI`, `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL`, with and without a right key or a payload column selected - return the same results as with the analyzer; - `05023_join_several_disjuncts_right_keys` passes; - the `join` tests have the same six reference mismatches as the parent commit, all of them tests that read differently on the legacy planner (`00826_cross_to_inner_join`, `01115_join_with_dictionary`, `02220_array_join_format`, `02784_parallel_replicas_automatic_decision_join`, `04653_distributed_plan_auto_rewrite_in_to_join`, `04670_any_join_take_last_row_no_swap`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115465 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115301 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115684&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115684](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115684+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Store and ingest Prometheus native histograms in the TimeSeries engine
signals.text: ## Summary First slice of Prometheus native-histogram support for the `TimeSeries` engine (storage + ingestion). Today, `timeseries[].histograms[]` in a remote-write request is parsed and silently dropped with a 204; a Prometheus sender configured with `send_native_histograms: true` loses all histogram data. This PR makes that data storable and queryable via SQL: - **Storage**: a new optional `HISTOGRAMS` target table on the `TimeSeries` engine (alongside `DATA`/`TAGS`/`METRICS`), enabled with `SETTINGS store_native_histograms = 1` or an explicit `HISTOGRAMS [db.table | INNER ENGINE ...]` clause. One row per histogram sample, mirroring the `prompb.Histogram` message for lossless round-trip: `id`, `timestamp`, `flags` (is_float / counter-reset hint / gauge / stale marker), `schema`, `zero_threshold`, `count`, `sum`, `zero_count`, positive/negative spans and bucket values, and `custom_values` for NHCB (schema −53). Bucket values are stored as absolutes (int-flavor deltas are decoded at ingest). A `timeSeriesHistograms(db.table)` table function mirrors `timeSeriesData` for introspection. - **Ingestion**: `PrometheusRemoteWriteProtocol` reads `timeseries[].histograms[]` — both the int (delta-encoded) and float flavors — validates span/bucket consistency (rejecting the request with `INCORRECT_DATA`/HTTP 400 on malformed data), preserves counter-reset hints and stale markers, updates the tags table's `min_time`/`max_time` from histogram timestamps, and counts ingested histograms in a new `PrometheusRemoteWriteHistograms` profile event. The decoding is factored so a future remote-write 2.0 message path can reuse it. The vendored protobuf gains upstream's `custom_values = 16` field. - **Backward compatibility**: tables without the `HISTOGRAMS` target work exactly as before — `CREATE`, `ATTACH`, and remote writes are unchanged; histogram samples sent to such a table are dropped with a rate-limited warning (and the profile event), so the loss is at least observable, instead of today's silent drop. Everything stays behind `allow_experimental_time_series_table`. PromQL evaluation over histograms (`histogram_quantile` etc.), the HTTP query API JSON shapes, and remote-read output are explicitly out of scope for this PR and build on this storage layer. Open design questions (called out for reviewers): whether the `flags` gauge bit should be dropped as redundant with `counter_reset_hint == GAUGE`, and whether new tables should get the `HISTOGRAMS` target by default under the experimental flag rather than opt-in. ## Tests - Stateless: `CREATE`/`SHOW CREATE` round-trip with and without the target, external histograms-table validation, `timeSeriesHistograms()` reads, `ATTACH` of a pre-histogram definition. - Integration (`test_prometheus_protocols/test_native_histograms.py`): remote-write of int, float, NHCB, and stale-marker histograms with spans, zero bucket and negative buckets, asserting every stored column; mixed float samples + histograms in one request; drop-with-warning on a 3-target table; invalid spans and negative decoded counts → 400. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The experimental `TimeSeries` table engine can now store Prometheus native histograms: a new optional `HISTOGRAMS` target table (enabled with `store_native_histograms = 1`), ingestion of native histograms from the Prometheus remote-write protocol, and a `timeSeriesHistograms` table function for reading them. Previously such samples were silently dropped. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115685&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115685](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115685+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Perf: fuse TimeSeries tag extraction and NULL map
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Build the TimeSeries extracted-tag value and NULL map in one pass.** ## What changed `timeSeriesExtractTag` used to: - scan the groups and build a `ColumnString`; - scan every output string again with `getDataAt(i).empty()`; - build the nullable map in a separate loop. The collector already knows whether the requested tag was found during the first scan. This change lets it fill the final `ColumnString` and NULL map together. - Removes the second output scan. - Removes the separate NULL-map insertion loop. - Preserves the old empty-value NULL behavior. - Keeps the existing `Nullable(String)` result and missing-tag behavior. ## Why this is safe - The collector still uses the same group validation and shared lock. - Present tags write their value and the same empty-value check used previously. - Missing tags write the default string and a NULL bit. - TimeSeries SQL tag construction normally removes empty tag values before storing groups. ## Benchmark Added an isolated workload that extracts an early-hit tag (`tag00`), a late-hit tag (`tag15`), and a missing tag from 16-tag groups. It repeats 4,096 groups over 20 million rows with one thread and a large block size so tag lookup and NULL-map construction dominate the setup. ## Tests - Extended `03779_time_series_tags_functions` to check both present and missing tags with `isNotNull` and `isNull`. - Added a mixed-row test with alternating present and missing groups to verify NULL-map alignment. - Added `tests/performance/timeseries_extract_tag.xml`. - Compiled the changed translation units with the existing Release compile commands. - Ran `git diff --check` and validated the benchmark XML. Related to [#115656](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115656). That PR fuses tag-name and tag-value extraction for `timeSeriesTagsToGroup`; this PR fuses extracted values with NULL-map construction for `timeSeriesExtractTag`.

signals.title: Support asynchronous inserts in the Prometheus remote-write protocol
signals.text: The Prometheus remote-write protocol handler now honors the `async_insert` setting (enabled in the user profile or passed as a URL query parameter of the handler): data from multiple concurrent remote-write requests is batched in the asynchronous insert queue before forming parts, which reduces the number of parts created in the inner tables of a `TimeSeries` table under a high rate of small remote-write requests. Since `async_insert` is enabled by default, remote-write requests are batched by default; add `async_insert=0` to the handler URL or disable the setting for the user to keep the previous synchronous behavior. A request is acknowledged only after the data is flushed to all inner tables of the `TimeSeries` table, regardless of the `wait_for_async_insert` setting, because the remote-write protocol treats an acknowledged write as durable. If the flush fails, the request returns an error instead of an acknowledgement, so the sender retries it. Deduplication on flush is forcibly disabled on this path (both `deduplicate_insert` and `async_insert_deduplicate`, since the former overrides the latter): a flushed block combines data from multiple remote-write requests, so its hash differs on every retry anyway, and the inner tables of the `TimeSeries` engine handle duplicates themselves. Verified manually with a local server and real remote-write requests: a request without settings goes through the asynchronous insert queue and the data is visible immediately after the acknowledgement; `async_insert=0` keeps the synchronous path; four concurrent requests are flushed as a single batch insert; a failing inner table (a `CHECK` constraint on an external `DATA` target table) returns HTTP 500 with no acknowledgement and no data written. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The Prometheus remote-write protocol now supports asynchronous inserts: data from multiple concurrent remote-write requests is batched before forming parts, following the `async_insert` setting (enabled by default; add `async_insert=0` to the handler URL to keep the synchronous behavior). A request is acknowledged only after the data is flushed to all inner tables of the target `TimeSeries` table. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115688&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115688](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115688+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Rename refresh dependencies when restoring under a new name
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115645 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `RESTORE ... AS <new name>` leaving the `REFRESH ... DEPENDS ON` list of a refreshable materialized view pointing at the original database. The restored view refreshed in response to a table it no longer read, ignored refreshes of its own parent, and stopped refreshing entirely once the original database was dropped. ### Description `RESTORE DATABASE db AS db_restored` rewrote every table reference in a stored refreshable materialized view definition except the `REFRESH ... DEPENDS ON` list: ``` CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW db_restored.child REFRESH AFTER 1 SECOND DEPENDS ON db.parent ... AS SELECT a FROM db_restored.parent ^^ TO/FROM rewritten, DEPENDS ON not ``` `DDLRenamingVisitor::visit` dispatches on `ASTCreateQuery`, `ASTTableExpression`, `ASTFunction`, `ASTDictionary` and `ASTStorage`; `ASTRefreshStrategy` was missing, so the node was walked but never touched. The refresh scheduler keys its dependency graph on the full table name, so a dependency naming the pre-restore database occupies a different graph slot than the restored parent. Measured: refreshing the *source* parent fired the restored child, three consecutive refreshes of its *own* parent did not, and dropping the source database left the restored view at `MissingDependencies`. The fix adds the missing visit, running the renaming map over the dependency list exactly as the existing `create.targets` loop does. `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` already visits this node to qualify the same list at CREATE time, so this is the renaming counterpart of an established pass. The visitor is the only transform applied at all four sites that rewrite a stored definition, so this covers backup-side and restore-side renaming together, and the corrected definition is what gets persisted, so later `ATTACH`es are right with no separate fixup. A dependency pointing outside the restored set is left alone, and so is one whose table is not itself renamed by a `RESTORE TABLE ... AS`; the test pins both as controls. Backups already written are not affected: the defect was in the rename transform, not the backup, so restoring an existing backup with a fixed server gives the correct dependency (verified against a backup taken by an unfixed binary). No settings or formats change; a definition without `DEPENDS ON` is untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115689&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115689](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115689+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Wake idle streaming exchange sinks and sources on backward stop
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114806 When a `LIMIT` in a distributed plan is satisfied, the stop signal travels backward through the exchanges. It stalled at idle stages: a `StreamingExchangeSink` with an empty input waited only on its input port and did not read `NoMoreDataNeeded` from the socket, and a `StreamingExchangeSource` on a silent socket did not notice that its output port was closed, so it did not forward the stop upstream. Stages that no longer produce anything kept reading and computing until the query timed out. Now both wake while idle: each sink and source waits on a small epoll that holds the socket and a wakeup pipe written by `onUpdatePorts`. The sink asks for socket writability only while it has unsent bytes, so an idle socket does not cause a busy loop. The wire protocol is unchanged. Local in-memory exchanges have the same gap and are not covered here. In the new test the unfixed server hits `max_execution_time = 25` although the result is ready after ~2 s; fixed, the query ends in ~3 s and all worker tasks finish cleanly. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Distributed query plans (`make_distributed_plan`) now stop idle upstream stages promptly after a satisfied `LIMIT`: an idle exchange sink reads `NoMoreDataNeeded` as soon as it arrives, and an idle exchange source notices its closed output and forwards the stop upstream. Previously such stages kept reading and computing data that nobody consumes. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not report "Server died" when the server is stalled but alive
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115080 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112393 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel)` on master @ `756b18a3921e` reported a single failing leaf `Server died` while its own aggregate said `Failed: 0, Passed: 10925, Skipped: 164`. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=756b18a3921e9a5daec71d5c4413bfdad78a8275&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%20parallel%29 The server did not die. It stopped making progress process-wide at `22:14:47` for 116 s, ran for 31 s, stalled again for 107 s, then recovered on its own 89 s *after* the hung check had declared it dead, and shut down cleanly at the end of the job. What the artifacts say about those two stalls: - 0.34 s of CPU burnt across 224 s of wall time, and no `OSCPUWait` either - the threads were not starved, they were parked. - Not one log line, from any of the ~1400 threads, including the embedded Keeper and every `BackgroundSchedulePool` task; on resume they all logged in the same millisecond, and several reported `Execution took` 119-168 s. - The sampling profiler collected 99 samples/minute against a 24000/minute baseline, so the timer signals were not being delivered either. - The co-tenant `seaweedfs` hit its 5-minute heartbeat at `20:16:32.4298`, mid-stall, to the microsecond - the box was fine. - No `<Fatal>` line, no sanitizer report, empty `dmesg`, no failed test. That is a whole-process stop-the-world in the sanitizer runtime, not a ClickHouse deadlock, and it is not something the server can avoid. Root cause of the *report*: `check_server_liveness` spends at most ~165 s (10 attempts, 10 s socket timeout, back-off) and the caller turned "the probe gave up" straight into the abort. A failed probe says the server is not answering; it does not say the server is gone. So the verdict is now split by the evidence that is actually available, in a new `HungCheckMonitor`: - the server process is gone: abort on the first failed probe, at master's latency, unchanged; - the process is still there: keep probing, and only call it a hang after `GRACE_WITH_LIVE_PROCESS = 600 s` of silence. A server that really is deadlocked is still reported, just later, and the extra wait is bounded and small next to a multi-hour job. Not being able to tell whether a process is there (no `ps`, or a server on another host) reads as gone, so master's behaviour is kept whenever there is no positive evidence of a live process. `get_server_pid` picks the first server it can see, so in a multi-replica setup a surviving replica delays the verdict on a dead main server by the grace; it does not lose it. The re-probes inside the grace use a single attempt on a 10 s gate: the retry budget has already been spent proving the server unresponsive, and repeating it would block the parent loop for minutes per iteration. While the server answers, the probe is byte-for-byte what it was. Applied to the incident: the first probe would have failed at ~165 s, the server answered again at ~285 s, and the run would have continued with the other 2000 tests instead of being thrown away. Not claimed: this does not make the stall go away, and it does not touch the `Server died` leaf that #115080 renames or the probe scheduling that #112393 reworks. Both touch the same region, so the second to merge needs a rebase. Validation: `ci/tests/test_hung_check_alive_grace.py` drives the class on a fake clock with the probe and the PID lookup stubbed out - no server, no `ps`. 6 tests; four mutations (no grace, PID evidence ignored, no interval gate, always the full retry budget) each redden a named case. Full `ci/tests`: 817 passed, the 2 pre-existing `test_max_failures_exit_code` failures reproduce identically on pristine master here (they need a running server). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115692&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115692](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115692+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not assert scan-progress values decided by an async race in test_early_return_limit
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115661 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115661 `test_storage_delta/test.py::test_early_return_limit` pins two values an async interleaving decides. 5 hits in 90 days across three job families, two on master, so not parametrization-specific. Latest master failure: [`Integration tests (arm_binary, distributed plan, 1/4)` @ 0c80ff614e89](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=0c80ff614e89817cf0936f09d57f8d67b3bfb7d2&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%201%2F4%29) Root cause: the scan producer appends to a bounded deque and logs the LIVE queue depth (`List batch size is {}/{}`); consumers pop under the same mutex. With `s3_list_object_keys_size = 1` the capacity is one, so the last log legitimately reads `1/1` or `0/1` depending on which thread reaches the mutex first. `DeltaLakeScannedFiles` is incremented after both callback shutdown exits, so the count is 2 or 3 for the same reason. Both orderings are correct. Two test-only changes: - The assertion counting `List batch size is 1/1, shutdown: true` is **removed**, not relaxed: even relaxed it is implied by `assert first_check_hits > 0 or queue_check_hits > 0` three lines above, which runs first. A callback returning false cannot stop the producer reaching that batch log. - `assert scanned_files == 3` becomes `<= 3`, restoring the bound the test was written with: `a33799ba6fb63ee` added `scanned_files < 10`; `95e6f488a0917b` ("Make exact comparison in test") tightened it to `== 3` days later. `scanned_files > 0` bounds the other side. Validated with a forced-interleaving probe in the scan callback: unpatched fails with the CI signature on the drained ordering, patched passes on it. Deleting both callback shutdown exits makes it fail at `assert 997 <= 3`, so the bound still catches an early-return regression. 20/20 runs pass. The retained assertion is not race-proof either: both counters are logged inside the callback, so a shutdown seen by the parked producer skips it. That ordering has 0 of 38 failures in 90 days over 97538 runs, against 5 for the one removed here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115693&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115693](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115693+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid deep copy of AccessRights in getGrantQueriesImpl when it is only read
signals.text: ## What's Changed `getGrantQueriesImpl` used to unconditionally deep-copy the grantee's whole `AccessRights` tree: ```cpp AccessRights access = grantee.access; ``` `AccessRights` is a radix tree, and copying it is `O(number of nodes)`. For users with a huge number of per-table grants (e.g. tens of thousands), this deep copy becomes a serious bottleneck: it is executed on **every** `GRANT`/`REVOKE` (during serialization to `DiskAccessStorage`) and on every `SHOW GRANTS`. The tree is only *modified* when `final == true` (via `unionAccessFromRoles`, which calls `AccessRights::makeUnion`). In the common case (`final == false`) the tree is only read, so we can pass a read-only reference and avoid the deep copy entirely. ## Scope - `src/Interpreters/Access/InterpreterShowGrantsQuery.cpp` — avoid the deep copy when `final == false`. ## Motivation / observed impact On a production cluster (ClickHouse 26.6.1.1193), a user with ~11.6k per-table grants in one database: - A single `GRANT ... ON <table> TO <user>` took **5–28 seconds** on some replicas. - `system.query_log` showed the grant spending **99.9% of its time in user-space CPU**, with a `MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheckBytes` of up to **~500 MB**. - `system.trace_log` showed the hot spot was the recursive `Node::operator=` deep copy inside `serializeAccessEntity -> getGrantQueriesImpl`. - The same grant completed in **~100 ms** on replicas whose in-memory `AccessRights` tree was smaller, confirming the deep copy is the bottleneck. This change removes one of the three deep copies performed per grant (the one inside `getGrantQueriesImpl`). It is a safe, behavior-preserving optimization. ## Testing - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02000_grants_no_deepcopy.sql` + `.reference` verifying that `GRANT`, `SHOW GRANTS` and `REVOKE` behave identically. - Manual verification on the affected cluster: after applying the equivalent change, `SHOW GRANTS FOR <user>` completed in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds. ## Checklist - [x] Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement - [x] Changelog entry: "Avoid a deep copy of the AccessRights tree in `getGrantQueriesImpl` when it is only read, speeding up GRANT/REVOKE and SHOW GRANTS for users with many grants." - [x] Unit tests pass. - [x] Documentation is not required (internal implementation detail). Closes #115694

signals.title: Schema inference for freeform text formats
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Implement schema inference for **row** freeform text format. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/34006 Once this is done you *should* be able to ingest arbitrary tabular text files (ie. application logs) without specifying the structure (Template). *Example usage:* Read data from file ```sql SELECT * FROM file(<file_path>,'Freeform') ``` Describe data from file ```sql Desc file(<file_path>,'Freeform') ``` *How it is implemented* `FreeformFieldMatcher` houses an array of matchers that parse text data by escaping rules (JSON, CSV, Raw(but cutoff by whitespace), Quoted and Escaped). First, FreeformFieldMatcher will iterate over this set of matchers and generate as many solutions as possible. A `Solution` is defined as the order of the matchers to parse one row successfully associated with a score. The score here is generated by continuously adding the score of each field in the solution, specifically by the escaping rule and the type of the field. More specific fields (ie. DateTime) yield higher scores. For now we only generate solutions for the first row because the data is supposed to be *tabular* to we *should* be able to get an acceptable solution just by looking at one row. Then the solutions are sorted by score and they are check against `max_rows_to_check`. The first solution matches all of the `max_rows_to_check` would be picked as the final solution. Currently this works with CSV and syslog but more testing and tunings needs to be made for it to be in an acceptable state. From ```csv 1,2021-04-01 00:00:18,2021-04-01 00:21:54,1,8.40,1,N,79,116,1,25.5,3,0.5,5.85,0,0.3,35.15,2.5 1,2021-04-01 00:42:37,2021-04-01 00:46:23,1,.90,1,N,75,236,2,5,3,0.5,0,0,0.3,8.8,2.5 ``` we have ``` 1 2021 4 1 0 0 18 2021 4 1 0 21 54 1 8.4 1 N 79 116 1 25.5 3 0.5 5.85 0 0.3 35.15 2.5 1 2021 4 1 0 42 37 2021 4 1 0 46 23 1 0.9 1 N 75 236 2 5 3 0.5 0 0 0.3 8.8 2.5 ``` From ``` Nov 13 10:29:56 Tri chronyd[227]: Selected source PHC0 Nov 13 13:24:02 Tri kernel: [91566.562562] hv_utils: TimeSync IC version 4.0 Nov 13 13:24:02 Tri chronyd[227]: Forward time jump detected! ``` we have ``` Nov 13 10 29 56 Tri chronyd[227]: Selected source PHC0 Nov 13 13 24 2 Tri kernel: [91566.562562] hv_utils: TimeSync IC version 4.0 Nov 13 13 24 2 Tri chronyd[227]: Forward time jump detected! ``` *Update 2022-28-11:* With the new changes on increasing the search tree size, we now iterate over all matchers and don't exit early. However, a new field is added only if it has a better type score than the previous field or if no field other than type string has been found. This helps us to better parse the previous CSV example: ``` 1 2021-04-01 0 0 18 2021-04-01 0 21 54 1 8.4 1 N 79 116 1 25.5 3 0.5 5.85 0 0.3 35.15 2.5 1 2021-04-01 0 42 37 2021-04-01 0 46 23 1 0.9 1 N 75 236 2 5 3 0.5 0 0 0.3 8.8 2.5 ``` And also ClickHouse's logs: ``` 2022-11-17 11 7 30.825405 [395843] {345bf223-db80-4772-9a07-73542321e715::202211_15349_15604_53} <Debug> MergeTask::PrepareStage: Merging 6 parts: from 202211_15349_15599_52 to 202211_15604_15604_0 into Compact 2022-11-17 11 7 30.826372 [395843] {345bf223-db80-4772-9a07-73542321e715::202211_15349_15604_53} <Debug> MergeTask::PrepareStage: Selected MergeAlgorithm: Horizontal ``` *Update 2022-30-12:* Now we could parse and unmarshal JSON object fields into their own columns. *TODO:* - Make use of the SchemaCache to store the solution - Fix the new added test

signals.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signals.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. signals.title: [ClickHouse-58380] Implement Retries in distributed queries when server stopped during queries
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Add settings `distributed_query_retries` and `distributed_query_retry_interval_ms` (disabled by default): when enabled, a query to a `Distributed` table or to the `remote` table function is retried after a network error (`NETWORK_ERROR`, `SOCKET_TIMEOUT`, `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF`, e.g. when the remote server is stopped while the query is running). The query is retried on another available replica and only if no result data has been received from the remote server yet, so the result never contains duplicated rows. Queries executed with parallel replicas and cluster function tasks are not retried. While a retry is still possible, the progress reported by the remote server is deferred until the first block of result data (or the completion of the query), so the work replayed by a retry is not double-counted in read limits and quotas. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- The settings documentation is autogenerated from the setting descriptions in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58380 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=66791&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/66791](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F66791+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Display named Tuple columns in Pretty formats as subcolumns
signals.text: ### Changelog category: - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Named Tuple columns in `Pretty` formats are now displayed split into subcolumns, with the names of the elements in additional header (and footer) lines. Controlled by the new setting `output_format_pretty_named_tuples_as_subcolumns` (enabled by default). A named tuple rendered inside a single cell (e.g. nested in an `Array`, or when the new setting is disabled) is still displayed according to `output_format_pretty_named_tuples_as_json`. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/65388 Example: ``` SELECT 'hello' AS x, (1, 'world')::Tuple(a UInt8, b String) AS t ┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━┓ ┃ x ┃ t ┃ ┃ ┣━━━┳━━━━━━━┫ ┃ ┃ a ┃ b ┃ ┡━━━━━━━╇━━━╇━━━━━━━┩ 1. │ hello │ 1 │ world │ └───────┴───┴───────┘ ``` It works for all three styles (`Pretty`, `PrettyCompact`, `PrettySpace`), arbitrary nesting depth, and is mirrored in the footer: ``` SET output_format_pretty_display_footer_column_names = 1, output_format_pretty_display_footer_column_names_min_rows = 0; SELECT 'hello' AS x, (1, 'world')::Tuple(a UInt8, b String) AS t FORMAT PrettyCompact ┌─x─────┬─t─────────┐ ├───────┼─a─┬─b─────┤ 1. │ hello │ 1 │ world │ ├───────┼─a─┴─b─────┤ └─x─────┴─t─────────┘ ``` The implementation recursively flattens named Tuple columns into their elements before rendering, so all the existing width, row, and separator machinery works on the flattened columns unchanged; the hierarchy is kept as a small list of groups plus per-boundary junction levels, from which the extra header and footer lines are derived. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=78927&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/78927](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F78927+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: clean orphans from keeper snapshots
signals.text: This change makes ClickHouse Keeper able to recover from snapshots that contain orphaned nodes — nodes whose parent is absent from the snapshot. Before this change, such a snapshot made Keeper fail to start with an opaque internal error thrown by `updateValue` ("Could not find key"). This pull request replaces that with a clear, opt-in recovery path: - By default (`keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `false`), Keeper still refuses to load a snapshot with orphaned nodes, but now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` exception that reports the number of orphaned nodes and how to enable recovery. - When `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` = `false`, the orphaned nodes and all of their descendants are removed during startup, ACL usage counters and ephemeral bookkeeping are updated, and stale `numChildren` counters on surviving nodes are corrected, so Keeper can load the snapshot. Cleanup is strictly a startup recovery operation. A snapshot deserialized while the server is already running — for example, a follower applying a leader snapshot in `KeeperStateMachine::apply_snapshot` — is applied as-is and is never modified, so a follower cannot diverge from the rest of the cluster. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ClickHouse Keeper now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` error reporting the number of orphaned nodes (nodes whose parent is missing) when loading a snapshot that contains them, instead of failing with an opaque internal error. With the new setting `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` set to `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` set to `false`, such orphaned nodes (and their descendants) are removed during startup so Keeper can load the snapshot. The cleanup is performed only on startup, never while the server is running. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=95761&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/95761](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F95761+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Optimization of `GROUP BY` in the presence of `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Optimize `GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and `GROUP BY ... LIMIT` queries by maintaining a bounded heap during aggregation to prune groups that cannot appear in the result, significantly reducing memory usage and execution time for high-cardinality grouping. Controlled by the `enable_group_by_top_k_optimization` setting. Based on the initial implementation by [Dmitriy Terenichev](https://github.com/Dmitry909) ([#78553](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/78553)). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/72610 Query shapes that benefit from this optimization: - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key ORDER BY key ASC LIMIT N` -- single key, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT key, agg() FROM t GROUP BY key LIMIT N` -- single key, no ORDER BY - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, full ORDER BY match - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2, k3 ASC LIMIT N` -- 3+ keys, full match - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- composite keys, ORDER BY is a prefix of GROUP BY - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 1 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, k3, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2, k3 ORDER BY k1, k2 ASC LIMIT N` -- prefix 2 of 3 - `SELECT k1, k2, agg() FROM t GROUP BY k1, k2 LIMIT N` -- composite keys, no ORDER BY - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL ORDER BY URL ASC LIMIT N` -- String keys - `SELECT URL, count() FROM t GROUP BY URL LIMIT N` -- String keys, no ORDER BY Not supported (optimization is skipped): - `ORDER BY agg()` (ORDER BY aggregate function, not a GROUP BY key) (handled by [another PR](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/98607)) - `WITH TOTALS`, `HAVING`, `GROUPING SETS`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP` - `LIMIT WITH TIES` - ~~Non-final aggregation (distributed partial aggregation)~~ - `max_rows_to_group_by` is set - `rows_before_limit_at_least` mode (exact count) - a COLLATE on any of the matched GROUP BY keys (a COLLATE on a later ORDER BY column past the full key prefix cannot affect which groups qualify and does not disable the optimization) - ORDER BY columns that are not a leading prefix of GROUP BY keys <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=96630&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/96630](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F96630+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add settings `semi_join_compatibility` and `anti_join_compatibility` (default off) to optionally enforce SQL-standard preserved-side column visibility for SEMI and ANTI joins in the new analyzer. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/95738 <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches query analysis/identifier resolution around JOINs and can change query results or raise `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` when the new settings are enabled. signals.title: Columns Cache
signals.text: Implement the deserialized columns cache that keeps columns in memory. In comparison to the uncompressed cache, this saves time on deserialization and copying. Closes #82335. The cache identifies entries by table UUID, so it is only active for tables in databases that assign UUIDs (`Atomic` and `Replicated`); tables in `Ordinary` databases are silently excluded. The feature is gated behind the `EXPERIMENTAL` settings `use_columns_cache`, `enable_reads_from_columns_cache`, and `enable_writes_to_columns_cache`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Implement an experimental columns cache that keeps deserialized columns in memory for `MergeTree` tables. signals.title: Replace ExpressionAnalyzer with Analyzer for standalone expression compilation
signals.text: Replace legacy `ExpressionAnalyzer` with the modern Analyzer framework for standalone expression compilation across storage metadata, MergeTree operations, and query planning. This also rejects invalid `CHECK` constraints containing forbidden subqueries or table names, including `x IN other_table`; direct `x IN (SELECT ...)` remains supported. signals.title: Skip writing all-default columns during MergeTree INSERT
signals.text: ## Summary During MergeTree INSERT, columns whose values are entirely type-defaults (e.g., all zeros for `UInt64`, all empty strings for `String`, all `NULL`s for `Nullable`) are detected and excluded from the part's column list before constructing `MergedBlockOutputStream`. This avoids writing unnecessary `.bin` files (Wide parts) or data streams (Compact parts), saving disk space for sparse-update workloads where most columns in each INSERT are left at their type's default. The optimization is opt-in via the MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` (off by default). It additionally requires `serialization_info_version` to be set to `with_missing_columns` (the format version that records frozen defaults for missing columns), so that a cluster pinned to a lower version for compatibility never writes parts that older servers cannot read. The block itself is passed intact to the writer, so skip indices, projections, primary index, and min-max index are all computed from the full data. Reading a part that lacks a column fills it with type-defaults automatically — the same mechanism used by `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` on existing parts. To keep reads stable, a structured `missing_columns` array is recorded in the part's `serialization.json` (a new `WITH_MISSING_COLUMNS` serialization-info version). Each entry carries the column name and a `type_default` marker. On read, `fillMissingColumns` consults this marker and fills a missing column with its type-default even if the column later gains a new `DEFAULT` expression, so that a subsequent `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN ... DEFAULT` does not retroactively change the values that were actually inserted. The marker is propagated through merges, mutations, and on-the-fly `ALTER RENAME COLUMN`, so the inserted type-defaults survive part-lifecycle operations. The `MissingColumnInfo` struct also reserves a `DefaultKind::Expression` variant for future use (issue #92475: `ALTER MODIFY DEFAULT` freezes old expression into parts). This PR only writes `type_default` markers; reading an `expression` marker throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` to fail closed until Phase 2 implements expression evaluation. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/4968, https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92475 **On-disk format (`serialization.json`):** ```json { "missing_columns": [ { "name": "b", "default": "type_default" } ], "version": 2 } ``` **Changes:** - Add MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` (default `false`). - Add `IColumn::hasOnlyTypeDefaults` with optimized overrides for `ColumnVector`/`ColumnDecimal` (`memoryIsZero`), `ColumnString`/`ColumnArray` (zero offsets), `ColumnNullable` (all-`1` null map), `ColumnSparse` (no stored non-default values), and `ColumnTuple` (delegates to sub-columns). - Filter all-default columns in `MergeTreeDataWriter::writeTempPartImpl` (`skipEmptyColumnsOnInsert`). Columns with a `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS` expression are never skipped. A column is skipped only when `IDataType::getDefault()` coincides with the column's zero representation (`isDefaultAt(0)` on a column filled via `getDefault()`), which correctly excludes types like `Date32` (type-default 1900-01-01 ≠ memory-zero) and `Enum` (first declared value ≠ 0). Patch parts are excluded, and at least one physical column is always kept. - Gate the optimization on `serialization_info_version >= with_missing_columns`. The populating step is authoritative about the part format version, so `SerializationInfoByName::getVersion` never silently upgrades a part past the configured value (which would make older servers reject it during a rolling upgrade). - Record the missing columns in `serialization.json` via `SerializationInfoByName` (new `WITH_MISSING_COLUMNS` version). Only `type_default` markers are written; `expression` markers are rejected on read until Phase 2. The list is written in sorted order so that identical parts produce identical checksums on different replicas. - Propagate the missing-columns marker through the part lifecycle: through merges (`MergeTask`, for columns that end up absent from the merged part), through mutations (`MutateTask::getColumnsForNewDataPart`, including renames of missing columns), through compact-part renames (`splitAndModifyMutationCommands`), and through on-the-fly `ALTER RENAME COLUMN` on read (`IMergeTreeReader::fillMissingColumns` translates the requested name back through `alter_conversions`). - Add a stateless test with 46 cases covering: basic skip; all-default keeps one column; merges (horizontal and vertical); mutation; `Nullable`; key columns; `DEFAULT` expression not skipped; `Array`; `Tuple`; `ColumnSparse` source; compact parts; `LowCardinality`; stable values across `ALTER ... DEFAULT`; a non-zero-default `Enum`; marker across mutation/merge/rename after `ALTER DEFAULT`; version gate; DETACH/ATTACH TABLE; DETACH/ATTACH PARTITION; BACKUP/RESTORE; FREEZE; CHECK TABLE; MATERIALIZE COLUMN; CLEAR COLUMN; lightweight DELETE; chained mutations; INSERT SELECT; REPLACE PARTITION; ATTACH PARTITION FROM; ALTER ADD/DROP COLUMN; projections; FixedString; Map; mixed parts merge; Date/DateTime; pre-ADD-COLUMN + skip merge; type-changing mutation; compact-part rename+mutation; Date32 regression. - Add an integration test (`test_skip_empty_columns`) with 6 cases: replicated consistency; merge marker propagation across replicas; mixed-version version gate; backward-compat fallback for old parts; restart durability; REPLACE PARTITION across replicated tables. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree INSERT can now skip writing columns whose values are entirely type-defaults (zeros, empty strings, `NULL`s), saving disk space for sparse-update workloads. Enabled by the MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` together with `serialization_info_version = 'with_missing_columns'`. Missing columns carry frozen defaults in `serialization.json`, so a later `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN ... DEFAULT` does not retroactively change the inserted values. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is not required (bug fix, no new user-facing feature) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=98472&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/98472](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F98472+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
