signals.title: Add TLP and NoREC correctness oracles to the server-side AST fuzzer
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a lifetime bug in `ColumnAggregateFunction::convertToValues` that could produce incorrect results or an exception for `-State` aggregates combined with `-OrDefault` / `-OrFill` under `WITH TOTALS`, `ROLLUP`, or `CUBE`. The bug was found by the TLP and NoREC correctness oracles this PR adds to the server-side AST fuzzer (internal testing infrastructure, controlled by the new experimental `ast_fuzzer_oracle` setting, with a dedicated CI job running the oracle-enabled fuzzer against the release build). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Not a user-facing feature — this is internal testing infrastructure. --- **Summary** Integrates two metamorphic testing oracles from the SQLancer project into the built-in server-side AST fuzzer: - **TLP WHERE** (Ternary Logic Partitioning): for a query with `WHERE p`, verifies that `SELECT ... FROM t` produces the same sorted result set as `SELECT ... WHERE p UNION ALL SELECT ... WHERE NOT p UNION ALL SELECT ... WHERE isNull(p)`. - **NoREC** (Non-optimizing Reference Engine Construction): verifies that `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE cond` equals `SELECT countIf(cond) FROM t`. Instead of generating queries from scratch (as SQLancer does), the oracles check queries that the AST fuzzer already produces and executes successfully. Applicable queries must be simple SELECTs (no JOINs, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, LIMIT, QUALIFY, window/aggregate functions) with a WHERE clause against a real table. Non-deterministic functions are detected and skipped. On mismatch, throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` which crashes the server — making bugs immediately visible in CI. **CI integration:** - New job **"AST fuzzer (amd_release, oracle)"** in PR checks, using the release (RelWithDebInfo) build. - Enabled via `AST_FUZZER_ORACLE=1` environment variable which applies `ast_fuzzer_runs=1` and `ast_fuzzer_oracle=1` as server default profile settings. **Testing done:** - Oracle verified with 1000+ passes on non-empty tables (200–500 rows). - Found a real correctness bug during testing: `WHERE (x > 0) AND -2147483648` incorrectly returns 0 rows on MergeTree (INT_MIN truncated to `UInt8` → 0 in the filter path). <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Adds new oracle-execution paths and a new `ast_fuzzer_oracle` setting inside `executeQuery`, plus new CI jobs/config; although gated behind an experimental setting, it touches core query execution and introduces new failure/exit-code handling that could affect CI stability. > > **Overview** > Introduces an experimental `ast_fuzzer_oracle` mode that runs a new `QueryOracleChecker` after each successfully executed fuzzed SELECT, applying multiple metamorphic correctness checks (TLP variants, NoREC, DQP, identity predicate rewrites, and subquery wrapping) and throwing `AST_FUZZER_ORACLE_MISMATCH` on mismatches. > > Extends fuzzing/CI plumbing to support this mode: the AST fuzzer now preserves oracle-friendly query structure (`oracle_mode`), the client/fuzzer job detects oracle mismatches via a dedicated exit code with better log artifact upload, and PR/Master workflows add a new **"AST fuzzer (amd_release, oracle)"** job plus fuzzer config tweaks to enable the setting during that run. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 840494d51c91400e72706015de939dd1b2f0140f. signal.title: Stop copying a system table's metadata twice to set its comment
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> Noticed while profiling start-up for #112496. signal.title: Avoid overflow in the `uniq` aggregate function at cardinalities above ten billion
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/6078 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `uniq` aggregate function returned garbage (e.g. `18446743978444128518`) for cardinalities above roughly thirty billion, because its state kept only 32 bits of each hash and the correction formula overflowed. The state now additionally keeps a small sample of full 64-bit hashes (state version `1`) which the estimate switches to at about two billion elements: `SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000)` returns `99642145106` (−0.36%), and the estimate stays accurate (about 1%) up to trillions. Below two billion nothing changes: the estimates, the memory usage and the state format are exactly as before, and states written by older versions remain readable and merge correctly in mixed-version clusters. --- ### The bug The `uniq` state (`UniquesHashSet`, a BJKST-style adaptive sampling set) keeps hashes truncated to 32 bits. Beyond a few billion distinct values all `2^32` hash values fill up, and the collision-correction formula computes `round(2^32 * (log(2^32) - log(2^32 - res)))` with `res >= 2^32` — `log` of a non-positive number, and the cast of the resulting infinity/NaN to an integer is undefined behavior that produced the values reported in the issue. ### The fix The main sample stays in the historical 32-bit format, bit for bit — below two billion elements nothing changes at all: same estimates, same memory, same serialized bytes. In addition, the state maintains a small sample of full 64-bit hashes (the "wide" set): only one hash in `262144` enters it, and it is bounded by 16384 values (256 KiB), thinned out further beyond that. For normal states it is empty or tiny — about 4 values per million distinct elements — and `size()` switches to it once it has at least 8192 values, i.e. at about two billion elements, where its statistical error (~1%) meets the degrading precision of the 32-bit sample. The legacy formula is also clamped, so a saturated 32-bit estimate returns its saturation limit (~9.5e10) instead of the garbage above. The wide sample must be fed from the very first insertion — the high bits of the hashes of already-consumed elements are unrecoverable. This also rules out the reviewer-suggested variant of converting the state at a threshold: with parallel or distributed aggregation every partial state stays below any threshold, no 64-bit information is ever captured, and the merged estimate stays capped (~9.5e10) no matter the real cardinality — I implemented that variant and measured exactly this on `numbers_mt(50000000000)`. Feeding a heavily pre-thinned sample from the start gets the same memory profile without that trap. **State versioning** follows the `quantileDeterministic` scheme (#112052) exactly: version `1` (a flags byte, the main sample in the legacy layout, then the wide sample if present) is spelled out in fresh state types and pinned at DDL time; the default version stays `0` so unversioned persisted data keeps its layout; the wire version is derived from the negotiated revision (new constant `DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_UNIQ_STATE_VERSION_1 = 54493`), so an old peer receives plain version-`0` states. A version-`0` state simply carries no wide sample, and merging it degrades only the merged-in elements to the old 32-bit precision. ### Results ``` SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(2000000000) -- 2006192184 (+0.31%, still the 32-bit sample) SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(4000000000) -- 3979938734 (-0.50%, the 64-bit sample) SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(50000000000) -- 50090681348 (+0.18%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000) -- 99642145106 (-0.36%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(1000000000000) -- 1016359869734 (+1.6%) ``` Cross-version compatibility was verified against a real 26.7 server: all six mixed-version scenarios (raw state columns and partial aggregation states, both directions, plus a two-shard mixed `remote`) return exactly the value the old server computes natively (`1001943` for `numbers(1000000)`), since the main sample is identical. ### Costs - Memory and serialized size are unchanged below ~1 million distinct elements per state (the wide sample is empty for almost all states; `sizeof` of the state grows by one pointer). From there the wide sample adds `n / 16384` bytes, up to +50% (256 KiB over the 512 KiB main table) for multi-billion-cardinality states. - The insertion hot path gains one branchless check per value. The batched path detects the rare candidates without calls inside the loop, and the instruction count of `SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers(100000000)` is within 0.1% of master (wall-clock comparison on my machine was inconclusive due to load; the perf tests will tell). - Above two billion the estimate error is ~0.8-1.1% (8192-16384 samples) versus ~0.6% below — and versus garbage before this change. ### Two latent bugs of #112052 fixed on the way Both reproduce with `quantileDeterministic` on current master and were exposed by the new `uniq` version: - `ColumnBLOB::toBLOB` (parallel block marshalling) serialized the payload with the state version resolved from the local type, while `NativeWriter::write` announces the version derived from the negotiated revision, so the receiver lost sync inside the blob: `SELECT medianDeterministic(n, n) FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', default, t) GROUP BY n % 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_blocks_marshalling = 1, prefer_localhost_replica = 0` failed with `Skip degree in quantileDeterministic state is 120` (an exception, in a release build). - A view of a `ColumnAggregateFunction` (the result of a sort, filter, or index operation) and a plain copy of it dropped the state version, so `SELECT arraySlice(groupArray(x), 1, 1) FROM (SELECT medianDeterministicState(number, number) AS x FROM numbers(10) GROUP BY number ORDER BY number)` failed with `Cannot read all data`. ### Tests - A `gtest` suite for `UniquesHashSet`: the estimator at a simulated cardinality of `10^11`, the saturation clamp of the legacy formula, round trips of both formats, wide-sample merges with thinning, merges with legacy states, the insertion path feeding the wide sample, and rejection of corrupt states. - `05023_uniq_state_version_64bit_hashes`: version pinning, wire round trips of both versions, cross-version merges, and that the values below two billion are identical across versions. - `05024_aggregate_state_version_parallel_marshalling`, `05025_aggregate_state_version_in_column_views` for the two bugs above (covering both `uniq` and `quantileDeterministic`). - `05026_uniq_64bit_sample_above_two_billion` (`long`): an end-to-end four-billion-row check of the switch to the 64-bit sample; the result does not depend on the distribution of rows between threads. - Since the 32-bit sample is bit-identical to master, only the tests that print state type names or raw state bytes needed reference updates; all `uniq` value references below two billion are untouched. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115393&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115393](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115393+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Keep a text index direct read from widening a filter step's output header
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113320 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114460 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Cannot find input column ... on its position in inputs of expression actions DAG`) when a query has a `JOIN` above a table whose text-indexed column is used by both a `PREWHERE` and a `WHERE` text-search predicate. ### Description #114460, the fix for #113320, introduced the column retention this change works alongside. It is unreleased, so no released version is affected. On default settings, a `JOIN` over a table with a text index fails when the same indexed column is read by both a `PREWHERE` and a text-searchable `WHERE` predicate: ```sql SELECT t.id FROM tab AS t GLOBAL JOIN (SELECT toUInt32(number) AS rid FROM numbers(2)) AS r ON t.id = r.rid PREWHERE hasTokenCaseInsensitive(t.key, 'foo') WHERE hasAllTokens(t.key, 'foo'); -- Logical error: 'Cannot find input column key on its position in inputs of -- expression actions DAG, expected inputs [__table1.id, key], [__table2.rid]' ``` Found by the AST fuzzer ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111867&sha=775787f0654602c107b33178c068b3ef74665b35&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29), STID 2409-5283); that PR does not touch the planner. Root cause: the rewrite drops the indexed column from a filter DAG's inputs, but the column stays in the reading step's output header under its raw storage name because it is deliberately kept in the read set for another reader - the `PREWHERE`, or a row policy. `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` appends such an unmatched header column to its result. The rewrite runs in the second optimization pass, after all header reconciliation, so the widened header reaches the join, whose DAG inputs lack it. The retention step already computes which columns it keeps for another reader, and now makes each an input of the filter DAG at that same point, so nothing is appended to the output header. Both the `WHERE` and the `PREWHERE` rewrite go through that one step, and the column still reaches the reader that needs it. The test is the query above. Removing any one of its elements makes it succeed on the pre-fix binary. The test for issue 113320 stays green. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114771&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114771](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114771+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Avoid deep copy of AccessRights in getGrantQueriesImpl when it is only read
signal.text: ## What's Changed `getGrantQueriesImpl` used to unconditionally deep-copy the grantee's whole `AccessRights` tree: ```cpp AccessRights access = grantee.access; ``` `AccessRights` is a radix tree, and copying it is `O(number of nodes)`. For users with a huge number of per-table grants (e.g. tens of thousands), this deep copy becomes a serious bottleneck: it is executed on **every** `GRANT`/`REVOKE` (during serialization to `DiskAccessStorage`) and on every `SHOW GRANTS`. The tree is only *modified* when `final == true` (via `unionAccessFromRoles`, which calls `AccessRights::makeUnion`). In the common case (`final == false`) the tree is only read, so we can pass a read-only reference and avoid the deep copy entirely. ## Scope - `src/Interpreters/Access/InterpreterShowGrantsQuery.cpp` — avoid the deep copy when `final == false`. ## Motivation / observed impact On a production cluster (ClickHouse 26.6.1.1193), a user with ~11.6k per-table grants in one database: - A single `GRANT ... ON <table> TO <user>` took **5–28 seconds** on some replicas. - `system.query_log` showed the grant spending **99.9% of its time in user-space CPU**, with a `MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheckBytes` of up to **~500 MB**. - `system.trace_log` showed the hot spot was the recursive `Node::operator=` deep copy inside `serializeAccessEntity -> getGrantQueriesImpl`. - The same grant completed in **~100 ms** on replicas whose in-memory `AccessRights` tree was smaller, confirming the deep copy is the bottleneck. This change removes one of the three deep copies performed per grant (the one inside `getGrantQueriesImpl`). It is a safe, behavior-preserving optimization. ## Testing - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/02000_grants_no_deepcopy.sql` + `.reference` verifying that `GRANT`, `SHOW GRANTS` and `REVOKE` behave identically. - Manual verification on the affected cluster: after applying the equivalent change, `SHOW GRANTS FOR <user>` completed in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds. ## Checklist - [x] Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement - [x] Changelog entry: "Avoid a deep copy of the AccessRights tree in `getGrantQueriesImpl` when it is only read, speeding up GRANT/REVOKE and SHOW GRANTS for users with many grants." - [x] Unit tests pass. - [x] Documentation is not required (internal implementation detail). Closes #115694

signal.title: Reject invalid event numbers and durations in sequenceMatch patterns
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an `out_of_range` exception raised as an internal `Code: 1001` error when a `sequenceMatch`, `sequenceCount` or `sequenceMatchEvents` pattern contains the event number `0`, for example `sequenceMatch('(?0)')`. Such a pattern is now rejected with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. A temporal condition holding a lone sign, such as `sequenceMatch('(?1)(?t>+)(?2)')`, was silently treated as `(?t>0)` and is now rejected with `SYNTAX_ERROR`. ### Description Event numbers are 1-based, but the bound check validated only the upper bound, so `(?0)` passed it. The conversion to a 0-based condition index then underflowed `UInt64` to `SIZE_MAX`, and `std::bitset<32>::set()` rejected that with `std::out_of_range`. Thrown from the aggregate function constructor during analysis, it surfaced as an internal `Code: 1001` error and aborted the server in debug and sanitizer builds. Two further inputs reached the same state: an event number overflowing `UInt64`, and a sign with no digits, `(?+)`. In each case `tryReadIntText` fails after consuming a byte while its pointer overload discards the boolean, so the existing "Could not parse number" check does not fire and the output keeps its initialiser `0`. Adding the missing lower bound validates the parsed value and covers all three at once, error code and message unchanged. The sibling temporal branch shared that parse-success defect and is fixed here too, after review automation raised it: `(?t>+)` was accepted as `(?t>0)`. The duration is now read through the `ReadBuffer` overload so the boolean is available, and rejected when it is false. The position check is kept, because `tryReadIntText` also succeeds while consuming nothing for a leading non-digit, which is what rejects `(?t>)`. Only the sign form leaked; `(?t>-)` and an overflowing duration were already rejected, and `(?t>+5)` still equals `(?t>5)`. All three functions share this parser and were affected; all are covered by new assertions in `00222_sequence_aggregate_function_family`, which fail on an unfixed binary. One imprecision is left as is: an overflowing event number is reported as event number `0`. Found by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)`, `bitset set argument out of range` (STID 2508-34fb): https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115019&sha=7be817c59e288cab7aa329a76ed1ba65b9d555e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29. Also seen on `Stress test (arm_tsan)`. Both carrier pull requests are bystanders; the defect reproduces on pristine master. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115056&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115056](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115056+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1808` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Honour do_not_block_pipeline_on_failure for every non-ok job status
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107115 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109071 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description A job that sets `do_not_block_pipeline_on_failure` still blocked its whole downstream closure whenever it ended `ERROR` rather than `FAIL`. The two consumers disagreed. `hook_html.py:224` gates on `not result.is_ok()`, so dependees were correctly not marked `DROPPED`. `runner.py:910` gated on `result.is_failure()`, which is `FAIL`/`XPASS` only, so an `ERROR` was never exempted and the job emitted `pipeline_status=failure`. Every dependent job's guard is `!contains(needs.*.outputs.pipeline_status, 'failure')` over a transitive `needs`, so that one token skips the entire closure. The case that hits it: an integration shard exhausts its 7200 s parallel-phase budget and appends a synthetic `Timeout` child while every real test passes. One non-ok child means `force_ok_exit = True`, so the job declares itself non-blocking, but the same timeout sets the error flag and `set_error()` makes the status `ERROR`. That skipped 107 of 175 results on #107115 and 112 of 177 on #109071, including all five `Bugfix validation (*)` jobs. Because those never ran, `new_tests_check.py` read them as `PENDING` and failed `Finish Workflow` with "it's not actually a regression test for the fix", reporting a timeout in an unrelated shard as a verdict on the author's regression test. 8 occurrences across 8 PRs and 5 of the 6 shards in 30 days. `runner.py` now uses the same predicate as `hook_html`, extracted so it is reachable from a test. They have been asymmetric since the `runner.py` consumer was added in `b35b5fd41f28412`. `functional_tests.py:1527` passes the same flag after a path that can also end `ERROR`, so it is fixed by the same line. **Merge-blocking is unchanged.** `ready_for_merge` is computed from `job.allow_failure` alone (`native_jobs.py:1102-1117`) and never reads this flag; all six shards are `allow_failure=False`, so a failing shard still blocks the merge and still reports red. Only downstream dispatch changes. `new_tests_check.py` is left as it is: its strict check is correct once the jobs actually run. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Every mutation below was applied to production code and the suite re-run. | arm | mutation | result | |---|---|---| | 0 | the fix | 45 passed | | A | predicate reverted to `is_failure()` (pre-fix behaviour) | 11 failed, incl. the end-to-end shard shape | | B | exemption made unconditional, flag ignored (negative control) | 14 failed (every `flag=False` row) | | C | `hook_html` predicate drifted to `is_failure()` | 1 failed (the agreement pin) | | D | output site re-derives the status inline, helper left unused | 1 failed (the delegation pin) | | E | merge gate made to read the flag | 1 failed (the merge-gate pin) | | F | emitted token hardcoded, or overridden after the call | 1 failed each (the emit pin) | Arm B is what rules out a vacuous oracle: a test that ignored the flag would stay green. Arms D, E and F each redden exactly one test, pinning the seams nothing else covers: the call site the extraction created, the token actually emitted, and the merge computation the paragraph above rests on. The new test parametrizes every non-ok member of `Result.Status` (`FAIL`, `ERROR`, `XPASS`, `DROPPED`, `UNKNOWN`, `PENDING`, `RUNNING`) and all three ok members against flag on/off, asserts the two consumers reach the same verdict, reproduces the measured production shape (903 `OK` + 17 `SKIPPED` + 1 `Timeout`), and pins `allow_failure=False` on the six shards. Full `ci/tests`: 972 passed / 31 skipped / 8 failed with the fix, versus 927 / 31 / 8 on pristine `runner.py`. The same 8 pre-existing environment failures on both arms (`clickhouse was not found in PATH`); the delta is the new tests. Exactly two production `complete_job(` call sites pass this flag, and both are covered by this one line. The only other writer of `pipeline_status` is the config job's unconditional `success`. The remaining `is_failure()` uses are test-level row filtering or rendering, not job-level gating. </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1812` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Compute the transformed header once per step instead of per stream
signal.text: `ExpressionTransform` and `FilterTransform` recomputed their output header in every instance via `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` (constant folding over the whole DAG, one column per node), and `ExpressionStep` / `FilterStep` create one transform per stream — so pipeline construction paid O(streams × DAG size). `FilterTransform` even ran updateHeader twice per instance: once for the output header and once for the pre-removal `transformed_header` member. This came out of profiling why ClickBench Q29 (90 `SUM(ResolutionWidth + N)` aggregates, which the analyzer collapses into a single `sumCount` plus 89 scalar projections) still takes ~25 ms hot: on a 96-core machine, the single largest item of pipeline construction was `ActionsDAG::evaluatePartialResult` called from the `ExpressionTransform` constructor once per each of the 89 streams (~8 ms of ~23 ms total query overhead), via `ExpressionStep::transformPipeline` → `Pipe::addSimpleTransform` → `transformHeader`. ## Changes All output ports of a `Pipe` share one header, so the transformed header is now computed once in `ExpressionStep::transformPipeline` and `FilterStep::transformPipeline` and shared by all instances through new `ExpressionTransform` / `FilterTransform` constructor overloads that accept a precomputed header. The legacy constructors are kept for the remaining call sites; the legacy `FilterTransform` constructor now delegates and runs updateHeader once instead of twice. ## Results On the 96-core machine (12 runs, steady state, 100M-row table): - hot Q29 `SELECT`: ~24 ms → ~17 ms - `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` of Q29: ~19 ms → ~13 ms - `EXPLAIN PLAN`: unchanged (as expected) - `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` output and query result checksums are identical before/after; a 140-test stateless smoke run (filter/totals/`EXPLAIN PIPELINE`-heavy tests, including `02210_processors_profile_log*`) shows no regressions. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up query pipeline construction for queries with large expressions or many streams: the output header of `ExpressionTransform` and `FilterTransform` is now computed once per query plan step instead of once (twice for filters) per stream. For a ClickBench Q29-like query on a 96-core machine, this removes about a third of the hot query time. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115677&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115677](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115677+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: "Permissions for queries" docs for `readonly` mode falsely claims readonly=1 default for HTTP and is incomplete for readonly=2
signal.text: ### Documentation page /concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the issue The [documentation for `readonly` mode](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) is both incorrect and incomplete: ### Incorrect claim about HTTP GET using `readonly=1` [The docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) claim that HTTP `GET` queries use `readonly=1` by default. In reality, HTTP `GET` use `readonly=2` by default unless overridden by settings profiles. `POST` uses `readonly=0`, which is implied but not explicitly stated. E.g. with a default clickhouse docker container (`clickhouse/clickhouse-server:24.8`, clickhouse 24.8.14.39) with no config overrides or custom env-var injection: ```console $ curl -G 'http://localhost:8123/' --user 'default:' --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly')" 2 ``` It looks `HTTP GET` has used `readonly=2` since the beginning of the repo's history; see commit a33ab9cbe1a. It'd also make sense to explicitly mention that while GET _defaults to_ `readonly=2` if not otherwise set, this can be overridden by settings profiles (but _not_ by http listener configuration or http authentication server responses). With test cover for the assertions. ### `readonly=2` behaviour is unclear and underspecified The docs describe `readonly=1` fairly clearly, but the box-out section that carries most of the details has no mention of `readonly=2`. Nothing says that `readonly=2` disallows changing `readonly` mode, and the description for 2 says > When set to 2, allows the above plus: SET [...]" ... which doesn't exclude `SET readonly` so it's open to interpretation whether `readonly=2` blocks changing `readonly` at all, or what to. I actually suggest _not_ fixing this immediately. Instead I'd leave it under-specified and implement https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115695 to _permit_ `readonly=2` to transition to `readonly=1`, _then_ document the new behaviour and add a state-transition-table showing the permitted and blocked transitions. ### Confusing mention of `allow_ddl` for `readonly=1` in the boxout By explicitly naming two settings, this: > After setting readonly = 1, the user can’t change `readonly` and `allow_ddl` settings in the current session. implies that other settings may be changeable. This is clarified shortly after by: > Setting readonly = 1 prohibits the user from changing settings. but it's confusing. I suggest removing the first paragraph entirely, and instead adding to the main description that _Once readonly=1 is set in a session the user cannot change the `readonly` setting. Once readonly=2 is set in a session the user cannot set readonly=0._ ... with a note that currently readonly=2 prohibits a transition to readonly=1 too, but that's subject to change in future per https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115695 ### Additional context **There is duplicate documentation for the readonly setting at https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/constraints-on-settings#read-only** which is better overall, but doesn't mention or link to the docs for HTTP mode. Based on the `git blame` for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blame/master/src/Common/SettingConstraintWritability.h the `readonly=2` setting has existed for at least 4 years. I wasn't immediately able to find when the HTTP GET method started using `readonly=2`; it seems to have been the case as early as a33ab9cbe1a which is as close to the start of the repo's history as I could usefully get.

signal.title: Report malformed Parquet thrift metadata as INCORRECT_DATA
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113006 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog ### Description Reading a Parquet file whose Thrift metadata is corrupt reported `Code: 1001 STD_EXCEPTION`. That is an internal-error code: it tells the user nothing about the input and cannot be classified programmatically as a bad-file error. `apache::thrift::TException` derives from `std::exception`, so it was caught by the generic clause in `deserializeThriftStruct` and converted through `CreateFromSTDTag`. Catching `TException` before that clause and mapping it to `INCORRECT_DATA` fixes it. All five Parquet metadata struct types deserialize through this one function, so the change covers every carrier. Split out of #113006 on reviewer request, where this rode along with an unrelated Arrow IPC change and shared no file with it. The regression test asserts the error code on a file whose metadata is corrupted after writing. Removing the new catch clause and rebuilding makes it fail, so the assertion is on the fix rather than on incidental behavior. Found by mutation fuzzing. signal.title: Reuse LowCardinality aggregation mappings across blocks
signal.text: Previously dictionary position to aggregate state mappings were only valid within a block. For parts where there's only a single dictionary, this is too restrictive and resulted in repeated work. This moves the mapping cache to the aggregation method, matching its lifetime to the aggregation hash table. We keep the successful mappings while the dict remains unchanged. Non-shared dictionaries remain block local. This gives a very nice speedup to the benchmark in the previous commit: | Width | LC before | LC after | Change | |-----------------|----------:|----------:|-------:| | `UInt8` | 0.1220 s | 0.1158 s | -5.1% | | `UInt16` | 0.1703 s | 0.1395 s | -18.1% | | `UInt32` | 0.1884 s | 0.1489 s | -20.9% | | `UInt64` | 0.1952 s | 0.1513 s | -22.5% | | `UInt128` | 0.5676 s | 0.5649 s | -0.5% | | `UInt256` | 0.9354 s | 0.9206 s | -1.6% | | `String` (6 B) | 0.2535 s | 0.1598 s | -37.0% | | `String` (26 B) | 0.2521 s | 0.1630 s | -35.4% | | `String` (56 B) | 0.2689 s | 0.1655 s | -38.5% | The improvements for UInt128 and UInt256 will be there after #114982 is merged. The benefit is largest when many blocks share the same dictionary, because dictionary-position mappings are reused across those blocks. _AI assisted, scratching an itch I've had for a while._ ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve aggregation performance by reusing LowCardinality aggregation mappings across blocks. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114993&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114993](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114993+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix "Not-ready Set" for GLOBAL IN over an object-storage _path / _file filter
signal.text: `SELECT ... FROM s3(...) WHERE _path GLOBAL IN (SELECT ...)` over a path without globs threw ``` Logical error: 'Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'globalIn'' ``` `ReadFromObjectStorageStep::applyFilters` intentionally leaves the sets of `globalIn` / `globalNotIn` unbuilt, so that `ReadFromRemote` can attach an external table to them first. Plan optimization then moves the subquery plan of such a set into a `CreatingSetsStep` (`DelayedCreatingSetsStep::makePlansForSets`), which means the set is only created once the pipeline runs. `StorageObjectStorageSource::createFileIterator` prunes an explicit key list while the pipeline is being built, and its `buildSetsForDAG` call is a no-op for a set whose subquery plan is already gone, so the pruning expression was executed with a set that was not ready yet. `GlobIterator` is unaffected: it applies the same filter while listing objects, when the set is already built. Pruning the keys is an optimization - the same predicate is applied by the `Filter` step above the source - so skip it when a set is not ready. `buildSetsForDAG` now reports whether every set in the DAG ended up ready. Reproducer (deterministic, fails on `master`, passes with this change): ```sql SELECT * FROM s3(s3_conn, filename = 'x', format = CSV, structure = 'x UInt64') WHERE _path GLOBAL IN (SELECT 'no such path'); ``` The stress test hit it through an AST fuzzer query over `test_s3_race`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=1c3181d592a4aaeec15077107e15b7edab5bca8d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'globalIn'` exception for a `GLOBAL IN` subquery over the `_path` or `_file` virtual column of an object storage table (`s3`, `azureBlobStorage`, ...) whose path has no globs. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112968&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112968](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112968+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: readonly>0 does not restrict SET ROLE
signal.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour With `readonly = 1` set on the session by any means, `SET ROLE NONE` and `SET ROLE <other granted role>` still succeed. The [permissions-for-queries doc](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) describes `readonly = 1` as > you can only run read queries ... and lists which statement classes are refused, but doesn't explicitly say anything about `SET ROLE`. As `SET` is confined unless a settings profile explicitly permits it to be set in read-only mode, a reader would reasonably expect and assume that `SET ROLE` should also be confined. Users building read-only, locked-down sessions could easily rely on this unintentionally. But this allows an attacker to simply `SET ROLE NONE` or `SET ROLE` to another known role their session has access to in order to escape confinement. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce Deploy a basic clickhouse container, and: ### Setup **Setup (as admin user):** ```sql CREATE ROLE ro_role; GRANT SELECT ON system.one TO ro_role; CREATE ROLE other_role; CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; GRANT ro_role, other_role TO probe; ALTER USER probe DEFAULT ROLE ro_role; ``` ### Variant A: `readonly = 1` at connect time (`--readonly 1`) ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --multiquery --query " SET ROLE NONE; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " [] $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --multiquery --query " SET ROLE other_role; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " ['other_role'] ``` `SET` enforcement for variables works: ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 1 --query "SET max_threads = 3" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` ### Variant B: `readonly = 1` applied mid-session via `SET readonly = 1` This is what a gateway that wants to drop into a less-privileged session before executing user queries might do - but it doesn't actually work either. ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET ROLE NONE; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " [] $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET ROLE other_role; -- expected: refused; actual: succeeds SELECT currentRoles(); " ['other_role'] ``` Again `SET` enforcement for session variables and configuration works: ```console $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --multiquery --query " SET readonly = 1; SET max_threads = 3; " Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_threads' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` ### HTTP API and readonly=2 Similar behaviour for the HTTP API when running the queries using session-ids, if a settings profile is used to allow the initial connection to connect without the default `readonly=2` enforcement. Because the HTTP API's default `readonly=2` does allow `SET`, it's arguably more reasonable that it should permit `SET ROLE`, though still surprising. (Surprisingly, though, `readonly=2` does not permit the session to transition to the seemingly more-restrictive `readonly=1` mode). But it still isn't documented behaviour and is IMO still surprising. With the same `probe` user setup as above, using stateless GET (no sessions): ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE NONE' # expected given readonly=2: refused under readonly; actual: 200 OK $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE other_role' # expected given readonly=2: refused; actual: 200 OK ``` The same can be seen with HTTP sessions: ```console $ SID=$(uuidgen) $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' ['ro_role'] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE NONE' # succeeds $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' [] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET ROLE other_role' # succeeds $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT currentRoles() FORMAT TSV' ['other_role'] $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly') FORMAT TSV" 2 ``` The last query confirms `readonly = 2` is in effect. ### Expected behavior Either both `SET ROLE` statements are refused with `READONLY` (code 164) once `readonly = 1` is in force, matching the treatment of `SET max_threads = …`, _or_ the docs for `readonly = 1` explicitly call out that role membership is not covered. In the latter case another mechanism for one-way role transitions would be strongly desirable. ### Error message and/or stacktrace N/A ### Related issues and pull requests Related to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 which covers issues with role transitions and `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ... TO ROLE ...` Also to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115697 which flags issues in the docs around readonly mode. ### Additional context This isn't strictly a security bug because there's no documented claim about the interaction of `readonly = 1` and `SET ROLE`, but it's close.

signal.title: Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility with redundant parentheses
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114188 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix KeeperMap metadata compatibility during rolling upgrades when equivalent primary keys were serialized with different redundant parentheses. ### Problem KeeperMap stores the table definition in Keeper and previously compared its primary-key expression as formatted text. Builds that serialize the same expression as either `key` or `(key)` therefore reject an otherwise compatible shared table definition during a rolling upgrade, including during ATTACH/startup. ### Implementation - keep the existing writer spelling and never rewrite compatible shared metadata, so patched nodes do not strand unpatched peers during a rolling deployment; - parse stored and local primary-key expressions and normalize only redundant outer parentheses that wrap one complete expression; - require the remaining input to be exact normal formatter output, preserving strict rejection of malformed, terminated, commented, or genuinely different definitions; - use the same compatibility check in CREATE-against-existing-path and ATTACH/startup; - split columns from the primary-key section using its structural newline-delimited header. The reader-side implementation uses parser and formatter APIs present in both current master and 26.4. It does not depend on `formatIgnoringRedundantParentheses()` added by #114188, so the same compatibility rule can be backported to 26.4. ### Tests The stateless SQL regression covers both directions (`key` stored with `(key)` local and `(key)` stored with `key` local), verifies that compatible CREATE and ATTACH do not rewrite the Keeper znode, and checks data access after ATTACH. It also verifies rejection of a different key, malformed `(key`, and terminated `key;` metadata, plus a primary-key expression containing the metadata header text. Red-before was reproduced with embedded Keeper on official ClickHouse 26.4.5.143 and 26.7.1.1315: after changing stored metadata from `key` to `(key)`, DETACH + ATTACH left the table in `INVALID_STATE` (Code 668). signal.title: Do not admit non-clonable read steps into the MergeTree direct join
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103473 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Cannot clone ReadFromPreparedSource plan step` (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`) when joining against a `Buffer` table with `join_algorithm = 'direct'`. Such a right side is now declined with the same message as any other unsupported storage. ### Description `tryMakeDirectJoinWithMergeTree` admitted `ReadFromPreparedSource` as a right-side read step, then cloned the right plan unconditionally. That step has no `clone()` override, so the clone reached the throwing base `IQueryPlanStep::clone()`: ```sql CREATE TABLE t_left (id UInt64, name String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE t_right_mt (id UInt64, val String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE t_right_buf AS t_right_mt ENGINE = Buffer(currentDatabase(), t_right_mt, 1, 1000, 1000, 10000, 10000, 10000000, 10000000); INSERT INTO t_left VALUES (1, 'A'); SELECT * FROM t_left AS l LEFT JOIN t_right_buf AS r ON l.id = r.id SETTINGS enable_analyzer = 1, join_algorithm = 'direct'; -- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Cannot clone ReadFromPreparedSource plan step. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) ``` That arm never had a working case: `typeid_cast` matches the exact type, and neither `ReadFromPreparedSource` nor its subclasses implement `clone()`, so every plan it admitted threw. This removes it. The other two arms are kept, and `ReadNothingStep` (which does implement `clone()`) carries the empty-MergeTree case from #95935. The query now takes the pre-existing refusal for unsupported right-side storages, `Can't execute any of specified algorithms ...`, which is what a `Memory` or `StripeLog` right side already returns. This is the "make the exception message better" change @ vdimir asked for when he closed #103473 as not planned: `direct` does not support `Buffer`, so the right behaviour is the ordinary unsupported-storage refusal rather than a clone failure. It deliberately does not make `Buffer` work with `direct`. Two notes beyond the report. The failure is not limited to an empty underlying table as the issue title suggests: it also reproduces with a non-empty `Buffer` and with `INNER JOIN`. And it does not touch the second entry point @ zlareb1 reported, where correlated-subquery decorrelation clones the same step: that path does not go through this allow-list. Hence `Related:` below rather than `Closes:`. signal.title: Implement PromQL functions stddev_over_time() and stdvar_over_time()
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented functions `stddev_over_time()` and `stdvar_over_time()` (population standard deviation/variance). ### Description Implements `stddev_over_time(v range-vector)` and `stdvar_over_time(v range-vector)`, previously reported as not implemented. **Key Technical & Numerical Stability Highlights**: 1. **Welford's Algorithm & Chan's Parallel Merge**: Uses a running centered-moment `{count, mean, m2}` accumulator ($M_2 = \sum (x - \bar{x})^2$) in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesVarianceOverTime.h` updated per sample via Welford's formula and merged pairwise via Chan et al.'s parallel merge algorithm. This avoids catastrophic cancellation on large-magnitude counter series (e.g. byte counters $\sim 5 \times 10^8$, where raw $\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2 / N$ loses all precision and produces false zeroes or negative variances). 2. **Prometheus Staleness Handling**: Implements full Prometheus stale-marker (`0x7ff0000000000002`) semantics. Stale markers are flagged at ingestion (`is_stale_marker`), excluded from range-vector aggregations (`WHERE NOT is_stale_marker`) so target disappearance does not pollute range windows with NaNs, while remaining detectable by instant selectors to correctly report series absence. 3. **Non-Invertible Two-Stacks / Recompute Strategy**: Avoids floating-point `unmerge` subtraction on moments to prevent numerical cancellation and drift over long sliding windows. Registered `timeSeriesStddevToGrid`/`timeSeriesStdvarToGrid` in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp` and added the two `impl_map` entries in `applyFunctionOverRange.cpp` with `drop_metric_name = true`. **Verified numerically against Prometheus 3.5.0**: verified bit-for-bit accuracy against Prometheus 3.5.0 live responses, including cross-architecture (ARM64 vs x86_64) ULP tolerance handling in CI. **Testing**: SQL-level test (`04628_variance_timeseries_functions.sql`) covering empty/single/multi-sample windows and `AggregatingMergeTree` round-trips, plus integration cases in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` (including stale-marker ingestion and instant/range evaluations). This flips 12 queries of the PromQL compliance suite from unsupported to passed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112355&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112355](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112355+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hold the table lock across a lightweight UPDATE pipeline
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104431 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a server abort (`Logical error: Part patch-... doesn't exist`) when a `DROP TABLE` runs concurrently with a lightweight `UPDATE` on a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table. The update now holds the table's shared lock until its patch part is committed, so the `DROP` waits instead of removing it. ### Description Reported by @ alexey-milovidov on #104431: an `Upgrade check (amd_release)` abort with no fix on master, STID `3208-458f`, 4 hits on 4 unrelated PRs in 6 days ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104431&sha=7970f08a82eaf2ad5217d57a7796ae1c5e920030&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade+check+%28amd_release%29)). **What breaks.** A lightweight `UPDATE` racing a `DROP TABLE` aborts the server, release builds included: `Transaction::commit`'s `modifyPartState` sits in `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`, whose catch-all is `std::terminate`. **Root cause.** `InterpreterUpdateQuery::execute` takes `lockForShare` into a function-local holder and parks only the *storage* in the returned pipeline; `QueryPlanResourceHolder` keeps `storage_holders` and `table_locks` separately, so the lock dies when `execute()` returns, long before the sink commits the patch part. A concurrent `DROP` then takes the exclusive lock, `dropAllData()` clears `data_parts_indexes`, and the commit cannot find its own part. It needs a UUID-less database (`Memory`/`Ordinary`), where `DROP` removes data inline, hence the intermittency. **The change.** Move the already-acquired lock into the pipeline's resources, as the INSERT path does at `InterpreterInsertQuery.cpp:1297`. Three entry points: `InterpreterUpdateQuery::execute`, `InterpreterAlterQuery::executeToTable`, and `StorageAlias::updateLightweight`, which resolves a *different* storage and so needs the target's own lock, as `StorageAlias::read` does. `DELETE FROM` rewrites to `UPDATE` and is covered transitively. A concurrent `DROP` or `DETACH` now waits for an in-flight lightweight update, as it already does for `INSERT`. `TRUNCATE` takes no exclusive lock for `MergeTree`. **Validation.** New test `04905_lwu_drop_race_table_lock.sh`, one arm per fixed carrier. A pauseable failpoint parks the replicated sink between the patch-part rename and the commit, while the update still holds the lock; the arm then drops the table and waits for the drop to block on that lock. Nothing is timed, so an arm cannot miss a window or pass quietly. Aborts without the fix, passes with it, 50/50 green. <details> <summary>Both-directions matrix (every cell measured, Build IDs asserted against the running server)</summary> | binary | `UPDATE` | `ALTER ... UPDATE` | via `Alias` | |---|---|---|---| | base (fix reverted) `ea8e869d` | ABORT | ABORT | ABORT | | interpreters only `3651f11d` | pass | pass | ABORT | | full fix `1884b944` | pass | pass | pass | The middle row is the control that shows the `StorageAlias` change is necessary: with both interpreter fixes applied, the alias arm is the only one that still aborts. The lock demonstrably serializes the two queries: with the sink parked after the patch-part rename, the `DROP` becomes a waiting writer and stays one until the sink is released, then completes. Deadlock check: the change only extends the lifetime of a *Read* acquisition, and no sink on this path takes the table lock. `update_sequential_consistency = 1` and a following `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` both complete normally. </details> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1813` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: GRANT is extremely slow for users with many per-table grants
signal.text: ### Environment - ClickHouse version: **26.6.1.1193** (self-hosted, 4-shard × 2-replica cluster, 8 nodes) - Access storage: `local_directory` (`DiskAccessStorage`), ~366k grants total across 66 users - Affected user: `userX` with **~11.6k per-table grants** (11,683 GRANT statements, concentrated in one database) ### Symptom A single `GRANT ON CLUSTER xx_cluster SELECT, INSERT, ... ON db.table TO userX` takes **5–28 seconds** on some replicas, while completing in **~100 ms** on others. Because `ON CLUSTER` waits for the slowest replica, the whole cluster's GRANT is blocked for tens of seconds. ### Root cause (confirmed via trace_log) `system.trace_log` shows the hot spot is the **recursive deep copy of the `AccessRights` tree**: ``` DiskAccessStorage::writeAccessEntityToDisk -> serializeAccessEntity -> getGrantQueriesImpl -> AccessRights::operator= -> Node::operator= (recursive, 15+ levels) ``` `AccessRights` is a radix tree (`AccessRights.cpp`). `Node::operator=` copies every child recursively: ```cpp if (src.children) children = std::make_shared<Container>(*src.children); ``` For a user with ~11.6k per-table grants the tree is large, and a single `GRANT` triggers **three** deep copies / full traversals: 1. `update_func`'s `entity->clone()` (InterpreterGrantQuery.cpp:491) 2. `getGrantQueriesImpl`'s `AccessRights access = grantee.access` (InterpreterShowGrantsQuery.cpp:97) 3. `access.getElements()` traversal (AccessRights.cpp:903) ### Evidence For the same `GRANT` on the same table: | Node | Duration | MemoryAllocatedWithoutCheck | UserTime | |------|----------|-----------------------------|----------| | slow replica | 20–28 s | ~500 MB (116 allocs) | 99.9% of duration | | fast replica | ~100 ms | ~19 MB (16 allocs) | ~0.1% | `SYSTEM RELOAD USERS` temporarily resets the in-memory tree and drops the duration to ~20–46 ms, confirming the in-memory `AccessRights` tree size is the driver. ### Suggested fix Avoid the deep copy in `getGrantQueriesImpl` when the tree is only read (`final == false`): ```cpp const AccessRights & access = grantee.access; if (final) { AccessRights access_copy = grantee.access; unionAccessFromRoles(access_copy, grantee, access_control); getGrantsFromAccess(res, access_copy, grantees, access_control, attach_mode, with_implicit); } else { getGrantsFromAccess(res, access, grantees, access_control, attach_mode, with_implicit); } ``` This removes one of the three deep copies (the one in `serializeAccessEntity`/`SHOW GRANTS`). A more complete fix would be copy-on-write for `AccessRights::Node` (only copy the modified path), but that is a larger change. ### Workaround for users - Aggregate per-table grants into a role and `GRANT role TO user`, so the deep-copied object is the (smaller) role. - Periodically run `SYSTEM RELOAD USERS` after large batches of GRANTs.

signal.title: Support the Vortex file format
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added support for reading and writing the [Vortex](https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex) columnar file format (the `Vortex` input and output format). This closes [#87327](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The implementation uses the Rust `vortex` crate (v0.83.0) through a new C FFI crate `rust/workspace/vortex` (`_ch_rust_vortex`), following the same pattern as `prql` and `polyglot`. Data crosses the FFI boundary through the Arrow C Data Interface and is converted with the same `ArrowColumnToCHColumn`/`CHColumnToArrowColumn` code as the `Arrow` format. IO is delegated back to ClickHouse through callbacks: reads go through ClickHouse's own read buffers (range reads for seekable inputs, whole-file buffering otherwise), and the produced file is streamed into the output buffer. The library spawns no threads of its own: a scan is split into tasks that ClickHouse runs on its own thread pools (`max_parsing_threads` for decoding, `max_download_threads` for reads), writing is driven on the calling thread, and Rust panics are caught at the FFI boundary and turned into exceptions. Features: - Reading with projection pushdown: only the columns used by the query are read from the file. - Parallel reading (merged from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 by @m7kss1): the file is split into row ranges that are read, filtered, and decoded concurrently; nearby segment reads are coalesced into one request. Chunks are returned as soon as they are decoded, so the row order is not guaranteed unless `input_format_vortex_preserve_order` is set. - Schema inference and `count()`-only queries answered from file metadata without reading data. - Writing with the library's default adaptive compression (BtrBlocks-style cascading encodings + zstd), including a valid empty file for empty results. - Graceful errors on malformed and truncated files (fuzzer-friendly: no aborts, Rust panics become exceptions). Limitations (documented in `docs/reference/formats/Vortex.mdx`): - `Map`, `Int128`/`UInt128`/`Int256`/`UInt256`, `IPv6`, and `Interval` columns cannot be written (no corresponding Vortex type). - `String` and `FixedString` are written as Vortex `Binary` (ClickHouse strings are arbitrary bytes, while Vortex requires `Utf8` to be valid UTF-8). - The format is disabled in MSan builds: the MSan-instrumented library (with origin tracking) is so large that linking `unit_tests_dbms` overflows the 2 GiB `R_X86_64_PC32` relocation range (same approach as `wasmtime` and `delta-kernel-rs`). - Writing is single-threaded in this first version: the adaptive compressor samples many encodings per column, so writes are slower than `Parquet` — parallelism can be added later. Reading is parallel since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 was merged into this PR: on ClickBench, reads went from geomean ~26.8x slower than `Parquet` to ~1.2x, winning 9 of 43 queries (see the [benchmark results](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112950#issuecomment-5337908877)). Filter pushdown (added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114373, `input_format_vortex_filter_push_down`, on by default) lets the scan skip the statistics zones the predicate rules out and decode only the matching rows of the rest: on a file of 1 000 000 sorted values, `WHERE n = 500000` reads 66 KiB with the pushdown against 7.5 MiB without it. The most selective ClickBench queries are nevertheless still 1.5-5.5x slower than `Parquet`. The 127 new vendored Rust crates are added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74 (the `contrib/rust_vendor` submodule is bumped to that branch). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112950&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112950](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112950+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Publish the standalone WebAssembly SQL parser as a CI artifact
signal.text: ## Motivation `utils/wasm-parser` builds `src/Parsers` on its own, for a browser: a WASI reactor that answers whether a query parses, reports the error with a position, and pretty-prints, in 1.2 MB (280 KB brotli). Nothing in CI published it, so the only way to get the module was to build it — a wasi-sdk download and a few hundred translation units of full LTO. The module *was* built in CI, inside `tests/integration/test_wasm_parser`, but in a container that was torn down at the end of the test, with the result thrown away. ## What this does Adds a `Build (wasm_parser)` job that builds the two extreme configurations, runs `ctest` on each - `parser-cases` drives the module through `test.mjs` under Node.js, `parser-size` asserts the byte ceiling - and publishes both modules as the `CH_WASM_PARSER_BIN` artifact: ``` https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/REFs/master/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser.wasm https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/REFs/master/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser-no-formatting-no-dcl.wasm https://clickhouse-builds.s3.amazonaws.com/PRs/<pr>/<sha>/build_wasm_parser/parser.wasm ``` There is no JavaScript sidecar to go with them, unlike the Emscripten `Build (wasm64)` artifact: a consumer instantiates the `.wasm` itself and supplies the WASI preview1 imports. It is a job of its own rather than another `BuildTypes` entry in the `Build` matrix, because the project cross-compiles to `wasm32-wasip1` with a wasi-sdk toolchain that cannot be mixed into a tree configured for the host. So it runs in `clickhouse/wasm-builder` instead of `binary-builder`, and the two post hooks the other build jobs carry are left off - neither the master-head binary nor the build profile has a counterpart here. The job takes over from `tests/integration/test_wasm_parser`, which existed because nothing else notices when this module stops compiling, which it did within a day of being merged, twice over. It built the same two configurations and discarded them; it, its compose file and its `TEST_CONFIGS` entry are removed, so CI no longer performs the same full-LTO build twice. `clickhouse/wasm-builder` moves out of `ci/docker/integration` - it is a build-job image now, not a service an integration test spins up - and gains `python3`, which praktika needs in order to run the job script inside it. ## Verification The job was run locally through praktika, against this branch after merging `master`: | configuration | ctest | published | bytes | ceiling | | --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | | everything | 2/2 passed | `parser.wasm` | 1234449 | 1290000 | | no-formatting-no-dcl | 2/2 passed | `parser-no-formatting-no-dcl.wasm` | 805553 | 840000 | Both are ~3.5% above the size table in `utils/wasm-parser/README.md`, which has drifted from what `master` produces; still inside the ceilings, so `parser-size` passes. Re-measuring all four configurations to refresh that table is left for a separate change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not required for this category. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115673&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115673](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115673+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not re-read a partially cached segment's committed prefix from the source
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115070 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `ICacheProvider.h:107-109` puts the derivation of a tier's uncommitted tail on the caller: given `Lead::available`, fetch `[available.end(), range.end())`. `readThroughCaches` bound `lead.available` to a local, used it only for the covers-the-head early return, then dropped it - `MissTier` had no field for it. `fetch_lo` came from the miss range instead, and on the populating path a partial segment's miss spans its whole extent from `seg_left` (`DiskCacheProvider.cpp:651`), that range being the writer's fill geometry. So a partially cached read re-read that prefix; `write`'s append-only check discarded those bytes, making it wasted I/O, not wrong data. The read-only sibling emits the miss from `committed_end` (`:600-601`). This carries `available` into `MissTier` and derives the tail once, for `fetch_lo`/`fetch_hi` and the write loop. A tier whose prefix spans its range yields an empty tail and is skipped, so it cannot pull `fetch_lo` back to the segment start. The new coverage is a unit test because a segment committed to an arbitrary mid-point is not deterministically reachable from SQL - which is why 04511 was flaky rather than failing. Its five cases each fail on master; the suite is 44/44 here. Measured on `s3_cache_04511`, `ReaderExecutorBytesFromSource` on the warm reread: **1,325,913 -> 276,057** bytes, cold unchanged at 1,588,547. With `reader_executor_use_long_connections` a held connection can still bridge over the prefix; untouched here. Surfaced by two [`04511_reader_executor_disk_cache`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113518&sha=758c46640f6193b9a9770c3e76a599688e574b15&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_msan%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20sequential%2C%202%2F2%29) failures on 2026-08-20, one on master, both diffing only `warm_served_from_cache 1 -> 0`. That test and its `.reference` are unchanged: its `warm < cold` assertion was correct and was reporting this bug, having been adjusted for flakiness four times. It passes 50/50 under randomized settings and under those runs' settings. #115643 pins it to one thread so its oracle can be strict; measured here, the two compose - `warm = 0` needs the pin, and this cuts the multi-thread warm read it leaves. <details> <summary>Validation detail: warm-read source bytes per configuration, and the release-branch check</summary> Same fixture and probe each time; `warm/cold` ratio of `ReaderExecutorBytesFromSource`. The test's assertion is `warm < cold`, so a ratio near 1.0 is a near-failure. | threads / window | master | this PR | |---|---|---| | 8 / 1 MiB | 0.835 | 0.174 | | 8 / 256 KiB | 0.668 | 0.448 | | 8 / 64 KiB | 0.575 | 0.377 | | 4 / 1 MiB | 0.504 | 0.174 | | 16 / 256 KiB | 0.502 | 0.116 | | worst case | **0.835** | **0.504** | Build IDs: master `c877fb06499b8acdfd053c38051b7fd4c7e79737`, this PR `2ffe0b96223a5b47c2099d92b26cbbb4768786fd`; server identity asserted with `SELECT lower(buildId())` before each arm. `readThroughCaches`, `DiskCacheProvider.cpp` and `ICacheProvider.h` are absent from every active release branch (26.7 / 26.6 / 26.5 / 26.3 / 25.8), so the read-through cache path has never shipped. `use_reader_executor` was added in `996c1850` (2026-06-09), defaults to `false`, tier `EXPERIMENTAL`. No backport. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115664&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115664](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115664+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: TTL CLEAR INDEX for MergeTree parts
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107804 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78714 TTL CLEAR INDEX lets a MergeTree table keep secondary indexes for recent parts while dropping the physical index files from old parts. I recommend reviewing commit-by-commit. The motivating case is Observability log storage. For log tables, the raw data is not always the dominant cost. Text indexes can be very large, and most queries only touch recent data. We want to keep the index where it helps and stop paying for it on old parts that are rarely searched. Example syntax: ```sql TTL timestamp + INTERVAL 7 DAY CLEAR INDEX message_text ``` This follows the existing meaning of `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR INDEX`: remove the per-part index files, but keep the index definition in table metadata. Queries remain correct. Parts without the index just fall back to scanning. ## What this changes The patch adds a new table TTL action, `CLEAR INDEX`, and stores its per-part min/max TTL info in `ttl.txt` as `index_clear_ttl`. When a part is fully past the TTL for a target index, future maintenance may remove that index’s files from the part. If the table later reads that part, the secondary index reader already handles missing index files and simply does not use that index for that part. The patch also adds system table visibility: ```text system.parts.index_clear_ttl_info.{index_name,expression,min,max} ``` ## Merge behavior There are two cases. First, normal merges apply the TTL policy to their output. If a merge output is fully past the `CLEAR INDEX` TTL, the merge should not retain the target index files. This is important for late-arriving data: a tiny old insert should not cause a merge that rebuilds a huge old text index. Second, there is a dedicated TTL maintenance merge type: `MergeType::TTLClearIndex`. This is used for the case where a single old part has expired index files and does not otherwise need a merge. The first implementation is intentionally conservative: it selects one source part and produces one replacement part. Dedicated `TTLClearIndex` selection obeys the normal full-part merge byte and row limits. This keeps cleanup conservative when preserving the part would require copying unchanged files rather than hardlinking them. For eligible full-storage parts, the implementation uses a fast path: hardlink or copy unchanged files, omit the expired index files, rewrite checksums and metadata, and publish the replacement part. Projection directories are copied wholesale because the row set is unchanged. This avoids reading and rewriting the raw data. If the fast path is not safe, the code falls back to the normal rewrite path. The fallback may rewrite the part, but it still must not retain expired index files in the final output. Parts with incomplete TTL metadata are not selected for dedicated cleanup; `MATERIALIZE TTL` or an ordinary merge must first recalculate the current TTL rules. The fast path currently opts out for cases like packed part storage, UUID parts, legacy parts without metadata-version files, metadata version mismatches, patch parts, part-format changes, and projection subdirectories it cannot copy as-is. On remote or zero-copy storage, it copies unchanged files instead of hardlinking them. It handles packed skip-index archives by excluding dirty `skp_idx.packed` files from the hardlink/copy set and rewriting the archive for surviving packed entries. ## Rollout safety `TTLClearIndex` is a new merge type, and merge types are serialized in replicated MergeTree log entries. Older replicas would not understand a new merge type. For that reason, generation is gated by a setting: ```sql enable_ttl_clear_index_merge_type_generation ``` The default is off. The binary can parse and execute `TTLClearIndex`, but a server will not write that merge type to the replicated log unless the setting is enabled. The intended rollout is: 1. deploy code everywhere; 2. once every replica that can read the log understands `TTLClearIndex`, enable generation; 3. later we can consider changing the default. With the gate off, replicas will not schedule dedicated `TTLClearIndex` maintenance work. Regular merges can still apply the clear-index TTL to their outputs, which is safe because missing per-part index files are already supported. ## Interaction with `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` `CLEAR INDEX` is a TTL effect, so it respects the TTL merge blocker. If TTL merges are already stopped before a regular merge starts, the merge continues without applying clear-index TTL effects. If TTL merges are stopped after a merge has already decided to apply clear-index TTL effects, the merge is cancelled, matching existing TTL-delete behavior. ## Validation and edge cases covered The tests cover: - invalid target index names - per-part `index_clear_ttl_info` in `system.parts`, including the target index name - minmax index clearing - text index clearing - the late tiny insert case, where an old cleared part later merges with a small old part - adding `CLEAR INDEX` TTL to a table that already has old indexed data - TTL dependency recalculation after mutating a column used by the TTL expression - replicated execution with embedded Keeper - generation off vs generation on ## Things deliberately left conservative The fast path is narrow on purpose. Physically unsupported parts use the regular fallback, while parts with incomplete TTL metadata wait for recalculation. We can broaden the fast path later once we are comfortable with storage-specific details. The generation gate is also conservative. It is there to make rolling upgrades safe, not to disable all `CLEAR INDEX` TTL behavior. Possible follow-ups: - share more code with the existing `ALTER ... CLEAR INDEX` mutation path - add more schema-evolution tests around dropping or changing target indexes - add more direct instrumentation around which files were hardlinked vs copied in the fast path ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree tables now support `TTL ... CLEAR INDEX index_name`, which clears secondary index files from parts once all rows in the part are past the TTL. This can help to manage the lifecycle of large indexes on older data, to conserve disk space. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108069](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108069+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
