signal.title: Support safe type conversions in correlated subquery equivalence substitution
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113407 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101863 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Correlated subqueries with an equality on columns that differ only in nullability (e.g. `Int64` vs `Nullable(Int64)` under `data_type_default_nullable = 1`, as in TPC-DS Q35), or on native-number columns having a least common type (e.g. `Int32` vs `Int64`), are now decorrelated via equivalent-expression substitution instead of falling back to a CROSS JOIN with a post-join filter, avoiding severe memory growth on such queries. Closes #113407. --- ## Motivation The equivalent-expression substitution in `PlannerCorrelatedSubqueries` recorded an equivalence only when both sides of the correlated `equals` had exactly the same type. A correlated `EXISTS` whose join condition compares `Int64` with `Nullable(Int64)` therefore decorrelated through the CROSS JOIN fallback; at TPC-DS SF100 (Q35 with `data_type_default_nullable = 1`) the cross-joined intermediate grew without bound (35+ GiB and climbing before being killed, versus 1.72 s / 1.70 GiB with aligned column types). ## Approach The exact-type guard was load-bearing: correlated columns are `PLACEHOLDER` nodes typed with the outer column's type, and every decorrelated DAG declares that type for its inputs, so a substituted column of a different runtime type is a logical error during execution. The substitution therefore cannot simply alias a column of another type, nor cast to the common supertype — it must produce exactly the placeholder's type. Equivalence classes now track `(column name, type)` pairs. The recording guard admits, besides equal types, two verified-safe families: - nullability-only differences (any base type) — the equality predicate rejects `NULL`s; - native-number pairs with a least supertype — for them `equals` is mathematically exact (`9007199254740993 :: Int64 = 9007199254740992.0 :: Float64` is `0`), the supertype exists only when every type embeds losslessly, and `accurateCastOrNull` is exactness-checking, so value equivalence is transitive across a class. At substitution the chosen equivalent column is converted to exactly the correlated type: `toNullable` / lossless `CAST` when widening, `assumeNotNull` / `accurateCastOrNull` when narrowing. For the narrowing conversions a `FilterStep` is inserted below the renaming that drops rows whose value is `NULL` or does not convert exactly — such rows can never satisfy the recorded equality (a top-level AND-conjunct of an ancestor filter), and dropping them before `assumeNotNull` is required so that its arbitrary result for non-converting values cannot leak into aggregation keys (the aggregation decorrelation appends correlated identifiers as group keys). Pairs whose comparison semantics are not consistent with `CAST` keep the previous CROSS JOIN fallback: `Decimal` vs `Float` (comparison converts to `Float` and is inexact), `String` vs `FixedString` (comparison ignores padding), and supertype-less numeric pairs such as `Int64` vs `UInt64` or `Int64` vs `Float64`. ## Verification - The issue's reproducer plans with zero `cross` nodes and returns the same result as the fallback. - New stateless test `05023_correlated_subquery_equivalence_type_conversion` (12 cases: both nullability directions, widening/narrowing/sideways/float numerics with adversarial boundary values, scalar-subquery aggregation with an outer `0` vs inner `NULL`, guarded fallbacks) passed 6/6 runs under harness setting randomization. - A cross-check over 16 type pairs compared `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` / scalar `count()` results between substitution and the CROSS JOIN fallback on value pools with boundary values (`2^31±1`, `2^32±1`, `2^53`, `2^53+1`, non-integer floats) and `NULL`s — identical everywhere, and plan probes confirmed the substitution fires exactly for the admitted pairs. - The existing `correlated` stateless subset passes (3 environment-only failures in the local scratch setup: MinIO, test cluster, writable access storage). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signal.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. Key changes: - `user_files_policy` setting in `ServerSettings` with XML config example - `Context` stores `VolumePtr` and exposes `getUserFilesVolume`, `getUserFilesPaths`, `setUserFilesPolicy` - `StorageFile` supports disk-based glob matching via `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingOnDisk`, disk-based reads via `disk->readFile`, and disk-based writes via `disk->writeFile` - `FunctionFile` reads through disk I/O when volume is configured - All 13 callers of `getUserFilesPath` updated for multi-path validation - Helper overloads `pathStartsWith(path, vector)` and `fileOrSymlinkPathStartsWith(path, vector)` added - Integration test with local multi-disk and S3 (`s3_plain`) scenarios ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `user_files_policy` server setting to store `user_files` on a custom disk, including S3-backed disks. This allows customers to have a "scratch area" for files in ClickHouse Cloud, shared among all replicas. Note: keeping as a draft, because the code is not generalized enough. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Introduces a new storage-policy-backed path for `user_files` and rewires many read/write and path-validation code paths (including remote disks), which could affect file access semantics and security boundaries if edge cases are missed. > > **Overview** > Adds a new server setting `user_files_policy` that binds the `user_files` directory to a storage policy (enforced to *exactly one volume with one disk*) and stores the resolved `VolumePtr` in `Context`, with server startup applying it via `setUserFilesPolicy`. > > Updates user-files consumers to become disk-aware when a policy is configured: `file()`/`StorageFile` switch to `IDisk`-based globbing, reads, writes, schema inference and truncation (plus new helpers like `splitUserFilesAbsolutePath`, `userFilesPathExists`, and symlink-escape checks), while features that require local POSIX paths (`ATTACH ... FROM`, SQLite, `filesystem` table function, static HTTP `file://`, FileLog, several dictionary sources, error logger, etc.) now explicitly reject remote `user_files_policy` disks. > > Adds integration coverage for local-disk and `s3_plain` configurations, including globbing, absolute paths, traversal/symlink-escape hardening, write/append/truncate behavior, schema inference, and expected rejections (e.g. partitioned inserts under `user_files_policy`). > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 04b03ad8df769f756aa699f0eb7eb7fff624da1b. signal.title: index_granularity_bytes is a per-block average, not a per-granule cap: a skewed insert block makes Array(FixedString(N)) parts permanently unreadable and unmergeable (TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE)
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse (found while investigating a support escalation). ### Describe what's wrong `index_granularity_bytes` is documented as *"Maximum size of data granules in bytes"*. It is not a maximum — it is an average. The MergeTree writer computes **one** granule size for a whole block from the block's *average* row size, then applies that same row count uniformly across the block: `src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeIndexGranularity.cpp`, `computeIndexGranularity`: ```cpp else if (index_granularity_bytes != 0 && bytes_uncompressed >= index_granularity_bytes) { size_t granules_in_block = bytes_uncompressed / index_granularity_bytes; index_granularity_for_block = rows / granules_in_block; } ``` `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::fillIndexGranularity` then appends marks of exactly that size for every row of the block. So when a single block mixes tiny rows with large rows, the *average* comes out perfectly within `index_granularity_bytes` while the granules covering the large rows are orders of magnitude over it. For a block of `R` rows containing `D` contiguous large rows of `b` bytes each, the worst granule holds ``` min(D*b, R * index_granularity_bytes / D) <= sqrt(R * index_granularity_bytes * b) ``` so with `R = 8192` and the default 10 MiB cap, one granule crosses 1 GiB as soon as a single row reaches roughly 13 MB. This is bad on its own (read amplification, query memory). For `Array(FixedString(N))` it is worse than that: it produces a part that **cannot be read or merged at all, ever**. `SerializationFixedString::deserializeBinaryBulk` refuses any bulk read over 1 GiB: `src/DataTypes/Serializations/SerializationFixedString.cpp`, `deserializeBinaryBulk`: ```cpp if (unlikely(max_bytes > MAX_STRINGS_SIZE)) throw Exception(ErrorCodes::TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE, "Too large sizes of FixedString to deserialize: {}", max_bytes); ``` Once such a granule exists, `SELECT` fails, `OPTIMIZE` fails, and every mutation fails, because merges and mutations always read exactly one whole granule at a time and have no setting to read less: `src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeSequentialSource.cpp`: ```cpp void MergeTreeSequentialSource::updateRowsToRead(size_t mark_number) { const auto & index_granularity = read_task_info->data_part_info->getIndexGranularity(); if (mark_number < index_granularity.getMarksCountWithoutFinal()) current_rows_to_read = index_granularity.getMarkRows(mark_number); } ``` The part is not corrupt — the data is still reachable through a `SELECT` with a short enough read span — but nothing in the server can rewrite it, so the only recovery is `INSERT SELECT` into a fresh table. What makes this hard to notice is that every metric says the table is healthy. In the reproducer below the part reports `data_uncompressed_bytes / marks = 10420732` against a `10485760` cap, i.e. 0.6% *under* budget, while one of its granules holds 1.25 GiB. There is no per-granule size exposed in `system.*`, so the first symptom is the error. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce ### 1. The invariant violation, cheaply (6.6 MB, runs in 0.2 s) 100 rows of exactly `index_granularity_bytes` each, preceded by 4000 empty rows, all in one insert block. Every one of the large rows is one full cap's worth of data, so each must get its own granule. ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS skewed_granule; CREATE TABLE skewed_granule (k UInt64, arr Array(FixedString(16))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, index_granularity_bytes = 65536, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO skewed_granule SELECT number, arrayMap(x -> toFixedString('0123456789abcdef', 16), range(if(number >= 4000, 4096, 0))) FROM numbers(4100) SETTINGS max_block_size = 10000, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0; SELECT 'average looks compliant' AS what, round(data_uncompressed_bytes / marks) AS avg_bytes_per_granule, 65536 AS index_granularity_bytes FROM system.parts WHERE table = 'skewed_granule' AND active AND database = currentDatabase(); SELECT 'but one granule is not' AS what, max(rows_in_granule) AS rows_in_worst_granule, max(rows_in_granule) * 65536 AS bytes_in_worst_granule, 65536 AS index_granularity_bytes FROM ( SELECT rows_in_granule, sum(rows_in_granule) OVER (ORDER BY mark_number) AS end_row FROM mergeTreeIndex(currentDatabase(), skewed_granule, with_marks = 1) ) WHERE end_row > 4000 AND rows_in_granule > 0; ``` Result on 26.7.4.58 and on master: ``` average looks compliant 63646 65536 but one granule is not 40 2621440 65536 ``` 40 large rows in one granule, 2621440 bytes, 40x the cap. ### 2. The unreadable part (1.25 GiB) ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS poisoned; CREATE TABLE poisoned (k UInt64, arr Array(FixedString(16))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, index_granularity_bytes = 10485760, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; -- one insert block: 130048 empty arrays, then 1024 arrays of 81920 elements (1.25 MiB each) INSERT INTO poisoned SELECT number, arrayMap(x -> toFixedString('0123456789abcdef', 16), range(if(number >= 130048, 81920, 0))) FROM numbers(131072) SETTINGS max_block_size = 200000, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0, max_insert_block_size = 200000, max_memory_usage = 0; SELECT rows, marks, data_uncompressed_bytes, round(data_uncompressed_bytes / marks) AS avg_bytes_per_granule FROM system.parts WHERE table = 'poisoned' AND active AND database = currentDatabase(); -- 131072 129 1344274432 10420732 <- average is *under* the 10485760 cap SELECT sum(cityHash64(arr)) FROM poisoned; -- Code: 131 OPTIMIZE TABLE poisoned FINAL; -- Code: 131 -- the data is still there, reachable only with a short read span SELECT sum(cityHash64(arr)) FROM poisoned SETTINGS max_block_size = 512, use_query_condition_cache = 0; -- 13584573267723215872 ``` `1342177280 = 1024 rows * 81920 elements * 16 bytes`. Note that `SELECT sum(length(arr)) FROM poisoned` succeeds, because it only reads the `.size0` subcolumn — a useful way to inspect an affected table without touching the broken stream. ### Notes on reachability * No unusual settings are required. Disabling the insert squashing above only makes the reproducer deterministic. With completely default insert settings the same failure appears as soon as one incoming block spans the whole skewed range (source block of 131072 rows fails, 100000 rows does not) — `min_insert_block_size_bytes` merges small blocks but never splits a large one, so any client sending one big mixed block is exposed. * Under default `min_bytes_for_wide_part = 1 GiB` an affected part is always Wide, since exceeding the 1 GiB read limit requires more than 1 GiB of uncompressed data in the part. * Merges are also a source, though the default `merge_max_block_size_bytes = 10 MiB` normally prevents it. With an `AggregatingMergeTree` column of type `SimpleAggregateFunction(groupUniqArrayArray, Array(FixedString(16)))`, four individually readable parts merge into an unreadable one as soon as `merge_max_block_size_bytes` is set to `0` or to a large value; at the default, and with `merge_max_block_size = 512` alone, the merge output is fine. * `Array(String)` with an identical layout is unaffected: `SerializationString::deserializeBinaryBulk` has no equivalent cap. The oversized granules still exist, they just do not throw. * Reducing `index_granularity` does **not** help, because the reader coalesces consecutive granules into a single deserialization call (`MergeTreeRangeReader::DelayedStream`). With `index_granularity = 512` the same table still fails, on a read span of 33792 rows (66 granules). ### Expected behavior No granule should exceed `index_granularity_bytes` by more than one row, regardless of how row sizes are distributed inside the block being written. Secondarily, a large-but-valid read span should not be a hard error. The 1 GiB check guards a single up-front `data.resize` before `readBig` (added in e3dafdb865d12dbc9ad0ed38378cbfa574b15d99, "More hardening", 2022-09-18); it is not an on-disk format constraint, and `SerializationString` has no equivalent. Reading the span in bounded steps would preserve the hardening (a corrupt length would no longer cause any up-front allocation at all) while letting existing affected parts be read and merged again without a manual rebuild. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 131. DB::Exception: Too large sizes of FixedString to deserialize: 1342177280: (while reading column arr): (while reading from part .../all_1_1_0/ in table default.poisoned located on disk default of type local, from mark 127 with max_rows_to_read = 1024, offset = 0): While reading part all_1_1_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPool, algorithm: Thread). (TOO_LARGE_STRING_SIZE) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108243 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/20013 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108297 ### Additional context ### Relationship to #108243 / #108297 That fix addresses a different defect with the same symptom family: `ColumnAggregateFunction::byteSize` reports only pointers plus its own arena, so the writer under-measured the *input* to the averaging formula. It corrects the average for aggregate-state columns and does not touch the averaging itself, so intra-block skew still produces oversized granules there. It is unrelated to this report: `Array(FixedString(16))` and `SimpleAggregateFunction(..., Array(FixedString(16)))` are both `ColumnArray(ColumnFixedString)`, whose `byteSize` is exact — the writer here already saw the correct 1.34 GB — and the failure reproduces on builds that contain the fix. ### Recovery for an affected table No server-side operation can repair the part, because everything that rewrites data reads whole granules. `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` and `CLEAR COLUMN` succeed (they never read the column), lightweight `DELETE` succeeds, and everything else fails. `index_granularity_bytes` is readonly for all MergeTree engines, so it cannot be lowered in place either. The working recovery is a rebuild through a `SELECT` with a bounded read span: ```sql INSERT INTO new_table SELECT * FROM affected_table SETTINGS max_block_size = 512, use_query_condition_cache = 0, min_insert_block_size_rows = 0, min_insert_block_size_bytes = 0, max_insert_block_size = 512, max_threads = 1; ``` Both settings are needed: `use_query_condition_cache = 1` forces reads to round up to complete granules (`ceilRowsToCompleteGranules` in `MergeTreeRangeReader::startReadingChain`), so `max_block_size` alone does not shorten the span for a filtered read. Verified byte-for-byte: symmetric difference between source and rebuilt table is 0 rows, and the rebuilt table reads with default settings and survives `OPTIMIZE FINAL`. One case is unrecoverable by any means: a single row whose elements exceed 1 GiB (67108865 elements of `FixedString(16)` = 1073741840 bytes) cannot be read even at `max_block_size = 1`, since a granule cannot be smaller than one row. Worth checking before attempting a rebuild with `SELECT max(length(arr)) * 16 FROM t`, which is safe to run on an affected table because it only reads the offsets subcolumn.

signal.title: perf(native-proto): batch protocol messages by default
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Native protocol: Make batching protocol messages default and `sync()` api to ship immediately. This enables to send the end-of-query message sequence like (profile info, progress, profile events, end-of-stream, …) as one socket write instead of one packet per message. Removes a full round-trip of latency per query for clients on high-latency links whose connections idle between queries. ### Background and Rationale NOTE: **This is driven by one of the customer (low-latency system). Saw this additional RTT and saw latency spike. Their setup is egress is 30 ms DELAY from client -> server (RTT). They notice additional RTT between client and server.** The native protocol runs with `TCP_NODELAY`, so every buffer flush becomes its own small TCP packet. At the end of every query the server sends a burst of tiny messages back-to-back (profile info, progress, profile events, an empty block, logs, end-of-stream). Flushed one at a time, each takes a slot in the TCP congestion window. That is usually invisible, but not always. After a connection sits idle between queries, Linux resets the congestion window back to the route's `initcwnd` (`net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle`). If the end-of-query burst is longer than that window, the server has to stop and wait for an ACK before sending the rest (a full extra round trip). On a high-latency link this shows up as roughly 2x query latency for clients that idle between queries, which is exactly what a customer hit. The fix groups the whole end-of-query suffix into a single socket write instead of one write per message, so the burst fits in one flight. A `GroupedMessagesGuard` (see `src/Server/TCPHandler.h`) accumulates the messages and flushes once at end-of-stream. This covers every path that emits the suffix: the pulling `SELECT` path, the synchronous and asynchronous `INSERT` epilogues, and the completed-pipeline branch. Tested with an integration suite (`test_native_protocol_grouped_writes`) that counts the server's socket writes per query via the `NetworkSendCalls` profile event, plus an end-to-end latency test over a simulated 500ms-RTT link with a small `initcwnd`. ### See it in action You can use [Go program](https://gist.github.com/kavirajk/62dfcc661ba004cb09f5f59ea5d52750) with following environment setup (simulating customer setup) to reproduce the latency spike (additional RTT) #### Setup (Linux) ```bash # A private network stack named "chsrv" for the server process. sudo ip netns add chsrv # A virtual cable. One end (veth-host) stays on your machine; the other (veth-ch) # is pushed into the namespace. Traffic between them really crosses this "cable" # (two local IPs WITHOUT a namespace would short-circuit over loopback - that's # why the namespace is needed at all). sudo ip link add veth-host type veth peer name veth-ch sudo ip link set veth-ch netns chsrv # Addresses: your side is 10.99.0.1, the server side is 10.99.0.2. MTU stays 1500, # so segment sizes behave like a real network (loopback's 64KB MTU would not). sudo ip addr add 10.99.0.1/24 dev veth-host sudo ip link set veth-host up sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip addr add 10.99.0.2/24 dev veth-ch sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip link set veth-ch up sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip link set lo up # The fake WAN: delay every packet leaving the server by 32ms => client-observed # RTT = 32ms. (Requires the sch_netem kernel module - loads automatically now # that your kernel and /lib/modules match.) sudo ip netns exec chsrv tc qdisc add dev veth-ch root netem delay 32ms # THE LEVER: the server's initial congestion window, as a route metric. # 10 is the Linux default; 8 reproduces the customer; 4 is pathological. sudo ip netns exec chsrv ip route change 10.99.0.0/24 dev veth-ch \ proto kernel scope link src 10.99.0.2 initcwnd 8 ``` Validate the 30ms egress delay by a ping ```bash ping -c 3 10.99.0.2 ``` You should see ~30 ms ```bash PING 10.99.0.2 (10.99.0.2) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=4 ttl=64 time=32.2 ms 64 bytes from 10.99.0.2: icmp_seq=5 ttl=64 time=32.1 ms ``` #### Performance issue with CH 26.3 1. Run the 26.3 CH server (without the patch) ```bash mkdir -p /tmp/chdata cd ~/chbin wget https://builds.clickhouse.com/26.3/amd64/clickhouse sudo ip netns exec chsrv sudo -u "$USER" \ ./clickhouse server -- --listen_host=0.0.0.0 --path=/tmp/chdata/ ``` 2. Create the dataset ```bash ./clickhouse client --host 10.99.0.2 -q \ "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS benchmark_test (id UInt64) ENGINE=MergeTree ORDER BY id" ./clickhouse client --host 10.99.0.2 -q \ "INSERT INTO benchmark_test SELECT number FROM numbers(939)" ``` 3. signal.title: Do not merge patch parts across the data version of an existing part
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/98898 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113998 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Found patch part ... that intersects mutation with version ...` (`LOGICAL_ERROR`) on tables with lightweight updates. A merge of patch parts could produce a patch whose range of data versions spans the data version of an existing part; that patch can then be neither applied nor skipped, so every later operation on the partition failed and the replication queue stalled. Such merges are no longer assigned. ### Description A patch part is applied to a part either wholly or not at all: `patchHasHigherDataVersion` asserts that the patch's data versions are either all newer or all older than the data version of the part, and throws a `LOGICAL_ERROR` otherwise. Merging patch parts unions their ranges of data versions, so the merged range must not span the data version of any part in the original partition. The merge predicate took that boundary from `getCurrentMutationVersion`, that is from the mutations it still knows about. Those records are not durable, while the data version a mutation gave to the parts is: * `ReplicatedMergeTree` removes a mutation from `mutations_by_partition` when the cleanup thread drops the finished `/mutations` znode, and immediately on `KILL MUTATION`; * `MergeTree` removes it from `current_mutations_by_version` in `clearOldMutations`. Once the record is gone, every patch on either side of the boundary maps to the same version, the pair looks mergeable, and the merge produces a patch that spans a version the parts have already crossed. From then on `DETACH`/`DROP`/`MOVE`/`REPLACE PARTITION`, applying patches and building a mutations snapshot all fail on that partition, and debug and sanitizer builds abort. The fix takes the boundary from the data versions of the parts. For `ReplicatedMergeTree` they come from `virtual_parts`, which is `current_parts` + `queue`, so a version that only a queued `MUTATE_PART` has assigned is seen before that entry is executed — the pending-mutation case, which #113998 addresses from the queue side, is covered as well. The versions are collected only when the table has patch parts, so tables without lightweight updates pay nothing. No assertion is relaxed. The refused merge is never needed: the patch on the older side of the boundary is fully applied, so `clearUnusedPatchParts` drops it, and the patches on the newer side still merge with each other. This does not repair a patch that already spans a version on disk; such a table stays stuck until the patch is removed. The test is deterministic: it keeps the applied patch with `remove_unused_patch_parts = 0`, removes the finished mutation record with `KILL MUTATION`, and forces the merge with `OPTIMIZE ... PARTITION ID '<patch partition>' FINAL`. On master it aborts with the exact message; with the fix the merge is refused, the patches stay separate and the data is correct. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=0fc2db3239a1bd6dd6581f103473834687408b7d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29 The same `LOGICAL_ERROR` accounts for 23 stress-test failures across 8 distinct stacks and every build flavor between 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-16, the most frequent one being a merged patch part reported from `MergeTreeData::MutationsSnapshotBase`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115064&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115064](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115064+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115661 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115661 `test_storage_delta/test.py::test_early_return_limit` pins two values an async interleaving decides. 5 hits in 90 days across three job families, two on master, so not parametrization-specific. Latest master failure: [`Integration tests (arm_binary, distributed plan, 1/4)` @ 0c80ff614e89](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=0c80ff614e89817cf0936f09d57f8d67b3bfb7d2&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%201%2F4%29) Root cause: the scan producer appends to a bounded deque and logs the LIVE queue depth (`List batch size is {}/{}`); consumers pop under the same mutex. With `s3_list_object_keys_size = 1` the capacity is one, so the last log legitimately reads `1/1` or `0/1` depending on which thread reaches the mutex first. `DeltaLakeScannedFiles` is incremented after both callback shutdown exits, so the count is 2 or 3 for the same reason. Both orderings are correct. Two test-only changes: - The assertion counting `List batch size is 1/1, shutdown: true` is **removed**, not relaxed: even relaxed it is implied by `assert first_check_hits > 0 or queue_check_hits > 0` three lines above, which runs first. A callback returning false cannot stop the producer reaching that batch log. - `assert scanned_files == 3` becomes `<= 3`, restoring the bound the test was written with: `a33799ba6fb63ee` added `scanned_files < 10`; `95e6f488a0917b` ("Make exact comparison in test") tightened it to `== 3` days later. `scanned_files > 0` bounds the other side. Validated with a forced-interleaving probe in the scan callback: unpatched fails with the CI signature on the drained ordering, patched passes on it. Deleting both callback shutdown exits makes it fail at `assert 997 <= 3`, so the bound still catches an early-return regression. 20/20 runs pass. The retained assertion is not race-proof either: both counters are logged inside the callback, so a shutdown seen by the parked producer skips it. That ordering has 0 of 38 failures in 90 days over 97538 runs, against 5 for the one removed here. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115693&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115693](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115693+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Read the global settings under a lock in Context::getReadSettings
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62025 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a data race on the global `Context`'s settings. `Context::getReadSettings()` and `Context::getWriteSettings()` read the settings without a lock while the writers on that path hold `Context::mutex` exclusively, so a background thread opening a file during a settings change could read a torn value, including a `std::string_view` into a `String` setting being reallocated. `Context::setDefaultProfiles()` also adjusted settings outside the lock. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/62025 ### Description `Context::getReadSettings()` reads 51 settings through `getSettingsRef()`, an unsynchronized inline accessor, while the writers on that path hold the exclusive `Context::mutex` - a missing reader-side lock (the `checkSettingsConstraints`/`clampToSettingsConstraints` overloads are the exception, disclosed below). `getWriteSettings()` has the same shape, and the four throttler getters read their bandwidth setting the same way. Two of those settings are `SettingFieldString`, and the getter holds a `std::string_view` into the heap `String` while a concurrent assignment can reallocate it, so the consequence exceeds a torn scalar. `setDefaultProfiles()` was the other half: `applySettingsQuirks`, `adjustSettingsForMakeDistributedPlan` and `doSettingsSanityCheckClamp` ran after `setCurrentProfile` released the mutex, so a reader-side lock alone would exclude nothing. Free `getReadSettings()` falls back to the global context when there is no query context - the documented `system_profile` path for background work - so a background thread opening a file during startup reaches it. The report came from a Keeper changelog reader racing `setDefaultProfiles`, but the defect is in `Context`. Both getters now take a shared lock over the settings extraction and release it before the calls that follow, because this mutex cannot be upgraded and the throttler getters re-enter it exclusively. The throttler getters' own bandwidth reads are synchronized the same way, and `setDefaultProfiles`' trailing mutations move under the exclusive lock. The effective settings a server reports are byte-identical before and after. Scope is narrow: it makes the reported pair race-free, not all access to the global settings. Still unsynchronized and not addressed here: the five `checkSettingsConstraints`/`clampToSettingsConstraints` overloads reaching `doSettingsSanityCheckClamp` under a shared lock only, `reloadClusterConfig()`, `getBackupsThrottler()`, and 29 sites outside `Context` reading the global settings via `getSettingsRef()`. <details> <summary>Provenance and validation</summary> Issue #62025 reports this same race, also on a `String` setting; it was closed by #62309, which reordered one `clickhouse-local` caller and left the accessor unsynchronized. This report is from an internal ThreadSanitizer stress run, with no public CIDB hits for the stack in 90 days: it is rare, and the argument is the mechanism. Two tests in the existing `gtest_context_race.cpp`, neither carrying signal outside ThreadSanitizer. `GetReadSettingsRace`: reader threads calling both getters against a writer changing a `String` setting and an integer one; it reports on the unpatched tree in 3 of 3 runs, naming `getReadSettings` as the read and `setSettingWithLock` as the write, and is silent in 5 of 5 with the fix. `SetDefaultProfilesRace` covers the other half, where the trailing pass is the unlocked reader. Of the seven locks added, six were removed one at a time with the matching test required to report, at six distinct addresses; the seventh is `getWriteSettings`' own, driven by the same test through `s3_allow_parallel_part_upload`, which only it reads. Since this locks a hot accessor, deadlock was the main concern. `Context::mutex` is private and no `Context` method calls either getter, so there is no reverse entry, and the callees inside the locked region do not take it. Dynamically, a server with embedded Keeper and all four bandwidth settings non-zero, so the throttler getters reach their exclusive branch, served 263,251 queries at 2920 QPS under mixed load with no hang. Also green under ThreadSanitizer: `Context.*` (9), `Coordination*` (43), `Threading.*SharedMutex*` (12), and the Keeper suites `test_keeper_and_access_storage` (which guards the startup ordering `setDefaultProfiles` takes part in), `test_keeper_session`, `test_keeper_incorrect_config`, `test_keeper_block_acl`. An alternating A/B benchmark showed no measurable throughput change (base 3464 QPS, patched 3520, overlapping ranges). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115659&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115659](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115659+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **`timeSeriesFromGrid` bulk-copies values for dense rows.** ## What changed - Add a **dense-row fast path** to `timeSeriesFromGrid`. - Use **one `insertRangeFrom` call** for dense values. - Remove repeated **per-sample `insertFrom` calls** on that path. - Use ClickHouse’s existing **`memoryIsZero()` null-map helper** for nullable rows. - Keep the **existing sample-by-sample path** for rows containing NULLs. - Keep **timestamp generation** unchanged. - Keep **row ordering and result offsets** unchanged. - Add **mixed dense and sparse multi-row coverage**. - Add a **dense nullable row after a sparse row** to cover a nonzero nested-array offset. - Add a **dense negative-timestamp case**. - Add an **all-NULL case** for the sparse fallback. ## Why this is safe - **Input length validation is unchanged.** Every row still needs exactly `num_steps` values. - **Non-nullable rows are always dense**, so they can use the range copy directly. - **Nullable rows check only their row slice** of the null map before taking the bulk path. - Rows with **any NULL stay on the existing path**, including sparse and all-NULL rows. - For nullable values, the fast path copies the already-unwrapped **nested `T` column into the non-nullable result `T` column**. - The optimization changes only **how dense values are copied**. - **Timestamps, NULL filtering, row order, and offsets keep the existing behavior.** ## Benchmark Focused `timeSeriesFromGrid` benchmark on Apple arm64 with **Release/O3 binaries**. The baseline and patch used the same remaining build objects and differed only in `timeSeriesRange.cpp` (`std::none_of` versus `memoryIsZero`). Each case ran **10 identical queries in one `clickhouse local --multiquery` process**, with `max_threads = 1`, 4,096 grid points, 10,000 input rows, and `arraySum` over the returned values so the value payload was consumed. Times below are total wall time for the 10 queries. | Workload | Baseline | Patch | Change | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Non-nullable dense | 2.98 s | 2.51 s | **15.8% faster** | | Nullable dense | 2.24 s | 2.17 s | **3.1% faster** | | One NULL at first position | 3.49 s | 3.47 s | **flat** | | One NULL at final position | 3.55 s | 3.55 s | **flat** | | 10% NULL | 3.78 s | 3.80 s | **0.5% slower** | | 50% NULL | 2.66 s | 2.66 s | **flat** | A sample-width sweep at **256, 1,024, 4,096, and 16,384 points** showed the same shape. signal.title: clean orphans from keeper snapshots
signal.text: This change makes ClickHouse Keeper able to recover from snapshots that contain orphaned nodes — nodes whose parent is absent from the snapshot. Before this change, such a snapshot made Keeper fail to start with an opaque internal error thrown by `updateValue` ("Could not find key"). This pull request replaces that with a clear, opt-in recovery path: - By default (`keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `false`), Keeper still refuses to load a snapshot with orphaned nodes, but now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` exception that reports the number of orphaned nodes and how to enable recovery. - When `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` = `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` = `false`, the orphaned nodes and all of their descendants are removed during startup, ACL usage counters and ephemeral bookkeeping are updated, and stale `numChildren` counters on surviving nodes are corrected, so Keeper can load the snapshot. Cleanup is strictly a startup recovery operation. A snapshot deserialized while the server is already running — for example, a follower applying a leader snapshot in `KeeperStateMachine::apply_snapshot` — is applied as-is and is never modified, so a follower cannot diverge from the rest of the cluster. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ClickHouse Keeper now throws an actionable `CORRUPTED_DATA` error reporting the number of orphaned nodes (nodes whose parent is missing) when loading a snapshot that contains them, instead of failing with an opaque internal error. With the new setting `keeper_server.remove_orphaned_nodes_on_startup` set to `true` and `keeper_server.digest_enabled` set to `false`, such orphaned nodes (and their descendants) are removed during startup so Keeper can load the snapshot. The cleanup is performed only on startup, never while the server is running. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=95761&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/95761](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F95761+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114629&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114629](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114629+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: readonly=2 blocks transition to more-restrictive readonly=1
signal.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When a session/connection is in `readonly=2` mode, it is restricted from transitioning to `readonly=1` even though `readonly=1` should have a strict subset of `readonly=2`'s capabilities, and thus be a reduction in privileges. **What the docs say about it:** [The docs for readonly](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/permissions-for-queries#readonly) do not make any claims about transitions restricted by `readonly=2`. They claim for `readonly=1` that: > After setting `readonly = 1`, the user can’t change `readonly` and `allow_ddl` settings in the current session. > When using the `GET` method in the HTTP interface, `readonly = 1` is set automatically. To modify data, use the `POST` method. > Setting `readonly = 1` prohibits the user from changing settings. There is a way to prohibit the user from changing only specific settings. Also there is a way to allow changing only specific settings under `readonly = 1` restrictions. For details see [constraints on settings](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/configuration/settings/constraints-on-settings). But: 1. The **documentation is actually wrong**, as the HTTP interface sets `readonly=2` not `readonly=1` by default; 2. The **documentation makes no specific claims about what `readonly=2` constrains**; it only says > 2 — Read data and Change settings queries are allowed. which isn't particularly specific and doesn't describe if/whether `readonly=2` confines transitions to `readonly=1` or even to `readonly=0`. 3. The breakout passage about not being able to escape readonly once it is set only applies to `readonly=1`; it says nothing at all about `readonly=2` This ticket focuses on the IMO surprising inability to switch from a less to more restrictive readonly mode. I raised https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115697 for the wrong docs about the HTTP readonly mode etc. ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? Tested on 26.8.1.1731 & 26.3.17.1 ### How to reproduce ### Setup On a generic clickhouse docker container, assuming default no-auth admin: ```bash clickhouse-client --query " CREATE USER probe IDENTIFIED WITH plaintext_password BY 'x'; " ``` ### HTTP API test cases Using the HTTP API, which defaults to `readonly=2`: ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'readonly=1' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT 1 FORMAT TSV' Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode 'query=SET readonly = 1' Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` Show that `readonly=2` is in effect by default: ```console $ curl -sS -G 'http://probe:x@localhost:8123/' \ --data-urlencode "session_id=$SID" \ --data-urlencode "query=SELECT getSetting('readonly') FORMAT TSV" 2 ``` ### Native protocol test cases Same underlying issue as HTTP. `SettingsConstraints` refuses to modify `readonly` while any nonzero `readonly` is in effect. **From `readonly = 2` (HTTP-default-equivalent)** Single statement refused with `Code: 164 READONLY`: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 \ --query "SET readonly = 1" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) ``` **Multi-statement has the same error and `SELECT` never runs:** ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 --multiquery \ --query "SET readonly = 1; SELECT getSetting('readonly')" Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) (query: SET readonly = 1;) ``` Sanity check showing `readonly=2` really is in effect, and other settings can still be changed under it (as that's how `readonly=2` is distinct from `readonly=1`): ``` $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 \ --query "SELECT getSetting('readonly')" 2 $ clickhouse-client --user probe --password x --readonly 2 --max_threads 3 \ --query "SELECT getSetting('readonly'), getSetting('max_threads')" 2 3 ``` ### Expected behavior I **expected** the following state-transitions to be permitted: a. `readonly=0` -> `readonly=1` or `readonly=2` b. `readonly=2` -> `readonly=1` and all others blocked. The reality is that only (a) is allowed, and (b) is blocked: | Start state | Attempted transition | Result | |-----------------------------------|----------------------|----------------------------| | `readonly=0` (default) | `SET readonly=1` | ✅ succeeds | | `readonly=0` (default) | `SET readonly=2` | ✅ succeeds | | `--readonly 2` | `SET readonly=1` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 2` | `SET readonly=0` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 1` | `SET readonly=2` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 1` | `SET readonly=0` | ❌ Code 164 | | `--readonly 2` + `--max_threads 3`| (query time) | ✅ both settings applied | This is true for both HTTP and native protocols but because `readonly=2` is the default on the native protocol, it's easier to hit the issue. ### Error message and/or stacktrace `DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'readonly' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY)` ### Related issues and pull requests Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 ### Additional context This overlaps somewhat with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115691 in which `readonly=1|2` fails to restrict `SET ROLE`, and with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115551 where session profiles are not applied when role-transitions occur mid-session. All three are problems with confinement, privilege dropping and access control.

signal.title: Add query plan cache for complex queries (views, joins, subqueries)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add an experimental query plan cache supporting complex `SELECT` queries: views (including nested views), joins, `UNION`, `IN` subqueries and multiple tables over supported local table engines. When `allow_experimental_query_plan_cache = 1` and `enable_query_plan_cache = 1`, repeated identical queries skip query analysis and logical planning (the query is still parsed) while still executing against current data. `SYSTEM DROP QUERY PLAN CACHE` clears the cache; events `QueryPlanCacheHits`/`QueryPlanCacheMisses`/`QueryPlanCacheValidationMisses`/`QueryPlanCacheStaleMisses` and metrics `QueryPlanCacheBytes`/`QueryPlanCacheEntries` provide observability. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) --- ### Description An experimental **query plan cache** for `SELECT` queries that supports **complex queries** — views (including nested views), joins, `UNION`, `IN` subqueries and multiple tables over supported local table engines. It complements https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99309, which covers single-table `MergeTree` queries with a universalize/materialize design; this PR takes a different approach to reach query shapes where planning cost is actually concentrated (deep view chains, many joins). Unlike the query result cache, a plan cache hit still executes the query: only query analysis and logical planning are skipped (the query is still parsed, since the cache key is built from the parsed AST), so hits are transactionally consistent and always see current data. #### Design On a miss, the plan is built in the planner's existing `build_logical_plan` mode (the machinery used by distributed plan shipping), with a new `SelectQueryOptions::cacheable_logical_plan` mode that makes the logical plan self-contained: - Leaf reads are storage-agnostic `ReadFromTable` placeholders for any eligible local engine. - **Views are expanded at plan time** (only `StorageView`; a materialized view stays a leaf and is read from its target table like an ordinary table), recursively in logical mode (propagated through `StorageView::readImpl` via `SelectQueryInfo::build_logical_plan`), so the cached plan embeds the analyzed view bodies instead of deferring the expensive expansion to execution. - Key-value direct-join lookup steps (`JoinStepLogicalLookup`), which bind live storages into the plan, are not used; a regular join is planned instead and the physical join algorithm is chosen at materialization. Distributed and parallel-replicas logical plans do not set this mode and are unaffected. - The plan is serialized with the standard query plan serialization and built with `compile_expressions = 0` (JIT-fused function nodes cannot be serialized; the JIT still applies when pipelines are built from the plan). Both hits and misses execute through `QueryPlan::resolveStorages`, which re-binds every leaf to a fresh storage snapshot. #### Cache key and invalidation The key is the normalized AST hash, a hash of plan-affecting settings, the current database, the user and the sorted role set. Each entry stores a **dependency fingerprint over every referenced storage**, discovered from the plan's `ReadFromTable` leaves plus an AST closure through view definitions (which also catches tables referenced only from scalar subqueries): UUID, metadata version (or a schema content hash including the view body), and the row policy hash. Every hit revalidates all dependencies and re-checks `SELECT` access, so `DROP`/`CREATE`, `ALTER`, view redefinition (including **nested** views), row policy changes and permission revocation are handled transparently. #### Eligibility - Non-deterministic functions anywhere — including inside expanded view bodies — make a query uncacheable (`arrayJoin` is exempt: it is multi-valued but pure). - Scalar subqueries are evaluated during analysis and baked into the plan as constants, so they are gated behind the opt-in setting `query_plan_cache_allow_scalar_subqueries`. - Table functions, temporary tables, system tables (except `system.one`), remote/`Merge` storages and views whose SQL security is not `INVOKER` (`DEFINER` and `NONE`) are rejected. - Plans containing steps without serialization support (e.g. window functions) execute normally and are simply not stored. #### Performance, proven on DOOMbench [DOOMbench](https://github.com/cedardb/doombench) is a DOOM-like raycasting engine implemented entirely in SQL; its `screen` query renders a frame through a deep chain of views over joins, unions, array joins and scalar subqueries. Ported to ClickHouse SQL, the workload is **query-analysis-bound**: profiling showed `IQueryTreeNode::getTreeHash` and analyzer resolution dominating, and `SELECT ... LIMIT 0` was as slow as the full query. With the plan cache (local server, single connection): | DOOMbench frame render | median | speedup | | --- | --- | --- | | cache off | 551-577 ms | — | | cache on (hit) | 227-246 ms | **2.4x** | | cache on, `max_threads = 4` | 148-176 ms | **3.3x** | On hits the analyzer cost disappears from profiles (`getTreeHash`: 25.8k samples → 174); the remaining time is genuine execution. Correctness validated on the same workload: frames are byte-identical between cache off/miss/hit, game-state mutations are visible on every cached render (HTAP freshness), nested view redefinition is picked up immediately, and `rand()` inside a view body refuses to cache. #### Notes - This PR includes the `ActionsDAG` input-constant serialization fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107124 as its first commit; it will be rebased once that PR is merged. - The miss path executes through the same logical-plan machinery as hits, so hit and miss behavior is identical by construction; storage-specific planning shortcuts (e.g. trivial `count()`) are not applied to cache-enabled queries. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99309 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107124 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107125&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107125](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107125+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Sync `BackupImpl` lock-file handling and the Cloud-only resume state
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 This is the public side of the private pull request above, and most of it is that sync. The shared files both touch -- `BackupImpl.h`, `BackupImpl.cpp`, `BackupSettings.h`, `BackupSettings.cpp`, `BackupFactory.h` -- are identical here and there, down to the blank lines, so `Check public build` can overlay the private ones unchanged and later syncs have nothing to reconcile in them. What stays private is where continuing an interrupted backup is implemented, because nothing outside ClickHouse Cloud resumes one. The part that changes this build is the lock-file handling. `open` runs from the constructor, so a failure there leaves no backup behind for anything else to clean up: whatever `open` does not undo, nothing will. It now removes the lock it created when anything that follows throws -- the verification, the rest of claiming the destination, and opening the archive. Otherwise the lock outlives the failed attempt and fences the destination against every later one, which cannot match it either: a retry picks a fresh backup UUID, so the orphaned lock belongs to nobody, and every subsequent `BACKUP` to that destination fails until someone deletes the file by hand. `removeLockFile` now reports whether the destination still holds the lock. `checkLockFile(false)` is false both for a foreign lock and for one it could not read, so a caller could not tell "not ours" from "unknown" while the lock was still there; `tryRemoveAllFiles` reports that as a failure rather than claiming the destination is clean. `createLockFile` asks for the lock with `writeFileIfNotExists` and, when that fails, compares what is there against what it would have written: its own contents mean a concurrent backup, a completed `.backup` means the backup already exists, and a lock that has since disappeared rethrows the original failure rather than guessing. `writeFileIfNotExists` is only exclusive where the storage can be -- `S3` and `Azure` implement it, every other writer falls back to an ordinary write. ### Known gaps Two of them, both predating this change and both worth naming rather than implying they are fixed. `File`, `Disk` and `Memory` destinations still have no exclusive create, so two backups started against one of them can each write `.lock`, each verify their own contents, and both proceed. The comparison above detects a lock that is already there; it cannot order two writers racing to create one. Closing this needs an exclusive create in those writers. An archive whose type `createArchiveWriter` refuses -- an unsupported extension, a compiled-out library -- still leaves the archive object behind, because the buffer it is given is created before the type is checked. The lock is removed, but the next attempt finds the archive and reports the destination as an existing backup. ### The rest Behind `CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, and compiling to nothing here: `CreateParams` carries the resume parameters, `open` hands them to a `BackupResumer` this build does not have, and the places that read them are the ownership check before anything becomes visible, the timestamp a continuation republishes, the lock a continuation is allowed to find, and the manifest it does not write again. `BackupSettings` carries the two batch-size settings that bound the work a continuation redoes; a macro list cannot hold a preprocessor conditional, so the conditional selects the list. `BackupImpl` keeps one member, `metadata_already_published`. So this build behaves as it did: it writes its own timestamp and always publishes metadata. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `BACKUP` no longer leaves a lock file behind in its destination when the attempt that created it fails before writing anything -- whether it fails while claiming the destination or while opening an archive. No later backup could match such a lock, so every retry to the same destination failed until the file was deleted by hand. Backups to `S3` and `Azure` destinations also create the lock exclusively, and a lock that belongs to another backup is reported as a concurrent backup rather than as whatever error the storage returned. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115387&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115387](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115387+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1800` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix uncompressed Keeper snapshots being written as empty files
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115388 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed Keeper snapshots being written as empty files when `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format` is disabled. The server logged `Created persistent snapshot` but the snapshot file was 0 bytes, and the node then refused to start with `CORRUPTED_DATA`. Closes #115388. ### Description With `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format=false`, every snapshot written to a local disk came out as a 0-byte file, and the node could not restart afterwards. The reported recovery is to delete the snapshot, which ClickHouse's own message calls data loss. Root cause: `KeeperSnapshotManager::writeSnapshotFile` wraps the snapshot file buffer in a `CompressedWriteBuffer` **by reference** on the non-zstd branch, while the zstd branch moves ownership into the compression decorator. `CompressedWriteBuffer` deliberately does not finalize the buffer it writes into, and it declares no `sync()`, so `finalize()` only moved the compressed blocks into the file buffer's 1 MiB memory buffer and `sync()` never reached the file descriptor. `writer.reset()` then destroyed a non-finalized `WriteBufferFromFile`, whose destructor only closes the fd. Snapshots under 1 MiB compressed came out empty; larger ones were truncated to a multiple of the buffer size. The by-reference wrap was correct when introduced, because `~WriteBufferFromFile()` called `finalize()` at the time. That destructor finalize was later removed as a general policy change, which turned this call site into a data-losing one without touching it. `f1ab91191041d8f` is present in all active release branches. The fix finalizes and syncs the file buffer on the non-zstd branch, which is what the two sibling write paths in this file already do. The other three snapshot write paths were checked and are correct as written. The on-disk format is unchanged, verified rather than assumed: the bytes the fixed path produces are md5-identical to those written through `serializeSnapshotToBuffer` plus `serializeSnapshotBufferToDisk`, so existing snapshots stay readable. Tests: two `TEST_P`s in `gtest_coordination_snapshot.cpp`, each covering both compression settings - one round trip through the fixed path, one asserting a failed fsync is surfaced and the partial files cleaned - and an integration test that forces a snapshot and restarts the node. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115553&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115553](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115553+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1802` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Retry a job image pull that failed DNS resolution
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113611 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113611 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Retry the praktika job's Docker image pull when the registry proxy's name fails to resolve, so a transient DNS failure no longer kills the whole job before any test runs. ### Description The retried job image pull added in #113611 declines to retry a DNS resolution failure, so the job aborts with zero tests run. From a failing job's log: ``` Run command: [timeout --verbose 300 docker pull clickhouse/stateless-test:...] failed to copy: ... dial tcp: lookup dockerhub-proxy.dockerhub-proxy-zone on 127.0.0.53:53: server misbehaving Retry 1/3: command failed, exit code: 1 No retryable errors found, stopping retries ERROR: command failed after 1/3 attempt(s), exit code: 1 ``` **Root cause.** `_IMAGE_PULL_RETRY_ERRORS` allowlists transport-class phrases. Go's resolver renders a SERVFAIL as `server misbehaving`, absent from that list, so a transient DNS blip takes the `break` path meant for permanent errors and the pull's non-fatal failure falls through to the implicit `docker run` pull, which has no retry wrapper. **The change** adds that one phrase: a nameserver was reached and answered badly, so the same name can resolve on a later attempt. `no such host` is deliberately not added: that is NXDOMAIN, i.e. permanent, so a misnamed image host would burn all three attempts instead of failing fast, and it has 0 occurrences in 90 days. A broader substring (`dial tcp`, `lookup `) was rejected for the same reason, since both prefix NXDOMAIN too. A new arm pins that the NXDOMAIN line is still not retried. **Breadth.** 4 jobs across 4 pull requests in 30 days, 0 on master, each carrying this phrase in the pull's own stderr. Each produced 0 test rows while sibling jobs on the same commit produced 55 to 950, so a whole check is lost, not one test. **Validation.** The suite drives the real `Shell.run` loop, so its arms exercise the production matcher. Without the fix the new arms report 1 attempt instead of 3; with it, 25 passed, identical over 30 runs. No related open issue found. <details> <summary>New test arms and their controls</summary> The new arm feeds the verbatim production line rather than a bare phrase, because there the phrase is the tail of a nested resolver error inside a URL. It carries its own negative control: the same line matched against the allowlist with the entry removed must stop after one attempt. Without that control the arm could not distinguish this entry working from some other entry already matching, which is what the pre-fix job disproved by stopping after attempt 1. Note also that the two errors in the log above differ, which is why the gap looks covered: the retried attempt got `server misbehaving`, the later `docker run` got the allowlisted `connection refused`, by which point no retry wrapper is in play. Only the second reaches the CI database, so the pull's own error appears only in the job log. | Arm | Pre-fix | Post-fix | |---|---|---| | `test_each_transport_phrase_is_retried[server misbehaving]` | 1 attempt (red) | 3 attempts | | `test_the_production_dns_failure_is_retried` | 1 attempt (red) | 3 attempts, `on_retry` reports the phrase | | its in-arm control (entry removed) | 1 attempt | 1 attempt | | `test_the_permanent_resolver_failure_is_not_retried` (`no such host`) | 1 attempt | 1 attempt | | `test_permanent_error_is_not_retried`, `test_named_permanent_errors_are_not_retried` | green | green | Deleting the entry reddens exactly the 2 arms that pin it and no others; widening it to `dial tcp` reddens the NXDOMAIN arm, so that arm is load-bearing rather than decorative. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115555&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115555](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115555+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Bound the response wait of the GCP OAuth token request instead of inheriting the caller's request timeout
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109455 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang of up to one hour in `BACKUP`/`RESTORE ... TO S3`, GCS disks and the `s3` table function when the named collection sets `http_client = 'gcp_oauth'` and the Google OAuth2 token endpoint accepts the connection but never answers. The bearer token request no longer inherits the caller's data transfer request timeout; its response wait is bounded at 10 seconds, matching the STS `AssumeRole` request cap. ### Description Found in CI: `BACKUP TABLE ... TO S3(<collection with http_client = 'gcp_oauth'>)` sat for 695 s with `read_rows: 0` until the test budget expired and the job reported `Some queries hung`. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107108&sha=7b0f0efd7803a3f3a603fe10adf92811bf16f468&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20DBReplicated%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%203%2F3%29 `BackupIO_S3.cpp` sets `requestTimeoutMs = 60 * 60 * 1000` because backup data transfers can legitimately take that long. That single value becomes both the send and the receive socket timeout, and `PocoHTTPClientGCPOAuth` reuses the same `timeouts` member for its bearer token round trip, so a credential request that should take milliseconds parked in the TLS header read for an hour (`SecureSocketImpl::mustRetry` under `HTTPHeaderStreamBuf::readFromDevice`). The S3 endpoint in the failing case is plain HTTP on localhost, so the TLS peer can only be the hardcoded Google token URL. This bounds the response wait of that round trip at 10 seconds, independently of the data transfer timeouts, at both mint sites (explicit ADC triple, and the metadata service branch). The connect timeout is left as the caller set it: `metadata_service` is a user-configurable host, so its connect budget belongs to the deployment that configured it, and connect was never the unbounded phase (`BackupIO_S3` already bounds it at 10 s). Data plane requests keep the full hour, and an already tighter timeout is kept. The 10 s matches the STS `AssumeRole` request cap, so it is named once in `S3Defines.h`. Validated against a mock that accepts and never answers: the value passed before was still blocked after 40 s, the value passed now fails in 10.0 s. Exactly one request arrived in each arm, so `backup_restore_s3_retry_attempts` (default 1000) does not multiply the mint. Not bounded here: session creation is retried up to 5 times, each attempt carrying the caller's connect budget, and the mint is not cancellation aware within the 10 s. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115531&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115531](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115531+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1803` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix the Upgrade check silently validating against a stale previous release
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The Upgrade check starts a previous release, then upgrades to the build under test. `tests/ci/get_previous_release_tag.py` picks that baseline, and can silently pick one far too old. On PR #114376 commit `e1cb0dee5e9` it picked `v25.1.4.53` for a `26.8.1.1` build; that old server aborted on shutdown, reported as `Received signal 6` unrelated to the PR. Two commits earlier it resolved `v26.7.3.19`. 4 of 47 recent runs were affected. Report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114376&sha=e1cb0dee5e9bd972e9bbbdd8cd8d971ad1e39ee1&name_0=PR&name_1=Upgrade%20check%20%28amd_release%29 Root cause: when no candidate on a page could be used, an unbounded `while not found:` advanced to page 2, 3 and answered from there. `/releases` returns entries roughly newest-created first, not in version order, and each later page's newest release is older than the previous page's newest (measured across all 9 pages), so page 1 holds the newest release overall. The only diagnostic was `logger.debug` under `basicConfig(level=INFO)`. This resolves from the first page only. A candidate still needs an uploaded package, so a release whose packages are still publishing keeps falling back to the previous patch release, now logged at WARNING rather than DEBUG. Three cases now raise: a first page with no usable candidate, a page shorter than the 100 requested, and an answer that is its page's oldest entry, which cannot show that no newer release precedes it. `upgrade_runner.sh` turns those nonzero exits into a job failure. No C++ change is needed: the abort is a use-after-free in `25.1`, fixed in `2920d338ea4` (#81473, released in `v25.6.1.3206`), so master and every active release branch carry the fix. Tests were removed at review request. The Upgrade check's digest now lists both release helpers `upgrade_runner.sh` runs, the resolver and `download_release_packages.py`; without them a change to either leaves the job cache-skippable, the same failure mode fixed here. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112974 (hardens the API helper; edits the same digest list, so whichever merges second rebases). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115228&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115228](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115228+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1805` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Do not build statistics for non-physical columns
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114791 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` on every `INSERT` into a table that declares `STATISTICS(...)` on an `ALIAS` or `EPHEMERAL` column, which made such tables read-only. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114791 `CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, b UInt64 ALIAS a + 1 STATISTICS(basic)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a` is accepted, and then every `INSERT` fails `Code: 10 ... Not found column b in block`, so the table is read-only. `materialize_statistics_on_insert` defaulting to `true` in 26.8 exposed it. **Root cause.** The `ColumnsStatistics` constructor collects every column with a non-empty statistics description without checking how the column is stored, and the insert path builds those with `build`, which does `block.getByName`. An `ALIAS` column is computed on read and never appears in the written block, so the lookup always throws. Merges use `buildIfExists` and skip absent columns, which is why they kept working. Such statistics are already unsupported in `addImplicitStatistics` and `ALTER ... ADD STATISTICS`. **The change.** Drop non-physical columns from the collector the insert path builds, in `MergeTreeDataWriter`, using the existing `ColumnsDescription::hasPhysical`. `build` stays strict, because its type-mismatch check is a deliberate diagnostic, so an absence for any other reason is still an error. A newly issued `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS <col>` naming such a column is still rejected before enqueue. An already queued one instead skips it, so a command persisted by a pre-upgrade server drains rather than retrying forever in the background task. `ALL` skips such a column and stays usable. **Deliberately unchanged.** The declaration stays accepted but inert: every candidate rejection site is also the ATTACH/startup or replica-addition path, so a check there would stop existing affected tables from loading. `DROP STATISTICS` stays permissive and recovers such a table. Covered by `02864_statistics_ddl`, which fails on master with `Code: 10` and passes with the fix. The queued-mutation drain under the old mutation analyzer is not covered by a test: it needs the server-level `use_analyzer_for_mutations` override, which a stateless test cannot set.
