signal.title: Nullable(Array) stages 1-2: type foundation and collision-free substream names
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115394 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 Stages 1 and 2 of the staged `Nullable(Array(T))` implementation described in the RFC, ClickHouse/ClickHouse#115394. Internal machinery only: **the type is still unreachable from any query**, and there is no user-visible change. `DataTypeFactory` continues to reject the string `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, so this cannot be reached through DDL, a table function's column list, or any function that takes a type by name. That boundary is itself pinned by a test, so opening it in a later stage is a deliberate change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. The two stages ship together because Stage 1 alone has no production caller — `makeNullableAllowingArray` would land exercised only by unit tests. Stage 2 is the first thing that uses it. They are separate commits. ### Stage 1: the type-level foundation `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable` keeps returning `false`, permanently. That predicate is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and each encodes an assumption about which types can be wrapped. Leaving its meaning untouched means no existing code path can begin producing `Nullable(Array(...))` on its own; only code that explicitly opts in can. `makeNullableAllowingArray` is that opt-in and it is the only door — the constructor it uses is private, reachable through a single friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. The cost is that `canBeInsideNullable` now answers `false` for a type that can in fact sit inside `Nullable`. Two consequences are pinned by tests so they are deliberate rather than discovered later: `makeNullable` rejects an array, and `makeNullableSafe` silently returns the array unwrapped instead of throwing. The second is how a `Nullable(Array)` could be quietly degraded to `Array`; the sites where that matters are audited in a later stage. ### Stage 2: collision-free substream names `Nullable` appends `.null` to a stream name and `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1` and so on, while array *elements* contribute no component at all. A `Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))` column would write two different null maps to the same file. A second, structured naming scheme inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements, and is selected per column from the type as stored in the part: ```text Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.nested Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.null c.array.nested Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))) -> c.size0 c.array.null c.array.array.size0 c.array.array.nested.null c.array.array.nested Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c (unchanged) ``` Types legal today keep byte-identical names, so existing parts stay readable with no migration and no format version bump. ### Testing Expectations are derived from real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than hand-built substream paths. That distinction turned out to matter: `SerializationNullable` emits its null-map substream and pops it before recursing, so a path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs. The real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and the naming code branches on whether a null map precedes the final substream. Expectations written against constructed paths can be entirely self-consistent and still disagree with what is written to disk. The criteria are stated as properties over a corpus rather than as spot checks: - **No existing stream name changes.** Asserted as a proof rather than a sample: for 28 currently-legal types the structured scheme is never selected, neither by type nor by any enumerated path. If it is never reached then the legacy naming code is the only code that runs, and this change does not modify it. - **Typed and untyped callers agree** for every legal type, so a column cannot be written under one set of names and read under another. - **All names distinct** for thirteen shapes placing `Nullable(Array)` inside arrays, tuples, maps and variants — including their substream cache keys and their prefix/suffix substreams. - **Subcolumn reads resolve to files the writer produced.** 31 unit tests across the three suites; the full `unit_tests_dbms` suite is green at 22732 passed, 0 failed. ### Two things worth a reviewer's attention **The substream-to-name mapping existed in three places** — `getNameForSubstreamPath`, a full copy, and a partial per-element copy — and the full copy had already drifted: it was missing `MapBucketIndexes`, so a bucketed `Map` holding a `Nullable(Array)` would have lost that name component and could have written two streams under one file name. Both copies are gone, replaced by `ISerialization::getLegacyNameForSubstreamPath`. **The naming scheme cannot be decided from the substream path alone.** The path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The column type is load-bearing, and a caller that does not supply one cannot be answered correctly. Where the path proves a type was needed — `NullableElements` above an array substream can only come from a `Nullable` directly over an `Array` — resolving a name without one now raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than quietly returning a legacy name no writer produced. A test asserts this guard never fires for any currently-legal type. Ensuring every MergeTree caller passes the type is an explicit obligation for the next stage. ### Attribution The design and a substantial amount of the code originate in ClickHouse/ClickHouse#104816 by @zhanglistar, which was closed in favour of this staged implementation. Both commits carry a `Co-authored-by` trailer. The blocker analysis that shaped the design is @Avogar's, and the resolutions to it are @alexey-milovidov's. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115464&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115464](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115464+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Find a LowCardinality needle equal to the type's default value
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112953 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`, `indexOf`, `countEqual`, `mapContainsKey`, `mapContainsValue` and `Map` subscript returning "not found" for a constant `LowCardinality` needle equal to the element type's default value, such as an empty `String` or a zero number. ### Description **The problem.** A constant needle equal to the element type's default value is never found in an `Array(LowCardinality(T))` or a `Map` with a `LowCardinality` key. No exception, so a `WHERE` on such a predicate silently drops rows: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a Array(LowCardinality(String))) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t VALUES (['', 'a']); SELECT has(a, '') FROM t; -- 0, expected 1 ``` Likewise for `0` over the numeric types, a NUL-padded `FixedString` and the `1970-01-01` `Date`, while `m['']` returns `''` instead of the stored value. Any non-default needle is correct. Reproduces on 26.5 to 26.7. **Root cause.** A `LowCardinality` dictionary reserves prefix slots for the default and NULL values, and `ReverseIndex` is built with `num_prefix_rows_to_skip`, so the reserved slot is never indexed. `ColumnUnique::uniqueInsertData` compensates for that on the write path; the read path had no counterpart. **The change.** `ColumnUnique::getOrFindValueIndex` now performs the same default-slot match as the write path. `ReverseIndex` is untouched, so no write behaviour moves. That slot becoming reachable brings two equality details. The lookup casts the constant into the element type without reporting loss, so `UInt64(256)` arrived as `UInt8(0)` and would match the default; that slot now answers only if the element type can represent the constant. And a dictionary can hold `-0.0` and `0.0` as separate entries while the shortcut has room for one index, so a zero constant over a float element type is left to the value-comparing path, as `indexOfAssumeSorted` already is. The new test covers both call sites. Lookup timing is unchanged. **Overlap with #112953.** That open PR declines this same shortcut for every float element type, subsuming the float-zero decline here, and the two conflict textually; whichever merges second should keep the broader decline and drop this one, collapsing the duplicated representability predicate to one copy. Non-float types are independent of it.

signal.title: Fix out-of-bounds read in `formatRowNoNewline` with empty rows
signal.text: Fixes a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline`. When a row is formatted to an empty result (for example, an empty string with the `RawBLOB` format), the newline-stripping logic could rewind the shared write buffer into the previous row's bytes, producing non-monotonic `ColumnString` offsets and a `size_t` underflow in the string size. Functions consuming the result could then return incorrect results or raise a logical error. The trailing newline is now stripped only when the current row actually emitted at least one byte, which keeps the offsets monotonic. The cursor is also kept within the current working buffer so the decrement never moves it before the buffer start after a flush. Added a regression test in `tests/queries/0_stateless/04512_format_row_no_newline_empty_row_underflow.sql`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a bug in the function `formatRowNoNewline` that could produce incorrect results or a logical error when a row is formatted to an empty result. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115669&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115669](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115669+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix out-of-bounds read of the LowCardinality saved-hash array
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/29782 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114993 Reported on master, no issue open for it, by `AST fuzzer (amd_tsan)` as a ThreadSanitizer heap-use-after-free at `src/Common/ColumnsHashing.h:248` on thread `MergeMutate`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=a753fdf104bb824600ebd63fd8fe20fc8deabbf2&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed an out-of-bounds read of the cached dictionary hashes when aggregating or joining on a `LowCardinality(String)` key whose dictionary grows while it is being aggregated, reachable from `TTL ... GROUP BY`. It could yield a wrong hash, and a reported heap-buffer-overflow in sanitizer builds. ### Description `IColumnUnique::tryGetSavedHash()` memoized the dictionary hash array on first use and returned a bare `const UInt64 *` with no length. `ReverseIndex::calcHashes()` sizes it from the dictionary size at that moment, and `ReverseIndex::insert()` afterwards grows only the internal copy, so nothing extended the published one. Consumers cached the bare pointer and indexed it with a current dictionary position, past the end. Only String and FixedString keys have such an array. `TTL ... GROUP BY` reaches this from ordinary SQL: `TTLAggregationAlgorithm` builds its aggregate columns once per block, grows the dictionary in place row by row, and aggregates once per key run, so later runs index positions the first run's snapshot never covered. This publishes the array as a `std::span` derived from a single owned column, so data and length always describe the same buffer, and bounds-checks all six read sites: a position inside the span uses the memoized hash, one outside takes the existing branch that hashes from the key. That branch runs today for every numeric dictionary, so no new code path appears. Both consumers are fixed: `HashMethodSingleLowCardinalityColumn` (aggregation, where it was reported) and `LowCardinalityKeyGetterForJoin` (joins, same unbounded pointer), as is the dictionary cache, which would otherwise resurrect an unbounded pointer on a hit. I did not produce a join query that overflows. #29782 fixed the lifetime half of this contract; this fixes the bounds half. Validation: a new stateless test kills the server during `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL` on master under a sanitizer build and passes with this change, 50 of 50 runs under randomized settings. The sanitizer build is the oracle, not the SQL assertion. Reverting only the bounds check brings the report back, and results are byte-identical before and after. <details><summary>Validation detail</summary> Reproduced locally with the same frames as the linked report, under ASan, which additionally attributes the overflowed region to `ReverseIndex::calcHashes` via `tryGetSavedHash` on the first `executeOnBlock` and reports the read as exactly 8 bytes past a 144-byte (18-slot) allocation. Instrumenting the out-of-range branch on the reproducer shows it taken over a thousand times with a snapshot of 2 entries while positions reach 9 and beyond, so without the check those reads are all out of bounds. Reproducer: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (k LowCardinality(String), d DateTime, v UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k TTL d + INTERVAL 1 SECOND GROUP BY k SET v = sum(v), d = max(d) SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, index_granularity = 1024, merge_with_ttl_timeout = 100000; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000, now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY, number FROM numbers(200000) SETTINGS max_insert_block_size = 200000; OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; ``` Existing coverage could not reach this: `03774_ttl_group_by_lowcardinality.sql` uses numeric LowCardinality types, where there is no saved-hash array. Taking the fallback branch cannot split a group: the memoized value comes from `StringViewHash`, which is also the `HashMap` default hash for these keys, over the same bytes `getDataAt` returns. GROUP BY and join results over String, Nullable(String), FixedString and numeric keys are byte-identical on both binaries. Eight concurrent clients running GROUP BY, spilling GROUP BY, `uniqExact` and a `parallel_hash` join over one shared dictionary return identical correct results with no sanitizer reports, exercising both sides of the publication exchange. #114993 changes the mapping caches in the same file without touching the saved hash, so the mechanisms are independent, but it extends cache lifetime across blocks here and will likely conflict textually. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115604&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115604](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115604+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1799` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Avoid server abort on type mismatch during partial result evaluation
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110048 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97411 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Constant folding during query planning no longer executes a function whose argument type differs from the type the function was resolved for during analysis. Such a mismatch used to raise a `LOGICAL_ERROR` while the output header was being computed, which is an assertion failure in debug and sanitizer builds. Folding is now skipped instead, and a genuinely invalid query still reports a recoverable `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT` error from the normal execution path. ### Description `ActionsDAG::updateHeader` matches header columns to DAG input nodes **by name only**, then runs `evaluatePartialResult` to compute the output header. A function node, by contrast, is resolved once during analysis: the overload is picked and the return type computed for a fixed set of argument types. If partial evaluation is handed an input column whose type differs from the one the function was resolved for, `executeActionForPartialResult` used to execute the function anyway. That trips a `LOGICAL_ERROR` inside the function body (for example `FunctionUnaryArithmetic`: "`negate`'s argument does not match the expected data type"), and because `handle_error_code` routes `LOGICAL_ERROR` to `abortOnFailedAssertion`, a debug or sanitizer build aborts the whole server process during planning rather than failing the one query. **Fix.** Before executing a `FUNCTION` node in partial evaluation, compare each argument column's type against the type recorded in `function_base->getArgumentTypes()`. If any of them differs, skip the fold: it is only an optimization, and the node's declared result type is already known from analysis. - With `input_rows_count == 0` (header computation) an empty column of the declared result type is produced, so header computation proceeds. - With `input_rows_count == 1` (the callers reached from JOIN rewrites, shard skipping and virtual-column path extraction) the column is left null. Those callers treat any non-null output as a definitive folded value, so a fabricated one could silently change a JOIN rewrite or skip the wrong shards; a null routes them through their existing "unknown value" path. The comparison is exact rather than wrapper-stripped, because `isNullable` derives its value from the argument type alone: its result type is `UInt8` either way, so a wrapper-only difference would produce a definitive but wrong value that no result-type check can catch. `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` need the same treatment, because both used to pass a value through while keeping the declared type computed during analysis. That hid the mismatch from the check above and let a downstream function execute on an incompatible column anyway. Both now carry the argument's actual type, which is what `ExpressionActions::executeAction` already does in its own `ALIAS` and `ARRAY_JOIN` cases. One result type cannot be instantiated: `DataTypeFunction`, the result type of a captured lambda, inherits `IDataTypeDummy::createColumn`, which throws `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. The column is left null in that one case. Since a capture is normally a child of the higher-order function consuming it, that function then reports a recoverable `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, whereas executing the stale capture raises `Cannot capture column N because it has incompatible type`, another `LOGICAL_ERROR` abort. (`DataTypeNothing` and `DataTypeSet` derive from the same base but do override `createColumn`, so they are built normally.) **Scope.** In production the mismatch was produced by a concurrent `EXCHANGE TABLES`. The query does hold its table object, lock and metadata snapshot for its whole lifetime (`InterpreterSelectQuery.cpp:635-656`), so the held storage is never swapped. What drifts is that the old analyzer resolves the table name a second time for the analyzed column types (`getTableExpressions.cpp:118`, reached from `joined_tables.resolveTables()`), and an exchange changes what that second resolution returns. The per-query storage cache from #97411 is what keeps those two resolutions consistent; #108728 defeated it and #110048 restored it, which is what `03915_exchange_tables_race` races for. This change is therefore no longer the fix for that race; it hardens the planning path itself so that any argument-type mismatch degrades to "do not fold" instead of aborting the server. I left the changelog category as `Bug Fix` because the abort was user-visible on released builds before #110048, but I am happy to move it to `Not for changelog` if you prefer, given that the root cause is now fixed upstream. **Testing.** Coverage is a unit test rather than a functional one, because the race is an inherent TOCTOU and cannot be reproduced deterministically. Since `updateHeader` binds header columns by name only, the mismatch can be injected directly, single-threaded, with no race at all. `src/Interpreters/tests/gtest_actions_dag_partial_result_type_drift.cpp` covers a strict function (`Float64` resolved, `Int256` supplied), a wrapper-only difference through `materialize`, the same mismatch behind an `ALIAS` and behind an `ARRAY_JOIN`, the wrong-value hazard via `isNullable` at `input_rows_count == 1`, a captured lambda both as a terminal output and consumed by `arrayMap`, and a non-mismatched constant that must still be folded. Verified in both directions on a debug build. Against master's `executeActionForPartialResult` the first case aborts the test binary with `Logical error: 'Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Int256'` through `updateHeader` -> `evaluatePartialResult` -> `executeActionForPartialResult`; with the fix all eight cases pass. Each hunk was also reverted individually and fails only its own case, and forcing the guard to fire unconditionally fails only the still-folds-a-constant case. Full unit suite: 22357 tests pass. `03915_exchange_tables_race` passes 10 out of 10 runs. **Known residuals, both pre-existing on `master` and deliberately not addressed here.** I measured each one against a build with this branch's `ActionsDAG.cpp` replaced by master's, and the behaviour is identical, so neither is caused or widened by this change: - The add-time fold in `tryFoldFunctionToConstant` does not perform this check. Handing `addFunction` a `function_base` resolved for one type together with a differently typed constant child raises `Unexpected return type from negate. Expected Float64. Got Const(Int256)`. This diff does not touch that path, and adding the check there would alter DAG construction for every query on a scenario I could not reach from SQL. - At `input_rows_count == 1` with `allow_unknown_function_arguments`, a type-sensitive folder above a node whose column is unknown can still fold from the type alone. Two shapes: `identity -> isNullable` over a `Nullable(String)` yields `0` where the real chain would yield `1` (unchanged from `master`), and an `ARRAY_JOIN` whose argument stopped being an array leaves the declared nested type in place, so `isNullable` above it also folds to `0`. Closing this properly needs an explicit "unknown" marker propagated through descendants, which changes the `evaluatePartialResult` contract for every caller. I tried the two local shortcuts and neither works: clearing the type outright makes the unit-test binary abort and then segfault, because a null type in a `ColumnWithTypeAndName` breaks downstream consumers; handing up the argument's own type does not help, because the parent compares against the type it was itself resolved for. So this is a separate design decision rather than part of an abort-avoidance fix. Happy to follow up on any of these if you would like them in scope. This branch also takes master's version of `03915_exchange_tables_race` verbatim: master rewrote that test after this branch forked it (pinning `enable_analyzer` and capping concurrent clients so the flaky check does not run out of memory), and those changes belong with #110048's coverage rather than here.

signal.title: Fix logical error in optimize_or_like_chain with aggregate/window function on LIKE LHS
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a logical error (`Function node with name '...' is not resolved as ordinary function`) that could occur with `optimize_or_like_chain` enabled when an aggregate or window function appeared on the left-hand side of a `LIKE`/`ILIKE`/`match` inside an `OR` chain. ### Description Found by the BuzzHouse fuzzer (STID 3477-117d) on [this CI run](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107567&sha=16ccfffe167f14e51996ce4ec16384f92e4d15d0&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_msan%29). Not caused by that PR — it is a trunk analyzer bug the fuzzer happened to surface there. `isExpressionNonDeterministic` in `ConvertOrLikeChainPass` guarded its `getFunctionOrThrow()` call with `FunctionNode::isResolved()`. `isResolved()` returns true for aggregate and window functions too (it only checks that the function pointer is set), but `getFunctionOrThrow()` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` when the function kind is not `ORDINARY`. So a resolved aggregate (e.g. `count()`) or window function nested under a `LIKE` argument in an `OR` chain tripped the assertion — an exception in release builds, an abort in debug/sanitizer builds. Fix: guard with `isOrdinaryFunction()` instead, matching the existing correct guard in `PlannerExpressionAnalysis`. Aggregate/window functions are never non-deterministic-in-scope-of-query at this point, so recursing into their children is sufficient. Minimal reproducer (aborts before the fix on a debug build): ```sql SET optimize_or_like_chain = 1; SELECT toString(count()) LIKE '%1%' OR toString(count()) LIKE '%2%' FROM numbers(3); ``` Covered by `tests/queries/0_stateless/04545_optimize_or_like_chain_aggregate_lhs.sql` (aggregate and window variants, plus an ordinary-function control that must still collapse). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110641&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110641](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110641+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Promote exponentialTimeDecayed window-functions to aggregate-functions
signal.text: ## Motivation `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` already exist and are documented as aggregate functions, but their current implementation is a special window-function implementation in `WindowTransform`. They do not provide mergeable aggregate states that can be persisted and combined with aggregate combinators such as `-State` and `-Merge`. This prevents incremental time-decayed aggregation in engines such as `AggregatingMergeTree`: data has to be evaluated through the window path instead of being aggregated independently in multiple batches and merged later. This PR adds regular, mergeable aggregate implementations for those three names while preserving the existing window implementation and its behavior. ## What changes For the regular aggregate form, each state keeps the weighted sum and sum of weights at the greatest timestamp observed by that state, plus that timestamp. When a row or another state has an older anchor, it is moved to the newer anchor with: `exp((older_time - newer_time) / decay_length)` The existing semantics are unchanged: `decay_length` is the interval after which a contribution has weight `1/e`. It is not a half-life. With the default `exponential_time_decay_aggregate_function_calculation_budget = 0`, the state representation makes independently built states mergeable with the same calculation. Input rows do not need to be timestamp ordered, and different row orders and batch distributions produce the same mathematical result subject to normal `Float64` rounding. A positive calculation budget opts into approximate aggregation using calculation index timestamps. For sums, the index is the time when the absolute contribution or state reaches unit magnitude; counts use the corresponding total-weight index; averages consider both numerator and denominator indexes. A state more than the configured number of decay lengths behind the dominant state is discarded before evaluating `exp`. This makes the cutoff depend on remaining significance rather than source age. Approximate results near the cutoff can depend on row order or merge grouping, and signed sums that nearly cancel can have larger relative error. The aggregate forms accept numeric timestamps, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64`. ### Finalized decaying values The sum and count aggregate forms return the experimental parameterized type: `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` The decay length is part of the type. Its tuple-compatible storage is canonicalized as `(sign, signed_unit_time, decay_length)`, where `unit_time = anchor_time + decay_length * ln(abs(value))` is the timestamp at which the curve has unit magnitude and `signed_unit_time = sign * unit_time`. Zero has the canonical form `(0, 0, decay_length)`. This representation makes native sorting and relative comparisons match the curve values at any common timestamp for values with the same decay length. Comparisons across different decay lengths are rejected. The redundant decay-length marker is checked against the type parameter when a value is evaluated or combined, preventing incompatible values from being silently mixed through layout-compatible custom-tuple paths. Values can be constructed/aggregated with: `exponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)(value, time)` A finalized decaying value can be aggregated again without repeating the decay length: `exponentialTimeDecayedSum(decaying_value)` When the input is `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)`, the decay length is inferred from its type and the result has the same parameterized type. This gives the closure property required by `SimpleAggregateFunction`, so it can be stored directly in `AggregatingMergeTree`: ```sql CREATE TABLE decaying ( key UInt64, value SimpleAggregateFunction( exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(60)) ) ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree ORDER BY key; ``` The scalar helpers are: - `exponentialTimeDecayingValueAt(value, target_time)` — evaluate the same exponential curve before, at, or after its anchor, including at `now()` / `now64()`; - `exponentialTimeDecayingDecayLength(value)` — read the decay length encoded in the type; - `exponentialTimeDecayingAdd(a, b)` — combine two values at their greatest anchor. The `+` operator uses the same addition logic for two decaying values. Different decay lengths are rejected. `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg` continues to return `Float64`. All new regular-aggregate and decaying-value behavior is experimental and disabled by default behind `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. ## Effect on the existing window functions The existing window-function implementation remains in place. Window calls continue to use the previous frame-based implementation, retain their `Float64` result, and do not require `allow_experimental_time_decay_aggregate_functions`. This PR also corrects the function documentation to consistently call the parameter `decay_length` and describe the existing `1/e` decay semantics. ## Correctness and tests Stateless tests cover: - regular aggregation and `-State` / `-Merge`; - direct aggregation of finalized `ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length)` values; - direct `SimpleAggregateFunction(exponentialTimeDecayedSum, ExponentialTimeDecayingFloat64(decay_length))` storage and merging in `AggregatingMergeTree`; - different input orders and batch distributions, including reproducibly generated randomized inputs; - numeric, `DateTime`, and `DateTime64` time arguments; - the experimental setting in enabled and disabled forms; - forward and backward value evaluation, addition, decay-length lookup, and rejection of inconsistent/mixed decay lengths; - native sorting and all relative comparison operators, including negative, zero, and positive values; - exact-default, bounded-cutoff, and state-merge calculation-budget behavior; - signed values, empty input, nullable paths, canonical reconstruction, and large-time decay/underflow cases. The implementation uses `Float64` accumulation. As with other floating-point reductions, large signed values that nearly cancel can expose order/grouping-dependent rounding. Stronger reproducibility for that case is intentionally left for a separate improvement if feedback shows it is important in practice. ## Benchmark status There are no end-to-end ClickHouse benchmark results yet. The benchmark already posted in the PR discussion is a standalone C++ microbenchmark of the decay formulas. It showed the expected benefit from avoiding redundant `exp` evaluations in the merge/value paths, but it excludes ClickHouse aggregation, column access, serialization, scheduling, and `AggregatingMergeTree` overhead and therefore is not evidence of end-to-end query throughput. An end-to-end benchmark, preferably a ClickHouse performance test covering state creation and state merging, is still pending. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental mergeable `exponentialTimeDecayedSum`, `exponentialTimeDecayedAvg`, and `exponentialTimeDecayedCount` aggregate forms, including a parameterized decaying-value type that can be stored directly with `SimpleAggregateFunction` in `AggregatingMergeTree`, while preserving the existing window-function behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110934&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110934](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110934+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Avoid per-row heap allocations in blocked Myers edit distance
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improved the performance of `levenshteinDistance` (and `editDistance`) for medium-length strings on ARM by avoiding per-row heap allocations in the blocked Myers code path. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106595 Fixes the ARM regression reported in #106595: `string_similarity` query `0` (`SELECT avg(levenshteinDistance(randomString(300), randomString(300))) FROM numbers(10000)`) was about +12.6% slower on Neoverse-V2. Root cause: the blocked Myers path (`BlockMyersEditDistance`, used for byte needles of 257..8192 bytes) allocated its per-row scratch buffers on the heap once per row through `VectorWithMemoryTracking`: the pattern-mask table `tbl` and the `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` bit vectors. Each allocation pairs a `malloc`/`free` with a `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomic update. On ARM those atomic updates are comparatively expensive, so this per-row churn showed up as the regression. Only this path was affected: the single-word Myers widths (`ByteEditDistanceMyersImpl`, needles up to 256 bytes) already use fixed stack scratch, which is why the other `string_similarity` queries did not regress. Fix: hold the per-row buffers in `PODArrayWithStackMemory`. It keeps an allocation up to its inline capacity in an inline buffer (no heap allocation, no `CurrentMemoryTracker` atomics) and transparently spills to a tracked allocation above it. The per-row allocation is therefore eliminated across each buffer's inline range, and the buffer management is a single idiomatic type instead of a hand-rolled stack-array + tracked-vector + raw-pointer split (suggested by @ nikitamikhaylov). The inline range differs per buffer because their shapes differ: - `VP`/`VN`/`HP`/`HN`/`D0` hold one `Word` per block (1 KB each), so a 128-block inline buffer covers the full 8192-byte blocked-Myers range. - `tbl` is the ASCII pattern table, `256 * num_blocks` words (one row per byte value), so it is 256x larger per block. Its inline buffer covers needles up to 8 blocks (512 bytes, 16 KB); a full-range inline table would be about 256 KB, so longer needles transparently spill `tbl` to a tracked allocation while the bit vectors stay inline. The reported regression (300-byte needles, 5 blocks) is fully on the inline path for every buffer. Correctness: distances are unchanged. `02884_string_distance_function`, `03369_function_arrayLevenshtein` and `04125_array_levenshtein_types` pass, and a differential check of `editDistance` and `editDistanceUTF8` against a brute-force DP reference (1392 random pairs) matches exactly, including the block and inline/spill boundary lengths (64/128/192/256/512/8192). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Bound submodule cache population so it cannot kill the Config Workflow job
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114811 `Config Workflow` computes the workflow matrix, so when it dies no build and no test job is scheduled. On a submodule cache miss it clones 141 submodules inside its own `timeout=600` budget, and when that does not finish praktika SIGTERMs the job, silently dropping the matrix: the public `26.5` run at `f724d2da9360` recorded 4 checks against 102-155 on healthy commits, and the run still looks finished because `Finish Workflow` reports success afterwards. 7 occurrences over 7 refs in 30 days, including a release branch and three backport PRs. This bounds the clone with `timeout -s KILL` at 600s, above p99 494.5s and the slowest population that currently succeeds (517s), and raises the job cap to `SUBMODULE_CACHE_POPULATE_TIMEOUT_SEC + 600`, 1200s by default, above the 828s worst case (600 clone + 44 tar and upload + 184 rest of the job). Deriving the cap keeps it above the step bound under a per-repository override; were the two equal the job watchdog would fire first. A test pins that ordering. Per @ maxknv's review the step now fails when the cache cannot be populated, instead of reporting `OK` and accepting a miss. Accepting it only degrades cleanly if every dependant can run its own `git submodule update`; dependants clone unauthenticated while this path can use the App installation token, so under `ENABLE_SUBMODULE_CLONE_AUTH` a private submodule is unreachable to them and continuing would schedule checkout failures whose cause is no longer visible. The bound is what makes the timeout reportable: a job-level SIGTERM leaves no result at all. `retries` is dropped because `Shell.check` applies `timeout` per retry, not as a total. Verified by driving the real function both ways: an exhausted budget fails with the hash unset and nothing uploaded, a generous one still populates the cache. YAML regeneration is unchanged.

signal.title: Fix a wedged mutation after a patch-mode lightweight delete
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115570 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` (`Not found column _row_exists in block`) that permanently blocked all further mutations of a `MergeTree` table after a lightweight `DELETE` run with `lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'` was followed by a heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` and then by another mutation rewriting all columns. Closes #115570. ### Description Closes #115570. A lightweight `DELETE` in patch mode supplies `_row_exists` from a patch part, not from the source part's own columns, so `MutateTask` synthesizes a `READ_COLUMN{read_for_patch = true}` command for it. For a mutation that rewrites all columns, `MutationsInterpreter` correctly omits the mask from its output header: that mutation applies the mask on read and physically drops the masked rows, so the new part must not carry a mask. `getColumnsForNewDataPart` disagreed with it. Its `_row_exists` entry derived the answer from a command proxy, which is true for that synthetic command, so the mask was added to the new part's column list while the pipeline block did not contain it. The part writer enumerates the column list and looks each name up in the block, so it threw on the first write and the mutation was re-queued forever. Every later mutation queued behind it, leaving the table unmutable until `KILL MUTATION`. `_row_exists` was the only entry in that loop asking a command proxy. Its siblings `_block_number` and `_block_offset` already ask the pipeline header, and two other sites in this file already treat the header as the mask authority, so I made `_row_exists` ask it too. The second disjunct is kept: it preserves an existing on-disk mask for a partial rewrite. I validated by row-set equality against `lightweight_delete_mode = 'alter_update'`, the mode that does not wedge, rather than by the exception disappearing: same rows, same checksum, same per-part mask layout. A partial `ALTER UPDATE` still materializes the mask and hides the deleted rows, so no lightweight-deleted row is resurrected. All three commands that rewrite all columns (`DELETE`, `APPLY DELETED MASK`, `REWRITE PARTS`) reproduce and are fixed. Not addressed here: a deterministically failing mutation is still re-queued indefinitely. That is a separate retry policy question, and fixing the exception removes the wedge. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115665&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115665](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115665+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Switch the default compression to ZSTD(3) for table data and network
signal.text: Switch the default compression in ClickHouse from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`, for both on-disk table data and network communication. ### Motivation `LZ4` has been the default for a long time and optimizes for speed, but `ZSTD(3)` gives substantially better compression ratios at a still-modest CPU cost, reducing both storage footprint and network traffic out of the box. ClickHouse Cloud already uses a stronger default; this aligns the self-managed defaults. ### What changes - **On-disk table data.** `CompressionCodecFactory::getDefaultCodec` now returns `ZSTD(3)` instead of `LZ4`. For `MergeTree` column data the built-in default is *size-aware*: when a column specifies no codec and no `<compression>` server-config case matches, `CompressionCodecSelector::choose` uses the faster `LZ4` for parts smaller than 100 MB and `ZSTD(3)` for larger parts, so freshly inserted data starts as `LZ4` and the bigger parts produced by background merges switch to `ZSTD(3)`. The direct `getDefaultCodec` users — the `Log` family, part checksums, the HTTP `compress=1` output, the `StripeLog` data stream, and the persistent `Set`/`Join` files — are not size-aware and switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. External temporary (spill) files are unaffected: they keep their own `temporary_files_codec` default (`LZ4`). - **Network.** The defaults of `network_compression_method` (`LZ4` → `ZSTD`) and `network_zstd_compression_level` (`1` → `3`) are changed, so the native client/server and Distributed (server/server) protocol uses `ZSTD(3)` by default. The changes are recorded in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so the `compatibility` setting restores the previous behavior for these paths. The distributed-query streaming exchange (`StreamingExchangeSink`) does not read `network_compression_method` and always uses the server default codec; this is safe because each frame is self-describing (the receiver auto-detects the codec) and the exchange is a transient, same-version channel — `StreamingExchangeProtocol` rejects peers on a different protocol version, so a stream is never read back by a node expecting a different codec. - **Upgrade safety.** The append-only `Log`/`TinyLog`/`StripeLog` engines resolve the default codec at write time, so a table written before the upgrade (`LZ4`) and appended to after it (`ZSTD(3)`) ends up with mixed-codec blocks in one file. Their readers now pass `allow_different_codecs = true` (as the `MergeTree` reader already does) so such files still read back correctly. The legacy custom-frame Keeper snapshot format (`compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format = false`) is pinned to `LZ4` so it stays the documented format. Columns, tables, and connections that specify a codec or method explicitly are unaffected — with one exception: streams written through the built-in default codec directly, which ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config. The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files (written by `SetOrJoinSink` and `StorageJoin::mutate` through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with no codec), and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`, via `MergeTreeDataPartChecksums::write`) always follow the new default; see the changelog entry below for the per-path rollback. ### Validation Built locally and verified against the new binary: - A `MergeTree` table created with no explicit codec follows the size-aware default: small parts report `LZ4` and parts larger than 100 MB report `ZSTD(3)` as their `default_compression_codec` in `system.parts`. Direct `getDefaultCodec` streams (e.g. `StripeLog`) report `ZSTD(3)` regardless of size. - `system.settings` shows `network_compression_method = ZSTD` and `network_zstd_compression_level = 3`. - End-to-end `SELECT`/`INSERT` over the native protocol with default (now `ZSTD`) network compression work; all of `LZ4`/`lz4hc`/`zstd`/`none` still work and an invalid method still errors with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`. - The `02995_new_settings_history` consistency check passes (both setting changes are recorded). - The on-disk byte-dump tests (`02047_log_family_*_data_file_dumps`) were regenerated for the new default: `Log`/`TinyLog` keep `LZ4`-pinned columns, while `StripeLog`'s shared `data.bin`/`index.mrk` reflect the `ZSTD(3)` default (it uses `getDefaultCodec` and ignores the per-column codec). Size-sensitive stateless and integration tests that assert compressed byte sizes were pinned back to `LZ4` (cache segment sizes, distributed-batch corruption offsets, full-disk thresholds, frozen-part checksums). The CI performance comparison does **not** measure this tradeoff: the harness pins the built-in default codec to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/config.d/compression.xml`) and `network_compression_method` to `LZ4` (`tests/performance/scripts/config/users.d/perf-comparison-tweaks-users.xml`) on *both* the reference and the tested server, deliberately, so the report measures query logic rather than drowning in expected codec regressions. It therefore serves only as a regression filter for the non-codec parts of this change; the storage/network-vs-CPU tradeoff of `LZ4` → `ZSTD(3)` itself is a well-known property of the two codecs and is not measured by this pull request's CI. Documentation updated accordingly, including the `Native` format and protocol specifications and the `<compression>` config examples. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The default compression method is changed from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. For client/server and server/server network communication it switches uniformly to `ZSTD(3)`. For on-disk table data, `MergeTree` column data now uses a size-aware built-in default — parts smaller than 100 MB use `LZ4` and larger parts use `ZSTD(3)` — while the direct built-in-default streams (the `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and part checksums) switch uniformly from `LZ4` to `ZSTD(3)`. This improves compression ratios and reduces storage and network usage out of the box, at a modest increase in CPU usage. None of the on-disk or HTTP paths are controlled by `compatibility`; the previous behavior can be restored per path as follows. For client/server and Distributed network compression, use the `compatibility` setting (or set `network_compression_method = 'LZ4'`). For `MergeTree` column data, set a column/table `CODEC(LZ4)` or configure the server `<compression>` default to `LZ4`. For the `Log`/`TinyLog` engines, set a column `CODEC(LZ4)` (their default does not consult the `<compression>` config). The `StripeLog` data stream, the persistent `Set`/`Join` backup files, the HTTP `compress=1` framed output, and `MergeTree` auxiliary streams such as part checksums (`checksums.txt`) use the built-in default codec directly — they ignore per-column codecs and the `<compression>` config — so they always use the new `ZSTD(3)` default and have no runtime rollback; reading stays correct because every compressed frame is self-describing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108786&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108786](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108786+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Query cache on disk, backed by the filesystem cache
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361 The query cache can now additionally store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache (an entry of the `filesystem_caches` section of the server configuration), selected per query with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`. Compared to the in-memory query cache, this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Design, following the RFC in the issue: - The entries are ordinary filesystem cache entries, indistinguishable from other data in the same filesystem cache: they are not held from deletion, they are evicted by the same rules, and there are no specific limits on their total size or number other than the limits of the filesystem cache itself. The keys are hashed with a salt so that they cannot intersect with other keys in the filesystem cache. - No extra in-memory state is kept: all metadata needed to validate an entry (TTL, user id, roles, the shared flag) is serialized into the entry itself, followed by the result payload in `Native` format, compressed with the codec from the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_codec` (default `ZSTD(3)`; reading is independent of the setting because the compressed frames are self-describing). - The on-disk cache works independently of the in-memory cache and can separately be enabled for reads and/or writes with the new settings `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk` and `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk` (both `true` by default, activated by setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`). If both caches are enabled for reads, the lookup is attempted first from memory and only on a miss from disk. If both caches are enabled for writes, the result is written to both. A result served from memory is not written to disk. - A stale (expired TTL), partially evicted, corrupt, or inaccessible (another user's non-shared) entry is treated as a cache miss; stale entries are overwritten on the next write. - Introspection of the on-disk entries in `system.query_cache` is out of scope, per the issue. New profile events: `QueryCacheOnDiskHits`, `QueryCacheOnDiskMisses`, `QueryCacheOnDiskReadBytes`, `QueryCacheOnDiskWrittenBytes`. Tests: `05019_query_cache_on_disk_local` proves persistence across process restarts (separate `clickhouse-local` invocations sharing one filesystem cache directory, including a cached non-deterministic result, TTL expiry, and disabled reads); `05020_query_cache_on_disk` covers the server path with user isolation, sharing via `query_cache_share_between_users`, and error cases (unknown cache name, invalid codec). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The query cache can now store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache: this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Select the filesystem cache with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`; see also the new settings `query_cache_on_disk_codec`, `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk`, and `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk`. Closes [#115361](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115382&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115382](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115382+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: CI: refuse LLVM coverage verdicts on incomplete measurements, make coverage profiles kill-safe
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The `LLVM Coverage` gate fails a PR when total line coverage drops more than 0.3 pp below the master baseline. Both totals are merged from 21 per-shard `.profdata` artifacts that are deliberately `optional=True`, and nothing verified that either side had all of them. A shard profile can vanish while every check stays green (a corrupt `.profraw` aborts the producer merge, `-failure-mode=warn` silently discards a corrupt input, a zero-length `.profraw` is accepted silently). Both error directions occur: - A short PR side fails an unrelated PR. Observed twice in the last 60 days, both times the same missing file `it-amd_llvm_coverage_4_8.profdata` with all 21 shard jobs green: [PR 110186](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110186&sha=0b33f54bc8089ea3560397c589e93dc6aec92d47&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage) ("dropped 0.50 pp" on a 102-line PR) and [PR 105844](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105844&sha=66107bb44ab45a490e839225eb096e46204e5e86&name_0=PR&name_1=LLVM%20Coverage). - A short master run writes a low baseline into the CI DB, so a later real regression passes. This direction produces a PASS and is invisible in any failure count. The invariant established here: a verdict comes only from two complete measurements. - Every coverage producer (functional, integration, unit) names its profile after its own artifact (`<artifact>.profdata`), so the filename carries the shard identity. Producer merges use `--failure-mode=any` and skip zero-length `.profraw` inputs: a shard with invalid data publishes nothing instead of a silently short profile. Artifacts stay `optional=True`, so a missing profile never reddens a green test job. - The `LLVM Coverage` job compares the expected file set against what arrived and merges an explicit file list instead of a `*.profdata` glob. On a missing or invalid shard it reports `SKIPPED` naming the shard, and withholds every comparative output: no verdict, no GitHub comment, no `llvm_coverage.info` artifact, no CI DB row. A genuine tooling failure (report generation) still stays RED. - Baseline completeness needs no metadata: the diff script already selects the first master ancestor that has an `llvm_coverage.info`, and after this change such an `.info` exists only for complete runs. (Transitional: for the first ~30 master commits after merge, pre-change ancestors are still selectable, which is exactly today's behaviour.) - Under coverage, the integration sequential test phase runs regardless of how many parallel tests failed (`MAX_FAILS_BEFORE_DROP`), so a green shard cannot silently publish a profile that is short by the whole sequential phase. - Root cause of the recurring shard 4/8 loss: `LLVM_PROFILE_FILE` in merge mode writes the profile only at process exit, and integration tests `SIGKILL` servers on purpose; a kill inside that multi-second write leaves a half-written `.profraw` whose header makes `llvm-profdata` abort with `LLVM ERROR: out of memory` ([llvm/llvm-project#50970](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/50970), open since 2021). Coverage builds now compile with `-mllvm -runtime-counter-relocation` and run with `%c` (continuous mode): the counters are memory-mapped into the profile, which is valid at every instant, so a kill at any moment loses nothing and corrupts nothing. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112832, which establishes the same invariant via a completeness sidecar published next to `llvm_coverage.info`, a manifest fingerprint, and a two-pass baseline selector. Withholding the `.info` on incomplete runs makes the sidecar unnecessary, and the profile naming plus set check shrink to ~40 lines. Accepted residuals of the simpler design: a session-timeout-truncated shard can still publish a valid short profile, and on the rare day the coverage artifact manifest itself changes, verdicts are unreliable until master republishes. Not covered here (pre-existing, unchanged): the diagnostics of the diff-report script, addressed separately by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115225. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115623&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115623](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115623+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/metadata
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Adds Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` support for `TimeSeries` tables.** ### Description This adds the Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` endpoint backed by the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table. The endpoint returns the metric type, help text, and unit for each metadata object in the format expected by Prometheus-compatible clients. ### Why this matters - **Prometheus-compatible tools** use `/api/v1/metadata` to discover **metric types, help text, and units**. - Without this endpoint, clients need separate configuration or lose this metadata when using ClickHouse as a Prometheus-compatible endpoint. - The `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table remains the **source of truth** for this metadata. Supported parameters: - `metric` filters the response to one metric family. - `limit` limits the number of metric families. `limit=0` returns no families. - `limit_per_metric` limits the number of unique metadata objects returned for each family. Zero and negative values mean no per-family limit. Other details: - Metadata objects are unique for each metric family and returned in a stable order. - `FINAL` is used whenever the Metrics target supports it, including wrapped targets. If a remote replica rejects `FINAL` before response output starts, the metadata query retries without it. - Metadata parameters stay endpoint-local and are not treated as ClickHouse settings. - The generated query uses the normal query pipeline and is recorded in `query_log`. - Access to the configured `TimeSeries` table and related table functions is checked. - The endpoint works with dedicated handlers and the combined `/api/v1` handler. - TimeSeries target reads carry the original user and exact active-role snapshot across shards, even when `push_external_roles_in_interserver_queries=0`. - Authenticated target scopes always contain fully qualified physical `{database, table}` names. A missing database on a Distributed target is resolved before authentication, and empty or malformed scopes are rejected. - `StorageTimeSeriesTargetProxy` keeps transaction, streaming, and MergeTree capabilities visible to the planner. Planner checks also unwrap proxies so Distributed shard pruning and parallel-replica analysis continue to work. - `StorageTableProxy` remains transparent for table-function INSERT validation. Forwarding proxies are still rejected, and Buffer target-function writes fail explicitly because their destination would require separate write authorization. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - unique metadata across multiple parts and stable results after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`. - JSON escaping for quotes, backslashes, newlines, tabs, and Unicode. - metric filtering, both limit parameters, invalid limit values, and high-cardinality metadata. - primary-key filtering, aliases, `prefer_column_name_to_alias`, and wrapped `FINAL` targets. - query logging, endpoint and table-function access control, and unknown endpoint handling. - fully qualified target scopes and role propagation with both values of `push_external_roles_in_interserver_queries`. - lazy table proxies and the explicit Buffer target-function INSERT error. - GET/HEAD, unsupported methods, dedicated handlers, and the combined `/api/v1` handler. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation was added to the Prometheus protocols page. It covers the handler configuration and supported parameters. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114038&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114038](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114038+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support `Merge` tables with plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/67770 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972 Lets a `Merge` table be read with parallel replicas, implemented on top of the plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`). `ReadFromMerge` is opaque to the parallel-replicas plan transformation: it unites the pipelines of its per-table subplans instead of their plans, so the underlying `MergeTree` reads do not exist yet while the plan is transformed. An eligible `ReadFromMerge` is therefore expanded into a plan-level `UnionStep` over those child reads, right before the reads to distribute are collected. A `Merge` then has exactly the shape the transformation already distributes - a union of `MergeTree` reads - so the reads are coordinated across the replicas, and the steps above the `Merge` (aggregation, joins) are distributed as well, without any `Merge`-specific code in the coordinator, in the serialization or in the local plan. The expansion is off by default, gated by the new setting `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, and takes effect only together with `parallel_replicas_plan_based`. A `Merge` is read by a single replica when one of its children is not a plain `MergeTree` read, when the read is `FINAL`, or when no table matches its regexp. This is an alternative to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110972, which implements the same feature on the legacy (query-tree-based) path. There, the query text is reshipped and every replica re-analyzes it, which needs a fail-close handshake (`parallel_replicas_designated_table`, `_freshness_checked_tables`, `_merge_child_tables`) to guard against the set of underlying tables differing across replicas or changing between planning and reading. The plan-based path ships a serialized plan fragment with the tables already resolved, so none of that is needed. Tests: three new stateless tests - the core feature and its negative cases (`04907`), the query shapes a `Merge` can be read with, including the `merge` table function, a filter on the `_table` virtual column and reading in order with a limit (`04908`), and `Merge` tables inside JOINs on either side of the join (`04909`). Each of them checks the results against non-parallel execution and asserts through the plan how the query was distributed. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A `Merge` table can now be read with parallel replicas: the reads from the underlying `MergeTree` tables are coordinated across the replicas, and the aggregations and joins above them are distributed too. Enabled by the new setting `parallel_replicas_allow_merge_tables`, which takes effect together with `parallel_replicas_plan_based`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115001&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115001](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115001+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix PromQL timestamp and duration overflow at Int64 boundary
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reject PromQL timestamps and durations that exceed the Int64 range.** ### Summary PromQL timestamps and durations can be passed as floating-point values. ClickHouse scales them and converts them to Int64. `INT64_MAX` is rounded to `2^63` when represented as `Float64`. The previous upper-bound check used `>` and allowed that value to reach the conversion even though `2^63` is outside the Int64 range. Converting it to Int64 is undefined behavior. The upper-bound check now rejects equality as well. ### Tests - Add a timestamp regression for the finite floating-point boundary. - Add a duration regression for the same boundary. - Compile the changed C++ translation unit. - Run `git diff --check`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115682&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115682](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115682+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject truncated/incomplete AI text function responses
signal.text: The AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) could silently return a truncated answer. When a provider stops early — most commonly by hitting the `max_tokens` limit — it reports this in the response, but the shared base class `FunctionBaseAI` never inspected the signal and returned whatever partial text came back. For example, `aiGenerate('Write three sentences about the ocean.', map(..., 'max_tokens', '5'))` returned the fragment `The ocean covers more than` with no error. This change normalizes each provider's native stop reason (OpenAI `finish_reason`, Anthropic `stop_reason`) into a canonical `FinishReason` enum, so the base class can make a single completeness decision without knowing the provider dialect: - `Truncated` (token/context limit) → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_TRUNCATED`. - `ContentFilter` (OpenAI `content_filter`, Anthropic `refusal`) and `ToolCall` → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_INCOMPLETE`. - `Complete` (natural end, or a caller stop sequence such as Anthropic `stop_sequence`) and `Unknown` (unrecognized reason) are accepted, so benign non-`stop` reasons are not misclassified as truncation. The rejection is thrown inside the existing per-row `try`, so it is non-retriable (retrying would hit the same limit) and honors `ai_function_throw_on_error`: with `1` the exception propagates; with `0` the row becomes the column default. `aiEmbed` is unaffected (embeddings have no finish reason). Integration tests in `test_ai_functions` cover truncation (throw + graceful), content-filter, an accepted unknown reason, and the Anthropic `stop_sequence` (must not throw) and `max_tokens` (must throw) cases. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) now reject truncated or otherwise incomplete provider responses (e.g. when the model hits the `max_tokens` limit) instead of silently returning partial output. Behavior follows the `ai_function_throw_on_error` setting. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111830&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111830](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111830+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Mongo queries: keep whole documents in a JSON column
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58394 Adds two ways to run MongoDB queries against ClickHouse: - a **wire protocol endpoint** (`mongo_port`), so MongoDB drivers and tools such as `pymongo` and `mongosh` can connect to ClickHouse as if it were a MongoDB server; - a **query dialect** (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`), so MongoDB shell syntax can be sent over the usual ClickHouse interfaces. This continues @scanhex12's https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 - it holds all of its commits - and changes how a collection is stored, which is what the review of that pull request asked for (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493#discussion_r3771132310): a collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in one `JSON` column rather than a column inferred per field of the first document. ```sql CREATE TABLE db.users (`_id` String, `json` JSON) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY `_id` ``` The document goes into the `JSON` column, whose paths are its fields, and its object id into the `_id` column, which is the primary key. A document may then hold a field that no document before it had, may leave out a field another one has, and `$exists` answers what it means. A table that was created in ClickHouse keeps its own columns, and a field of a query names the column of the same name there, so an application can also be pointed at a table that already holds the data. A read of the documents as they are stored selects them next to the types of their paths, so a date reads back as a BSON date and an integer as an `int32`/`int64` of its width. The integration tests of `test_mongo_protocol` say what each shape answers now - a collection of documents where that is what is tested, a table created in ClickHouse where the test is about a column - and 75/75 of them pass. **This is a draft** because a few things of a document collection are an explicit error rather than an answer: an `update` of it, an index over a path, the `mongo` dialect over it, the element-wise match of an array by equality or `$in`, `$unwind` of a path, and the accumulators that read a number. They are the next commits; every one of them is listed in `docs/en/interfaces/mongo.md` and pinned by a test in the meantime. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol endpoint (the `mongo_port` server setting) and a MongoDB query dialect (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`) for basic collection operations. A collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in a `JSON` column. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114577&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114577](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114577+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
