signal.title: Fix Arrow export of JSON, Dynamic, QBit and AggregateFunction
signal.text:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115023 Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/91170 The `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types_as_binary` fallback wrote a column with no first-class Arrow mapping by calling `IColumn::getDataAt` per row. That method exposes a column's contiguous in-memory bytes, which most of the types reaching the fallback do not have: - `ColumnObject` (`JSON`), `ColumnVariant` (hence `ColumnDynamic`) and `ColumnQBit` throw `Method getDataAt is not supported`, so `SELECT ... FORMAT Arrow` failed on them — after the schema message had already been written, leaving the client with a truncated stream; - `ColumnAggregateFunction::getDataAt` returns the `AggregateDataPtr` itself, so exporting an aggregate state silently wrote raw heap addresses instead of the state, both corrupting the data and disclosing server addresses. Before the fallback existed these types were rejected with a clear `UNKNOWN_TYPE`, so both are regressions introduced together with the setting: ``` -- 26.4, before #91170 SELECT '{"a":1}'::JSON FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 50. The type 'JSON' of a column 'j' is not supported for conversion into Arrow data format. (UNKNOWN_TYPE) SELECT sumState(number) FROM numbers(3) FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 50. The type 'AggregateFunction(sum, UInt64)' ... (UNKNOWN_TYPE) -- 26.5 .. 26.8 SELECT '{"a":1}'::JSON FORMAT Arrow; -- Code: 48. Method getDataAt is not supported for Object(max_dynamic_paths=1024, max_dynamic_types=32). (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) SELECT sumState(number) FROM numbers(3) FORMAT Arrow; -- succeeds, writes 00D0A9C9D37F0000 ``` The fallback now serializes each value through `ISerialization`, whose `serializeText`/`serializeBinary` are pure virtual and therefore defined for every type, so the "do not fail a `SELECT *`" property that motivated the setting holds by construction instead of depending on an unrelated method's implementation status. The aggregate state written in binary mode is the `RowBinary` encoding and deserializes back into the original `AggregateFunction` type. `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types` (`throw` / `text` / `binary`) replaces the boolean, adding a `text` mode that writes what `CAST(col AS String)` would produce — useful for the BI clients that drive `SELECT *` over Arrow Flight SQL, and the workaround users had to apply by hand for `JSON`. Its default, `binary`, is the previous behavior, and its `SettingsChangesHistory` entry has identical previous and new values so `compatibility` never marks it changed. The boolean keeps working with full effect (`0` means `throw`, `1` means `binary`) and is only consulted while the new setting is left at its default, so an explicit mode wins whichever order the two are set in. Both writers — the native Arrow IPC one behind `FORMAT Arrow`/`ArrowStream` and the Apache-Arrow-library one behind Arrow Flight SQL — make the accept/reject decision in the schema converter, before the schema message is written, so a rejected type can no longer abort a stream whose schema the reader has already accepted. Both serialize the values with the query's own `FormatSettings`, so a setting the serialization depends on (`output_format_binary_write_json_as_string`, `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers`, …) produces the same payload whichever writer serves the query. An opaque column is tagged in both writers with the `clickhouse.opaque` Arrow extension name and the original ClickHouse type name in `ARROW:extension:metadata`, so a consumer can tell it apart from a genuine string or binary column. Per the Arrow extension-type convention a reader that does not know the extension name ignores the metadata and sees the plain storage type, so no existing consumer changes behavior. `StorageArrowFlight::ArrowFlightSink` built its converter settings from scratch and never consulted the setting, so it always used the struct default. It now resolves the mode from the query context like the other Arrow Flight call sites, which makes `INSERT INTO ... ENGINE = ArrowFlight` of an `AggregateFunction` column follow the setting; `throw` reproduces the previous behavior exactly. `JSON` and `Dynamic` cannot reach that sink, because the storage rejects a dynamic-structure column when the table is created and the table function takes its header from the remote schema. Verified against a local ClickHouse Arrow Flight server as well as `FORMAT Arrow`: `SELECT *` over a table with `JSON` and `AggregateFunction` columns returns them as `clickhouse.opaque`-tagged `binary` fields carrying the ClickHouse type name, with a neighbouring `String` column left untagged; `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types = 'text'` switches them to tagged `string` fields holding the text; and the payloads match the native writer byte for byte under the serialization settings above. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `SELECT ... FORMAT Arrow` failing with `Method getDataAt is not supported` for `JSON`, `Dynamic` and `QBit` columns, and silently exporting heap addresses instead of the aggregate state for `AggregateFunction` columns. Added the `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types` setting (`throw` / `text` / `binary`, default `binary`) which supersedes `output_format_arrow_unsupported_types_as_binary`.

signal.title: Make a table read by a scalar subquery in a CONSTRAINT a loading dependency
signal.text: Attaching a table analyzes its constraints in `InterpreterCreateQuery::getConstraintsDescription`, and the analysis executes the scalar subqueries of a constraint expression. The tables such a subquery reads were not registered as loading dependencies, because `DDLLoadingDependencyVisitor` only looks at functions, dictionary sources and the storage definition. Nothing prevented dropping such a table, and the server did not start afterwards - attaching the dependent table threw `UNKNOWN_TABLE` and loading the metadata failed: ```sql CREATE TABLE t1 (id UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); CREATE TABLE t2 (conversation UInt64, CONSTRAINT c CHECK (SELECT id FROM t1 LIMIT 15) IN (conversation)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); DROP TABLE t1; -- accepted, and the server cannot start anymore ``` The referential dependency was recorded, since `DDLDependencyVisitor` visits `ASTTableExpression`, so `check_referential_table_dependencies = 1` rejected the `DROP`. But that setting is off by default, and it is the loading graph that the default `check_table_dependencies` check and the `DROP DATABASE` drop order (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97057) use. A constraint declaration is now visited, and the tables of every subquery that the analysis executes are added to the loading dependencies. Subqueries which the analysis does not execute - the right argument of `IN` and the argument of `exists`, see `ExecuteScalarSubqueriesMatcher::visit` - are skipped, because what they read is needed only when the constraint is checked, not to attach the table. That keeps `02916_joinget_dependency`-style patterns working, in particular `02841_not_ready_set_constraints`, which drops the table read by an `x IN (SELECT ...)` constraint on purpose. Seen in CI as a `Cannot start clickhouse-server` stress failure, e.g. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110231&sha=4de836223549fd5224ca017b8c1a28e344ce38e9&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_msan%29 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114918 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87369 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115648 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A table read by a scalar subquery inside a `CONSTRAINT` is now a loading dependency of the table that declares the constraint. Previously such a table could be dropped, after which the server did not start, because attaching the dependent table executes the subquery. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114923&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114923](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114923+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Report an HTTP handler config error as itself, not a listen failure
signal.text: Report an HTTP handler config error as itself, not a listen failure Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114883 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): An invalid `<http_handlers>` configuration is now reported with its own error instead of being wrapped into `NETWORK_ERROR "Listen [host]:port failed"`. Previously, when `listen_try` was in effect, the error was only logged as a warning about `<listen_host>` and the server started without serving HTTP at all. The same applies to the Prometheus listener on `prometheus.port`, to the Keeper control endpoints on `keeper_server.http_control`, and to `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP` in `clickhouse-local`, which blamed `listen_host` and `http_port`. ### Description `Server::createServers` built the HTTP and HTTPS handler factory tree inside the `createServer` callback, whose only error handler is about listen addresses. So a handler-configuration error surfaced as ``` Code: 210. DB::Exception: Listen [0.0.0.0]:8123 failed: Code: 318. DB::Exception: Unknown handler type 'x' in config here: http_handlers.rule.handler.type. (INVALID_CONFIG_PARAMETER) (NETWORK_ERROR) ``` which points at the socket layer instead of the real cause. With `listen_try` it is not reported at all: it becomes a warning advising the operator to change `<listen_host>`, and the server starts without HTTP. `clickhouse-local` reaches the same two exits from `SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP`, naming `listen_host` and `http_port` while both are correct. Handler construction is configuration validation and cannot fail for any socket reason, so I hoisted it above `createServer` at all four sites, behind a port guard matching `createServer`'s own early return, so a server without `http_port` still does not parse `<http_handlers>`. The custom-protocol block a few lines up already does this. `createServer.cpp` is untouched, so a genuine bind failure reports byte-identically before and after, for both `listen_try` values. Worth weighing: a server that today starts silently without HTTP on an invalid handler configuration will now refuse to start. I believe that is the safer direction, but it is a behaviour change. On a runtime reload the update is abandoned with the error reported to the caller, while the process and unrelated listeners keep running; with `listen_try` the reload used to complete and leave the listener silently gone. Every other listener reading a handler section wrapped its factory the same way and is hoisted behind the same guard: the Prometheus listener on `prometheus.port`, and the Keeper control endpoints on `keeper_server.http_control`, in `clickhouse-keeper` and embedded in `clickhouse-server`. That is the whole family. <details> <summary>Test coverage</summary> One integration case per exit of the error handler (plain, and `listen_try`), one for the HTTPS listener, two for the standalone Prometheus listener, one locking each port guard, two for the runtime reload path (HTTP and Prometheus), plus stateless tests covering `clickhouse-local` and `clickhouse-keeper`. Each case reddens if its own half of the fix is reverted. The HTTPS listener has its own textual copy of the construction, so it needs its own case: it configures `https_port` with `http_port` removed, which leaves HTTPS the only reader of `<http_handlers>`. Verified by mutation, restoring the pre-change shape for HTTPS alone reddens that case and no other. The unconfigured-port cases are deliberately not both-directions arms (they pass before the change too, because the parse already sat behind the same condition); deleting a guard makes the matching case fail, verified for the Prometheus one by rebuilding with the guard removed, which refuses startup instead. The reload cases assert on the error returned to the `SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG` caller. `updateServers` reuses `createServers`, so it re-enters the hoisted code; before the change the reload returned success while HTTP, or the Prometheus handler change, was silently dropped. The Prometheus one first requires its listener to be serving, so it cannot pass against a build that never started it. A genuine bind failure on an occupied port, and a valid handler configuration, are the negative controls: both behave identically before and after, in both `listen_try` settings, so the new assertions discriminate the diagnosis rather than merely detecting a refusal to start. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115548&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115548](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115548+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix reading `Arrow` files that validate the arbitrary bytes of unobservable slots
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111996 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111534 The Arrow specification leaves the value bytes of unobservable slots undefined: slots that are null at their own or an ancestor level (a struct's nulls do not have to be repeated in its children's validity), slot ranges no list offset references, and union child slots not selected by their row's type id. The native `Arrow` IPC reader ran value-level validation — the `Date32` range check, dictionary index bounds, `BinaryView` view checks, the raw-byte width sniff for `IPv6` and the big integers — over every slot before applying null maps, so spec-valid files failed to read. It also copied those undefined bytes into the result, so they surfaced as values whenever an ancestor null map is dropped, which is what reading a nullable struct as a plain `Tuple` does. ClickHouse produces such files itself: `Date32` arithmetic does not clamp the stored day number and `nullIf` keeps the original payload under the new null mask, so the writer stores an out-of-range day number under a null slot and the reader then refuses to read it back. ```sql INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('t.arrow', 'Arrow') SELECT nullIf(x, x) AS d FROM (SELECT toDate32('9999-12-31') + 100 AS x); SELECT * FROM file('t.arrow', 'Arrow'); ``` ``` Code: 321. DB::Exception: Arrow IPC date32 value 2932996 is out of the allowed Date32 range [-719528, 2932896] ... (VALUE_IS_OUT_OF_RANGE_OF_DATA_TYPE) -- but should work fine ``` The same failure occurs one level deeper with a nullable struct read as `Nullable(Tuple)` (with `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type`): the child of a NULL struct row can hold garbage while its own validity marks it valid, so only the composed ancestor validity reveals the value is unobservable. Both reading paths are now driven by one composed invisible-rows mask: value-level validation skips those rows, and every leaf decodes them as the type default instead of copying the undefined bytes — including the `fixed_size_binary` leaves the ClickHouse writer uses for `UUID`, `IPv6` and the 128/256-bit integers, and the self-describing Arrow `uuid` extension type. `04513` covers the crafted `pyarrow` files where the garbage is reachable only through composed visibility; `04512` covers the ClickHouse round trip. Two notes on scope: - The first version of this pull request fixed the Apache Arrow library reader as well. That reader was removed from the `Arrow` formats in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111996, so those changes are gone and `input_format_arrow_use_native_reader` no longer selects anything. `ArrowColumnToCHColumn` still validates the bytes of null slots the same way, but it is now reachable only through `ArrowFlight` and DeltaLake, so that is left for a separate change with its own coverage. - Reading a nullable struct as a plain `Tuple` drops the struct null map, and the NULL row's element values now read as type defaults rather than as the payload the producer left behind — `04493` records that (`ORC`, whose null map does reach the tuple elements, shows `NULL`s for the same file, so the defaults are the closer of the two answers). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix reading `Arrow` and `ArrowStream` files that carry arbitrary bytes in unobservable slots: values hidden by null rows (at their own or an ancestor level), unreferenced list ranges and unselected union children are no longer validated and no longer surface as values, but decode as type defaults. Previously such spec-valid files could fail with errors like `VALUE_IS_OUT_OF_RANGE_OF_DATA_TYPE`, including files written by ClickHouse itself. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110531&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110531](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110531+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Perf: format PromQL instant-vector timestamps once per block
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **PromQL instant-vector responses reuse the formatted evaluation timestamp within each result block.** ## What changed - Format the instant-vector timestamp once per result block. - Reuse the serialized timestamp for every returned series in that block. - Keep label and value serialization unchanged. - Keep empty blocks from accessing row zero. ## Why this is safe - Instant-vector finalization requires the start and end times to be equal. - The generated query uses `<start_time> AS timestamp`, so every row has the same timestamp. - The cached text lives only for one result block. - Multi-block responses still format each block independently. - Empty results keep the existing behavior. This removes repeated `getInt()` calls and decimal-to-text formatting from the per-series loop. signal.title: Cross-compile ClickHouse for Windows
signal.text: Draft. Cross-compiles `clickhouse.exe` for `x86_64-w64-windows-gnu` (mingw-w64 + clang + lld → a native PE, no emulation layer and no MSVC licence). The goal is `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` running natively on Windows. **State: it links, it has never been run.** The development host is aarch64 and its Wine has no x86-on-ARM emulator, so everything here is compiled and linked but not executed. That is the next step and needs an x86-64 Windows machine. ``` programs/clickhouse.exe: PE32+ executable for MS Windows 6.00 (console), x86-64 520 MB · imports ADVAPI32, IPHLPAPI, KERNEL32, USER32, WS2_32, dbghelp, msvcrt ``` Every import ships with Windows, so the binary is a single self-contained file. Linux builds and links `clickhouse` unchanged after every commit in the branch. CI builds `clickhouse` for Windows on every pull request, so the port cannot silently regress. ## What is here The runtime (libc++/libc++abi/libunwind with SEH, compiler-rt builtins), 117 contribs behind a self-maintaining CI gate, all of Poco — whose Windows layer had been deleted from this fork and is restored from upstream 1.9.3 — every library under `src`, and `programs`. Roughly 900 of the changed lines are one mechanical class: `std::filesystem::path` used where a `String` is wanted, which compiles on POSIX through an implicit conversion that does not exist on Windows. Implemented natively rather than stubbed, because a client needs them: terminal size and console encoding, raw console mode and keystroke reading, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Break, socket liveness, `statvfs` via `GetDiskFreeSpaceEx`, file mapping, `pread`, per-thread CPU time, `setThreadName`, `isLocalAddress`, `readpassphrase`, and a `WakeupFd` built on a loopback socket pair (a Windows pipe cannot be waited on alongside sockets). Compiled out with the reason recorded at each site, all server-side or POSIX-only: the sampling profiler and signal handlers (Windows reports faults through SEH), `ThreadFuzzer`, the `fork`-based watchdog, `ShellCommand` and everything built on it, the pseudo-terminal features, and the `su`/`docker-init`/`install` tools. ## Known gaps - Not executed, as above. - `-g0` on Windows: a PE image cannot exceed 4 GiB and the DWARF alone is several times that, and PE has no `.gnu_debuglink` equivalent to carry it separately. A crash symbolizes to module and offset, not file and line. - No `Epoll` backend, so nothing that polls sockets through it works yet. - Local syslog, archives (`libarchive` needs a hand-written Windows `config.h`), conditional writes to the local object storage (they need `flock` on a directory and sub-second modification times), and the web terminal report `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. `docs/en/development/build-cross-windows.md` has the build instructions and a per-subsystem inventory of what remains. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112185 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112767 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a cross-compilation target for Windows (`x86_64-w64-windows-gnu`), producing a native `clickhouse.exe`. The build is not yet tested at runtime. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112824&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112824](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112824+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add support for S3Queue mode='exclusive'
signal.text: This patch adds a third mode to the S3Queue engine: `exclusive` mode turns off all file tracking and synchronization in ZooKeeper. S3 file processing will be tracked only locally via in-memory structures of this ClickHouse server process. This mode is meant to support high-throughput, high-volume ingestion scenarios. In our particular case, we have a minio instance on each of our ClickHouse nodes, with S3Queue pointing to 127.0.0.1. Exclusive mode allows ingesting many terabytes of data per day while avoid file framing boundary and buffering issues. (S3 multipart uploads solve the buffering issue for ingestion clients.) We have been running our ClickHouse cluster with these patches for many years with no issues. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Adds support for mode='exclusive' in S3Queue engine, for high-throughput and self-hosted scenarios. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110552&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110552](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110552+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hash the type-derived parameter in the ALP, FPC and GCD codecs
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `ALP`, `FPC` and `GCD` omitting their type-derived parameter from the codec hash. In a Compact part the writer shares one compressed stream per distinct codec hash, so two columns of different value width under the same codec collided and shared one codec object carrying the wrong width. This rejected valid inserts with `CANNOT_COMPRESS` when the widths disagreed, and otherwise compressed one of the columns worse than it should have. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 `MergeTreeDataPartWriterCompact::addStreams` keys compressed-stream reuse on `codec->getHash()` with no key-equality fallback, so a hash collision is an object-identity collision. Three codecs resolve a parameter from the column type, keep it out of the codec description AST, and hash only that AST, so two columns of different width shared one codec object and the loser of the race got the other's width: - `ALP` and `FPC` derive `float_width`. With `Float64` declared first the shared codec carries `float_width = 8`, a `Float32` granule is not a multiple of 8, and `ALP` throws `Code: 270 ... data size 404 is not aligned to 8 (CANNOT_COMPRESS)`. A mixed-width `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)` reaches the same throw, since the codec is resolved per substream. `FPC` ceil-divides instead of throwing, so its half is ratio-only: measured +10.0%. - `GCD` derives `gcd_bytes_size`, so the divisor width depended on declaration order and the ratio suffered. Data round-trips either way, because the width is in the GCD block header. Added on review request so the class stays revertable as one change; #113798 fixes the same `updateHash` for its own `is_signed_type` and goes forward independently. The fix adds the missing field to each hash, matching `SZ3`, `DoubleDelta`, `Gorilla`, `T64` and `Delta`, which already hash their type-derived width. Wide parts were never affected: one stream per column. Two consequences worth noting. Codec hashes also gate `can_substitute_codec_arguments`, a whole-codec flag, so `Tuple(Float32, Float64) CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` now shows as `CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` rather than `CODEC(FPC(12), LZ4)`; `Delta` and `Gorilla` already behave this way, same-width tuples still resolve, and a bare `CODEC(FPC)` still means level 12. No format change: each codec records the parameter in its own block header, so existing parts stay readable both ways. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, base `f9dd35fa7f57bbd8ec97be53c15acd82848a98f1`. ALP/FPC (build id `a0327326e75c88c307e5efda56857c3df38552c7`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `INSERT`, default table, f64 then f32, 101 rows | `Code: 270 ... 404 is not aligned to 8` | 101 rows, Compact part | | `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)`, default table | `Code: 270 ... 12012 is not aligned to 8` | 1001 rows, values round-trip | | ALP mixed vs two single-column tables | 234896 vs 228332, order dependent | 228332 == 228332 | | FPC mixed vs two single-column tables | 238887 vs 217185 | 217185 == 217185 | GCD (build id `bb612f0c6681bdde02436c553770393ff66f63fe`, pre-fix control `0a3b06892a5a9cafc8bc2c68a19d5fe9dff3f312`): | Check | Before | After | |---|---|---| | `UInt16` + `UInt64` mixed vs two single-column tables | 80815 vs 80830 | 80830 == 80830 | | declaration order invariance (`u16, u64` vs `u64, u16`) | 160544 vs 160540 | identical | | round-trip on the mixed table | 20000/20000 | 20000/20000 | | same tables as Wide parts (control, no stream sharing) | already equal | already equal | `04861_codec_hash_type_derived_params` (renamed, since it no longer covers only float width) fails on the parent commit and passes with the fix; the two new GCD assertions were verified to redden independently, 5/5 runs failing before and 10/10 passing after under randomized settings, and 4-way self-parallel runs pass. A control build patching only `ALP` left the `FPC` numbers at exactly 238887, confirming the `FPC` measurement is not leaking from the `ALP` change. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114189&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114189](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114189+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add a TOLERANCE clause to ASOF JOIN
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109034 `ASOF JOIN` matches the closest row however far away it is, so a trade can be matched against a quote from hours earlier. `TOLERANCE` bounds that distance: ```sql SELECT trades.time, trades.price, quotes.bid FROM trades ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes ON trades.symbol = quotes.symbol AND trades.time >= quotes.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND ``` The bound is inclusive. With `ASOF LEFT JOIN` a row whose closest match is out of tolerance is kept with default or `NULL` values on the right, following `join_use_nulls`, which is what `pandas.merge_asof(tolerance=...)` does. With `ASOF JOIN` it is dropped, like a row with no match at all. It can be written as an `INTERVAL`, or as a plain number in the units of the `ASOF` column. For a `DateTime64(3)` column `TOLERANCE 5000` and `TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND` are the same bound. ### Implementation notes The bound is converted into the units of the `ASOF` key once, during planning, so the join implementation compares it against key values directly with no per-probe conversion. `findAsof` already returns the closest match in the direction the inequality fixes, so if that one is out of bounds no other can be closer and the probe has no match. The interval unit is read from the result type rather than from the shape of the expression: `INTERVAL 5 SECOND` is written `toIntervalSecond(5)` but is constant folded during resolution into a constant whose value is `5` and whose type is `IntervalSecond`, so treating it as a bare number silently means five milliseconds against a `DateTime64(3)` key. ### Rejected rather than approximated - `MONTH`, `QUARTER` and `YEAR`, which are not fixed lengths of time. - An `INTERVAL` against an `ASOF` key that is not a date or time, where the unit would be undefined. - A bound finer than the key's resolution, such as `INTERVAL 1 MICROSECOND` against `DateTime64(3)`, which would otherwise round down to "exact matches only". - A negative bound, which nothing can satisfy. - `enable_analyzer = 0`, which builds `TableJoin` without the query tree the bound travels on and would silently ignore it. - `full_sorting_merge`, which matches through `IColumn::compareAt` and so has ordering but not distance. The planner falls back to another enabled algorithm; if only `full_sorting_merge` is enabled the query fails. Each of these silently returns matches further away than the query asked for if it is accepted instead, which is the failure this clause exists to prevent. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `TOLERANCE` clause to `ASOF JOIN`, bounding how far apart the left and the matched right value of the `ASOF` column may be, so that stale rows are not matched. The bound can be given as an `INTERVAL` or as a number in the units of the `ASOF` column, for example `ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes ON trades.symbol = quotes.symbol AND trades.time >= quotes.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 5 SECOND`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115530&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115530](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115530+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: fix loading old S3 tables with globbed paths
signal.text: Before ClickHouse `26.6`, `S3` tables could use a path like `**.parquet` together with `PARTITION BY`. These tables were read-only, so ClickHouse ignored `PARTITION BY`. https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/86746 changed this in ClickHouse 26.6. https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107437 also changed how the default strategy is selected. ClickHouse now tries to use either `hive` or `wildcard`. Neither works with this kind of path unless it contains `{_partition_id}`. Because of this, tables created before 26.6 can fail to load after an upgrade. Use the old behavior for these tables when `partition_strategy` is not set. Invalid strategies that users set explicitly still fail. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114705 ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix loading old S3 tables with globbed paths and `PARTITION BY` after upgrading from versions before 26.6. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115277&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115277](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115277+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Silk fibers integration
signal.text: Splits the silk runtime integration out of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275, so that it can be reviewed on its own. This adds the plumbing that lets ClickHouse run work on [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fibers, without yet putting any subsystem on them. - `Silk::initializeFiberScheduler` / `Silk::destroyFiberScheduler`, called by the server when the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting is enabled. The fiber stack size is configurable through the `silk.fiber_stack_size` configuration key (320 KiB by default, which leaves enough room for OpenSSL handshakes). - `FiberLocal` - fiber-local storage. A fiber can migrate between operating-system threads, so it must not observe another fiber's `thread_local` state; the values of the registered slots are swapped in and out on every fiber switch instead. `current_thread` (`ThreadStatus`), the OpenTelemetry tracing context, and the memory-tracker and exception blockers are moved to it. - The silk thread-local-storage sanitizer: an LLVM pass in `utils/silk-thread-local-storage-sanitizer` that instruments every `thread_local` access and aborts when a fiber touches raw thread-local storage. Without it, a variable that was not migrated to `FiberLocal` produces silent corruption rather than a diagnostic. It is enabled in the debug and ASan CI builds. - `Silk::ConnectionPool` and `Silk::streamSocketFactory` - a `Connection` pool and a socket factory that suspend the calling fiber instead of blocking the operating-system thread. `PoolBase` and `ConnectionPool` are templated on the lock and the condition variable to make that possible, and `ConnectionPool` stays an alias of the `std::mutex` instantiation, so the existing call sites are unchanged. - Memory that the runtime maps outside the C++ heap - fiber stacks and `io_uring` rings - is charged to `total_memory_tracker` through silk's mmap accounting hooks. - The low-level silk runtime counters are exported to `system.asynchronous_metrics` under a `Silk` prefix. - `Common/Fiber.h` and `Common/FiberStack.h` are renamed to `Common/StackfulCoroutine.h` and `Common/CoroutineStack.h`. They implement the boost-context coroutines used by `AsyncTaskExecutor`, which are unrelated to silk fibers, and having two different things called "fiber" in the same codebase is confusing. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added experimental support for the [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fiber runtime, enabled with the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting. When it is enabled, the server initializes the silk fiber scheduler at startup, so that subsystems supporting it can run their jobs on fibers instead of occupying an operating-system thread while waiting for I/O. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112667&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112667](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112667+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
signal.author: mstetsyuk

signal.title: Support Iceberg tables in Unity Catalog and Delta Lake tables in Glue Catalog
signal.text: ## Motivation Both AWS Glue and Databricks Unity Catalog are general-purpose metastores that can host tables in multiple open table formats. In practice: - Unity Catalog supports `DELTA`, `ICEBERG`, `PARQUET`, `CSV`, etc. as `data_source_format`. Iceberg-managed tables in UC have become common (Databricks "Managed Iceberg"). - Glue Data Catalog routinely stores Delta tables alongside Iceberg ones, distinguished by the `table_type` table parameter (`ICEBERG` vs `DELTA`, or by the presence of a `_delta_log/` directory under the storage location). Today ClickHouse hardcodes a single table format per catalog: - `UnityCatalog` accepts only `DELTA` — `src/Databases/DataLake/UnityCatalog.cpp`. - `GlueCatalog` accepts only `ICEBERG` — `src/Databases/DataLake/GlueCatalog.cpp`. As a result, users with mixed-format warehouses cannot expose all of their tables through a single ClickHouse `DataLakeCatalog` database — Iceberg tables in UC are reported as unreadable, and Delta tables in Glue are reported as unreadable. We should drop this assumption and choose the metadata reader per table, based on what the catalog reports. ## Current architecture (relevant pieces) - `DataLake::ICatalog` — `src/Databases/DataLake/ICatalog.h` — catalog interface. Returns `TableMetadata` which carries location, schema, credentials, and optional `DataLakeSpecificProperties` (currently just `iceberg_metadata_file_location`). - `DatabaseDataLake::getConfiguration` -- switches on `catalog->getCatalogType()` and `DatabaseDataLakeStorageType` (S3/Azure/HDFS/Local/Other) to return a hardcoded `Storage{S3,Azure,Local,HDFS}{Iceberg,DeltaLake,Paimon}Configuration`. The choice between Iceberg and Delta is currently a static property of the catalog type: - `UNITY` branch always returns a `*DeltaLakeConfiguration`. - `GLUE` branch always returns a `*IcebergConfiguration`. - The actual table-format-specific metadata reader is selected at template instantiation time via `DataLakeConfiguration<BaseStorageConfig, DataLakeMetadata>` — `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/DataLakeConfiguration.h`. There is no runtime polymorphism on the metadata reader per table within one configuration object. - `getConfiguration` is invoked from `DatabaseDataLake.cpp:646`, after `tryGetTableMetadata` has already been called and `DataLakeSpecificProperties` are available. So at the call site, we already know everything we need to know per table — we just lack a way to thread the "format" through. ## Proposed design ### 1. Add a per-table format to `TableMetadata` Introduce a `DataLakeTableFormat` enum in `src/Databases/DataLake/ICatalog.h`: ```cpp enum class DataLakeTableFormat : uint8_t { Iceberg, DeltaLake, Hudi, Paimon, Unknown, }; ``` Add `setTableFormat` / `getTableFormat` to `DataLake::TableMetadata`. This is the single source of truth that catalog implementations populate per table. ### 2. Teach catalogs to detect both formats - **`GlueCatalog::tryGetTableMetadata`** -- Replace the strict `table_type == "ICEBERG"` check with: - `table_type == "ICEBERG"` → `DataLakeTableFormat::Iceberg`, keep current `metadata_location` resolution. - `table_type == "DELTA"` → `DataLakeTableFormat::DeltaLake`, location points at the table root; no `metadata_location` parameter is expected (the `_delta_log` directory under `Location` is what `DeltaLakeMetadata` reads). - **`UnityCatalog::tryGetTableMetadata`** -- Remove the hardcoded `READABLE_TABLES`/`READABLE_DATA_SOURCE_FORMAT` filter (lines 36-37). Inspect both `securable_kind` and `data_source_format`: - `data_source_format == "DELTA"` → `DataLakeTableFormat::DeltaLake`. - `data_source_format == "ICEBERG"` → `DataLakeTableFormat::Iceberg`. For managed UC Iceberg tables, also retrieve the metadata file location (UC exposes it under a different field than Glue — needs verification against the UC `GET /tables` response, likely via the Iceberg REST shim that UC ships with). - Keep the existing `setTableIsNotReadable` path for anything we still don't recognise (e.g., `PARQUET`, `CSV`). - Vended credentials code paths in both catalogs are format-agnostic and need no changes. ### 3. Route to the right configuration in `DatabaseDataLake::getConfiguration` Change the signature of `getConfiguration` to take the table format as an extra argument, and within the `UNITY` and `GLUE` branches dispatch on it: ```cpp case DatabaseDataLakeCatalogType::GLUE: switch (format) { case DataLakeTableFormat::Iceberg: return std::make_shared<StorageS3IcebergConfiguration>(...); case DataLakeTableFormat::DeltaLake: return std::make_shared<StorageS3DeltaLakeConfiguration>(...); ... } ``` The call site at `DatabaseDataLake.cpp:646` already has the `TableMetadata` in scope, so it can pass `table_metadata.getTableFormat()` directly. For "fake" (`Other`) storage tables, fall back to `StorageLocalIcebergConfiguration` as today — the goal there is just `SHOW CREATE TABLE`, not reading.

signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/series
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ****Prometheus HTTP API:** implement **`/api/v1/series`** for **`TimeSeries`** tables.** ### Why this matters **Prometheus clients** use **`/api/v1/series`** to discover the label sets stored for active series. This endpoint is used by **Prometheus-compatible tools** such as **Grafana** when they need to populate metric and label selectors. ClickHouse **`TimeSeries` tables** can store labels in the main **`tags` Map**, in dedicated columns configured with **`tags_to_columns`**, or in a mixture of both layouts. The endpoint needs to expose the **same logical series** regardless of how those labels are stored. ### Description This PR adds **Prometheus `/api/v1/series` support** for **`TimeSeries` tables**. The endpoint is available through both a **dedicated `/api/v1/series` handler** and the **combined `/api/v1` handler**. It supports **GET requests** and **`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` POST requests**. Supported parameters: - **`match[]`** selects series by metric name and label matchers. Repeated parameters are combined as a **union** and overlapping results are returned only once through **deduplication**. - **`start` and `end`** select series overlapping the requested **time range**. - **`limit`** limits the number of returned series and reports when the response was **truncated**. ### Changes - **Selector parsing:** parse Prometheus series selectors with equality, inequality, regular-expression, and negative regular-expression matchers. - **Storage compatibility:** support metric names, labels in the **`tags` Map**, dedicated tag columns, and mixed rows that use both storage layouts. - **Label normalization:** normalize missing labels to the **Prometheus empty-value semantics** and include the full logical label set in each response. - **PromQL compatibility:** support quoted label names and anchor regular expressions to the **complete label value**. - **Input validation:** validate selectors and timestamps before executing the query. - **Time ranges:** apply the time-range filter when trusted min/max data is available. When it is not available, keep the request valid and return the **compatible candidate superset** allowed by the Prometheus API. - **Result limits:** support zero and positive limits, exact-limit responses, truncation reporting, and invalid-value errors. - **Access control:** read the underlying series metadata through the **`TimeSeries` table-function path** after checking access to the configured **`TimeSeries` table**. Unknown routes are resolved before authorization, so they keep the normal **404 response**. - **Existing endpoints:** apply the configured **`TimeSeries` table access boundary** consistently to the existing Prometheus query endpoints. - **Query lifecycle:** run the generated query through the **normal query pipeline** and keep **query logging** and **query completion handling** intact. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - **Matcher operators:** metric-name and label selectors with all matcher operators. - **Repeated selectors:** repeated **`match[]`** parameters, selector unions, and overlapping-result deduplication. - **Storage layouts:** Map labels, dedicated tag columns, missing labels, mixed carriers, conflicting carriers, and **`__name__`**. - **Regex and names:** quoted label names and whole-value regular-expression anchoring. - **Selector validation:** invalid and unbounded selectors, including the valid **`{host!~".*"}`** case. - **Time ranges:** two-sided, one-sided, inclusive, and invalid time ranges. - **Min/max behavior:** requests with and without trusted min/max metadata. - **Limits:** zero, exact, positive, maximum, and invalid **`limit`** values. - **HTTP methods:** GET and form POST requests. - **Authorization:** wrapper-only **`SELECT` grants**, access checks for all query endpoint families, and unknown-route handling. - **Observability:** query completion records and the existing query API limit behavior. Also ran **Python syntax checks** and **`git diff --check`**. ### Documentation **Documentation is written.** The **TimeSeries engine documentation** now covers the Prometheus handler configuration and the **`/api/v1/series` endpoint parameters**. ### Stack This is the **base PR** for the follow-up Prometheus API endpoints: - **#114868** adds **`/api/v1/labels`**. - **#114869** adds **`/api/v1/label/<name>/values`**. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114867&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114867](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114867+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Deny mergeTreeProjection and mergeTreeIndex reads that bypass a SELECT row policy
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> No related public open issue found. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reading projection data with the `mergeTreeProjection` table function no longer bypasses a SELECT row policy defined on the parent table. Such a read is now denied with `ACCESS_DENIED` when a non-trivial SELECT row policy exists. The `mergeTreeIndex` table function is likewise denied when the row policy references one of the index columns being read. ### Description `mergeTreeProjection(db, table, projection)` reads a projection's parts directly. Projection parts contain materialized rows of the parent table, so the read returned rows that a SELECT row policy on the parent is meant to hide. Any user with `SELECT` on the table could read hidden rows. `mergeTreeIndex` had the same gap, exposing per-granule index metadata (marks, primary key and column min/max). PR #95480 added the missing `SELECT` grant check to these functions but did not consider row policies. Reproduction (before this PR the last query returns all 4 rows): ```sql CREATE TABLE users (id UInt64, name String, department String, salary UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'Alice','engineering',100000),(2,'Bob','finance',120000), (3,'Carol','engineering',110000),(4,'Dave','hr',90000); ALTER TABLE users ADD PROJECTION proj (SELECT id, name, salary ORDER BY id); ALTER TABLE users MATERIALIZE PROJECTION proj; OPTIMIZE TABLE users FINAL; CREATE USER restricted NOT IDENTIFIED; GRANT SELECT ON default.users TO restricted; CREATE ROW POLICY rp ON users FOR SELECT USING department = 'engineering' TO restricted; -- as restricted: returns only Alice, Carol (policy enforced) SELECT * FROM users; -- as restricted, before this PR: returns all 4 rows (policy bypassed) SELECT * FROM mergeTreeProjection('default', 'users', 'proj'); ``` Fix: - `StorageFromMergeTreeProjection::read()` denies the read when a non-trivial SELECT row policy exists on the parent. The policy cannot be re-applied here: a projection may aggregate rows or omit the policy's filter columns entirely (as in the example above, where `department` is absent from the projection), so hidden rows still leak even when those columns are absent. A column-overlap check is therefore insufficient for projections; a full deny is required. - `StorageMergeTreeIndex::readImpl()` exposes only index metadata, so it gets the narrower column-overlap guard already used by `mergeTreeTextIndex`: deny only when the policy filter references one of the storage columns whose index data is being read. An always-true policy (`isAlwaysTrue()`) does not trigger the deny, and reads without a row policy are unaffected. Test: `tests/queries/0_stateless/04401_mergetree_projection_row_policy.sh`.

signal.title: Fix an unkillable hang when dropping a low-sorting-name TimeSeries table
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114259 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a hang when dropping a `TimeSeries` table whose name sorts lexicographically below its inner tables' names, for example `` DROP TABLE `-ts` `` or dropping a materialized view declared with `ENGINE = TimeSeries`. The drop self-deadlocked on the DDL guard and could not be cancelled with `KILL QUERY`. ### Description `DROP TABLE` of a `TimeSeries` table never returned and could not be killed when the table's own qualified name sorted below its inner tables' names: ```sql SET allow_experimental_time_series_table = 1; CREATE TABLE `-ts` ENGINE = TimeSeries; DROP TABLE `-ts`; -- hung forever ``` A materialized view's inner name is `.inner_id.<uuid>`, which always sorts below `.inner_id.metrics.<uuid>`, so dropping an `MV ... ENGINE = TimeSeries` hung too. **Root cause.** `executeDropQuery` takes the DDL guard for the inner table, then synthesizes an `ASTDropQuery` for that same table without setting `no_ddl_lock`, so the nested interpreter takes the guard for the identical name again. `DDLGuard::table_lock` wraps a non-recursive `std::mutex`, so the thread deadlocks against itself. A mutex wait is not a cancellation point, so `KILL QUERY` could not land and the guard stayed held for the server's lifetime. `need_ddl_guard = true` comes from one call site, `StorageTimeSeries::dropInnerTableIfAny`, which requests the inner guard only when the parent name sorts first. That predicate is correct and is kept: guards must be taken in increasing name order. Only its comment was wrong, claiming the inner name is "almost always less", which holds for `MaterializedView` but not `TimeSeries`. **The change.** `executeDropQuery` now sets `no_ddl_lock = need_ddl_guard`, so the inner name is guarded exactly once, by the caller, across the nested execute. `InterpreterCreateQuery` sets the same field for the same reason. The fix is inert for the other ten call sites, which all take the `need_ddl_guard = false` default. The `ddl_guard` null check is pre-existing hardening. **Validation.** Both shapes time out before the fix and succeed after, while a high-sorting-name control passes on both builds. Eight concurrent drops serialize and complete and the name is reusable afterwards, so the guard is still taken and released. New test `04920` covers both shapes and asserts no inner table is left behind.

signal.title: Propagate OpenTelemetry trace context into AsyncTaskExecutor fibers
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112738 The OpenTelemetry trace context is stored in a `FiberLocal`, but the fibers created by `AsyncTaskExecutor` (`ConnectionEstablisherAsync`, `PacketReceiver`, `RemoteQueryExecutorReadContext`) started with an empty fiber-local context. Remote queries of a distributed query were parented directly to the trace context supplied by the client, bypassing the spans of the initiator, and no spans were produced for the async tasks themselves. ## Changes - `AsyncTaskExecutor` captures `OpenTelemetry::CurrentContext()` on the thread that constructs it and installs a `TracingContextHolder` inside the fiber routine. This seeds the fiber-local context from the creating query and opens one span per task execution, named after the executor (`ConnectionEstablisherAsync`, `PacketReceiver`, `RemoteQueryExecutorReadContext`). It is a no-op when tracing is not enabled. - `FiberLocal` is now a per-type singleton (obtained via `FiberLocal<T>::instance`, the constructor is private). The address of the single object keys the per-fiber data, so a fiber suspended on one thread and resumed on another resolves to the same data. ## Span hierarchy change Remote queries now descend from the initiator through the `Connection::sendQuery` CLIENT span instead of appearing as direct children of the client-supplied trace context: ``` client span └─ query (initiator) └─ Connection::sendQuery [CLIENT] └─ query (remote server) ``` The expectations of `01455_opentelemetry_distributed` are updated accordingly: only the initial query span is now a direct child of the input trace context. A new test `04869_opentelemetry_async_remote_query_spans` covers the async paths, including `use_hedged_requests=1` (asserting `ConnectionEstablisherAsync` and `PacketReceiver` spans) and fiber cancellation. This is the first part of the distributed tracing improvements discussed in the linked issue ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Propagate the OpenTelemetry trace context into the fibers used for asynchronous connection establishment and remote query execution (hedged requests, `async_socket_for_remote`, `async_query_sending_for_remote`). Spans of remote queries in a distributed query are now correctly parented under the initiator's `Connection::sendQuery` span instead of being attached directly to the client-supplied trace context, and each asynchronous task execution produces its own span. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114813&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114813](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114813+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Accept PromQL line comments at EOF
signal.text: ### Description PromQL line comments currently require a newline, so valid queries with a trailing comment at EOF, such as `up # trailing comment`, are rejected by ClickHouse. Prometheus consumes line comments through CR, LF, or EOF and skips comment tokens before parsing the expression. This change matches that behavior, regenerates the checked-in ANTLR lexer artifacts, and adds coverage for EOF, LF, CRLF, adjacent comments, and comment-only input. Upstream references: - [Prometheus lexer](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L874-L882) - [Prometheus line-ending handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/lex.go#L1123-L1125) - [Prometheus parser comment handling](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse.go#L2817-L2855) - [Prometheus comment-only query test](https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/main/promql/parser/parse_test.go#L3206-L3220) ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Accept PromQL line comments that end at EOF.**

signal.title: Pin actions/checkout to a commit SHA in praktika-generated workflows
signal.text: `zizmor` flags `actions/checkout@v6` in every praktika-generated workflow as an unpinned action reference (528 occurrences across 24 workflows) — pinning to a mutable tag lets whoever controls that tag change what code runs in CI without review. Pin it to the `v6.1.0` commit SHA in the `yaml_generator.py` template that emits the checkout step, and regenerate the workflows. While at it, also pin `actions/setup-python`, `actions/upload-artifact`, and `actions/download-artifact` in the same templates for consistency, since they share the same unpinned-tag issue even though no current job exercises those addons. This only touches the `uses:` line of the checkout step in each generated workflow — verified with `git diff` that no other line changed. `zizmor` confirms `unpinned-uses` findings drop from 534 to 6; the remaining 6 are `ClickHouse/checkout@v1` and `docker/setup-buildx-action@v3` in workflows that are not generated by praktika, out of scope for this change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Not for changelog (CI-only change, no changelog entry required).

signal.title: Hand the connection to the built-in web UI pages over `postMessage`
signal.text: The built-in web UI pages — `/play`, `/docs`, `/dashboard`, `/schema`, `/merges`, `/jemalloc`, `/processors-profile`, `/binary` — take their connection from their own query string, which cannot carry a password: a URL ends up in browser history, `Referer` headers, server access logs and proxy logs. Only `/webterminal` could be handed credentials by the page embedding it, in a `postMessage` message. Every page now speaks that same exchange: ``` page -> host {type: 'clickhouse-hello'} host -> page {type: 'clickhouse-credentials', url, user, password} ``` The page announces itself as soon as it can apply a connection, and the host answers. The page has to speak first because a host that opened it with `window.open` cannot observe when a cross-origin document became ready, and an embedded page would otherwise race its host's `load` handler. Having adopted a connection, each page redoes what it had already loaded with the previous one, so the handover also works when it arrives after the page started querying: `/play` re-probes the credentials, `/docs` rebuilds its cross-link name cache and re-runs the displayed search, `/dashboard` and `/processors-profile` chain their reload behind the load already in flight (two concurrent loads would otherwise duplicate charts, or let a stale failure overwrite a good listing), `/schema` and `/jemalloc` reload, and `/binary` drops its cached tiles and redraws. ## Opening `/docs` from `/play` The Documentation icon in the `/play` sidebar is the first user of the handover. A plain click opens `/docs` through `window.open` — the anchor's `rel=noopener` would sever the handle — and hands the whole connection over, so the documentation search runs against the same server as the same user without the password appearing in a URL. A middle or modifier click keeps the browser's native new-tab handling, which carries `?user=` only, since such a window has no link back to `/play`. ## Security A reply is accepted only from the one window that opened or embeds the page, and only from an exact origin: the page's own, `https://console.clickhouse.cloud`, `https://console.clickhouse-staging.com` or `https://clickhouse.com`. The list is exact rather than a domain suffix on purpose — every ClickHouse Cloud service endpoint is a `*.clickhouse.cloud` host that serves content of its owner's choosing, and a trusted host can aim a page at a server of its own through `url`, which the user may then type credentials into believing it is still their own service. `webterminal.html` gated its own exchange on such a suffix and now uses the same exact list. `url` is optional and defaults to the server the page already points at, but the credentials are replaced wholesale: a message that names only a server cannot attach credentials it did not carry to it, which is what keeps a password filled in by the browser's password manager for this page's origin from following a `url` elsewhere. Outbound, credentials are always sent with an exact target origin, never `'*'`; the readiness announcement carries no secrets, only the fact that the page exists, which its host knows already. Verified in Chromium against a mock endpoint: the `/play` → `/docs` handover, the handover into an iframe for all eight pages, rejection of a handover from an untrusted origin and from a same-origin window that is not the page's host, the wholesale credential replacement, and the exactness of the origin list for all nine pages (`https://myserviceendpoint.clickhouse.cloud`, `https://evil.clickhouse.com`, `http://console.clickhouse.cloud` and `https://console.clickhouse.cloud.evil.com` are all rejected). The committed test asserts that every served page implements both halves of the exchange and that its origin list stayed exact. The protocol is documented in `docs/concepts/features/interfaces/web-ui-embedding.mdx`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The built-in web UI pages (`/play`, `/docs`, `/dashboard`, `/schema`, `/merges`, `/jemalloc`, `/processors-profile`, `/binary`) can now be handed their connection — server URL, user and password — in a `postMessage` message by the page that opened or embedded them, instead of taking it from their own query string, where a password would be recorded in browser history, referrer headers and access logs. `/play` uses this when opening `/docs`, so the documentation search connects to the same server as the same user. A page accepts a connection only from the window that opened or embeds it, and only from an exact list of trusted origins. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115067&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115067](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115067+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Measure the compressed size of aggregate states in `estimateSizeOfCompressedState`
signal.text: `Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` estimates how many bytes the aggregate states would take when a replica sends them to the initiator, which is how automatic parallel replicas decides whether distributing a query pays off. It builds a `CompressedWriteBuffer` over a `NullWriteBuffer`, but serializes the sampled states into the `NullWriteBuffer` directly and then reads that buffer's counter: ```cpp NullWriteBuffer wb; CompressedWriteBuffer wbuf(wb); // never written to ... aggregate_functions[j]->serialize(place + offsets_of_aggregate_states[j], wb); ... wbuf.finalize(); res += it ? static_cast<size_t>(table.size() * wb.count() / ((it + period - 1) / period)) : 0; ``` So nothing is ever compressed and, despite the function's name and its own `We only interested in the size of compressed state` comment, it returns the plain serialized size. `recordAggregationStateSizes` then stored that single number as all three of `bytes`, `sample_bytes` and `compressed_bytes`, which pins the compression ratio of the aggregation-state statistics to 1. `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes`, documented as `Mirrors the logic of Aggregator::estimateSizeOfCompressedState` for in-order aggregation, feeds the same `AggregationState` counters via `estimateCompressedColumnSize` and does measure the compressed size - so two producers of one statistic disagreed on what it means. This change serializes the sample through the compressing buffer and returns the sample's uncompressed and compressed sizes alongside the extrapolated total, letting the existing compression-ratio machinery in `RuntimeDataflowStatisticsCacheUpdater` apply the states' real ratio. Taking the ratio from the sample rather than compressing the extrapolated size also keeps the per-compressed-block framing overhead out of the extrapolation, where multiplying it by `table.size() / num_samples` would have inflated it. **Effect on the estimate.** Only queries whose output is dominated by compressible aggregate states move. That is exactly the shape that showed up as a CI failure of `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` on master: `query_28` (`MIN(Referer)` states over a two-level hash table with many groups) estimated 59335657 bytes against a recorded 23722663, a ratio of 2.4996 that left the test's 2.5x bound no margin. Reading the estimates out of the failing job's server log, the ten other queries in that test match their recorded values within 1.00..1.41x, because their output is dominated by aggregation keys or by output columns, both of which were already measured compressed. So the recorded values expect the compressed size and this defect is why that one entry looked wrong. **Two small-sample corrections found while validating this in CI.** The compressed format writes a checksum and a block header in front of every block, so a sample of a few bytes comes out of `CompressedWriteBuffer` larger than it went in and the derived ratio drops below one, *inflating* the estimate. With an early conversion to a two-level hash table (`group_by_two_level_threshold=1`, which the test randomization sets) every one of the 256 buckets holds a handful of states and every per-bucket sample is dominated by that framing, which is what made `04034_autopr_dataflow_cache_reuse_between_different_queries` fail on the first run of this pull request: the two cache-reusing queries lost parallel replicas. When the states are really sent, the framing is amortized over `min_compress_block_size` of data, so such a sample is now reported as incompressible rather than as expanding, keeping the ratio at 1 - exactly what the caller assumed before the ratio was measured at all. The new test `04653_autopr_state_size_estimate_small_buckets` pins `group_by_two_level_threshold` to 1 and fails without that. Reviewing the same statistic end to end also turned up the mirror-image defect on the in-order-aggregation side, reported in review: `recordAggregationStateColumnSizes` totalled `IColumn::byteSize`, which for a `ColumnAggregateFunction` whose states live in a foreign arena (as `AggregatingInOrderTransform` hands them over) counts one pointer per row, so arena-backed states - `min(String)`, `groupArray`, `uniqExact` - were under-counted. That column is now sized from its serialized states too, sampling at most as many of them as the hash-table producer samples per bucket. **Recorded values.** The values in `03634_autopr_output_bytes_estimation` are empirical and need `test.hits`, so they are re-measured from this PR's own CI run rather than guessed - the test reports every query that lands outside the 2.5x band, and I will update whatever it reports. `query_1` and `query_20` are single `count()` states whose estimate becomes the ~29-byte compressed-block framing instead of a 2-3 byte varint; the test's `NOT (res.2 < 100 AND res.3 < 100)` guard already covers those. Verified so far: both changed translation units pass a full `-fsyntax-only` typecheck against master. The estimate itself is validated by CI, since reproducing it needs the stateful dataset. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111981 That PR is the interim, test-only fix for the master CI failure linked below: it re-records `query_28` as the ~58 MB the estimator currently reports. **The two changes touch the same line and are mutually exclusive.** If #111981 merges first, this PR must set `query_28` back to the post-fix measurement (expected to land near the original 23722663); if this PR merges first, #111981 should be closed as unnecessary. https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=5baed0f5a10c333cd220b9646d6ef4647425079d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20parallel%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the estimation of the size of aggregate states used by automatic parallel replicas: it measured the serialized size of the states instead of their compressed size, overestimating how much data a replica would send for queries that aggregate into large, compressible states. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111985&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111985](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111985+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Take the Cascades planning node count from the plan, not the ambient context
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115545 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113422 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115398 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the node count the Cascades optimizer plans for when `distributed_plan_workers_num` and `distributed_plan_execute_locally` are set inside a subquery's `SETTINGS` clause. The count was re-read from the ambient query context, which for a separately-planned subquery holds the outer query's values, so the subquery was planned for the configured worker cluster instead of the requested number of workers, and on a server with no worker cluster a valid query was rejected with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`. Closes #115545. ### Description A scalar subquery gets its own `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings`, but `CascadesOptimizer::buildContext` resolved the node count through `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount(getQueryContextOrThrow())`, the query-level context, i.e. the outer query's. It read both settings from there, while two lines below taking `distributed_plan_execute_locally` from `optimization_settings`. Measured on `90a20ccf81cd348`: with a worker cluster configured, a subquery asking for 4 workers under an outer query asking for 8 was planned for 8 (wrong parallelism, silent). With no cluster the count resolved to 0 and a valid query was refused with `Code 344 SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`, while the same settings applied to the whole query answered correctly. Every setting involved is experimental and off by default, so this needs an unusual but supported configuration. Same defect class as #113422 (merged), at a consumer it did not touch, and the fix extends that seam. `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings` gains the missing `distributed_plan_workers_num` field, and `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount` takes both settings as parameters, keeping `context` only for the server-level worker configuration, which cannot differ per subquery. The Cloud discovery lease in `TaskToHostMap` gets the same value, otherwise the planner would use the subquery's count while the lease still leased the outer one. That branch is Cloud-only and untested here. The new test asserts the resolved node count via `system.text_log`. It fails on master and passes with the fix; reverting only the argument at the call site reddens it again while the top-level control arm stays green. The `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` half needs a server with no worker cluster, which stateless CI never provides, so it rests on the counted arms over the same reads. Also noticed, not fixed here: `sort_settings` and the statistics hint in the same function are read from the ambient context too. Neither has a measured consequence, and both are separate root causes, so I am not raising them. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115571&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115571](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115571+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
