signal.title: Record an index's absent columns when materializing it on a wide part
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114990 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112484 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes an unreleased regression from #112484 (`master` only): `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE INDEX` produced an index that never prunes when the indexed column had been added by a metadata-only `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` and the part is wide. No stable release carries #112484, so no changelog entry and no backport are owed. ### Description Reported by @ clickgapai. #112484 merged on 2026-08-15 and is an ancestor of no release branch, so only `master` is affected. **What breaks.** `ADD COLUMN c ... DEFAULT ...` on a wide part is metadata-only, so the part holds no bytes for `c`. A following `MATERIALIZE INDEX idx` writes the index files but does not add `c` to the part's column list, and since #112484 the reader refuses an index whose columns the part does not describe. The index occupies disk and never prunes: `Granules: 16/16` on the reporter's fixture versus `1/16` before, results correct both ways. **Root cause.** `splitAndModifyMutationCommands` has two branches. The compact one turns an index's required-but-absent columns into `READ_COLUMN` commands; the wide one had no such step, so `c` never enters `updated_header` and `getColumnsForNewDataPart` erases it. The missing type is the defect, so the fix belongs on the write side. **The change.** On a wide part, `MATERIALIZE INDEX` now also reads the index's absent columns, so the part records them at the type the granules were built from. The column list belongs to the part, so it records the column only when every other index holding files there either does not read it or has its granules rebuilt by this same mutation: a carried-over granule keeps its build-time type, so recording the column now would hand the reader a matching type for a stale granule. What the mutation rebuilds is decided from its own commands, and an undecidable index counts as carried over, keeping the pre-fix behaviour. Compact parts and the reader are untouched, so every #112484 refusal holds. **Cost.** The mutation now writes column data: +247 bytes before, +806,931 after on a 200k-row wide fixture; the next merge writes it anyway. No format, serialization or default change, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry. <details> <summary>Validation, rejected alternative, known-unfixed shape</summary> **Rejected alternative:** recording build-time types in a new per-part file - a format change needing ~9 seams, a protocol bump and upgrade/downgrade paths. **Known-unfixed:** on a part with orphan index files (#109595) `hasSecondaryIndex` is true, so the read is suppressed and the index stays inert - the status quo, never wrong results. | arm | absent arm | control arm | |---|---|---| | pristine master | `16/16` (inert) | 1/16 | | this PR | `1/16` | 1/16 | Counts identical with and without `use_skip_indexes` in every cell; the control prunes on both. Four mutation arms cover the restriction, each red on the build missing its guard: without it, a hardlinked granule's column is rewritten at the new type and the next read attempts a 4 EiB allocation; keyed to the index named in the command rather than the column, a second index over that column has its stale granules re-enabled and the next read aborts; without the rebuilt-sibling exemption, a batched update that does rebuild the sibling still suppresses it, leaving the new index inert - covered both for a sibling reached by a named column and for one reached via a TTL target. Tests: `04869_skip_index_stale_type_absent_column` gains cases 26 (the regression), 26b (subcolumn index, absent parent recorded), 27, 28 (two indices, one absent column), 29 and 30 (rebuilt sibling). Cases 11/22/23/24 moved from `ADD COLUMN` to a column TTL expiry, since the fix makes the old route no longer leave a column absent; each gained an `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` refusal assertion, and every such assertion now pins the granule count rather than matching a substring. `04246_materialize_index_force_recalc` (the #104872 compact tripwire), `04165`, `04870` and `04871` pass unchanged; 250/250 across a 50-run randomized loop. Unrelated columns stay hardlinked (by inode), so the mutation does not escalate to a full part rewrite. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115055&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115055](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115055+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Make `arrayCount` return `UInt64` and rewrite `length(arrayFilter(...))`
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/2120 --> `arrayFilter` builds an array of the elements that pass the predicate, and `length` then throws that array away and keeps only its size. `arrayCount` computes the same number without materializing anything. ```sql SELECT length(arrayFilter(x -> (x >= 2), arr)); -- becomes SELECT arrayCount(x -> (x >= 2), arr); ``` The rewrite is a new query tree pass in the spirit of the existing `RewriteArrayExistsToHasPass`, controlled by the new `optimize_rewrite_array_filter_length_to_array_count` setting (on by default). A new node is built rather than rewriting the `arrayFilter` node in place, because the filtered array can be referenced elsewhere in the query tree, where it is still an array. `arrayCount` counted into `UInt32`, which silently wrapped for a row whose array has more than `4294967295` matching elements, while `length(arrayFilter(...))` counts through `ColumnArray::Offset` and is exact. It now counts into `UInt64` and returns `UInt64`: this fixes the overflow of `arrayCount` itself, and makes the rewrite value-preserving for arrays of any size. The result type of `arrayCount` therefore changes from `UInt32` to `UInt64`; the values are unchanged. Because `length` and `arrayCount` now have the same result type, the rewritten node needs no `CAST`, and the pass only rewrites when the two result types match. Since this changes the stable public signature of an existing function, the previous behavior is kept behind the new compatibility setting `array_count_legacy_uint32_result` (default `false`): setting it to `true` restores the `UInt32` result type, and it is wired into the settings changes history, so `compatibility = '26.7'` (or older) restores it automatically on the servers where it is set. For distributed queries, the setting (like any setting) is forwarded from the initiator to the shards, so a query initiated by a server that has it set behaves exactly as before on every shard. The one case it does not cover is a rolling upgrade with a *not-yet-upgraded initiator*: an old server does not know the setting and cannot forward it, so type-sensitive expressions evaluated locally on already-upgraded shards (for example, `byteSize(arrayCount(...))`) observe `UInt64` there, while the initiator still converts the top-level result to its own `UInt32` header. To keep such queries fully unchanged during the upgrade, set `array_count_legacy_uint32_result = 1` on the upgraded servers for the users under which shard-side queries execute (with an interserver `secret` configured that is the initiator's current user; otherwise it is the user from the cluster definition or the `remote` table function - the simplest robust approach is to enable it for all users of the upgraded servers), and remove it once the whole cluster is upgraded. This is documented in the `arrayCount` documentation and in the setting's description, and both directions of the mixed-version scenario are pinned by the integration test `test_backward_compatibility/test_array_count_return_type.py`. In legacy mode the rewrite does not fire, because the pass requires the result types to match. Measured with the setting toggled on the same binary (release, aarch64), best of five, before the `CAST` was removed: | query | setting off | setting on | | |---|---|---|---| | one 30M-element array, half the elements pass | 0.38 s | 0.33 s | 1.15x | | one 30M-element array, all elements pass | 0.40 s | 0.31 s | 1.29x | | one 10M-element `String` array | 0.40 s | 0.37 s | 1.08x | | 5M rows x 32-element arrays, unpredictable predicate | 1.42 s | 1.29 s | 1.10x | | 1M rows x 8-element `String` arrays | 0.25 s | 0.22 s | 1.14x | | 5M rows x 32-element arrays, half the elements pass | 1.41 s | 1.48 s | 0.95x | The gain grows with the array length, which is where the copy that `arrayFilter` does starts to cost something. The last row loses 5%: for short arrays the copy is cheap, `ArrayCountImpl` counts the filter with a scalar loop while `arrayFilter` copies with vectorized code, and the cast to `UInt64` added a column of its own - that cast is no longer generated. I did try replacing that scalar loop with `countBytesInFilter`, but its vectorized path is `__SSE2__` only, so on the aarch64 machine I measured on it made no difference and I dropped it rather than commit something I could not verify. It may be worth doing separately, measured on x86. Found while profiling https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/2120, where `length(arrayFilter(x -> (x >= 2), arrayEnumerateUniq(...)))` is applied to a single array of 60 million elements. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/2120 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `arrayCount` now returns `UInt64` instead of `UInt32`, so that it is exact for arrays with more than 4294967295 matching elements; set the new setting `array_count_legacy_uint32_result` to `true` (or use `compatibility = '26.7'`) to restore the previous result type. During a rolling upgrade, set `array_count_legacy_uint32_result = 1` on the upgraded servers for the users under which shard-side queries execute (the simplest robust approach is to enable it for all users of the upgraded servers), so that distributed queries initiated by not-yet-upgraded servers (which cannot forward the setting) keep the previous behavior on upgraded shards; remove it after the upgrade is complete. In addition, `length(arrayFilter(func, arr))` is now rewritten to `arrayCount(func, arr)`, which counts the matching elements instead of building an array of them only to take its size - up to 1.29x faster on long arrays, controlled by the `optimize_rewrite_array_filter_length_to_array_count` setting. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113023&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113023](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113023+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Schema inference for freeform text formats
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Implement schema inference for **row** freeform text format. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/34006 Once this is done you *should* be able to ingest arbitrary tabular text files (ie. application logs) without specifying the structure (Template). *Example usage:* Read data from file ```sql SELECT * FROM file(<file_path>,'Freeform') ``` Describe data from file ```sql Desc file(<file_path>,'Freeform') ``` *How it is implemented* `FreeformFieldMatcher` houses an array of matchers that parse text data by escaping rules (JSON, CSV, Raw(but cutoff by whitespace), Quoted and Escaped). First, FreeformFieldMatcher will iterate over this set of matchers and generate as many solutions as possible. A `Solution` is defined as the order of the matchers to parse one row successfully associated with a score. The score here is generated by continuously adding the score of each field in the solution, specifically by the escaping rule and the type of the field. More specific fields (ie. DateTime) yield higher scores. For now we only generate solutions for the first row because the data is supposed to be *tabular* to we *should* be able to get an acceptable solution just by looking at one row. Then the solutions are sorted by score and they are check against `max_rows_to_check`. The first solution matches all of the `max_rows_to_check` would be picked as the final solution. Currently this works with CSV and syslog but more testing and tunings needs to be made for it to be in an acceptable state. From ```csv 1,2021-04-01 00:00:18,2021-04-01 00:21:54,1,8.40,1,N,79,116,1,25.5,3,0.5,5.85,0,0.3,35.15,2.5 1,2021-04-01 00:42:37,2021-04-01 00:46:23,1,.90,1,N,75,236,2,5,3,0.5,0,0,0.3,8.8,2.5 ``` we have ``` 1 2021 4 1 0 0 18 2021 4 1 0 21 54 1 8.4 1 N 79 116 1 25.5 3 0.5 5.85 0 0.3 35.15 2.5 1 2021 4 1 0 42 37 2021 4 1 0 46 23 1 0.9 1 N 75 236 2 5 3 0.5 0 0 0.3 8.8 2.5 ``` From ``` Nov 13 10:29:56 Tri chronyd[227]: Selected source PHC0 Nov 13 13:24:02 Tri kernel: [91566.562562] hv_utils: TimeSync IC version 4.0 Nov 13 13:24:02 Tri chronyd[227]: Forward time jump detected! ``` we have ``` Nov 13 10 29 56 Tri chronyd[227]: Selected source PHC0 Nov 13 13 24 2 Tri kernel: [91566.562562] hv_utils: TimeSync IC version 4.0 Nov 13 13 24 2 Tri chronyd[227]: Forward time jump detected! ``` *Update 2022-28-11:* With the new changes on increasing the search tree size, we now iterate over all matchers and don't exit early. However, a new field is added only if it has a better type score than the previous field or if no field other than type string has been found. This helps us to better parse the previous CSV example: ``` 1 2021-04-01 0 0 18 2021-04-01 0 21 54 1 8.4 1 N 79 116 1 25.5 3 0.5 5.85 0 0.3 35.15 2.5 1 2021-04-01 0 42 37 2021-04-01 0 46 23 1 0.9 1 N 75 236 2 5 3 0.5 0 0 0.3 8.8 2.5 ``` And also ClickHouse's logs: ``` 2022-11-17 11 7 30.825405 [395843] {345bf223-db80-4772-9a07-73542321e715::202211_15349_15604_53} <Debug> MergeTask::PrepareStage: Merging 6 parts: from 202211_15349_15599_52 to 202211_15604_15604_0 into Compact 2022-11-17 11 7 30.826372 [395843] {345bf223-db80-4772-9a07-73542321e715::202211_15349_15604_53} <Debug> MergeTask::PrepareStage: Selected MergeAlgorithm: Horizontal ``` *Update 2022-30-12:* Now we could parse and unmarshal JSON object fields into their own columns. *TODO:* - Make use of the SchemaCache to store the solution - Fix the new added test

signal.title: Do not treat the CFI build as a sanitizer build in the test harnesses
signal.text:
### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Closes: #115122 Two test harnesses decide whether a build is a sanitizer build by testing `CXX_FLAGS LIKE '%-fsanitize=%'`. The `amd_cfi` profile adds `-fsanitize=cfi-vcall,cfi-derived-cast` (`CMakeLists.txt:527`), so the substring matches even though `-DSANITIZE=` is empty: - `tests/config/install.sh:227` installs `config.d/trace_log_no_symbolize.xml`, so `TraceLog.cpp:298-299` inserts a zero-length array into `symbols` and `lines`, failing the two `03150_trace_log_*` tests. - `tests/integration/helpers/cluster.py:5152` `is_built_with_sanitizer()` makes 50 no-argument call sites across 35 integration test files skip themselves, `test_trace_log_build_id` saying "trace_log is disabled with sanitizers", which is not true under CFI. Both now test `-DSANITIZER`, which `cmake/sanitize.cmake:30` puts into `SAN_FLAGS` and which reaches `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` in all 5 branches of `if (SANITIZE)` and nowhere else. The named `address` / `thread` / `memory` checks keep testing `-fsanitize=`. **The reporter's open question is answered, and negatively: official release builds are not affected.** `amd_cfi` and `amd_release` differ by exactly one flag (`-DENABLE_CFI=1` versus `-DBUILD_STANDALONE_KEEPER=1`), so ThinLTO with split-debug and stripping is already the shipped configuration. Validated on the exact binary from the failing job (build ID `e3992b92...`): with the override present both `03150_*` tests fail; with the patched script both pass. That binary is now classified as not sanitized while a real ASan binary still is, the regression risk this PR's ASan/TSan/MSan lanes cover. No existing check can show the `03150_*` tests green: `WeeklyCFI` on master runs only build, integration and stress (`ci/workflows/weekly_cfi.py:30-34`), and the stateless `amd_cfi` lane arrives with #115036, still open. Since both consumers react by skipping work, a revert would stay green, so `ci/tests/test_cfi_not_a_sanitizer_build.py` pins both predicates against the measured `CXX_FLAGS` of nine profiles, running the installer's own function with a stub `clickhouse`. It runs on every PR, and both predicate files are now `CI Tests` digest inputs so a later edit cannot reuse a cached pass. #113107 edits the same block, so whichever lands second may need a rebase. [CI report.](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=30c47a7d9420ba1e86365979016e7765cbc080da&name_0=WeeklyCFI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_cfi%2C%20parallel%29)
Other users of an -fsanitize string test, left unchanged (click to expand) I checked every in-tree consumer of the same "is this a sanitizer build" idea and changed the two that are reachable under CFI and change test outcomes: | consumer | reachable under CFI? | why left alone | |---|---|---| | `install.sh:92` `is_fast_build` | no | its only call site needs `FAST_TEST=1`, whose only producer builds with `-DENABLE_THINLTO=0` and no CFI, and CFI without ThinLTO is a cmake `FATAL_ERROR` | | `tests/clickhouse-test:5135` `collect_build_flags` | yes | already correct: it maps sanitizer names, so CFI yields no flag and `SANITIZED` stays false. It must keep the name map to emit per-sanitizer `no-asan`/`no-tsan` tags, which a boolean marker cannot express | | `tests/docker_scripts/upgrade_runner.sh:171` | no | there is no `amd_cfi` upgrade job | | `tests/integration/test_userspace_page_cache/test.py:31` | yes | its own local probe, run before the cluster starts so it cannot use the helper. The consequence is one extra container under CFI, not a wrong result | | `ci/jobs/scripts/functional_tests/setup_log_cluster.sh:102` | yes | the value is only echoed, never read again anywhere in the tree - a dead diagnostic | `Stress test (amd_cfi)` also runs `install.sh` on master, so that predicate is exercised there, but that suite asserts nothing about symbolized `trace_log`. Each remaining one is a separate question with no observed consequence today, so widening this PR to them would be unmeasured churn.

signal.title: Do not delete staged Iceberg files when a catalog commit outcome is unknown
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed data loss on catalog-backed Iceberg tables when a write's catalog commit was accepted but its response was lost: the staged files of what had become the table's current snapshot were deleted, leaving the table unreadable. The catalog step now confirms the outcome first, and one it cannot establish is reported as `UNKNOWN_STATUS_OF_TRANSACTION` with the files kept. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112081 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115390 **What breaks.** A catalog-backed Iceberg write stages `v<N>.metadata.json`, then points the catalog at it. A commit the catalog had **accepted** but whose response was lost read as "the commit did not happen", so the caller deleted the staged files of what was by then the current snapshot. This is the catalog half of the family #112081 names; #115390 fixes the storage one. **Root cause.** `RestCatalog::updateMetadata` returned `false` for any `HTTPException`, and `GlueCatalog::updateMetadata` threw one error code for any AWS failure. `false` means "another writer won, retry", and all three destructive call sites clean up on it, so a third outcome, "cannot tell", had nowhere to go. **The change.** Each outcome is classified where the information exists. The REST commit POST becomes single-attempt, because a re-POST is refused by the requirement the first attempt satisfied, making every status ambiguous. A 409 is then a proven lost race; a non-retryable status, and any failure raised before the request reached the wire, keep their error and their cleanup; anything else reconciles against the `main` ref. Glue reconciles every failed outcome, since its client retries `UpdateTable` with no per-request pin; it reads the raw `metadata_location`, as the derived one matches the staged file. Only an unresolved outcome becomes `UNKNOWN_STATUS_OF_TRANSACTION`, which the cleanup handlers skip. An orphaned file is recoverable; a deleted snapshot is not. **Validation and scope.** Twelve REST and six Glue integration arms cover the insert, delete and compaction commit paths, asserting on object existence and readability; 30 of 30 repeated runs pass. Reverting the reconciliation, single-attempt pin, pre-dispatch guard, 409 branch, non-retryable branch or a cleanup guard each reddens a named arm. `updateSchema` and `EXPIRE SNAPSHOTS` are out of scope, as neither deletes staged files on failure; `DeltaLakeSink` commits through a Delta transaction, not this interface. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115580&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115580](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115580+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Disable the map element to subcolumn rewrite by default and revert the PREWHERE grouping change
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111879 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99200 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107988 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111954 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107912 ### Description In 26.3 we added bucketed serialization for the `Map` data type together with an analyzer rewrite of `m['key']` (internally `arrayElement(m, 'key')`) into the Map key subcolumn `m.key_<key>`, so that only the relevant bucket is read from disk. The bucketed serialization turned out to be imperfect and is planned to be reimplemented as a separate type. For regular (non-bucketed) `Map` serialization this rewrite can be harmful (for example, it complicates subcolumn size estimation) and gives no benefit for single-key lookups. **1. New setting.** `optimize_map_element_to_subcolumn` (default `false`) gates only the `{Map, arrayElement}` transformer in `FunctionToSubcolumnsPass`. All other `Map` subcolumn optimizations (`mapKeys`, `mapValues`, `length`, `empty`) keep following `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns`. The new setting takes effect only when `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` is also enabled. This only disables the automatic rewrite; reading the `m.key_<key>` subcolumn explicitly still works, and query results are unchanged either way. **2. Revert of the PREWHERE grouping from #107988.** That change made `MergeTreeWhereOptimizer` and `tryBuildPrewhereSteps` group conditions by physical storage column instead of by the exact column set, so that several `m['kN']` subcolumn reads share one read step. Its only purpose was to compensate for the rewrite: with the rewrite disabled, all `m['kN']` conditions reference the same column `m` and the original exact-column-set grouping already places them into one step. The grouping also introduced a correctness regression, #111879: a guard condition and a throwing expression over subcolumns of the same column (for example `payload.longitude IS NOT NULL` and a `CAST(tuple(...), 'Point')` over `payload.latitude`) became adjacent and were merged into one read step. All conditions of a step are evaluated on the same unfiltered block, so the throwing expression ran on rows the guard had rejected. Measured with the repro from #111879 on pre-built binaries: | binary | result | |---|---| | master before #107988 (`cd3c529cd3a`) | `66666` | | master with #107988 | `CANNOT_INSERT_NULL_IN_ORDINARY_COLUMN` | | this branch | `66666` | Reverting instead of adding a new heuristic keeps this change small enough to backport. Improving subcolumn read sharing in PREWHERE will be done separately on `master` and does not need backporting; #111954 is superseded by this change. The serialization part of #107988 (`ISerialization` cache keys, whole-map caching in `SerializationMapKeyValue`, the `SerializationSparse` refactor) is kept — it is unrelated to #111879 and still shares reads between subcolumns of the same column inside one read step. **Expected performance comparison results.** By default `m['key']` again reads the whole `Map` column, as before 26.3, so query shapes that read map elements are slower than on `master`, where the rewrite is enabled: `get_map_value` and the shapes in `tests/performance/map_subcolumns_prewhere.xml` (the setting opt-in was removed from that test so it measures the default path). This is the intended consequence of disabling the rewrite; enabling `optimize_map_element_to_subcolumn` restores the previous behavior. **Out of scope.** With `enable_multiple_prewhere_read_steps = 0` the whole PREWHERE is a single step, so no guard can protect a throwing expression and the repro still throws. This is pre-existing and unrelated to the rewrite: master before #107988 (`cd3c529cd3a`) already throws in that configuration, and it involves `JSON` subcolumns, not `Map`. The new test pins the setting to `1` because it is randomized in CI. **Tests.** `04815_prewhere_guard_throwing_expression_subcolumns` is a regression test for #111879. `04814_optimize_map_element_to_subcolumn_setting` covers the new setting and pins its value, because `clickhouse-test` randomizes it. The tests that assert the rewrite (`04000`, `04513`, `03989`, `04040`, `04207`) enable the setting explicitly. All 177 `prewhere`-named stateless tests were compared against a pre-revert binary and none changes behavior. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new setting `optimize_map_element_to_subcolumn` (disabled by default) that controls rewriting `m['key']` into the `Map` key subcolumn `m.key_<key>`. It is disabled by default because the bucketed `Map` serialization it relies on is being reworked. Also reverted the PREWHERE condition grouping that was introduced for that rewrite, which caused `CANNOT_INSERT_NULL_IN_ORDINARY_COLUMN` when a guard condition and a potentially throwing expression, such as a `CAST`, read subcolumns of the same column, for example a `JSON` or `Map` column. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114150&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114150](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114150+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Aggregation pushdown below JOIN in the Cascades optimizer
signal.text: ## Motivation Queries like `SELECT count() FROM t1 LEFT JOIN t2 ON t1.key = t2.key GROUP BY t1.key` aggregate after the join, although most of the aggregation work can be done on one join input before the join. When the pushed side has few distinct group keys, aggregating first shrinks the join input dramatically. This is the classic *eager aggregation* transformation (Yan & Larson, VLDB 1995). It is not always a win — with nearly-unique group keys the extra aggregation is pure overhead — so it is implemented as a cost-based alternative in the Cascades optimizer: the memo keeps both plans and the cost model picks. ## What is implemented A new transformation rule `AggregationPushdown` with two variants: - **Partial pushdown**: a partial aggregation (`final = false`) below one join input, and a `MergingAggregated` step above the join. The pushed side's group keys are extended with every column of that side referenced by the join condition and residual filter, which makes all rows within a partial group indistinguishable to the join — the join then filters or duplicates whole groups uniformly, and merging `m` duplicated copies of a state equals processing the underlying rows `m` times. This is semantically exact, including for `ALL` joins with fan-out, and requires no uniqueness knowledge. - **Full pushdown**: when every `GROUP BY` key belongs to the pushed side, the join-condition columns are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, and the strictness rules out duplication (`ANY`/`SEMI`/`ANTI` with the join kind matching the pushed side), the aggregation stays final below the join and no merge is needed. When legal, it strictly dominates the partial variant and is emitted instead of it. The legality matrix was derived from the hash-join implementation and independently re-verified during review. Notably, `ANY INNER JOIN` is excluded from the matrix entirely: it emits at most one row per join *key* (`setUsedOnce`), not per probe row, so pushing aggregation below it would change results. The correctness test contains a tripwire scenario against future wrong enablement. Safety rules encoded in the rule (each bails out and leaves the classic plan): the pushed side must never be null/default-extended by the join (an unmatched preserved row would otherwise carry an empty aggregate state and silently contribute nothing); global aggregation (`GROUP BY ()`) is excluded (an empty join output must still produce one row); all aggregate arguments must resolve to the pushed side; `join_use_nulls`/`USING` type-changing joins, grouping sets, `overflow_row`, `max_rows_to_group_by`, in-order aggregation, and name collisions between the two sides are all rejected. Supporting changes: - `MergingAggregatedStep` gets an opt-in `allowInputWithoutAggregatedChunkInfo` mode (join output chunks carry no `AggregatedChunkInfo`, and special column representations must be materialized before merging). The `only_merge` aggregator consumes keys and states positionally, so the rebuilt join projects keys first, then state columns. - **Wire format**: the new mode is serialized as flag bit 64 of `MergingAggregatedStep`, gated behind query plan serialization version 9 (bumped from 8). On a mixed-version cluster the plan fails at plan time with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` (naming `SET cascades_aggregation_pushdown = 0` as the escape hatch) instead of a remote runtime error. Note that the version bump also excludes version-8 replicas from parallel-replicas distributed plans, per the documented design of `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION`. - `AggregatingStep::rebaseOntoInput` re-bases an aggregation onto a new input with a different key set; new memo helpers build the three-level (partial) and two-level (full) alternatives. The rule is gated by the new `EXPERIMENTAL` setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (default on) and takes effect only together with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`. ## Testing - `04926_cascades_aggregation_pushdown`: EXPLAIN plan shapes for both variants and both sides, stat-hint steering in both directions, guard negatives (`FULL`, `ASOF`, `INNER ANY`, `join_use_nulls`, grouping sets, global aggregation, mixed-side aggregate arguments), executed queries with hand-verified values (including fan-out multiplicity and mixed equi+residual conditions), and a 3-join task-budget sanity check. - `04927_cascades_aggregation_pushdown_correctness`: 22+ scenarios, each executed with the optimizer on and off with identical results (fan-out duplication, unmatched rows, multi-key and expression join keys, residual conditions, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`avg`/`uniqExact`/`countIf`, keys from both sides, `SEMI`/`ANTI`/`ANY`, keys-only `GROUP BY`, empty inputs, full-pushdown cases), plus plan-shape canaries proving the pushed plans actually fire for the test's tables. - The full `*cascades*` and `*merging_aggregated*` stateless test sets pass locally on a test-config server. One pre-existing test (`04330_cascades_activation_gating`) pins the new setting off in one case whose own assertion (about subplan broadcasting) would otherwise be made vacuous by the new, cheaper plan. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added aggregation pushdown below `JOIN` (eager aggregation) to the experimental Cascades optimizer as a cost-based alternative: a partial aggregation is performed on one join input before the join and merged above it, or, when the join provably neither duplicates nor null-extends the aggregated side and the join keys are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, the aggregation is pushed below the join entirely. Controlled by the new setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (enabled by default; takes effect only with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`). --- 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115354&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115354](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115354+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: TimeSeries: optional TTL'd recent samples table preferred by PromQL for short time ranges
signal.text: On a large `TimeSeries` table the most frequent queries — alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards — pay primary-key analysis over the whole multi-billion-row samples table and read one full granule per series: on a 71.4B-sample corpus a bare instant selector takes 0.85 s cold to return a few hundred points. When the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a fourth target table (`RECENT SAMPLES`) mimicking the samples table, plus an inner materialized view `.inner_id.recentsamplesmv.<uuid>` copying `id`, `timestamp`, `value` into it on every insert. The recent table adds `PARTITION BY` from `recent_samples_partition_by` (default `toDate(timestamp)`), `TTL toDateTime(timestamp) + toIntervalSecond(<ttl>)` with `ttl_only_drop_parts = 1`, and `recent_samples_index_granularity` (default 8192). PromQL selector reads (`prometheusQuery`, `prometheusQueryRange`, the HTTP API, remote read) prefer it whenever the selector's whole range fits in the TTL window (`min_time >= now() - TTL`) — safe because `ttl_only_drop_parts` drops a part only when all its rows have expired. The preference can be disabled with the new query setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. Off by default; not supported in `Replicated` databases yet (the inner materialized view would get a different UUID on every replica). Measured on a 71.4B-sample / 30-day / 413k-series corpus (40 PromQL queries, cold geomean vs the same binary without the feature): rules 5x (bare selector 0.85 s → 0.03 s, alert 1.9 s → 0.20 s), 30m dashboards 3.5-4.3x, 6h 1.4x, 24h 1.1x, overall 1.6-1.7x; results value-identical to 1e-15. A TTL of ~3 days is the sweet spot: it covers the intraday horizon including `offset 24h` panels at +10% disk, and avoids the regression seen with a 10d TTL, where 7d-range queries switch to the recent table and get 15% slower than on the single sorted part. Hourly partitioning is a wash overall and multiplies part count 24x, so day partitioning is the default. The cost is ingest: a fresh remote-write load of 1.3B samples slows from 324 s to 455-475 s (−30% throughput) — hence opt-in; a dedicated batched sink instead of the generic materialized-view chain is a possible follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TimeSeries` tables can now keep a "recent samples" table: when the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a TTL'd copy of the samples table (partitioned by `recent_samples_partition_by`, by day by default) fed by an inner materialized view, and PromQL queries whose time range fits in the TTL window automatically read from it, making alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards several times faster on large tables. The preference can be disabled with the new query-level setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115441&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115441](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115441+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Docs: Bring the insert deduplication guide up to date
signal.text: The guide `Deduplicating inserts on retries` no longer matched the code. It presented `insert_deduplicate` as the query-level switch and named `insert_select_deduplicate` for `INSERT ... SELECT`. Both are superseded. `deduplicate_insert` is the main switch and defaults to `enable` since 26.2, `deduplicate_insert_select` governs `INSERT ... SELECT`, and `insert_select_deduplicate` is obsolete. The guide also said nothing about asynchronous inserts, although they are deduplicated by default since 26.2. Changes to `docs/concepts/features/operations/insert/deduplicating-inserts-on-retries.mdx`: - New `Settings that control insert deduplication` section. It separates the table-level requirement (a deduplication log) from the query-level one, and lists `deduplicate_insert`, `deduplicate_insert_select`, `insert_deduplication_token`, and `deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views` with their current defaults. - New `Precedence` subsection and a `Legacy and obsolete settings` table, plus a note on how the `compatibility` setting affects the 26.2 defaults. - New `Deduplication for INSERT ... SELECT` section. It defines when a `SELECT` is stable and documents the four values of `deduplicate_insert_select`. - New `Deduplication for asynchronous inserts` section. It covers the per-user-query deduplication granularity, the `DuplicatedAsyncInserts` and `SelfDuplicatedAsyncInserts` events, and the materialized view restriction. - Corrected the statement that non-replicated tables deduplicate by default. `non_replicated_deduplication_window` is `0`. - Corrected the materialized view section. `deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views` is enabled by default since 26.2. Changes to `docs/snippets/_async_inserts.mdx`: the snippet still claimed that deduplication is disabled for asynchronous inserts and must not be enabled with dependent materialized views. That restriction was removed by https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/89140. English content only. The locale trees are generated. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/66003 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/89140 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Documentation (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115575&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115575](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115575+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Don't use JSON skip indexes for combined literal+sub-object subcolumns
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107039 --> `tryMatchJSONSubcolumnToIndex` rejected the sub-object prefix `^`, but not the combined prefix `@`, so ``json.@`a`` was matched against a `JSONAllPaths` index as a path literally named `` @`a` ``. No granule contains such a path, so all granules were pruned: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE isNotNull(json.`@\`a\``); -- 0, wrong SELECT count() FROM t WHERE isNotNull(json.`@\`a\``) SETTINGS use_skip_indexes=0; -- 2 ``` Reject the `@` prefix as well. Both prefixes are now recognised as the prefix character followed by a back-quote (the rule `tryGetPrefixedSubcolumn` uses), so ordinary paths like `` json.`@timestamp` `` keep using the index. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a filter on a combined literal+sub-object `JSON` subcolumn (``json.@`a``) was analyzed against a `JSONAllPaths` skip index: the subcolumn was treated as a path literally named `` @`a` ``, so all granules were skipped and the query returned fewer rows than it should. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114873&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114873](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114873+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Bound the Cascades cluster node count by the distributed-read bucket limit
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A very large `distributed_plan_workers_num` no longer makes the server abort with a `std::length_error` when the experimental `make_distributed_plan` and `enable_cascades_optimizer` are enabled. Such a node count is now rejected with `INVALID_SETTING_VALUE`. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109770 That PR capped the sibling setting the same way. Found by `AST fuzzer (arm_asan_ubsan)`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105987&sha=58887a838b23240918d8f9e717a4bed777136134&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) (unrelated carrier PR). Reproduces deterministically: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t SETTINGS enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, make_distributed_plan = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 9223372036854775807; -- std::length_error in sliceMarksAcrossBuckets; the server dies in a debug build ``` `buildContext` resolves `cluster_node_count` from the internal query parameter, from `distributed_plan_workers_num`, or from the configured worker cluster, checking only for zero. The `ParallelRead` rule passes it through as the read's bucket count, and `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets` sizes a vector to it as its first statement, before the 256 ceiling already threaded in is consulted. `buildContext` now also rejects a resolved count above `max_distributed_read_buckets`, beside the existing zero check. Bounding the resolved value covers all three sources of the count and every consumer of it: the read buckets, the layer budget `FINAL` derives from them, and the exchange fan-out sized from the count. Not inside `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets`, which `FINAL` legitimately calls with `target_buckets * 16`-derived counts before grouping the layers into at most 256 tasks. Behaviour change: a count above 256 that did not reach the plain slicer (`257`, a `FINAL` read, or a worker cluster above 256 replicas) is planned today and is now refused. Such a plan reads serially but can still scatter to that many exchange destinations, which is the memory cost this same ceiling already bounds for the sibling settings. @ davenger, say so if you would rather bound the setting itself (a worker lease count) or clamp. `04320_distributed_plan_read_rejects.sql` gains seven arms: both sources of the count, both read paths, and three positive controls (256 accepted on the plain and `FINAL` paths, plus a rule-based query with a huge `workers_num` untouched). It fails on unpatched master with `server died`, and passed 50/50 runs with the fix. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115398&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115398](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115398+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Pin the ORC corrupt-stripe-footer test blob to valid hexadecimal
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114924 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `04856_orc_corrupt_stripe_footer` builds its fixture with `unhex('<blob>')`, and the blob contained one non-hex character: a `\0` escape that the SQL parser turns into a NUL byte landing on the first half of a hex pair. `unhex`'s result for a non-hex character is [documented as implementation-defined](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/functions/encoding-functions#unhex), so that byte is whatever the current decoder produces - `0xF0` today. It is what truncates the stripe footer. Any legal change to hex decoding moves it, the footer stops being corrupt, ORC parses it cleanly, and both expected error lines disappear while the well-formed control arm keeps passing. The test then silently asserts nothing about the abort that #114924 fixed. On #91993 (optimised hex decode) it fails 57/57 runs with randomized settings and 58/58 without: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=91993&sha=2b0b6ff04a0320e586cea3455a4b9a1d08a5327e&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_debug%2C%20parallel%29 The first commit replaces that escape with the valid digit `f`, which yields the same nibble from a valid character: `unhex(old) = unhex(new)`, so the ORC reader receives a byte-identical 289-byte input and `.reference` is unchanged. Every decoder agrees on all 22 valid hex characters, so the fixture no longer depends on implementation-defined behaviour. Coverage is exactly preserved; no setting is disabled and no tag is added. Because both revisions decode identically, the ORC assertion cannot tell them apart on today's decoder, so a second commit adds a shell guard requiring the literal to be even-length `[0-9a-f]`. Without it, reverting the one-character fix would leave the test green. The guard runs before any side effect and exits non-zero with a message on stderr. Validated by varying only that byte on one binary: `0xF0` (the fix) and `0xFF` both produce the two expected error lines, `0x00` reproduces the CI diff exactly. 50/50 runs pass with and without randomized settings. `02477_single_value_data_string_regression.sql` has the same fragility and is deliberately left alone, since #91993 already rewrites it as an explicit byte literal. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115583&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115583](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115583+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1788` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Bind an unqualified dictGet name to the current database
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85181 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/44301 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46424 The dictionary name of `dictGet` and its variations is resolved against the current database of the server that *evaluates* the function. A shard of a `Distributed` table evaluates it in a session whose current database comes from the cluster configuration — `default` unless `<default_database>` is set — and not from the initiator. So: ```sql USE demo; SELECT code, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code) FROM demo.test; ``` fails on the shards with ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Dictionary (`dict_test`) not found: In scope SELECT __table1.code AS code, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', __table1.code) ... FROM demo.test_local AS __table1. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` and — worse — when a dictionary of the same name also exists in the shard's own database, no error is raised at all and the values of the *wrong* dictionary are returned silently. This binds the name in the analyzer, while the current database of the initiator is still known, so the bound name travels to the shards inside the query tree. The old analyzer already does the same in `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` for the query it sends to the shards. The binding happens after the projection names of the arguments have been calculated, so the column name of the expression stays exactly as it was written by the user: `dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code)`, not `dictGet('demo.dict_test', 'value', code)`. `qualifyDictionaryNameWithDatabase` leaves the name alone when it is already qualified, when it belongs to an XML dictionary, and when no such dictionary exists in the current database — in the last case the name may still be meant for a dictionary that only exists on the shards. Notes: - The `EXPLAIN SYNTAX run_query_tree_passes=1` references of the inverse dictionary lookup tests now show the bound name; only the printed query changes there, no result changes. - Existing test `04054_dictget_unqualified_name_distributed` deliberately runs in the `default` database so that the shard can resolve the unqualified name, which is why it never caught this. The new test runs in the test's own database with `prefer_localhost_replica = 0`, which is what makes the shard query travel over a real connection. - The old analyzer keeps failing here with `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK`, because the header it computes on the initiator keeps the unqualified column name while the query it ships to the shards carries the qualified one. Fixing that needs a separate change, so the new test is tagged `no-old-analyzer`. - `joinGet` has the same defect (`Table default.jt does not exist. Maybe you meant demo.jt?`); its first argument is a table name with temporary-table and access-control semantics of its own, so it is left for a separate change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `dictGet` and its variations in distributed queries: an unqualified dictionary name is now bound to the current database of the initiator, instead of being resolved against the current database of each shard, where it either was not found or resolved to a different dictionary of the same name. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115541&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115541](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115541+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1789` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Reject a bare carriage return in HTTP header names and values
signal.text:
`HTTPHeaderFilter::checkAndNormalizeHeaders` rejected an embedded line feed (`
`) in HTTP header names and values, but not a bare carriage return (``). A lone `` also terminates a header line, so a value such as `tokenX-Injected: evil` could still smuggle a second header into an outgoing request (request/response splitting). This rejects `` alongside `
`, for both header names and values, in the shared filter. This covers the callers that route header names/values through `HTTPHeaderFilter` — the SQL-facing paths where headers are supplied per query: the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, S3/Web configuration, and the DataLake/REST catalogs. Outbound HTTP clients that build headers without this filter (for example the AI providers and the BigQuery client, whose header values come from named collections, OAuth tokens, or DDL configuration) are not affected by this change; enforcing the same invariant at the shared HTTP send path for those clients is left to a separate follow-up. Deferred from #110313 to keep that pull request focused on refactoring. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110313 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reject a bare carriage return (``), in addition to a line feed (`
`), in HTTP header names and values that pass through the HTTP header filter. This closes an HTTP header injection (request/response splitting) gap for features that pass user-provided headers, such as the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, and data lake catalogs. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1790` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add setting to use packed storage for parts in busy partitions
signal.text: Adds the `MergeTree` table setting `max_number_of_parts_in_partition_for_full_part_storage_on_insert`. When a partition already contains at least the configured number of committed active parts, a newly written part that would otherwise use `Full` storage uses `Packed` storage instead. Newly inserted parts in partitions with many active parts are likely to be merged soon, so writing each part file separately provides little value. The setting is disabled by default. It applies across insert sources and part levels, including level 1 parts produced by `optimize_on_insert`; projection parts inherit their parent part's storage type. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `MergeTree` setting `max_number_of_parts_in_partition_for_full_part_storage_on_insert` to use `Packed` storage for newly inserted parts in partitions that already contain many active parts, avoiding a separate-file layout for parts that are likely to be merged soon. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114049&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114049](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114049+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add stateless and fuzzer jobs to the WeeklyCFI workflow
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100419 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112152 The `amd_cfi` build is the only test build with ThinLTO enabled — the same compile profile as official release builds — so besides CFI violations the WeeklyCFI workflow also catches ThinLTO-only behavior differences that no other CI job can see. The latest example is the `__functional` frame-name suppression surfaced by `test_crash_log` in the weekly runs of 2026-07-20 through 2026-08-10 and fixed in #112152. This PR broadens the workflow's coverage: - **Stateless tests** (parallel + sequential lanes, mirroring `amd_debug`). `clickhouse-test` now detects the CFI build from `-fsanitize=cfi` in the `CXX_FLAGS` row of `system.build_options`, so tests that cannot pass in this build profile can carry a `no-cfi` tag (the same generic `no-<flag>` skip mechanism the sanitizer builds use). CFI is deliberately not treated as a sanitizer: it has near-zero runtime overhead, so tests tagged `no-sanitizers` still run under CFI. - **AST fuzzer and BuzzHouse**: fuzzers assert only on crashes, never on exact query output, so the build profile cannot produce false positives there, and fuzzing reaches virtual-call combinations the curated suites never exercise. The fuzzer job configs are shared out into `_common_ast_fuzzer_job_config` / `_common_buzz_fuzzer_job_config`; master and PR workflows are unchanged. Not added, and why: unit tests (`ENABLE_CFI` is incompatible with `ENABLE_TESTS` — ThinLTO is disabled when building tests), performance comparison (it compares against the non-CFI master-head binary, so results are uninterpretable), upgrade/compatibility checks (version and data compatibility are orthogonal to CFI instrumentation), Keeper Jepsen (requires the standalone `clickhouse-keeper` build, which the CFI build omits). **Validation (complete):** the workflow was temporarily switched to a `pull_request` trigger (same approach as #100419) and all ten `amd_cfi` jobs passed on `baf56e50335` — stateless parallel + sequential, integration 4/4, stress, AST fuzzer, and BuzzHouse ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=baf56e50335c45adf2afb691d0a1ef72f49c8bc6&name_0=WeeklyCFI)). The schedule-only trigger is restored in the final commit. The first run surfaced two findings, both filed: a probabilistic server crash in gRPC response compression (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115121) and empty `symbols`/`lines` in `system.trace_log` under this build profile (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115122 — the two `03150` tests are left enabled, so the weekly stateless lane stays red until it is fixed; this workflow does not gate PRs). Workflow: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/workflows/weekly_cfi.yml ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115036&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115036](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115036+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the situation There's a table with json event and two materialized columns from it. signal.title: Use the primary key index for first-tuple-element conditions and `pointInEllipses`
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54805 Follow-up to #112956, which taught `KeyCondition` to use the primary key index for `pointInPolygon(coord, [...])` with a `Point` key column. This PR closes the remaining gaps of the same shape: 1. **Conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column** (`coord.1 < 100`, `tupleElement(coord, 1) = 5`, or access by element name for named tuples) now use the primary key index. Tuple values are ordered lexicographically, so the first element is a non-strictly monotonic function of the tuple; it is analyzed through the regular monotonic-functions chain (`FunctionFirstTupleElementOfKey`), so composed chains such as `coord.1 + 1 <= N` and `NOT` also work. Other elements are not monotonic w.r.t. the tuple order and remain unanalyzed. 2. **`pointInEllipses(x, y, x0, y0, a, b, ...)`** over key columns now uses the primary key (and minmax) index. The analysis stores the union bounding box of the ellipses as a rectangle ring and reuses the existing `pointInPolygon` evaluation unchanged, in both the regular and the lightweight analysis paths. The box follows the function's exact semantics: an ellipse with a non-positive or `NaN` parameter matches no point (the function's own bounding-box check never passes for it); if all ellipses are empty, the condition folds to `ALWAYS_FALSE`; a non-finite box declines the analysis. The atom only ever reports `{maybe, maybe}` or `{no match, maybe}`, so `NOT pointInEllipses` stays correct. 3. **`pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), ...)` and `pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, ...)`** — the point written as the two elements of one tuple-typed key column — resolve to the single-key-column form from #112956, deriving the point's bounding box from the range of the tuple key column. Previously this natural rewrite silently disabled the index. ```sql CREATE TABLE points (coord Point) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY coord; INSERT INTO points SELECT (number, number) FROM numbers(100000); SELECT count() FROM points WHERE coord.1 <= 25000; -- Before: 100000 rows read (full scan). After: 26/100 granules. SELECT count() FROM points WHERE pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, 0., 0., 5000., 5000.); -- Before: full scan. After: 6/100 granules. ``` Note: the reference outputs of the two new tests were computed analytically (counts from the data distribution, granule counts from `index_granularity = 1000`); if CI reports a formatting difference in the `EXPLAIN` lines, I will update the references from the CI output. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Use the primary key index for conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `coord.1 < 100` for a table ordered by a `Point` column), for `pointInEllipses` over key columns, and for `pointInPolygon`/`pointInEllipses` with the point written as the two elements of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), [...])`). Follow-up to [#112956](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115482&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115482](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115482+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Cascades node count still re-read from ambient context; subquery SETTINGS rejected
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With no stateless worker cluster configured, a scalar subquery that scopes `make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4` in its own `SETTINGS` clause is rejected with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` ("make_distributed_plan with enable_cascades_optimizer cannot determine how many nodes will run the query"). The identical settings on the top-level query run fine and return the right answer.** - **Root cause:** `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount` derives the planning node count from the ambient query context instead of the settings the plan is being built with. This is the same ambient re-read of `distributed_plan_execute_locally` that this PR removes from `createExchangeLookup`, `createDistributedQueryExecutor` and `TaskToHostMap`; the planner-side consumer was left behind. `buildContext` itself takes the plan's value two lines later (`context.distributed_plan_execute_locally = optimization_settings.distributed_plan_execute_locally`, Optimizer.cpp:93), so one function reads the same setting from two different sources. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `optimizeTreeSecondPass` -> `CascadesOptimizer::CascadesOptimizer` -> `buildContext` ([`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp:80`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp#L80)) calls `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount(query_context)` where `query_context` is `CurrentThread::get().tryGetQueryContext()` (Optimizer.cpp:51) -> [`src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1190`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp#L1190)/1193 reads `distributed_plan_workers_num` and `distributed_plan_execute_locally` from that ambient context. For a separately-planned subquery the ambient context is the outer query's, so both settings read their outer values (0/0), the function falls through to the configured worker cluster size (0 on a plain server), and Optimizer.cpp:83 throws. **Affected locations:** - [`src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1193`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/QueryPipeline/DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp#L1193) — getCascadesPlanningNodeCount: ambient read of distributed_plan_execute_locally and distributed_plan_workers_num - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp:80`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/90a20ccf81cd3/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/Cascades/Optimizer.cpp#L80) — buildContext passes the CurrentThread query context, while line 93 uses optimization_settings for the same setting **Impact:** On a server with no `stateless_worker_client` cluster - the configuration the error message itself names as supported for `distributed_plan_execute_locally` - a valid query is refused purely because its distributed-planning settings sit in a subquery's `SETTINGS` clause instead of the outer query's. Where a worker cluster IS configured the query is not refused but is planned for the cluster's node count instead of the requested `distributed_plan_workers_num`, i.e. the wrong parallelism. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `90a20ccf81cd3`). ### How to reproduce ```python On a server with a default config (no `stateless_worker_client` section): CREATE TABLE t1 (key UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY key; CREATE TABLE t2 (key UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY key; INSERT INTO t1 SELECT number FROM numbers(100); INSERT INTO t2 SELECT number FROM numbers(100); -- works, returns 100: SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0; -- same settings scoped to the subquery, fails with SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED: SELECT (SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0); -- repeating both settings on the outer query makes it succeed again, proving the ambient read: SELECT (SELECT count() FROM t1 INNER JOIN t2 ON intDiv(t1.key, 2) = t2.key SETTINGS make_distributed_plan = 1, enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4, enable_parallel_replicas = 0, max_rows_to_group_by = 0) SETTINGS distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 4; Or run: cd tests/integration && pytest test_distributed_plan_subquery_settings/test.py -v ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 100 100 (both the query-level and the subquery-scoped form return 100) ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Client failed! Return code: 88, stderr: Received exception from server (version 26.8.1): Code: 344. DB::Exception: Received from 172.18.0.2:9000. DB::Exception: make_distributed_plan with enable_cascades_optimizer cannot determine how many nodes will run the query. Configure a stateless worker cluster, or set `distributed_plan_workers_num` (also required for `distributed_plan_execute_locally` with ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Take the node count from the settings the plan is built with: add `distributed_plan_workers_num` (alongside the existing `distributed_plan_execute_locally`) to `QueryPlanOptimizationSettings` and have `buildContext` pass those values to `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount`, leaving only the config lookups (worker cluster / discovery service) on the context. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - `getCascadesPlanningNodeCount` also sizes Cloud discovery leases (`#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD`, DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1197); switching its source of `distributed_plan_workers_num` changes that path too and should be reviewed by someone with Cloud context. - DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp:1220 reads `distributed_plan_workers_num` from a context as well; that call is on the execution path where the context is the query's own, so it was not investigated further. Found during automated review of [PR #113422](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113422). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr113422_001` </details> cc @groeneai @alexey-milovidov @davenger (from #113422)

signal.title: Lossy-codec rejection skips partition-key columns; pruning drops matching rows
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With a lossy codec (`SZ3`) on a column used in the partition key, the same predicate returns fewer rows when partition/part pruning is used than when the rows are scanned: `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400` returns 91 while `SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t` over the same table returns 92. 6 of 1000 rows sit in a partition that contradicts their own read-back value.** - **Root cause:** The new check's column set is the sorting key only, although the failure mode it guards against (a value derived from the pre-compression block being stored separately from the lossily-compressed data) applies identically to the partition key, whose value and minmax index are also derived pre-compression. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `MergeTreeData::checkProperties` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033)) iterates only `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()`. `getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()` ([`src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h:247`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h#L247)) is never consulted, so `PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)` with `i CODEC(SZ3(...))` is accepted. The partition value and the part-level `minmax_i.idx` are computed by the writer from the pre-compression block, while the data stream is written lossily - so `KeyCondition` prunes on values the part no longer contains. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033) — new lossy-codec check iterates only getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey() - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1052`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1052) — throw BAD_ARGUMENTS; the message names only the sorting key **Impact:** Silent wrong results: a query whose predicate touches the partition-key column returns fewer rows than the same predicate evaluated over a full scan, and rows are stored in a partition their own value contradicts (so `DROP PARTITION`, `_partition_id` filters and partition-wise merges all act on the wrong rows). No error is raised at any point. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `6c8e5b1397b5f`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a4e07fd3-1f5d-45c5-a666-4202ab5427be) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- no-fasttest: needs sz3 library -- no-random-settings, no-random-merge-tree-settings: SZ3 is lossy and its output depends on how the data -- is split into compressed blocks -- A lossy codec on a column of the partition key: the partition value and the part minmax index are -- computed before compression, so they contradict the values that are read back. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; CREATE TABLE t_lossy_partition_key (k Int64, i Float64 CODEC(SZ3('ALGO_INTERP_LORENZO', 'REL', 0.01))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100); INSERT INTO t_lossy_partition_key SELECT number, number * 1.1 FROM numbers(1000); SELECT countIf(toString(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)) != _partition_id) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3; SELECT countIf(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400; SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 0 91 91 91 91 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 6 91 92 91 92 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Extend the loop's column set to the partition key: iterate over the union of `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()` and `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()`, and generalise the message to name the key that the column belongs to. Alternatively, restrict the PR title/changelog to the sorting key and file the partition-key hole separately. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - Secondary skip indexes on a lossy column are the same shape of hazard (index built pre-compression); three probe shapes failed to produce a divergence because the codec error stayed inside the granule range, so this is unproven rather than ruled out. Found during automated review of [PR #114531](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114531). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114531_001` </details> cc @groeneai @rschu1ze (from #114531)
