signal.title: Shipped sort gate ignores WITH FILL: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1`, any `SELECT ... ORDER BY <col> WITH FILL` fails with `Code: 48. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED)`. The same query on the same binary returns rows with `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 0` (classic parallel replicas) and with `enable_parallel_replicas = 0`.** - **Root cause:** `sortingCanBeShipped` delegates the shippability decision to `SortingStep::isSerializable()` (SortingStep.h:160-163), which inspects only the sort TYPE and `scatter_partitions` - never the sort DESCRIPTION. A `WITH FILL` sort is `Type::Full` with `scatter_partitions == 0`, so it passes the gate although `serializeSortDescription` hard-rejects it. `subtreeIsShippable(parent_node)` cannot catch it either: the unserializable `FillingStep` sits ABOVE the sorting node, outside the checked subtree. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** applyParallelReplicas.cpp:307 accepts the lift when `sortingCanBeShipped` (:377-379) is true -> the sort is cloned into the fragment at :320 -> the fragment is serialized for the replicas -> `SortingStep::serialize` (SortingStep.cpp:730) calls `serializeSortDescription`, which throws for any element with `with_fill` (SortDescription.cpp:310-311). **Affected locations:** - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:379`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L379) — sortingCanBeShipped - gate that lets a WITH FILL sort into the shipped fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:320`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L320) — partial_sorting_node.step = sorting_step->clone() - puts the WITH FILL sort description into the fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h:160`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h#L160) — isSerializable() checks only type and scatter_partitions, not the sort description - [`src/Core/SortDescription.cpp:310`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Core/SortDescription.cpp#L310) — serializeSortDescription throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED for desc.with_fill **Impact:** Every `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` query (with or without LIMIT, with or without INTERPOLATE, with `parallel_replicas_local_plan` 0 or 1) is rejected outright once `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled. `WITH FILL` is a common gap-filling idiom for time-series dashboards, so enabling the setting breaks those queries wholesale. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `a4efc96a3f8ce`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL under plan-based parallel replicas returns the same rows as local execution. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_pr_with_fill; CREATE TABLE t_pr_with_fill (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO t_pr_with_fill SELECT number * 4 FROM numbers(5); SET enable_analyzer = 1; SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1; SET parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1; SET max_parallel_replicas = 3; SET cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost'; SET parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1; SET parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1; -- CI randomizes automatic_parallel_replicas_mode; pin the manual mode so the split engages. SET automatic_parallel_replicas_mode = 0; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_replicas = 0; SELECT '---'; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2; DROP TABLE t_pr_with_fill; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19020. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) (query 14, line 20) (in query: SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2;) ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Reject a sort whose description carries `WITH FILL` before shipping it. Narrow fix: add `&& std::none_of(desc.begin(), desc.end(), [](const auto & c) { return c.with_fill; })` to `sortingCanBeShipped`. Broader fix (also covers `tryMakeDistributedSorting` and any future consumer): make `SortingStep::isSerializable()` return false when any element of `result_description`/`prefix_description` has `with_fill`, mirroring the check `serializeSortDescription` already enforces. Trade-off: the broader fix costs read-in-order for WITH FILL queries under plan-based parallel replicas - the same state as before this PR. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - A window pre-sort WITHOUT `PARTITION BY` (`OVER (ORDER BY a)`) is also newly shipped by this rule and is not covered by 04909 (which only tests the excluded partitioned case). It planned cleanly in EXPLAIN here, but could not be executed locally. Found during automated review of [PR #114315](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114315). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114315_001` </details> cc @devcrafter @nickitat (from #114315)
signal.author: clickgapai

signal.title: ReplicatedMergeTree replica becomes permanently readonly (Code 122) when power loss reverts an applied ALTER's local metadata commit; force_restore_data / RESTART REPLICA / RESTORE REPLICA all fail to recover
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong When a `ReplicatedMergeTree` replica applies an `ALTER` (its `/replicas/<r>/metadata_version` znode is durably advanced in [Zoo]Keeper) but the local side of that commit — the rename that replaces `metadata/<db>/<table>.sql` — is reverted by a power loss, the replica can never start again: `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread` fails initialization with `Code: 122` `Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and logs `Initialization failed, table will remain readonly`. The state is permanent across restarts, and none of the documented recovery paths repair it: | Recovery attempt | Result | |---|---| | restart the server | same `Code: 122`, still readonly | | `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t` | still readonly | | `flags/force_restore_data` + restart | still readonly (the flag only skips part sanity checks) | | `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` | refuses: `Replica path is present at ... - nothing to restore` | The only way out is `SYSTEM DROP REPLICA` plus re-creating the replica (or hand-editing the `.sql` file to match ZooKeeper). The window is real on default settings: the `ALTER`'s local metadata commit is `writeMetadataFile` of an fsynced `.sql.tmp` (`fsync_metadata = 1` covers only the file content) followed by `DatabaseAtomic::commitAlterTable` doing `renameExchange`/`replaceFile` with no fsync of the file or parent directory — the same never-made-durable commit rename described in #111348, and the code itself carries `/// NOTE: replica will be lost if server crashes before the following rename` right at that spot. On ext4 the rename becomes durable only when the journal happens to commit, so a power cut within that interval rolls the local file back to the pre-`ALTER` structure while the replica's own `metadata_version` znode (updated durably in Keeper as part of applying the `ALTER_METADATA` entry) stays advanced. On the next start the replica's recorded metadata version claims the new structure while the local file carries the old one, and the attach thread refuses. A normal lagging replica (killed before applying the `ALTER`) recovers fine — its local structure and its `metadata_version` znode are consistently old, so the queued `ALTER_METADATA` entry replays. The brick needs exactly the torn state this unfsynced rename produces: znode ahead, local file behind. Since initialization refuses before the queue is even loaded, the `ALTER_METADATA` replay that would repair the structure never gets a chance to run. Secondary effects observed while the replica sits in this state: its `/replicas/<r>/parts` set keeps hundreds of stale entries for parts that no longer exist locally (the startup fetch-or-remove reconciliation also never runs), and the broken local parts accumulate in `detached/`. Observed organically first: a 3-replica cluster under a concurrent INSERT/mutation/DDL workload where one replica's data directory sat on a dm-flakey device that lost power (drop_writes + remount) while the other replicas and Keeper stayed durable — 2 of 5 such runs on 26.8 ended with the recovered replica permanently readonly with `Code: 122`. The deterministic reproduction below simulates only the rename rollback, which is what the device power loss does by itself. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — 26.8.1.1708 (official master build), deterministic with the reproduction below; also observed under real device power loss. ### How to reproduce Two `ReplicatedMergeTree` replicas (`r0`, `r1`) of one table over one Keeper, each server with its own data directory: ```sql -- on both replicas: CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/t', '{replica}') PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id; -- on r0: INSERT INTO t SELECT number, number, 0 FROM numbers(100); ``` 1. Save a copy of r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. 2. `ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c UInt32` (on either replica); wait until r1's `t.sql` contains the new column (the `ALTER_METADATA` entry applied; r1's `/replicas/r1/metadata_version` znode advanced). 3. Kill r1's server (`kill -9` — any crash). 4. Write the saved pre-`ALTER` content back into r1's `metadata/default/t.sql`. This simulates the power-loss rollback of the never-fsynced commit rename (#111348's mechanism); under a real device power cut inside the filesystem journal window this step happens by itself. 5. Start r1. r1 logs `ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread: Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure` and `system.replicas.is_readonly` stays `1` forever. `SYSTEM RESTART REPLICA t`, the `flags/force_restore_data` flag and `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t` all fail as in the table above. A control run without step 4 recovers to `is_readonly = 0` immediately. ### Expected behavior An applied `ALTER` whose local metadata commit was lost to power loss leaves the replica in a state its own queue already knows how to repair — the replica's structure is simply behind ZooKeeper's. The replica should reconcile the local metadata from ZooKeeper (or reapply the `ALTER_METADATA` diff) instead of refusing initialization forever, or at minimum `force_restore_data` / `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA` should cover this state. Alternatively, making the metadata commit rename durable (fsync the parent directory when `fsync_metadata` is enabled) closes the window at its source. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` <Error> default.t (ReplicatedMergeTreeAttachThread): Initialization failed, table will remain readonly. Error: Code: 122. DB::Exception: Table columns structure in ZooKeeper is different from local table structure. Local columns: ... ``` `SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA t`: ``` Code: 36. DB::Exception: Replica path is present at /clickhouse/tables/t/replicas/r1 - nothing to restore. If you are sure that metadata is lost and that replica path contains some garbage, then use SYSTEM DROP REPLICA query first.. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct open reports of the same unfsynced-commit-rename mechanism with different consequences: #111348 (table-level `DROP`/`RENAME`/`EXCHANGE` on an Atomic database silently revert) and #111802 (`ON CLUSTER` DDL marked finished in Keeper while one host's local effect is lost, never retried). This report is the `ReplicatedMergeTree` column-`ALTER` flavor, where the outcome is not a silent revert but a replica that permanently refuses to initialize, with no working documented recovery short of dropping and re-creating the replica.
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Parts written by an INSERT concurrent with DROP PROJECTION keep the dropped projection; after any mutation CHECK TABLE permanently fails with UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` that is still running when `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PROJECTION` commits keeps using its metadata snapshot from query start, so the parts it writes after the drop still materialize the dropped projection (`.proj` directory on disk and an entry in the part's `checksums.txt`). Nothing ever reconciles those parts: the drop's cleanup mutation was created before their block numbers, so it never rewrites them, and every later ordinary mutation hardlinks the orphaned `.proj` directory into the new mutated part. Beyond the false alarm, merges are blocked wherever affected and clean parts coexist in one partition: merge assignment refuses ranges whose parts have differing projection sets, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `OPTIMIZE ... PARTITION` permanently fail with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE` (`Parts have different projection sets: {} in '...'`), and the partition can never merge down. In that mixed state nothing non-destructive heals it: `DETACH PARTITION` + `ATTACH PARTITION` re-attaches the part still carrying the orphaned `.proj` (renumbered, still failing `CHECK`), `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR PROJECTION <dropped name> IN PARTITION` completes without removing the directories, and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. `OPTIMIZE FINAL` heals only the uniform case where every part in the partition carries the same orphaned projection set (they merge together and the merge drops the unknown projection). The lasting symptom appears as soon as any mutation rewrites such a part: `CHECK TABLE` permanently fails for the mutated part with `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` (`Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj`), although every data file is intact and all rows are readable. The un-mutated ancestor part passes `CHECK TABLE` (it is covered by the unknown-projection tolerance), so the table degrades from "checks clean" to "permanently reports broken parts" at the first mutation, which for an operator is a corruption alarm that never clears. On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the background part-check thread (`ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix`) logs the same `Part has broken projections` for the part, on every replica that has it. The unknown-projection tolerance in `checkDataPart` (added for parts that legitimately carry a projection dropped while they were detached) removes the unknown `.proj` entries from the in-memory checksums and sets `is_broken_projection` with a comment saying the caller can then handle it gracefully — but the entries are not erased from `projections_on_disk`, so the `require_checksums && !projections_on_disk.empty()` branch right below throws `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` anyway (`src/Storages/MergeTree/checkDataPart.cpp`, "Found unexpected projection directories"). A mutated part takes the `require_checksums` path, which is why the throw fires exactly for the mutation descendants. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Reproduces on 26.8.1.1708 (official master build) and on 26.4.1.1, so it is long-standing, and on both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree` (2-replica cluster: `CHECK TABLE` returns 0 on both replicas). ### How to reproduce Against any running server (the race window is the INSERT's runtime, ~5 s here, so the interleaving is reliable): ```bash clickhouse-client -q "CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id" clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t ADD PROJECTION p1 (SELECT part, sum(val) GROUP BY part)" # slow INSERT: the metadata snapshot is taken at query start clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, sleepEachRow(0.05)*0 + number, 0 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS max_block_size=10, min_insert_block_size_rows=10, max_insert_threads=1" & sleep 1.5 # DROP PROJECTION commits while the INSERT is still running clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t DROP PROJECTION p1" wait # any ordinary mutation over the affected parts clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t UPDATE val = val + 1 WHERE id < 50 SETTINGS mutations_sync=2" clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t" # 100 - data is fine clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1" # 0 clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=0" | grep $'\t0\t' ``` The same end state is reached with asynchronous mutations (`mutations_sync=0`); the synchronous form above is only for determinism. In this repro all parts of the partition carry the orphaned projection, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` merges them and heals the check. When the partition mixes affected and clean parts (one more concurrent INSERT after the drop is enough), `OPTIMIZE` fails with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE: Parts have different projection sets` and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. It survives server restarts. ### Expected behavior Either the INSERT does not materialize a projection that was dropped before its parts were committed, or parts that legitimately carry a since-dropped projection keep passing `CHECK TABLE` after mutations, matching the graceful-handling intent already present in `checkDataPart` for the un-mutated case. A part whose data files are all intact must not be reported broken forever, and its presence must not permanently block merge assignment in its partition. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0_8_8_0_12 0 Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) (version 26.8.1.1708 (official build)) ``` On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the same error surfaces through the background part check: ``` Part `0_7_7_0_11` has broken projections. It will be ignored. Broken projections info: Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) 5. DB::checkDataPart(...) 7. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartImpl(String const&, bool) 8. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix(String const&, std::optional<long>*, bool) 9. DB::StorageReplicatedMergeTree::checkDataNext(std::shared_ptr<DB::IStorage::DataValidationTasksBase>&) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct from #100413: that issue covers a fetch-side flavor where `checksums.txt` references a `.proj` directory that was never transferred (`NO_FILE_IN_DATA_PART`). Here no detach, attach or fetch is involved — an `INSERT` racing `DROP PROJECTION` plus one mutation is enough, and the direction is inverted: the `.proj` directory exists on disk but is unknown to the table metadata.

signal.title: Record TopK-filtered granules in the query condition cache
signal.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Granules fully filtered by the dynamic threshold of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) read are now recorded in the query condition cache, so repeat runs of such queries skip them at the mark-selection stage instead of re-reading and re-filtering most of the table. On the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes (`SELECT SearchPhrase FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> '' ORDER BY EventTime LIMIT 10`), a warm run drops from ~95M rows / ~12000 granules read to ~1.3M rows / ~160 granules, and from ~15–30 ms to ~8 ms on a 96-core machine. The `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) optimization pushes a dynamic `__topKFilter` threshold into the `MergeTree` read as a PREWHERE, dropping rows that cannot beat the running top-N. But the granules it emptied were never recorded in the query condition cache: the PREWHERE write path in `MergeTreeSelectProcessor::read` rejects non-deterministic conditions, and `__topKFilter` is one. Only the downstream WHERE `FilterTransform` wrote entries, at whole-chunk granularity, which learns almost nothing (a single surviving row voids the attribution of the whole chunk) — measured on hits, warm runs still selected 11766 of 12348 granules and re-read ~95M of 100M rows. The original out-of-tree build of this optimization (PR #81944, commit `2e2f594308f4` plus the follow-up making the TopN dynamic filters deterministic and reusable for the cache) recorded them and skipped ~98% of granules on warm runs — that is the 2–3x Q24/Q26 gap measured in issue #114639. Recording these granules is sound: for a fixed plan and data, the running threshold only tightens, so a granule none of whose rows survive the filter contains no row that could reach the final top-N, regardless of the threshold trajectory. The entries are keyed with the TopK plan salt (`TopKFilterInfo::condition_hash`: sort column, type, `LIMIT`, direction, `NULLS` direction, collation locale, number of sort columns, and the part-set snapshot), mirroring what the WHERE write path already does since #104478/#110507 — only the same TopK plan over the same part set ever reuses them. Changes: - `isDeterministicAllowingTopKFilter` (two identical static copies in `updateQueryConditionCache.cpp` and `ReadFromMergeTree.cpp`) moved into `VirtualColumnUtils`. - The TopK salt is plumbed to the reader via `MergeTreeReaderSettings::query_condition_cache_top_k_salt`. - The PREWHERE write path accepts a `__topKFilter`-bearing condition when the salt is present, folding the salt into the cache key. Any other non-deterministic condition is still never cached. - The PREWHERE consult path (`filterPartsByQueryConditionCache`) applies the salt exactly when the PREWHERE contains `__topKFilter`, so the keys match the write side; deterministic user PREWHERE conditions keep using plain, unsalted entries shared with non-TopK queries. - `04217_query_condition_cache_topk` and `04242_query_condition_cache_topk_collate` pin exact cache entry counts, which double (each TopK plan now writes a WHERE entry and a PREWHERE entry per part). - New test `04891_query_condition_cache_topk_prewhere_granules` isolates the PREWHERE write path with a WHERE-less TopK query (on current master such a query writes no cache entries at all), asserts that the ASC and DESC plans do not share granule decisions, and that a warm run selects fewer marks. - New performance test `topk_query_condition_cache.xml` with the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes over `hits_100m_single`. Measured on the 100M-row single-part ClickBench `hits` (96-core aarch64, hot, interleaved runs): warm Q24/Q26 at 0.007–0.009 s, on par with the original bench-opt build (0.009–0.011 s), against 0.015–0.03 s for current master; warm runs read 159 of 12348 granules against master's 11766. A first run with an empty cache shows no measurable overhead (0.016–0.019 s with the mechanism on and off). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114639 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110507 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114659&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114659](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114659+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Text index: fix wrong result when a LIKE pattern contains an invalid backslash escape
signal.text: The index-side tokenizers drop a backslash which does not form a valid LIKE escape sequence, while row-level matching keeps it as a literal, so the index searched for a token the value never produced and pruned granules holding matching rows. Index analysis now declines such patterns and falls back to row-level evaluation. Fixes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115578. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix invalid backslash escape characters in text, tokenbf_v1 and ngrambf_v1 indexes. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115634&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115634](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115634+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add --dump-schema option to clickhouse-client and clickhouse-local
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/60681 Adds a `--dump-schema[=<db1,db2,...>]` option that dumps `CREATE DATABASE`/`CREATE TABLE`/`CREATE DICTIONARY`/`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`/`CREATE VIEW` statements for one or more databases, or all non-system user databases if no value is given, to stdout, then exits — similar to `pg_dump --schema-only`. Tables are ordered (via `TablesDependencyGraph`, the same class `DatabaseCatalog` uses to load tables at startup and backups use to order their restore; ties within a level broken by `(database, name)` for determinism) using every dependency signal `system.tables` exposes, combined: `loading_dependencies_*` (dictionaries), inverted `dependencies_*` (a materialized view's source — recorded only on the source row, not the view), `target_database`/`target_table` (a materialized view's `TO` target, explicit or implicit), and — since the server tracks none of this for plain views at all (`DROP TABLE` on a view's source succeeds even with the view still referencing it) — a best-effort scan of each view's stored, server-formatted `SELECT` text for other dumped tables' names. A genuine dependency cycle is a clear error rather than being silently reordered. This is entirely a client-side feature: `system.tables.create_table_query` and `SHOW CREATE DATABASE` already give the server-computed DDL text, so no server-side or wire-protocol changes are needed — the new code (`src/Client/SchemaDumper.{h,cpp}`) just issues a couple of queries over the existing connection (same pattern as `Suggest.cpp`) and prints the results in dependency order. `--dump-schema` also accepts a comma-separated database list (`--dump-schema=db1,db2`), and two modifiers: - `--dump-schema-exclude=db1,db2` dumps all user databases except the listed ones (rejected if combined with an explicit database list — the two are mutually exclusive ways of selecting the same thing). - `--dump-schema-dir=<path>` writes one `<database>.sql` file per dumped database into that directory (created if it doesn't exist, e.g. `mkdir clickhouse-lab && clickhouse-client --dump-schema --dump-schema-exclude=... --dump-schema-dir=clickhouse-lab`) instead of writing everything to stdout. Database names are escaped with `escapeForFileName` before being used as filenames; two target databases whose escaped names collide case-insensitively are rejected unconditionally (regardless of the destination filesystem's actual case sensitivity — reliably probing that portably isn't worth it when the point of a dump is to be replayed somewhere else later anyway), rather than one silently overwriting the other's file. Per-database write failures are detected instead of reported as success, and when a table in one dumped database depends on a table in another, the files (and their confirmation lines) are ordered — and a note printed — so replaying them in the printed order works; a database-level circular dependency (distinct from, and not implied by, a table-level cycle) is rejected with a clear error since no file order could satisfy it. A few things worth calling out for review: - Implicit materialized-view storage tables are excluded from the dump (recreated automatically by their owning `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` statement) — but only when confirmed to be a *live* materialized view's own target with the generated-name shape (`.inner_id.*`/`.inner.*`), not merely name-shaped like one, so a real user table literally named `` `.inner.foo` `` stays in the dump. Orphaned mid-refresh leftovers (`.tmp.inner_id.*`/`.tmp.inner.*`) are filtered by name, since they're never any live target. - `--dump-schema` forces non-interactive mode (like `--query`/`--queries-file`) and is rejected if combined with either of them, so its stdout is never mixed with an interactive banner, warnings, or another query's output. For `clickhouse-local`, it's also rejected combined with `--file`/`--structure`. `--dump-schema-exclude`/`--dump-schema-dir` are rejected if `--dump-schema` itself isn't given — all validated in `processConfig()`, before `connect()`, so a plain argument mistake fails fast instead of after a connection attempt (which could otherwise block on an interactive password prompt). - Verified end-to-end via real replays into a fresh `clickhouse-local` instance: a source table with a materialized view (implicit storage), a dictionary, a plain view, a view-on-view chain, and an explicit `TO` target, named so that alphabetical order alone would produce an unreplayable dump without the fix; single/list/exclude/all-databases selection; `--dump-schema-dir` output with a genuine cross-database dependency; the case-insensitive filename collision guard (using a case-sensitive APFS volume to stand in for a Linux source, confirming both that `Foo`/`foo` coexist there and that the guard fires when dumping them); and all the rejection cases (unknown database, combined with `--query`/`--file`/`--structure`, list + exclude together, dir without `--dump-schema`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `--dump-schema[=<db1,db2,...>]` option to `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` that dumps `CREATE DATABASE`/`CREATE TABLE`/`CREATE DICTIONARY`/`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`/`CREATE VIEW` statements for the given database(s), or all user databases if no value is given, to stdout in dependency order, then exits — similar to `pg_dump --schema-only`. `--dump-schema-exclude=<db1,db2,...>` skips the listed databases when dumping all of them, and `--dump-schema-dir=<path>` writes one `<database>.sql` file per dumped database into that directory instead of stdout. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114098&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114098](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114098+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix a renamed and dropped column being read from the wrong file while the mutation is pending
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114562 ## Problem A column that is renamed, dropped and added again in one `ALTER` silently returns the **dropped** column's data instead of its own default, while the mutation is still pending: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64, h UInt8 DEFAULT 0) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() SETTINGS min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0, min_rows_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO t SELECT number + 100, 0 FROM numbers(1000); SET alter_sync = 0; -- mutation left pending ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b, DROP COLUMN b, ADD COLUMN b UInt64 DEFAULT 7; SELECT count(), min(b), max(b) FROM t; -- 1000 100 1099 <- the old `a` values -- expected: 1000 7 7 ``` No error and nothing in the log; it affects `Wide` and `Compact` parts alike. The added `b` is a different column from the one that was dropped, so its rows have to come from its `DEFAULT`. **Scope.** This fixes the answer while the mutation is pending. Once the mutation has materialised a `Wide` part still returns the dropped column's data — a separate, pre-existing defect that lives in `MutateTask`, see the follow-ups at the end. ## Root cause `AlterConversions` records a pending drop under the name the command used: ```cpp else if (command.type == DROP_COLUMN) { dropped_columns.emplace(command.column_name); } ``` while every consumer of `isColumnDropped` asks about a column under the name it has **in the part**: - `IMergeTreeReader::isColumnDroppedByPendingMutation` takes the name out of `columns_to_read`, which is built from `getColumnInPart` and therefore already has the rename mapping applied (`IMergeTreeReader.cpp:81`); - `injectRequiredColumnsRecursively` passes `column_name_in_part` (`MergeTreeBlockReadUtils.cpp:119`). Without a rename the two names are identical, so the hazard those checks exist for — a column dropped and re-added under the same name, whose data in the part is stale — behaves correctly. That is why this was never noticed. With a rename they diverge: the part holds `a`, the drop is recorded for `b`, the check asks about `a`, finds nothing, and the reader streams the `a` file into the new `b`. ## Solution Consume the ordering in `DROP_COLUMN`, where both halves of it are needed anyway. Commands arrive as issued, so the renames recorded so far are exactly those preceding the drop; the entry that gives the drop its part-side name is also the entry the drop makes obsolete, so one lookup does both: ```cpp auto name_in_part = command.column_name; auto it = std::ranges::find(rename_map, command.column_name, &RenamePair::rename_to); if (it != rename_map.end()) { name_in_part = it->rename_from; rename_map.erase(it); } dropped_columns.emplace(std::move(name_in_part)); ``` Every existing caller of `isColumnDropped` already passes a part-side name, so all of them become correct at once and none of them changes. Retiring the mapping matters on its own. `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b` used to leave **two** entries pointing at `b` — from the dropped `a` and from the live `c` — and the lookup returns whichever comes first, so `b` read the wrong column. Writing a `RenamePair` as `to <- from`, where `to` is the name in the metadata and `from` the name in the part, and remembering that `dropped_columns` now holds part-side names: | # | command | what happens | `rename_map` | `dropped_columns` | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | `RENAME a TO b` | not chained, insert | `[b <- a]` | `{}` | | 2 | `DROP b` | `b <- a` gives the part's `a` and is erased in the same step | `[]` | `{a}` | | 3 | `RENAME c TO b` | `b` is free, insert | `[b <- c]` | `{a}` | `getColumnOldName("b")` then answers `c`, and `a` stays dropped so nothing reads it. Both halves are needed to get this right: | variant | `min(b), max(b)`, want `5000 5999` | |---|---| | `master` | `100 1099` — the **dropped** column's data | | part-side drop only | `0 0` — the default | | both | `5000 5999` ✔ | ### Why in the drop and not when the name is taken over Retiring the entry in `RENAME_COLUMN` instead — erase whatever maps onto the new target and is already dropped — reads as the more targeted fix, and it is where the first two commits of this PR put it. It has to cover two paths, though, because a rename can reach the freed name through a chain: `RENAME c TO d, RENAME d TO b` updates the existing `d <- c` entry in place rather than appending, so an erase placed on the appending path alone leaves `[b <- a, b <- c]` again. That variant does not misread — it fails outright, because `b` resolves to the dropped `a` and the part-side name reaches the storage snapshot: ``` Code: 16. DB::Exception: There is no column a in table. (NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE) ``` Reaching it takes `ReplicatedMergeTree`: a single `ALTER` rejects transitive renames (`Transitive renames in a single ALTER query are not allowed`), and `StorageMergeTree::alter` always waits for the previous mutation before a metadata change (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:548`, *"alters should be executed in sequential order"*), so two of them can never both be pending there. Doing it in the drop is the same thing one step earlier and needs no case analysis: a mapping onto a dropped name simply never exists, so `RENAME_COLUMN` has nothing to clean up and the chained path needs no special handling. The two were measured equivalent on both the read path (all of `04872`) and the materialisation path (the mutation run to completion with `alter_sync = 2` for `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, ADD b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b, RENAME c TO b`, `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` and the chained Replicated case — byte-identical results). ### Why not fix it in the reader Checking the renamed-to name in the reader as well looks equivalent and is wrong. The opposite command order produces exactly the same `AlterConversions` state, and `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames` already pins the required behaviour for it: ```sql ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN value2_old, RENAME COLUMN value2 TO value2_old; ``` Here the drop hit a *different* column that merely carried that name, and `value2`'s data is live and must be readable as `value2_old`. The only thing separating the two situations is where the drop sits among the renames, which the readers cannot see. Measured with the reader-side variant applied, live data is replaced by defaults: ``` dropped, then the name reused by a rename -1000 100 1099 +1000 0 0 ``` Hence the ordering has to be consumed at construction time. ### Tests `tests/queries/0_stateless/04872_read_renamed_then_dropped_and_readded_column.sh` — seven cases: the defect on `Wide` and on `Compact`, the `RENAME/DROP/RENAME` case above and its chained variant, plus three controls that must not move — drop-and-re-add without a rename (what the check was written for), a pending rename with no drop, and the mirror case. The chained case runs the `ALTER`s with the partition detached and then attaches the part carrying the old column names to a table whose merges are stopped, so the mutations stay unapplied while it is read — the same shape as `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`. Verified on a local server that it is load-bearing: with the retirement placed on the appending path of `RENAME_COLUMN` it fails with `NO_SUCH_COLUMN_IN_TABLE`, while the non-chained control passes either way. Because the two possible wrong answers fail in opposite directions, the result is checked three ways: | variant | the defect | the mirror case | |---|---|---| | `master` | `1000 100 1099` ✗ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | | reader-side variant | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 0 0` ✗ | | this change | `1000 7 7` ✔ | `1000 100 1099` ✔ | `01281_alter_rename_and_other_renames`, `01278_alter_rename_combination`, `03905_chained_rename_column_mutation`, `04053_alter_add_rename_column_in_single_query` and `04011_detach_rename_attach_column` all pass. ### Notes for reviewers - **The retirement relies on the command sequence reaching `AlterConversions` without gaps, and it does.** Metadata mutations are exempt from every `params` switch — `needIncludeMutationToSnapshot` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:653`, *"Metadata mutations must be included into the snapshot regardless of the parameters"*) and `addSupportedCommands` (`MergeTreeData.cpp:704`) both admit `RENAME_COLUMN` and `DROP_COLUMN` unconditionally, so no caller can ask for a snapshot holding the renames but not the drops. Per-part filtering then takes a contiguous suffix, never a middle slice: both `getOnFlyMutationCommandsForPart` implementations walk in reverse and *stop* at the first mutation at or below the part's version (`StorageMergeTree.cpp:3549`, `ReplicatedMergeTreeQueue.cpp:2355`). A gap would need `RENAME a TO b` in the window with `DROP b` cut out, but the drop is the newer of the two, so cutting it necessarily cuts the rename that created the entry as well. Order is a documented contract: *"@return list of mutation commands in order: oldest to newest"* (`MergeTreeData.h:617`). The chained-rename collapsing that predates this PR rests on the same property. The replicated loop iterates by `mutation_version` while testing `alter_version`, so the suffix is contiguous only if the two are co-monotonic, and they are: the single site that creates a mutation entry with `alter_version != -1` (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7092`) does so in one `tryMulti` that also carries `set /metadata` with a CAS on the current metadata version (`StorageReplicatedMergeTree.cpp:7001`, and `alter_version` is that version plus one) and `set /mutations` with a CAS on its own version. Either CAS makes two of them serialise, and the sequential number is assigned inside that atomic commit, so the k-th alter mutation to commit gets both the larger sequence number and the higher metadata version. `mutate` — the other creator — leaves `alter_version` at `-1` and is handled by the loop's other branch. Confirmed by reading the raw znodes through `system.zookeeper`: with `ALTER UPDATE`s interleaved between the renames the metadata subsequence is `1, 2, 3, 4` in znode order, and ten concurrent renames from separate clients land as `alter_version` `1..9` matching the znode sequence exactly. - `isColumnDropped` now consistently answers about part-side names. That matches all four existing call sites, so it is a fix rather than a contract change for them, but a future caller holding a metadata name would have to resolve it first. - **Overlaps with #114562, in a way that is safe in either merge order.** That PR adds a second lookup in the empty-candidate accounting loop of `injectRequiredColumns`, mapping a part name forward to its renamed-to name and testing the drop under that, so that a single-statement `RENAME a TO b, DROP b` is recognised as accounted for. This change makes the *first* lookup answer that correctly, because the drop is then already recorded as `a`, so the second lookup becomes dead code once both are in. It is deliberately left in place here rather than removed pre-emptively: while only #114562 is merged the second lookup is what makes that case work. A small cleanup to delete it belongs after this merges. signal.title: Check access rights in EXPLAIN QUERY TREE and EXPLAIN SYNTAX
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78938 `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE` and `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` (in the analyzer) resolve the query and dump table metadata such as column names and types, but unlike `EXPLAIN PLAN` they do not build a query plan. The `SELECT` access check that the planner performs in `prepareBuildQueryPlanForTableExpression` was therefore skipped, so a user with no privileges could read the column names and data types (including `Enum` element lists) of tables they are not allowed to access, while `SELECT`, `EXPLAIN PLAN` and `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` are correctly rejected. This adds a `SELECT` access check for every table referenced anywhere in the query tree (including tables inside subqueries in expressions such as `WHERE x IN (SELECT ... FROM t)`). The check mirrors the planner: it validates access to the columns that are actually read, with the trivial-count fallback (access is granted if at least one column is accessible) for queries that read no specific column, e.g. `SELECT count() FROM t`. As a result, a user with a column-level grant sees the same behavior as for a plain `SELECT` (`EXPLAIN QUERY TREE SELECT granted_col FROM t` is allowed, `... other_col ...` is denied). `buildQueryTree` only builds the tree; table identifiers are bound to storages and columns are resolved by the query analysis pass. The check runs on the resolved tree: on `query_tree` directly when the passes already resolved it, or on a throwaway resolved copy otherwise (e.g. `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE run_passes = 0`, which intentionally dumps the unresolved tree, so the tree that gets dumped is unchanged). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `EXPLAIN QUERY TREE` and `EXPLAIN SYNTAX` not checking access rights on the referenced tables, which allowed a user without privileges to read table column names and data types. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110180&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110180](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110180+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Allow unknown settings in query plan serialization
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114184 Adding a plan setting has meant bumping `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION` and gating the write on it — twice already, for versions 5 and 7 — because the settings of a step were written as a name and a typed binary value. A reader that met a name it did not know could not tell where the value ended, so `QueryPlanSerializationSettings::readBinary` threw `UNKNOWN_SETTING`. That fenced off far more than the feature being added: the name goes into every plan that touches the step, so a setting a given plan cannot even use made that plan unreadable to the previous release. Fencing a feature is what the step registry does, by rejecting an unknown step. Plan settings are now written the way query settings have always travelled between client and server (`SettingsWriteFormat::STRINGS_WITH_FLAGS`): name, flags, and the value as a string of its own length. A reader steps over a name it does not know and keeps its own default for it, and rejects the plan only when the name carries `IMPORTANT` — the flag that already means "affects query results, cannot be ignored by older versions". Which form is written is decided by the version of the stream, which `QueryPlan::serialize` already negotiates as the minimum of ours and the peer's, so a peer below version 9 keeps receiving the old form and nothing changes for it. The plan settings that decide a result rather than a way of producing it are marked `IMPORTANT` accordingly: the row and byte limits of `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` with their overflow modes, the two-level aggregation thresholds, `empty_result_for_aggregation_by_empty_set`, `join_any_take_last_row`, `totals_auto_threshold`, and the two settings that decide how aggregation states are laid out. The existing per-setting gates stay — peers below version 9 still need them — but a setting added from now on needs one only when it belongs in that group. `gtest_query_plan_settings_skippable` covers the round trip of every declared setting type through its string form, the old form at the previous version, an unknown setting being skipped, and an unknown `IMPORTANT` setting being rejected. The 58 stateless tests that set `serialize_query_plan` were run against the new format locally (56 pass; two fail only for want of `s3_disk` and `https_port` in the local server config). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A query plan serialized with `serialize_query_plan = 1` no longer becomes unreadable to a peer that does not know one of the plan's settings: a setting the peer can ignore is skipped, and only one whose absence would change the query result is rejected. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115627&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115627](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115627+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Detect stream filename collisions within a single column
signal.text: `MergeTreeData::checkColumnFilenamesForCollision` only compared stream file names *across* columns. Two streams of one column that render to the same file name were silently deduplicated before that comparison, so the column was accepted at CREATE/ALTER and the part was then written with both streams in one file: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (c Nullable(JSON(`null` Int64))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t VALUES ('{"null":1}'), (NULL); SELECT c FROM t; -- Code: 33. Too many marks in file .../c.null.cmrk2 ... (CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA) ``` The same collision spread over two columns was already rejected, so this only removes an asymmetry. The new branch follows the existing convention: `BAD_ARGUMENTS` at CREATE and ALTER, a logged error on attach so an already broken table still attaches and can be repaired manually. Columns whose streams collide only as *subcolumn* names, not as file names, stay allowed (``Array(Tuple(`size0` UInt64))``, ``Tuple(`a` String, `a.size` UInt64)``) - they read back correctly, and such tables may already exist. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed accepting a column whose two serialization streams map to the same file name (for example ``Nullable(JSON(`null` Int64))`` or ``Tuple(`a` Tuple(`b` UInt64), `a.b` UInt64)``). Such a table was created successfully, but its parts were written with both streams in one file and could not be read, merged or checked. Creating such a column now fails with `BAD_ARGUMENTS`, as a collision between two different columns already did. Existing tables still attach, with the collision logged. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115632&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115632](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115632+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Transform JOIN hash table payload to row major
signal.text: Resolves [#97883](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/97883) Introduce an alternative layout for hash table payload in hash joins, where fixed and contiguous columns under a certain size are transformed into one row-major block of data. Before the change: ``` col1 Int32 col2 String col3 UInt8 col4 Float64 ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ │ .... │ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └────────────┘ └──────────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┘ row N → col1[N], col2[N], col3[N], col4[N] ``` After the change: ``` ROW STORE (col1 + col3 + col4, contiguous per row) col2 String (columnar) ┌──────────┬──────────┬────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ col1 │ col3 │ col4 │ ← row N (record) │ .... │ ← col2[N] ├──────────┼──────────┼────────────┤ ├──────────┤ │ col1 │ col3 │ col4 │ │ .... │ └──────────┴──────────┴────────────┘ └──────────┘ ``` ### Rational: The row-major format allows the output construction to be a tight loop over each column, basically one pointer load and data copy: ``` for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) { const char * row_store_ptr = row_store_ptrs[i]; col->insertData(row_store_ptr + value_offset, value_size); } ``` In comparison the columnar version has to do more work: load columns[j], row_numbers[j], replicated_columns access, insertFrom ... For the following query `SELECT * FROM rs_probe_200m l JOIN rs_right_10m r ON (l.k % toUInt64(10000000 / 0.9)) = r.k FORMAT Null` from `04054_hash_join_with_row_store.sql` the perf counters for `LazyOutput::buildOutput` in `AddedColumns` look as follows: ``` ┌─variant────────────────────────────┬─query_id─────────────────────────────┬─runtime_ms─┬───────instr─┬──────cycles─┬──────cmiss─┬──brmiss─┬───ipc─┬─cmiss_per_kinstr─┬─brmiss_per_kinstr─┐ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 9d2d6886-2ad7-430f-af2c-6c7cd32f3808 │ 1621 │ 11393048228 │ 31974507197 │ 1470246364 │ 5892574 │ 0.356 │ 129.05 │ 0.517 │ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 56b33013-8bec-4d7a-a415-2a06beb14bf6 │ 1633 │ 11547943445 │ 31874206968 │ 1484117664 │ 6265932 │ 0.362 │ 128.52 │ 0.543 │ │ row-major-enabled-multi-threaded │ 65583fa7-9ce0-4426-95eb-977251d38f75 │ 1708 │ 11338601601 │ 31825721703 │ 1468670383 │ 5921051 │ 0.356 │ 129.53 │ 0.522 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 5ff1b154-3c3f-40c6-bae9-f6cf0feafe81 │ 2548 │ 15453833738 │ 58322156979 │ 2636461094 │ 9533242 │ 0.265 │ 170.6 │ 0.617 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 6e92c1d4-8432-4a79-a6cc-85e38232116d │ 2580 │ 15400954730 │ 58683032344 │ 2623136775 │ 9455570 │ 0.262 │ 170.32 │ 0.614 │ │ row-major-disabled-multi-threaded │ 133f384f-c09a-4e12-9e69-85b61272a360 │ 2686 │ 15419169622 │ 59548322941 │ 2647601264 │ 9746405 │ 0.259 │ 171.71 │ 0.632 │ │ row-major-enabled-single-threaded │ 20039e91-b5dc-4b4a-8e22-f4451f6067be │ 30610 │ 9046504977 │ 16964398066 │ 995568814 │ 3235355 │ 0.533 │ 110.05 │ 0.358 │ │ row-major-disabled-single-threaded │ a3f9a822-dae6-45c1-9a4e-63e87a3592e8 │ 56821 │ 15279361788 │ 27940919919 │ 1167368997 │ 4694553 │ 0.547 │ 76.4 │ 0.307 │ └────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┴─────────┴───────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────┘ ``` ### Changes: - A `RowDataStore` that takes a set of columns and lays them in row major format. It exposes access to individual rows and the layout of each row (offset and size of fields in a row). - New `IColumn` interfaces that handle building the output columns from the row store, used manly by `AddedColumns.cpp`. - Two new settings to control the row-major transformation: - min_columns_for_hash_join_row_store: the minimum number of columns that must be suitable to the transformation to apply. - min_rows_ratio_for_hash_join_row_store: Minimum estimated ratio of join output rows to build-side rows to enable transforming hash join payload to row-major. Used in the planner to decide when to enable the optimization. - A runtime feedback loop that tracks the number of hash table matches from a join and feeds it to the next execution of the join instead of relying on the estimated join output: - The match count is only published when the probe phase fully completes. - Only joins that went through the join reorder optimizer get a cache key. - Plans serialized to distributed workers don't collect or use the feedback. ### Limitations: 1. Only supports fixed and contiguous types and nullable version of them. Supporting non fixed rows would make the row-major layout non-uniform between rows and output column construction loop would not be as tight anymore. Also transforming unbounded unfixed types to row major could be very heavy. 2. ColumnReplicated might get materialized. The decision is made based on the column state the join sees in the first block. If it's ColumnReplicated the column is excluded from the row store, if it's not the column is included and it's replicated in a future block it get's materialized. 3. If spilling occurs, the row stored data is split back into columns for now. In a follow up we can make the row store a column and spill it as is. ### Build overhead: | Type | Rows | Columns | avg per worker thread (ms) | |---|---|---|---| | Int64 | 2M | 8 | 28.2 | | Int64 | 1M | 16 | 31.9 | | FixedString(16) | 1M | 8 | 24.6 | | FixedString(16) | 2M | 4 | 21.5 | ### Benchmarks: #### from `04054_hash_join_with_row_store.sql`: | # | Right table | Match | Join | Before (s) | After (s) | Speedup | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 0 | `rs_right_100k` | 0.9 | INNER | 0.265 | 0.237 | 1.12× | | 1 | `rs_right_100k` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.182 | 0.178 | 1.02× | | 2 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.108 | 0.525 | 2.11× | | 3 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.532 | 0.335 | 1.59× | | 4 | `rs_right_100k_nullable` | 0.9 | INNER | 0.350 | 0.249 | 1.41× | | 5 | `rs_right_100k_nullable` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.216 | 0.183 | 1.18× | | 6 | `rs_right_10m_nullable` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.607 | 0.553 | 2.91× | | 7 | `rs_right_10m_nullable` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.698 | 0.357 | 1.95× | | 8 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.9 | FULL | 1.652 | 0.916 | 1.80× | | 9 | `rs_right_10m` | 0.3 | FULL | 1.424 | 0.861 | 1.65× | | 10 | `rs_right_1m_x10` | 0.9 | INNER | 2.239 | 1.554 | 1.44× | | 11 | `rs_right_1m_x10` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.825 | 0.641 | 1.29× | | 12 | `rs_right_1m_nullable_x10` | 0.9 | INNER | 3.771 | 1.820 | 2.07× | | 13 | `rs_right_1m_nullable_x10` | 0.3 | INNER | 1.372 | 0.771 | 1.78× | | 14 | `rs_right_mixed_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 1.596 | 1.249 | 1.28× | | 15 | `rs_right_mixed_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 0.759 | 0.628 | 1.21× | | 16 | `rs_right_wide_10m` | 0.9 | INNER | 6.158 | 1.979 | 3.11× | | 17 | `rs_right_wide_10m` | 0.3 | INNER | 2.563 | 1.111 | 2.31× | ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Introduce an alternative layout for hash table payload in hash joins, where qualifying columns are transformed into one row-major block of data in order to speed up join output reconstruction. Controlled by two new settings: `min_columns_for_hash_join_row_store` (default 3, the minimum number of fixed-size payload columns that triggers the row-major layout; set to 0 to disable) and `min_rows_ratio_for_hash_join_row_store` (default 2, the minimum estimated ratio of join output rows to build-side rows to enable the transformation).

signal.title: Reject a lossy codec on columns backing the partition key
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114406 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115533 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114531 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER TABLE` now reject a lossy codec such as `SZ3` on a column used in the partition key. ### Description Follow-up to #114531, which added this check for the sorting key only. #115533 reported the same problem for the partition key, and @rschu1ze asked for it to be covered too. A partition value and a part minmax index are both computed from the block before compression, so they record the exact input while the data on disk decompresses to a different value. Pruning trusts that metadata and discards parts that do hold matching rows. With `i Float64 CODEC(SZ3('ALGO_INTERP_LORENZO', 'REL', 0.01))` and `PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)` over 1000 rows, 6 rows read back a value contradicting their own partition, and a pruning query returns 91 rows where a full scan returns 92. Not a regression from #114531: the same numbers reproduce on an earlier build. The change extends the existing loop in `MergeTreeData::checkProperties` to the partition-key columns and generalises the message. Per-substream lossiness resolution is reused unchanged, so type wrappers and codec chains behave as before. `CREATE` and `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` both reach the check; `ATTACH` stays exempt, so existing tables stay loadable. Two costs, both already carried by the shipped sorting-key check, verified. The check is keyed on column names, since neither key accessor exposes substreams, so a provably exact key such as `PARTITION BY length(arr)` over `Array(Float64) CODEC(SZ3(...))` is now rejected although only the lossless sizes substream is read (measured: 82611 payload values differ from what was written, yet no row lands in the wrong partition and pruning is exact). And a table created earlier with a lossy partition-key column refuses further `ALTER`s while that codec remains, the metadata entry stalling on an upgraded replica in a mixed-version cluster. Tests were added to `04791_lossy_codec_key_column`: the partition key through a plain expression, through an `Array` element and through a `MATERIALIZED` column, plus the `ALTER` path and accepted cases. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115626&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115626](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115626+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject WITH FILL bounds that do not fit the ORDER BY column type
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109454 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109216 --> `WITH FILL FROM`/`TO` values are converted to a type wide enough for the arithmetic - `Int64` for every integer column type - while the generated values are written into a column of the column's own type, which truncates whatever does not fit its range. A truncated value wraps around, so the filled stream stops being monotonic while the query plan keeps claiming that it is still sorted by the fill columns. `DISTINCT` in order relies on that claim and reads the stream as a sequence of sorted runs, so it deduplicates within wrong ranges: ```sql SELECT count() FROM (SELECT DISTINCT x, s FROM (SELECT toUInt8(5) AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025)); ``` returns `1024` instead of `257` in a release build, because `WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025` over a `UInt8` column generates `1..255, 0, 1..255, 0, ...`. In a debug or sanitizer build the same query aborts in `DistinctSortedStreamTransform` with `Equal values are not contiguous within the range assumed to be sorted`, which is what the AST fuzzer hit: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109454&sha=b0030d87c1f4e4b31d2766c17286e42492a2da94&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29 https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109454 The fuzzer query is unrelated to that pull request; the abort reproduces on `master`: ```sql SELECT DISTINCT x, isZeroOrNull(materialize(true)), s FROM ( SELECT 5 AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC NULLS LAST WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 10 INTERPOLATE (`s` AS concat(s, 'A')) LIMIT 1048576 UNION ALL SELECT 5 AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC NULLS LAST WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025 INTERPOLATE (`s` AS concatAssumeInjective(s, 'A')) LIMIT 1048576 ) ORDER BY s ASC; ``` ### Fix Reject `FROM`/`TO` values that cannot be represented in the type of the `ORDER BY` column with `INVALID_WITH_FILL_EXPRESSION`, next to the existing check that rejects negative bounds for an unsigned column type. This matches how the equivalent `Date`/`DateTime` bound mismatch is already rejected (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/30421). `TO` is an exclusive bound, so it may still be outside of the range as long as the values that filling actually generates fit: `WITH FILL FROM 0 TO 256` over a `UInt8` column keeps generating `0..255`, and so does `WITH FILL FROM 0 TO 257 STEP 3`, which stops at `255`. The last generated value is known up front only when `FROM` and a plain numeric `STEP` are given. Without `FROM` the sequence is anchored at a data value, so which values are generated is known only at execution time: `WITH FILL TO 257 STEP 3` over a `UInt8` column stops at `254` when the data ends at `11` but reaches `256` when it ends at `13`. Still, whenever filling generates anything at all, its last value lands within one step before `TO`, so such a bound is rejected only when even the value one whole step away from `TO` (clamped towards zero, so that anchors close enough to `TO` to generate nothing keep being accepted) does not fit the column type - that is, only when filling provably wraps for every possible anchor. An `INTERVAL` step performs its calendar arithmetic in the column's own native type, so unlike a plain numeric step it wraps around within the column domain and can never reach a `TO` outside of it: filling would generate wrapped-around values forever (it does on current master, e.g. `SELECT toDate(0) AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL FROM toDate(0) TO 70000 STEP INTERVAL 100 YEAR` never terminates). Such a `TO` is therefore rejected regardless of `FROM` - but only when it is out of range in the fill direction. A `TO` out of range against the fill direction (e.g. `ORDER BY d DESC WITH FILL TO 70000 STEP INTERVAL -1 YEAR` over a `Date` column) is a guaranteed no-op instead: every possible anchor is already past it, filling never takes a single step, and the bound is accepted - the same clamp towards zero as in the numeric case. `STALENESS`, which is allowed only without `FROM`, replaces `TO` as the effective bound whenever it comes first, so the sequence can stop arbitrarily far below `TO` and such a `TO` is not checked either. Float and Decimal bounds are not checked: they saturate instead of wrapping, and a `Float64` bound is generally inexact in a `Float32` column, so requiring exact representability there would reject ordinary queries. On top of the storage range, the calendar arithmetic of an `INTERVAL` step clamps at the boundaries of the representable calendar - the `[0000-01-01, 9999-12-31]` window of `DateLUTImpl`, taken in the local civil calendar of the column's time zone, so for `DateTime64` the boundary in raw ticks shifts by the UTC offset (the last reachable second of a `DateTime64(0, 'Etc/GMT-14')` column is `253402250399`, not the UTC `253402300799`) - and for `Date32` and `DateTime64` that window is strictly narrower than the storage type. A `TO` beyond the calendar boundary in the fill direction fits the storage type but can never be reached: the filling keeps generating the clamped boundary value forever (it does on current master, e.g. `SELECT toDate32('9999-12-31') AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL TO 3000000 STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR` never terminates). Such a `TO` is rejected against the calendar limits, scale-aware for `DateTime64`. For `Date` the calendar clamp coincides with the `UInt16` storage boundary, and `DateTime` wraps within `UInt32`, where any in-range `TO` stays reachable from some anchor, so the storage check covers those two. Beyond reachability, for `Date32` and `DateTime64` the values between the calendar boundary and the boundary of the storage type are invalid in themselves: no conversion produces them (they all clamp at the calendar boundary), yet a `FROM` bound in that gap is materialized into the column as is and serialized as the clamped boundary date - a spurious duplicate of the genuine boundary value next to it (e.g. `SELECT d FROM (SELECT toDate32('2000-01-01') AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL FROM -719529 TO -719528 STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR)` on current master returns a `0000-01-01` row holding the day number `-719529`, which is not `0000-01-01`). The representability check therefore tests bounds of these two types against the calendar window (in the local civil calendar of the column's time zone for `DateTime64`), not just the storage range: an out-of-calendar `FROM` is rejected for any kind of step - like a `FROM` out of the storage range already is - and a numeric-step `TO` is rejected when the last value generated under it provably lands in the gap, under the same rules as the storage range. The last-generated-value computation covers the `Decimal64`-carried `DateTime64` bounds as well as the `Int64`-carried types: a numeric step over `DateTime64` advances raw ticks of the column's scale, and ticks beyond the calendar do not wrap but are equally invalid (they all serialize as the clamped boundary date). Finally, the calendar clamp makes an `INTERVAL` step able to stagnate: adding the interval to a value whose result would leave the calendar returns the value unchanged, so the sequence can stop advancing strictly below a perfectly representable `TO` and never terminate (e.g. `WITH FILL FROM toDateTime64('9999-06-01 00:00:00', 0, 'UTC') TO toDateTime64('9999-12-31 00:00:00', 0, 'UTC') STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR` hangs on current master). With an explicit `FROM` the whole sequence is known up front - `FillingRow::next` advances it by one application of the step function at a time - so it is walked at construction time with the same step function, under a bounded budget (65536 steps), and rejected when it provably stagnates before reaching `TO`. The walk mirrors the runtime step exactly, so it can never misjudge a terminating sequence; a fill whose stagnation lies beyond the budget (a fine-grained step over a huge span) is accepted as before. The same walk rejects a step that turns back instead of stagnating: the calendar arithmetic is performed in the storage type of the column, so a step whose result would leave that type wraps around (e.g. `WITH FILL FROM toDateTime('2106-01-01 00:00:00', 'UTC') TO 4294967295 STEP INTERVAL 100 YEAR` jumps from 2106 back to 2069 and keeps cycling below `TO` forever on current master). The value such a step wrapped from is above the type maximum, hence above `TO`, so the sequence has already overshot the bound and every value generated from there on is spurious - out of order and past the `TO` the query asked for - whether or not the wrapped-around walk happens to land beyond `TO` later on and terminate. For data-dependent paths whose effective bound comes from the next input row or `STALENESS`, `FillingRow::next` checks every generated step at runtime. A step that does not advance in the sorting direction now throws `INVALID_WITH_FILL_EXPRESSION`, preventing both wrapped rows and non-terminating fills. The stateless test covers the `Int64` between-rows overflow case. ### Changelog category Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry Reject `WITH FILL` bounds and steps that would wrap, generate non-monotonic output, or never terminate. ### Documentation entry - [x] Documentation is not required. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112650&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112650](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112650+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix read_rows/read_bytes/written_rows/written_bytes in system.query_thread_log
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105246 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `read_rows`, `read_bytes`, `written_rows` and `written_bytes` in `system.query_thread_log` reporting a thread lifetime running total instead of the values for the logged query. Rows of long-lived pooled threads, in particular the query's initiating `HTTPHandler` thread, were affected. ### Description `ThreadStatus::progress_in` and `progress_out` live as long as the OS thread, and the four progress columns are read straight off them. Nothing ever cleared them, so for a pooled thread the row reported everything that thread had ever served. Worker threads get a fresh `ThreadStatus`, so the victim is the row with `thread_id = master_thread_id`. `ThreadStatus::initPerformanceCounters()` already exists for this, runs on attach to a thread group, and says "Clear stats from previous query if a new query is started". It resets `performance_counters` and `memory_tracker` but never these two members, which predate it. The fix adds them. Before the fix, over HTTP on one connection, four identical `SELECT`s each reading 200000 rows: | `query_log.read_rows` | `query_thread_log.read_rows` | same row's `ProfileEvents['SelectedRows']` | |---|---|---| | 200000 | 1000000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1200000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1400000 | 200000 | | 200000 | 1600000 | 200000 | After the fix all three agree. Four identical `INSERT`s behaved the same way on `written_rows`, and are covered. One semantic point to confirm, since it is a choice: this reset runs per attach to a thread group, not per query, so a thread logged on several rows for one query reports each attach cycle separately. `ProfileEvents` on the same row already behaves this way, so the two become consistent rather than gaining a new convention. Populating the columns from `SelectedRows`/`InsertedRows` instead was rejected: it redefines them and would tie them to `log_profile_events`. Query-level accounting is untouched: `query_log`, `system.processes`, `max_rows_to_read`, leaf limits, throttling and quotas read the separate `QueryStatus` object, and I checked each of those. The test drives the queries over HTTP on one keep-alive connection: over the native protocol the reads happen on a separate pipeline thread, so the initiating thread's row would assert nothing. It fails on master. @PedroTadim <details> <summary>Validation</summary> - Negative control on a pristine master binary: all four assertion lines move (distinct `read_rows` 1 to 4, distinct `written_rows` 1 to 4, and every column comparing a progress value against `ProfileEvents` moves on both arms). Reproduced under randomized settings too. - New test passes on the fixed build, 50 of 50 randomized runs, and 12 concurrent copies over 6 workers. - Of the ten other stateless tests touching `query_thread_log`, the eight runnable in my sandbox still pass; the remaining two need a listener this sandbox does not provide, and neither reads the four columns. - Verified `progress_in`/`progress_out` on `ThreadStatus` have two writers (`CurrentThread::updateProgressIn`/`Out`), one reader (the log site), and no other reference in `src/`, `programs/`, `base/`, `utils/`. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115596&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115596](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115596+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Re-land aggregate function `gini` in the `sum` family
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113868 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112280 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): New aggregate function `gini`, which calculates the [Gini coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gini_coefficient) of a column of finite, non-negative numeric values. The result ranges from `0` (all values equal) towards `1` as inequality grows; for a sample of `n` values the maximum is `(n - 1) / n`. `NaN` values are skipped, while infinite and negative values are rejected. The function returns `Float64` and consumes `O(n)` memory. ### Description Re-lands the `gini` function that #113868 reverted, following the option-2 spec @ Manerone gave in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113763#issuecomment-5217284116. `gini` now registers and folds exactly like `sum`. Relative to #112280 it drops the `getArgumentsThatCanBeOnlyNull` override, `.returns_default_when_only_null = true`, and the `argument_type->onlyNull()` branch in the creator, and touches no file under `src/AggregateFunctions/Combinators/`. The property was doing the work: it made `AggregateFunctionFactory::getImpl` skip its only-null guard and build a real `gini` over `Nullable(Nothing)`, so `gini(NULL)` returned `Float64` `nan` where every `sum`-family function folds to `Nullable(Nothing)`. Without it the fold happens in the `Null` combinator first, which is why `createAggregateFunctionSum` has no equivalent. It also drops `getOwnNullAdapter`, at @ Manerone's request in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114643#issuecomment-5354588069. Keeping it left `gini` the only function in the family whose plain and wrapped forms disagreed on nullability: the `Null` combinator consults that hook only on the object it wraps directly, and for `giniIf` / `giniDistinct` that is `AggregateFunctionIf` / `AggregateFunctionDistinct`, whose own adapters win. So `gini(x)` stayed `Float64` while `giniIf(x, c)` became `Nullable(Float64)`. Dropping it gives parity on the runtime axis too: over a `Nullable` column every form returns `Nullable(Float64)`, `NULL` when no non-`NULL` value qualifies and `nan` when fewer than two do. Non-nullable input is unchanged. Validated against `sum` on the same binary: every literal-`NULL` and `Nullable`-column cell matches its `sum` counterpart, and non-nullable results are unchanged from #112280. Docs: `gini.mdx` plus its slug-map, navigation and redirect entries are restored from their merged state in #114314, which #113868's revert had removed as collateral; the generated region is regenerated from the `FunctionDocumentation` block by `ci/jobs/scripts/docs/autogenerate/autogenerate_docs.py` (`--check` clean) and the page keeps its hand-written header. The slug-map row is needed, not cosmetic: without it the nightly generator resolves no Mintlify destination and fails for this page. The `pr-autogenerated-docs` label is what lets a page carrying the markers pass the generated-region guard, as the guard's own message asks for. cc @Manerone <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114643&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114643](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114643+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
