signal.title: Do not attach a cache writer to a detached file segment
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110029 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Cache file segment is in detached state`) when reading through the filesystem cache with the experimental `use_reader_executor` setting. The regression was introduced by #110029 and is not in any release, so no backport is owed. ### Description Related: #110029 **The problem.** `BuzzHouse` aborts the server with `Cache file segment is in detached state, operation not allowed`, on two unrelated PRs, first seen 8h41m after #110029 merged. CIDB STID `4043-43b7`, [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113382&sha=97396ecebc7bcb7ee4d4921c71d1cfdd071a2895&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29). **Root cause.** `FileCache::getOrSet` can hand back a synthetic `DETACHED` placeholder rather than a real segment: `getImpl` fabricates one when the covering segment is being evicted or removed, and another when the range exceeds `bypass_cache_threshold`. Such a placeholder is outside the cache metadata, holds no bytes, and the downloader role cannot be acquired on it. `DiskCacheProvider::resolve` classified it as a *writable* miss, because `segmentCommittedEnd` falls back to the write offset, which for a placeholder equals the segment start. It attached a `DiskCacheWriter`, and `ReaderExecutor::readThroughCaches` then called `claimLeadRole` on it, whose `getOrSetDownloader` hit `assertNotDetachedUnlocked`: a `LOGICAL_ERROR`, aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds. **The change.** `resolve` now emits a writer-less miss for a detached segment, so those bytes are read from source and nothing is cached. The legacy paths already do this: `CachedOnDiskReadBufferFromFile` dispatches `State::DETACHED` to a cache bypass before acquiring any role, and `CachedOnDiskWriteBufferFromFile` skips write-through caching on `isDetached()`. `claimLeadRole` was the only one of the five non-test `getOrSetDownloader` callers reachable with a detached segment; the assertion is a correct caller contract and stays. **Reachability.** `src/IO/DiskCacheProvider.cpp` exists on no active release branch (25.8, 26.3-26.7), and #110029 is an ancestor of none of them, so no released version can reach this. `use_reader_executor` is experimental and off by default; the abort affects the `BuzzHouse` checks, which randomize it as a session setting, plus anyone opting into the experimental path. **Validation.** Deterministic, no fuzzer needed: the test arms the existing failpoint `file_cache_simulate_evicting_segment`, which makes every segment the cache reports a placeholder. Without the fix the server dies with the CI stack; with it the test passes, 50/50 randomized. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115070&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115070](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115070+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads for parallel manifest decoding
signal.text: Reading an Iceberg snapshot's data files requires walking the snapshot's manifest list and decoding each manifest file. `IcebergIterator` currently does this with a single background producer thread, so for tables with many manifest files the manifest walk is serial and can dominate query planning time. This adds an opt-in, experimental setting `iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads` (`UInt64`, default `1`). At the default value of `1` behavior is unchanged. With a value greater than `1`, `IcebergIterator` builds N data-file iterators that share one atomic counter over the snapshot's `manifest_list_entries` and spawns N producer tasks; each producer claims the next manifest index via `fetch_add`, so manifests are decoded cooperatively with no overlap, and the last producer to finish closes the queue. The effective thread count is clamped to the number of manifest files. Delete-file manifests are still drained serially, since data-file pruning depends on the full delete set. A new `ProfileEvent` `IcebergParallelManifestDecodeThreadsSpawned` reports how many producer threads were spawned. Tests: a unit test for the shared-index claim contract, a stateless test for the setting, and an integration test asserting result parity across thread counts (including a query with an `IN` filter, which exercises concurrent lazy materialization of the shared filter set). ### Changelog category: - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental setting `iceberg_parallel_manifest_decode_threads` that decodes Iceberg manifest files using multiple threads during query planning, speeding up reads of tables with many manifest files.

signal.title: Parallelize Iceberg delete-manifest processing
signal.text: ### Problem `IcebergIterator`'s constructor synchronously drains every DELETE manifest in the snapshot before it starts the background data-file producer: ```cpp auto delete_file = deletes_iterator.next(); while (delete_file.has_value()) { if (delete_file.value()->parsed_entry->equality_ids.has_value()) equality_deletes_files.emplace_back(std::move(delete_file.value())); else position_deletes_files.emplace_back(std::move(delete_file.value())); delete_file = deletes_iterator.next(); } std::sort(equality_deletes_files.begin(), equality_deletes_files.end()); std::sort(position_deletes_files.begin(), position_deletes_files.end()); producer_task.emplace(...); ``` This means: 1. **Query startup is blocked** on a sequential walk of all DELETE manifests. Each manifest fetch is an object-storage round-trip; their parsing is independent and fully parallelizable. 2. The data-file producer thread does not start until deletes are fully loaded — wasted overlap with the network-bound delete reads. For snapshots with many delete manifests (large copy-on-write / merge-on-read tables under heavy update load), this dominates planning time. ### Proposed approach **Parallel delete-manifest fetch.** Replace `SingleThreadIcebergKeysIterator` walking DELETE manifests one-by-one with a worker pool that fetches and parses K manifests concurrently. `ManifestFileIterator` is already thread-safe internally (atomic `current_row_index`, mutex-guarded output vectors), so the only change is to dispatch multiple manifest fetches in parallel and merge the results.

signal.title: clickhouse-local: HTTP/TCP listener aborts the whole process on a routine client socket error (KillingErrorHandler)
signal.text:
**Component:** clickhouse-local · **Version:** 26.8.1.1774 (official build, arm64 macOS; the listener feature is new in 26.8) · **Severity:** crash / DoS of the local server ## Summary `clickhouse-local` can now expose network listeners with `SYSTEM START LISTEN TCP/HTTP` (new in 26.8). When it runs **non-interactively** (piped/non-TTY stdin — i.e. exactly how you'd run it as a background server), it installs Poco `KillingErrorHandler`, whose handler calls `std::terminate()` on **any** exception that reaches a Poco thread's error handler. A connection-handler thread routinely throws on benign client behaviour — e.g. a client that resets a keep-alive socket mid-response. `clickhouse-server` swallows these via `ServerErrorHandler` (log-and-continue). In `clickhouse-local` the same exception hits `KillingErrorHandler` → `std::terminate()` → `abort()`, killing the entire process (and, with a persistent `--path`, taking down the served database). A **single** client doing "keep-alive request → RST" in a loop kills the listener in ~4 seconds. ## Reproduction Fully self-contained (no auth, no data, no special query). Needs `clickhouse` ≥ 26.8 and `python3`. ```bash CH=/path/to/clickhouse DIR=$(mktemp -d) cat > "$DIR/cfg.xml" <<EOF <clickhouse><logger><level>trace</level><log>$DIR/ch.log</log><errorlog>$DIR/ch.err</errorlog><console>0</console></logger></clickhouse> EOF # keep stdin open (non-interactive server path) so the listener stays up mkfifo "$DIR/in"; ( exec 9>"$DIR/in"; sleep 120 ) & "$CH" local --path "$DIR/data" -C "$DIR/cfg.xml" --http_port 18124 --interactive \ -q "SYSTEM START LISTEN HTTP" < "$DIR/in" & SRV=$! sleep 2 curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18124/ping" # -> Ok. SRV=$SRV python3 - <<'PY' import socket, struct, threading, os, time def alive(): try: os.kill(int(os.environ["SRV"]),0); return True except OSError: return False REQ=b"GET /?query=SELECT%201 HTTP/1.1
Host: x
Connection: keep-alive

" LINGER0=struct.pack("ii",1,0) # SO_LINGER on, 0s -> hard RST on close def churn(): while True: try: s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1",18124),timeout=2) s.sendall(REQ); s.recv(20) # read part of the keep-alive response... s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_LINGER,LINGER0); s.close() # ...then RST except Exception: pass threading.Thread(target=churn,daemon=True).start() # ONE thread is enough t0=time.time() while time.time()-t0<20: if not alive(): print(f"*** clickhouse-local ABORTED after {time.time()-t0:.1f}s ***"); break time.sleep(0.2) PY ``` Observed: `*** clickhouse-local ABORTED after 4.3s ***`, and the parent shell reports `Abort trap: 6` for the clickhouse process. Reproduced consistently at 1, 2, 4, 8, and 48 concurrent connections (always ~4.3s). Originally hit organically with an ordinary application using `clickhouse-connect` and a keep-alive connection pool pointed at a `clickhouse-local` listener — it crashed within a few requests under concurrency. ## Crash Two escaping exceptions observed, both the same scenario (client reset mid-response), both fatal via the same handler: ``` Terminate called for uncaught exception: Poco::Exception. Code: 1000, e.code() = 22, Invalid argument: Invalid argument 0. Poco::Exception::Exception(...) 1. Poco::InvalidArgumentException::InvalidArgumentException(...) 2. Poco::Net::SocketImpl::error(int, String const&) 3. Poco::Net::SocketImpl::<socket op> # EINVAL on the reset keep-alive socket ... 7. Poco::ErrorHandler::handle(Poco::Exception const&) # -> KillingErrorHandler 8. Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start() 9. Poco::Net::TCPServerDispatcher::run() ``` and ``` Terminate called for uncaught exception: 5. DB::WriteBufferFromHTTPServerResponse::cancelWithException(...) # "Write buffer has been canceled" 6. DB::HTTPHandler::trySendExceptionToClient(...) # sending an error to a reset socket throws 7. DB::HTTPHandler::handleRequest(...) 8. DB::HTTPServerConnection::run() # exception escapes the handler 9. Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start() 10. Poco::Net::TCPServerDispatcher::run() ``` Then `signalHandler → abort → terminate_handler → std::__terminate → Poco::ErrorHandler::handle → TCPServerConnection::start` (SIGABRT). ## Root cause `programs/local/LocalServer.cpp` (v26.8.1): ```cpp is_interactive = stdin_is_a_tty && (... ); if (!is_interactive) { /// We will terminate process on error static KillingErrorHandler error_handler; // :1152 Poco::ErrorHandler::set(&error_handler); // :1153 } ``` `src/Common/ErrorHandlers.h`: ```cpp class KillingErrorHandler : public Poco::ErrorHandler { void exception(const Poco::Exception &) override { std::terminate(); } // :15 void exception(const std::exception &) override { std::terminate(); } void exception() override { std::terminate(); } }; class ServerErrorHandler : public Poco::ErrorHandler { void exception(const Poco::Exception &) override { logException(); } // :26 <- log & continue ... }; ``` `clickhouse-server` installs the tolerant handler — `programs/server/Server.cpp:2007`: ```cpp static ServerErrorHandler error_handler; Poco::ErrorHandler::set(&error_handler); ``` `KillingErrorHandler` was a reasonable choice while non-interactive `clickhouse-local` was a one-shot batch tool (fail the run on any error). But now that the **same non-interactive path** can start network listeners, a per-connection socket exception — which `Poco::Net::TCPServerConnection::start()` catches and forwards to the global `Poco::ErrorHandler` — terminates the whole process instead of dropping one connection. Note the interaction: `--interactive` is downgraded to non-interactive whenever stdin isn't a TTY, so any scripted/daemonized invocation that serves connections gets `KillingErrorHandler`. ## Suggested fix When listeners are (or can be) active, connection-thread exceptions must not be fatal. Options, smallest first: 1. Install `ServerErrorHandler` instead of `KillingErrorHandler` once `SYSTEM START LISTEN` brings servers up (or whenever `server_ports`/listeners are configured). ~2 lines at the listener-start site; preserves `KillingErrorHandler`'s batch-mode semantics for the pure one-shot path. 2. Or ensure the HTTP/TCP connection handlers never let socket exceptions (`SocketImpl` errors, `WriteBufferFromHTTPServerResponse::cancelWithException`) escape `HTTPServerConnection::run()` in local mode, so the global error handler is never reached for routine client resets. Option 1 matches how `clickhouse-server` already behaves and is the minimal change. ## Impact Anyone using the new `clickhouse-local` listener as a lightweight embedded/loopback ClickHouse server (the emerging "clickhouse-local as a server" pattern) can have the process aborted by ordinary client-side connection resets — trivially triggered, no auth required. With a persistent `--path`, the served database goes down with it (data is safe on disk; availability is not). --- *Verified end-to-end on 26.8.1.1774 (official build), macOS arm64.* --- > *Generated by [Nerve](https://github.com/ClickHouse/nerve)*

signal.title: Perf: reserve TimeSeries tag vectors by row
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Reserve the final per-row capacity when converting TimeSeries tag arrays.** ## What changed - Count the separate tag name/value pairs already present in the function arguments. - Reserve array tags and separate tags together for each row. - Cover empty `Array(Nothing)` and `NULL` arrays when separate tags are provided. ## Why this is safe - The array offsets contain the exact number of array tags in each row. - The number of separate tag pairs is known from the validated arguments. - `reserve()` does not change tag order, sorting, duplicate removal, or output. - Empty and `NULL` array paths only reserve when separate tags are present. ## Benchmark Local Release build with `max_threads=1` and `max_block_size=65536`. The benchmark used 2M rows and three measured runs after one warmup per case. Each row used the same tag value modulo 10,000, and only the number of array tags changed. | Array tags per row | Before | After | Change | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 1 | 0.35 s | 0.35 s | 0% | | 4 | 0.93 s | 0.62 s | 33% faster | | 8 | 1.38 s | 1.00 s | 28% faster | | 16 | 2.75 s | 2.25 s | 18% faster | | 32 | 6.06 s | 5.10 s | 16% faster | These are array-only calls, where the extra-tag count is zero, so the measured hot path is unchanged by the mixed-tag fix. The end-to-end ingest gain depends on how much time is spent in this path. ## Tests - Run `git diff --check`. - Existing `03779_time_series_tags_functions` coverage includes array tags with separate tags and empty arrays with separate tags. - The revised helper is included in the PR CI build.

signal.title: Add `borrow_from_cache` object storage and `memory` metadata types
signal.text: Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache using ephemeral `FileSegment`s. Each stored object is backed by a cache segment held alive via `FileSegmentsHolder`; when released, the cache reclaims the space. Add a new metadata type `memory` that keeps all file-to-blob mappings and directory structure entirely in memory with no persistence. On server restart all data is lost, which is acceptable for the intended use case of temporary tables. Configuration example: ``` disk(type=object_storage, object_storage_type='borrow_from_cache', metadata_type='memory', cache_name='some_cache') ``` ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A new object storage type and metadata type suitable for temporary tables. Add a new object storage type `borrow_from_cache` that allocates space in a named filesystem cache and holds it from eviction. Add a new metadata storage type `memory` that keeps the mapping in memory. For example, this could allow creating temporary tables with custom engines in the Cloud without using S3. signal.title: Look up the SSH key and support ssh-agent in clickhouse-client
signal.text: `--ssh-key-file` can now be specified without a value. In that case the key is looked up the same way as `ssh` does it: - the identity files configured for this host in `~/.ssh/config` and in `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`; - the default identity files, such as `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`; - the keys held by the `ssh-agent`. A key held by the `ssh-agent` is preferred, because it does not need a passphrase. It is also used when `--ssh-key-file` names a key file that the agent holds - an encrypted key that was added with `ssh-add` no longer asks for the passphrase. Signing with the agent is implemented in `SSHAgent`, a small client of the agent protocol, which produces the same `SSHSIG` signature as `SSHKey::signString` does for a local key (for RSA keys it asks the agent for `rsa-sha2-256`, because agents sign with SHA-1 by default and the server rejects that). The configuration is read with the parser of `libssh`, so `Host` and `Match` sections, `Include`, and the `%`-tokens of `IdentityFile` and `IdentityAgent` (`%C`, `%d`, `%h`, `%i`, `%L`, `%l`, `%n`, `%p`, `%r`, `%u`) work the same way as in `ssh`. `IdentitiesOnly yes` is honored: the ssh-agent is not asked for an arbitrary key when none of the configured identity files exists. The client reports the key it has chosen: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user abcuser --ssh-key-file Using the SSH key 'the key of abcuser' from the ssh-agent. ``` Two related changes of the existing behavior: the passphrase is now asked only if the key file is really encrypted (before, `--ssh-key-file` always asked for it), and the message about a key that cannot be imported now names the file. Tests: a new stateless test `04908_ssh_key_file_lookup` covers the default identity file, an `IdentityFile` with the `%r` token, an `ed25519` key from the `ssh-agent`, an `ssh-rsa` key from the `ssh-agent` with an empty `~/.ssh`, `IdentityAgent none`, and `IdentitiesOnly yes`. `03780_failed_ssh` no longer expects the passphrase prompt. The existing `test_ssh_keys_authentication` integration tests pass. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `clickhouse-client` accepts `--ssh-key-file` without a value: the key is looked up the same way as `ssh` does it - the identity files configured for the host in `~/.ssh/config`, the default identity files, such as `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, and the keys held by the `ssh-agent`. Authentication with a key held by the `ssh-agent` is now supported, and it does not need a passphrase. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115072&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115072](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115072+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libssh/pull/15

signal.title: Enable the consecutive-keys cache for fixed-size aggregation keys
signal.text: The `keys128` and `keys256` aggregation methods had `consecutive_keys_optimization = false`, so aggregating data whose keys arrive in long runs of equal values (e.g. anything grouped by a fixed-size key that is a prefix of the table sort order) paid a full hash-and-probe per row. Enabling the existing `LastElementCache` for these methods (including the two-level variants) skips the hash table entirely within a run, at the cost of one wide key compare per row; the aggregator's adaptive hit-rate machinery already disables the cache on random keys, verified by a random-key `keys256` microbenchmark showing no regression (3.88 s baseline vs 3.82/3.88 s). On clustered keys (runs of ~200k equal `Tuple(UInt64, UUID)` values, 400M rows) this saves ~10% of aggregation CPU. Session: ad94609b-7b39-4f96-af16-7947efc50974 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Aggregation by fixed-size keys of 17-32 bytes (the `keys128`/`keys256` methods, e.g. `GROUP BY` a `UUID` or a `Tuple(UInt64, UInt64)`) now uses the consecutive-keys cache, making aggregation of sorted or clustered data up to 10% faster; the cache disables itself adaptively on random keys. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115155&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115155](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115155+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Database context not preserved in distributed queries when using dictGet function
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong When executing a distributed query that uses the dictGet function to access a dictionary, the database context is lost on remote nodes, causing "**Dictionary not found**" errors even when the dictionary exists. **Version Affected**: ClickHouse 25.7.1.3997 (still reproduces on 26.3) ### How to reproduce **​Cluster Configuration**: 2 shards, 1 replica ​**Component**: Distributed query execution with dictionary functions ### Steps to Reproduce ```sql -- Create database demo CREATE DATABASE demo on cluster 'all' ENGINE = Replicated('/clickhouse/default/demo', '{shard}', '{replica}'); -- Create test Dict CREATE DICTIONARY demo.dict_test ( code Int32, value String ) PRIMARY KEY code SOURCE(FILE(path './user_files/test.ndjson' format 'JSONEachRow')) LAYOUT(COMPLEX_KEY_HASHED) LIFETIME(0); -- Create local table CREATE TABLE demo.test_local(code Int32) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree() ORDER BY code; -- Create Cluster table CREATE TABLE demo.test(code Int32) ENGINE = Distributed('demo', 'demo', 'test_local', rand()); -- Execute sql use demo; SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; ``` ### Expected behavior The query should successfully resolve the dictionary reference on all cluster nodes since: - The dictionary exists in the same database on all nodes - The query is executed within the demo database context ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` -- Exception: /** Received exception from server (version 25.7.1): Code: 36. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000. DB::Exception: Received from ch-2:9000. DB::Exception: Dictionary (`dict_test`) not found: In scope SELECT __table1.code AS code, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', __table1.code) AS `dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code)` FROM demo.test_local AS __table1. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) **/ select hostname,type,current_database,query,databases,tables from cluster('demo','system.query_log') where initial_query_id='4c9b4549-be34-4c37-b635-024eb53fa70d'; /** Row 1: ──────the space key to toggle the display of the progress table. hostname: ch-1 type: QueryStart current_database: demo query: SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; databases: ['demo'] tables: ['demo.test','demo.test_local'] Row 2: ────── hostname: ch-1 type: ExceptionWhileProcessing current_database: demo query: SELECT code,dictGet('dict_test','value',code) FROM demo.test; databases: ['demo'] tables: ['demo.test','demo.test_local'] Row 3: ────── hostname: ch-2 type: ExceptionBeforeStart current_database: default query: SELECT `__table1`.`code` AS `code`, dictGet('dict_test', 'value', `__table1`.`code`) AS `dictGet('dict_test', 'value', code)` FROM `demo`.`test_local` AS `__table1` databases: [] tables: [] **/ ``` ### Additional context The database context from the initiating node is not properly propagated to remote nodes during distributed query execution, particularly when resolving dictionary references. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115541 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1789` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix Keeper CORRUPTED_DATA after cross-segment writeAt crash (#112101)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Fix ClickHouse Keeper refusing to start with `CORRUPTED_DATA` after a crash during cross-segment Raft log truncation (`writeAt`), which could leave an acknowledged log entry stranded behind stale changelog segments. Closes #112101 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Detail When `Changelog::writeAt` rewrote an entry in an earlier changelog segment, later segments were removed asynchronously and the rewrite could be fsynced/acked before those unlinks finished. A crash in that window left a duplicated index in the earlier file plus stale higher-index files; startup treated the gap as unrecoverable corruption. This change waits for those `RemoveChangelog` operations **outside** `writer_mutex` before appending the rewrite (durability ordering; no lock cycle with the remove thread). Startup still reports `CORRUPTED_DATA` for changelog gaps so recovery stays manual. ### Test plan - [x] `gtest_coordination_changelog` / `ChangelogTestWriteAtPreviousFile` — after cross-segment `write_at`, superseded changelog files are already gone before the rewrite is acknowledged <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114003&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114003](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114003+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix GCD codec behavior on signed values
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78190 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed GCD codec handling of signed fixed-width values with negative numbers. Previously it computed the divisor from signed values directly, which could miss the common divisor and significantly reduce compression efficiency for signed integer and decimal columns. It now computes the divisor from magnitudes for signed types while preserving existing behavior for unsigned types and decompression. ### Description GCD pre-processing was using signed values directly when discovering the common divisor. For signed fixed-width storage types, negative values could therefore spoil divisor discovery and make CODEC(GCD) compress much worse than expected, even though the data still had a large common divisor in magnitude. The fix makes CompressionCodecGCD compute the divisor on unsigned magnitudes for signed types, and threads signedness from the column type into codec instantiation so Int* and signed Decimal* columns use the correct path. This also handles the signed-minimum edge case safely by avoiding signed negation overflow. Unsigned behavior is unchanged. The type-agnostic fallback is kept deliberately unchanged: unlike T64, GCD still does not throw when type information is unavailable and falls back to the 1-byte unsigned path. That preserves correctness for cases such as default_compression_codec or CODEC(Default) resolution without a concrete column type, but signed data on that path may still compress less efficiently because signedness is unknown. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113798&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113798](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113798+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Lower KeeperTCPHandler 'Client has not sent any data' log from warning to info
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/18005 `KeeperTCPHandler` logs `Client has not sent any data` at `LOG_WARNING` when a connection is opened but no data is received (the `in->eof()` branch). The same message in the server's `TCPHandler` was lowered from warning to info in #18005, but `KeeperTCPHandler` — a separate copy of the same pattern — was never updated, so it still logs at warning. Any TCP health check against the Keeper client port trips this on every probe. In particular, the ClickHouse Keeper operator's default `tcpSocket` liveness probe opens and closes a connection to the client port every few seconds, producing a steady stream of warning-level lines. This brings `KeeperTCPHandler` in line with `TCPHandler`. The nearby `LOG_WARNING` for a genuine protocol-header read error is intentionally left unchanged. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ClickHouse Keeper now logs the "Client has not sent any data" event at `Information` level instead of `Warning`, matching the server's TCP handler. This avoids spurious warnings from TCP health-check probes (for example Kubernetes `tcpSocket` liveness probes) that open and immediately close a connection to the Keeper client port. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111217&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111217](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111217+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. The `Chimp` numbers in the previous revision of this description were measured against an older encoder revision and are omitted; the qualitative picture for `Chimp` — robust on non-decimal data, slow Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113575&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113575](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113575+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signal.title: Assert the socket timeout exception instead of wall-clock time in test_secure_socket
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112938 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `test_secure_socket` guarded each of its three timeout arms with `assert end - start < 10`. That bound measures host load, not the behaviour under test, so it fails on a loaded CI host even when the timeout is honoured. It failed at 35.47 s here: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112938&sha=81483c13ee7fed39a69f62b13e5a98827ae7357a&name_0=PR&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%2C%20db%20disk%2C%20old%20analyzer%2C%204%2F6%29 Root cause is a whole-host scheduling stall, not a timeout defect: unrelated periodic tasks and another pytest worker froze over the same window. CIDB over 90 days: 4 failures, 0 on master. The three literals are replaced by an assertion on the `SOCKET_TIMEOUT` exception each arm must produce, which is what the test means: `receive_timeout=5` is honoured instead of the query hanging on the remote's `sleep_in_send_data_ms = 1000000`. Each arm also asserts the socket description its own code path formats, so an ignored `async_socket_for_remote` or `use_hedged_requests` cannot collapse two arms. Arm 1 had none before. Two `assert error.find("DB::ReadBufferFromPocoSocket::nextImpl()") == -1` guards go too: vacuous since `89205d78a688793` moved `nextImpl()` to `ReadBufferFromPocoSocketBase`, so `find()` returned -1 always. The per-arm assertions cover their intent. `send_timeout` drops from 5 to 4 so the asserted `5000 ms` is attributable: at 5 both settings render the same value, so a regression reading the send timeout on the read path stayed green. It goes below `receive_timeout` rather than to its default because a blocking secure read waits `max(receive_timeout, send_timeout)`, so raising it left the assertion unchanged while elapsed time went to 9.10 s at 9 and 300.11 s at the default. Hang detection is unchanged (`pytest.ini` sets `timeout = 900`). Latency tightness is given up: the asserted `5000 ms` is the configured value the message prints, not the elapsed time. Widening was rejected, that bound already went 6 to 10 in `ed6363b88bd1b43` and failed again. Every assertion is mutation-validated both ways, each mutation reddening only its intended arm. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115572&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115572](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115572+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1786` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Normalize the plan check in 04061_analyzer_inline_view
signal.text: `04061_analyzer_inline_view` pinned the full `EXPLAIN` output, including the step description of `ReadFromRemoteParallelReplicas`, which embeds the whole query sent to the replicas. That makes the reference sensitive to unrelated changes in query formatting, and it breaks outright once reading with parallel replicas is planned differently: the step is then called `ReadFromParallelReplicas` and it is not wrapped into `Expression (Convert distributed names)`. Print the plan with `description = 0`, drop the `Expression` steps and fold both names of the reading step into one, so the check keeps asserting what the test is about - the shape of the plan built for an inlined view - without depending on how reading from the replicas is planned. signal.title: Fix lost text index optimization for queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/issues/68580 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/93545 A query that filters on a text index and also has `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` could stop using the index to answer the filter, and read and tokenize the whole text column instead: ```sql SELECT count() FROM (SELECT id, v FROM t WHERE hasToken(s, 'error') ORDER BY v DESC, id LIMIT 10) ``` The two optimizations did not compose: the one that speeds up `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` reshaped the plan in a way the text index optimization no longer recognized, and it silently fell back to reading the column. Nothing indicated this in the query plan or the logs, and the results stayed correct, but the query got much slower and used much more memory. On a full-text search benchmark over ~30M rows the affected queries took ~300 ms and ~500 MB instead of ~30 ms and ~15 MB. Whether a query was affected depended on the order of the columns in `SELECT`, which made it look arbitrary: `SELECT v, id ... ORDER BY v` was fine while `SELECT id, v ... ORDER BY v` was not. All the settings involved are enabled by default. Both optimizations now apply together. A `TRACE` log entry was also added for the remaining cases where the text index optimization cannot be used, so a silent fallback is visible in the logs. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a performance regression where a query combining a text index filter with `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` stopped answering the filter from the index and read the whole text column instead. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115586&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115586](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115586+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix flaky test `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit`
signal.text: Fix a flaky test. Without `exact_rows_before_limit`, `rows_before_limit_at_least` is set from `LimitByTransform`, which counts the rows it emitted before `LIMIT` stopped the pipeline. That count depends on the block size of the sorted stream, and `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit` pins it with `max_block_size = 1`. When settings randomization enables external sorting, `MergeSortingTransform` merges its spilled runs into blocks of at least 128 rows, so `LIMIT BY` sees a whole batch of groups at once and the counter reports a larger value — 5 instead of 3 on the failing run. The queries in the test are tiny (50 rows), but `max_block_size = 1` makes `MergeSortingTransform` account for 50 single-row chunks by their allocated size, which crosses the randomized `max_bytes_before_external_sort` threshold and spills to disk (confirmed by `ProfileEvents['ExternalSortWritePart'] = 2`). The fix disables external sorting in the test. Minimal reproducer of the CI failure: ``` --optimize_read_in_order 0 --max_bytes_before_external_sort 156659 --max_bytes_ratio_before_external_sort 0 --allow_merge_tree_settings --ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization 0.0 ``` Verified locally: with the fix, 210 runs of the test over randomized combinations of `max_block_size`, `max_threads`, `optimize_read_in_order`, external sort/group-by thresholds, `prefer_external_sort_block_bytes` and MergeTree serialization settings all match the reference; without it, the same sweep reproduces the mismatch (including on the "unsorted" query, which reported 9). The sibling tests `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit_mem` and `03408_limit_by_rows_before_limit_dist` were checked under the same sweep and are not affected. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=bddae8d728ac67d24e7c4f102e87b4a3c552322b&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_msan%2C%20WasmEdge%2C%20parallel%2C%201%2F3%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115644&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115644](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115644+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Mixing lightweight and heavyweight mutations permanently wedges a MergeTree table (`NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK: _row_exists`)
signal.text: ## Describe the bug After a lightweight `DELETE` and a heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` have both run on a MergeTree table, a subsequent heavyweight `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` fails with ``` Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _row_exists in block. There are only columns: k, v, g, s, t, ver, sign, _block_number, _block_offset. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` The mutation is **retried forever**. It never completes and never gives up, so every later mutation on that table queues behind it and the table can no longer be mutated at all. The statement itself returns `Code: 341 ... (UNFINISHED)`, but the entry stays in `system.mutations` with `is_done = 0`. No TTL, skip index, projection, replication or concurrency is required. ## How to reproduce ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS sh SYNC; CREATE TABLE sh (k UInt64, v UInt64, g UInt32, s String, t DateTime, ver UInt64, sign Int8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY (k % 4) ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1, min_bytes_for_wide_part = 0; INSERT INTO sh SELECT number, number * 7 % 1000000, number % 50, concat('s', toString(number % 200)), now() + INTERVAL 10 YEAR, 1, 1 FROM numbers(60000); SET mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2, lightweight_deletes_sync = 2; DELETE FROM sh WHERE k % 3 = 0 SETTINGS lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'; ALTER TABLE sh UPDATE v = v + 1 WHERE k = 1; DELETE FROM sh WHERE k = 1 SETTINGS lightweight_delete_mode = 'lightweight_update'; ALTER TABLE sh DELETE WHERE k = 1; -- Code: 341 ... (UNFINISHED) SELECT mutation_id, is_done, parts_to_do, latest_fail_reason FROM system.mutations WHERE table = 'sh' AND NOT is_done; ``` **Actual** ``` mutation_13.txt 0 1 Code: 10. DB::Exception: Not found column _row_exists in block. There are only columns: k, v, g, s, t, ver, sign, _block_number, _block_offset. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK) ``` The row stays in `system.mutations` indefinitely with a growing retry count. **Expected:** the `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` completes, exactly as it does when the preceding lightweight `DELETE`s are absent. ### It is not merely "still running" The mutation makes no progress and never will. `parts_to_do` is unchanged after minutes, while `latest_fail_time` keeps advancing, i.e. it is looping on the same failure: ``` mutation_id: mutation_13.txt is_done: 0 parts_to_do: 2 <-- same value 140 s later age_s: 140 since_last_fail_s: 66 <-- still actively re-failing ``` And the table is no longer mutable — the next statement fails immediately, naming the wedged mutation: ```sql ALTER TABLE sh UPDATE v = 1 WHERE k = 99999 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2, alter_sync = 2; -- Code: 341. DB::Exception: Exception happened during execution of mutations -- 'mutation_13.txt, mutation_14.txt' ``` Recovering the table requires `KILL MUTATION`. ## Notes on the shape of the trigger - Both mutation styles are needed. A table that only ever receives lightweight mutations, or only ever receives heavyweight ones, never wedges. - Only the **first** lightweight `DELETE` needs a broad predicate; the other three statements work with `WHERE k = 1`. It also has to be non-aligned with the partition key: with `PARTITION BY (k % 4)`, `k % 3 = 0` reproduces but `k % 2 = 0`, `k % 100 = 0` and `k < 30000` do not. So what matters is that the first lightweight delete masks off a partial, non-partition-aligned subset of *every* part. - `lightweight_delete_mode` may be either `'lightweight_update'` or `'lightweight_update_force'`; both reach it. - Independent of `TTL`, of `minmax` / `set` / `bloom_filter` skip indexes, of projections, and of `ReplicatedMergeTree` — first observed on a replicated table with indexes and projections, then reduced to the plain table above. ## Impact The table becomes permanently unmutable: no further `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, `ALTER UPDATE` or `ALTER DELETE` will complete, because the failing mutation is never retired and blocks the queue. Recovery requires `KILL MUTATION`. Because the failure is a retry loop rather than a terminal error, it also burns a background mutation slot indefinitely. ## Root cause Two places independently decide whether a mutation "updates the `_row_exists` mask", and they disagree when the only signal is a pending patch rather than an explicit assignment: - `MutateTask.cpp::isDeletedMaskUpdated`, which decides the **new part's physical column list** (`getColumnsForNewDataPart`), treats a synthesized `READ_COLUMN(_row_exists, read_for_patch=true)` command as "yes, the mask is updated". That command is added whenever a part has an unresolved patch touching `_row_exists` (a pending lightweight delete). So `_row_exists` is kept in the new part's schema. - `MutationsInterpreter::prepare()`, which decides what the **pipeline actually writes**, explicitly excludes that same signal: ```cpp /// The _row_exists mask is handled by APPLY_DELETED_MASK, not as a data column. if (command.type == MutationCommand::READ_COLUMN && command.read_for_patch && command.column_name != RowExistsColumn::name) patch_updated_columns.insert(command.column_name); ``` Its own `deleted_mask_updated` flag only flips on an explicit `UPDATE _row_exists = ...` assignment, never on this `READ_COLUMN` signal. For a plain `UPDATE`, the mismatch is harmless: untouched columns are hardlinked from the source part, so `_row_exists` never goes through the writer. It only surfaces when the mutation is `DELETE` / `APPLY_DELETED_MASK` / `REWRITE_PARTS` (`affectsAllColumns() == true`), which forces a full rewrite (`MutateAllPartColumnsTask`) that writes every declared column through the pipeline. `MergeTreeDataPartWriterWide::addStreams` then expects `_row_exists` in the block and throws `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK` when it isn't there. Confirmed against a live repro: the server-side stack trace resolves the throw to `block_sample.getByName("_row_exists")` inside `addStreams`, and `system.mutations` / `system.parts` / `system.parts_columns` show exactly the state this explanation predicts — an active patch on `_row_exists` sitting on the one part the failing `DELETE` touches. ## Suggested fix Teach `MutationsInterpreter::prepare()`'s command scan to also set `deleted_mask_updated = true` for the excluded case, mirroring `isDeletedMaskUpdated`: ```cpp // src/Interpreters/MutationsInterpreter.cpp, around line 741 if (command.type == MutationCommand::READ_COLUMN && command.read_for_patch) { if (command.column_name == RowExistsColumn::name) deleted_mask_updated = true; else patch_updated_columns.insert(command.column_name); } ``` `deleted_mask_updated` is already a member used the same way for the explicit-assignment case a few dozen lines below, so this is a single-function, single-file change (~6-line diff hunk), plus a regression test. **Not yet verified**: this is a proposed direction from static analysis of the two disagreeing code paths, not a built and tested patch — I have not compiled ClickHouse with this change or confirmed it resolves the repro without regressing anything else. ## Related - #67314 — same `NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK: _row_exists` error on v24.6, triggered by lightweight deletes followed by `MATERIALIZE PROJECTION`. Closed; the final comment attributes it to a mutation still running asynchronously. The case here involves no projection at all, and the evidence above shows the mutation is looping rather than progressing. - #61985 — same error message on v24.3 while changing a TTL column, closed without a repro ("should be verified in a recent version"). This report is that verification, on 26.8, with a deterministic reproducer.

signal.title: Do not hold the DDL guard during TRUNCATE
signal.text: `TRUNCATE TABLE` held the table's DDL guard while removing data, and truncate can wait for running merges or for other replicas to process `DROP_RANGE`. Any DDL on that name — including background threads that need it — was blocked for that whole time. Release the guard before `IStorage::truncate` for databases with UUIDs, matching `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which never took it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TRUNCATE TABLE` no longer blocks concurrent `DROP`, `RENAME` and other DDL queries on the same table while the data is being removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114672&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114672](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114672+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: A `WHERE` predicate on an `arrayJoin`'d column can be rewritten into `arrayFilter` so the array is filtered before expansion
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse customer ### Use case Queries that unnest one or more `Array` columns with `arrayJoin` (or `ARRAY JOIN`) and then select a few specific elements in `WHERE` are a very common pattern (tag/label arrays, event attribute arrays, key-value arrays stored as parallel arrays). Today ClickHouse first materializes the full expansion and only then applies the filter, so a query that ultimately returns one row per source row can transiently produce `length(A) * length(B) * length(C)` rows per source row. The work and the memory spent on those rows is unnecessary, and with several `arrayJoin` calls in one query it's multiplicative. Example: ```sql SELECT arrayJoin(A) AS a, arrayJoin(B) AS b, arrayJoin(C) AS c FROM t WHERE a = 'X-A' AND b = 'X-B' AND c = 'X-C'; ``` is equivalent to, but much slower and more memory hungry than, the manual rewrite: ```sql SELECT arrayJoin(arrayFilter(x -> x = 'X-A', A)) AS a, arrayJoin(arrayFilter(x -> x = 'X-B', B)) AS b, arrayJoin(arrayFilter(x -> x = 'X-C', C)) AS c FROM t; ``` ### Describe the solution you'd like Add an optimization that pushes a WHERE conjunct that constrains an arrayJoin'd column into an arrayFilter over the source array, i.e. rewrite `arrayJoin(expr) AS a ... WHERE f(a)` into `arrayJoin(arrayFilter(x -> f(x), expr)) AS a` and drop the conjunct from WHERE when it becomes redundant. Conditions under which the rewrite is applicable: 1. The predicate is a top-level conjunct of WHERE (an AND operand). OR across different array-join columns must not be rewritten. 2. The conjunct depends on exactly one arrayJoin'd column. Other columns it references must be row-constant (not produced by an arrayJoin); those are captured by the lambda, which arrayFilter already supports. A conjunct relating two different arrayJoin'd columns (e.g. a = b) cannot be rewritten. 3. The predicate must be deterministic and stateless (exclude rand, runningAccumulate, neighbor, and anything else whose result depends on evaluation order or position in the stream). 4. Multi-array `ARRAY JOIN a, b` is not supported ### Describe alternatives you've considered Writing `arrayJoin(arrayFilter(...))` by hand. This works and is the current workaround. ### Additional context _No response_

signal.title: Mac OS security dialogs due to self-extracting binary distribution
signal.text: The official Mac OS builds are currently shipped as self-extracting executables (e.g. `clickhouse-macos-aarch64`). Recent Mac OS releases have additional checks for unsigned/untrusted executable files, which means you have to go through multiple hoops (four dialogs and a non-obvious button in Settings) to allowlist the binary, and this has to be done after each minor upgrade. (With previous Mac OS versions, it was two dialogs which was slightly more bearable.) Clickhouse's self-modification appears to reset and drop the permission needed to execute. So you end up with a non-executable `clickhouse` after `brew upgrade`. Possible low-friction solution is to just ship the Mac OS binaries as a standard non-self-modifying gzip executable. (Alternatively, it might be possible to make the Mach-O header look like a valid gzip stream and locate the data such that you can gunzip it, or might be possible to preserve the security metadata while self-extracting, or might be possible for the homebrew packager to pre-run the binary once and re-install the permissions on the result, but life's too short.)

signal.title: Fix a logical error when materialized views share one target table
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/104448 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a `Block structure mismatch` logical error on `INSERT` into a table that several materialized views write to, when the target table's metadata is changed concurrently. Each view's sink is now built from the same metadata snapshot as the header feeding it. ### Description A table reached through N materialized views is visited N times while insert dependencies are collected, because `DependencyPath::popBack` removes the node from `visited`. `observePath` re-read the target's metadata every visit and published it into the builder-wide `metadata_snapshots` unconditionally, so the **last** visit won, while `output_headers` is keyed per view and keeps the snapshot of the visit that observed it. `createSinkImpl` pairs the two: `RemovingSparseTransform` from `output_headers.at(view_id)`, the sink from `metadata_snapshots.at(inner_table_id)`. If the target's metadata is replaced between two visits, an earlier view's sink is built against a snapshot its header did not come from, and `Chain::addSink` -> `connect` throws: ``` Logical error: 'Block structure mismatch in function connect between RemovingSparseTransform and MemorySink stream: different number of columns: k UInt32 UInt32(size = 0), v UInt32 UInt32(size = 0), w UInt32 UInt32(size = 0) k UInt32 UInt32(size = 0), v UInt32 UInt32(size = 0)' ``` The share lock `observePath` takes is a drop lock, so it does not prevent this: `ALTER` takes `alter_lock`, and `StorageObjectStorage`'s schema refresh calls `setInMemoryMetadata` with no lock at all. The fix stores the storage handle, its snapshot and its share lock only on the first observation, then adopts that snapshot and re-derives the materialized-view pointer from the stored handle, so a node's published artifacts all describe one storage as seen once. A view is itself re-visitable, and that pointer picks the branch and supplies `getTargetTableId`. It sits after the stale-dependency validation, which keeps its fresh read, and before `output_headers` is filled. Where both reads would return the same value the adopted handle *is* that value, so behaviour is unchanged. Reproduced on `Memory` and `MergeTree` targets by racing `INSERT` against `ALTER ADD/DROP COLUMN`: pristine master aborted 4 of 4 runs, the fix survived 4 of 4. A gtest pins the invariant; two mutation arms confirm both halves load-bearing. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113518&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113518](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113518+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL functions sort_by_label() and sort_by_label_desc()
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the PromQL functions `sort()`, `sort_desc()`, `sort_by_label()` and `sort_by_label_desc()` in the experimental PromQL dialect for `TimeSeries` tables. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes: `sort_by_label(v instant-vector, label string, ...)` and `sort_by_label_desc(v instant-vector, label string, ...)` sort the elements of an instant vector by the natural sort order of the given label values, in ascending and descending order respectively. Several label names may be provided; earlier labels take precedence and later ones break ties. A missing label is treated as an empty string (matching Prometheus). ### Description This adds the PromQL sorting-by-label functions to the experimental PromQL-to-SQL converter: - `sort_by_label(v, label, ...)` — sort ascending by the given label values. - `sort_by_label_desc(v, label, ...)` — sort descending by the given label values. Unlike `sort()` / `sort_desc()` (which order by sample value), these order by the *natural* sort order of the requested label values, so numeric segments compare numerically (e.g. `host1, host2, host10, host20`). Multiple labels are supported: earlier labels take precedence, later labels break ties, and the full label set is appended as a deterministic final tiebreaker. A missing label is treated as an empty string. Implementation notes: - Grammar: added `sort_by_label` / `sort_by_label_desc` to `PromQLLexer.g4` and regenerated the ANTLR lexer. - Lowering: `applySortFunction` orders the vector at the call site (in PromQL these are ordinary vector functions, so outer transforms must keep the order they produce): it materializes the argument grid and builds a rank map `sort_group` → `sort_rank` fixing each series' position. The map is carried through series-preserving transforms, re-keyed by group-changing ones (metric-name dropping, `label_replace()`/`label_join()`), discarded by aggregations, and `finalizeSQL` joins it and emits `ORDER BY sort_rank`. - Errors: at least two arguments are required, and every label argument must be a string. Testing: - Parser unit tests in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp`. - Stateless test `04556_promql_sort_by_label` covering single-label natural ordering, descending order, multi-label ordering with the missing-label/tiebreak behaviour, and the argument-count / argument-type errors. - Nested regressions in the stateless tests (`abs(sort(...))`, `-sort(...)`, `label_replace(sort_desc(...), ...)`, `abs(sort_by_label(...))`) checking that outer functions keep the order produced by an inner sort* call. - sort*/sort_by_label* checks in `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_evaluation.py` comparing against real Prometheus, and re-enabled the tests that were disabled as nondeterministic without `sort_by_label()`. > [!NOTE] > Per review, this PR supersedes #112826: it contains both the `sort()` / `sort_desc()` commit and the `sort_by_label()` / `sort_by_label_desc()` work, and is intended to be merged instead of that PR.

signal.title: Fix ANY/SEMI RIGHT JOIN with OR conditions emitting rows twice or losing matches
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112640 `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` emit every row of their right table at most once, and exactly once when the row has a match. With several OR-ed conditions in `ON` the claim for that was taken with a single CAS on the head row of the matched key's `RowRefList`, while `addFoundRowAll` then emitted every row of that list and discarded the result of the per-row `setUsedOnce` it called afterwards. With `OR` a right row is reachable through several keys in several hash maps, so a per-key claim does not partition the right rows: a list whose head row was claimed through another condition was skipped whole, orphaning its other rows, and a list whose head row was still free re-emitted rows another left row had already taken. Some right rows then appeared twice and others lost their match — padded with defaults for `ANY RIGHT JOIN`, dropped entirely for `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` — varying from run to run with the probe order under `max_threads > 1`. The claim is now taken per emitted row: `addFoundRowAll` claims a row before appending it and skips the rows whose CAS it loses, and returns whether it appended anything so the left row is filtered in only then. A single disjunct keeps the per-key claim, which is exact there, since one key owns all of its rows. The residual-condition path (`joinRightColumnsWithAdditionalFilter`) already claimed per row and is unchanged. Besides writing `ANY RIGHT JOIN` / `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` directly, this is reached by a plain `ANY LEFT JOIN` whenever the planner swaps the tables (`query_plan_join_swap_table`, `auto` by default), which is how the issue was reported. Measured on the reported query before and after, at `max_threads = 8`: 20 of 60 runs returned 5 or 6 rows for a 4-row left table, now 60/60 return 4. On a 1000-row shape, `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` returned 200 rows instead of 1000; `ANY LEFT JOIN` padded 416–736 rows with defaults although they had a match, and with `max_joined_block_size_rows = 7` also returned 1008 rows for 1000 left rows. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `ANY RIGHT JOIN` and `SEMI RIGHT JOIN` with several `OR`-ed conditions in the `ON` section returning some rows of the right table twice and losing the matches of others. A written `ANY LEFT JOIN` was affected too, because the planner may swap the tables and execute it as `ANY RIGHT JOIN`.

signal.title: Test: merge memory is not bounded by max_memory_usage (merge OOM repro)
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107389 --> Draft. A test demonstrating that a background merge's memory is **not** bounded by the per-query `max_memory_usage` setting. ### Motivation In the AST fuzzer run for #107389 ([CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107389&sha=ec12cb3ce0a49a403226cb0668b092f02a2fa3f6&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%2C%20targeted%2C%20old_compatibility%29)) the server was OOM-killed even though the fuzzer runs queries **sequentially** and no single query peaked above 1.69 GiB. During the steepest part of the memory climb there were *zero* foreground queries running — only background merges. The fuzzer's `INSERT`s left behind parts (large arrays from `arrayResize`, very wide schemas up to 1796 columns) that the background merge subsystem then combined; that memory accumulates across query boundaries and is governed by the global / background-pool trackers, not by the per-query limit. A merge runs under its own memory tracker — a child of the global `Background process (mutate/merge)` tracker — created in `ThreadGroup::createForMergeMutate`. `configureMemoryTrackerFromSettings` never installs `max_memory_usage` as the merge tracker's hard limit, so the per-query limit does not constrain a merge at all. ### What the test does - Creates a `MergeTree` table and inserts two parts of large arrays (forcing a horizontal merge). - Sets a tiny `max_memory_usage` (20 MB). - Runs `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` — the merge **completes** despite the limit. - Confirms via `system.part_log` that the merge's `peak_memory_usage` (~110 MiB observed) is far above the per-query limit. The test asserts behavior with a generous margin, so it does not literally OOM-kill the CI server (that would be destructive and flaky). It reliably reproduces the *condition* that leads to OOM: a merge consuming memory the per-query limit never sees. It is intended as the regression/repro basis for extending the memory-overcommit mechanism to merges (today `OvercommitTracker` only selects victims from `ProcessList`, i.e. user queries; merges — which are restartable and therefore cheaper to cancel than queries — do not participate). ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107410&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/107410](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F107410+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not qualify an expression alias in the right argument of IN with the default database
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/94894 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/76356 `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` when the view query used an expression alias as the right argument of `IN`: ```sql CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW myview TO mydestination AS SELECT 'foo' AS object WHERE (object IN ('foo', 'bar') AS objects) AND object IN objects; ``` ``` Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression or table expression identifier `default.objects` in scope SELECT 'foo' AS object WHERE ((object IN ('foo', 'bar')) AS objects) AND (object IN (default.objects)). (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` assumed that an identifier in the right argument of `IN` is a table name and qualified it with the current database, so the stored view query could not be resolved, while the same plain `SELECT` worked. The similar code in `MarkTableIdentifiersVisitor` checks the query aliases before marking such an identifier as a table; now `AddDefaultDatabaseVisitor` does the same: it collects the expression aliases of each select query (visible in nested queries, but not leaking into the enclosing query) and leaves matching identifiers intact, so that a real table name in the right argument of `IN` is still qualified. #76356 fixed the same problem for aliases defined in the `WITH` clause; this covers aliases defined elsewhere in the query. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` error when creating a materialized view whose query uses an expression alias as the right argument of `IN`. signal.title: Parsing a Tuple to JSON fails when a string field stores unencoded binary data
signal.text: ### Company or project name Use Case: I am ingesting event data to a self-hosted clickhouse instance that may include fields with raw binary objects without an encoding. Due to the dynamic nature of the upstream sources (potentially breaking schema changes at any given restart) I want to use JSON for the dynamic pathing and type inference it provides. ### Describe what's wrong The String data type from my understanding is used to store binary data of any description and does not need to necessarily be utf8 encoded data, in fact string assumes no encoding. However, when a string column with binary data is part of a tuple that is parsed to JSON, the parsing fails when converting, seemingly due to the fact that the strings may contain invalid utf-8 characters. The error I have seen is as below. Received exception from server (version 26.7.1): Code: 117. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:9000.
