signal.title: Add with_source parameter to the JSON type storing the JSON text in the __source sub-column
signal.text: ## Motivation Reading a whole `JSON` value as a `String` (`toString(json)`, or just selecting the column in a text format) is expensive: it reads every sub-column of the JSON column — all typed paths, all dynamic paths and the shared data structure — and constructs the JSON object back for every row. Applications that store JSON documents and ship them back verbatim pay this on every query. ## What was added The `JSON` type accepts a new parameter `with_source`. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in a separate `String` sub-column `__source`: ```sql CREATE TABLE test (json JSON(with_source=1)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO test VALUES ('{"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42}'); SELECT json, json.__source FROM test; ``` ``` ┌─json─────────────────┬─json.__source─────────────┐ │ {"a":42,"b":"Hello"} │ {"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42} │ └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ ``` Reading `json.__source` reads a single sub-column. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such a column write the stored text instead of constructing it from the object (it saves the construction, not the reading of the column). The text is stored exactly as it was inserted. Where the original text is not available it is created from the object itself, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON: values restored from an aggregation or `JOIN` key, binary input without the JSON text (structured `RowBinary`), nested `JSON(with_source=1)` type hints (only the top level column gets the original text), and results of functions creating JSON objects such as `mergedJSONPatch`. `__source` is reserved in such types: a top level JSON key with this name is rejected during parsing, and the name cannot be used as a type hint or in the `SKIP` section. Nested keys with this name are fine. Adding or removing the parameter with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` always rewrites the data. The stored text is not a part of the value: it doesn't participate in comparison, so two values with the same content but different formatting stay equal and are grouped together. ## Implementation notes - The text is stored in a separate `String` column inside `ColumnObject` and serialized into its own named `ObjectSource` sub-stream, so `json.__source` is a static sub-column resolved the same way a named tuple element is. The sub-stream exists in all `Object` serialization versions except `STRING`, where the JSON text is the payload itself, and no `Object` serialization version was bumped. - In binary type encoding the JSON type version is bumped to `1`, and version `1` is written only for types that actually have `with_source=1`, so encodings of all other types stay byte-identical and readable by older servers. - `ColumnObject` keeps its type to create the text when the original is not available; the serialization for it is built lazily on first use, so nothing is built for columns that never need it. - The aggregation key representation (`serializeValueIntoArena`) deliberately stays canonical, i.e. it doesn't include the text; otherwise values differing only in formatting would form different `GROUP BY` groups while comparison says they are equal. ## Limitations - Text created from the object is written without the settings used during parsing, so with `json_type_escape_dots_in_keys` enabled keys with dots appear in it escaped (`{"a%2Eb" : 42}`). - `Native` in JSON-as-string mode transmits the constructed text unless `output_format_json_type_use_source` is set. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `with_source` parameter to the `JSON` data type. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in the reserved `__source` `String` sub-column, so reading the whole value as a string is a single sub-column read instead of reading every path and constructing the JSON back. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such columns write the stored text. The text is kept as it was inserted; where the original text is not available (for example for values restored from an aggregation key) it is created from the object, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON. A top level JSON key named `__source` is not allowed in such types. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115477&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115477](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115477+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reload a persisted `url()` table with the storage its creation selected
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104437 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server that refuses to start after a table was created with `CREATE TABLE ... AS url('http://host/**/', ...)` while `allow_experimental_url_wildcard_from_index_pages` was enabled. Loading such a table's metadata re-evaluated the experimental check and failed with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`, aborting startup. ### Description Reported by @ bacek on #104437, where `Stress test (amd_tsan)` failed with `Cannot start clickhouse-server` after a fuzzer created `url('/**/', JSONEachRow, 'x int')`. No fuzzer is needed: enable the setting, create such a table, restart with the default. Root cause is one defaulted parameter. `ITableFunction::execute` declares `bool is_insert_query = false`; `CREATE ... AS url(...)` passes `true` explicitly (`InterpreterCreateQuery.cpp:2403`), while metadata replay (`DatabaseOnDisk.cpp:117`) passes nothing. `TableFunctionURL::getStorage` computes `use_web_wildcard = !is_insert_query && ...`, so the two take opposite branches for the same stored table: creation builds a plain `StorageURL` and never reaches the experimental check, replay builds `StorageObjectStorage` and does. The check is dead at creation and live only on replay, and metadata loading rethrows. The fix treats a definition arriving with stored columns as a persisted one being replayed, so it resolves to the storage creation selected. The check is not suppressed, it becomes unreachable because the correct branch is taken. Suppressing it would instead enable index-page expansion with the setting disabled and give the table a read-only storage. `ENGINE = URL` was already fixed this way in 64abbdd31d85b15 ("Gate `URL` wildcard experiment check to creation"). Behaviour change: a persisted glob `url()` table that today rebuilds as `StorageObjectStorage` after a restart now rebuilds as the `StorageURL` its creation built. Both carriers are covered by the one change and both are tested: explicit structure, and `structure = 'auto'` via `StorageTableFunctionProxy` (the surface of an earlier `test_url_wildcard_schema_inference` failure). `urlCluster` cannot persist a table. The creation-time check in `getActualTableStructure` is deliberately untouched, since a columns-less `CREATE` reaches it before `execute`. Querying `url()` directly still requires the setting. Out of scope: the check stays dead at creation, so `CREATE` with a glob still succeeds with the setting off. `ytsaurus()` has the same problem by another mechanism. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104437&sha=bee15ffc5ec3d2a9b5479bd1fbc197ac6458eebc&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115095&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115095](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115095+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: [ClickHouse-58380] Implement Retries in distributed queries when server stopped during queries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Add settings `distributed_query_retries` and `distributed_query_retry_interval_ms` (disabled by default): when enabled, a query to a `Distributed` table or to the `remote` table function is retried after a network error (`NETWORK_ERROR`, `SOCKET_TIMEOUT`, `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF`, e.g. when the remote server is stopped while the query is running). The query is retried on another available replica and only if no result data has been received from the remote server yet, so the result never contains duplicated rows. Queries executed with parallel replicas and cluster function tasks are not retried. While a retry is still possible, the progress reported by the remote server is deferred until the first block of result data (or the completion of the query), so the work replayed by a retry is not double-counted in read limits and quotas. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- The settings documentation is autogenerated from the setting descriptions in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58380 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=66791&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/66791](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F66791+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix `STREAM BOUNDED` returning no rows on a stale enrichment round
signal.text: Caused by: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110653 `MergeTreeData::scheduleStreamingJob` read the visible parts *before* it iterated the registered subscriptions, so a subscription registered in that window was credited with an enrichment round computed from a parts snapshot taken before it existed. For a subscribing stream that is harmless — the next round fixes the cursor. For a bounded stream it is not: `handleBoundedReconfiguration` treats the first completed round as authoritative, so an empty stale round makes the source finish immediately and the query silently returns fewer rows (usually none) than were committed before it started. That is how `04545_streaming_queries_bounded` failed on master. The first query in the test (`STREAM BOUNDED` over the still-empty table) triggers the background streaming job; the job snapshots an empty part set and is then descheduled; by the time it reaches `executeOnEachSubscription` the two `INSERT`s and the second query have already run, so the second query's subscription is handed that empty round: ``` empty 0 -all 10 45 450 +all 0 0 0 ``` CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=8d5be603139a198bdfd2ea225d2e998554316178&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20parallel%29 The fix collects the subscriptions first and reads the parts only afterwards. Everything in the collected list was registered before the collect, so the parts snapshot is at least as fresh as every subscription served from it. A subscription registered after the collect is picked up by the next round instead: its own `triggerStreamingSubscriptionEnrichment` re-schedules the job even while the job is running, because `BackgroundSchedulePoolTaskInfo::execute` re-queues a task that was scheduled during execution. `executeOnEachSubscription` is replaced by `collectSubscriptions`, which returns strong pointers under the shared lock — the callback form invited exactly this ordering mistake, and there was only one caller. The race is timing-dependent (one failure in 2629 master runs of this test over 90 days), so there is no deterministic functional test for it; the added unit tests cover the `collectSubscriptions` contract the fix relies on, including that a subscription registered after a collect is not part of that round. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a race that could make a `STREAM BOUNDED` query return fewer rows than were committed before it started, usually none. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115543&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115543](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115543+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1779` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Stop resolving the UTC time zone in `TimezoneMixin`
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> While profiling `clickhouse local --query "SELECT 1"` it turned out that almost all of the run happens before the query: the query itself took 1ms of a 45ms run. This is one of the sources of that startup work, split out of #112496. `TimezoneMixin` resolved the UTC time zone in its constructor, in addition to the named or default one. Building a `DateLUTImpl` walks ~146k days through cctz, about 70M instructions, and `DataTypeDateTime` / `DataTypeDateTime64` get constructed just to name a column type — for example when building the schemas of the system tables — without ever touching UTC. Only the serializations need UTC, for ISO output and for the `best_effort` parsers, so `SerializationDateTime`, `SerializationDateTime64` and the `DateTime` / `DateTime64` nodes of `JSONExtractTree` declare their own `utc_time_zone` member instead. The cost is then paid once per formatter rather than once per named type. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Naming a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` type no longer builds a UTC time zone lookup table that nothing reads, which makes constructing these types — and therefore starting up `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` — faster. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115488&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115488](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115488+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1780` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Add min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds to compact partitions that no longer receive inserts
signal.text: ## Summary Closes #79697. Reworked per review: the previous `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... MERGE SMALLPARTS` syntax is reverted. Instead this adds an opt-in `MergeTree` setting, `min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds`, addressing the issue's use case in the background merge selector itself (similar in spirit to #105454). When set to a non-zero value and every part in a partition is at least that many seconds old — i.e. the partition no longer receives inserts — the `Simple` and `StochasticSimple` merge selectors: - consider all part ranges in that partition for merging, bypassing the base heuristic that otherwise refuses "unbalanced" merges of a large part with small ones, and - skip the right-tail heuristic that removes small parts from the right side of a candidate range. Each merge still respects `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool`, so a partition larger than that limit converges to a few max-size parts. Unlike `min_age_to_force_merge_seconds` with `min_age_to_force_merge_on_partition_only`, the partition does not have to fit into a single merge, and unlike plain `min_age_to_force_merge_seconds`, actively written partitions are unaffected. The default is `0` (disabled), preserving existing behavior. Merged parts start with age 0, which re-arms the threshold, so compaction of an idle partition proceeds in naturally throttled rounds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `min_partition_age_to_force_merge_seconds` `MergeTree` setting: when every part in a partition is at least this old, the `Simple` and `StochasticSimple` merge selectors compact the partition's parts (including its tail of small parts) within the `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool` limit. ### Documentation entry: - [x] Documentation is generated from the setting description in `MergeTreeSettings.cpp`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: Publish a failing job step's cause to CIDB, not just the failure count
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description A job's summary line carried only `Failures: N/M`. When a job dies in a step outside the node named by `result_name_for_cidb` (`Install ClickHouse`, `Start ClickHouse Server`), that count is the only text in the job's own info, so the cause reaches neither CIDB's job-level row, nor the report page, nor the GitHub issue body. It survives only inside `job.log`. 152 failing master job instances land in this shape over 30d; at `b03544a19bc` the failing `Start ClickHouse Server` node carried 301 lines and CIDB got 13 bytes ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=b03544a19bc3e7046b8ac5eb6467bf444f295038&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_debug%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%20s3%20storage%2C%20parallel%29)). `_add_job_summary_to_info` now names each failing direct child after the count line. The count line stays first and keeps its exact old text, so readers and queries written against it keep matching. Fixing it here rather than in `cidb.py` lifts every surface that renders a job summary, per review. Two bounds, both measured. `from_commands_run` puts the cause near the front in its error-centered branch but at the tail in its default branch, so a one-ended trim drops it in one of the two; the trim keeps both ends. And a job whose direct children are test cases already publishes a row per case, so naming all of them grew this row with the failure count (40 cases gave 120 KB); at most the first few are named. Not addressed: a job whose info is already non-empty when the summary runs, so a later fallible sibling (`Collect logs`) still publishes no cause. That predates this change, identically, and reaching it needs the final result tree at serialization time. `Keeper Stress` naming a `result_name_for_cidb` no child carries is likewise unchanged. Validation: `ci/tests/test_job_summary_names_failed_step.py`, 21 cases including both payload branches, both trim directions, the per-shape bound, and the path through the real publisher. 15 mutations, one per property, each reddens the suite; the whole `ci/tests` suite passes. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115526&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115526](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115526+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL aggregation operator limit_ratio
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented the aggregation operator `limit_ratio()`. ### Description Implements the PromQL `limit_ratio` aggregation operator, which was previously rejected at parse time: ``` limit_ratio(r scalar, v instant-vector) ``` For each aggregation group it keeps a deterministic, reproducible ratio `r` of the input series (`r` in `[-1, 1]`; out-of-range values are clamped, matching Prometheus). The selection uses the same stable per-series sampling key as `limitk` (`timeSeriesGroupToSamplingKey`, a fixed-seed hash of the series labels), normalized to an offset in `[0, 1)`: ``` keep a series if (r >= 0 AND offset < r) OR (r < 0 AND offset >= 1 + r) ``` so `r` and `-r` keep complementary subsets, `r = 0` keeps nothing, and `|r| = 1` keeps everything, matching Prometheus semantics. Like `limitk`, `limit_ratio` does not aggregate: the selected series are returned unchanged, and their labels (including the metric name) are preserved. `by` / `without` grouping is supported. **Implementation** - `limit_ratio` is added to the `impl_map` in `applyLimitAggregationOperator.cpp`, reusing the existing collect / per-time-step mask / unzip pipeline and the `limitk` sampling keys. A new `is_ratio` flag on `ImplInfo` selects a `getRatio()` helper that keeps the ratio a `Float64` clamped to `[-1, 1]` instead of truncating it to a `UInt64` count via `convertScalarToK()`. The index-selection lambda filters the non-null series by the ratio condition above. `isLimitAggregationOperator()` now dispatches `limit_ratio` automatically. - The operator name is added to the `AGGREGATION_OPERATOR` rule in the PromQL lexer (`PromQLLexer.g4`) and the ANTLR C++ is regenerated (`PromQLLexer.cpp` / `.interp`). **Testing**: new parser cases in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp` (plain and `by`-grouped); new stateless test `04555_promql_limit_ratio.sh` validating the whole/empty/complement ratios, out-of-range clamping, the complementary and reproducible subsets selected for `r` and `-r`, and label preservation end to end against a multi-series TimeSeries table. signal.title: Label "submodule changed" only when a submodule actually changed
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) The `submodule changed` label is applied by matching the `contrib/` path prefix: ```python if "contrib/" in " ".join(changed_files): pr_labels_to_add.append(Labels.SUBMODULE_CHANGED) ``` Most of `contrib/` is not submodules. The `contrib/<lib>-cmake/` directories are ClickHouse's own build glue, `contrib/CMakeLists.txt` is ours, and some directories under `contrib/` are ordinary in-repo trees — `contrib/antlr4-grammars` and `contrib/antlr4-grammars-cmake` are not registered in `.gitmodules` at all. Editing any of them gets a PR labelled as changing a submodule although no gitlink moved. **Of the 77 open PRs currently carrying the label, 33 contain no submodule change at all.** I measured this by taking each PR's diff and looking for `Subproject commit` lines, which is what a gitlink change always renders as — that catches bumps, additions and removals without depending on any `.gitmodules` baseline. Representative cases: | PR | `contrib/` files touched | gitlink changed | | --- | --- | --- | | #63057 | `contrib/arrow-cmake/CMakeLists.txt` | no | | #88857 | `contrib/jwt-cpp-cmake/CMakeLists.txt` | no | | #78494 | `contrib/datasketches-cpp-cmake/CMakeLists.txt` | no | | #80177 | `contrib/CMakeLists.txt`, `contrib/aws-sdk-cpp-*/CMakeLists.txt` | no | | #107200 | `contrib/datasketches-cpp-cmake/include_patched/…` | no | | #113173, #112861, #114558 | `contrib/antlr4-grammars…/PromQLLexer.{g4,cpp,interp}` | no | This decides the label from the submodule lifecycle instead, using only the data the hook already has — the PR's changed-file list and the checkout's `.gitmodules`: - a **bump** leaves `.gitmodules` untouched, but the submodule path is in the changed-file list and is still registered, so the path intersection catches it; - **adding**, **removing** and **renaming** a submodule all edit `.gitmodules` itself, so that file appearing in the changed-file list is the signal. Both conditions are needed. A removal is invisible to the path intersection, because the removed path is no longer registered at the head — and a removal that forgets to clean up `.gitmodules` leaves the entry in place, where the intersection catches it. `ci/tests/test_pr_labels_submodule_changed.py` pins the whole lifecycle. Against those cases: | implementation | wrong | | --- | --- | | `contrib/` substring match | 3 of 11 — the `-cmake` glue and grammar false positives | | head `.gitmodules` paths only | 1 of 11 — the removal | | this PR | 0 of 11 | One thing this PR deliberately does not change: the label is only ever added, never removed, so a PR that once touched `contrib/` keeps it afterwards. That accounts for 9 of the 33 above, which touch no `contrib/` file at all today. Worth knowing when checking this fix against an existing PR — the stale label will not clear by itself.

signal.title: Add byte-weighted bytes_to_do and progress to system.mutations
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114678 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `system.mutations` now exposes byte-weighted mutation progress: `bytes_to_do` (the on-disk size of the data parts that still need to be mutated) and `progress` (an estimated finished fraction from 0 to 1, including the live fraction of the parts currently being rewritten). Part counts are a poor work proxy — parts are unequal in size and a regular merge can retire many pending parts at once — so the byte view is the honest one; the docs gain an "Estimating mutation progress" section with an equivalent parameterized-view recipe for older releases. Implements the conclusion of the research on the issue in two layers: **Columns** (`bytes_to_do` UInt64, `progress` Float64 in `system.mutations`): derived on read like `parts_to_do` — no persisted state, no replication protocol or znode format change. For plain `MergeTree` the sizes ride along the existing per-part scan in `getMutationsStatus`; for replicated tables the queue keeps returning name-only statuses under its state lock and the storage resolves sizes afterwards, so no parts lock is ever taken under the queue mutex (parts gone by then were retired and contribute nothing). The in-flight fraction comes from the merge list (`system.merges` rows with `is_mutation = 1`). Values are estimates by nature: a merge can retire pending parts at any moment, making `progress` jump forward. **Docs**: an "Estimating mutation progress" section on the `system.mutations` page explains why part-count percentages mislead and ships a parameterized-view recipe computing the same number on releases without the columns (the view was validated live against a running mutation, including a merge collapsing 9 pending parts mid-run), plus cross-links from `system.merges`, `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, and the knowledge base. The stateless test asserts exact values on both engines: with merges stopped (which parks mutation tasks), `bytes_to_do` equals the active parts' total size and `progress` is 0; after completion the entry reports 0 and 1. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114850&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114850](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114850+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Implement PromQL range function double_exponential_smoothing
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 > **Note:** stacked on #112855 (`ts_of_*`), which is itself stacked on #112851 (`first_over_time` / `mad_over_time`). Until those merge, the diff here also shows their changes; once they are merged this PR will show only the `double_exponential_smoothing` commit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented the range function `double_exponential_smoothing()`. ### Description Implements the PromQL `double_exponential_smoothing` (Holt-Winters double exponential smoothing) range function, which was previously rejected at parse time: ``` double_exponential_smoothing(v range-vector, sf scalar, tf scalar) ``` For each grid point it smooths the samples in that point's staleness window (in timestamp order) with the smoothing factor `sf` and trend factor `tf`, and returns the last smoothed value. Both factors must be constants in the open interval `(0, 1)` (an out-of-range factor produces a query error, matching Prometheus's panic). At least two samples are required in the window, otherwise the series is dropped for that grid point. The metric name is dropped, matching Prometheus. **Implementation** - One new templated grid aggregate, `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesDoubleExponentialSmoothing`, exposed as `timeSeriesDoubleExponentialSmoothingToGrid`. It takes two extra scalar parameters (`sf`, `tf`) after `(start, end, step, window)`, keeps the window's `(timestamp, value)` samples in a `SlidingSum` (a non-invertible summary; `SlidingSum` recomputes per grid point) and runs the Holt-Winters level/trend recurrence in timestamp order — modelled on `timeSeriesMadToGrid`. Registered inline in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp`, where `sf`/`tf` are validated to be in `(0, 1)`. - `applyFunctionOverRange` is refactored to expose `applyAggregateFunctionOverRange`, which lowers a range vector to an aggregate over the window and appends extra scalar parameters after `(start, end, step, window)`. A dedicated translator `applyFunctionDoubleExponentialSmoothing` validates the three arguments (a range vector plus two constant scalars in `(0, 1)`) and threads `sf`/`tf` into the aggregate parameters. - The function name is added to the PromQL lexer (`PromQLLexer.g4`) and the ANTLR C++ is regenerated (`PromQLLexer.cpp` / `.interp`) — this keyword was not in the lexer, so the name would otherwise fail to parse. **Testing**: new parser case in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp`; new stateless test `04554_promql_double_exponential_smoothing.sh` validating the smoothed values (verified against the Prometheus algorithm), two different `(sf, tf)` pairs, metric-name dropping, the fewer-than-two-samples drop, and out-of-range factor errors end to end against a multi-series TimeSeries table.

signal.title: Wait for the worker cleanup before force-killing the test workers
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113393 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description No related open issue; found while investigating `Stress test (*)` jobs failing with only ` script exit code: 1`. `do_run_tests` stopped a run by SIGTERMing each worker and waiting `join(timeout=10)` before SIGKILLing it. That worker's SIGTERM path reaches `kill_process_group`, which on a sanitizer build sleeps **60** seconds, so every worker got 10 seconds for a 60 second cleanup and died inside that sleep. Two consequences. The sanitizer report is truncated, which is what the grace in `1a76ce9b81ce3fc` exists to collect. And `p.kill()` reaches only the worker, not the test's process group, whose PGID file is already unlinked, so the test's `bash` and `clickhouse-client` survive. The harness's random query killer then kills that leaked client and the orphaned `bash` writes `Terminated` into the log descriptor it inherited. Landing while the job packages the logs, `tar` exits 1 on `file changed as we read it`, killing the job *before* the hung check. The wait is now derived from the delays cleanup sleeps for, so the two cannot drift apart again; `ddc6bcfbd68a761`'s SIGTERM, wait, SIGKILL, wait escalation is unchanged. Workers clean up concurrently, so the grace is one monotonic deadline for all of them, and a ceiling rather than a sleep. It bounds one cleanup invocation, not the whole cleanup: a worker owning several process groups pays the sleeps per group and its later groups are still cut short. No wait is shorter than the previous 10 seconds, so nothing regresses. Remaining gaps below. Aggregate shutdown grows: N wedged workers cost 70 + (N-1)*10 seconds on a sanitizer lane, 80 + (N-1)*10 with stacktrace capture, against N*10 before, so about +60s on 16 workers. Cheap against losing a report, but it is CI wall-clock. A unit test pinning the budget was removed on review request, so it rests on the CI stop-path runs. <details> <summary>Affected runs, validation, #113393</summary> All four are sanitizer lanes over three weeks, `base_ref=master`. In each the worker log stops after the `SANITIZED`-gated print, never reaching `Killing process group`, and the archived log is 11 bytes short. Release and debug lanes, which skip that sleep, show none. Also uncovered: the stacktrace collection, an uninterruptible sleep, and `spawn` workers (`aarch` names), which have no cleanup. - [`57ffb33`, PR 111575, `arm_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111575&sha=57ffb330ff3e3da66a99a2c8dfa6f4a49ffddc27&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) - [`5639d68`, PR 107736, `arm_tsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107736&sha=5639d68fe32623687d7dba60a6f72a58ffd1603b&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29) - [`542bb86`, PR 112951, `arm_msan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112951&sha=542bb86022afb31800274d59fcd836d8c7dfc159&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_msan%29) - [`6e15957`, PR 114695, `amd_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114695&sha=6e159579fc017f42673653cf0db45fc03ac9090d&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29) Before the test was removed, eleven mutations each reddened it distinctly (flat 10s, no `kill()` escalation, unbounded wait, sleep instead of ceiling, per-worker budget, either delay dropped, floor gone, wall-clock deadline, call site reverted). End to end with real processes, the pre-change shape leaks the `bash` and writes those 11 bytes 3/3; this change eliminates it 3/3. #113393 (mine, open) extracts this same sequence into `quiesce_workers_and_reap()` and keeps `p.join(timeout=10)` verbatim, relocating this defect without fixing it. Complementary (that one reaps orphaned groups, this one stops creating them) but textually conflicting. I can rebase onto it or fold this in there. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115403&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115403](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115403+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix lazy materialization OOB and a Merge LOGICAL_ERROR from unused text index virtual columns
signal.text: <!-- Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix an out-of-bounds read (release) / logical error (debug) in the lazy materialization optimization, and a logical error in `Pipe::unitePipes` for `Merge` tables, when the direct-read-from-text-index optimization leaves an unused index virtual column in the read header of a `MergeTree` table with multiple `text` indexes. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111422 `TextIndexDAGReplacer::replace` rewrites text-search predicates into `__text_index_*` virtual columns, recording one per rewritten node, then runs `removeUnusedActions()`. When the rewrite keeps a different index's virtual column (or the original expression), the first virtual's input becomes unreferenced, but `result.added_columns` was not re-filtered, so `createReadTasksForTextIndex` still appended that orphaned column to the `ReadFromMergeTree` output header. `removed_columns` was already reconciled against the surviving inputs; `added_columns` was not, and that asymmetry is the bug. The fix collects the rewritten virtuals as candidates while walking the DAG and only populates `added_columns` after `removeUnusedActions()`, keeping a candidate when its input is in the surviving-inputs set already computed for `removed_columns`. The reading step's header then matches what the plan consumes, and a redundant index read goes away. One orphaned column causes two user-visible failures, both fixed: 1. **Lazy materialization out-of-bounds read** (the reported issue). `optimizeLazyMaterialization2` builds its `required_columns` mask positionally from the input headers above the reading step, which never contain a read-only virtual column. The mask ends up shorter than that step's header and the pass indexes a `std::vector<bool>` past its end: out-of-bounds read in release, `cols.size() == required_columns.size()` assertion in debug. 2. **`Merge` table logical error.** With `text` indexes on both `mapKeys(map)` and `mapValues(map)`, the `mapKeys` virtual wins the predicate and the `mapValues` one is left registered but unreferenced. Under `SELECT count()` nothing else is read, so the dead virtual becomes the indexed child's only output column while a non-indexed sibling's header stays empty. `Pipe::getCommonHeader` picks the first non-empty header and `unitePipes` asserts the empty sibling against it: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream`, a server abort in debug and sanitizer builds. `02346_text_index_bug111422` covers the first shape. The new `04563_text_index_merge_heterogeneous_children` covers the second, which the first cannot reach (no `merge()`, no bare `count()`). It pins the two runner-randomized settings it depends on per setting, not with a blanket tag. <details> <summary>Validation of the new test</summary> Debug build of this branch, memory-capped server, per-slot ports. | arm | build id | result | |---|---|---| | master `f9801d5649` (no fix) | `c29b56ab…` | aborts: `Block structure mismatch in Pipe::unitePipes stream: different number of columns` (`Block.cpp:308` <- `Pipe.cpp:316` <- `QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:263`) | | this branch, reconciliation loop removed | `fd96fd28…` | aborts: `Column __text_index_idx_map_values_equals_… already added for reading` (`ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4765`); via the test runner: `ClickHouse server died` | | this branch, unmodified | `a0a422da…` | passes byte-for-byte, and 50/50 randomized runs | The pre-fix signature differs between the two bases because this branch's merge-base predates the `already_has_direct_read` re-entry gate (`optimizeDirectReadFromTextIndex.cpp`, `6253632d8da4`): without that gate the pass visits the step twice and the same over-registration trips the duplicate guard before a pipe is united. Same defect, two assertions. Both pinned settings were verified load-bearing and effective: with the pins removed, a client injecting `query_plan_direct_read_from_text_index=0` or `query_plan_text_index_add_hint=0` turns the `EXPLAIN` assertion vacuous (`1 0` -> `0 0`); with the pins present the test matches the reference under either injection and under both together. Full `text_index` suite on this branch, base vs with the new test: 157 -> 158 tests, 7 -> 6 failures, **zero new failures**. All shared failures are environmental on a bare slot server (missing stateful `test.hits` dataset, no `localhost:9000`, and four debug-build 600s timeouts). </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111467&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111467](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111467+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add memory_eviction_score query setting for memory reservation eviction order
signal.text: Adds an experimental per-query `memory_eviction_score` setting (`Int32`, default `0`) that controls the order in which queries' memory reservations are evicted when their workload is under memory pressure. A query with a higher `memory_eviction_score` is evicted first; queries with an equal score keep the existing largest-reservation-first order. Negative values make a query less likely to be evicted. The eviction victim is now selected by `(memory_eviction_score, reservation size)` instead of reservation size alone. When every query keeps the default `memory_eviction_score = 0` the selection is identical to before, so there is no behavior change unless the setting is used. The setting only has an effect when a `MEMORY RESERVATION` resource is configured for the workload (experimental workload scheduling). signal.title: Fix timezoneOffset losing the whole-day component of the UTC offset
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115281 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `timezoneOffset` (alias `timeZoneOffset`) returning an offset wrong by exactly one day for time zones whose UTC offset differs from their 1970-01-01 offset by a whole day, such as `Pacific/Kiritimati` and `Pacific/Apia` after they crossed the international date line, and for most zones before 1970. This also fixes `parseDateTime`, `parseDateTimeOrNull`, `parseDateTime64`, `parseDateTimeInJodaSyntax`, `EXTRACT(TIMEZONE_HOUR / TIMEZONE_MINUTE ...)`, `formatDateTime`'s `%z`, `toUTCTimestamp` and `fromUTCTimestamp`, which consume that offset. Closes #115281. ### Description Reported by @ PedroTadim in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115281#issuecomment-5327580058. `timezoneOffset` did not read the offset, it reconstructed it as `(lut[index].date - lut[epoch].date) % 86400` plus `offset_at_start_of_epoch`. That difference is `days * 86400 - (offset_now - offset_epoch)`, so the modulo keeps only the sub-day part of the change since the epoch and discards any whole-day part; the date-line zones stayed pinned at their pre-jump offset, correct before the jump and wrong after. Separately, `%` takes the sign of the dividend, so on a pre-epoch day the remainder is negative, the `res > 43200` wrap never fired, and the result came out near `+86400` instead of a small negative offset. The fix computes the offset directly as `day_number * 86400 - lut[index].date`: local midnight is that many seconds of local time from the epoch, and `date` is the UTC instant of the same midnight. Exact for either sign, no modulo, no wrap branches. The same-day `amount_of_offset_change` correction is unchanged. All 12 in-tree call sites checked. Seven were wrong and are repaired by this one change: the function itself, the `parseDateTime` family (including a zone named in the format string), `EXTRACT(TIMEZONE_HOUR / TIMEZONE_MINUTE ...)`, `formatDateTime`'s `%z`, and `toUTCTimestamp` / `fromUTCTimestamp`. The other five reduce the offset modulo a day (`CAST ... AS Time` / `Time64`, `localtime`), so an exact one-day error already cancelled; the test pins those as controls. Over all 597 rows of `system.time_zones` at 14 instants from 1900 to 2300, against Python `zoneinfo` as an independent oracle: 500 wrong samples across 307 zones before, 18 after, all 18 being `tzdata` differences between the bundled 2025a and the system 2026a. All 488 changed samples differ by exactly one day, so nothing sub-day moved. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Both directions through `tests/clickhouse-test`: on the base master debug snapshot (build id `09e3d57a4bbe30cd`) `01252_weird_time_zone` fails with a 39-line reference diff; with the fix (build id `485b33ed0bf6e99c`) it passes, including 50 of 50 randomized runs. `unit_tests_dbms --gtest_filter='*DateLUT*:*DateTime*:*Date*'` passes 7906 tests, so no calendar component moved. The `timezone` stateless suite passes 42 of 42. Six failures in the wider `datetime` and `extract` suites are pre-existing gaps in my local environment (no `remote()` cluster config, no parquet/iceberg fixtures, no `test.hits`) and reproduce identically on the base binary. New arms: the seven reported zones after their jump; the same zones before it and `Pacific/Chatham` (+13:45) as controls that must not move; the pre-1970 class; agreement between `parseDateTime*` and `toDateTime`; the other offset consumers; the modulo-a-day consumers as regression controls; DST transition days; agreement between the in-range and out-of-range paths; and a sweep over `system.time_zones` with no zone list hardcoded, comparing the reported offset to rendering the instant as local text and reading it back as UTC. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115332&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115332](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115332+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Enforce settings constraints on nested SETTINGS and SET name = DEFAULT
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109473 Two code paths mutated session or query settings without calling `checkSettingsConstraints`, so an authenticated user could override a setting an administrator had locked with `CONST`, `readonly`, `MIN`/`MAX`, or a feature tier. Where those constraints are the tenant-isolation boundary, this breaks multi-tenant isolation. ### A nested `SETTINGS` clause was applied unchecked `QueryTreeBuilder::buildSelectExpression` applied a `SELECT` node's `SETTINGS` clause to the per-node context copy with no constraint check. A clause on an outer query is validated by `InterpreterSetQuery::applySettingsFromQuery`, but a clause inside a subquery, a CTE, or a view's inner query reached only the analyzer. The Planner then read the mutated context, so with `additional_table_filters` - a documented row-level isolation mechanism - the user read other tenants' rows: ```sql -- rejected SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}; -- accepted before this change, returning every tenant's rows SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}); ``` There were no `checkSettingsConstraints` call sites anywhere in `src/Analyzer`, `src/Planner` or `src/Processors`. The legacy interpreter has always checked the same clause in `InterpreterSelectQuery`, so the analyzer becoming the default silently dropped the check. ### `SET name = DEFAULT` was applied unchecked The parser stores `SET k = v` in `ASTSetQuery::changes` and `SET k = DEFAULT` in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, and only the former was validated before `Context::resetSettingsToDefaultValue` applied the compiled-in default. So `SET readonly = DEFAULT` cleared a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile and re-enabled `INSERT`, `CREATE` and `DROP`, and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` cleared a resource cap. The same gap existed in the Arrow Flight `SetSessionOptions` reset branch, whose value-assignment branch already checked. ### A `profile` change was not checked against the constraints it installs A `SET` statement was validated as a whole before it ran, but a `profile` change among its settings replaces the constraint set halfway through it. So a single statement overrode the very constraint that the profile it names installs, while the same settings applied as two separate statements were rejected: ```sql -- rejected SET profile = 'p'; SET max_execution_time = 999; -- accepted before this change, for a profile p with max_execution_time = 10 CONST SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = 999; SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = DEFAULT; ``` ### The fix A new `SettingsConstraints::checkCanReset` validates a reset request, reached through `Context::checkSettingsConstraintsForDefaults` from both `InterpreterSetQuery` entry points, the Arrow Flight reset branch, and the analyzer: * For a built-in setting the compiled-in default is checked as the new value, via the new `Settings::getDefaultValue`, so min/max, `CONST`, tier and source restrictions all apply. Resetting a setting that already holds its default stays allowed, including under `readonly = 1`, because the constraint checker skips a change equal to the current value. * A custom setting has no compiled-in default - resetting it erases it - so only its writability is checked. This matters: erasing a `CONST` custom setting that a row policy reads through `getSetting` is exactly how the reported isolation boundary was broken. `buildSelectExpression` also no longer ignores a nested `SETTINGS name = DEFAULT`, which was previously a silent no-op; it is now checked and applied as a reset. It is applied to the subquery's context only and is not recorded on the `QueryNode`, so it stays invisible to the consumers that read a subquery's settings off the query tree - as it was when the clause was dropped outright. That limitation is documented at the call site and tracked in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115415. For the `profile` case, `InterpreterSetQuery` now checks the rest of the statement against the constraints the profile installs. That requires the profile to have been applied first, so the checking runs on a scratch copy of the context and nothing is applied to the real one until all of it passes: a rejected statement leaves the session alone rather than applying the profile and dropping its own tail. The changes are then applied in one call with the original list, so the order in which they take effect - and therefore which assignment wins - is unchanged. ### Behaviour change A `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view - the default for `CREATE VIEW` - whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails. This restores the behaviour of the legacy interpreter, which has always checked that clause. An administrator can keep such a view working with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER`, because `getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext` switches to the definer, whose constraints then apply. Note the limit of that workaround: it copies the invoker's changed setting *values* while switching the user, so a `CONST`/`MIN`/`MAX` constraint does not travel and the view works, but a `readonly = 1` value does travel and the inner clause is rejected even under `DEFINER`. A `readonly` user reading a view whose inner query sets a setting therefore has no workaround other than removing the clause from the view. ### Testing `05019_settings_constraints_reset_and_nested` covers, in a `CONST`-constrained session: a rejected `SET x = DEFAULT`; a no-op reset of an already-default setting still being allowed; a `CONST` custom setting resisting erasure; a nested `SETTINGS` clause rejected in a subquery, in a CTE, and in the `= DEFAULT` form; an unconstrained nested clause still working; and a `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view still reading while its `INVOKER` equivalent is rejected. It also pins down that a `SETTINGS` clause written after a nested `UNION` or `INTERSECT` is rejected: the parser attaches such a clause to one of the member `SELECT`s rather than to the compound query, so it is covered by the same check, whichever member it lands on. `05021_settings_constraints_set_profile_in_same_query` covers the `profile` case: an explicit value and a reset after the `profile` change both rejected against the profile's constraints, the profile left unapplied by a rejected statement, an assignment before the `profile` change still allowed, the profile's constraints in force afterwards, and an unconstrained setting after the change still applying. `05020_settings_constraints_readonly_user` covers a user under a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile: `SET readonly = DEFAULT` and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` both rejected, the session still readonly afterwards, and a nested `SETTINGS` clause unable to lift the user's row filter. One existing test needed a fix. `04102_hash_join_stress_test` used `SETTINGS max_joined_block_rows = 100` inside a subquery; the setting is called `max_joined_block_size_rows`. The misspelling went unnoticed because `Settings` accepts custom settings, so `Settings::set` stores an unrecognised name instead of rejecting it, and the `SQL_`/`custom_` prefix validation lives in `AccessControl::checkSettingNameIsAllowed`, reached only from `SettingsConstraints::checkImpl`. The same clause on a top-level query has always been rejected with `UNKNOWN_SETTING`; only the nested form escaped. The name is now spelled correctly. The Arrow Flight reset branch is not covered by a test: there is no functional-test harness for the Arrow Flight server, and the change there is the same three lines as its sibling value-assignment branch. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a settings-constraint bypass. A `SETTINGS` clause inside a subquery, a CTE or a view's inner query, `SET <name> = DEFAULT`, and a setting assigned or reset after a `profile` change in the same `SET` statement, now all enforce settings constraints, so none of them can be used to leave readonly mode or to override a `CONST`, `MIN` or `MAX` constraint. Note that a `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails, matching the behaviour of the old analyzer; use `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for such a view. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115397&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115397](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115397+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signal.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. signal.title: Support PromQL count_values
signal.text: **TL;DR** - **Adds** PromQL `count_values` support for ClickHouse `TimeSeries` data. - **Matches** Prometheus value-label, grouping, float-formatting, and stale-marker behavior. - **Includes** integration tests, compliance cases, and user documentation. **Why this matters** - **PromQL compatibility:** Queries using `count_values` can run through the ClickHouse PromQL path instead of being rejected as unsupported. - **State metrics:** This is useful for counting how many series currently have each value, such as service states, status codes, or rollout phases. - **Existing queries:** Users can keep Prometheus queries that already use `by()` and `without()` without rewriting them for ClickHouse. - **Correct results:** Matching label and float semantics is important for dashboards, recording rules, and alerts that compare ClickHouse results with Prometheus. Adds native lowering for the PromQL `count_values` aggregation operator over ClickHouse `TimeSeries` data. **What changed** - **PromQL lowering:** Adds `count_values` to the PromQL-to-SQL aggregation path. - **Value labels:** Formats every sample value as a Prometheus label string and stores it under the requested label name. - **Grouping:** Applies the generated value label before `by()` and `without()` grouping, matching Prometheus label-set behavior. - **Counting:** Counts equal values for each output label set and evaluation step. - **Sparse results:** Packs the counts back into the vector-grid shape and keeps missing samples as `NULL`. - **Float formatting:** Adds a dedicated formatter for `Float32` and `Float64` values. - **Label validation:** Accepts non-empty valid UTF-8 label names and rejects empty names. - **Special values:** Covers `NaN`, `+Inf`, `-Inf`, `-0`, and large values such as `1e21`. - **Stale markers:** Filters the Prometheus stale-marker payload without dropping regular `NaN` values. **Tests** - **Integration coverage:** Adds `by()` grouping, UTF-8 label names, empty labels, stale markers, and float-formatting cases. - **Compliance coverage:** Adds `by()`, `without()`, empty-vector, dynamic `time()`, and invalid-label cases. - **Validation:** Python test files compile successfully and the patch passes whitespace checks. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added native PromQL-to-SQL lowering for `count_values` over ClickHouse `TimeSeries` data. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Implement PromQL range functions ts_of_first/last/min/max_over_time
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 > **Note:** stacked on #112851 (`first_over_time` / `mad_over_time`). Until that PR merges, the diff here also shows those changes; once it is merged this PR will show only the `ts_of_*` commit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL: implemented range functions `ts_of_first_over_time()`, `ts_of_last_over_time()`, `ts_of_min_over_time()` and `ts_of_max_over_time()`. ### Description Implements the four PromQL "timestamp of" range functions, which were previously rejected at parse time: - `ts_of_first_over_time(v range-vector)` / `ts_of_last_over_time(v range-vector)` — the Unix timestamp (in seconds) of the earliest / latest sample in each grid point's staleness window. Keeps the metric name. - `ts_of_min_over_time(v range-vector)` / `ts_of_max_over_time(v range-vector)` — the timestamp of the minimum- / maximum-value sample. On ties the latest (largest-timestamp) sample wins, and a `NaN` value loses to any real value, matching Prometheus `compareOverTime`. Drops the metric name. All four return a Float64 Unix timestamp in seconds. **Implementation** - One new templated grid aggregate, `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesTsOfToGrid`, exposed as `timeSeriesTsOfFirstToGrid` / `timeSeriesTsOfLastToGrid` / `timeSeriesTsOfMinToGrid` / `timeSeriesTsOfMaxToGrid`. It keeps the selected sample of each window in a `SlidingSum` (a non-invertible summary; `SlidingSum` recomputes per grid point) and returns its timestamp divided by the timestamp scale multiplier so the result is in Unix seconds regardless of the `DateTime` / `DateTime64` timestamp type. Registered inline in `AggregateFunctionTimeseriesHelpers.cpp`. - All four functions are wired through `applyFunctionOverRange`'s `impl_map` (`ts_of_min`/`ts_of_max` drop the metric name, `ts_of_first`/`ts_of_last` keep it). - The function names are added to the PromQL lexer (`PromQLLexer.g4`) and the ANTLR C++ is regenerated (`PromQLLexer.cpp` / `.interp`) — these keywords were not in the lexer, so the names would otherwise fail to parse. **Testing**: new parser cases in `gtest_PromQLParser.cpp` for all four functions; new stateless test `04553_promql_ts_of_over_time.sh` exercising earliest/latest-timestamp selection, minimum/maximum-value selection with latest-on-ties, metric-name keeping/dropping, and out-of-window series exclusion against a multi-series TimeSeries table, with values verified against Prometheus semantics.

signal.title: Support column matcher expansion for default value expressions and index expressions
signal.text: This PR closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92266 Support column matchers in column `DEFAULT`, `ALIAS`, `MATERIALIZED`, and `EPHEMERAL` expressions, and in data skipping index expressions. This allows expressions such as `*`, `COLUMNS('...')`, `COLUMNS(a, b)`, `EXCEPT`, `APPLY`, and `REPLACE` to be expanded before expression validation and execution. ~~The change also adds `namedTuple` function to make matcher-expanded named tuple expressions ergonomic in tests and user queries.~~ The tests cover these use cases, direct and indirect cyclic default-expression dependency detection, and nested matcher expansion. ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry: - Support column matchers such as `*` and `COLUMNS` in column default value expressions, `DEFAULT`, `ALIAS`, `MATERIALIZED`, and `EPHEMERAL` expressions, and in data skipping index expressions. ### Note ~~About the newly added `namedTuple` function: I read the previous discussions in [1], [2], and [3], and my impression is that the existing `enable_named_columns_in_function_tuple` setting is not very discoverable. A separate function name may make the intention clearer and the feature easier to use, especially in this use case. It also avoids changing the behavior of the existing tuple function, so it should not introduce compatibility issues. signal.title: Make Jepsen node setup wait for apt's dpkg locks
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description The nightly `ClickHouse Keeper Jepsen` check reported ERROR for **all 24 workloads** on master `90a20ccf` ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=90a20ccf81cd348372f1406facf7544efa445f75&name_0=NightlyJepsen&name_1=ClickHouse%20Keeper%20Jepsen)): `0 successes / 24 crashed` and no `:valid?` line anywhere, so it produced no linearizability signal while reporting a red that reads like a Keeper defect. All 24 died in `jepsen.os.ubuntu/setup!` (`ubuntu.clj:22` -> `debian.clj:117`) before any test body ran: `E: Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend ... (unattended-upgr)`. **Root cause.** `debian/install` runs a plain `apt-get install` with no lock-wait option, and apt's default `DPkg::Lock::Timeout` is `0`, so it exits 100 the instant the lock is held. Nodes are scaled 0 -> 3 at job start, so each is seconds old, and Ubuntu's apt-daily timers carry `Persistent=true`, firing the missed run at once on boot. **Change.** A new `jepsen.clickhouse.os` wraps `ubuntu/os`: stop the two apt-daily timers (best effort, never the services), write a `DPkg::Lock::Timeout "600"` drop-in, assert via `apt-config dump` that apt resolves that timeout, fetch the package lists once per node, then delegate. The three `:os` sites point at it; `server/db.clj` reaches its Keeper node via `(:os test)`, so that 4th node is covered too. **Validation.** Nightly-only and PR-gated on `jepsen-test`, so it cannot go green here. Holding the lock with `fcntl.lockf` and running Jepsen's exact argv: without the drop-in `rc=100` in 0.06 s with that error; with it `rc=0` after the 30 s hold, package installed. Pinning the timeout back to `"0"`, or malforming the file, re-breaks it. Checked on Ubuntu 20.04/22.04/24.04 through Jepsen's real sshj remote. Post-merge: 3 nightlies at 0 of 24 failures, with neither error string in `job.log`. **Not fixed, deliberately.** 2026-07-16's 15/24 is a different cause (SSH `session-error`, no dpkg-lock hits). Baking the packages into the AMI would be more robust, but is unreachable from here. <details> <summary>Why the lists lock needs a separate step, and why neither apt's cache nor its exit status is the postcondition</summary> `DPkg::Lock::Timeout` covers the dpkg frontend lock only. The same automatic apt run also holds `/var/lib/apt/lists/lock` during its update phase, and 6 of the 26 historical lock hits on this check are lists-lock ones, so the lists are fetched by a step that retries only while apt reports that lock held. Four candidate apt-native timeouts for that lock were tested and all fail in 0-1 s. Its postcondition is neither apt's cache files nor its exit status. Measured: an `apt-get update` that failed to take the lock still *creates* `/var/cache/apt/pkgcache.bin` having fetched zero indexes, so a freshness check reads that as success and suppresses the update `ubuntu/setup!` would run. And the status misreports both ways: **0** when every fetch failed and no index was written, **100** when one configured source is broken while every index that matters was fetched. So the step counts the *package* indexes apt can read afterwards (`apt-get indextargets`, restricted to `Created-By: Packages`; needs no root, takes no lock), and a non-lock failure is judged by that count rather than being fatal on its own. The restriction matters because apt lists one record per target, so Translations/DEP-11/CNF appear beside the package indexes: a node with the Release files but no package index reports a positive *total* while `apt-get install ntpdate faketime` finds no installation candidate. Measured on apt 2.8.3, as targets/package-indexes: 30/15 populated (install resolves) - 22/11 one mirror host unreachable (accepted) - 30/15 a 404 suite made the update exit 100 (accepted) - 15/**0** package indexes missing, auxiliary ones present (rejected) - 0/0 lists emptied, and after the lock-failed update above. `Created-By:` is present on apt 2.0.10, 2.4.14 and 2.8.3, and in the stock state package-indexes equals the total on all three. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115637&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115637](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115637+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.author: slimtom95

signal.title: Apply `SETTINGS` from the `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` definition to it's inserts
signal.text: ### Feature description Currently, query-level settings that affect MV writes (e.g. `deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views`) can only be controlled via the INSERT statement or user profiles. They propagate correctly from the INSERT context to the MV's write context, but there is no way to declare them on the `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` definition itself. The existing workarounds all require controlling the insert caller rather than the MV: - Set the setting on every INSERT statement (requires all callers to cooperate) - Set the setting in the user profile of the inserting user (requires controlling which user performs inserts, or creating a dedicated profile per use case) Neither approach lets the MV owner encode the intended behavior directly in the MV definition, where it is most discoverable and closest to the logic it affects. ### Proposed solution Allow a `SETTINGS` clause on `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` that would be applied to the MV's internal write context, overriding the session/profile value for that specific MV. Example: ```sql CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TO target_table SETTINGS deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views = 0 AS SELECT ... ``` ### Settings that would be valuable at the MV level | Setting | Why | |---|---| | `deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views` | Pin dedup behavior on the MV regardless of the caller | | `materialized_views_ignore_errors` | Currently all-or-nothing across all MVs — per-MV would let you mark specific MVs as best-effort without silently swallowing errors in critical ones | | `async_insert` | Force the MV's writes through the async insert path without requiring the insert caller to set it — useful for high-fanout MVs where MV writes shouldn't block the source insert | | `insert_deduplicate` | Control whether the MV's write to the target table deduplicates at all | | `insert_quorum` / `insert_quorum_timeout` | Per-MV write quorum for replicated targets — some MVs may need strong consistency, others don't | | `max_insert_block_size` | Tune memory/throughput tradeoff per MV independently of the source insert block size | ### Use case The MV owner wants to declare write behavior as part of the MV definition itself — making it self-contained and not dependent on how callers or user profiles are configured. This is especially useful when the MV is part of a shared schema managed independently from the inserting services. ### Related - `deduplicate_blocks_in_dependent_materialized_views` - Similar precedent: `CREATE TABLE ... SETTINGS`, `POPULATE` clause on MVs

signal.title: Parquet: map TIME logical type to Time64
signal.text: The native Parquet reader currently maps both `logical.TIMESTAMP` and `logical.TIME` (and the deprecated converted types `TIMESTAMP_MILLIS`/`TIMESTAMP_MICROS`/`TIME_MILLIS`/`TIME_MICROS`) to `DataTypeDateTime64`. That was fine before ClickHouse 25.6, when there was no time-of-day type, but it now produces the Parquet analogue of #104038: when the target column is `Time64` and `session_timezone` is non-UTC, the `DateTime64 -> Time64` cast (PR #90310) shifts the value by the timezone — silent data corruption for a value that has no date/timezone to begin with. This PR splits the schema-converter branch so that: - `logical.TIME` / `TIME_MILLIS` / `TIME_MICROS` → `DataTypeTime64(scale)` (timezone-unaware). - `logical.TIMESTAMP` → `DataTypeDateTime64(scale, timezone)` (unchanged). It also extends `is_output_type_decimal` to recognize `Time64` so min/max stats stay enabled when the output column is `Time64`, and removes the stale comment that claimed ClickHouse has no time-of-day type. While covering explicit type hints in the test (`SELECT * FROM file(..., 'Parquet', 't Time')`), I hit a second pre-existing gap from 25.6: `Time64 -> Time` was never registered as a cast — it threw `CANNOT_CONVERT_TYPE` because `IsDataTypeNumber<DataTypeTime>` is `false` (it inherits `DataTypeNumberBase<Int32>`, not `DataTypeNumber<Int32>`). Before this PR the path went `DateTime64 -> Time` and returned a wrong, timezone-shifted value; after the Parquet fix it would have thrown. The second commit adds an inline `Time64 -> Time` branch in `ConvertImpl` that divides by the scale multiplier — no timezone offset, because both Time64 and Time are timezone-unaware seconds-of-day. A new stateless test `04277_parquet_time_of_day` covers: - Schema-less inference (Parquet `time32[ms]`/`time64[us]`/`time64[ns]` → `Nullable(Time64(3/6/9))`; `TIMESTAMP` stays `Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC'))`). - Import into `Time64(scale)` columns under `session_timezone = 'Asia/Shanghai'` (values must not shift). - Explicit type hints under non-UTC session: `Time64(3)` / `Time` / `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')` / `Int64`. Review follow-up: making `Time64 -> DateTime` legal also exposed that `ToDateTimeMonotonicity` treated `Time64` sources as monotonic, while the cast wraps negative time-of-day values with the default `date_time_overflow_behavior = 'ignore'` (`-00:00:01` -> `2106-02-07 06:28:15`), i.e. it drops at zero. `toDateTime` now reports non-monotonic for `Time`/`Time64` sources; the regression test `04828_time64_to_datetime_not_monotonic` shows that without the guard the key condition prunes every granule and range/point queries over a `Time64` key silently return empty results. The Parquet docs (`docs/reference/formats/Parquet/Parquet.mdx`) are updated for the new `TIME` -> `Time64` mapping. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Parquet `time32`/`time64` columns being read as `DateTime64` and then silently shifted by `session_timezone` when inserted into a `Time64` target column. Parquet `TIME` logical types now map directly to `Time64`, and a previously-missing `Time64 -> Time` cast is added. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106019&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106019](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106019+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
