signal.title: [RFC] Nullable(Array) support: staged implementation
signal.text: ## Status Accepted design, staged implementation in progress. Supersedes #105192. This RFC replaces the earlier draft RFC #105192 by @zhanglistar. That document, together with the exploratory implementation in #104816, is the direct ancestor of everything below: the stream-naming approach, the framework treatment of null rows, the gating strategy and a large body of tests all originate there. #104816 was closed in favour of a staged implementation by the core team, and its code is reused with attribution (`Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits that carry it). Thanks also to @Avogar for the original blocker analysis, which shaped the design, and to @alexey-milovidov for the resolutions to it. ## Goal Allow the array value itself to be `NULL`, distinctly from an empty array: ```sql NULL::Nullable(Array(UInt32)) != []::Array(UInt32) ``` This is not the same as `Array(Nullable(T))`, which already works and makes *elements* nullable. Arrow, ORC, Parquet, Spark, Hive and JSON producers all distinguish "list field absent or NULL" from "list present but empty", and ClickHouse currently cannot represent the difference, so those reads are lossy. ## Non-goals - `Nullable(Map(...))`. `Map` is physically `Array(Tuple(keys, values))`, so it depends on this work, but it is out of scope. - Changing the rule that `Map` keys cannot be nullable. - Flipping `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()`. See below — this is a deliberate and load-bearing decision, not an omission. ## Core design **`DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()` keeps returning `false`, permanently.** `Nullable(Array(T))` is constructible only through `makeNullableAllowingArray`, which reaches a private `DataTypeNullable` constructor via a friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. This is the single most important property of the design, and the reason is not the one an earlier revision of this document gave. It is not primarily about blast radius during the rollout. `canBeInsideNullable` is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and those places do two different jobs: 1. **Handle a `Nullable(Array)` that already exists** — serialization, subcolumn extraction, the nullable subcolumn creator, `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple`. 2. **Decide whether to *produce* a `Nullable`** — `getLeastSupertype`, `makeNullableSafe`, cast resolution. Only the second kind would behave differently if the predicate were flipped. The first kind needs explicit `Nullable(Array)` handling either way, because once the type can be created at all, this code has to cope with it. And the second kind is where flipping the predicate becomes a user-visible result-type change for queries that have nothing to do with this feature. This was measured rather than reasoned about: `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()` was flipped to `true` on a scratch branch, the server rebuilt, and the same queries run against both binaries with every gate off. | Expression | predicate `false` (today) | predicate `true` | | --- | --- | --- | | `splitByChar(',', materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(String)')))` | `Array(String)`, value `['']` | `Nullable(Array(String))`, value `NULL` | | `extractAll(materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(String)')), '.')` | `Array(String)` | `Nullable(Array(String))` | | `bitmaskToArray(materialize(CAST(NULL,'Nullable(UInt8)')))` | `Array(UInt8)` | `Nullable(Array(UInt8))` | These are ordinary functions on ordinary types. No `Nullable(Array)` column is involved and nothing experimental is enabled. The mechanism is `makeNullableSafe` in `IFunctionOverloadResolver::getReturnTypeWithoutLowCardinality`: with the predicate `false` it returns the array type unchanged, and with the predicate `true` it wraps it. Every function that uses the default nulls implementation and returns an array is affected, and the change is semantic, not cosmetic — `splitByChar(',', NULL)` yields `['']` today and `NULL` after. **That change cannot be gated.** The `compatibility` setting is implemented by replaying old *setting values* — `SettingsChangesHistory` entries are `{setting, old value, new value, description}` — so a behaviour change is only reversible if a setting is read at the point of decision. Function return-type computation reads no settings, and `canBeInsideNullable()` is a property of a type object rather than of a call site: a `DataTypePtr` does not know which session created it, and the predicate is consulted during background merges, metadata load and distributed query fragments, where a session setting is not a defined concept. The exploratory work tried to make an equivalent predicate settings-aware for the `Tuple` case and had to reach for `Context::getGlobalContextInstance()`, documenting that "config changes for global context settings are applied after server restart" — global state with a restart caveat, which is not gating. So flipping the predicate would be an unconditional result-type change with no `compatibility` value and no individual setting that restores the previous behaviour. Conversely, building genuine dual behaviour would mean keeping the explicit per-site decisions described here *and* adding a second branch at each — more code than the current design, not less. `Nullable(Tuple)` is the cautionary example rather than a counter-example. Its predicate is `true`, and the consequence is observable today, by a different route — the `Tuple` branch of `getLeastSupertype`: ```sql SET enable_nullable_tuple_type = 0; SELECT if(0, tuple(1), NULL); -- \N, of type Nullable(Tuple(UInt8)) ``` The gate does not contain the type: with the setting explicitly disabled you still get real `Nullable(Tuple)` values, because type inference never consults it. We are deliberately more conservative in light of how much corner-case work that feature required after merge. For the avoidance of doubt, one thing that does **not** change when the predicate is flipped is array-versus-`NULL` supertype resolution. `if(1, [1], NULL)` returns `Variant(Array(UInt8))` with the predicate either way, and `NO_COMMON_TYPE` either way when the `Variant` fallback is disabled, because the array branch of `getLeastSupertype` bails at "some of them are Array and some of them are not" before any nullable wrapping. An earlier revision of this document claimed otherwise; see the correction log. ### What this costs `canBeInsideNullable()` now returns `false` for a type that demonstrably *is* inside `Nullable`. That is a permanent, accepted cost rather than a transitional one: - Any guard of the form `if (t->canBeInsideNullable())` reachable by a `Nullable(Array)` value must be extended with `|| isArray(t)`. We already missed one — see the known-defect section below. - `makeNullableSafe` returns its argument unchanged for `Array`, silently degrading `Nullable(Array)` to `Array` rather than throwing. There are 32 such call sites. - **Every `canBeInsideNullable` guard added anywhere in the codebase from now on is wrong for `Nullable(Array)` by default.** This is the real long-term price, and the Stage 4 audit is what bounds it. Do not attempt to "clean this up" later by flipping the predicate. There is no gated path back. Identifying every reachable instance is the **call-site audit**, delivered in Stage 4 (below). This is the audit @Avogar asked for in #104816, reframed: the question is not "are 75 files correct" but "which sites can a `Nullable(Array)` value actually reach, and which of those need to change". ### Gating A single session setting, `allow_experimental_nullable_array_type`, gates **every user-facing path that can produce the type** — not only DDL. That includes `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER`, table-function column lists, and the functions that accept a type by name (`toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST`). Internal C++ construction is ungated. This makes the gate a single clean seam between internal machinery and external interface, which is what the staging below is built around. ## MergeTree serialization ### The collision Stream names come from `getNameForSubstreamPath`. `Nullable` appends `.null`; `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1`, …; array *elements* add no name component at all, only a nesting level. ```text Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.null c <-- collision ``` Two distinct null maps would share one file name. Shipping that would corrupt data. ### Resolution A second, *structured* naming scheme, used only for columns whose type requires it (`needsStructuredSubstreamNames`), which inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements: ```text Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.null element null map c.array.nested element data Nullable(Array(UInt32)): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.nested element data Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))): c.size0 outer array offsets c.array.null inner nullable array's null map c.array.array.size0 inner array offsets c.array.array.nested.null element null map c.array.array.nested element data ``` Note that the outer null map and the array offsets keep their plain `.null` and `.size0` names; only the streams below an array element acquire the `.array` component. This is the naming the implementation actually produces, verified by driving real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than by reasoning about substream paths — see the correction note at the end of this issue. Every currently-legal type keeps byte-identical legacy names, so existing parts remain readable with no migration and no format version bump. Selection is **per column, from the type as stored in the part**, on both read and write, so a single query can span old and new parts, and unaffected columns inside a part that contains a structured column keep their legacy names. `columns_substreams.txt` records the actual on-disk substream names for Compact parts and is the source of truth on read. Not in `serialization.json`, which describes serialization kinds and statistics rather than physical file names. Not a global part format version bump, since the change is column-scoped and must coexist with legacy names in the same part. ### Requirements this must meet These are the acceptance criteria for Stage 2, and they are stronger than what #104816 demonstrated: 1. **No legacy stream name changes for any currently-legal type.** The property is that the structured scheme is never *selected* for such a type, neither by the type nor by any path enumerated for it: the legacy naming code is then the only code that runs, and it is not modified. The corpus must reach the shapes where a stream name is decided, and a corpus of static types enumerated from the top level does **not** reach all of them. Two that it misses, both of which produced real regressions: - types materialised at runtime inside `Dynamic` and `Object` columns — a JSON dynamic path holding `Array(Nullable(T))` carries an array and a null map on one path, exactly like `Nullable(Array(T))` but in the opposite nesting; - subcolumn serializations produced by `NullableSubcolumnCreator`, which are not the column's own streams. Treat "proven over a corpus" as a claim about the corpus, and state which shapes it reaches. 2. **Collision-free names for arbitrary nesting** of `Array`, `Nullable`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic` and `Object`, including substream cache keys and prefix/suffix substreams. 3. **A single source of truth for names.** #104816 duplicated the substream-to-name switch, and `Object`/JSON substream types are added to `master` continuously, so a duplicate will drift. 4. **The column type is required, and losing it must not fail silently.** *(Revised — see the correction log.)* This was originally stated as "one naming oracle, or a proven equivalence between two". That is not achievable: the path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The same path requires different names for different types, so no path-only oracle exists and the two arms are not competing answers to one question — the path-based arm covers `Dynamic`/`Object` columns whose static type does not reveal the runtime variant. The hazard is therefore not disagreement between arms but a caller that supplies no type at all: it silently receives legacy names for a structured column. What is required instead: - where the substream path *proves* a type was needed, resolving a name without one raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than returning a name no writer produced; - the divergent case above is pinned by a test, so the reason the type is required is documented where a reader will look; - a test asserts the guard never fires for any currently-legal type; - **every MergeTree caller passes the column type** — an explicit obligation for Stage 3, verified there rather than assumed. ## Subcolumns The outer null map must propagate into subcolumns: ```sql SELECT a.null FROM t; -- UInt8 SELECT a.size0 FROM t; -- Nullable(UInt64), not UInt64 ``` `NullableSubcolumnCreator` handles this, **in Stage 6 rather than alongside the naming work**. Note that bare `Array(T).null` must stay an invalid Dynamic subcolumn path: the null map belongs to the `Nullable` wrapper, not to the array, so `getSubcolumn(42::Dynamic, 'Array(UInt64).null')` must keep failing rather than returning an all-ones map. `.size0` needs none of this — it resolves to `Nullable(UInt64)` through the ordinary path, because `UInt64` passes `canBeInsideNullable`. The creator's array case only matters when the extracted subcolumn is *itself* an array, such as a tuple-element subcolumn inside a nullable array. Two constraints on that work, both learned the hard way: - It must not change the subcolumn type of `Nullable(Tuple(... Array ...))`, which is legal today. Wrapping arrays unconditionally moves `Nullable(Tuple(x Array(T)))`.`x` from `Array(T)` to `Nullable(Array(T))`. - Reaching the *outer* null map of a `Nullable(Array)` as a subcolumn is still an open question. Marking hidden null maps as subcolumn-bearing is not the answer: `NullMapHidden` exists to let a nested `null` subcolumn win, and un-hiding it makes the null map shadow `Nullable(JSON).null`. ## Function execution framework `defaultImplementationForNulls` unwraps nullable arguments, runs the function on the nested columns and patches the result. When the result type cannot be `Nullable` — historically true for `Array` — it substitutes defaults for null rows. Left alone, this silently turns a `NULL` array into `[]` for roughly 70 unmigrated array functions. The contract: - For an array-returning function with a `Nullable(Array)` argument, the result type becomes `Nullable(Array(...))`. - Array arguments are normalised to empty at null rows before the call, so functions that have not been individually migrated still see well-formed offsets. - The row null map is the OR of the input null maps, and is re-applied to the result. - A function may opt in to producing the nullable result itself via `preserveNullableArrayResultForDefaultNulls`, for cases like `arrayElementOrNull` where the function's own null semantics must win. This is deliberately narrower than #105192 proposed. That draft sketched four separate framework capabilities; one opt-in virtual plus automatic normalisation turned out to be sufficient, and the smaller surface is easier to reason about. **Ordering constraint:** the framework must land before the gate opens. Otherwise the type is storable but silently lossy through most functions, which is worse than not having it. ## Semantics | Expression | `NULL::Nullable(Array(T))` | `[]::Array(T)` | `[x]::Array(T)` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `isNull(a)` | `1` | `0` | `0` | | `length(a)` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `empty(a)` | `NULL` | `1` | `0` | | `a.size0` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `arrayElement(a, 1)` | `NULL` | default | `x` | | `arrayElementOrNull(a, 1)` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `x` | | `arrayMap(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | `[f(x)]` | | `arrayFilter(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | filtered | Questions #105192 left open, now resolved: - **`arrayJoin` / `ARRAY JOIN` over `Nullable(Array)` is explicitly unsupported** and throws `TYPE_MISMATCH`. Row-cardinality semantics for a NULL array have no obviously correct answer, and silently treating it as `[]` would defeat the purpose of the type. Revisitable later; not blocking. - **Aggregate functions treat a NULL array as any other NULL value.** Aggregates that skip nulls skip null arrays; those that collect values may collect them where the result type can represent them. This falls out of the existing `Null` combinator rather than needing per-function work. - **Formats never infer the type by default.** Inference is behind its own separate setting, `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`. ## Staged implementation One pull request per stage, each targeting `master`, merged before the next opens. | # | Stage | Content | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Type and column foundation | `makeNullableAllowingArray`, private constructor, `ColumnNullable` exception. `DataTypeFactory` still rejects the type string, so the type is constructible from C++ only and unreachable from any query. | | 2 | Serialization and substream naming | Structured naming, cache keys, deserialization order, plus the four requirements above. Still unreachable from SQL. | | 3 | MergeTree wiring, gate opens | Typed stream names, wide and compact readers and writers, `columns_substreams.txt`, merges, mutations, `ALTER`. `DataTypeFactory` starts accepting the type string, and `validateDataType` / `InterpreterCreateQuery` begin enforcing the gate: the factory is permissive and the entry points are restrictive. Paths not yet migrated throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. | | 4 | Function framework and audit | The framework contract above, the full call-site audit, and the `unwrapNullableTuple` fix. | | 5 | Array functions and aggregates | Migration by category; `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` throws replaced with real behaviour. | | 6 | Remaining creation paths | The functions that take a type by name — `toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST` — each gated. User documentation. | | 7 | Formats, explicit schema only | Arrow, Arrow IPC, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON, Native, plus the `Native` format specification. | | 8 | Schema inference | Behind `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`, including schema-cache keys. | | 9 | Stabilisation | Fuzzing, performance and storage overhead, beta decision. | Stages 1 and 2 are verifiable by unit tests only, since the type cannot be named in a query. That is deliberate: it makes "internal machinery only" a checked property rather than an intention, and Stage 3 flipping it becomes a visible change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. Stage 3 introduces the gate rather than Stage 6 so that Stages 4 to 9 are testable with ordinary stateless tests. Between Stages 3 and 5 the type is reachable only with the experimental setting explicitly enabled, and any path not yet migrated **throws** rather than returning a wrong answer. Substituting `[]` for `NULL` in the interim was considered and rejected: it would ship exactly the defect this feature exists to remove. ## Known defect inherited from the exploratory work `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple` substitutes defaults for an `Array` field of a `Nullable(Tuple(...))`, so a NULL struct's list field becomes `[]`. It is reached from the ORC, Arrow and Arrow IPC readers when a nullable struct sits inside a list. Reproducer, against an Arrow file holding `Array(Nullable(Tuple(x Array(Int32))))` whose second element is `NULL`: ```sql SET allow_experimental_nullable_array_type = 1; SELECT a FROM file('nt.arrow', Arrow, 'a Array(Tuple(x Nullable(Array(Int32))))'); -- [([1,2]),([])] -- expected [([1,2]),(NULL)] ``` The requested type *is* honoured (`toTypeName` reports `Nullable(Array(Int32))`) but the value comes back as `[]` with `isNull() = 0`. Cause: the branch tests `elem_type->canBeInsideNullable()`, which is `false` for `Array` by design, so the default-substitution path is taken before the hinted type is applied. Fixed in Stage 4. This is not a regression — with the gate disabled the same hint is rejected outright — but it is an instance of the exact conflation the feature exists to remove, occurring inside the feature. It was found by chasing a single `canBeInsideNullable` call site, which is the argument for completing the audit before the gate widens. ## Testing matrix - **Types:** `Nullable(Array(T))`, `Nullable(Array(Nullable(T)))`, `Array(Nullable(Array(T)))`, multidimensional, inside `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic`, `Object`, `Nested`. - **Storage:** wide and compact parts, old-part reads, merges, mutations, projections, materialised views, `ALTER`, `columns_substreams.txt` integrity. - **Subcolumns:** `.null`, `.size0`, nested `sizeN`, tuple subcolumns inside arrays. - **Functions:** every array function by category; `if`, `multiIf`, `CAST`, `accurateCastOrNull`, `IN`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`. - **Aggregates:** `groupArray`, `groupUniqArray`, `arrayReduce`, combinators, state serialization. - **Formats:** `Native`, `Values`, `JSONEachRow`, CSV, TSV, Arrow, ArrowStream, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON. - **Fuzzing:** AST fuzzer, function stress, serialization round-trip. ## Related - Supersedes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 ## Correction log **2026-08-19, stream names.** The stream-name example in *MergeTree serialization → Resolution* originally showed `c.array.size0` for the array offsets and `c.array` for the element data. Both were wrong. They were carried over from #105192 and the exploratory implementation's own documentation, and had never been checked against the code. The cause is worth recording, because it also invalidated the exploratory work's unit tests for this area. The naming decision for a stream depends on what precedes the final substream in its `SubstreamPath` — in particular on whether a null map precedes it. `SerializationNullable::enumerateStreams` emits the null-map substream, then **pops it** before recursing into the nested type, so the path seen while naming the array's own streams contains no null map. A hand-built path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs in production; the real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and it takes a different branch. Expectations written against hand-built paths were therefore self-consistent and simultaneously wrong about two of the four streams. Combined with a shell test whose `Before drop:` listing was never actually emitted, the on-disk naming for this feature had no accurate test and no accurate documentation. The fix on our side is to derive every naming expectation from a real `enumerateStreams` walk, and to state the acceptance criteria as properties over a corpus of types rather than as spot checks on constructed paths: - the structured scheme is never selected for any type that is legal today, which is what makes "no existing stream name changes" a proof rather than a sample; - a caller that has the column type and one that does not must produce identical names for a legal type; - all stream names of a type containing `Nullable(Array)` are distinct, at arbitrary nesting depth. **2026-08-19, criterion 4.** Restated. The original wording asked for a single naming oracle or a proven equivalence between two, which is not achievable — the naming of a stream genuinely depends on the column type and not only on the substream path. The revised criterion and its rationale are in *Requirements this must meet* above; the reasoning and what replaced it are in the Stages 1–2 comment on this issue. **2026-08-20, the rationale for `canBeInsideNullable`.** The *Core design* section originally justified keeping the predicate `false` as a blast-radius decision: 105 call sites, too many to audit safely. That reasoning is real but weak, and it would expire once the feature reached GA, inviting a future contributor to flip the predicate as cleanup. The section now gives the argument that actually holds. The call sites split into those that must handle an existing `Nullable(Array)` (unchanged by a flip) and those that decide whether to create one (changed by a flip) — and the second group is precisely where a flip becomes a user-visible result-type change, from `Variant(Array(T))` to `Nullable(Array(T))`, that the `compatibility` mechanism cannot express, because that mechanism replays setting values and a type-level predicate cannot read a setting. The consequence is that the decision is permanent, and that the explicit opt-in call sites are the correct long-term shape rather than debt to be repaid. **2026-08-20, the mechanism behind the `canBeInsideNullable` decision — previous correction was wrong.** The 2026-08-20 revision above claimed that flipping the predicate would change `if(1, [1], NULL)` from `Variant(Array(UInt8))` to `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, via the nullable wrapping in `getLeastSupertype`. That was incorrect, and it does not reproduce. The `canBeInsideNullable` check in question is in the `Tuple` branch of `getLeastSupertype`; the `Array` branch exits earlier with "some of them are Array and some of them are not" and never reaches a nullable wrap. The claim was checked the direct way — flipping the predicate on a scratch branch, rebuilding, and running the same queries against both binaries. `if(1, [1], NULL)` is `Variant(Array(UInt8))` with the predicate either way. The same experiment found the mechanism that does hold, and it is a stronger argument than the one it replaces: `makeNullableSafe` in `IFunctionOverloadResolver::getReturnTypeWithoutLowCardinality` starts wrapping array return types, so ordinary functions change their result type and their semantics — `splitByChar(',', NULL)` moves from `['']` to `NULL` — for every user, with nothing experimental enabled and no setting read anywhere on that path. The section above now states the measured before-and-after and names the correct mechanism. **2026-08-20, criterion 1 and the placement of subcolumn null-map propagation.** Criterion 1 was described as proven over a corpus. It was proven over the corpus that existed, which enumerated static types from the top level and therefore reached neither `Dynamic`/`Object` paths materialised at runtime nor subcolumn serializations produced by `NullableSubcolumnCreator`. Both shapes turned out to decide stream names, and both produced regressions in existing tests. The criterion now says which shapes a corpus has to reach. The *Subcolumns* section also read as though `NullableSubcolumnCreator`'s array handling belongs with the naming work. It is now scheduled for Stage 6, with the two constraints that the first attempt violated.

signal.title: Wrong result: optimize_trivial_count_query makes count(arrayJoin(arr)) return the table's row count instead of the number of array elements
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong - With the default `optimize_trivial_count_query = 1`, `SELECT count(arrayJoin(arr)) FROM t` returns the number of rows in the table instead of the number of array elements. - arrayJoin is a row-multiplying operator, so the aggregate must observe the post-expansion stream. The trivial-count optimization replaces the entire table read with a stored row counter and never evaluates count's argument, so the ARRAY JOIN expansion is silently dropped. No error, no warning. - The optimization rests on the premise "the number of rows the aggregate sees equals the number of rows stored in the table." That holds for `count()`, `count(1)` and `count(non_nullable_col)`, but arrayJoin breaks it, and nothing in the guard list checks for it. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a93a2cb4-e0f1-450b-a97e-0acef509da3b ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬──────────┐ │ Query │ Result │ Correct? │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) │ 2 │ ✗ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0 │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(*) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin(A) ...) │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ sum(length(A)) │ 5 │ ✓ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴──────────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior - The `count(arrayJoin(A))` should return the total number of array elements across all rows, equivalent to sum(length(A)). ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115227 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1681` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.5.3`, `26.6.4.4`, `26.5.8.6`, `26.3.21.6`, `25.8.31.12` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Remove CatBoost integration
signal.text: Removes the CatBoost integration: the `catboostEvaluate` function, the `system.models` table, the `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S)` queries and the matching `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` privilege, together with their documentation, tests and the bundled model artifacts. The `CANNOT_LOAD_CATBOOST_MODEL` and `CANNOT_APPLY_CATBOOST_MODEL` error codes are intentionally kept so their numbers are not reused. Refs: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/70771 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/45052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Removed the CatBoost integration. The `catboostEvaluate` function, the `system.models` table and the `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S)` queries are no longer available. Queries, views and grants referring to them have to be migrated before the upgrade: in particular, revoke `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` from all users and roles beforehand, because an access entity whose grants still mention the removed privilege cannot be parsed on startup. Also let any in-flight `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL(S) ON CLUSTER` entries drain from the distributed DDL queue before the upgrade: upgraded hosts can no longer parse such entries and will finish them with an error status instead of executing them. The same applies to persisted table metadata: a table whose column `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS` expressions, secondary indices, constraints, projections, partition/order/sample keys, or TTL expressions still reference `catboostEvaluate` cannot be loaded after the upgrade (`UNKNOWN_FUNCTION`), so drop or rewrite such definitions beforehand. The revoke also has to cover every other carrier of serialized grants: a `GRANT SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` line in the `grants` section of `users.xml` must be removed as well, because it can no longer be parsed and the server then refuses to load the users configuration at startup; on clusters with replicated (Keeper-backed) access storage, revoke the privilege before upgrading any replica, because with the default `access_control_improvements.throw_on_invalid_replicated_access_entities = 0` an upgraded replica that reads a user or role still carrying `SYSTEM RELOAD MODEL` from ZooKeeper cannot parse it and silently drops that entity from its in-memory copy (set `throw_on_invalid_replicated_access_entities = 1` to fail loudly instead); and access backups (`BACKUP ... ACCESS`) taken while the grant was still present cannot be restored with `RESTORE ... ACCESS` on the new version, so re-create such backups after the revoke. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109710&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109710](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109710+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Validate Iceberg metadata file path for null bytes
signal.text: A null byte in the `iceberg_metadata_file_path` setting causes `std::length_error` in filesystem path operations. Since `std::length_error` is a `std::logic_error`, the exception handler in `executeQuery.cpp` treats it as a logical error and aborts the server in debug/sanitizer builds. Reject paths containing null bytes with a proper `BAD_ARGUMENTS` exception instead. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/96811 https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100176&sha=32a8de2243259ca5c69f22e0599aa41189972a69&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_tsan%29 https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/100176 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix exception when Iceberg metadata file path setting contains a null byte. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.4.1.110` (included in `26.4` and later) - Backported to: `26.3.21.5` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Reject duplicate storage namespaces within a policy
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/88808 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107484 Two top-level disks in the same storage policy could resolve to the same underlying storage namespace. During `MergeTree` startup, the table scans every disk in its policy, so the same part can be loaded twice and one copy can be removed as a duplicate. If both disk objects refer to the same physical data, this removes the only copy and causes data loss. The previous fix in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107484 compared every configured `encrypted` disk globally. That rejected safe configurations where separate tables use equivalent custom disks through separate single-disk policies. In particular, it broke `03820_plain_rewritable_over_another_disk_with_same_path` for `encrypted` disks layered directly over and through a cache on the same `s3_plain_rewritable` storage. This change keeps the absolute-path, normalization, and delegate-boundary validation for `encrypted` disk paths, but moves duplicate namespace validation to `StoragePolicy`. Only top-level disks visible to the same policy are compared. This rejects the configuration that can make one table scan the same namespace twice, while allowing equivalent disks used by separate policies. The validation applies to configured, reloaded, and programmatically created policies and also covers wrapper/delegate and non-encrypted disk aliases. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reject storage policies whose top-level disks resolve to the same underlying storage namespace, which could cause data loss after a server restart.

signal.title: Do not drop a named collection that a detached table still uses
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96181 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/77366 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110529 A table detached with a plain `DETACH TABLE` keeps its metadata file, so the server attaches it again on the next start. It is gone from `DatabaseCatalog` though, so `isTableExist` returns false for it, and the `check_named_collection_dependencies` check (added in #96181) treated its dependency as a stale leftover of a failed `CREATE TABLE`: it removed the dependency and let `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` succeed. The `ATTACH` replayed at startup then threw `NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST`, which aborts loading the metadata, and the server did not start at all. This is how the `Stress test (arm_tsan)` job fails on master with `Cannot start clickhouse-server`: the AST fuzzer makes `04320_url_engine_dispatch_partition_and_format` leave its `URL(named_collection)` table detached (the test's `ATTACH TABLE` never reaches the server), and the test then drops the named collection. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=8aad759007771032aa94d7f4eee3e18103dd63c3&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29 ``` Application: Caught exception while loading metadata: Code: 722. DB::Exception: Waited job failed: Code: 695. DB::Exception: Load job 'load table test_3.04320_..._n' failed: Code: 669. DB::Exception: There is no named collection `04320_..._nc`: Cannot attach table `test_3`.`04320_..._n` from metadata file store/e5b/.../04320_..._n.sql from query ATTACH TABLE ... ENGINE = URL(`04320_..._nc`, format = 'JSON'). (NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST) ``` The same signature accounts for 6 of the 8 `Cannot start clickhouse-server` failures with a missing named collection in the last 60 days (per `play.clickhouse.com`); the other two come from `03822_named_collection_drop_dependency_check`, which drops the collection with `check_named_collection_dependencies = 0` on purpose, and are the case #110529 handles by tolerating the missing collection at startup. ### Changes Per review feedback, the implementation is a simple in-memory bookkeeping in `NamedCollectionFactory` (an earlier revision inspected the metadata the detached table would be attached from, which required probing database disks and sweeping metadata directories after renames): - `DETACH TABLE` (and `DETACH DATABASE`, for every table inside) moves the dependencies of the table into a list of (collection, database, table) entries. - `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` is refused with `NAMED_COLLECTION_IS_USED` while an entry for the collection exists. - `ATTACH` does not remove the entry by itself: the dependencies are registered while the engine arguments are resolved, and the attach can still fail after that (an unknown format name, a failure creating the storage), leaving the table detached — the entry must keep protecting it. Instead, the entry is removed by the events that prove the metadata under that name is gone or harmless: `DROP TABLE`, `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY`, and `RENAME` of the (necessarily re-attached) table; `DROP DATABASE` removes the entries of the database's detached tables, and `RENAME DATABASE` re-keys them. The `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` check itself removes nothing: the table's existence in `DatabaseCatalog` is racy against in-flight attaches and detaches (the table can exist while nothing in the drop query has validated its live dependency), so the drop path is read-only and every recorded entry refuses the drop. - `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` does not record an entry: a permanently detached table is not loaded at startup, so dropping a collection it references cannot break the server start. A later explicit `ATTACH` of such a table fails cleanly with `NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST` and is recoverable by recreating the collection. - The list lives in memory only, which is consistent across a restart: a plainly detached table is attached again at the next start, where regular dependency tracking picks it up, and a permanently detached one records no entry at all. The list is deliberately imprecise in one direction: a stale entry may keep refusing the drop for a while after the detached table itself is gone, or after the table was attached back (until the table is dropped or renamed). In exchange, the `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` path performs no disk access at all. - A `RENAME TABLE` that moves a table between an `Ordinary` and an `Atomic` database changes the identity the dependency is keyed by: the move into `Atomic` assigns a fresh UUID to the table and the move out of it drops the UUID, while a dependency is keyed by the UUID for tables of `Atomic` databases and by the name for tables of `Ordinary` ones. The rename interpreter only knows the names, so the entry used to keep the identity the table had before the move and nothing found it afterwards: the detach recorded no entry and, for the `Atomic -> Ordinary` direction, the drop check even classified the entry of the still attached table as a leftover of a failed `CREATE` and dropped the collection from under it. `DatabaseOnDisk::renameTable` now re-keys the entries of the moved table to its new `StorageID`, where both identities are known. `EXCHANGE` is unaffected: it is only supported between two `Atomic` databases, where the UUIDs do not change. - A table of a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1` is attached as a `StorageTableProxy` and its real storage is built only on the first access, so the engine arguments are not resolved at load time and the dependency on the named collection they name stayed unregistered. `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` was then allowed while such a table still referenced the collection - breaking it at the first access with `NAMED_COLLECTION_DOESNT_EXIST` - and a `DETACH` of it had no dependency to move to the list of the detached ones, so the protection above silently disappeared in that mode. `DatabaseOrdinary::loadTableLazy` now registers the dependency straight from the metadata, via the new `tryGetUsedNamedCollectionName` helper. An identifier first argument counts as a collection reference only for the engines that resolve their arguments through named collections (a new `StorageFactory::StorageFeatures::supports_named_collections` flag) - for other engines an identifier means something else, e.g. a cluster name for `Distributed` - and for them the signal is time-stable: whether the collection currently exists is deliberately not checked, so the dependency of a collection that is missing at load time (say, after a drop with `check_named_collection_dependencies = 0`) protects it when it is recreated later. The exception is `Remote`/`RemoteSecure`, where the same identifier is also a valid positional argument - a cluster name - when the named-collection lookup does not resolve (marked by the new `StorageFeatures::named_collection_argument_is_ambiguous`; every other flagged engine treats an unknown collection as an error, not as a fallback to a positional form). For them the helper decides from the shape of the argument list first, replicating the decision the engine's own argument parsing would make on the same metadata - which is exactly what a non-lazy load of it does. A `key = value` second argument occurs only in the named-collection form: no positional signature of `Remote` accepts one there, so `parseRemoteFunctionArguments` reports a missing collection instead of reparsing the arguments positionally, and the shape alone proves the reference - the dependency is registered without looking at the collection namespace, exactly as for the unambiguous engines, so a collection missing at load time is protected when it is recreated later. Only a genuinely positional-looking list (`Remote(cluster, system, one)`) or a bare `Remote(x)` consults the namespace, because there the meaning of the stored definition itself depends on it, and the engine resolves it the same way at the same moment. `SETTINGS` are skipped when the shape is examined, as `parseRemoteFunctionArguments` does. `MongoDB` and `MaterializedPostgreSQL` were the only flagged engines whose eager argument resolution did not pass the dependent table to `tryGetNamedCollectionWithOverrides` (they registered the dependency at the lazy load but not when the storage is built); they now pass it, so both load modes register the same dependency. `addDependency` ignores an exact duplicate, because the same dependency is registered again when the proxy is materialized. Tables created with `CREATE TABLE ... AS f(...)` need no lazy branch: a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1` deliberately loads them eagerly as a `StorageTableFunctionProxy` (see `DatabaseOrdinary::shouldLazyLoad`), and that load registers the dependency via `ITableFunction::getUsedNamedCollectionName`. - The cleanup of stale *active* dependencies (leftovers of a failed `CREATE TABLE`, pre-existing from #96181) no longer treats the table's absence from `DatabaseCatalog` alone as a proof of staleness: the dependency of an in-flight `CREATE`/`ATTACH` is registered while the engine arguments are resolved, before the table is committed to the catalog, and a concurrent `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` could prune it and drop the collection while the create later succeeds — recreating the broken metadata this PR fixes. The creating query holds the `DDLGuard` of the table name for the whole window between the registration and the commit, so the drop re-checks the table's existence under that guard before pruning: once the guard is acquired, no create is in flight, and the table's absence proves the entry is stale. (Entries with an empty database name come from dictionaries defined in the configuration files, which are not created through DDL; they are pruned as before.) The pruning removes only the exact stale entry (the collection and the recorded database, table and UUID): `CREATE TABLE ... UUID` can reuse the UUID of a failed create under a different table name, which the guard of the recorded name does not synchronize with, and removing everything under the UUID would erase the live dependency of such an in-flight create — the collection it uses could then be dropped from under the committed table. A new `create_table_pause_before_commit` failpoint keeps a create inside the window for the tests. ### Documented behavior impact `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` now rejects a collection that a detached table or a table in a detached database references, where it previously succeeded (and left a server that could not start). This is what `check_named_collection_dependencies` already promises - "Check that DROP NAMED COLLECTION will not break tables that depend on it" - so the documented behavior of the setting does not change, and setting it to `0` still allows the drop. No documentation update is needed. ### Verified locally (release build) - Before: `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` + `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = URL(nc)` + `DETACH TABLE` + `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` succeeds, and the server then fails to start with the exact error chain above (exit code 210). Same with `DETACH DATABASE`. - After: the drop is refused, the collection stays, the table attaches back, and a restart of a server with the detached table present succeeds. - `04660_drop_named_collection_detached_table`, `04698_drop_named_collection_detached_after_rename`, and `04823_drop_named_collection_broken_attach` (all new, covering plain `DETACH TABLE` (blocks the drop), `DETACH TABLE ... PERMANENTLY` (does not block; the later `ATTACH` fails cleanly), `DETACH DATABASE`, `Ordinary` databases, renames of the table and of the database before and after the detach, stale dependencies of failed `CREATE TABLE`, and an `ATTACH` that fails after the dependencies were registered — the drop stays refused), and `04836_drop_named_collection_inflight_create` (new, runs `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` against a `CREATE TABLE` and an `ATTACH TABLE` paused between the dependency registration and the commit to the catalog: the drop blocks on the `DDLGuard` and is refused), and `04840_drop_named_collection_cross_engine_rename` (new, moves a table between an `Ordinary` and an `Atomic` database in both directions and then detaches the table and its database), and `04848_drop_named_collection_reused_uuid` (new, prunes the stale entry of a failed `CREATE TABLE ... UUID` while a create of a different table reusing the UUID is paused inside the window: the drop of the old collection succeeds, and the drop of the collection the new table uses stays refused; verified to fail without the fix), plus `03822_named_collection_drop_dependency_check` and `04003_named_collection_drop_dependency_check_dict` pass. - `test_named_collections/test.py::test_drop_while_used_by_lazily_loaded_table` (new integration test: a table using a named collection in an `Atomic` database with `lazy_load_tables = 1`, a server restart so the table comes back as a never-accessed proxy, and the drop refused both while it is attached and after `DETACH TABLE`). It is an integration test because the hole is only reachable once the in-memory list is empty, i.e. after a restart: without one, the `DETACH DATABASE` that precedes `ATTACH DATABASE` leaves its own entry behind and that entry refuses the drop on its own. Verified that it fails without the fix (the drop succeeds) and passes with it. - `test_drop_collection_recreated_under_lazily_loaded_table` (new integration test: the collection is dropped with `check_named_collection_dependencies = 0`, the server restarts while it is missing, and the drop of the recreated collection is refused; verified to fail without the fix), and `test_drop_not_used_by_lazily_loaded_distributed_table` (new integration test: a collection named after the cluster of a lazily loaded `Distributed` table is droppable; passes before and after, pinning the behavior). - `test_drop_collection_recreated_under_lazily_loaded_remote_table` (new integration test: an `ENGINE = Remote(nc, database = 'system')` table in a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1`, the collection dropped with `check_named_collection_dependencies = 0`, a restart while it is missing, and the drop of the recreated collection refused - the unambiguous `key = value` shape registers the dependency from the AST alone), and `test_drop_not_used_by_lazily_loaded_remote_table` (new integration test: a collection named after the cluster of a lazily loaded `ENGINE = Remote(cluster, system, one)` table, created after the table, is droppable after a restart; verified to fail without the fix - the drop was refused with `NAMED_COLLECTION_IS_USED` by the unrelated table), and `test_drop_while_used_by_lazily_loaded_table_function` (new integration test pinning that a `CREATE TABLE ... AS bigquery(collection)` table in a database with `lazy_load_tables = 1` keeps blocking the drop after a restart, before the first access and after a `DETACH TABLE`: such tables are loaded eagerly as a `StorageTableFunctionProxy`, which re-registers the dependency; passes without any code change, confirming no lazy table-function branch is needed). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed the server failing to start after a named collection was dropped while a detached table (or a table in a detached database) still referenced it. `DROP NAMED COLLECTION` now counts detached tables as dependents and is refused with `NAMED_COLLECTION_IS_USED`, as `check_named_collection_dependencies` already does for attached tables. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112805&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112805](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112805+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Iceberg writer serializes day/hour partition transforms as non-canonical `days`/`hours`, breaking external readers (pyiceberg: UnknownTransform)
signal.text: **Describe what's wrong** The Iceberg writer serializes the `day` and `hour` partition transforms under the non-canonical plural names `days` / `hours` in the table metadata. The [Iceberg spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#partition-transforms) defines the transform names as `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour` (singular), and that is what other writers emit. Spec-following readers do not recognize the plural forms: pyiceberg 0.10.0 parses them as `UnknownTransform(transform='days')`, so a ClickHouse-written time-partitioned Iceberg table silently loses its partition information (and with it partition pruning) in external readers. The writer is also internally inconsistent: the *sort order* serialization path maps the same functions to the canonical singular names (`{"toRelativeDayNum", "day"}, {"toRelativeHourNum", "hour"}` in `parseFunction`, `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`), while the *partition spec* path emits the plural (`getPartitionField` writes `"days"` / `"hours"`, same file). `year` and `month` are emitted correctly in both paths. ClickHouse's own reader is lenient (`parseTransformAndArgument` accepts `day`, `date`, `days`, `dates`, …), so the bug is invisible in ClickHouse-only round-trips — it only breaks interoperability, which is the main reason to write Iceberg metadata in the first place. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Reproduces on master 26.8.1.1375, on every write. **How to reproduce** ```bash clickhouse local --path . --query " CREATE TABLE t (k Int64, ts DateTime) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('\$PWD/ice/', 'Parquet') PARTITION BY (toRelativeDayNum(ts)) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; INSERT INTO t SELECT number, toDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00') + number * 3600 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS allow_insert_into_iceberg = 1; " grep -ho '"transform" : "[^"]*"' ice/metadata/*.json | sort -u ``` **Expected behavior** ``` "transform" : "day" ``` **Actual behavior** ``` "transform" : "days" ``` And through pyiceberg 0.10.0: ```python from pyiceberg.table import StaticTable t = StaticTable.from_metadata('ice/metadata/<latest>.metadata.json') print([repr(f.transform) for f in t.spec().fields]) # ["UnknownTransform(transform='days')"] ``` `PARTITION BY (toRelativeHourNum(ts))` produces `"transform" : "hours"` with the same result. `toYearNumSinceEpoch` / `toMonthNumSinceEpoch` correctly produce `year` / `month`. Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: GRANT has no TO ALL, while CREATE ROW POLICY / SETTINGS PROFILE / QUOTA all accept it
signal.text: ### Company or project name Multi-tenant application built on ClickHouse's native access control (RBAC). ### Use case Building multi-tenant applications on ClickHouse's own access control means expressing "any authenticated principal may write here" -- the mail-slot pattern, where many principals may `INSERT` into a table and only the owner may `SELECT` from it. There is currently no way to grant a privilege or a role to every user. `GRANT ... TO ALL` is rejected as an unknown role, even though the same server accepts `ALL` as a live all-users target in three neighbouring statements, and as a live all-roles set in `SET DEFAULT ROLE`. **Version:** `26.7.1.1315` (official build). Also reproduced on `26.7.3.19` and `26.7.1.706`. All refused with `Code: 511 UNKNOWN_ROLE`: ```sql GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; -- Code: 511. There is no role `ALL` in `user directories` GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; -- Code: 511 GRANT pub TO ALL; -- Code: 511 (granting a role, not a privilege) ``` Accepted on the same server, same session: ```sql CREATE ROW POLICY rp ON t.reg USING 1 TO ALL; -- ok CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE sp SETTINGS max_threads = 4 TO ALL; -- ok CREATE QUOTA q FOR INTERVAL 1 hour MAX query_inserts = 9 TO ALL; -- ok SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO g1; -- ok (all *roles*, live) ``` Full reproduction: ```sql CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS t; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t.reg (h String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY h; CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS pub; CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS g1 IDENTIFIED WITH no_password; -- accepted: ALL as a live target set CREATE ROW POLICY IF NOT EXISTS rp ON t.reg USING 1 TO ALL; CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE IF NOT EXISTS sp SETTINGS max_threads = 4 TO ALL; CREATE QUOTA IF NOT EXISTS q FOR INTERVAL 1 hour MAX query_inserts = 9 TO ALL; SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO g1; -- refused: the same word as a grantee set GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; GRANT pub TO ALL; ``` ### Describe the solution you'd like `TO ALL` and `TO ALL EXCEPT ...` on `GRANT`, matching the sibling statements: ```sql GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL; GRANT INSERT ON t.reg TO ALL EXCEPT g1; GRANT pub TO ALL; ``` The storage machinery for a live "all users" marker appears to exist already. ClickHouse stores two such sets today, both flag-based and future-proof rather than expanded at execution time: - `SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO alice` is stored as `default_roles_all = 1` in `system.users`; a role granted to alice next month auto-activates. - `CREATE ROW POLICY / SETTINGS PROFILE / QUOTA ... TO ALL` applies to users created after the statement ran. Only the `GRANT` grammar refuses the same concept for grantees. Alternatively, if the asymmetry is deliberate -- e.g. the rule is *`ALL` is accepted where an object is applied to users (a policy, a profile, a limit) and refused where a capability is given to them* -- a sentence in the `GRANT` documentation recording that decision, and the recommended pattern instead, would resolve this entirely. ### Describe alternatives you've considered Without `TO ALL`, "everybody" has to be an application-maintained role granted at every `CREATE USER`. That is workable but fragile in a specific way: **one missed grant makes the role silently mean "everybody created before the omission."** There is no error, and the only way to detect the drift is to audit every account against the role (e.g. a cron diffing `system.users` against `system.role_grants`). ### Additional context The grant grammar has broadening syntax on two of its three positions and none on the third -- `GRANT <privileges> ON <objects> TO <grantees>`: | Position | Syntax | Semantics (verified on 26.7) | |---|---|---| | objects | `db.*` | live wildcard -- future tables covered | | privileges | `ALL` | snapshot -- expands to 45 rows in `system.grants` at grant time; privilege types added by later upgrades not included | | grantees | -- | nothing; `TO ALL` refused with Code 511 | So `ALL` currently has four meanings in the access-control grammar: a privilege set (snapshot), a granted-roles set in `SET DEFAULT ROLE` (live), an all-users target on row policy / settings profile / quota (live), and a grantee set on `GRANT` -- the only one that does not exist. A note on the documentation: https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/grant gives the grammar as `TO {user | role | CURRENT_USER}`, so the behaviour matches the documented syntax. The confusion is that the same page documents the *privilege* `ALL` -- easy to read as a grantee at a glance. Nothing on the page mentions that the sibling statements accept `TO ALL` as a target set.

signal.title: MaterializedPostgreSQL: coordinated Replicated/Shared nested tables for HA
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/47655 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` can now create its nested tables as `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree`/`SharedReplacingMergeTree` for high availability, using a new Keeper-based single-active-worker coordination of the replication slot. Controlled by the new settings `materialized_postgresql_table_engine`, `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and `materialized_postgresql_replica_name`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The three new settings and the coordinated-failover mechanism are documented in the embedded `Documentation` blocks of `DatabaseMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp` and `StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp`, from which the published engine pages are generated. --- ## Problem The nested tables that `MaterializedPostgreSQL` auto-creates were hardcoded to plain `ReplacingMergeTree` ([`StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/src/Storages/PostgreSQL/StorageMaterializedPostgreSQL.cpp)), so the engine could not be made highly available (issue #47655). Simply allowing `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` is unsafe on its own: a PostgreSQL logical replication slot permits only **one** active consuming session, so two ClickHouse replicas consuming the same slot would race on `pg_replication_slot_advance` and silently drop WAL. ## Solution Allow the nested engine to be `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` / `SharedReplacingMergeTree`, **gated** behind a new Keeper-based coordination that elects exactly one active worker — the same pattern used by `S3Queue`, the Keeper-coordinated `Kafka` engine and refreshable materialized views: - The active worker holds an ephemeral `/leader` node under `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and is the only replica that consumes the slot. - Standby replicas create the nested tables as replicas of the same replicated tree and receive data (including the initial snapshot) through ClickHouse replication, without touching the slot. - When the active worker's Keeper session ends, a standby wins `/leader` and resumes consuming from the slot's `confirmed_flush_lsn` — no reload, no duplication. PostgreSQL's own single-active-session rule on the slot is the ultimate backstop against double-advance during a handover. A graceful stop of the active worker (`DETACH`, a non-last `DROP`, server shutdown) does not wait for that: it releases `/leader` with a **confirmed** removal - the node lives under the server's shared Keeper session, which outlives the database, and nothing re-enters the election on that replica after shutdown, so an unconfirmed (lost-response) removal is resolved on the spot with owner- and version-checked re-checks instead of leaving a stale node that would keep every peer on standby for as long as that session lives. - The slot and the publication are **shared state**, and the whole lifecycle honors that: - A durable `snapshot_completed` marker in Keeper records that the initial snapshot loaded every table. A new leader may resume from `confirmed_flush_lsn` only when the marker exists; otherwise the previous worker died mid-snapshot, and the new one **clears the nested tables**, drops the slot and redoes the snapshot from scratch, so pre-slot rows cannot be lost. Clearing first is required for correctness: a row the dead worker had copied and that PostgreSQL then `DELETE`d has no counterpart in the new snapshot, so without a clear the stale copy would survive (a `ReplacingMergeTree` collapses duplicate keys by `_version` but never turns a now-absent row into a tombstone). The marker is fenced on the live leadership session: it is written through the Keeper session that backs `/leader` (in a multi-request with a check on `/leader`), the snapshot load aborts as soon as that session is lost, and a consumer is never started over a dead leadership session - so a worker deposed mid-snapshot can never mask its successor's replacement snapshot with a stale marker. The redo of the snapshot is fenced the same way: a worker whose leadership session is no longer alive aborts before truncating the nested tables (re-checked per table) and before dropping or recreating the shared slot, so a deposed worker cannot wipe the tables its successor has already reloaded or discard the slot the successor just created. A startup attempt that fails before a consumer got running (most importantly, a coordinated single-table engine whose one snapshot load failed) aborts instead of starting a consumer with nothing to apply - which would advance the shared slot's `confirmed_flush_lsn` while applying no rows - and releases the leadership so a healthy peer can take over. That release never leaves a stale leadership claim behind: a `remove` of `/leader` that could not be confirmed does not prove the node survived, so the claim is dropped in either case, and a leader node this replica created under the current Keeper session but no longer tracks is recognized (by its stored replica name and its owning session) and removed on its next election attempt - a replica never keeps acting as the active worker, or touches the shared slot and snapshot state, without provably holding `/leader`. - A second coordinated `CREATE DATABASE` adopts an existing publication instead of dropping it from under the active worker. - Every replica registers itself under `<keeper_path>/replicas`; dropping the database on one replica keeps the shared slot/publication for the others, and only dropping the last replica removes them from PostgreSQL (fail-close when Keeper is unavailable). The last-replica decision is fenced on the shared `replicas` node so concurrent `DROP DATABASE` on different replicas cannot both act as last, it removes the replica's registration only atomically with winning that fence - a replica that is not the last one keeps its registration until its local nested tables are actually gone, so even a server killed mid-drop stays visible to every later last-replica check - and it runs even for a `DROP DATABASE` issued immediately after a restart, before the background startup task has rebuilt the replication handler. - Recreating a coordinated database right after dropping it is safe: the nested tables are dropped without the delayed-drop window (so their shared Keeper subtrees do not outlive the `DROP DATABASE`), the snapshot insert is never silently deduplicated against block hashes surviving from a previous incarnation of the shared table, a publication leaked by an incompletely dropped setup (no surviving coordination state in Keeper) is dropped by a fresh `CREATE` instead of silently adopted with its stale table set, and a refused (failed) drop never leaves the replica silently dead: every refusable Keeper step of the pre-data teardown runs before the replica's consumer is stopped, and if the drop still fails after that point - the last replica's removal of the shared coordination nodes, or the deletion of this replica's own local nested tables (e.g. Keeper disappearing while a nested replicated table removes its own Keeper metadata) - replication is rebuilt in the background - for the database engine through a new generic `IDatabase::onDropDatabaseFailed` hook that discards the stopped handler and re-runs the startup task, for the single-table engine by re-arming the handler's retrying startup path - so the replica rejoins the setup once Keeper is reachable again. - All replicas of one coordinated setup must agree on the naming-affecting settings (`materialized_postgresql_table_engine`, `materialized_postgresql_schema`, `materialized_postgresql_schema_list`, `materialized_postgresql_tables_list_with_schema`) and must replicate the same PostgreSQL source — the same source database and, for the single-table engine, the same source table (so a single-table engine and a database engine can never share one keeper path): these determine how the ClickHouse names of the shared nested tables and the names of the shared slot and publication are derived. The first replica publishes a canonical fingerprint of them at `<keeper_path>/naming`; a disagreeing replica is rejected — synchronously at `CREATE` time when the setup already exists in Keeper, and fail-close at startup before it registers itself — instead of adopting the same publication yet building a disjoint replicated tree that never receives the other replicas' data. - The shared **table set** is fenced the same way, *before* any nested table is built: the first replica publishes its derived set at `<keeper_path>/table_set`, and a replica whose derived set differs is refused fail-close (the shared publication - from which joining replicas later derive their set - is only created by the elected active worker, so without this fence two fresh replicas starting concurrently could silently build diverging nested tables on one keeper path). The refusal converges by itself once the publication exists, because joining replicas then derive their set from the publication, which was created from the fenced set. - The last-replica teardown is generation-safe: winning the last-replica fence atomically (in one Keeper multi-request) creates an ownership token at `<keeper_path>/teardown`, which is removed only after the shared PostgreSQL slot/publication have actually been dropped. While the token exists, a fresh coordinated `CREATE` on the same keeper path is rejected (synchronously by validation and fail-close at startup), so the pending by-name drops can never delete a new setup's freshly created slot/publication. A replica recovering its own refused drop reclaims its own token, and a retried drop resumes its earlier teardown instead of leaking the slot. - Per-table and database-wide destructive changes are refused (`NOT_IMPLEMENTED`) in coordinated mode: `ATTACH TABLE` / `DETACH TABLE PERMANENTLY` / `DROP TABLE` / `RENAME TABLE` / `EXCHANGE TABLES`, and a database-wide `TRUNCATE DATABASE` / `TRUNCATE ALL TABLES FROM`. Each would only change the local replica (or wipe its copy of the shared replicated data) while the shared publication, tables list, slot/snapshot marker and peer replicas keep the old state, silently diverging the replicas. Recreate the database with an updated `materialized_postgresql_tables_list` instead. New settings (both the database engine and the single-table engine): | Setting | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `materialized_postgresql_table_engine` | `ReplacingMergeTree` | `ReplacingMergeTree` / `ReplicatedReplacingMergeTree` / `SharedReplacingMergeTree` | | `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` | (empty) | opt-in gate that enables coordination; supports the `{shard}` macro; a per-replica/per-server macro (`{replica}`/`{server_uuid}`, including reached through a config macro) is rejected at `CREATE` time, and so is `{uuid}` unless the DDL carries the UUID (`ON CLUSTER`, a table inside a `Replicated` database, or an explicit `UUID '...'` clause) so that it is provably identical on every replica, and so is a misspelled/unsupported macro (in this path or in `materialized_postgresql_replica_name`) — both settings are macro-expanded during validation exactly as the handler expands them later | | `materialized_postgresql_replica_name` | `{replica}` | replica identity for coordination and the nested replicated engine; must resolve to a distinct value on every replica, which is enforced: the `/replicas/<name>` registration node stores the owning replica's identity, and a name already registered by another replica is rejected (synchronously at `CREATE` time when the registration is already visible); it must also resolve to a single Keeper node name (empty or containing `/` is rejected, since a nested path under `/replicas` would break the last-replica bookkeeping); together with `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` it forms the coordination identity of the replica, which is treated as immutable once the setup exists: a configuration-only change of a macro these settings expand through is refused at startup, while a `DROP` tears down the identity persisted in the nested tables; a name change made in the one window where the registration already exists while no nested table does yet is recovered from the registration itself, which stores an owner identity no macro feeds into, so the stale registration is removed (on startup and on drop) instead of keeping `<keeper_path>/replicas` non-empty forever and stopping every future drop from becoming the last-replica drop | The replicated/shared engines require `materialized_postgresql_keeper_path` and vice versa (coordination with a plain `ReplacingMergeTree` would leave the standbys without data), and coordination is mutually exclusive with `materialized_postgresql_use_unique_replication_consumer_identifier` (which gives each replica its own slot). Coordination also requires Keeper/ZooKeeper to be configured on the server: a coordinated `CREATE DATABASE` on a server with no Keeper is rejected synchronously at `CREATE` time rather than being accepted and left retrying in the background. All of this validation also applies to a user `ATTACH DATABASE` / `ATTACH TABLE` that spells out the full definition - it is fresh user input, exactly like a `CREATE`; only replaying an already-persisted definition (server startup, and the short `ATTACH` syntax, which re-reads the stored definition) is exempt. signal.title: Rename `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`
signal.text: Renames the MergeTree setting `allow_experimental_adaptive_codec_selection` to `enable_adaptive_codec_selection`. The `allow_experimental_` prefix is the pre-tier way of gating a feature. The `EXPERIMENTAL` tier in the declaration already carries that information and is exposed as `tier` in `system.merge_tree_settings`, so the prefix duplicates it in the one place that is expensive to change later: the name. When the feature graduates, a prefixed name has to be renamed and the old spelling carried as an alias forever. That is why the tree already holds `allow_experimental_analyzer` -> `enable_analyzer`, `allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type` -> `enable_nullable_tuple_type` and `allow_experimental_database_iceberg` -> `allow_database_iceberg`. With the tier doing the gating, graduation becomes a one-word change. `enable_` matches the neighbouring MergeTree booleans (`enable_block_number_column`, `enable_block_offset_column`, `enable_mixed_granularity_parts`). **Why this can be a plain rename.** The setting was added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111834 and has not shipped in any release: its `SettingsChangesHistory` entry sits in the unreleased `26.8` block, which this PR updates in place. So there is no alias, no `MAKE_OBSOLETE` and no compatibility entry, and nothing for `compatibility` to revert. The tier stays `EXPERIMENTAL` and the default stays `false`; only the name changes. The autogenerated settings reference pages (`docs/reference/settings/merge-tree-settings/allow-experimental.mdx`, the manifest, the settings explorer and the legacy-route map) still spell the old name. They are generated from a binary's introspection tables by the nightly docs job (`ci/jobs/docs_autogen_nightly.py`), so they are deliberately not hand-edited here and the setting will move to its new group page on the next run. Hand-written prose in `docs/reference/statements/create/table.mdx` is updated. signal.title: Fix wrong results for non-boolean conditions taken out of `and`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/112236 `and` implicitly converts its arguments to booleans, so any non-zero value is true. When a query plan optimization takes a part of a conjunction away and a single conjunct is left as the new predicate, that conjunct was converted with a cast to the type of the original predicate. A cast is not a boolean conversion: it maps values like 256 or 0.1 to 0, so rows whose condition value is a non-zero multiple of 256 silently disappeared. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (id UInt32) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(600); SELECT count() FROM t AS l LEFT JOIN t AS r ON l.id = r.id WHERE r.id AND l.id = r.id; ``` returned 597 instead of 599, the rows with `id = 256` and `id = 512` were dropped. `mergeFilterIntoJoinCondition` moves `l.id = r.id` into the JOIN and leaves `CAST(r.id, 'UInt8')` as the filter: ``` Filter column: CAST(id AS UInt8) ``` The same happens in `ActionsDAG::removeUnusedConjunctions` when a conjunct is pushed down and the filter column is still needed in the result. That one is reachable without a JOIN, and the value of the condition was wrong there as well (the raw value instead of a boolean): ```sql SELECT count(), sum(f) FROM ( SELECT id, (id != 1000 AND s) AS f FROM (SELECT id, sum(id) AS s FROM t GROUP BY id) WHERE id != 1000 AND s ); ``` returned `597 597` instead of `599 599`. It only converted floating point types, now every non-boolean type is converted. Both places now wrap the remaining conjunct into `and(x, true)`, the same way `toBoolIfNeeded` does it in `JoinStepLogical.cpp`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results when a non-boolean condition, such as a bare integer column in `WHERE`, is left alone after the other conditions are merged into the JOIN condition or pushed down. Rows whose condition value was a non-zero multiple of 256 were skipped. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
